en: Part I, Chapter 1: The Sūtra on the Proposition {1,1}.
At the commencement of the Vārttika, conforming to the practice of the learned, he first performs an auspicious invocation: "Viśuddha... (Pure...).

For it is observed that the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭas*) in all undertakings is preceded by the performance of auspicious rites (*maṅgalācaraṇa*). An auspicious rite consists of the praise and salutation of deities and so forth.

Since this [rite] is invariably connected with the commencement of another fruitful action and lacks fruit in itself, its status as a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to that other action is determined by the maxim: "That which is without fruit in the proximity of that which has fruit is a subsidiary to it. This being established, and given that an undertaking extends until its completion, [the rite serves to ensure the completion of the work].

The fruit is the completion of the rite without obstacles. According to the maxim that "the injunction of what is not required is weaker than the injunction of what is required," the postulation of another fruit is weak. Therefore, just as the traditional rules regarding study periods (*adhyāya*) and non-study periods (*anadhyāya*) are for the sake of ensuring the uninterrupted study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*), so too is this [rite]. This is the meaning: he whose body of knowledge is purified.

He is described as such. The Blessed One’s knowledge is pure because the causes of knowledge are not defiled by passion and other afflictions; and his body is [pure] because it is not born from a womb and is devoid of the various sufferings of the womb. Furthermore, the statement that "the three Vedas are his eye" is a figurative expression, because he illuminates the meaning of the Vedas clearly, without doubt, and without error. And it is "divine" because its range extends to objects beyond the senses. It is "elemental" (bhautika) [in the sense of being composed of the elements].

For the [ordinary] eye has as its object things that are present, whereas this [vision] is divine, having as its object the future and so forth. And the Blessed One is the cause for the superior [state], which consists in the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful. "To him who bears the crescent moon"—that is, to him who wears a digit of the moon. *Namaḥ* (salutation). Although the fivefold [manifestations] beginning with the physical form (*vigraha*) will be refuted in the section on the deities (*devatādhikaraṇa*), [they are mentioned here].

Nevertheless, just as in the case of the *ājya* and other *stotras*, the fruit belongs to the principal rite itself through the praise of the deity performed in this manner; thus, there is no fault. // 1 //

{1,2} Now he performs praise and salutation to the teachers of knowledge—beginning with the words "having prostrated. First, I salute those teachers who, like suns, cause the lotuses of their disciples' intellects to blossom; thereafter, I shall compose the *Vārttika*. This will be by their very grace, through both the visible instruction on the reality of the meaning and the invisible [grace] arising from praise and salutation. For even following the teacher and so forth...
They take the *ācārya* alone as their authority. By the inclusion of the term "vārttika," he remedies what was poorly stated and supplies what was not said.

By the word "mīmāṃsā," he shows that this is a treatise on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), and thus demonstrates that there is no fault in the refutation of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth in accordance with logic. And by the word "śloka," he shows that we shall dispel [objections] through the expansion of brevity. Therefore, this work is for the most part already summarized in the aphorisms (*sūtra*).
The intended meaning is that those who are attentive and desirous of knowledge will cultivate [this] for the sake of the goal. // 2 //

Now, regarding those virtuous people who, out of regard for the conduct of the world, strive for the benefit of others even while disregarding their own self-interest—those whose sole purpose is the welfare of others—the author says: "Therefore, the wise... Those who are *asūyavaḥ* are envious; others than these are *anasūyavaḥ*, meaning non-envious. // 3 //

But for those who are impartial and, by means of an investigation into merits and defects, reject that which possesses defects and accept that which possesses merits—for their sake, he requests a specific examination with the words "na cātra" [and not here]. [That is to say:

"May you examine both the merits and defects simultaneously in this my treatise, which possesses both merits and defects. Otherwise, if one disregards the merits and examines only the defects, then even non-existent defects would appear to those whose minds are solely intent on perceiving faults."

Now he speaks with a rebuke directed at the wicked—beginning with "From where [could they have]...": "How could we, who do not tolerate even the faults found in the works of others, admit faults into our own treatises? And it is not fitting for wise scholars to seize upon faults that we ourselves have not admitted. // 5 //

{1,3} Now, those who are envious will surely disparage my composition. Therefore, he says "nirdoṣatve" (in order that there may be no discouragement of those desiring to hear by pointing out its defects). Even regarding liberation and heaven, which possess well-known excellence, atheists dispute; they say: "Worldly pleasure and pain are [respectively] heaven and hell."
Thus it is said. Regarding liberation (*mokṣa*), there is dispute starting from its very existence. For some say that liberation does not exist;
others, however, call liberation a stream of consciousness free from the coloring of all objects; others, the cessation thereof;
and still others, a state characterized by the total destruction of all specific qualities of the self (*ātman-guṇa*), which is unsurpassed, born of non-attachment to objects, and endless.
It is a mass of bliss. Furthermore, both those in the past and those in the present deny the nature of ultimate liberation through various conceptual constructions arising from delusion. // 6 //

Moreover, even if those who desire to listen find faults in my composition, I am nonetheless beyond reproach. For I do not state anything independently; rather, as I proceed according to the scriptures, any lapse that has occurred—even if unavoidable by chance—must be overlooked.
Indeed, no desired object whatsoever is entirely free from defects. However, having remedied the defects, one should rely upon the virtues;
thus he says: "By means of scripture" (*āgama*). For this is the path of the virtuous, known as following scripture. Thus, in this case, there are predominantly virtues alone.
As for the defects, even if they exist to some extent, they are like non-existent things due to their scarcity and should therefore be disregarded. // 7 //

Let it be granted for now that the words of great poets like us, which follow the sacred scriptures (*āgama*), are beautiful. Even for another person who possesses faith and follows the path of the Three Vedas (*trayī*), a mode of speech—even if undertaken in some casual way, or being laborious and of little substance—is beautiful.
But ours, being of great substance and produced without effort, is exceedingly beautiful; thus he says: "Just as... (verse 8).
[Objection: But why is a *vārttika* being composed for Mīmāṃsā, which is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [of the Vedas]?

Let the Vedas themselves be explained directly. To this he replies: "Mīmāṃsā. When the Vedas themselves are explained by means of the sequence of doubt, prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*), and final conclusions (*uttarapakṣa*), they truly captivate the mind, but not through the method of commentaries on the *mantras* and *brāhmaṇas*. Since it is only through Mīmāṃsā that they are explained in such a manner, my desire to compose a *vārttika* upon that very [system] increases. // 9 //

[Objection: But surely there are ancient treatises even within Mīmāṃsā; why then exert yourself in vain? To this he says: "For the most part" (*prāyeṇa*). The *Lokāyata* is the system of the nihilists (*nāstika*). It has been brought to such a state by a compendium of various heterodox doctrines.

This effort has been made in order to place it back upon the path of those who believe in the afterlife (*āstika*). One should understand that the suffix *-kta* is used here in the sense of expressing a wish (*āśaṃsā*) for a future action. // 10 //
Thus ends the introduction.

Now he shows the purport of the aphorism with the word "atha" (now). For this first aphorism is composed to state the purpose (*prayojana*), which is the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this treatise under the name of *dharma*. The term "first" indicates its position as the locus for the statement of the purpose.

Thus he demonstrates: although it was not explicitly stated that "dharma is its purpose," nevertheless, by declaring that "dharma is the object of the desire to know" (*jijñāsā*), and because knowledge that does not result in human welfare is undesirable, it is indicated that dharma, as something constituting human welfare, is the purpose; thus it is called a "sūtra. And by the word *kṛta*, it is shown that this [work] is artificial (*kṛtrima*).

Therefore, he shows that even if [the text] is explained as being aimed at the cessation of residing in the teacher’s house at its conclusion, it does not entail any fault. For in the case of an eternal [text], whatever is stated is authoritative exactly as spoken. But in the case of a human composition, even if it appears to have another meaning through the force of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is established as having that other meaning [only] by the power of those other means of valid cognition. // 11 //

Now, what is the purpose of stating the aim? Let the treatise itself simply be composed. For it is not proper for one desiring to compose a treatise to state its aim, as such a statement lies outside the treatise itself. Furthermore, what is the purpose of this [statement]? If it is argued that "due to a specific purpose, there is engagement with the treatises by those who desire to hear," that is not so; for wise persons do not act in this way merely because of a human word.

It is appropriate to have confidence that this refers to the *artha* (wealth/interest), especially because a specific reason is seen. Otherwise, those who hear the treatise might suspect that even though it has another purpose, it was stated by the author merely as a means to induce people toward *dharma*, and they would not place their trust in it. Therefore, since a statement of the purpose [alone] would yield little result, he says: "of all... (*sarvasya*).

Even regarding some other treatise—whether worldly, such as the rules for cooking rice, or something else—that can be accomplished with little effort, people do not respect it if its purpose has not been stated; how much less so in the case of Mīmāṃsā? Thus, it is proper to state the purpose at the commencement of a treatise. As for the objection that there is no confidence in the words of a person, that is not so, because of the distinction between a reliable and an unreliable person. For the Commentator will say: "And if [the source] is from a trustworthy person," and Jaimini also says: "Or rather, when the cause [of error] is not perceived, those [words] employed should be understood [as authoritative]. (1.3.7)

Thus it is said. As for the claim that he speaks while desiring to deceive, that is not so; for it is impossible for this great seer to utter a falsehood, nor is any motive for deception perceived in him.

If [the motive were] "let the listeners proceed," what would he gain from them—whether they be fruitless or productive of demerit—if they were made to proceed under the pretext of dharma? On the contrary, it would result in demerit.

If he were to cause his disciples to wander in error, a great fault would accrue to him; nor can it even be imagined that one who is supremely righteous would practice unrighteousness. Furthermore, it is not possible to suppose that the author of a *tantra* would err regarding the purpose of that *tantra*. Therefore, because the possibility of error or deception is non-existent [in such cases], the traditional recollections (*smaraṇa*) of the sages, such as those concerning the *Aṣṭaka* rites, have their root in the *Śruti*; this was established in the section on *Smṛti* (Jaimini Sūtra 1.3).
It will be stated [later]: "If there were no trust in the words of all persons, even that [trust] would be undermined"; thus, it is appropriate to state the purpose. // 12 //

[1] "Various horses" [2] and "of everything indeed"— by means of this interrogative intonation (*kāku*), [the author] illuminates the specific distinction that is implicitly contained within the *Mīmāṃsā*, [expressing it as] "called *Mīmāṃsā*. For other treatises are indeed restricted to having only the literal meaning (*vācya*) as their subject matter.
6} Grammar and the other [sciences]. This science called Mīmāṃsā, however, relies upon many other sciences—such as the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs—which serve as its means.

For its purpose cannot be determined correctly unless those [other sciences] are understood as they truly are. Therefore, it is logical that this [Mīmāṃsā], being accumulated both in terms of its means and its own essential nature, cannot fail to inspire even the desire to hear it among listeners, even if its specific purpose has not yet been stated.
The statement of the purpose. // 13 //
[3] Where is that distinction [4] which is capable of determining a single manifest object at the end? [5] That... [KHA] / [KA] / [KHA]

Moreover, even if those seeking knowledge—thinking that other sciences for which no purpose has been stated are purposeless—should not know them, or should fail to understand them correctly because they engage with them through weak faith, nevertheless, the attainment of harm does not occur on account of those [sciences] being unknown or poorly understood. In this case, however, regarding Mīmāṃsā, if the path of reasoning consisting of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is unknown or poorly understood, there is an absence of discrimination; consequently, one might mistake the prima facie position itself for the final conclusion.

Thinking thus, they would act accordingly. In that case, due to the non-performance or improper performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, they would incur great misfortune; therefore, Mīmāṃsā must be practiced with effort. This he states in two verses beginning with *vidyāntareṣu*. Now, one might object: even if one is ignorant of other sciences, [the fault] certainly remains. For instance, one who is ignorant of grammar...
Even so, one who employs an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) at a sacrifice incurs sin. For it is heard in scripture: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa must not speak like a barbarian (*mleccha*);

for an incorrect word is indeed a barbarian. It is replied: Who says that there would be no fault even in the lack of knowledge of other sciences? However, the distinction lies in the degree—whether [the ignorance] is slight or great. For Mīmāṃsā consists of the application of reasoning capable of removing ignorance, doubt, and error regarding all sciences. Therefore...
When this [ignorance] is not known, nothing at all is known. Therefore, one encounters great misfortune.
For this very reason, it is said: "It is a great fault. (14–15)
[6] One should obtain that [knowledge], and for this reason, one must investigate it with diligent effort.

Therefore, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*), asserting that it is appropriate for the authors of the Sūtras to state the purpose themselves. Now, one might ask: even so, why did Jaimini not disregard the effort that was to be made by the authors of the Bhāṣya and others, just as Pāṇini [did]?
To this he says "that which": how indeed could the authors of the Bhāṣya and others say anything other than what was already stated by that Jaimini?

Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, who could know what kind of purpose those who act according to their own will might declare? For instance, regarding grammar, the purpose which was overlooked by the author of the *sūtras* has been conceptualized in many ways by various commentators. To illustrate: having first stated that "there is merit (*dharma*) in the knowledge of correct words," it was subsequently stated that "there is prosperity (*abhyudaya*) in usage preceded by the science. This is indeed true.
It is indeed appropriate, first of all, to state the purpose. [16]
[8] Now, if this is so,
why was the fault committed by Jaimini not swallowed up?
For this reason, it is also appropriate for the author of the Sūtras to state that "this is the connection of this treatise with this purpose."

Disciples do not care to listen even to that whose purpose is unknown or whose relationship [to that purpose] is not understood. Therefore, he raises the objection that its relationship must be stated along with its purpose: "siddhārtham" (for the sake of establishing the subject matter). // 17 //

He addresses this by saying "the treatise. At the very moment it is stated that "this is the purpose of this treatise," the relationship between those two—characterized as that between the means and the goal—is already stated by implication. Furthermore, the authors of the sūtras do not record with words a matter that has already been established by implication, for that would result in the undesirable consequence of [the work] no longer being a sūtra. // 18 //

Now, even if the author of the Sūtra did not explicitly state the relationship separately from the purpose, it may nevertheless be clarified by the commentators. For when the relationship is clearly explained, listeners proceed to engage with the work. For this very reason, the relationship is also clearly demonstrated in other treatises; for instance, following a question from a disciple:
He says "siddhiḥ" (accomplishment) because it is stated in the *Arthamālā* that the *tantra* was composed by Kaṇabhuj. // 19 //

[10] However, when the connection has not been made clear, listeners—suspecting that the author of the aphorisms (*sūtrakāra*) is merely engaging in incoherent prattle because commentators have failed to clarify the relationship—might consider the treatise and its purpose to be entirely unrelated.
Anticipating this, he says: "As long as... (verse 20).

He refutes this with the words "here" (*iha*). He thinks as follows: "In that case, the authors of the *Vārttika* indeed trouble themselves over what was not stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. But here, since the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself has raised the objection—'Is *dharma* well-known or unknown?'—the relationship will be stated either by [the words] 'or it is meaningful' (*arthavat*) and so forth; therefore, the relationship need not be stated separately."
However, one should strive specifically for the commentary on the *Sambandhabhāṣya*. // 21 //

[11] Furthermore, someone here might say this: "Just as later commentators do not state the connection separately, so too it is improper for the author of the *Bhāṣya* to state the connection, because the connection of the treatise— characterized by its immediate succession to the act of study— has already been stated by the author of the *Sūtras* himself through his use of the word *atha*."

For example, after the question of a disciple, Kāśyapa stated: "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma," meaning "we shall compose the treatise. To that, he replies: "And not even... For the word *atha* expresses a relationship characterized by immediate succession between the desire for knowledge and the action of study; yet those two actions are external to the treatise, being merely common instances of the general category of "desiderative" (*sannanta*) verbal formations.
This is the delusion of those who consider the *jijñāsā* and the *mīmāṃsā* to be one and the same. // 22 //

[12] He states with the two verses beginning "Even that which... that a relationship that is separate and not apprehended is purposeless. For in the system of Kaṇāda, a relationship consisting of immediate succession to an action (*kriyānantarya*) is shown. Indeed, it was stated there by the commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*): "What is *dharma*?"

Having considered these five questions raised by the student, he says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain Dharma. And the connection consisting of the succession of teachers is as stated here by some: Brahmā or Maheśvara taught the Mīmāṃsā to Prajāpati.
"Prajāpati [taught] it to Indra, Indra to Āditya," and so forth. "Parvan" means divisions; "guruparvan" means the divisions of the gurus;
the analysis of the compound *guruparvakrama* is "the sequence of the guru-divisions. And in this context, only two kinds of relationship are applicable.

For when that relationship exists—whether its form is present or absent—no distinction is perceived by the listener regarding engagement with or withdrawal from the treatise, nor is there any knowledge concerning the subject matter of the treatise; rather, engagement and withdrawal are the effects of injunctions and prohibitions.
It is through these two that [the author] indicates those [injunctions and prohibitions]. // 23–24 //

Since this [present] connection is purposeless, those who wish to state a connection as a constituent part of the commentary on the Sūtras must state a connection that is both supported by reasoning and purposeful. He says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to indicate that this has been done here in the Śābara Bhāṣya; for the word *avatāra* (introduction) is derived from the root *tṛ* with the prefix *ava*, in the sense of "that by which the treatise (*śāstra*) is introduced," using the suffix *ghañ* in the non-agentive sense.

In the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*), the suffix *ghañ* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.3.19, *ca kārake saṃjñāyām*. This [treatise] is both an introduction to the science (*śāstra*) and a connection (*sambandha*); thus, it is called "the connection that is the introduction to the science. And it has been stated that this [connection] is characterized by the means (*upāya*) and the goal (*upeya*). // 25 //

He now investigates the commentary, [beginning with] the word "loka. An objection is raised: surely only that meaning with which the commentary is consistent is fit to be explained; why then do you set forth six meanings? To this he replies: "in accordance with the author of the commentary. What is meant by this is that the commentary is consistent everywhere. But how can a single sentence have multiple meanings?

For he will state that there is unity of sentence (*ekavākyatā*) due to the unity of meaning, according to the principle: "Because of the unity of meaning, there is one sentence. Therefore, he says: "of that which is employed" (*prayuktasya*). This is the intended meaning: this sentence is employed by a person. However, persons are observed to employ even a single sentence that possesses multiple intentions after having understood the meaning through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example: "The white [dog] runs; [he is] of the Alambusas... [and so on].

Regarding the word "yāti": in the Vedic context, however, this rule holds that a single [word] has a single meaning. For in that case, the comprehension of the meaning follows the word exactly, because there is no other means of valid cognition [to contradict it]. As it has been said: "People may employ a single word even when it possesses multiple intended meanings..."

Thus [it ends]. Now, one might object: since it occurs in close proximity, it is more appropriate that the purpose of this commentary is merely to critique the word *atha* found in the first sūtra; how then can it serve as a component for the explanation of every sūtra occurring throughout the entire treatise? To this he says: "From the beginning. He thinks as follows: this sentence is employed at the very outset of everything; therefore, from this point on, it belongs to the position of being an introduction to the entire collection of sūtras.

Thus, no specific distinction is obtained from the location [of the word *atha*]. On the contrary, by virtue of the force of the plural number (*iti bahuvacana*), the nature of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, it is clearly revealed that its scope extends to all the Sūtras. Now, one might object: "In that case, since the Bhāṣya—forming a single syntactical unit with the passage beginning 'This word *atha* is used in the world' and so on—clearly reveals itself as having the purpose of refuting the word *atha*, such a unity of syntactical construction would not otherwise be possible."

Therefore, he says: "separately" (*pṛthak*). There are five alternative interpretations for that which is separated from the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and ending with "it would entail excessive effort" (*yatnagauravaṃ prasajyeta*). However, when it forms a single syntactical unit [with the preceding], the meaning is simply the refutation of the word "then" (*atha*). // 26 //
[13] This has been understood.

[14] Now, for the sake of easy comprehension, he enumerates the six meanings beginning with "origination" (*utpāda*): "the entire exposition," and so forth. And these will be explained in their respective appropriate places. // 27 //

He first explains the general commentary (*sarvavyākhyā*) with the words "the common" (*sādhāraṇī*). For the author of the *Bhāṣya* has provided two kinds of commentary on the *Sūtras*: one is the general [commentary], beginning with the words "In this world," and so forth; the other is the specific [commentary] pertaining to each individual *Sūtra*. For it is held that the wise grasp the meaning through both summary and detailed exposition. // 28 //
[15] Here, however, the Commentator has indicated the method of operation by showing that those words which are well-known in the world for certain meanings should, where possible,
be understood as having those very same meanings in the Sūtras; thus he says, "not by means of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth."
Cessation. Thus, here both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and cessation (*nivṛtti*) have first been shown according to their essential nature; furthermore, cessation is preceded by engagement.
Likewise, having first stated the well-known words (*pada*), the sūtras were subsequently presented as having those very meanings. Therefore...

In every instance here, the author of the *Vārttika* expresses the intended meaning (*tātparya*) through a specific arrangement of words—namely, "activity" (*pravṛtti*). By employing the two terms "activity" and "cessation" (*nivṛtti*), he demonstrates that the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated that the aphorisms proceed in exactly two ways, through activity and cessation. Furthermore, by means of this specific sequence, he shows that even for the author of the *Bhāṣya*, cessation is to be explained as being preceded by activity.

He demonstrates this. Thus, by intending to show the sequence between the word and the sūtra, he indicates that even for the author of the Bhāṣya, the meaning of the sentence is intended to be preceded by the meaning of the words. This is the sense: this activity, namely, that one must grasp the well-known meanings [of the words],...

The meaning is that one should grasp those words according to their well-known conventional meanings. Furthermore, regarding the cessation of syntactical defects such as ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth, it means that in the case of the *sūtras*, no interpretation of their meaning should be made through ellipsis and the like. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* says, "when possible. He states its meaning:
"in the case of words not contradicted by Vedic statements. That is to say, in the case of words that do not conflict with the statements of the Vedas.

In the case of the *sūtras*, there is an inclination toward adopting the well-established meaning and an avoidance of [unnecessary] ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) and the like, but this does not apply when some words—even in *sūtras*—are mutually contradictory; in such cases, there is a reversal of what is adopted and what is avoided. This very point has been stated by the phrase "when possible. Thus, when consistency with the Vedas is possible, this [method] must be followed and not otherwise. // 29 //
[16] Show [17] the proximity to the goal [18] when it exists (KHA).

Now, it may be argued that it is indeed appropriate for the operation [of the suffix] to apply to the words (*pada*). But how can there be a cessation based on the *sūtra*, given that it is the words themselves that are introduced as the primary subject and thus deserve to be referred to by the pronoun "of these" (*eṣām*), since linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) occurs with respect to the primary subject? For when it is said, "This staff stands upon the heap of bricks; strike with it," it is not understood that one should strike with the heap of bricks.

"But rather, [it is] by means of the staff. Since the pile of bricks (*iṣṭakākūṭa*) is employed as a qualifier of the staff, similarly here too, specific words [within] the sūtras are not subject to reference. Therefore, he says: "of the ellipsis" (*adhyāhārasya*). This is the meaning: only where ellipses and the like would otherwise result is it appropriate to prohibit them.

Because a negation presupposes that which is to be negated, and those two [the object and the agent] are not possible within the individual words here. "Supply" (*adhyāhāra*) consists in the introduction of an additional word capable of completing an incomplete sentence;

however, that is not possible with respect to the words, because it is impossible for a word to be deficient in its usage due to corruption (*apabhraṃśa*). "Transposition" (*vyatyāsa*), on the other hand, is the conceptualization of something separated; it is the shifting of what is situated in one place to another. But this is not possible in the case of a word whose nature consists of a base (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*) fixed in their respective order.

Because it would entail the loss of the word [itself]. Therefore, it is the *sūtras* alone—possessing the possibility of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth—that deserve to be referred to by the pronoun "these" (*eṣām*). But surely, the postulation of modification (*vipariṇāma*) and quality (*guṇa*) are properties of words (*pada-dharma*) alone; for it is a word that undergoes modification, whether as a base (*prakṛti*) or as a suffix (*pratyaya*). For example: *pratigṛhṇīyāt* becomes *pratigrāhayet*.

Thus it occurs; and from "remoteness" (*viprakarṣa*) [the form] "because of remoteness" (*viprakarṣāt*) also occurs. The conceptualization of secondary qualities (*guṇakalpanā*) is also within the scope of words.

This will be explained in the context of words such as *autpattika* and others. However, in sentences (*vākya*), neither of these two is possible. For a collection of words does not undergo modification, nor does it become secondary. Therefore, there is no difference whatsoever between the word and the sūtra. It is said:

For a sentence is indeed not some distinct reality separate from the words; rather, it is simply the words themselves, which have attained a state of syntactic unity through their embrace of a single purposeful action. Therefore, it is logical that even a property of the word should persist [in the sentence].

Consequently, since the assumption of modification (*vipariṇāma*) and quality (*guṇa*) in sentences occurs by way of the words, the status of the sentence as the substratum for negation is established.

However, since there is no possibility whatsoever for the properties of sentences to apply to a mere word, it is not appropriate to prohibit them; therefore, it is correct that the pronoun "these" refers to the sūtras in order to prohibit [the application of] ellipsis and so forth. // 30 //

In this regard, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), while stating the purpose of all the commentaries, has said: "Thus, it is the Vedic sentences themselves that are investigated by these [Sūtras]. The meaning of this is as follows: since the Sūtras have already been explained by means of a common commentary, they need not be explained again; rather, it is the Vedic sentences whose meanings have been fully understood through those [Sūtras] that must be explained. This is incorrect, for it has been stated:
"The commentary on the Sūtras is twofold: common and specialized.
Since the Sūtras are touched upon even by the specialized commentary, how can the restriction "only Vedic sentences" be justified?
To this he says: "The word 'eva' [is used]. For the rejection of the specialized commentary is intended to avoid the burden of excessive effort.

Furthermore, excessive elaboration (*gaurava*) would occur in a commentary composed like that of a logician (*tārkika*), through such things as the detailed analysis of word-divisions (*padaccheda*). But here, we shall not do so. Therefore, there is no fault in making a restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇa*) because only a small specific point contained within the Sūtra needs to be stated. The Bhāṣya also states: "Otherwise, an excessive burden of effort (*yatnagaurava*) would result. This is its meaning:

First of all, the Vedic statements themselves must be explained. However, if this explanation were described as having both the Vedas and the Sūtras as its scope, it would result in excessive effort. Therefore, he says: "of this" (*asya*). While explaining the Bhāṣya, [the author] refers back to the explanation under discussion with the word "of this," following from the statement that [the Vedic statements] are to be explained. If, in this context, both the Vedas and the Sūtras were being explained, [it would lead to the aforementioned difficulty].

Consequently, an excessive effort and weightiness would result in the repetition of the explanation. For even when there is a difference in substance, the repetition of an action is observed, as in the expression, "the Brahmins ate eight times. Here, an objection is raised: [19] "By the well-known...

Since the acceptance of the well-known meaning and the avoidance of *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) and the like are already established by themselves when there is no contradiction, what is the point of saying this? He replies:
—There is no fault. For the commentary (bhāṣya) does not have as its subject matter that which has not already been established, unlike the Veda. // 31 //

[19] Even though the meaning is established by its own force, nevertheless, for one who thinks that the restatement of a meaning already well-understood without being explicitly stated appears as if it required a further purpose, [the author says]: [20–21] ... with respect to such a person.

He states the purpose [of the treatise]: "As a constituent part of the commentary" (*vyākhyāṅgatva*). For one who observes that in another system (*tantra*) there are elements such as ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or technical terminology (*paribhāṣā*) like *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, and who consequently applies those here as well—for his sake, the nature of this scripture is defined by this [work], establishing that in Mīmāṃsā, an interpretation free from ellipsis and the like is indeed appropriate. // 32 //
[21] Even for us, those [arguments] are not [sufficient]; [22] furthermore, because they yield but meager results, there is likewise dissatisfaction with them.

He explains that [position] differently, saying "in other commentaries" (*vṛttyantareṣu*). For certain individuals, such as Bhavadāsa and others, have described non-worldly (*alaukika*) meanings for words in their various commentaries; these are being censured by this *bhāṣya*. Indeed, until a distinction is demonstrated—either by exposing the defects in previous works or by proclaiming the excellence of one's own work—[the former position remains untenable].

[23] Otherwise, the listeners would not care to listen. For those envious people who claim that this author is merely stealing from previous works with slight variations, it would be appropriate for them to discourage those desiring to hear; therefore, the criticism of others is indeed purposeful. // 33 //
[23] Where, then, has your honor perceived a non-worldly (alaukika) object of apprehension such that you thus reproach us? To this he says: "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*).

Here, "the world" (*loka*) refers to the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), wherein word and meaning are perceived. In that context, the very state of being separate words is what constitutes "now, therefore."
It is observed between two words, as for example: "Having eaten, he now goes.

It does not mean that because he has not eaten, he therefore does not go; rather, the connection between these two is not one previously seen as mere immediate succession (*ānantaryamātra*). And even as for the connection in "Now, therefore, the definition of the remainder" (*atha ataḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam*, JaiSū 3.1.1) and "Now, therefore, he sacrifices to Agni with the Agniṣṭoma," [the same applies].

Even there, the immediate transgression (*ānantarya*) is to be experienced solely as a result of the word "atha. And Bhadantāsva said: "The word 'atha'—as in 'lāthātaḥ' or 'atha ataḥ'—is employed in the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*)."

"It proceeds" (vartate). Therefore, the fact that this collection of words has that purpose (*tādarthya*) cannot be established without the technical rules (*paribhāṣā*), etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), he indicates connection with others and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). // 34 //

[26] Now he applies the commentary to these [points], beginning with the word "well-known" (*prasiddha*). For Bhavadāsa has denied that the word *ataḥ* has the sense of a logical reason (*hetu*), and has instead imagined that its scope is an unestablished immediate sequence (*anantarya*). And this [is untenable] as long as the established meaning is possible. [27]

It has not been stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* in the passage beginning with "kāryam iti loke" that [the conventional meaning] must be adopted; rather, the adoption of the well-known meaning is possible here. For Jaimini has not introduced his own technical terminology here in the manner that Pāṇini did in "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pā. 1.1.1). Therefore, it should be understood that this point was expressed by the phrase "sati sambhave" (when possible). For what harm has been done by the well-known meaning, such that one should bypass what is established by its own natural force and resort instead to an unfamiliar sense?
Thus, the meaning is postulated. // 35 //
[27] Thus it is said (KHA).

[28] Furthermore, even though this is so, when the meanings of the words of the Sūtras— which are constructed based on what is well-known— are being explained, and likewise regarding the Vedic sentences...
He says that [the objection] "it would entail excessive effort and weightiness" was stated by the words "otherwise... and so forth, meaning: "one suffers over the meaning of the Sūtra.

This refers to when the meanings of the Sūtra's words are being explained according to one's own imagination, and furthermore, regarding the Vedic sentences, there is [effort] on the part of the author of the book through the composition of the textual arrangement, on the part of the commentator through his explanation, and on the part of the listener...
For a great effort is required for the hearing and retention of a vast treatise. // 36 //

But as for one who thinks: "In the composition of a work of superior quality, listeners will take interest in hearing it simply from the act of listening; what is the use of this base ingratitude that robs them of their multitude of virtues?"—to him he introduces another point: "He will not explain. For this author of the Commentary, immediately after the recitation of the Sūtra, cites Vedic passages and, by distinguishing between the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) and the conclusive (uttarapakṣa) positions, proceeds to determine the meaning.

He will make an effort [to explain the meaning], but he will not take care to provide a detailed commentary on the constituent parts of the sūtras. In that case, a doubt might arise among the listeners: "Is it perhaps because of ignorance that he has neglected the sūtras, or rather because they are useless?"

"Or because it is well-known. Thus, this unskilled commentator—who set out to compose a commentary on the sūtras yet neglected them—commits an error. He remedies this fault by declining to provide an explanation: "We are not ignorant, nor are these sūtras meaningless."
Because they are dependent upon the meaning of the injunctions (*codanā*), they are not to be explained and have therefore been left aside. // 37 //
[29] Why would they not resort to them?

Furthermore, what is the reason for their dependence on the meaning of the injunctions? To this he says: "Because of the effort. But why is no effort made regarding the sūtras? To this he says: "Because of being fruitful," using the suffix *tavya*. For the Vedic sentences are indeed fruitful.

Because of the proximity of the means of knowledge regarding sacrifices that possess results; whereas the sūtras themselves are without results, they lack such proximity. For this very reason, the meaning of the injunction (codanā) alone must be approached by means of the sūtras acting as instruments;
the sūtras, however, should not be disregarded as being merely subordinate means. Thus, it is these [sūtras] that serve to clarify the Vedic sentences themselves.

It should be understood that this was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. For here he teaches the primacy of the Vedic sentences, since he indicates them as being "investigated" while connecting them with the nominative case; whereas the Sūtras are indicated with the instrumental case, as in "by these. Now, it may be granted that the Sūtras alone need not be explained because they lack a direct fruit; however, let both [the Sūtras and the Vedic sentences] be explained.

And since the sūtras consist of Vedic statements, he says: "Neither of the two. [This means that] in explaining both, one would incur the burden of a futile effort. It should be understood that this has been stated by the passage beginning with "But otherwise... and so forth. Now, it may be argued: "True, there is a burden of effort, but it is not futile; for the meaning of the sūtra is not known unless it is explained."

And one who is ignorant of that [grammar] is not able to know the meaning of the Veda, because grammar is the means to that end. Therefore, he says: "of the word-meanings. He thinks as follows: it is true that the Sūtras are the means for knowing the meaning of the Veda; however, they do not have their meanings easily understood when unexplained. First of all, the word-meanings are indeed well-known in the world. Precisely through that worldly renown...
And since the meaning of the sentence, which is preceded by that [word-meaning], is also well-established, nothing remains that requires further explanation. // 38–39 //
It should be understood that these are investigated by means of the [thirty] investigations (*vicāra*). Here, in this context, he states—
beginning with the word "thus" (*evaṃ*)— that the commentary (*bhāṣya*) fits this position even better than all other explanations.

For in the previous case, non-existence was merely figurative because the detailed explanation was brief; here, however, the explanation of the entire Sūtra is completely rejected. Thus, there is the justification for both the emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*) and the avoidance of the burden of effort. Now, with the desire to state another position, he refutes this position as well, beginning with "the division of words, etc."—because [this view] does not perform the division of words and so forth.

Therefore, those who subsist on the *Bhavadāsa-tantra* have falsely proclaimed that "this [author] is not a new commentator and does not understand the meaning of the Sūtras," in order to destroy the enthusiasm of those seeking knowledge.
In reality, however, he indeed expresses the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Sūtras and performs the examination of what is deficient or redundant here and there;
thus he says, "he indeed expresses. But where does he observe redundancies and so forth? To this he says: "Indeed..."

"Regarding the term 'incapable' (*aśakta*): [the opponent] raises an objection right at the *codanā-sūtra* itself, saying, 'Is it not the case that this sūtra is incapable of expressing these two meanings—that dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) and not by the senses and so forth, and that dharma is a beneficial purpose (*artha*) and not a harmful one (*anartha*)? For if both are intended to be expressed, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result. Having thus raised the objection, [the author replies: 'But that [objection applies] only to Vedic [sentences]... "

He will resolve this by stating that [the definition] does not apply to the Sūtras. Similarly, immediately after defining the Yajus, it was stated for the purpose of making known the measure of a Yajus—namely, how much constitutes a single Yajus: "A single sentence is that which has a single meaning, provided that if it were divided, there would be a syntactic expectancy" (Jaimini Sūtra 2.1.46). The meaning of this is: as many words as have a single purpose, and which, when divided, possess syntactic expectancy, [constitute a single sentence].
"Those many [words] constitute a single sentence. An example is the mantra: *devasya tvā savituḥ prasave*.

For here, the purpose is to manifest the primary act of offering (*nirvāpa*), which is qualified by all the qualifiers beginning with "of the god Savitṛ. And since all the parts beginning with *devasya tvā* and ending with *nirvapāmi* are distinct yet mutually expectant, [the whole forms a single sentence]. Of the god...

Since it has been established that the passage beginning with *tvā* and ending with *nirvapāmi* constitutes a single sentence, the Commentator, wishing to explain the purpose of its constituent parts, asks: "Now, for what purpose are both [criteria] stated in the Sūtra—namely, 'this is one sentence because of the unity of meaning' and 'it is expectant when divided'? In this regard, the purpose is as follows:

It has been stated: for there are some [expressions] that have a single meaning, yet are not expectant (*sākāṅkṣa*) with respect to a division [of syntactic units]. For example: "May Bhaga divide you two; may Pūṣan divide you two; may Aryaman divide you two," and so forth. Here, while all [these expressions] express a single act of division and thus possess a single meaning, they nevertheless attain the status of distinct sentences (*nānāvākyatva*). However, when there is no division [of syntactic units], there is expectancy.

If [the definition of syntactic unity] were based merely on having a single meaning through qualification, then all [mantras] would result in being a single sentence. Likewise, if it were stated only that "there is expectancy in the case of division," then [the following two mantras] would constitute a single sentence: "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well-pleasing with a stream of ghee;
sit upon it, O immortal one, and take thy stand, O essence of rice, being well-disposed."

Thus, the syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) of these two [sentences] is established because they are mutually expectant (*sākāṅkṣatva*) when divided. The phrase "he should sit upon that" (*tasmin sīdet*), being thus divided, remains expectant, because its function consists in referring back (*parāmarśa*) to what was previously mentioned, which would be untenable without that [prior mention]. Furthermore, even though there is mutual expectancy when divided, there is a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) due to the difference in purpose; for there are indeed two purposes therein: that of the former [sentence], and...
The preparation of the seat and the placement of the northern cake—having thus stated the purpose of both, [the author] concludes at the end:
"Therefore, it has been correctly formulated in the Sūtra. Similarly, there is the Sūtra: *viśaye prāyadarśanāt* (Jaimini 2.3.16).

It was stated there that this Sūtra is non-explanatory because the example is not understood. For here, in a case of doubt (*saṃśaya*), the observation of what is predominant (*prāyadarśana*) is indicated as the reason. In that regard, we do not know what the doubt is.
Or where is there doubt?
Having raised the objection as to which proposition the "observation of what is generally seen" (*prāyadarśana*) serves as the reason, this was resolved according to the opinion of the *Vṛttikāra*.
For the *Vṛttikāra*, having cited the example, "One should sacrifice a calf, for cattle are fond of calves," investigated: "What..."

Is this an injunction for a sacrifice, or is it merely the consecration of the calf? This point has been raised as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) by means of an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), in order to dispel the doubts of the dull-witted. For it is observed that the root *ālabhati* (to touch/sacrifice) is connected with a sacrifice when joined with a living being as the substance, as in:
"The initiated one who sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma. Therefore, this [act] here also, because of its connection with a living being as the substance...
The thought "it is for sacrifice" arises, leading to a lack of doubt. To remove that, this was stated: "In a case of ambiguity, [the meaning is determined] by the observation of what is predominant.

Its meaning is as follows: this verb *ālabhati* (he slaughters) is mentioned in close proximity with the purificatory rites for the calf (*vatsasaṃskāra*). Therefore, the understanding arises that this [verb] also refers specifically to the purificatory rite for the calf due to its association, just as the word "foremost" (*agrya*) written in a context mostly consisting of "foremost" things is understood as such. But is this not a mere indicative mark (*liṅga*)?
This indicative mark (*liṅga*) illuminates what has already been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

it does not, however, establish it. Therefore, it must be explained from where this object is obtained for which this is the indicative mark. It is said: First of all, in this case, the sacrifice is not perceived directly as it is in the injunction "one should sacrifice with Soma" (*somena yajeta*). Nor is it inferred like the animal sacrifice of the *Dīkṣā* ritual and so forth; for in that case, the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the connection between the substance and the deity is the cause for understanding the sacrifice. But here—

We do not perceive the substance as being connected with a deity, because there is only the scriptural mention of the substance itself. Therefore, this touching (*ālambha*) of the calf is a refinement (*saṃskāra*) having a visible purpose; for when it is touched, it will cause the cow to low. Much of this kind has been explained by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), and thus it should be inferred. Therefore...
If the explanation of the Sūtras were rejected, everything of this kind and more would result as being contradictory to the author of the Bhāṣya.
As for the reason stated for the rejection— that the Sūtras are merely means for knowing the meaning of the Vedas,
and therefore what is the use of explaining them?— [this is not so].

"But the goal (*upeya*) alone, which is the meaning of the Veda, must be explained by means of these [auxiliaries] acting as instruments. He refutes this with "And not... Since they are indeed the means (*upāya*), for that very reason they themselves must all the more be explained. For one who is ignorant of the means is not capable of determining the goal. But surely, if those [auxiliaries] are also being explained, they would become things yet to be accomplished (*sādhya*); and what is unestablished cannot be established by that which is itself unestablished. It is said in reply: even though it is unestablished, a means may be established by another.
It is employed for the sake of an effect, just as a sacrifice—accomplished through its constituent substances and deities—is employed in the production of a result (*phalabhāvanā*);
and just as means of proof that are not established for one party are nonetheless able to establish the probandum when they are established by other means. [41–42]
[32] Thus, beginning with these words and ending with those, when analyzed, they exist here [33] [34]. (KHA)
[35] All that has been said is [36] this (KHA) [37] and in this (KA) it shall be (KHA).
[38] That which he will cause to be heard; (KA) what [40] by another means, having attained the object, (KHA)

[41] It has been established that for one who is ignorant of the means (*upāya*), there is no determination of the goal (*upeya*). But for one who has already understood the meaning of the Veda through other means, what is the use of a commentary on the Sūtras? Therefore, he says: "Not from another. For those who have indeed understood the meaning of the Veda from another source alone—[for them...]

These sūtras were not composed by Jaimini for the sake of this [particular] meaning, nor were they explained by the author of the commentary (bhāṣyakāra) for that purpose. Rather, the sūtras were composed and the commentary was provided by the author for the sake of those who are ignorant of other matters. And yet, such persons do not deduce the meaning of the sūtras without [first receiving] an explanation; nor are they left with an undetermined understanding of the sūtra-meaning.
Since they are determining the meaning of the Veda, the effort expended in explaining its meaning is appropriate. // 42cd //

Regarding what was stated [in verse 42], "because the meanings of words are well-known," he refutes that with the words "of the rejection": for the fact that the meanings of words are well-known would result in the Vedic sentences themselves being inexplicable.
For even in those [Vedic sentences], it is precisely the same words and word-meanings that are well-known in common worldly usage. As he will state: "Those very [words] which are worldly..."

"The words are those very same ones; they are the same in the Vaidika [context]; their meaning is also that very same one. This is what was meant by the statement "because the meaning is the same" (tulyārthatvāt).
For the word-meanings are indeed the same in common usage, in the Vedas, and in the Sūtras. // 43 //

[42] Furthermore, it has been said (KHA): "Now, if it is argued that although the word-meanings (*padārtha*) are indeed well-established in the Vedic sentences, nevertheless, because the specific mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) regarding the sentence-meanings (*vākyārtha*) is not determined, doubts arise accordingly; therefore, an exposition (*vyākhyāna*) is undertaken there to dispel them."
Since that [objection] is the same regarding the Sūtras as well, he states—“the meaning of the sentence”—in order to show that the rejection of its explanation is improper. 44.

Moreover, this commentator, while rejecting the [forced] explanation of the Sūtras, would have stated quite clearly that they "are not to be explained" if he intended a total rejection. Since he achieves his rejection merely by prohibiting explanations corrupted by defects such as textual interpolation (*adhyāhāra*), it is understood that he does not exclude an explanation free from such defects; thus he says: "It is not to be explained. (45)
Thus, since this position of rejection contradicts the established interpretation [of scripture],
and because the two previous criticisms of all interpretations are trivial and lack significant purpose,
and because the middle criticism specifically results in an accusation of malice;

He states that "of this" [commentary]—the purpose is indeed *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification), which yields great fruit by refuting the alteration of Vedic sentences resulting from fallacious reasoning, and which is difficult to understand unless explicitly stated: "of this. // 46 //

[43] First, he states the scope of the enumeration—meaning "pertaining to the Veda" (*vaidika*)—by means of the suffix *-anta*. For the *sūtras* are intended for the purpose of explaining the sentences of the Vedas. Therefore, these [sūtras], even when grasped according to their literal hearing, are capable of providing the collection of reasonings (*nyāyakalāpa*) for determining the meaning of the Vedic sentences.
They indeed do offer [the alternatives]. Only in certain cases does an opposition between them arise.

Thus, when there is a mutual contradiction between the Veda and the Sūtra as they are accepted according to their literal hearing, the *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) pertains to that subject. Having thus understood the scope, he states its essential nature with the words beginning "tatra" and ending with "itinyeyam. Regarding the subject of contradiction:

For even this [rule] prevents the natural tendency to accept a Sūtra exactly as it was heard and grasped; namely, that one should accept the well-known meaning and avoid supplying ellipses (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth—provided there is no contradiction with the Veda. However, in the event of a contradiction, the Sūtra must be explained by means of supplying ellipses and other methods, while the Vedic sentence itself should be interpreted exactly as it was heard. This is what is being taught here. Now, is it the case that a Vedic sentence must always be interpreted exactly as it was heard?

"No," he says, "because there is a contradiction. For where there is a mutual contradiction between two Vedic statements, one of them must indeed be interpreted through methods such as *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) and so forth. Just as, due to the contradiction with the statement regarding the giver (*dātṛ*) understood from the opening [passage], the statement regarding the receiver (*pratigṛhītṛ*) found in the conclusion was shown to refer to the giver. For it has been stated thus: "As many horses as one might receive... [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.9].

"One should cause [the recipient] to accept" (pratigrāhayet). This, however, is an example of modification (*vipariṇāma*). As for elision (*adhyāhāra*) and the other [methods of interpretation], they have not been explained in detail here regarding Vedic sentences for fear of prolixity. // 47–48 //
[44] dhe. vedavi (KHA) [45] t pra (KA) But surely, when there is applicability in both cases, it constitutes a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). As it has been said:

In that case, it is stated that "exclusion" (*parisaṃkhyā*) occurs when there is the possibility of application both here and elsewhere. However, in this instance, the literal acceptance of the sūtra is not applicable for either of the two cases— contradiction or non-contradiction— for it never happens that a subordinate factor (*guṇa*), having been adopted according to its true sense as conforming to the principal factor (*pradhāna*), should lead the principal factor to be interpreted otherwise.

It is possible. Moreover, the Vedic statement is eternal, whereas the Sūtra is non-eternal; for this reason as well, it is not fitting for the latter to compete with the former. Consequently, when there is a conflict with the Veda, the adoption of the Sūtra exactly as it was heard does not follow [as a necessary rule]. Therefore, what is the purpose of an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) intended to prevent that? To this he says: "Just as... He thinks as follows: It is true that this logic applies when there is a conflict with the Veda.

"The Sūtra is being treated otherwise. To those who are led astray by fallacious reasoning, the Commentator provides a refutation with the words "The world... and so forth in the Bhāṣya. For listeners who are thus deluded might think: "There is no difference whatsoever between the Vedic sentences and the Sūtras. Just as the Veda is an authority regarding Dharma," [so too must be the Sūtras].

Thus, since even the determination of the meaning of the Vedas cannot be accomplished without the Sūtras, there is no difference between the Veda and the Sūtras for us. Nor is there any other intrinsic distinction between the sentences of the Veda and the Sūtras. To begin with, the words and word-meanings are identical in both cases; as for the sentence, which consists of the syntactic connection of words that are mutually expectant, semantically appropriate, and proximate, this applies equally to both the Vedic and the Jaiminīya (Sūtra) texts.
And indeed, neither of those two requires anything such as an ellipsis (adhyāhāra). This is what he says: "by the power of the sentence" (vākyasāmarthya). // 49-50 //
[46] "It is indeed this" (KHA);
[47] "not another" (KA); [48] "of the three... (A).

But surely, it is not possible for both contradictory meanings to be established simultaneously; therefore, since it is settled that one or the other must be incorrect, it was previously stated that the Sūtra should be interpreted otherwise because it is subordinate. To this, he says: "Because of impossibility. For those who desire knowledge possess diverse inclinations; thus, they sometimes understand the relative strength and weakness regarding what is primary and what is subordinate in accordance with the Vedas.

They interpret the Sūtra differently. Sometimes, those who have developed a profound reverence for their Teacher reflect thus: "How could Jaimini, who knows a thousand logical arguments, fail to perceive an inconsistency within our own sphere of experience? We consider it certain that the meaning of the Vedic revelation is consistent precisely with the way he has explained it; otherwise, by following a single Śruti at the expense of many Śrutis, one would result in the destruction of the entire corpus of revealed scripture. Thus, due to such differences in reflection, there is an option (vikalpa).
Thus [ends verse] 51.
[49] Having understood the relative strength and weakness of the means of knowledge, [50] the meaning of the Veda is established through reasoning;
or else, when both possess equal force, there is an option between them. However, in this case, during the stage of determining the meaning of the Veda—

The sūtras fall first. As long as they do not involve contradiction, they present themselves as things to be accepted exactly as heard. And a listener whose intellect has been occupied by those [sūtras] from the very beginning would sublate only an injunction that falls into a subordinate position. For it will be stated that there is a sublation of the subordinate in accordance with the primary, or that the primary [is stronger] because of the prior injunction.

"Like the world" (Jai. 12.2.23). He says this: "by virtue of being primary. By the word "proper," he indicates the purpose of the restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*). For if there were no restrictive injunction, the sublation of the proper injunction by a fallacious argument (*nyāyābhāsa*) would result. But how is it proper?

An objection is raised: [It might be argued that] the sūtras are subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), while those [commentaries] intended for their explanation are primary (*pradhānabhūta*). Indeed, it is not proper to alter the primary in accordance with the subordinate;
for subordinates are employed so that the primary may be accomplished without defect. But what [happens] when the primary itself is defective?

By means of the qualities (*guṇaiḥ*). For this very reason, he will state later: "And in the case of a conflict between a subsidiary and its quality, [the quality prevails] because it exists for the sake of that" (*Jaimini Sūtra* 12.2.25). And this principle is an exception (*apavādaka*) to the preceding principle of favoring the principal (*mukhya-anugraha-nyāya*). For this very reason, the sublation of the time of the principal initiation (*dīkṣā*) in accordance with the time of the primary sacrifice has been shown. For it has been said: "Initiation on the *parvan* day, and the pressing (*sutyā*) on the *parvan* day. Therefore, it is well stated.
"Righteous," [he said]. // 52 //
[51] Indeed,

having established a *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusive specification) through the two alternatives of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and restriction (*niyama*), which apply to both cases, [the author] applies the commentary (*bhāṣya*) specifically to this point. [52] (KHA) (KA) Thus.
"—By the word 'tena' (by that). The mention of "non-contradiction with the Vedas" is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*), which also implies non-contradiction with logical reasoning (*nyāya*).

Thus, the meaning is this: having restated what is already established—namely, the acceptance of well-known meanings and the avoidance of *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) and so forth—it is enjoined that there must be the possibility of non-contradiction. But even in this view...

Three faults ensue. To explain: for a rule proceeding by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*) in the form "when possible," it must be stated that its purpose is the negation of others in the form "not when impossible. In that case, there results both the abandonment of its own primary meaning and the assumption of a non-primary meaning. Furthermore, it follows that one would have to accept the sūtra exactly as it is heard in both cases—whether there is a contradiction or no contradiction.

That [general rule] is sublated; therein, it is a case of sublation by what has been previously established (*prāptabādha*). Therefore, by what distinction is this restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) introduced? It is said: if there were a general statement to the effect that "whether a conflict exists or not, one must adhere to the literal sense of the Sūtra," then one would have avoided the three faults. However, when one proceeds to postulate a general statement based on a fallacious reasoning, one perceives the direct instruction (*pratyakṣopadeśa*) stating "when possible."

At that time, the general statement has not yet acquired its own nature; therefore, there is no contingency of the three defects, such as contradiction with what has already been obtained (*prāptabādha*). Since it is only an injunction of what is not yet established (*aprāptavidhi*) when such a possibility exists, one might ask: "If [the result] would be obtained even without an injunction, what is the use of an injunction? Upon examining its purpose, the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is understood to be the fruit. However, in the ultimate sense, this is indeed an injunction of what was not previously established. As he will state regarding the mantra for the girdle (*raśanāmantra*):
[53] This is indeed a rule of non-attainment; therefore, this is the certainty regarding the mantra.
[54] He who... i.

It has been stated that the enumeration [of the topics] is by way of their results. Therefore, it should be understood that this very point is being enjoined here by the word "artha" (meaning/purpose). // 53 //

[55] Now, intending to demonstrate through examples in the sūtras the conceptualization of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and other devices regarding matters of contradiction, he first states an example of ellipsis:
"of those entitled to the remnants" (*śeṣabhājām*). For Jaimini will indeed state: "Or rather, it should belong to those entitled to the remnants" (Jai. 6.4.3).

Thus [ends the citation]. Here, indeed, having cited the remaining ritual acts such as the *iḍā* and the *prāśitra*, it will be investigated: if by chance there occurs a deficiency of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) that was taken for the sake of these [acts], should another oblation then be brought in, or should one offer from the remnant?

"Or there may be a loss of the ritual action. Regarding this, it was stated: "Or rather, he may be one who partakes of the remnant. This does not adopt the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), because of its connection with the word "or" (*api vā*). Nor is it the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), because there would be no prima facie position [to counter]. Furthermore, in the immediately preceding section, when the sacrificial material intended for the principal rite was destroyed, the prima facie position—that the offering could be made from the remnant by taking a portion—was adopted and then refuted; for, as the final conclusion states, "on account of the specific scriptural injunction, another [material] must be used."
Regarding the statement "one should bring it" (Jai 6.4.2):

if, by means of taking up another substance, that [action] is connected here immediately after the arrival of another substance, then a contradiction with another principle arises. For it has been established [in Jai 4.1.28] that the subsidiary rites (śeṣakāryāṇi) apply when there is a connection with an existing portion of the substance at its production.

Since the lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*) has been established by this section (*adhikaraṇa*), [the opponent might argue: "Now, by bypassing the subsequent position (*uttarapakṣa*), the connection would be that 'the cutting off from the remnant (*śeṣa*) for those entitled to the remnant should occur according to their purpose'.

That too is incorrect, because the remnant is connected with another disposal (*pratipatti*), and because there is no connection with the disposal of a lost part. Therefore, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indeed contrary to the Sūtra, as it involves the introduction of a different substance.

Alternatively, having accepted the established conclusion (*rāddhāntita*), he will demonstrate the supply of the word "omission" (*lopa*) by stating that there would be an omission for those entitled to the remainder.

Thus, this is the meaning of the sūtra: since *iḍā*, *prāśitra*, and so forth—which partake of the remainder—lack the capacity to employ other substances, and because the existing remainder is connected with another disposal (*pratipatti*), there would be an "omission," that is, simply non-performance. // 54 //
[56] That [57] is established [58] or it comes to be. That.
[59] Regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*):

[60] He illustrates their transformation through the effects beginning with the *ḍā* [suffix], stating "due to remoteness. For there is the animal to be sacrificed (*savanīya-paśu*) and the cup for the Aśvins (*āśvina-graha*).

"Having taken the *trivṛt* [rope] and having encircled the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), one dedicates the animal for Agni (*āgneya*) belonging to the *savanīya* [offering]; at each pressing (*anusavana*), the *savanīya* sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are offered. And there exist the *savanīya* animal-cakes (*paśupuroḍāśa*). In that regard, it being established that the primary (*tantrin*) ritual duties (*dharma*) assist those that are incidental (*prasaṅgin*), [the following applies].

In order to establish that the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) fall within the framework of the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*), the Sūtra states: "And because of the animal's distance [from the other rites], it is prescribed in the middle of the framework" (Jaimini 12.2.32).
However, this [Sūtra], as it is taken literally, is not capable of explaining the intended meaning. For "distance" (*viprakarṣa*)...

In this context, that which ends in the nominative case is understood as the probandum (*sādhya*). The phrase "because of its prescription within the *tantra*" ends in the ablative case and thus functions as the reason (*hetu*). However, that is incorrect. For the "remoteness" (*viprakarṣa*) of the animal consists in its connection with the three times, such as the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), and that is established by an explicit scriptural statement (*pratyakṣavacana*), not something to be proven. Indeed, it is heard [in scripture] thus: "They proceed with the omentum at the morning pressing; with the sacrificial cake..."

"At the midday pressing [they are performed] with the limbs; at the third pressing [they are performed with the animal]. Even this prescription within the middle of the *tantra* (the ritual framework) is something to be established, not something that requires a statement of reason. Therefore, a transformation of the first and fifth case endings will be explained. Because of the distance of the animal sacrifice—since it pervades the three times beginning with the morning—the placement of the *puroḍāśas* occurs within the *tantra* of the animal sacrifice. For the animal sacrifice indeed pervades even the time of the *puroḍāśas*. However, the *puroḍāśas*...

They do not extend as far as the conclusion of the *svasavana*. Therefore, since the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) fall within the framework of the animal sacrifice (*paśutantra*), the performance [of rites] for the sake of the animal becomes applicable to the cakes. And this very point has been cited by the author of the *Vārttika* in its modified form as "due to remoteness" (*viprakarṣāt*). He provides an example of the assumption of an intervention with the words "by a word" (*padena*). For it will be stated thus in the section concerning the Veda (*vedādhikaraṇa*).

The Vedas consist of collections of words (*padasaṅghāta*), and collections of words are seen to be composed by persons, such as those concerning objects like blue lotus groves. Therefore, these [Vedas] are also artificial (*kṛtrima*). To demonstrate this specific point, there is this sūtra: *loke sanniyamāt prayogasannikarṣaḥ syāt* (Jaimini).

And here, the word *prayoga*, separated by the word *sanniyamāt*, is to be connected immediately after the word *loke*. Thus, the meaning is this: in the world, the employment of words (*śabdaprayoga*) is characterized by a restriction (*sanniyama*).

It is logical that [the cognition] consists of a correct connection [of the sense organs], because of the contact of the eye and other senses with the object; however, this is not the case in the Veda, because its subject matter is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriyārthatvāt*). And although this example applies equally to both "transformation" (*vipariṇāma*) and "interposition" (*vyavahita-kalpanā*), since "transformation" has already been discussed, it is cited here specifically as an illustration of mere interposition.
Thus it should be understood. // 55 //
[61] That which is seen [62] by the pure [63] merits.
[64] Therefore, [KHA] [65] this is not as it was heard, because it is an expression intended [to convey a specific meaning] based on a connection [with that intention], [KHA].

He provides an example of an intervention by a *sūtra* with the words "by the *sūtra*. For this is taught in the *Samhitā*: "One who has vomited *soma* should offer a *caru* oblation of *śyāmāka* grain to Soma-Indra. In that regard, there is a doubt: is the *caru* for Soma-Indra intended for ordinary (*laukika*) vomiting of *soma*, or for Vedic (*vaidika*) vomiting? On this point, [the *sūtra* states]: "And the case of the impairment of drinking is like that" (Jaimini 3.4.38).

Thus, an extension (*atideśa*) has been made from the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the initial deliberation on the sentence regarding the *aśvapratigraheṣṭi* sacrifice. Therein, having cited the passage—"As many horses as one might receive in gift, so many four-pot-sherd offerings to Varuṇa should he perform"—it was deliberated: "Is this [the rule for] the receipt of a horse in a worldly context..."

Is this an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, or is it Vedic? In this regard, the sūtra for the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is: "But because of the fault, the *iṣṭi* should be performed in the case of the worldly [act]" (3.4.34).
For this *iṣṭi* is for the purpose of destroying a fault, since it is heard in connection with a fault. Indeed, they recite thus: "Varuṇa seizes him who accepts a horse. And this fault...

This [practice] exists in the world but not in the Veda, because the horse-sacrificial fee (*aśvadakṣiṇā*) is prescribed for the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rites. Thus, the prima facie view being that it is a worldly practice, it was stated: "Or rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), because there is no possibility of a transgression; therefore, it should be understood as pertaining to the sacrifice" (3.4.35).
The meaning of this is: this is not an *iṣṭi* sacrifice for the purpose of expiating a fault, because there is an absence of any fault.

For the occurrence of the defect consisting in Varuṇa’s seizure resulting from the acceptance of a horse is not apprehended through perception or other means of knowledge. Therefore, the mention of the defect is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda). Since there is no basis for postulating a [specific] result and because of the commonality of being Vedic, it remains established that [the prohibition] is Vedic;
yet, this was further investigated: let it be Vedic, indeed.

But does that [sacrificial rite] belong to the giver or to the receiver? In this regard, the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "And it is not enjoined for the giver, because of the difference between the acts" (3.4.36).

Its meaning is as follows: because of the difference between the acts of giving and receiving; and here, since the text says "as many horses as one might receive," the sacrificial rite (*iṣṭi*) is not enjoined for the giver, but rather for the receiver—the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*).

This being the prima facie view, it is stated: "That [rite] should belong to the officiating priest because of the indicative mark" (3.4.37). The meaning of this is as follows: this belongs to the *ārtvija*, that is, to the sacrificer who is the giver of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In that case, this sacrifice belongs to the giver. Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is the indicative mark? It is the force of the preceding and following words contained within the sentence concerning the horse-gift sacrifice (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*). For therein—
It is heard in the Śruti: "Prajāpati led the horse to Varuṇa"; having proclaimed the giver, one should accept [the gift] at the end.

And that [injunction], having fallen upon a cognition already occupied by the giver—which was first understood and free from contradiction—is understood as referring specifically to the giver. Therefore, it is modified to "one should cause [the recipient] to accept. Thus, in this case, the rule regarding the mishap involving the drinking of Soma is likewise [to be applied]. (3.4.38)

Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—that "on account of the mark (*liṅga*), it should apply to the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*); and because the action is not enjoined, there is no distinction of acts; or rather, it is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) because of the impossibility [of the literal sense]; therefore, it should be understood as applying to the sacrifice"—is extended from the preceding discussion, being separated by three *sūtras*.
