This is the meaning: the sacrifice for the mishap involving drinking (*pānavyāpad-iṣṭi*) ought to be like that, just as was stated in the prima facie view regarding the horse-gift sacrifice (*aśvapratigraheṣṭi*) and others. Why? Because:

Because of the scriptural mention of a defect. For it is thus heard in scripture: "He who vomits Soma is indeed deprived of his sensory power and vigor. And this loss of sensory power and vigor occurs when one vomits after drinking a worldly elixir (*rasāyana*), but not in the case of the Vedic [rite]. Since, in all primary and modified Soma sacrifices, the consumption of the Soma is established by the mere act of drinking, this was the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). To this, the following rebuttal was provided: "But because of the defect, it would apply to the Vedic [rite]" (3.4.39).

Thus [it is said]. For the purpose of *rasāyana*, the drink is indeed for the sake of emesis (*vamana*). For when the body has been purified by emesis, stability arises through the continuous process of the proper digestion and transformation of food. However, it is understood from the wording of the mantra, "The acceptance of Soma is until its proper digestion; thus it is dear to my limbs," that the ritual acceptance of Soma ends with proper digestion. Therefore, in that very context, when a mishap involving the drinking occurs due to emesis, [the following rite] is for the purpose of removing that [mishap].
The *caru* [is the offering]. Thus, although there is an intervention by three sūtras, the singular number in the word "sūtreṇa" is used with reference to the collection as a whole. // 55 //
[67] It will be explained;
[68] the assembly;
[69] thus it was previously proposed.
[70] Therefore,
[71] regarding the statement "the officiating priest" (*ṛtvij*),
[72] this is preceded by an investigation into the sentence concerning the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*).
[73] Exhaustion [74] Vomiting (KA) [75] Emetic therapy (KA)

He provides an example of the alteration of a sūtra with the words "paśu" (animal). For in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there are the Agniṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anubandhya animals. There also exist the sacrificial duties pertaining to animals, such as the ritual bringing forward (*upākaraṇa*) and so forth. A doubt arises: do these [duties] apply to all animals without distinction, or only to the Agniṣomīya or the Savanīya? In this regard, since they would prima facie apply to all animals due to the absence of any specification, [the author] states [the following] in order to demonstrate the specific restriction.
"The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice is common to all [animals], because there is no distinction in the context" (3.6.18).
This [sūtra], as it was originally understood, conveys a meaning contrary to what is intended; thus, Āpideva has explained it:

"The ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice would be common to all if there were no distinction in the context. However, there is indeed a distinction in the context, [namely] that [the animal] belongs to Agni."

For the ritual duties have been prescribed with reference to the *savanīya* animal sacrifice by such statements as "a sacrificial animal (*paśu*) is to be offered at the *agniṣṭoma*"; therefore, having adopted the position that these duties are for the sake of the *savanīya* because they are recorded within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *savanīya*, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that they are for the sake of the *agnīṣomīya* on account of their position (*sthāna*). For it is on the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*), which is the position of the *agnīṣomīya*, that these duties are prescribed. Therefore...

They are for that purpose alone. As for the claim that there is a *prakaraṇa* (contextual setting) for the *savanīya* [offerings], that is not so; for since the animals and their ritual properties are recited within the *prakaraṇa* of the Jyotiṣṭoma, no specific distinction is obtained from the context.
[The text states: "On the following day, having drawn the Āśvina cup and having encircled the sacrificial post with a triple-twisted cord, one dedicates the *savanīya* animal to Agni."

This is the origin of the *savanīya* offerings. If they were originated on the previous day, it would be impossible here to enjoin the time subsequent to the *āśvina* cup by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to them, because time is not something that can be enjoined as a subordinate element (*anupādeya*). For it is the ritual action that is enjoined in relation to a time, not the time in relation to the ritual action. In that case, there would be a distinction between rituals (*karmabheda*) according to the principle of the section on "another context" (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*), and thus there would be the fault of the excessive assumption of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa-kalpanā-gaurava*). This might be argued: [the injunction] "with the omentum at the morning pressing... [is intended].

As for the argument that "they proceed" means that because of the postponement of the ritual action produced on the previous day, no further injunction for other actions is possible upon its completion here, and thus it must be determined that the passage refers to qualities not to be adopted—that is incorrect. For the performance of the *vapā* (omentum) is merely a subsidiary (*aṅga*). It cannot postpone the primary action together with its subsidiaries produced on the previous day, because primary actions do not depend on their subsidiaries. Therefore, [the injunction applies to] the cup for the Aśvins.

Thus is the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*). And in this way, by referring back to that [originative injunction] through the statement "the goat for Agni" (*āgneyam ajam*) and so forth, the prescription of the subordinate qualities (*upādeyaguṇavidhāna*) becomes possible; thus it is established that both sentences are viable, and that the prescription of the *savanīya* animal for the following day is indeed proven. But the former [sentence] is for the purpose of prescribing the qualities. And it has been said:
[76] There is no [77] proof here; [78] therefore, it does not deserve to be connected with the meaning. (KHA)
On the Upavasatha day, there is a re-statement of the Savanīya;
their origination and ritual procedure follow after the drawing of the Āśvina cup.

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, it is established that the ritual properties (dharmas) are for the sake of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice because of their location. What is this so-called "alteration of the sūtra"? It is replied: this is the postulation of a restriction (*vyavadhāraṇakalpanā*). Where a matter appears in one way but is described otherwise by the force of the context, that is the postulation of a restriction. Now, is this not included among [the methods such as] *adhyāhāra* (supplying ellipses) and the rest? It is replied: it is not this...

The word "etc. (ādi) expresses a fixed arrangement because it denotes a variety [of types]. It is indeed appropriate to describe even such defects of sentences as these, which consist of various ways of supplying ellipses (adhyāhāra). // 56 //
[79] Thus it is said; [80] gradually; [81] what, moreover, is this?

[82] He illustrates the distinction between different sentences (*vākya-bheda*) within a single section (*māṇāntara*) by means of the three quarters beginning with "agnayaḥ. For he will state: "They serve all purposes because they have been employed, and the fires [serve all purposes] because they belong to their own time" (3.7.39).

[83] And here, having taken the position that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are engaged through selection and maintenance, exist for the sake of all actions—both worldly and Vedic—[84] it is stated: "Or rather, on account of the specific direction, it should be for Vedic rites" (12.2.3).

In this [passage], the determination of the function according to its application (*yathāviniyoga*) has been stated. On account of the syntactical unity (*ekavākyatā*) with that, there arises the notion that the same [principle] should be considered regarding the fires (*agni*) as well. That is incorrect; for in the sūtra, "The sacrificial ground (*vihāra*) should accomplish the purpose of worldly [acts] because of its capacity" (12.2.1), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was taken on the grounds that it serves the purpose of all actions, both worldly and Vedic, yet it was [subsequently] restricted to Vedic acts due to the specific direction [of the text].

In this context, the phrase "it may be" (*syāt*) is used because it has been established that [the fires] serve the purpose of the Vedic rites as specified. Therefore, having separated the statement "all those [rites] have all purposes because they are employed" (*ataḥ te sarvārthāḥ prayuktatvāt*), the fires are explained elsewhere with the words "and the fires, because they have their own time" (*agnayaś ca svakālatvāt*).

For in that [other] place, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was stated as follows: just as in the case of the rule "for whom there is a ladle made of *khadira* wood," the fact that the ladle is made of *khadira* is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*).
In the sūtra *prakṛtau vā dviruktatvāt* (3.6.2), it was explained that [the term] refers to the meaning of the archetype (*prakṛtyartha*);
likewise, the fires (*agnayaḥ*) are also only for the sake of the archetype. To this, the reply is given: *agnayaś ca svakālatvāt*.

The meaning of this is as follows: The fires (*agni*) are for the sake of both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the ectype (*vikṛti*). Why? Because they have their own time (*svakālatvāt*). For they are not enjoined with reference to either the archetype or the ectype; since they are enjoined independently (*anārabhyāmnānāt*), it is logical that, because no specific distinction is perceived, they serve the purpose of both. Furthermore, whatever serves as the means—such as the oblation, the sacrificial offering, or the cooking—in connection with the fires is directly heard in scripture (*pratyakṣaśruta*) for both the archetype and the ectype. Therefore, due to the lack of distinction in the means and the lack of distinction in the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is logical that the fires serve all purposes. Likewise, [the rule states]: "In the *abhyudayeṣṭi*, the removal of the milking should possess its own ritual properties" (9.4.41).

The two sūtras, *apanayo vārthāntare vidhānāt* (9.4.43), which appear as a single syntactic unit, have been explained by breaking them apart. For instance, in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, curd (*dadhi*) and milk (*payas*) are prescribed as the primary substances to be offered: "Curd for Indra on the new moon day; milk for Indra [on the full moon day]."

"Regarding the phrase 'on the new moon day': first, the sacrificial gifts (deyadharmas) must be prepared. Furthermore, following the performance of the occasional rite (naimittika), it is prescribed: 'If the moon should rise before the oblation has been set aside, he shall divide the rice grains into three parts;
those that are of medium size, he shall offer as a cake on eight potsherds (aṣṭākapāla-puroḍāśa) to Agni Dātra; those that are the largest, he shall [offer] to Indra..."

"One should offer a *caru* of curd to Pradātṛ; those [grains] that are least husked, one should offer as a *caru* in boiled milk to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Regarding this, there arises a deliberation as to whether the curd and the milk are entitled to the status of being the substance to be offered (*deyadharma*) or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that they are not entitled; for here the *caru* is the substance to be offered, while the curd and the milk serve merely as substrates (*adhikaraṇa*), having been assigned a subordinate role (*guṇabhāva*) in relation to the *caru*, as indicated by the phrases "a *caru* in curd" and "a *caru* in boiled milk. [The Siddhāntin replies: This is not so. The curd and the milk are indeed entitled to the status of being the substance to be offered. For the *caru* is prepared from them; it is precisely because the *caru* is produced from the curd and the milk that they are designated as its substrates. If they were not intended to be the substance to be offered, they would not have been mentioned as the locus of the preparation. Therefore, since the curd and the milk are the very material from which the *caru* is made, they are themselves the offerings. Thus, the curd is the offering to Pradātṛ, and the milk is the offering to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. This is established by the principle that when a substance is processed into another form, the former is the material cause and thus the actual offering. Therefore, the curd and the milk are the substances to be offered.

It has been stated: upon the removal of the milk, the curd and the milk would remain endowed with their own respective properties even at the time of the rising [of the offering], because there is no abandonment of what was previously understood to be the intended substance to be offered. However, their status as the locus (*adhikaraṇatva*)—known by implication from the fact that they are boiled together with the rice grains because they share the same deity—is not capable of reducing them to the status of subordinate qualities (*guṇabhāva*). This is observed...
And there is also the designation of that which is the principal element as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). For example: "One portion consists of precious jewels in a golden vessel;
that belongs to Devadatta; [another] portion consists of abundant gold in a silver vessel; that belongs to Yajñadatta.
Here, the portion is understood together with the vessel itself. Likewise here too, the sacrificial pap (*caru*) is the portion for the deity together with both the curd and the milk.

Thus it is established that the *deyadharma* (gifts to be given) must be performed for both curd and milk. Regarding the statement "or there is a removal because of the prescription for another purpose," since the sūtra "the removal of milking at the *abhyudaya*" asserts the removal of those very *deyadharma*s previously promised by the word *vā*, one might suspect a contradiction with logic; therefore, it has been explained elsewhere [as applying] to the *paśukāmeṣṭi*, where there are two [substances] prescribed by different words similar to the sentence of the *abhyudayeṣṭi*.

"The removal of curd and milk as the objects of donation occurs because they are prescribed for another purpose, namely for the cooking of the *caru*. He provides an example of the assumption of secondary qualities (*guṇakalpanā*):

"But these assumptions of qualities (*guṇakalpāḥ*) have been made [in the rule] *autpattikas tu*. Regarding the term "assumptions of qualities" (*guṇakalpāḥ*): an assumption (*kalpa*) is the act of assuming; an assumption of qualities is an "assumption of qualities. For a word that, by virtue of its secondary quality (*guṇa*), denotes one thing is assumed to apply elsewhere in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).

As in the case of "the boy is fire": the word *agni* (fire), which denotes the universal (*jāti*) of fire, indicates an individual (*vyakti*) belonging to that class; thereupon, through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of qualities such as tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) inherent in that [individual], it applies to the boy who possesses those qualities. And it has been said:
[84] Just as you [85] even though alone [86] do not prevent...
it is held that the cognition of that which is inseparably connected to the denotatum occurs through the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); however,
the figurative usage (*gauṇatā*) is accepted because of the application [of the word] due to its connection with the qualities of the object being characterized (*lakṣyamāṇa*).

Thus, here in the *Autpattika-sūtra*, the word *autpattika*—by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) "existing at the time of origin" (*utpattau bhavaḥ*)—denotes the impermanence of the three things, namely the word, its meaning, and their relationship; consequently, because it expresses the opposite of the intended permanence, it is understood as being used figuratively (*gauṇa*) due to the impossibility of the intended [literal] sense. For the word "origin" (*utpatti*) [is applied here] by connection with the quality of existence (*sattā*) inherent in that which is being produced, as characterized by the process of originating.

That which exists between word and meaning is secondary (gauṇa). Consequently, it is stated that the relationship is dependent upon the essential nature of the word and its meaning. And because that essential nature is eternal, the relationship is also eternal; thus, the intended point is established. Likewise, regarding the sacrificial sessions (satra) such as the Ādityānāmayana and others, when there arises a doubt as to whether the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) or to the year-long sacrifice (āyamana), one first proposes that it belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice due to the commonality of being a "group of days" (ahargaṇa).

By the rule *gavyasya ca tadādiṣu* (Pāṇini 8.1.18), the concluding ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *gavya* sacrifice is indicated; however, this word *gavya* is not well-known in any specific sacrificial variation (*kratubheda*). Nor is it capable of denoting the intended *gavāmayana* sacrifice. Therefore, because its primary sense is impossible in this context, it is explained as being used figuratively (*gauṇa*). This...

Furthermore, [the word *go*] is primary when it refers to a limb of a cow or a product thereof, because of the traditional rule: "The suffix *yat* is applied after *go* and *payas*" (Pāṇini 4.3.160). Thus, this [word *go*], while primarily denoting a specific relationship, becomes used figuratively (*gauṇa*) with respect to the Gavāmayana sacrifice, which possesses a general relationship characterized by being included within that [specific one]. For in the Gavāmayana, it is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—"The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session" (*gāvo vā etat satram āsata*)—that the cows are the performers.

There exists a connection with the *go* [cow]. Thus, the meaning is this: in rites such as the *ādityānāmayana*, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *gavāmayana* applies because of the commonality of being a *ayana* (sacrificial session), and because it exceeds [the requirements of] a simple *ayana*. Similarly, regarding the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there are optional variations of the *sāmidhenī* verses, such as "one desiring stability should recite twenty-one," and so forth. Since it is established that the completion of the number [of verses] occurs through the introduction of additional mantras (*āgama*), when these [mantras] are being brought in...
Regarding the *ṛc*s, there is a doubt: should they be inserted at the end, or in the middle between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī* verses?
In this matter, since the insertion of adventitious elements (*āgantūnām*) should follow the established order, it might initially seem they belong at the end;

however, it has been stated that they belong in the middle between the *samidhyamānavatī* and the *samiddhavatī*. Why? Because it says: "This is the *samidhyamānavatī*, that is the *samiddhavatī*; that which is between them is the *dhāyyā*. Thus, [the *dhāyyās*] belong to the *dhāyyā*s.

Because of the praise [of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*] as being between the *sāmidhenī* verses, their placement in the interval is determined. Likewise, the indicative mark (*liṅga*) "because they are seen at the end of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*" (5.3.6) has been taught. But that is incorrect, because the two primary [metres], the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*, are absent at the end; rather, it is by means of the *triṣṭubh*.

Because [the term] "he puts on" (*paridadhāti*) is seen at the end of a *triṣṭubh* verse, this [rule] refers to that intention: when the verses being brought forward are in the middle, the two [verses] beginning with *samiddhavatī* occur at the end;
and since those two, taken together, are equal in number to a *triṣṭubh*, it occurs at the end of a *triṣṭubh* due to the commonality of number.

Even so, it must be stated that [the word *triṣṭubh*] is seen at the end [of the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* verses]. True. Nevertheless, because the *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* have the function (*kārya*) of the *triṣṭubh*—as understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "The *uṣṇih* and *kakubh* are indeed the vigor (*vīrya*) of the *triṣṭubh*"—the term *uṣṇih-kakubh* is applied to the *triṣṭubh* by metaphorically attributing the name of the effect to the cause (*kāraṇe kāryopacāra*). Similarly, when it is established in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of one hundred and twelve [cows], there is an equal distribution among the sixteen officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).

Furthermore, when there is doubt as to whether [the shares] are unequal because no specific rule is heard, the equality of the portions is stated; then, a distinction is shown on the grounds that the measure of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) follows the measure of the ritual action, as such is observed in the world.
And again, an indicative mark (liṅga) is taught: "And because of the observation of a distinction, it is so at the rising [of the sun]."

And here, by the word *abhyudaya* (prosperity), the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is indicated because it is a means to prosperity. For in that context, regarding the sequence of initiations (*dīkṣā*) as stated in such passages as "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the master of the house," the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are designated by technical names (*samākhyā*) such as "he initiates the half-sharers" (*ardhin*), "he initiates the third-sharers" (*tṛtīyin*), and so forth.

The connection with *ṛddhi* and so forth has been restated. And this [connection], being a modification (*vikāra*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, would be impossible without a disparity in the portions within the archetype (*prakṛti*);
thus, the disparity serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*). But was it not said that these are "figurative derivations" (*guṇakalpa*)?

Here, in the case of the two words *autpattika* and *gavya*, a figurative description (*guṇavāda*) has been shown in some way; however, in the case of the words *uṣṇih* and *kakubh*, there is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*).

But since there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the word *abhyudaya*, how can they be called "conceptualized as qualities" (*guṇakalpāḥ*)? To this it is replied: because of the commonality of being a secondary mode of operation (*jaghanyavṛtti*), or because of the presence of the indicative mark (*liṅgasamavāya*), they are called "conceptualized as qualities," just as in the expression "he places the breath-beings" (*prāṇabhṛta upadadhāti*); thus, there is no fault. // 58 //

[88] Regarding the passage beginning with “he initiates you as a *brahmán*,” etc., for one who does not even accept a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*) because he considers the attainment of both [alternatives] to be too weak, the author states a different point in response: “the author of the Sūtras” (*sūtrakāra*). For the author of the Bhāṣya encourages his students and himself by means of praise for the author of the Sūtras. [89] By this very author of the Sūtras, through well-known...
Thus, the meanings of words have been expressed by the words themselves;

no technical convention (paribhāṣā) has been established here, as in the case of [the rules for] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*. Therefore, since their meaning is understood without difficulty, it is appropriate to listen to and explain these very words. // 59 //

[89] Regarding those who, thinking that whether there be praise or no praise the purpose remains the same, do not pay heed to the praise, this commentary is intended to refute the word "atha" (therefore) with respect to them; thus he says: "bhavitavyam" (it must be so). This refers to that which has attained syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the phrase "bhavitavyaṃ tu tena" occurring prior to this point.
Alternatively, this commentary provides a refutation of the word "atha" by establishing its syntactic unity with the preceding phrase, "tat tu vedādhyayanam. // 60 //
He connects the commentary with the first limit [of the definition]: "by means of words whose meanings are well-known. // 61 //

He applies the commentary according to the second interpretation: "for its meaning is well-known. The meaning is that a word whose meaning is well-known is appropriate because it must indeed be so. He raises an objection, saying "even though it is well-known," [arguing] that since the adoption of a well-known meaning has already been stated for cases other than the refutation of the word *atha*, the explanation of words such as *atha* is inappropriate. // 62 //

He refutes this: "Some say it is for the sake of illustration. Others, however, argue: "Let those words whose meaning is well-known and not confused by other commentators not be explained. But these two words, *atha* and *ataḥ*, have been interpreted by Bhavadāsa as having the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Therefore, let us set aside [his view] and establish that the word *atha* alone has the sense of immediate succession."

This must be stated. Just as it is well known that the word *atha* has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) from the eighth chapter onwards—as in the rule *atha viśeṣalakṣaṇam* (Pāṇini 1.2.45)—so too [the author] says "some say" by way of refutation. Furthermore, the commentary on both [sūtras] was set aside for fear of excessive prolixity; and since Vedic sentences have not yet been explained here, if they were to be considered in this context, the Bhāṣya would be rendered entirely irrelevant. Therefore, the explanation of the sūtra alone is indeed appropriate.
He says: "And not," [verses 63–64].

[90] Or rather, that which was stated as the adoption of a well-known meaning is itself [91] challenged because of the absence of a *vṛtti* (commentary) and because the word *atha* cannot possibly have the sense of "immediacy" (*ānantarya*). Thus he says: "Or rather. He applies the *Bhāṣya* to this very point with the words: "If," etc.; therein, the author of the *Bhāṣya* [proceeds] with the words beginning with "In that case," and so forth.

This refutes the acceptance of a well-known meaning [for the word *atha*]. For if a well-known meaning were accepted, the meaning of the word *atha* would be "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), and since that is not possible through the preceding *vṛtti*, one would be forced to resort to the assumption of an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and so forth. In this case, the passage beginning with "it must be" (*bhavitavyam*) should be explained as a refutation of the word *atha* based on its status as a general term followed by a specific one (*sāmānyaviśeṣottaratayā*). // 65 //

[91] He offers another explanation for the word *vā* (or): "Regarding the study of the Veda. This is the intended meaning: the word *atha* is not explained because it is difficult to understand without an explanation; rather, under the guise of explaining the word *atha*, something else entirely is what the author of the commentary intends to convey.

And this very point can be demonstrated through the sequence of objection and resolution once the meaning of the word *atha* has been stated. For instance, when the word *atha* is explained [as signifying "immediately after"], it follows logically that the postponement (*utkarṣa*) of bathing—which would otherwise occur immediately after the study of the Veda—is inferred by the force of the visible purpose of the Smṛti injunction for study, namely "having studied, one should bathe. Thus, the explanation of the word *atha* is indeed appropriate. // 66 //

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya, having proposed with the words "it must be so" (*bhavitavyaṃ tu tena*) that the word *atha* has the sense of immediate succession (*ānantarya*), stated the reason for this—namely, its well-known meaning—with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*). He explains that [reason] as follows: "if it were meaningless" (*anarthaka iti*). For if the meaning of the word *atha* were immediate succession, its well-known meaning would be maintained; however, if it were either meaningless or had some other meaning, its established usage would be contradicted.

Therefore, some prior occurrence is understood in order to provide the justification for the immediate sequence (*anantarya*) following the hearing [of the scripture]. But is it not observed that the word *atha* also serves the purpose of indicating a new topic (*adhikāra*), as in "Now, the instruction on words" (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*)? Consequently, how can its being used for another purpose constitute a contradiction of conventional usage?
It is said in reply: For in that case, [the word *atha*] indeed...

Since the instruction on words (śabdānuśāsana) itself will be the subject matter further on, it is logical that [the word "therefore"] has the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*). However, because there is no introduction of a topic regarding the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) here, it is well said that if [the word "therefore"] were intended for another purpose, its established usage would be contradicted.

[92] Regarding this point, there is a commentary stating that the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) would follow immediately after any other action as well. Having raised this objection, he provides the resolution:
"qualified," etc. This is the intended meaning: although [the inquiry arises] from the specific mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the investigation of the meaning of the Veda...

The one characterized by the wearing of marks (*liṅgin*) who is distinguished by the study of the Vedas is understood from what was mentioned immediately prior; nevertheless, because he was not explicitly mentioned in the aphorism (*sūtra*), this point has been raised. [68]

[93] As for the meaning of what is further raised—the word "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*)—this is the intended sense: Jaimini is not like Manu and others who teach for the sake of unseen results (*adṛṣṭārtha*);
rather, by this [word], immediate succession is taught.

Therefore, that whose immediate sequence has a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārtha) is understood to be "immediate" (ānantarya). The study of the Veda itself has a visible purpose in the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā), which consists of the investigation of the meaning of the Veda, because without it, that [inquiry] would be impossible. Thus, it is implied by that [inquiry]. Consequently, the objection that [the inquiry] was not stated in the aphorism (sūtra) is not tenable. // 69 //
But how is the study of the Veda implied by the fact that its purpose is directly perceived? To this he says: "By which... [70] //

Nor is the instruction intended for the sake of immediate sequence after some particular action, because such a sequence is constantly present due to its unavoidable nature; thus he says: "while being performed" (kriyamāṇa). // 71 //

One might object: "Since destruction is not possible even without volition (*saṃkalpa*), effort (*prayatna*), and so forth, the study of the Veda is implied by its having a perceptible purpose. Anticipating this objection, he says: "By volition and so forth. (95)
[94] He dispels the doubt regarding the desire to know [Brahman].
(KHA) {1,34} Having thus established the immediate succession following the study of the Vedas, he concludes: "Therefore," etc. // 73 //

The *Bhāṣya* states: "Furthermore, even before the study of the Veda. He [the opponent] objects to this with the words: "Of another as well. Since the study of the Veda has been rendered irrelevant by the passage beginning with "For this is not so," then at that very time, the inquiry into Dharma would necessarily occur either before or after the study of the Veda, or immediately following any other action; thus, the repeated mention of "before" (*prāk*) is redundant.

Regarding this, the explanatory passage for the refutation begins with "tādṛśīm" and so forth. He objects to that [refutation] with the words "pūrveṇa" (by the former). Since the acquisition of Vedic study has already been stated by the very phrase "for when that [study] exists, that [knowledge] is possible," what is left unsaid that he would state again by saying this? // 75 //
[96] Here, having raised another objection, he first states the refutation of the initial challenge with two and a half verses beginning with "vakṣyamāṇam" [97].
For it has not yet been established here that Vedic statements are authoritative; and Jaimini will explain those very statements.

This is not understood even thus. Therefore, since the inquiry into the Dharma—such as the veneration of caityas and so forth—is occasioned immediately after the recitation of the words of the Buddha and others, the objection is indeed appropriate. // 77 //
[97] Thus, even by means of the end of the censure,
[98] there is also censure (KHA); [99] it is the word of the Buddha and so forth (KA).
Having thus resolved that the objection applies to one who lacks direct knowledge (*anabhijña*), he offers another resolution with the two [verses] beginning with "Or rather" (*yad vā*).

The meaning is this: even in a sūtra such as "Having studied the Veda, one should then desire to know Dharma," there is indeed room for the same objection; for both [conditions] are intended—namely, that it is neither "without having studied" nor "after doing something else. And since that [objection] is improper because it would result in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) due to the difference in the phrasing of the words, [the other resolution is offered]. // 79 //

He elaborates on this very split of the sentence with the two [verses] beginning with "having studied" (*adhītyaiva*). For there is indeed one sentence: "Having studied the Veda, one should then desire to know dharma" (*adhītyaiva vedam atha dharmajijñāsā*). If that sentence enjoins "only after having studied the Veda," then, because it does not enjoin immediate succession (*ānantarya*), the desire to know dharma would follow even after other acts, such as the ritual bath (*snāna*) or union with a wife who shares the same religious duties (*sahadharmacāriṇī-saṃyoga*). Now, if, out of fear of this [undesired consequence], immediate succession is resorted to, then for one who desires to know dharma after having studied, only immediate succession would be enjoined.

If it were the case that the desire to know dharma for one who has not studied the Veda is not prohibited, then [the objection] would follow even prior [to such study]. However, the intention to express both [meanings] is indeed improper because it entails a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*). But, considering what will be stated later, this is not so; thus, in response to the objection, the phrase "even prior to the study of the Veda" should be construed by reversing its order [with the preceding clause]. Furthermore, [it applies to] "prior to the study of the Veda."

The meaning is this: although the meaning of the Veda is to be investigated, nevertheless it is proper to investigate it first of all. For every object that is to be abandoned or acquired is first of all desired to be known; for by means of that knowledge, one may either abandon it or acquire it. As for that object which is not established without investigation, [one should investigate] it first.

If, on the other hand, one investigates [the matter] by taking this very point as the basis for what has been lost [in the opponent's argument], then that would occur unintentionally. We shall state that "such is the case" is the very answer to this objection as well. // 81 //

[100] [The author of the *Nyāyāvalī* now justifies the *parihārabhāṣya*: "from the words of the Buddha, etc. That, however, refers to the study of the Veda, as will be seen from the upcoming consideration; thus, it was stated that the study of the Veda constitutes the *vṛtti*. This was said without taking that [point] into account, based on a failure to consider what is about to be stated.

The objection that "this is not so" has been answered by the description of the nature of the inquiry (*jijñāsā*)—namely, that this inquiry into Dharma consists of the investigation of the various meanings of the Veda which is about to be undertaken—by the words "of such a kind. Therefore, because it serves as a rebuttal to the objection, there is no redundancy. And this is so when one does not yet take into account what is to be said later.
Having explained the commentary by way of question and answer, he applies the same response even to the objection regarding "contemplation" (*ālocana*), stating:

"Previously. As for the objection raised—that the sentence would be split by the presentation of both [contemplation and study]—that is refuted by the fact that [the passage] is concerned solely with immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), since it is impossible to enjoin the act of study if that were its primary purpose. Furthermore, the objection "even previously" remains; that too is answered by the phrase "of such a kind."

Because the study of the Vedas as a prerequisite is obtained through the very capacity for the desire to know (*jijñāsā*); indeed, this [desire] cannot be undertaken by one who has not acquired the Veda. For this very reason, the claim that it is proper to desire to know Dharma even prior to study is also refuted by this. Such a desire—which serves as the basis for manifold types of inquiry—is impossible to carry out without the study established by that inquiry. However, one who studies after having already performed the inquiry would, due to the inquiry requiring a long duration to complete, cause the period of study to be exceeded.
One would fall into the state of a *vrātya*. Nor is it the case that one who has not studied the Veda is unable to comprehend its meaning;

thus, the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) is preceded by the study of the Veda undertaken without prior critical reflection. As for what was said—that undertaking [the Veda] without reflection is an act devoid of intelligence—who has ever said that the undertaking is "with intelligence"? It is those who desire one's welfare [who say so].

His father and others indeed cause this boy—who has not yet perceived the welfare of the next world—to engage [in these activities]. Furthermore, observing his peers who are engaged day after day without ceasing in the study of their own sacred recitations (*svādhyāya*), he understands in general: "Surely some prosperity will result for them from this action; otherwise, why would they be incited by their fathers and others, who are themselves laboring and desiring their welfare? Having understood this, I too shall practice accordingly.
For one who thinks, "I shall attain the highest good," engagement [in practice] occurs quite naturally of its own accord. // 82 //
[101] This young brahmin also [102] likewise [103] follows this.

Regarding this, there is another point: "Furthermore, we do not here teach a prohibition of the desire to know dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) prior to the study of the Veda"—this is the *Bhāṣya*. He states its meaning with the words "not at all" (*naiva*). Neither of these two meanings proposed by the previous [opponent], expressed through those two turns of phrase, is intended to be stated by this Sūtra; rather, it is the study of the Veda. Immediately following that, both [the desire to know dharma and the knowledge of dharma] naturally follow.

[105] By the force of the Smṛti injunction, "That for the sake of which one should investigate, and having studied which one should perform the ceremonial bath (snāna)," there is a departure from the presence of the teacher's family. To the question, "How indeed could one who has not yet returned home (asamāvṛtta) investigate the meaning of the Veda? this Sūtra was stated with that very purpose, as indicated by the words beginning with "api ca" and so forth.
[104] It is held; [105] it is stretched; [106] by the arrow.
Considering this commentary to be incomplete, some have supplied missing words and provided an explanation;

he introduces that [interpretation] with the words "immediate succession" (*ānantaryam*). For this sūtra, since its purpose is the cessation of residing in the teacher’s house (*gurukula-vāsa*), neither the study (*adhyayana*) nor the immediate succession is intended to be expressed. However, the commentary is observed to concern itself merely with the injunction for study and the prohibition [of other activities], exactly as it was heard.
Therefore, this should be explained by supplying the words "nor do we learn of any subsequent [act]" and interpreting it as a negation of both modes of expression. // 84 //
[107] No; [108] none whatsoever; [109] so many;
that much.
[110] That which is grasped [111] is understood as the negation of mere name [112].

Now, it may be objected that the meaning of a sentence is not a collection of unrelated word-meanings, and in this sūtra no such connection between word-meanings is observed by which the cessation of residing in the teacher’s house could be understood. On the contrary, the injunction of immediate succession to Vedic study is perceived through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). Therefore, that alone is logical; to this he says: "It is not prohibited," [referring to] one who has not yet studied the Veda.
Since one who is incapable of performing all ritual actions lacks the qualification [for Vedic study], the desire to know Dharma is already precluded by fate alone;

what, then, is the purpose of prescribing the rule of study? Furthermore, immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not taught for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), as is the case with Manu and others.

And it has been stated that Jaimini does not teach for the sake of an unseen result. Therefore, by the force of the immediate succession of study—which has a visible purpose—the cessation of residence in the teacher’s house is established.
It is resorted to by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). // 85 //

[113] Veśaḥpa (KHA), having thus presented the position of supplying ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), refutes it with the words "immediate succession" (*ānantarya*). This is the intended meaning: for indication (*lakṣaṇā*) occurs precisely because the literal meaning of what is heard is untenable. And if the expression were one of immediate succession...

What is the seed (the basis) for this secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*)? Therefore, by relying solely on the explicit expression of immediate sequence (*ānantarya*), if one were to accept the literal meaning of the words, it would follow that the purpose is merely perceptible (*dṛṣṭārthatva*); thus, the object made known through secondary indication—the non-performance of the bath—is what is enjoined. In this way, there will be no violation of the natural sense of the commentary as it stands. // 86 //

{1,38} By what connection, then, is the immediate succession (*ānantarya*) taught such that it indicates the absence of ritual bathing? To this he says: "perceived" (*pratīta*). This is the intended meaning: the existence of one contradictory factor is pervaded by the cessation of its opposite. Therefore, when the desire to inquire into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) occurs immediately after the study of the Vedas, [the absence of bathing is indicated].

At that very time, because the period immediately following study is occupied by that [initiation], the ritual bath (*snāna*) which is its obstacle is precluded. For one does not take the bath without having returned from the teacher’s house; nor is one who has already returned permitted to desire to know the Dharma. Just as study is not accomplished without a teacher, so too is the knowledge of Dharma not accomplished without it.

The same applies to the knowledge of the meaning as well. Therefore, when it is stated that "the inquiry into Dharma (dharmajijñāsā) must be undertaken immediately after the study," since there is the possibility that the nature of immediate succession would have a visible purpose, the interpretation characterized by the absence of the ritual bath (snāna) is appropriate.
[Objection: Granted, when one of two contradictory things is occupied by the other, the latter is excluded. But from where does the contradiction arise? Immediately after the study...

Indeed, by the force of the Vedic injunction inferred from the Smṛti rule "one should bathe after having studied," he will perform the ritual bath (*snāna*). Thereafter, he will begin an inquiry into the meaning of the Vedas, which possesses a doubtful purpose; therefore, he says: "the contradiction is simultaneous. This is the intended meaning: for one who has engaged in study by the force of the injunction for study—which has a visible purpose—does not deserve to desist prior to hearing the Mīmāṃsā. For there is only one [duty] for the initiated youth.

The subject matter of the scripture begins with the syllable *praṇava* and concludes with the deliberation on the office of the officiating priest (*ārtvijya*). Therefore, since both [the injunctions] present themselves simultaneously, their contradiction is logical. [Objection: Since two contradictory things cannot coexist, let one be sublated. It is logical that the investigation into the nature of Dharma—which, though established by reasoning, is weaker—is sublated by the force of the Vedic revelation inferred from the Smṛti rule, "Having studied, one should bathe."

Therefore, he says: "Weakness [of the Smṛti] results from its contradiction of the Veda. He thinks as follows: the meaning of the injunction "one's own Vedic study (svādhyāya) is to be performed" is that one should understand the meaning by means of the Vedic study once it has been performed. If, therefore, one were to bathe immediately after the study, one would transgress this sacred tradition (āmnāya). And that is improper, because it would entail the sublation of a directly perceived Vedic revelation (śruti) in favor of a Smṛti.

Furthermore, because it would entail the reversal of the relative strength and weakness between the root and the root-source; therefore, it is logical that the weaker act of bathing should be set aside in accordance with the stronger desire to know Dharma.
[116] vantaṃ vedā (KHA) [117] ptadha.

But what is this Veda which prevents one from bathing after having studied it? Is it not already stated that the scriptural injunction "one's own portion of the Veda should be studied" implies that the purpose of the scripture extends up to the comprehension of its meaning; thus, by performing the bath immediately [after study], that purpose would be frustrated? This would indeed be so if the study were for the sake of understanding the meaning. However, this [study] is merely instrumental to the injunction regarding the office of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), because no specific qualification (*adhikāra*) is heard in the injunction for study itself. And since the performance [of study] is obtained through the impulsion of the injunction regarding the office of a teacher, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, [the objection does not apply].

Because such an assumption is untenable. Therefore, although the injunction [for study] itself lacks a specific qualification (*adhikāra*), it becomes established by conforming to the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), which does possess a qualification. In the injunction for becoming a teacher, however, the qualification belongs only to one who desires the status of a teacher. But how can the injunction for becoming a teacher endeavor to impel the study of the Veda, which is not even a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that injunction? [Just as] the *prayāja* offerings and so forth...

For it is logical that those [rites] studied within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are subordinate members (*aṅga*) of them, and thus they are performed along with them. However, the study of the Veda, being studied as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), cannot be determined by direct statement (*śruti*) or other means to be a subordinate member of anything. This is indeed true. Nevertheless, even though it is not a subordinate member, study is nonetheless beneficial to the mandate (*niyoga*) of the teacher’s office (*ācāryaka*). Therefore...

Therefore, that [study] is employed by means of that [initiation], just as the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is employed by means of the injunctions for the sacrifices. But what is the benefit to the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) through study?

Listen: one becomes a teacher by teaching after having initiated [the pupil]. And teaching is not possible without study; therefore, study has teaching as its ultimate purpose. Furthermore, in the case of the recitation of "what is already existent" (*bhūta*) and "what is to be brought into being" (*bhavya*), that which is already existent (*bhūta*) is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being (*bhavya*). Thus, the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is taught for the sake of the act of teaching.

Thus, [the injunction] has the purpose of accomplishing the study [of the Veda]. Consequently, because the syllables of the *svādhyāya* are directed toward another end, the meaning—though perceived—is not intended to be expressed. And a meaning that is not intended to be expressed does not necessitate investigation (*vicāra*). Therefore, since the obligation of the teacher is fulfilled by the mere study of one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya-adhyayana*), the *Mīmāṃsā* need not be commenced; we do not perceive any contradiction between this and the traditional rule regarding the ceremonial bath (*snāna-smṛti*).

To this it is replied: as for the claim that study is prompted by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), we do not know what this "injunction to become a teacher" is. If you think it is the rule, "One should initiate an eight-year-old Brahmin and teach him," then the "beloved of the gods" (the opponent) is ignorant of injunctions. By this [sentence], it is not enjoined that "one should bring about the status of a teacher"; rather, it is enjoined with respect to the act of teaching.

It is understood that an eight-year-old Brahmin is the qualified person [for study]. But is it not the case that here one does not hear "an eight-year-old Brahmin should study," but rather "one should cause an eight-year-old to study"? True. Yet injunctions (vidhi), even when primarily concerned with the activity of the instigator (prayojaka), are seen to be concerned with the activity of the one being prompted (prayojya); as for example in the Aveṣṭi sacrifice: "One desiring food should cause him to sacrifice with this [offering]," and "One desiring offspring [should cause him to sacrifice] with the Atirātra."

And [the text says], "one should cause him to sacrifice. Now, one might object: since the rule states that the *ātmanepada* ending occurs after the root *nī-* when the sense is "acting as a teacher" (*ācāryakaraṇe*), it must be understood that one should accomplish the status of a teacher (*ācāryatva*) by means of the initiation (*upanayana*). This is not so. Here, the initiation is not understood from the *ātmanepada* ending to have the status of a teacher as its primary purpose; rather, the status of a teacher is a secondary consequence (*ānuṣaṅgika*) of the initiation which is for the sake of the boy (*māṇavaka*), just as the status of being the recipient of the *vaiśvadevī* offering is a secondary result of the act intended for the sake of the *iḍā*.

From the bringing of the curds, there follows the sacrifice of the whey; for the prescription of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) for the root *nī* (to lead) is intended to signify that the result of the action does not accrue to the agent. However, if the initiation (*upanayana*) were for the sake of making someone a teacher (*ācārya*), it would have to intend the result of the action for the agent himself. Therefore, the rule "one who is eight years old" is not an injunction for the act of becoming a teacher. Now, if it is thought: "We shall infer the injunction for becoming a teacher, for it is recorded in tradition (*smṛti*): [text continues]
[118] Having initiated a disciple and taught him the Veda, that twice-born man [is called an Ācārya]. [119] But he who, having brought a disciple near, should teach him the Veda...
They declare that teacher to be one who possesses both the ritual manuals (kalpa) and the secret teachings (rahasya).

Thus [it is argued]: "The Vedic revelation (*śruti*) shall be inferred to mean that one should bring about the status of a teacher (*ācāryaka*) by means of initiation and instruction, which serve as the root of this Smṛti rule. This is not so. For the root is inferred to be similar in nature to the Smṛti statement itself. Just as, upon perceiving a statement regarding the duty to perform the Aṣṭakā and other rites, a Vedic revelation concerning that very duty—namely, "the Aṣṭakā should be performed"—is likewise inferred; yet in the present case, the status of a teacher is not [brought about] by initiation and the like.

"One should perform [it]"—this is the statement of the Smṛti. Nevertheless, since worldly people apply the term "teacher" (*ācārya*) to one who initiates and teaches, [the author] shows that the meaning of the word "teacher" is indeed established by common worldly usage. How, then, can an injunction regarding what ought to be done be inferred from this restatement of an already established fact? Furthermore, "teaching" (*ācāryaka*) is not something non-worldly (*alaukika*), like the *āhavanīya* fire and so forth; for the word *āhavanīya* refers to that which is produced by the *ādhāna* rite, the *pavamāna* oblations, and so on.

It is logical that one who is intent upon a specific, extraordinary excellence is [called] one who possesses an "extraordinary purpose" (*alaukikārtha*). However, the word *ācārya* is used figuratively for one who initiates [a student] and bestows the Veda.
[120] Regarding the Smṛti... (KA)

[121] "One should cultivate [the mind] by bringing [the disciple] near and giving him the Veda; he is thus called an Ācārya," according to the Smṛti. In this way, however, it is merely a matter of visible worldly results, like that between a disciple and a teacher.
The office of a teacher is not something supernatural. Furthermore, the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*) is to impel one toward what has not yet been undertaken.

Since one engages in the office of a teacher spontaneously—whether for the sake of wealth or fame—what is the point of enjoining it? Therefore, this claim that "study is prompted by the injunction to become a teacher" is merely a conventional assertion made by those with empty hearts. And how could this [injunction] apply to one who possesses the auxiliary requirements (*itikartavyatā*) such as vows and observances?

The injunction for Vedic study is the motivator [of the act]. For teaching, being untenable without study, may motivate mere study by way of its worldly form. Therefore, since the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (svādhyāya) is not subservient to anything else, it cannot be subject to a prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) on the grounds that its meaning is unintended.

As for what was said—that initiation (*upanayana*) is a constituent part of the injunction regarding the status of a teacher (*ācāryatva*), and that the Vedic text "having initiated [the pupil], one should effect the status of a teacher through teaching" is inferred—here, because the suffix *-tvā* is heard, it is understood that the initiation has the same agent as the production of the status of a teacher. And there can be no single agent except when there is a unity of performance (*prayoga*). Nor can there be such unity except through the relationship of principal and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*).

In the injunction for the rite of initiation (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), it is established that the subsidiary act of initiation (*upanayana*) occurs together with its subsidiaries. When considering through what means this [initiation] might provide assistance, it is determined—by observing the very nature of initiation—that the bringing near (*sādana*) of the one to be initiated (*upaneyya*) is the means.
Furthermore, the one to be initiated is not a subsidiary if he is to be ineffective.
In view of that activity, the study of the Veda is enjoined following the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). And that [study] is beneficial to the injunction for teaching.

Therefore, it is precisely that [study] which is employed by the injunction for teaching through the medium of initiation. And it has been said: "How is the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*) the motivator? For that [teaching] is mediated by initiation."

To this it is replied: the injunction for study cannot be applied in this manner, because [upanayana] is neither a subordinate part (*aṅga*) nor a benefactor (*upakāraka*) of that injunction. Furthermore, as for the claim that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subordinate part of teaching (*adhyāpana*) because they share a common agent, that is not correct. For we clearly understand from the connection with the accusative case in the rule "one should initiate a Brahmin boy at eight years of age" that initiation is a subordinate part of the twice-born boy who is being initiated.

We understand that the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) exists. And because of its connection to study—expressed in the injunction "one should teach him"—its fitness for being a sacrament (*saṃskāra*) is indeed appropriate. Therefore, initiation is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the injunction of study by means of the student; thus, even though there is the injunction "having initiated him, one should effect the status of a teacher (*ācāryatva*) through teaching," initiation itself is not an auxiliary to that injunction [of becoming a teacher], since in cases where the purpose has already been fulfilled, [the initiation] serves merely to indicate the time.

Because it is established as such. For example, in the injunction "Having sacrificed with the Darśapūrṇamāsa, one should sacrifice with Soma," there is no mutual relationship of primary and subsidiary between those two, since both have their own independent purposes;

so it must be here as well. Granted that initiation (*upanayana*) is a subsidiary of teaching; however, that consists merely in bringing [the pupil] into proximity. Therefore, let only that much be employed by the injunction for the production of the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*).

However, the auxiliary element of study (*adhyayanāṅga*), being endowed with specific mantras and so forth, does not function as a means of valid knowledge when employed by this [person], because it lacks authority. Nor is there an acquisition of a specific qualification through the context of entitlement (*adhikāra*), as in the case of the *phalacamasa* cup. For in that case, the act of drinking mentioned in the section concerning the consumption of *soma* as an auxiliary to the sacrifice pertains specifically to that auxiliary consumption. But here, it is not so.

Because there is no [inherent] qualification (*adhikāra*). Nor can this be like the *juhū* ladle. For that [ladle], not having abandoned its connection to the sacrifice, is recognized as being that very same thing even when merely mentioned at a distance. Initiation (*upanayana*), however, is the act of bringing near and is divided into many types; thus, there is no basis for understanding it as something specific. Or, let it be granted that the specific initiation is a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*).

And let that [injunction] be applied by him; yet, it is not possible for the application of the study [of the Veda] to occur through that [injunction]. For it has been stated that this [injunction] is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to the study. And an auxiliary being drawn along does not draw the primary (*pradhāna*), because primary elements do not function under the control of their auxiliaries. Therefore, in no way can the injunction regarding the production of the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) be the motivator (*prayojaka*) of the study. Furthermore, why would the injunction of study be established through the motivation of the injunction regarding the production of the status of a teacher? Someone might be enjoined to something in a particular place.

Such indeed is the nature of an injunction (*niyoga*). Therefore, if this [teacher] does not himself enjoin [the student], he would forfeit his status as an injunction precisely because of that. If it is argued that he depends on another [injunction] because he lacks the qualification (*adhikāra*) himself, we say no; for the qualification has already been stated. It was stated that "an eight-year-old Brahmin is qualified.
For whoever is the purpose for which a rite is performed, he is the one qualified therein. And since study is the duty of the boy (*māṇavaka*), one should cause him to study.
This is understood from the injunction;

for this [injunction] is not intended merely to enjoin the nature of teaching itself, since one engages in it for the sake of livelihood even without such an injunction. Furthermore, the injunction for study (*adhyayana-vidhi*), which has no explicitly stated qualification (*aśruta-adhikāra*), requires a qualified agent. Indeed, it is not known by whom the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied.

Thus, by the force of the required injunction (*apekṣita-vidhi*), this [text] is indeed an instruction for the person authorized to study, stating "one should cause him to study. Therefore, the meaning is: "An eight-year-old Brāhmaṇa should study. Consequently, it has already been explained that this [injunction] is directed toward the activity of the one being prompted (*prayojya*), by means of the activity of the prompter (*prayojaka*). Now, if it is thought that the boy does not understand that the study is for his own sake and thus does not engage in it—

If this is so, then one would not engage in action even for the sake of the teacher, thinking, "I do not understand it. If you argue that the teacher himself prompts [the student] for his own sake, then the teacher's capacity to prompt is equally applicable to the student's own purpose. For he, desiring the student's welfare, knows that "this action brings about the student's prosperity. Thus, another who desires his welfare will prompt him, since he does not act by himself due to ignorance.

It is like [the injunction regarding] a woman in her own domain, or like the *sthapati-isti* sacrifice in the case of a Niṣāda. Furthermore, even if study were prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), no reason is found for the non-intentionality of the meaning; thus, if one performs mere study because it conforms to oneself, one does not destroy the inherent capacity of words to convey meaning.

Moreover, since the requirement for the office of a teacher (*ācāryakaniyoga*) is fulfilled by the mere act of reciting and studying the text itself, the function of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*) has no other purpose;

therefore, there is no reason whatsoever for the non-intentionality of the meaning. Or, let it be that other injunctions lack intentionality regarding their meaning because they serve as a means for the injunction concerning the office of a teacher.

Nevertheless, it is not possible to present the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) without undertaking Mīmāṃsā; for even the determination of the meaning of the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*) depends for its very existence upon the collection of logical principles found within Mīmāṃsā. If it is argued that this [injunction] also has its meaning unintended (*avivakṣitārtha*), because it is denoted by the term "one's own Vedic study" (*svādhyāya*), we say no. For an imagined injunction that has not been actually studied cannot be denoted by the term "one's own Vedic study. And if that [imagined injunction] were to have its meaning unintended—

If there were a desire to express one meaning, and then a further desire to express another meaning for that very purpose, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And when a stable determination is possible, it is not logical to describe the meaning of the scripture as being unsettled. Therefore, it is better that the injunction for the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*) has an invisible result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), rather than having an unsettled status by virtue of being subordinate to the injunction for becoming a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*). For in this way, the natural orientation of words toward their own meanings is preserved.
It is not a case of denial. Nor does it follow that the entire Veda would lose its authority on account of following a single type [of contradiction];

for he will state later that "when there is a conflict between many and few, the few is improper," and "when there is a concurrence of contradictory properties, the property of the majority shall prevail" (12.2.22).

Thus, since those learned in the principles of logic say, "One should sacrifice an individual for the sake of the family," the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) that this [text] does not intend to convey its literal meaning is not tenable. [122] The injunction regarding the teaching of the *dadhi* [offering], [123] the injunction regarding the teaching of the [Veda].
[124] another (KHA) [125] or for the sake of the teacher (KHA) [126] ... they surpass (adhya) ...

[127] Furthermore, regarding what has been established here: even though the study of the Veda is impelled by the injunction to become a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇavidhi*), its purpose is not merely the completion of that injunction, because that would be extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Rather, it is logical that the very knowledge of the meaning which is observed to arise in the student is its purpose. For whatever action is performed by an agent, it is for the sake of that agent.

Because it is seen to be so. Now, one might object: "The entry into the scope of the injunction that impels action (*prayojaka-vidhi*), which occurs first, is stronger than the knowledge of the meaning, which occurs later. Therefore, we cannot maintain that the purpose of study is for the sake of the student. For what [later factor] could set aside the fact that the purpose of the injunction regarding the appointment of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa-vidhi*), understood first, is subsequently superseded by something else? It is not so; because even prior [to the latter], there is no comprehension of a connection with any other scope (*adhikāra*).

Because it is not heard [in scripture]; and because, since the performance [of study] can be established by being prompted by something else, a postulation [of an independent injunction] is untenable—just as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others. Therefore, study prompted by the injunction for becoming a teacher remains precarious when there is no connection to a specific purpose, because all injunctions culminate in a qualification for action (*adhikāra*). Thus, this person who has studied the Veda along with its auxiliary limbs, [proceeds] in the interim before the study of Mīmāṃsā...

And thus the qualification [for ritual action] is accomplished. For at that time, having understood the meaning of the individual words, one who comprehends the meaning of the sentence realizes, "This action is for my sake. And this is logical: that the knowledge of the meaning required by the sacrifice is connected as its purpose.
In this way, even when prompted by another, since the focus on the meaning is not obstructed, it is indeed appropriate that Mīmāṃsā exists for the purpose of investigating that [meaning].

This is untenable. For there is no purpose for any injunctions other than the fulfillment of the meaning of the mandate (*niyoga*), such that an injunction—even one whose performance is prompted by another—would require a further purpose. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate such a purpose even for obligatory (*nitya*) rites.

It might be argued: "Even in the absence of a requirement from the injunction, the knowledge of the meaning produced from the object itself must not be lost"—thus [they claim] there is the knowledge of the meaning.

"It is not necessarily understood that [the meaning] has arisen from the purpose. This is not so. For even in the case of the oblation (*homa*), since that which arises from the purpose—such as the modification of the sacrificial offering (*havirvikāra*) and so forth—would result in being the objective. If it is argued that the knowledge of the meaning required by the ritual (*kratu*) is not like the modification of the sacrificial offering and so forth, we say: no.

Because if there were no orientation toward the meaning, there would be no performance of the ritual; what then would be required by what? [The requirement is] the bestowal of the fruit upon the agent.

Furthermore, the result of ritual actions is not certain, because there is deviation in the case of the officiating priests' duties. Therefore, we see no evidence for the view that the injunction to study has its own purpose—that is, the purpose of the instigating injunction (prayojaka-vidhi)—and thus does not have the [Vedic] meaning as its primary goal. Moreover, the postulation of a qualification (*adhikāra*) in the middle [of the process] is not a factor for engaging in the action. Even if it were to occur, it would terminate in one's own obligation (*sva-niyoga*) alone. For in this way, the student understands: "The purpose of the injunction is indeed eternal; it is mine to be accomplished. And thus, for the sake of fulfilling that obligation—

And since the purpose [of the Veda] is its recitation (*svādhyāya*), it does not have the meaning as its primary aim. Even though a meaning is perceived, like the previous [case], it is not intended [by the injunction]; thus, it is simply not to be investigated. Therefore, because this position lacks the appeal of being critically examined, the investigation into the injunction for study must be stated exactly according to the *Vārttika*. That is now stated: "The Veda... (*svādhyāyo*)...

Furthermore, an injunction is heard here: "It is to be studied" and "One should study one's own Veda. Moreover, it is the natural characteristic of all injunctions that they have as their object an activity directed toward a result.

Thus, having moved beyond the study of the Veda—which by itself does not constitute a human goal—one desires a fruit that consists of a human goal. Since study itself is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it is cast into the role of a means (*sādhana*). Consequently, this meaning arises: "By means of study, one should accomplish some desired end for the person. And since that [end] has not been specifically mentioned, it follows by the force of the sacred tradition (*āmnāna*), as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others.

Heaven alone is postulated as the fruit desired by all those who study. But surely, since the act of studying is mentioned in grammatical coordination with the word *svādhyāya* (one's own Veda) ending in the accusative case, it is understood that the study itself is the primary object. Consequently, the meaning of the sentence remains: "One should purify one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) by means of study. And yet, the *svādhyāya* is not something incapable of being purified, like the flour-particles (*saktu*).

Because it serves as the means for the knowledge of rituals that yield results, there is no room for postulating another result [for the study of the Veda]. No; because there is no application [of the Veda to that end].

Indeed, no scriptural injunction (*śruti*) is found that applies the Veda as one's own recitation (*svādhyāya*) toward the knowledge of its meaning. Therefore, since there is no authority for its being for that purpose, it does not deserve to be a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, the Veda is an already existing entity (*bhūta*), whereas the act of study is something to be accomplished (*bhavya*).

When an existing thing (bhūta) serves the purpose of a future thing (bhavya), its purpose is seen; otherwise, one would have to assume an unseen purpose (adṛṣṭa), and that is not logical. Therefore, by setting aside the specific application (viniyoga), the meaning of the scripture is properly established as: "One should effect the purification of the Veda through the act of study. Furthermore, since the study of meaningless utterances such as *huṃ* and *phaṭ* occurs, knowledge of meaning is not universally applicable [to all parts of the Veda]. Thus, for those [mantras], the study results in an unseen purpose.

If that were so, it would be like the "half-old woman" fallacy (*tadardhajaratīyam*), because one would be postulating both a seen and an unseen purpose for a single injunction. Therefore, it is more logical that it has only an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) in its singular form.
But surely, as in the case of the *Rātrisatra*, since a fruit is mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it is proper to rely on that; for it is heard:
"Whatever sacrifice he studies, by that very sacrifice his desired goal is attained. Thus, the attainment of the fruit of the sacrifice belongs to the study.

[This refers to] the fruit. Now, it might be argued that this fruit does not belong to the first study from the teacher, but rather is for the purpose of memorization and so forth. That is not correct; because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended for memorization and so forth is connected to the first study by way of extension (*atideśa*). Therefore, according to the principle of the *rātrisatra*, it is appropriate to assign the fruit residing in the explanatory passage itself through a transformation (*vipariṇāma*).

This might be so if the *arthavādas* were extended by their own inherent form; but this is not the case, because the extension of the scriptural injunction (*śāstra-atideśa*) has been refuted. Here, it is merely the incitement (*prarocanā*) produced by the *arthavāda* that is required by the injunction to study (*adhyayana-vidhi*) for the sake of establishing a connection; therefore, it is impossible to assume a modification of the words regarding the various substrates and results. Consequently, this interpretation is also untenable.

It is logical that, as in the case of the Viśvajit sacrifice and others, it is appropriate to assume that its fruit is indeed heaven (*svarga*). Therefore, having studied for the sake of heaven under a teacher, one should bathe immediately thereafter by virtue of the Smṛti rule regarding the ceremonial bath (*snāna*); whether one subsequently investigates the doubtful and purposeful meaning of the Veda or not, in any case, the purpose of the injunction for study is fulfilled.
Since it is "accomplished," we do not perceive any contradiction with the Veda in any way. As it is said in the world: [text fragment].
[130] As it has been stated regarding those [KA];
[131] the state of having three meanings (KHA); [132] by way of uniformity (KHA).
For the study of this [text] indeed consists merely in the recitation of its meaning.

[136] Regarding this, it is said: from the injunctions "one's own Veda should be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*) and "one should study one's own Veda" (*svādhyāyam adhīyīta*), it is clearly understood that the Veda (*svādhyāya*) is the object (*karman*) of the act of studying. Furthermore, a displacement of the application (*viniyogabhaṅga*)—as in the case of the groats—is not appropriate; for the groats are devoid of both past and future utility.
They do not merit [the status of] *saṃskāra*, nor is there such recitation (*svādhyāya*),
because it is useful for future application. For here, immediately after the study, there is the grasping of syllables,
and from that, the determination of words.
From that, there is the recollection of the meanings of the individual words; from that, the cognition of the meaning of the sentence; and from that, the performance [of the action].

Therefore, since "prosperity" (*abhyudaya*) is attained through a succession that results in the acquisition of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), there is no room for the postulation of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) based on a mere reversal [of the order of words]. For as long as a visible result, however remote, can be perceived, one must follow that alone. Thus, in these Vedic passages (*brāhmaṇavākya*), the fruit of the principal sentences is the communication of rituals that possess a fruit.

The subsidiary sentences (*aṅgavākya*) provide the manifestation of the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), which consists of both visible and invisible purposes, by way of being directly contributive (*sannipatyopakāraka*).

The explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) establish the excellence of the subject matter required by the injunctions. The names such as *udbhid* and others enjoin qualities and results. And the Upaniṣads [function] by way of establishing a conscious agent (*kartṛ*) who is fit for the enjoyment of results pertaining to the afterlife.
It should be understood that this constitutes the demonstration of the authority of the entire Veda. Furthermore, some mantras serve to illuminate the ritual acts being performed;

however, for those whose visible purpose is not apparent, one must postulate an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) pertaining either to the sacrifice or to the person. Yet, it is not proper to abandon a visible purpose observed elsewhere simply because of that [postulated] unseen purpose. This applies to both the mantras and the Brāhmaṇas taught by the injunction for the study of one's own Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya-adhyayana-vidhi*).

When it comes to the occasion of postulating a purpose (*prayojana*), it is only logical to postulate a purpose according to the capacity [of the means]. In that regard, since no visible purpose for *hum* and so forth is possible, they serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*) in contexts such as silent recitation (*japa*) and the Brahma-sacrifice (*brahmayajña*). Furthermore, it is observed that those elements which fall within the scope of a single performance injunction (*ekaprayogavidhi*)—such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and threshing (*avaghāta*)—possess both visible and invisible purposes. Therefore, one must not necessarily maintain a uniformity of nature (*aikarūpya*) in all cases. Thus, this...

The summary of the meaning of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): Since the study of the Veda has its fruit in the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) pertaining to the next world, the purpose of the injunction for study does not extend to the comprehension of the meaning; therefore, it is not necessary that the meaning of the Veda be investigated immediately thereafter.
