Consequently, there is no contradiction between the Smṛti rule regarding ritual bathing (*snāna*) and the injunction for study. And since that which is not contradicted does not deserve to be set aside even if it is weaker—this is the prima facie view. The final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows:

But— since it is understood that the Veda (svādhyāya) is to be refined by the act of study, when the expectation arises as to what one should do with the Veda once studied, the Veda is applied to the knowledge of its meaning by virtue of suitability;
and since that [knowledge] pertains to this world, [the injunction to study must have a worldly purpose].

Furthermore, because [the result] is seen immediately thereafter, it is not logical to postulate a result such as heaven—which is unseen, occurs in the hereafter, and is separated [from the action]. Thus, when the Veda, having become an instrument (karaṇa) by the rule "one should understand the meaning through the studied svādhyāya," requires an auxiliary (anugrāhaka), Mīmāṃsā—falling within the category of the procedure (itikartavyatā) due to its suitability—occurs immediately after the study [of the Veda]. Consequently, it contradicts the bath (*snāna*) which occurs at its own specific time; therefore, since the Śruti is more authoritative, the sublation of the Smṛti regarding the bath is rightly established. Thus, the [objection] concerning the bath is well-stated.
Therefore, there would be sublation. // 88 //
[137] The determination of the meaning [is achieved] through the teaching of the meaning;
[138] there is no room for the postulation of the unseen [if one relies on the teaching]. [139] KA.
[140] But [141] if [142] for him indeed there is no...
[143] For those who have no other [refuge], [144] only the vision of the various kinds [of Buddhas] (KHA) is to be relied upon (KA).

[146] Because it is not an object [of the injunction], [147] (KHA) [and because] here the Bhāṣya states that the purpose of study is seen [in this world], the immediate sequence [of study] would be contradicted. (KA)

"But this meaning may be [obtained] through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However, because the demonstration that the study [of the Veda] has a visible purpose would be redundant, and because the meaning [of the phrase] "but this meaning may be [obtained] through figurative indication" was not understood, it was abandoned by certain commentators. He states that [objection] first with the words "it has a visible purpose" up to "by some. But he himself [retains it], because it exists in ancient manuscripts.

He provides the resolution: "That is said. This is the intended meaning: previously, by the commentary beginning with "And not for one who has studied the Veda," it was shown that the suffix *ktvā* expresses mere priority in time (*pūrvakālatāmātra*), not immediate succession (*ānantarya*). Nor does this contradict the fact that such study has a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*); thus, non-contradiction with the Smṛti was demonstrated. Now, however, even if the word *ktvā* denotes immediate succession, [the following applies].

Nevertheless, since it would be contrary to the Vedas to accept the entire meaning of the Smṛti [literally], it is better to take it as a definition (*lakṣaṇā*). When "immediacy" (*ānantarya*) is stated as a specific temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), only the mere fact that study occurs prior to that [initiation] is indicated by the definition. For in this way, there is no contradiction with study that serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). // 90 //

He states another way in which [the word] is not in contradiction with *smṛti*: "By the word *grantha*," etc. Regarding the form of the root *iṅ*, there is a contradiction because of the rule *neṇaḥ*.

And this statement is made as a concession (*anvāruhyavacana*), so it is not to be taken too seriously. For the word *adhi* is an inseparable associate (*nityasahacarita*) of the root *iṅ* and constitutes a part of it;
indeed, its usage alone has never been observed before. Therefore, the established meaning of the whole belongs to the root *iṅ*; [not to the root] *iṇ*.

Furthermore, there is the well-known meaning of the individual parts [of the word *adhyetavya*], and that is weaker than the established meaning of the whole. Moreover, since the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyādhyayana*) is heard in the form "having studied" (*adhītya*), it is understood as referring specifically to that [Veda]; therefore, it is also not reasonable to assume that the purpose is the acquisition of knowledge. // 91 //
[148] Regarding the word *artha* (KA), the commentary states: "And this bathing is not enjoined for an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). He explains that as follows: "But he who...
For indeed, when there is no such contradiction between Śruti and Smṛti, there is merely the act of immersion for one who has not returned from the teacher's house.

The injunction "having studied, one should bathe" prescribes bathing as a primary act for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), similar to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth. Alternatively, it is thought that bathing—which consists of a refinement of the person (*puruṣasaṃskāra*)—is prescribed as an auxiliary to the primary act of study, accompanied by mantras and other elements, for the sake of an unseen result, like the act of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*).
To this, the following response will be stated. // 92 //

To this, he now states the answer with two verses beginning with "here" (iha). For in the case of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), a rule has been stated that he shall not bathe; thus, there is a restriction such as non-bathing and so forth. However, no specific limit of time was established therein. Consequently, there arises an expectation for a conclusion, namely: "for how long [is this to be observed]? If this is so, what follows? To this he says: "therefore" (*tataḥ*). When a rule is expected, its purpose is seen to be practical utility.

Otherwise, the injunction for bathing would have an invisible (transcendental) purpose; and that is not appropriate when a visible purpose is possible. Therefore, by the force of this requirement, the phrase "having studied, one should bathe" indicates bathing as the very cessation of the restriction against bathing and so forth. For that [indicated] bathing is the opposite of non-bathing, and the existence of an opposite is pervaded by the cessation of its contrary. Thus, by means of bathing, there is the indication of the cessation of the restriction against bathing.

This is indeed logical. Since [the duties] such as residing in the teacher’s house (*gurukula-vāsa*) are concomitant with that [state of non-bathing], their cessation is also indicated by the cessation of that [non-bathing]. Now, it is certainly reasonable that the cessation of non-bathing is indicated by bathing, because two contradictory things cannot coexist. But what is the reason for the cessation of the duties such as residing in the teacher’s house? And since residing in the teacher’s house and so forth are concomitant with the rules of non-bathing and the like, they are brought to an end by the cessation of those [rules].

What has been stated is incorrect; for that [instruction] is appropriate only in the case of an object within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Just as in the world, when at the time of a meal one receives the instruction to "wipe the bare ground," there arises an implied instruction to wipe all the implements of the meal associated with that ground, such as conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and so forth.

However, since *śruti* and *smṛti* have as their scope only that which is explicitly mentioned, it would be improper to include [the rules regarding] "those who associate with [others]" and so forth. It is said in reply:
this would indeed be so if the *smṛti* rule, "Having studied, one should bathe," were based on *śruti*.
But this [rule] is based on *nyāya* (logical reasoning). And this *nyāya* is the same for the cessation of all duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*). Which [is it]?

Furthermore, listen to this: for the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), such as dwelling in the teacher’s house and so forth, are auxiliary to the study of the Veda; they are brought to an end upon the completion of that study, according to the principle that "the vow [ends] upon the completion of the sacrifice. Therefore, it is logical that there is a conclusion of all the duties of a religious student—such as tending the sacred fires and fueling them—which is characterized by the cessation of the restriction against bathing. This point, however, should be understood as having been stated in the Bhāṣya with the words, "But this [is said] by means of figurative indication" (*lakṣaṇayā*), and so on. // 94 //

[149] Thus, he now concludes the meaning of the section with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the sense: that which was explained as the word *adhyayana* having the meaning of "comprehension," and that which was stated regarding the word *snāyāt* having the meaning characterized by the cessation of the restrictive rules such as the prohibition against bathing; [all this is established].

Likewise, regarding what was stated—that the word *atha* in the phrase "Now, therefore, the desire to know Dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*) signifies the absence of the ritual bath (*snāna*) prescribed by the Smṛtis, which would otherwise follow immediately after Vedic study—and that in all such cases the reason is its having a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatva)—[this is now addressed]. // 95 //

[150] Thus, [151] he here raises an objection—up to the words "having bathed"—as follows: "For it has been stated that weakness [of Smṛti] arises from its contradiction of the Veda. And in this way, there would be a contradiction of the Veda if the meaning of the Veda [were as the Smṛti claims].

It would have to be disregarded in every respect. However, if—following the injunction of the *smṛti*—one bathes immediately after Vedic study and, perceiving the doubtful yet purposeful meaning of the Vedas, desires to investigate it, then no contradiction with the Veda is observed; thus, there is no conflict regarding the bath. To one who argues in this way, he states the reply, ending with "evam" up to "snānabādhanam. This is the meaning: even if [the bath were performed] immediately following [study] in accordance with the *smṛti*,...

If bathing were intended to be merely that much, then here [in this context], various kinds of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites are also prescribed to be performed subsequent to the bath. If those too are to be followed, then there would be a total contradiction with the Veda; moreover, one who has not investigated the meaning of the Veda is not capable of performing even those rites correctly.

Furthermore, one who is ignorant has no entitlement [to perform rites]. For it will be stated later: "And one who is ignorant is not enjoined. Therefore, even if one must follow the Smṛti for some distance, its sublation must eventually be asserted. It is better, therefore, that the bathing which first presents itself as contradictory—on the grounds of having studied the Veda—is sublated. Thus, as long as one is unfit for the performance of obligatory and occasional duties due to not having studied the Veda, [the prohibition of bathing remains in force].

As long as one does not perform those [obligatory acts], one does not incur transgression. One would incur transgression by failing to perform them only if one were qualified through having studied the Vedas;

however, an ignorant person is unable to perform them, and one cannot know [the rites] without inquiry. Therefore, it is appropriate that the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*) follows immediately after Vedic study.
This has been stated on the grounds of subsequent possibility; in the ultimate sense, however, it is for the sake of fulfilling the requirement of the injunction to study.

The fact that one who has begun [the study] ought not to desist before hearing the Mīmāṃsā is a matter brought about solely by the force of the injunction for Vedic study (*adhyayana-vidhi*). For a primary act does not reach completion if it is performed without its auxiliary parts (*aṅga*). As he will state later: "The primary act together with its auxiliaries [is enjoined] because of the unity of the verbal expression. (Sūtra 1.1.25) // 98 //
[152] But for one who speaks [153] (KHA) [154], it approaches (KA).
[155] Indeed, the action [156] (KHA); having thus established the sublation of memory, he cites the very locus here— “so this”— with the particle *iti* used in the sense of *iva*.

The meaning is that, just as in the case of the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), the order of scriptural mention (*śrutikrama*) is understood to be set aside by the requirements of the purpose (*artha*). For it has been stated in the section concerning the subversion of order (*kramakopa-adhikaraṇa*)—namely, "Subversion of order occurs through purpose and word" (JS 5.4.1)—that here, having cited the examples "He offers the Agnihotra" and "He cooks the gruel," it will be deliberated: should one cook after having offered, or...?

"Or rather, it should be offered after being cooked. Regarding this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position—based on the authority of the textual sequence (pāṭhaprāmāṇya)—is that "one should cook after having offered. To this it is replied: there is a sublation (bādha) of the textual sequence by the sequence of meaning (arthakrama). For here, the textual sequence must be overridden by the force of the purpose.

Indeed, if one were to perform the rite according to the textual sequence, the purpose would not be accomplished; for cooking is for the sake of the oblation (homa), and it [the cooking] is performed subsequent to the oblation.

It would be purposeless. Furthermore, a *homa* sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the *āhavanīya* fire. Therefore, cooking must come first, and then the *homa*. Similarly here as well, although the sequence of bathing is understood through the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) of the suffix *-ktvā*, which denotes immediate succession to study, it must nevertheless be set aside by the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of making study serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). If that [sequence] were accepted, the very purpose of the injunction for study would be subverted. Even the sequence of the Vedic text (*śrutikrama*) is set aside in accordance with the requirements of the purpose (*arthānusāreṇa*).
The author of the *Ṭīkā* has stated in the section concerning the sublation of sequence (*kramabādha*) that "this is because everything is for the sake of the purpose" (*arthārthatvāt sarvasya*).

He cites another such section right here: "between the subordinate and the principal" (*guṇapradhānayoḥ*). He will state [later]: "And in the case of a conflict between the quality of a subsidiary (*aṅga*) and [the time of] the principal, [the former prevails] because it is for its sake" (*aṅgaguṇavirodhe ca tādarthyāt*, 12.2.25).
And in this context, it will be explained that the time of the *Dīkṣaṇīyā*—which is a subsidiary—is set aside in accordance with the time of the *Sutyā*, which is the principal.

Because the subsidiaries exist for the sake of the principal; for when there is a conflict with the principal, [the subsidiary] would be purposeless. Likewise here, the Smṛti prescribes the sequence between study and the ceremonial bath (snāna) by stating, "Having studied the sequence, one should bathe. And it is undisputed among all proponents that sequence is a subsidiary of those things that possess a sequence. Therefore, if this sequence were to be observed...
Consequently, study itself—which is the primary factor and has a perceptible purpose—would be subverted; and it is not proper to subvert the principal for the sake of the subordinate. // 99 //
[157] Not for the sake of wealth; [158] nor from grain; [159] nor from food.
[160] At the improper time, [161] by not being obstructed, one is afflicted; [162] he perishes. (KA)

Thus, it is established without dispute that, for the time being, there is an absolute sublation of memory. Now, since the relationship between the sublated and the sublator follows from contradiction—

Only that which is actually contradicted should be set aside. Since merely leaving the residence of the teacher’s family is an obstacle to the inquiry into Dharma, whereas the consumption of honey, meat, and so forth is not, those [latter practices] should not be set aside; thus he says: "Bathing," etc. (verse 100).
[165] But because of the non-delusive nature of the knowledge of phenomena, [166] it is not [the case that it arises] from speech; [167] therefore, it is not so.
Therefore, this is not a sublation of a portion of the Smṛti, but rather a sublation of the Smṛti in its entirety; thus he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 101 //

[169] Thus, indeed, having abandoned the duties of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*) such as [tending] fire and fuel, one becomes a graduate (*snātaka*; literally, "one who has bathed"). Since it is established by rule that "a graduate is always pure, fragrant, and habituated to bathing," the consumption of honey and other such things—though permitted by injunction—is not in contradiction with the inquiry into Dharma.

"That bathing should also be performed"—for this reason he says, "in the teacher's house. For the term *snātaka* is applied upon the cessation of all the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), not merely upon the cessation of a few duties such as tending the sacred fire. Therefore, as long as the departure from the teacher's house—which is one part of the entire complex of practices including the consumption of honey and so forth—is not completed, [the status of a snātaka does not arise].

To that extent, one is not yet a *snātaka*; thus, the cessation of the restrictive rules such as the prohibition against bathing does not result [in the status of a *snātaka*]. The meaning is that he does not attain the state of *snāna*. The word *snātaka* denotes the cessation of all the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). // 102 //

Thus he said. Having explained [the passage] beginning with "from *hā*" (*hād vini*), he states that very point in accordance with the formal application (*prayoga*): "from the teacher’s house" (*gurugehāt*). For as long as one does not turn back from, or depart from, the teacher’s house...

Until that point, he is not called a *snātaka*. Therefore, he does not obtain the duties (*dharma*) of a *snātaka*. If this is so, then let him not bathe; however, why would he not take a wife? Even one who has taken a wife, while residing with his teacher, still desires to know the *dharma*; therefore, he says "that" (*tat*). This refers to the bath performed by one who has departed from the teacher’s house and is endowed with the *mantras* and other requirements, because of that bathing there.
"The taking of another's wife is forbidden; a *snātaka* should take a wife of equal status. How, then, could this apply to one who has not yet performed the ceremonial bath (*asnātaka*)? // 103 //

[172] Or rather, because of this, the Bhāṣya here states: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe; let him not return from the teacher's house. That [statement] seems to have an inconsistent meaning.

It is observed [in the text]: "Having studied the Veda, one should bathe; let him not return from the teacher’s house. He separates that [passage] and joins it [to the previous], saying "having explained. For previously, after explaining the Smṛti statement with the commentary beginning "And this bathing is not for the sake of an unseen result," he has now restated that very same thing, meaning that "this is the meaning of this Smṛti. // 104 //

Surely, by the statement "let him not return from the teacher's house immediately," it is understood that there is a single textual unit [between the two rules]. What, then, is the reason for abandoning that [immediate sequence]? To this he says: "let him return. For immediate sequence alone is not the cause for a connection; rather, compatibility is also required. And in this case, because of the contradiction, there is no connection despite the immediate sequence. // 105 //

[174] Since this has been removed, how is it to be explained? To this he says: "By the word *atha*. For previously, the word *atha* was explained as having the purpose of removing the restriction regarding the end of residence in the teacher’s house (*gurukula*), by means of the commentary beginning with: "He did not return from the teacher’s house; how could he investigate the Vedic sentences? And there, no reason was given.

"Stated" means it was mentioned as it occurred to the mind in the context of the consequence that [the word *atha*] would have a purpose already seen in the Smṛti. For if the word *atha* were intended to signify immediate succession (*ānantarya*), it would be of unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, to avoid that, it is explained in another way as: "Let him not return from the teacher's house. Alternatively, only the cessation of residence in the teacher's house is set aside, not the entire meaning of the Smṛti.
Regarding this, he states the reason as follows: "of that alone" (tanmātrasya). // 106 //

[175] He explains this very point with the words "attained through Smṛti. Now, if the author of the Sūtras were to prohibit the consumption of honey and other such things— which is already established by Smṛti in the injunction "one should bathe after having studied the Veda"— while they are engaged in the inquiry into Dharma, he would be teaching something that has no visible purpose.
Because there is no contradiction; and that [contradiction] is not tenable. // 107 //

But as for one who, asserting there is no contradiction with the *Smṛti*, says this—"By the force of the *Smṛti*, having bathed immediately thereafter and entered the teacher's house, the Dharma will be investigated; thus there would be no contradiction"—to him he replies with the word "nivṛtya" (having turned back). For re-entering after having already gone out would serve an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Previously, this very objection was raised and refuted in a different manner [in the *Bhāṣya*]. Now, however, it is refuted according to the *Bhāṣya* by way of its serving an invisible purpose.
It is refuted; thus, there is no tautology. // 108 //
[176] [Objection: But how could entry have an unseen purpose? For its investigation has only a seen purpose. To this he says: "exit. The exit belongs to one who has already accomplished his purpose.

Departure would have a visible purpose; otherwise, it would have an invisible purpose. Therefore, by one who asserts that non-entry after having departed has an invisible purpose, it is effectively stated that cessation (nivṛtti) has an invisible purpose. // 109 //
Therefore, he now examines the word "ataḥ" (hence): [he says] "atha" (now).

At the very moment that the word "atha" has taught a sequence whose purpose is perceived (*dṛṣṭārtha*), since a sequence following mere action would have an unperceived purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), it was already stated [in verse 177] that the study of the Veda is the cause for determining the meaning of the Veda; so what is the use of the word "ataḥ"?
What does he mean by saying "it becomes fit"?
He means "fitness" (*yogyatva*). Because of the instruction regarding immediate succession, it is understood that one becomes fit for the knowledge of *dharma* through the study of the Veda;
however, the desire to know *dharma* (*dharmajijñāsā*) is not caused solely by that [study]. // 111 //

[178] One might object that by the word *atha* (now/therefore), it would have been stated merely that "such a person as this is fit for the knowledge of Dharma," and not that there is a specific cause;

therefore, he says: "the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Nor can it be said that study is established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) simply because no other cause exists; thus he says: "of the desire to know (*jijñāsā*). [112]

[179] It is not the case that he is unfit because of his desire for the fruit of the Dharma; rather, it is possible that [the desire for fame, etc. serves as a cause for the inquiry into the Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*). And since the inquiry into the Dharma has that as its cause, the objection that there would be no qualification for Śūdras is avoided by stating another solution: "The word *ataḥ*. Now, the word *atha*...
It has been stated that when [the author] teaches "immediacy" (*ānantarya*), he teaches the immediacy following the study of the Veda;
this is due to the force of the reason established by the word *ataḥ* which will be mentioned later. Otherwise, one might suspect that this word *atha* expresses some other meaning. // 113 //

Otherwise, he states the redundancy with the words "of the sublation of the bath" (*snānabādhasya*). Although it has been established by the word *atha* that the study of the Veda is the cause for the desire to know Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), nevertheless, because it expresses a different reason, the word *ataḥ* is not redundant. The word *ataḥ* declares the causality of the sublation of the bath. He reveals the reason for the sublation of the bath with the words "of one who is qualified" (*yogyasya*).
For one who has studied the Veda...

54} If one who has become fit for the performance of obligatory and occasional rites (*nitya-naimittika-anuṣṭhāna*) should fail to perform them due to ignorance, he would incur sin. Therefore, since it is not permissible to remain [in that state] once the Veda has been studied, one must strive immediately for the attainment of knowledge. // 114 //
[180] He gives (KHA);
[181] there is movement (KA);
[182] if this one is... (AVI).

Regarding this, the Bhāṣya states: "One should desire to know Dharma. There, having raised the objection that there is tautology because the suffixes *san*, *liṅ*, and *tumun* all express the sense of "desire," he resolves it by means of the difference in their objects—stating: "That which is expressed by *san*... First, the desire expressed by *san* pervades as its object precisely the internal cognition conveyed by the same word; that is to say, it has that [cognition] as its object. And by that much alone, that very [desire] is understood.

The meaning of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth is not "injunction" (*vidhi*) and the like. Although the root *iṣ* denotes desire (*icchā*), it is nonetheless not redundant because it expresses a different kind of desire. For instance, the object (*karman*) of the desire expressed by the desiderative suffix (*san*) is either an external property conveyed by another word, or it is the desire for knowledge.
Or rather, there are two desires for the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*). The distinction of actions is set forth for the purpose of clarifying the distinction between the desires.
Since the suffixes *liṅ* and *tumun* express both injunction (*vidhi*) and the identity of the agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), the difference in their scope is clear; thus, there is no tautology.
But what, then, is the purpose of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) in introducing a second desire here that was not mentioned in the sūtra?
One should rather say, "one should desire to know Dharma"; therefore, he says, "desire as formulated in the Sūtra. He thinks as follows:

just as a young student, being unfit for a command, is exhorted by the author of the Sūtra to engage in the knowledge of Dharma by means of the expression "one should desire to know Dharma" (dharmajijñāsā).

Thus, the commentator, following that very line of reasoning, stated a second desire which was not explicitly formulated in the Sūtra, asking how the desire formulated in the Sūtra could be brought about. Therefore, by the instruction regarding desire, the necessity of performing the action is also taught, because desire is preceded by that [intention to act]. Nor is desire not accepted, just like hunger. For instance, one person who is hungry eats; another, however, due to a weak digestive fire, is not hungry and yet desires even that [hunger] itself. (vv. 115–117)
[183] "Beginning with" [184] means also because of the distinction of objects [185] (KHA).
In that pond,
dharma arises from knowledge; it is the wandering of desire.

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya, while analyzing the compound *dharmajijñāsā*, stated: "The desire for dharma is *dharmajijñāsā*; for that is the wish to know it. He [the opponent] objects to this with the words "by the base form" (*prakṛtyā*). For where a compound with a dative case (denoting purpose) occurs, it is observed that the modified form (*vikṛti*) is compounded with the base form (*prakṛti*), as in "wood for a sacrificial post" (*yūpadāru*). However, there is no such compounding between things that are neither base nor modified, such as "a pot for cooking" (*randhanāya sthālī*).

"The mortar is for the purpose of threshing. Likewise, the author of the Vārttika stated that "the mention of both the original material (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*) must be made" in the case of a compound formed for the sake of one thing (*tādarthya*). This was not intended merely to demonstrate semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). Therefore, even in cases where there is no relationship of original material and modification, a compound certainly occurs wherever semantic capacity exists. Consequently, this is also the case in the expression *dharmajijñāsā* (enquiry into dharma), because of the presence of semantic capacity.

It must be stated that the *tādarthya* compound is justified because [the purpose] exists; for capability (*sāmarthya*) is impossible without a relationship of material cause and effect (*prakṛti-vikāra-bhāva*). Indeed, capability is the power to express the meaning of the analytical sentence (*vigraha-vākya*). And just as in the expression "a pot for cooking" (*randhanāya sthālī*), the heard dative case [indicates] even a pot that is not itself the material cause of cooking, being rather an external instrumental factor—

It illuminates that sense of being for the sake of something (*tādarthya*) in the compound *randhanasthālī* (“cooking-pot”) because that sense of being for the sake of something is weak. However, since the material cause itself—such as wood—undergoes transformation into the effect, such as a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), the sense of being for the sake of something is manifest;
thus, it is stated by analyzing [the compound] as *dāru yūpāya* (“wood for the sacrificial post”), which is even more easily understood than the compound *yūpadāru*. Therefore...

Thus, in the rule for forming compounds, the inclusion of the term "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) has been explained as pertaining to the relationship between the material cause and its modification (*prakṛti-vikṛti*), precisely because the sense of being "for the sake of that" is most evident in that context. And it has been said: "In the case of *padārtha* and so forth... [189].

[190] Or, in a compound denoting purpose (*tādarthya-samāsa*), [the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied] after [a word ending in] *prati*, provided that there is [the sense of] "for the sake of" (*vṛttatāyām*). [191–192] (KHA)
[193] For one engaged in cooking,
[194] because the external cause is clearly manifest, its purposefulness is not of that same nature.
[195] And just as a modification is clearly observed in relation to its primal nature (prakṛti), so it is here.

Thus, a compound based on the sense of "for the sake of that" (*tādarthya*) is not observed between a material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikṛti*), because in cases such as *aśvaghāsa* ("grass for horses"), a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) is resorted to.

However, in the case of the term *vaiyākaraṇa*, even though a compound exists, the case-ending is heard because the rule for non-elision (*aluk*) applies; therefore, it is indeed correct that the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) have the same meaning, even in the absence of a relationship of material cause and modification. This is the case with the compound *dharmajijñāsā*.
But this very point is the subject of dispute; therefore, this is not a compound. // 118 //

Having thus raised an objection, he provides the resolution: "For that" (*sā hi*). This is not a genitive compound (*caturthī-samāsa*); rather, like *aśvaghāsa* and other such examples, this is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). For it is analyzed as "she would wish to know that" (*tasya jñātum icchet*), using a word ending in the genitive case. [Objection: But how is the statement regarding the analysis, "the desire to know for the sake of Dharma" (*dharmāya jijñāsā*), to be explained? To this he says: "for the sake of Dharma" (*dharmāya*).
This is not a statement regarding grammatical case-formation (vigraha), but rather a demonstration of a specific meaning of the genitive case. // 119 //

Now, an objection is raised: "The dative case would follow. For if one intends to express the sense of *tādarthya* (being for the sake of that), the dative alone would indeed be required. However, [the author] refutes this by stating "merely a relation" (*sambandhamātra*) in response to the question of how the expression of *tādarthya* can occur when there is an intention to express a general relation. Indeed, the author of the Sūtras employed a genitive compound, *dharmajijñāsā*, with the intention of expressing a general relation. But since a general [relation] cannot exist without particulars, when there is a requirement for a specific [relation], it was the Commentator himself who—
The subsistence of that universal in a particular characterized by being for its sake (tādarthya) is described;
therefore, this too is not a fault. // 121 //

In this context, there is another commentary intended to demonstrate the nature of the inquiry into Dharma (*dharmajijñāsā*), namely: "What are its means of proof (*sādhana*)? What are the fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*)? Therein, he explains the term *sādhanābhāsa*: "The fallacious means of proof. [The question arises: How, then, is the meaning of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) a fallacious means of proof?

Therefore, he says: "the means of proof for another. For when that which is the means of proof for one thing appears as if it were the means of proof for another, it becomes a fallacious means of proof (*sādhanābhāsa*). // 122 //

This very point is clarified by the phrase "for the sake of the ritual" (*kratvartham*). For when things such as being made of *parṇa*-wood are stated to be for the sake of the ritual, they become mere semblances of a means toward human goals such as hearing auspicious verses; and when things such as the *godohana* vessel are stated to be for the sake of the ritual, they likewise become semblances of that [ritual]. Here, the Commentator asks: what is *dharma*?

Having stated that [the question] "What are its characteristics? has been explained by the *codanāsūtra*, he then states that [the questions] "What are its means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? and so forth have been explained by the *śeṣalakṣaṇa*. This appears somewhat inconsistent, for the term *śeṣalakṣaṇa* is well-known as referring to the third chapter (*adhyāya*). Furthermore, not everything—such as the means of accomplishment—is explained therein.

Anticipating the question "How so?", he says: "the definition of the subordinate" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*). This term "definition of the subordinate" is not employed with the intention of referring specifically to the third chapter;
rather, it is intended to encompass the remainder of the entire treatise. For this very reason, the singular number is used. // 123 //

In this regard, the Commentator, while raising an objection to the commencement of the treatise, stated: "Dharma must be either well-known or unknown. If it is well-known, it is not an object of inquiry; if it is unknown, it is all the more so. To this, [the opponent objects]:
"Since the negative particle (*nañ*) denotes non-existence, what kind of comparative suffix (*ātiśāyanika-pratyaya*) is this? For there can be no comparison of a negation."

Anticipating the objection that there might be some intrinsic distinction [in non-existence], he says: "It is well-known. This is true; there is no intrinsic distinction in non-existence. Nevertheless, because negation is dependent upon the object to be negated, it excels [others] through the excellence of that object. Thus, in this case, there is the absence of mere knowledge and desire regarding what is well-known, but not the absence of knowledge itself. However, in the case of what is not well-known, since both [knowledge and desire] are negated, an excellence is appropriate. The meaning is that, due to impossibility, it is neither desired nor known. // 124 //

Regarding this, the explanatory commentary (*parihārabhāṣya*) states: "Many learned persons hold conflicting views concerning *dharma*; for it is that which unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

He explains this [by saying]: "It is to be desired to be known" (*jijñāsya*). For wise people strive toward the definitive determination of that which is both doubtful and purposeful; and such is *dharma*. Therefore, this too is to be desired to be known.
Furthermore, what kind of doubt regarding the *dharma* is there, and what is its cause?

To this he says: "Regarding its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth. First, among the essential nature and other attributes of the *dharma*, people disagree in two ways: by means of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by means of the essential nature itself. The suffix [in the word *vipratipatti*] denotes the action itself (*bhāve*). And the Naiyāyikas hold that the disagreement of disputants (*vādin*) is the cause of doubt. Therefore, this is the doubt.

What indeed is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*: is it the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogi, or is it scriptural injunction (*codanā*)? It is precisely from this doubt regarding the means of valid cognition that there arises a doubt regarding its essential nature:
is *dharma* sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like, or is it the worship of a shrine (*caityavandana*) and the like? Thus, in the first quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]:

He states that a definitive conclusion must be reached: "by means of the [first] quarter. For here, validity will be established by refuting other possible means of knowledge and by refuting the possibility of invalidity. And through that establishment, the establishment of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is also accomplished.
In the [remaining] three quarters, however, the specific modes of the means of knowledge, which were promised by the question "of what kind? (*kathaṃlakṣaṇa*), are investigated. Validity...
This has been established right here. For this very reason, he says at the conclusion of the section [on the *pāda*]: "Thus, this status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) is well-known.
And in the section on *arthavāda*, he says: "of that which has an established status as a means of valid knowledge" (*siddhapramāṇabhāvasya*).

Furthermore, because the mode of that which possesses such [status] is not significantly different from the means of valid knowledge itself, the entire chapter is designated as the "Definition of the Means of Valid Knowledge" (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*). // 126 //
[196] Form, or [197] rather,
by means of its non-production [198].

Having thus stated the purpose of the first quarter-verse beginning with "of those who have perished" (*naṣṭasya*), he states the purpose of the subsequent tantra with the two verses beginning with "sthitaḥ": "For those who are ignorant, and for those who see only one path, or even for those of great learning, because of their doubts regarding the determination of the meaning of the statements, no certain understanding arises."

First, the doubt regarding the meaning and purpose of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names will be dispelled by the sections beginning with the *Arthavādādhikaraṇa*, through the demonstration of their utility for purposes such as praise (*stuti*). Furthermore, in the second [section], the doubt concerning the difference [of acts]—arising from the lack of difference in meaning among [verbs] such as *yajati*, *dadāti*, and *juhoti*—will be addressed by the section beginning with *Śabdāntarādhikaraṇa*. This is the general direction. Therefore, because their purposeful nature is still doubted, [the subsequent discussion follows].
"A treatise is to be composed. // 128 //
[200] And because of the non-manifestation of the Victors, [201] and because of being beyond [202] sight, (KHA)
Thus ends the first sūtra in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.

"An object characterized by an injunction is Dharma"—this is the opening aphorism of the treatise. He explains it as follows: "Dharma... The intention here is this: in the first aphorism, there was an inquiry into *dharma* in its specific sense;

with that in mind, the question "What is Dharma? was asked. And a specific [definition] is established through a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For according to the scriptures of the heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*), specific ritual acts such as the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*) constitute Dharma, whereas according to the Vedic scriptures, sacrifices (*yāga*) and the like do.

Therefore, here, with reference to dharma as established in its general form, the specific means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, *codanā*—is enjoined; and from that, the establishment of the specific nature of dharma follows.

As for the general essence of dharma, which consists in its being the means to achieve pleasure (*prīti*), that is indeed established without dispute by all proponents of philosophical views. For no one here disputes that dharma is the means to achieve pleasure.

Thus it is said. And likewise, those who maintain that dharma consists of human qualities say: "Dharma is that from which the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results. The Buddhists say it is a pure mental impression (*cittavāsanā*). The Ārhatas say it is meritorious persons (*puṇyāḥ pudgalāḥ*). All of these consider them to be *dharmas* solely by virtue of being means for achieving joy. For this very reason, he will state later that in this formulation of the statement, the word "object" (*artha*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*).

"It is obtained through a restatement of the meaning (*arthānuvāda*). This very mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) is the one intended by the author of the *Vārttika*. Otherwise, he will state that the word "meaning" (*artha*) would be impossible in both the case of an injunction and a restatement. [Objection: But surely, when a specific nature is required, the prescription of a specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is incoherent.

Therefore, he says: "of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth. When it is stated that "this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the category of *dharma*," since the establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) depends upon the means of valid cognition, it follows by implication that this has been said: "that which is made known by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the essential nature of *dharma*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) is included. As for the one who thinks that what was stated [in the previous verse] was intended to conceal the intended meaning:
He replies to that with the words "its own nature" (svarūpam). Here, the specific nature of a property already established in a general sense is being formulated as a sūtra. // 1 //
[203] Ṣaji (KA) [204] Tīti [205] Ṣābhidhāna (KHA)

[Objection: But if this is so, since when one [of the two] is prescribed, the other is not explicitly stated in the scripture (*aśrauta*), then the *Bhāṣya*—which states that "what is the means of knowledge (*dharma*) and what are its characteristics? is explained by a single sūtra alone—would be untenable. To this he says: "The pair. When one [element] is presented through direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), the other becomes explained by implication (*arthāt*).

Thus, in the prescription of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-vidhi*), the establishment of the essential nature (*svarūpa-siddhi*) is stated by implication; and even in the prescription of the essential nature (*svarūpa-vidhi*), the means of knowledge is established by implication.

He says: "In its own nature. When it is stated that "that which is characterized by an injunction (codanā) is Dharma," it follows by implication that the injunction is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for Dharma. For an entity devoid of a means of valid cognition is not capable of establishing its own nature. // 2 //

[206] For the sake of establishing the point, the author of the Bhāṣya has here explained the meaning of the term *codanā* as "an injunction (*vacana*) that impels one toward action" [207]. That is incorrect, because it is the impeller (*pravartaka*) that constitutes the *codanā*, whereas the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) and so forth are what possess that nature; therefore, he asks: "What is the beginning? The intention is as follows:
—It is true that the meaning of an injunction (*vidhi*) consists in the instigation of a mere cognition; however, its instigatory power does not reside in that alone.
For a person is enjoined as an agent toward their own activity. And that activity is the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), which consists of three factors.

Therefore, an injunction—which embraces the productive urge obtained through the force of the scriptural hearing (*śruti*) of the inclusion within a single verbal suffix—attains all its specific qualifications from that [productive urge].

It does not venture to impel a person [to action]. Furthermore, since the attainment of all those specific qualifications cannot be established without a sentence, it is rightly stated that "injunction" (*codanā*) is a sentence that impels [one to act]. Thus, having indicated the requirement for the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through the meaning of the individual components, the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) indicates the requirements for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). This is what is meant: "What... [and so forth].

A cognition that is complete with the factors to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth—required by the [inquiries] "by what means" and "how"—is capable of effecting an injunction that culminates in action;

for an entity devoid of those factors is unfit for performance. And this completion [of the cognition] comes from the sentence "one should do this by this means in this way"; thus, the sentence itself is the *codanā* (Vedic injunction). // 3 //
[207] They say:
[208] not [209] six perfections, nor... (KA) ...six.

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) stated, "For the injunction (*codanā*) [is the means of knowing] what has come to be," and so forth, for the purpose of demonstrating the validity or invalidity of the injunction and other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding *dharma*. That is incorrect;

since the Author of the Sūtras will state [this] in the two sūtras beginning with "satsamprayoge" and "autpattika," it would have been more appropriate for the Commentator to explain that very point there.

Therefore, why this labor over a matter that is not the proper field? To this he replies: "The injunction... The intended meaning is as follows: [the definition is] "that which is characterized by the injunction."

This is a compound word. A compound occurs only when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). And the semantic capacity of words consists in their expressing the relationship between a qualifier and a qualified. Furthermore, the relationship of qualifier and qualified among words does not exist without mutual exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). Therefore, because "being characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*) and [the absence thereof] mutually exclude one another, the injunction alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The two-fold restriction—that "injunction alone is the means of valid cognition"—is intended here. Since this requires a supporting rationale, the Commentator, following the lineage of Mīmāṃsā and unable to endure even for a moment a statement lacking logical justification, touched upon a slight trace of reasoning regarding the two-fold restriction right at the introductory sūtra, in order to establish the possibility [of the subject matter]. // 4 //
[210] ṇyapra [211] ta (KHA) [212] enduring, pra...

Regarding the restriction that "in this matter, this alone is the means of valid cognition," he first states a portion of the reasoning: "it is possible. In such matters, even those beyond the reach of the senses, the authority of the word is possible. Therefore, the authority suggested in the thesis will be established by means of a reason. He now demonstrates a portion of the reasoning for the restriction "only the Vedic injunction": [The text continues: "For the Vedic injunction is independent; it does not depend on anything else. And because it is independent, it is a means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous objects, just like the sense of sight with respect to color and so forth. Here, the meaning is as follows: the Vedic injunction is independent because it does not require corroboration from other means of knowledge. And because it is independent, it is a means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous objects, just as the sense of sight is a means of valid cognition regarding color and so forth. This is the portion of the reasoning. It is not the case that the independence of the Vedic injunction is unestablished, for its independence will be proven later. Nor is it the case that its being a means of valid cognition regarding supersensuous objects is unestablished, for that too will be proven later. Thus, the restriction "only the Vedic injunction" is established by means of this portion of the reasoning. Furthermore, the word "only" (eva) is used here to exclude other means of knowledge, such as perception and inference, which are incapable of apprehending supersensuous objects. [213] But how, then, can the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of verbal testimony be possible?

To this he says: "absolutely" (*atyanta*). For the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consists in their power to produce a cognition whose object is the thing itself (*arthagocara-jñāna*). That... [214] ...is [the definition].

And thus, it is indeed appropriate to consider the possibility of validity for words, since they produce cognitions even regarding things that are absolutely non-existent, such as the connection with a sky-flower. But if this is so, then just like that [non-existent object], invalidity would result;
thus, for one who seeks to establish validity, invalidity has ensued.

Therefore, he says: "by that. This is the intended meaning: for validity consists in the production of knowledge, which is the general rule (*utsarga*). That [validity] might be set aside in the case of human words, such as "the son of a barren woman goes," due to defects [in the speaker]. But in the case of non-human (Vedic) words, because of the absence of human defects and because they are inherently free from defect, their status as valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) will be established without being sublated. // 6 //
[214] Its validity (pramāṇatva) is that (sā); [215] it does not [216] attain [pu]. (KHA) (KA)

Regarding this, he states that by the word *codanā* in the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "for *codanā* [is] that which has come into being" (codanā hi bhūtam), it is intended as referring to verbal testimony (*śabda*) in general. He says: "codanā. He states the reason: "na hi" (for not...). For a prescriptive word (*vidhāyaka-śabda*) is the primary meaning of the term *codanā*. Since such a [prescriptive word] cannot have as its object that which has already come into being (*bhūta*) and so forth, it indicates verbal testimony in its general sense. // 7 //

[217] Regarding this point, he says "indriya" (the sense organ), explaining that "this is so here and thus from this. Since rivalry is possible only between two things of the same genus, only sound as a general category (*sāmānya*) can rival perception and the other means of knowledge, not its specific instances (*viśeṣa*). For there is a deliberation such as, "Should iron be brought, or wood? but not, "Is it iron, or is it *khadira* wood? // 8 //

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya has explained the meaning of the term *lakṣaṇa* (definition) as that by which something is characterized (*lakṣyate*). He then states—“it is merely the cause” (*nimittamātram*)—to clarify whether this refers to the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) or to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Regarding the alternative view that it is the *pramāṇa*, he sets forth various options for the means of valid cognition in order to expand the student’s understanding, saying “or it is the *pramāṇa*. This also applies to the case of “or it is the *pramāṇa*.”

The meaning is "the side" (pakṣa). For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka*), and the application of causal factors occurs according to one's intention. Therefore, whatever among the [factors] beginning with words and ending with the cognition of the sentence-meaning is intended as the most effective instrument (*prakṛṣṭasādhakatama*), that is the *pramāṇa*. In connection with the discussion of *pramāṇa*, he also shows the result (*phala*) by saying "of the former ones," namely, of words and so forth.

When the cognition of the sentence-meaning is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its result (*phala*) is [the cognition of that same meaning]. However, it must be presented as an intermediate operation (*antarālikavyāpāra*) of the instrument.

But when the cognition of the sentence-meaning itself is the valid means of knowledge, the result is the cognition of what is to be rejected (*hāna*) and so forth; thus one should distinguish between the two cases. // 10 //
[218] Regarding cognitions (jñāna):

[219] Is it not the case that, within the category of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cognition itself is also a definitional constituent? For that indeed is the means of valid cognition. [220] Therefore, how can there be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term *codanā*, which denotes a specific kind of word? To this, he says:
Regarding the term "knowledge" (*jñāna*):

its meaning is this—there is no rule that knowledge alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For it has already been stated that words and so forth possess the status of being means of valid cognition by virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). Furthermore, if knowledge alone were the means of valid cognition, then the word "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) would have been employed with that specific intention.

Nevertheless, by the word *codanā*, the cognition whose object is that [injunction] and its effect are indicated, provided the use of the term "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*) is intended with reference to them. However, if it is intended to refer to the cognition of the meaning of words and so forth, then the cognition which is the further effect of the cognition that is itself the effect of the word—namely, the cognition of the meaning of words and so forth—is indicated by the term *codanā*. For there exists a relationship through a causal chain even between the effect of an effect, which serves as the basis for indication (*lakṣaṇā*). // 11 //
[220] Indeed, that [221] is not necessarily known by [222] him.

[223] But regarding the sense of the cause (*nimitta*), in the case of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), a word (*śabda*), and a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) only between the two primary senses themselves; thus he says: "The cause," etc. (verse 12).

In this context, by the restrictive phrase "only [Vedic] injunction" (*codanāiva*), the possibility of *dharma* being within the range of the senses and so forth is excluded. That is incorrect; for *dharma* consists of substances and the like, and it will be stated in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* that these are indeed perceptible by the senses. Therefore, he says: "Substance... The meaning is this: it is true that substances and the like are *dharmas*, but not in their own essential form (*svarūpeṇa*). What then? [They are *dharmas*] as they are related to the performance of what is prescribed by the Veda. Thus, the restriction [in the sūtra] is not improper. Furthermore, since the word "only" (*eva*) is connected with the word "injunction," it does not exclude other means of knowledge such as perception. For example, when one says, "He eats only rice," it is understood that he eats rice and nothing else, but it is not thereby excluded that he eats it with curds and the like. Similarly, here too, the sense is that *dharma* is known through injunction alone, and not through anything else. However, it is not that other means of knowledge are excluded from its cognition. However, it exists in the form of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). Therefore, since it is not perceptible by the senses, there is no consequence of *dharma* falling within the range of the sense organs.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the generic form (*ākṛti*) is included. // 13 //
[224] By what nature, then, are these dharmas such that they are "to be known through the Veda"?

He shows this with the passage ending in *śreyaḥ* (the highest good). For substances and so forth exist by virtue of having the nature of being the power to accomplish the highest good (*śreyassādhana*). [225]

These are the dharmas. Their nature cannot be understood except through the Veda; for no other means of knowledge can proceed to establish that the *godohana* vessel and such things are means to the highest good (*śreyaḥ-sādhana*) without the scriptural injunction, "One desiring cattle should fetch water with the *godohana*," and so forth. He concludes the discussion on the supersensuous nature (*anaindriyikatva*) of dharma with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). // 14 //

[225] Having paid homage to the Self, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated here that "nothing other than the sense organs" means that the mere sense organs are incapable of being the *dharma*. However, this much alone does not justify the restrictive determination "codanā alone [is the means of knowing *dharma*]," because there remains the possibility of inference and other means being capable [of knowing it]. Therefore, he says: "[The mention of perception] is for the sake of illustration. For just as when the author of the Sūtras intended to state that all means of knowledge are not the cause [for knowing *dharma*], he said "that perception is not the cause," thereby indicating that mere perception is not the cause; so too here.

Thus, following that very style, the author of the Bhāṣya has described the incapacity of the sense-organs alone for the sake of illustration. Or rather, he says "nothing else" (*nānyat*) because the Bhāṣya must be interpreted as refuting the generality of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How then is the phrase "not the sense-organ" (*na indriyam*), which appears disconnected from what precedes, to be explained? To this he says: "Nothing else."

Regarding the word "tat" (that): the sense is that everything else is preceded by the sense-faculties (*indriya*), for when the sense-faculties lack power, [everything else] lacks power. Alternatively, having set aside the phrase "nānyat" (not other), he asks "what is the reason? and states "kiñca" (moreover/furthermore) as the reason, to be explained as before—that it is not the sense-faculty.
Thus he says: "kiñca. // 16 //
[226] It has been done.
[227] O Indriya, is it not the case that inference is capable regarding matters of this kind? (KHA)
Indeed, a past conjunction of fire and fuel is inferred from the embers; likewise, there is the cognition of future embers from the conjunction of fuel and fire.

Fire is remote from smoke, and a son is concealed by a wall or similar obstacle yet perceived by his voice; and a subtle substance is understood from its odor. Therefore, how can a universal negation be established? To this he says in two verses beginning with "Even though": it is true that inference is capable regarding the past and so forth.

But that [inference] does not arise without the cognition of a relation. And a relation is sometimes understood through generalities, as in the case of smoke in general with fire in general; and sometimes through particulars, as in the case of Rohiṇī and Kṛttikā. Yet, in neither of these two ways has any mark (liṅga) been perceived as being related to Dharma, which is eternal and beyond the senses.
By which there might be inference. // 18 //
[228] And here Andhabodha objects: "But surely," he says. For even a word does not convey meaning unless its relationship [to the object] has been grasped.

Because it is not understood by the ignorant, how then can an injunction consisting of words be an authority regarding dharma? He provides the rebuttal: "The word. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "But not... [229] What, then, is this? He says: "The meaning of the sentence. // 19 //
[229] Who is this? Surely there is no such thing as a sentence that is some transcendent reality (*atīndriya-tattva*) existing apart from the synthesis of all its letters and words.

Rather, it is the words themselves that, when combined, express the meaning. Therefore, how can a sentence whose relationship [to its parts] has not been grasped be the denoter of the sentence-meaning? [230]
Therefore, he says: "of the sentence. This fault would arise if it were accepted that the sentence is the signifier;

however, this is not the case. From what, then, does the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arise? To this he says: "of the word-meanings. But how can those [word-meanings] convey that [sentence-meaning] if their relationship [to it] has not been grasped? For it is not logical to postulate one thing upon the perception of another.

Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It might be argued that one who knows another [word] connected to that [meaning] infers the other; this is appropriate by virtue of the connection (*pratibandha*). Therefore, he says: "The relation" (*sambandha*). It will be demonstrated in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa* that words which are independent of the perception of a [direct] relation serve as the means of proof (*hetu*) for the meaning of a sentence, by virtue of their presence when that [sentence-meaning] is to be known. // 20 //
[230] There is no other commentary here besides this one, [231] nor is there anything else.
But surely, the *codanā* might express even an object that is not as it is, just like any ordinary worldly statement such as "There are fruits on the riverbank" and so forth. That is incorrect.
For how can the speech of some random person on the street be a point of comparison for the *codanā*? For the latter is indeed authorless (*apauruṣeyī*).
For the suspicion of defects in speech is based on human agency; therefore, how can there be a suspicion of its being otherwise?
Regarding this, some say that this commentary is intended to refute the thesis by means of an investigation into the power of words. Here...

It is said that by the *codanāsūtra*, it was asserted that the meaning of the Veda consists of what is to be done (*kārya*); this [point] is now challenged by the following: for if words do not touch upon objects, what is the point of this assertion regarding specific meanings for injunctions (*codanā*)? Indeed, all words do not, by their very nature, touch upon objects. For whatever sentence was once employed by someone in such a way as to possess a meaning, [it remains so].

For that very same thing, when free from all defects such as partiality (*kalā*) and inflation (*ādhmāta*), becomes otherwise false at another time. And this is not logical if there is no difference [in its nature]. As they say: "When sublation is impossible for that which possesses the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), those very characteristics themselves are sublated. Nor is this property observed in the case of means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) when they are functioning effectively; for [perception] free from defects such as cataracts (*timira*)—

It has been observed previously that the eye produces both correct and incorrect cognition. Furthermore, if the connection with an object were inherent, how could it produce cognition when the object is non-existent? For instance, even though a connection is sublated, it is understood from a word a hundred times over, such as "a herd of a hundred elephants on the tip of a finger. This has not been seen elsewhere; for indeed—

When a mother-of-pearl shell is perceived as silver by the eye, and a sublation arises in the form "this is not silver," it is the eye itself that again makes known [the object] as "not silver. But verbal cognition alone is unrestrained; it makes known its own object, whether that object is the domain of another or has been sublated by another means of valid cognition. Indeed, one who has not reflected upon the existence of ultimate reality, even while making an object known, makes it known in vain.

Thus we maintain. This has been stated: when a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that does not contact the object gives rise to a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), the counter-cognition (*pratipakṣavijñāna*) is no longer perceived as having that very [object] as its cause. In the case of verbal [cognition], however, even when a subverting cognition is clear, the counter-cognition arises again with the word itself as its cause, as in the case of "a hundred herds of elephants on the tip of a finger."
Thus [it is asked]. How, then, is there comprehension of meaning from a word?
They say it is conventional (*sāmayikī*). As they have said:
[234] *tī* means "three" (*bā*);
[235] *jā* means "birth" (*artha*).
And some maintain that this practice is the convention (*samaya*);
in brief, every word is the cause of intuition (*pratibhā*) through such practice.

Thus. In order to remove this objection, the following commentary is stated: "This is contradictory; it is said that [the word] expresses [something], yet it speaks falsely," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: it is a marvel that it makes an object known while not touching upon that object! For there is no relation between a word and its referent other than that of the signifier and the signified. And if this...
It makes the meaning understood;
how, then, could it be non-contacting with the object? It might be argued: "Non-contacting with the object is to be understood through a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*).

But this has already been stated: even when a subverting cognition exists, in the case of worldly sentences, knowledge arises from the word itself, as in the case of sentences such as "the finger [points at the moon]," and so forth.

Thus [you say]. Not so. You are ignorant of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator. In the case of "a hundred herds of elephants on the tip of a finger," it is the perception by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) that is sublated here, not the "hundred herds of elephants" themselves. For, in order to communicate to another an object perceived through another means of knowledge...

People employ sentences, and from that, only this much is understood from the word: "This person has been seen by him through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, in this case, it is precisely the perception of that object by means of another *pramāṇa* that becomes sublated.
However, in the case of a herd of elephants, the word is not a *pramāṇa*; thus, since [the knowledge] derived from that word was never even applicable, it is not sublated.

How, then, is the apprehension of the connection with the herd of elephants explained? This is an error based on the failure to grasp the distinction between word-meanings due to the defect of the proximity of words; it is not, however, a connection that is denotative [by the words themselves]. For in both the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what is denoted) and *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of what is connected), the basis is semantic competency (*yogyatā*). And there is no such competency in the case of the tip of a finger...

The capacity for performing the retention [of the Veda] is possible. Therefore, it is well said that "the word does not fail to touch its object," and thus the proposition regarding the specific nature of the object—that *dharma* is an object characterized by *codanā*—is established.
For it is based on that... [238] hi tanniba (KA).

We, however, do not accept these two objections and their refutations. Regarding what was first stated—that it is asserted in the *Codanā-sūtra* that the meaning of the Veda consists of things to be accomplished (*kārya*)—that is incorrect, because it contradicts the *Bhāṣya*.
For the author of the *Bhāṣya* has explained [the question] "What is Dharma? What is its definition? by means of that very same *sūtra*.

Having said this, he introduces the Sūtra. It would be more appropriate to state that one [aspect] of its measure and nature is based on scripture (*śrauta*) and the other is based on meaning (*ārtha*). And this has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The proposition that [the Veda] has action as its purpose is neither of Śabara nor of Jaimini.
Indeed, such a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of word-meanings is not seen in the *Codanāsūtra*; nor is there [any function] independent of the syntactical connection of word-meanings.

The meaning of the sentence is logical. But how does the assertion that [the Veda] has a purpose consisting of something to be accomplished (*kāryārthatā*) accord with the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? [Objection: Is it not the case that validity itself is impossible without having a purpose consisting of something to be accomplished? Therefore, the assertion that it has a purpose consisting of something to be accomplished is indeed consistent with the definition of a means of valid cognition. For a statement that does not have a purpose consisting of something to be accomplished cannot possess validity; for that [validity] is characterized by independence (*anapekṣā*). Nor can [it apply] to an already established fact (*siddhārtha*).
The statement becomes independent [of other means of knowledge]. For in its case, the occurrence of either a proof or a sublation is possible.

Among these, if a proof exists, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*); otherwise, it lacks authority because its object is sublated. It is for this very reason that the Vedic statements are also non-human (*apauruṣeya*). For being human-made consists in having an object already apprehended by another means of knowledge.

Furthermore, there is no production of words, phonemes, and so forth [from such causes]. Nor are humans capable of perceiving supersensible objects. Therefore, how could they compose words regarding supersensible matters? Thus, the declaration of a specific purposeful object will not be stated; this is the knowledge of the [author’s] intention.

To this we reply: as for the claim that [the Veda] is a mere restatement because its object is already established, that is incorrect. If it were to communicate an object already established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, being dependent upon that, let it be non-authoritative. However, even regarding an existent object, that which has as its own domain an object not within the scope of any other cognition—[is authoritative].

That [perception] is not dependent on that [other means of knowledge]. Now, if it is thought: "Perception and the other means of knowledge indeed have fully established objects; since they occur with respect to such specific objects, they render the means of knowledge redundant," that is not so. For a means of knowledge does not become redundant simply because another means of knowledge is possible, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For fire situated at a distance, though known through inference, can be perceived by one who approaches it; thus, its status as a means of knowledge does not lapse into redundancy. As for the claim that it is non-authoritative because its object is sublated...

Let it be so; however, when there is a subversion [of that cognition] such that "this is not thus," how could even that which has an established object as its domain—provided its object is uncontradicted—not be a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*)? If it is argued that even that is not a valid means of knowledge due to the possibility of a sublater (*bādhaka*), let that be the case for human compositions. But how could even an authorless (*apauruṣeya*) [text], despite having an established object, be suspected of being sublated?

For knowledge produced by non-defective causes is never sublated. And in the case of the word, there are no inherent defects; rather, it is the person who, in accordance with his own erroneous cognition, corrupts the word. But was it not said that it is difficult to maintain that what is established as an object is independent of a person? Is it now claimed that being beyond the senses constitutes independence from a person? Alas, if so, even the sentence "the sky-flower is fragrant" [would be independent].

It would follow that it is non-human (apauruṣeya). Yet, even for that [Vedic word], the object is not apprehended by any sense organ. This might be argued: "This sentence has a non-existent object, whereas a sentence with an existent object—one whose object transcends the senses—is non-human. But how can a Vedic sentence, which has an object consisting of something to be accomplished (*kārya*), have an existent object?
For its object, too, is not experienced through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Let it not be experienced; however, it is not rejected.

And it is understood from the word itself. However, the sentence "sky-flower" has its object negated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it makes known its meaning as "it does not exist. By which other means of valid cognition, then, is its object negated? It is certainly not by the positive means of valid cognition (*bhāva-pramāṇa*), because, having existence as their domain, they do not manifest non-existence. Furthermore, the negative means of valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) is simply not accepted by you.

[Objection: But surely there exists the cognition that "it exists" or "it does not exist," and that [cognition] will refute [your position]. [Response: Well then, sir, is that [cognition] a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one? It cannot serve to refute [anything] if it is invalid. And if it is a valid means of knowledge, it follows that there would be a sixth means of knowledge. [Objection: But surely, regarding a sky-flower, the statements "it exists" and "it does not exist" are contradictory. Therefore, because of this contradiction, the statement concerning a sky-flower has a non-existent object. What is the point here?

It is contradicted. For, in the case of an established entity, existence and non-existence, being understood as mutually contradictory, produce the cognition of a contradiction. However, there is no apprehension here of mutually contradictory existence and non-existence, because according to your own tenet, non-existence is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatvāt*). But surely—

There is, first of all, the linguistic usage "it exists" and "it does not exist. Let it not be that [this usage] is devoid of cognition; therefore, it will refute the existence of flowers in the sky. No, for words have their basis in objects, and contradiction pertains to objects. Furthermore, no object whatsoever is perceived for the word "does not exist. Nor does a word that lacks an object contradict another object. But is this word not indeed non-referential? For its object is simply the sky itself as distinguished from the flower. [Distinguished...]

69} Thus, it is inexpressible because there is no additional referent. To say "the sky is that which is designated by the word 'sky'" is a tautology; thus, there is no such thing as "non-existence," and this results in the fallacy of synonymy. If it is argued that "non-existence" is said when only the sky is perceived in the absence of its counter-correlate, the flower, then that [flower] would indeed not exist, and consequently the sky itself would likewise not exist. For that which is the locus of the term "does not exist" is precisely what is non-existent.

Worldly people think thus: "Therefore, the cognition that 'it does not exist'—whether it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not—is like the word 'it does not exist,' which does not negate a sky-flower; even that [cognition], being understood from its own words, must be something that exists. If, however, one wishes to say that such a thing simply does not exist, [then the following applies].

We do not deny the use of words; however, it has been stated that the actual existence of a thing cannot be denied. Therefore, for your venerable selves, the statement "a sky-flower exists" would result in being non-human (apauruṣeya) [in its status as a valid source of knowledge], because it refers to an object that is existent yet beyond the senses. Just as this [statement] has a non-existent object, so too the Vedic [scripture] has a non-existent object insofar as it refers to a causal purpose (*kāryārtha*) that is beyond the senses. For it cannot be said that a thing exists which is outside the scope of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and a causal purpose is not within the scope of perception or other such means.

Nor is it accessible through verbal testimony (*śabda*), because that which is not the meaning of a word cannot be the meaning of a sentence; and that which has not had its relation [to other words] grasped is not the meaning of a word; and because it is impossible to grasp a relation regarding that which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This will be explained in detail in the *Aupattika-sūtra* [JS 1.1.24–27].
Enough with this excessive agitation. Where there is no... (KHA) ...noble one. [242]
[243] Just as this is untenable, so too [244] *nāntarāgaḥ* (KA) [245] in the Vārttika.

Therefore, it is established that the Veda is not authorless (*apauruṣeya*) because it serves a purpose to be accomplished. How, then, is it so? Because it lacks prior and posterior limits.
