For that which has no prior or posterior limits reckoned is eternal, such as space. And since the Vedas are thus [without such limits], they are eternal. But what is this eternity of the Vedas? If it is the commencement of eternal phonemes and words, [then...]

This is the same in the case of worldly sentences. Now, if those [worldly sentences] are non-eternal because their sequence is non-eternal, then that same non-eternality applies equally to Vedic sentences. Therefore, there is no difference between human and non-human speech other than whether their objects fall within the scope of human authority or not. Or rather, let some specific distinction be stated; it is stated as follows: for [sentences] possess a sequence.

A sentence is said to consist of words. That [sentence] is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*) where a person composes the sequence independently; however, that is of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*) where the person is not independent in composing the sequence, but intends it exactly as the sequence was uttered by previous reciters. Furthermore, even though the manifestations of the sequence are impermanent, their status as identical or different is established on the basis of intermediate universals (*avāntarajāti*).

This will be discussed in the section on *śabda*. Furthermore, this very same method regarding the eternity of words will be demonstrated in that very place. As for one who thinks, "How can there be an absence of prior and posterior limits even in the Veda?", he should be told: first of all, the prior and posterior limits of the Vedas are not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor are they inferred (*anumāna*).

Because of an inverted inference. For in this case, the following is inferred: "The future time is not devoid of the Vedas, because it is time, just like the present time. In the same way, the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be shown regarding the past time as well. Furthermore, the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the Vedas has not been perceived by anyone. If it is argued that the Vedas were produced by Maheśvara at the beginning of the world, [then...]

No, because the world and so forth do not [originate] in that manner. Furthermore, there is no recollection of an author to the effect that "the Vedas were composed by someone at a recent time. Nor is it reasonable to assert that an author existed even though he is not remembered; for in the case of things like old wells, the non-recollection of an author might still be plausible due to the absence of a purpose [for remembering]. However, regarding the Vedas—which are produced for the sake of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)—there must be a recollection of a highly trustworthy author.
Who else would have faith in this? And he will say:
"Thus" (KHA) and "in the case of otherness" (KA).
"But Vedic usage does not exist without the recollection of an author.

Thus, in this way, its lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) is due solely to the absence of prior and posterior limits, and not because it has a purpose as an action (*kāryārthatayā*); therefore, that proposition is useless. Moreover, it is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*).

"Because the Mantras, Arthavādas, and Upaniṣads do not have that as their purpose. But surely, their status as being for the sake of action will be stated in the second chapter [of the *Śābarabhāṣya*]: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with an injunction" (1.2.7). And here too, the Commentator has said: "For an injunction (*codanā*) is capable of making known what has been, what is, and so forth," ending with those words. This is what is meant: while the injunction teaches only what is to be accomplished (*kārya*), it also makes known things such as what has already come into being.

But it does not establish [the meaning]. That is why it was said that "it is able to cause understanding. To this, it is replied: First of all, it was not stated in the *Arthavāda* section that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) have a purpose consisting of an action; rather, it was shown that those which have an existing state as their object (*bhūtārtha*) are connected to an injunction (*vidhi*) by way of praise.

Furthermore, the intention of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "For the injunction [refers to] what is existent" (*codanā hi bhūtam*) has already been explained immediately thereafter by the author of the Vārttika.

As for this meaning attributed to it—that an injunction (*codanā*) indicates what has already come into being (*bhūta*) and so forth, but does not bring it about—that is not correct. If it indicates what has already come into being and so forth, how is it that it does not bring it about? For there is no "bringing about" (*pratipādakatva*) other than "indicating" (*gamakatva*). Now, if it is by this manner of explanation that its focus on what is to be accomplished (*kāryaparatva*) is described, [then...]

For every class of words is directed toward an action and is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the essential nature of existing things (*bhūta*) and so forth; how then can Brahman—consciousness, bliss, without beginning or end—be established on the basis of the Upaniṣads? And for what purposeful action could the Upaniṣads possess authority? Is it not the case that even they are solely intent upon the necessity of performing a realization (*pratipatti-kartavyatā*)? Indeed, there is an injunction regarding knowledge (*jñāna-vidhāna*).

"The Self is to be known. This means that one should know the Self as consciousness and bliss. But how can the nature of the Self be established from a word whose primary purport is something other than itself? For a word whose primary purport lies elsewhere cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding another object;
on the contrary, it would lead to the opposite result.

This might be possible. For in common worldly usage, one observes the prescription of performing an action toward something that does not actually possess that nature; for example, "one should recognize a non-father as a father. Likewise, in the Veda, there is the injunction to meditate upon the *udgītha* in what is not the *udgītha*, namely the syllable *oṃ*:
"One should meditate on this syllable *oṃ* as the *udgītha*. It might be argued that the nature of the Self is established solely through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Thus [it is asked]: by what other means of valid knowledge? For transmigrating beings do not directly perceive Brahman—which is Being, Consciousness, and Bliss—as distinct from the aggregate of the body and the instruments of perception. Indeed, regarding the body alone as the self, they know the person to be suffering, impermanent, and insentient. However, there are those for whom the entire manifold of the body, senses, and so forth—manifested by the connection with beginningless ignorance that has been completely overturned—[no longer exists].

Those who have ascended to Brahman—which is the fruit, consisting of bliss, devoid of movement, and in which all distinctions between means of knowledge (*mātṛ*), objects of knowledge (*meyam*), and knowledge itself (*māna*) have been completely uprooted—what could they see, and by what means? Therefore, the nature of the Self cannot be established in any way. Consequently, neither through logical reasoning (*upapatti*) nor through the text (*grantha*), it is possible to maintain that the purpose [of the scripture] is merely to describe an effect (*kārya*). Thus, as for the purpose... [text fragment].
[249] Thus, it is not understood in anything [250]. (KHA) [251] In what...?

As for the claim that the proposition is undermined because words do not touch upon their objects—on the grounds that "they are not of such a nature"—that is incorrect. For instance: what is this "non-touching" of the object? If it means the absence of any relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, that is indeed admitted;
for no relation characterized by conjunction and the like is accepted between word and object. Or, if it means the failure to cause the cognition of the object, [then...]

Whence, then, is the cognition of meaning? If you say "from convention" (*samaya*), surely this very [issue] is the rejection of the [intrinsic] relation; for since the positions of [the relation being] dependent on each individual person and so forth are impossible, convention will be refuted [later].
Why, then, is effort expended here for the sake of refuting that? And as for what was said for the sake of refuting the lack of contact with the object—

In this case, the perception of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sublated, but not the [perception] "this is a herd of elephants. We do not understand what the meaning of that [statement] is. Mundane speech has as its object only that which is perceived by other means of valid cognition; how then could it be sublated by the sublation of those other means of valid cognition? It might be thought: "The other means of valid cognition make known an object delimited by specific place and time, such as this..."

"Now, [regarding] the phrase *atra ca* (and here): therefore, when there is a sublation of the connection with specific results such as [crossing] rivers and so forth, those [results] become sublated. But the word, denoting an object that is not delimited by space or time, does not become sublated by the sublation of a specific connection.
This is incorrect. For at any given time, the word denotes precisely that connection which is intended by the speaker at that very moment.

It is not merely the relation [of contact]. For there exists no universal residing in the specific relations between various fruits on the banks of many different rivers that could serve as the meaning of a word. Nor is it tenable to claim that the relation is denoted by the word while being unintended [as a specific one], because linguistic usage would fail due to a lack of consensus between the speaker and the listener. This is so even in the case of a statement regarding a specific instance, such as "There are fruits on the bank of the Narmadā."
What is the rebuttal? If it is argued that "there were [such persons] there, or there will be," we say no; for the statement "they exist" is a designation of the present.

Furthermore, when and where will such a person appear who will strive to avoid the contradiction regarding the meaning of words? To deny the comprehension of the connection [between word and object], however, is contrary to direct experience (*saṃvit*).

Thus it is. But if it is argued: "Every worldly sentence is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object, because it lacks validity with respect to the speaker's cognition. For it has been said: 'Moreover, from a human statement there arises the cognition, "This person knows it to be thus," but not [the cognition] "The object is thus. Therefore, there is never a sublation of the word-meaning. By speaking in this way, the proponent has effectively established that words do not touch upon (i.e., do not correspond to) objects."

"It does not touch upon the object as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even though it touches upon the object. Furthermore, let it be granted that it is not a *pramāṇa* with respect to the object itself; nevertheless, it is certainly a *pramāṇa* with respect to the speaker’s cognition. Therefore, since that [cognition] alone is the meaning of the word, even if that [cognition] is sublated, the sublation of the word's meaning is indeed difficult to avoid.
It might be thought: "The word is not a *pramāṇa* with respect to the speaker’s cognition by way of being expressive (*vācakatayā*)."
Because consciousness is inferential,
the word— which is understood as an effect having consciousness as its cause— inferentially indicates the consciousness that serves as its cause.

And there is no dispute that the cognition of a cause from an effect is inference. As it has been said: "Consciousness [is not a means of knowledge] because its cause is well-known. This is the secret of avoiding the charge of not touching upon the object. What else need be said here? A word is neither a means of knowledge regarding an external object nor regarding consciousness; therefore, it does not touch upon the object. Now, it might be argued: "The word is not for us..."

"It is not [a means of valid cognition] with respect to the object. For in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), the relationship between word and meaning is established as innate (*svābhāvika*).

However, in the world, because deviation is sometimes observed, or because sentences are dependent upon the authority of the speaker, they terminate in the speaker's cognition and do not produce certainty regarding the object. But in the Veda, since there is no speaker, its validity with respect to the object is not undermined. For indeed—

In that regard, it is said that "word functions as dependent upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That is not so. For a means of valid cognition does not become one whose object is non-existent simply because a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed in some instance. Indeed, the cognition of silver with respect to mother-of-pearl, though sublated, does not thereby become a cognition whose own object is something else; rather, due to a defect, it makes known an object that exists in one way but appears in another.
We shall explain this in the commentary (*vṛtti*) of the author.
[252] vitava (KHA) [253] thā bo (KA)

Therefore, here too, all verbal cognition has the object as its very domain; it is reasonable to say that only some of it becomes erroneous due to the influence of defects. Moreover, if there were no validity regarding the object in the speech of persons, how then could a specific cognition of the speaker be inferred? For cognitions are not, by their own nature, inferred unless they have attained an embrace with a specific object. Thus, one who desires to infer their specific character must necessarily [infer] their embrace with a specific object.
It must be said: an object that has not entered into the speaker’s cognition does not qualify that cognition. Furthermore, as some maintain:

since deviation is observed in the case of human statements, no certainty regarding the object arises; and an object that is not certain cannot be known, for there is no such thing as a cognition whose nature is non-certainty.

Therefore, even when the meaning of the sentence is not yet known, this reflection arises in the listener: "This trustworthy person speaks only a collection of words whose meanings are mutually compatible; therefore, he must certainly have known their connection. Thus, [the listener] infers the speaker's very knowledge of the connection. But for the listener, it is merely a reflection. That is incorrect. For how could the listener [infer] a specific connection that has not even ascended into his own intellect?

[The opponent] imagines [the speaker's cognition] as a qualifier of the speaker. If it is argued that one infers the cognition of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—thinking "this person composes this sentence because he perceives [the connection] precisely through the activity of the palate and other organs of an authoritative person (*āpta*)"—we say no. This is because [one would only be inferring] the mere cognition of positive concomitance. However, an inference of a cognition of a *specific* positive concomitance on the part of the speaker is not possible without the speaker’s own cognition of that specific [connection]. As for the question, "How can an object that is not yet certain be known?"...

Thus it is said. To this we reply: indeed, speakers are determined to be of three kinds—those whose status as authoritative has been established, those whose status as non-authoritative has been established, and those whose nature is undetermined as either. In all cases, there is certainly a determination regarding words. However, when the speaker’s status as authoritative has been established, the conviction that "this has been correctly understood by him" becomes firmly established; in the opposite case, it is subverted. When neither of the two statuses has been determined, [the result is doubt].

Even in the case of words, there is indeed certainty. However, because of occasional deviation (*vyabhicāra*), doubt arises as something adventitious. Nowhere is a word itself a cause of doubt. [Objection: Even so, since certainty regarding words follows the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*), a cognition that had previously arisen becomes obstructed by doubt upon seeing a deviation and thus ceases to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

And since it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) in a subsequent determination that follows a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), when will it ever become a valid means of knowledge itself? We reply: at its own time. And at its own time, this object was determined by that [cognition] which possesses the nature of arising and is of a doubtful character. And this much alone constitutes the validity of means of knowledge. Therefore, how could it be invalid? It serves only to eliminate doubt regarding the conventional usage of the term.
By means of reliability (*āptatva*), one relies merely on the absence of defects;

and this [reliability], common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), constitutes the default validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*) through the removal of suspected defects. Furthermore, it is not logical to claim that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for a listener who perceives an unprecedented object (*apūrva-artha*) not previously apprehended by other means of valid cognition.

For when it has been ascertained that "this is Caitra" from afar, and it is subsequently doubted due to some resemblance to Maitra, and then it is ascertained again that "this is indeed he," the previous cognition of Caitra does not become invalid.

Therefore, by means of the speaker's ascertainment of the validity [of his own cognition], the listener determines: "This [cognition] was indeed valid. Consequently, both of these are valid cognitions: namely, the cognition arising from the word and [the subsequent ascertainment].

And that ascertainment which follows the authority of the speaker occurs first through the determination of a previously unknown object; subsequently, however, it occurs through the removal of doubt. And it has been stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The two [cognitions] do not differ... [and] "...the cognition of the object... [is not].
[256] Rabhuvā [257] tī (KA, KHA) [258] d uttaraṃ (KHA)
"But the establishment of validity occurs because of the possibility of a cause consisting in the speaker's cognition.

As for what was said—that there is no cognition whose nature is non-ascertainment—that too is fit to be stated only after having defeated us. Cognition is fivefold: valid knowledge, error, doubt, recollection, and corroboration.

Let us distinguish them. Therefore, every verbal cognition, whether it be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not, has an object as its domain. And the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge and what is otherwise is based on the presence or absence of defects, just as in the case of perception and the other [means of knowledge]. As it has been said: "That whose instrument is defective, and that in which there arises the conviction 'this is false'..."

"That alone is the incorrect cognition, and nothing else. This does not refer merely to sensory perception (*akṣaja-jñāna*), because by stating "that alone is the incorrect cognition," it includes cognition in general. Furthermore, human speech is corrupted solely by the defect of the speaker, even if the word itself is inherently faultless. But surely, it is only a defective cause of cognition that corrupts the cognition?

Furthermore, it is the sound itself that is the cause of the cognition, not the speaker; for the latter is employed solely for the manifestation of the sound. Even when manifested by a defective speaker, how could the sound—which is entirely free from defects such as being muffled or blown—become the cause for producing an incorrect cognition? For words uttered by a defective speaker do not [corrupt the cognition] in the same way that cataracts and other ailments corrupt the eyes and other sense organs.

Defects are perceived. [Objection: No, because defects are diverse. For not all defects are of a single form; rather, based on the observation of their effects, only certain things are assigned to the category of defects in specific instances. Thus, in this case, just as the proximity of a *japā* flower is the defect in the perception of a gem’s redness, so too in verbal cognition, the proximity of an unintended and incompatible word is the defect. A person is considered defective by virtue of uttering [the words] in such a manner.

He refutes [the position regarding] verbal testimony (*śabda*). Therefore, the distinction between what is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and what is not within the realm of verbal testimony is established as being based on the presence or absence of defects. Now, if it is accepted that meaning is understood from words, then what is the response to the following objection: "In order to prove that [verbal testimony] does not touch upon the actual state of affairs, it was stated that even when an object is sublated, the cognition produced is based solely on the word"? In that case, what is the solution regarding [the status of] the word?

[This is] by way of avoiding the sublation of the meaning. That is what we wish to avoid. What here is difficult to avoid? For it is not the case that errors—such as the double moon, confusion of directions, a fire-brand circle, a yellow conch, or a reflection—which have their objects sublated, do not manifest again. Indeed, as long as the defect exists, they are produced once more by the very same eye. Therefore, in this case as well, as long as there is the proximity of words whose connection is impossible...

What is impossible about the arising of a cognition that does not correspond to reality? Therefore, these two [arguments] are neither a valid objection nor a valid rebuttal. [259] It is entirely [260] false.
(KHA) [260] It is indeed [KHA, GA] false.
Intending to describe it otherwise, he first states the intention of the *ākṣepa-bhāṣya*: "Because of [the claim of] eternality and so forth. This is the intention:

this objection belongs to the Buddhists and the Lokāyatikas. For they do not consider letters, words, or Vedic sentences to be eternal; nor do they regard them as being like the incoherent ravings of a madman.

They say that sentences such as "The cutting out of Prajāpati’s omentum" (prajāpativapā-utkhādana) are authoritative because they convey commendation (*prāśastya*) through syntactic unity with an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, it is appropriate to compare the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) to the words of some random street person; based on that similarity, one may infer their falsity.
Alternatively, he says "having accepted" (*abhyupetya*) to indicate that they are bringing forward a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) even while conceding [the Vedas'] eternality. Thus...

For he thinks thus: "If the Vedas are eternal, they will all the more lack authority. For a human statement may sometimes be authoritative when produced by a speaker endowed with virtues; but how could that which is eternal ever be authoritative? [Objection: But surely even a human statement is not authoritative by depending on the virtues of the speaker; rather, it is so by its own nature. For how...

Knowledge that has arisen, which is non-erroneous and free from doubt, will be authoritative. Therefore, what is the point of its being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), since it would instead incur a greater lack of authority?

To this he says: "By another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*). For how can human speech, whose object is a thing already perceived by another means of knowledge, [be authoritative] by its own power?
It will be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For memory, being dependent on another means of valid cognition, does not become a means of valid cognition in its own right.

And here there is a formal argument (*prayoga*): "The word of a person is not intrinsically a means of valid cognition, because it makes known an object already established by another means of valid cognition, just like memory. // 22 //

But surely, worldly practice is seen to proceed from the mere words of a trustworthy person independently [of other means of knowledge]. How, then, could that [practice] arise from something that is not intrinsically authoritative? To this he says: "Nūnam" (surely). For he thinks as follows: human speech concerns an object within the range of the speaker. Therefore, even when the object has not been perceived by oneself, one concludes, "Surely this object was experienced by the speaker. Thus, the basis for the statement of a trustworthy person is preceded by the speaker’s own experience.
The opinion of one who accepts valid means of knowledge is logical; however, being an authoritative person (*āptatva*) is not the cause of validity by virtue of some unperceived form.
But he who engages with human [utterances] while disregarding other means of valid cognition might indeed be thwarted. // 23 //

[261] Why is it that such a cognition is not appropriate? To this he replies with the example: "not from what belongs to oneself. Thus, having established that in worldly statements validity is dependent upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he applies this same principle to the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) with the word "likewise" (*tathā*). // 24 //
But how could a cognition that has arisen, which is free from doubt and free from error, become non-authoritative by means of another means of knowledge?

To this he says: "By that" (*tena*). For when it has been established that the authority of all words is dependent upon another means of knowledge, and since the Veda is accepted as eternal, there is an absence of any other means of knowledge in the form of a speaker; then how will it be authoritative?

For knowledge that is independent and lacks a determinate cause cannot be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, merely because a cognition has arisen as an intuition (*pratibhā*), it is not accepted as valid. Therefore, knowledge arising from the Veda is not a valid means of cognition, because of its independence, like intuition and the like. // 25 //

He states another application [of the argument] to be demonstrated: "svarga... (beginning with "heaven"). The phrase "having as their object the relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth" is stated for the purpose of establishing the reason (*hetu*), namely, that [the meaning] is not apprehended by perception and the other means of knowledge. For one might think: "The meaning of a sentence is indeed *bhāvanā* (productive activity).
And that is either motion (*spanda*) or effort (*prayatna*). In any case, it is apprehended by perception and the rest; therefore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*)."
To this it is replied: for someone, there is an activity (*kriyā*) or cultivation (*bhāvanā*) by means of something;

although that [activity] is perceptible in its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), it is understood from verbal testimony alone as consisting in the relationship between the end to be accomplished and the means.

For this very reason, the supersensible nature (*atīndriyatva*) of *dharma* will also be established. The object of verbal testimony is precisely the relationship between the end to be accomplished and the means.

For the meaning of the word "one should bring about" (*bhāvayet*) is not that one should bring about a specific relationship between a means and an end—such as sacrifice and heaven—that has not yet been established.

Therefore, it is established [that the Veda possesses authority] because its subject matter is not accessible through perception and other means of knowledge. And in this context, it should be understood that when the Materialist (*Lokāyatika*) employs his argument, the words of the Buddha serve as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), whereas when he employs his own argument, the words of the Materialist himself serve as the example. // 26 //

Regarding this very point to be proven, he states another example and reason with the words "or else" (*yad vā*). Since it is established that the eternal Vedas were not composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), the lack of authority of the Vedas follows from their eternity, just like space (*vyoman*) and so forth. This is the formal argument (*prayoga*) for those Buddhists who assert that space is eternal. // 27 //

[262] He states another example (KHA). Now, following the logic of the quarrel between the dog and the boar (*śvavarāhakalahanyāya*) and by way of conceding the positions of the Naiyāyikas and others, the proponent—who for the time being stands within the school of the Nāstikas—states a formal argument (*prayoga*) against the Mīmāṃsaka, beginning with "Or if" (*yadi vā*). That is to say: if it must necessarily be asserted that the Vedas are a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), [then... [263] ...he says "or if. If it is absolutely necessary to state that the Vedas are authoritative...

However, let it be stated that the authority of the Veda follows from its being spoken by Him, just as the Vaiśeṣikas have asserted. As for this claim made by the Mīmāṃsakas—that the Vedas are eternal and authoritative—that is utterly remote from the truth and corrupted; such is the sense. Furthermore, by the word "all," one should eliminate the suspicion of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*) with respect to human instructions on perceptible matters and the instructions of Manu and others.
He refutes [the opponent's view]. Thus, the meaning is this: the Vedic injunctions, even those whose objects are seen or unseen, have as their subject matter *dharma*.

The point to be proven (*sādhya*) is that they depend upon a person for their authority (*prāmāṇya*). "Because they are sentences, like the speech of a person. Having stated the thesis (*pratijñā*) that "or [they are] not intrinsically authoritative," he states those same reason and example: "or [they are] not intrinsically [authoritative]. (28)

Having proposed the thesis that "validity" (*prāmāṇya*) or "the subject" (*dharmin*) is dependent on humans, one must prove that it is "dependent on humans. One must state the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), namely: "because it is connected with words, like invalidity" (*aprāmāṇyavat*); thus he says, "or validity. Here too, the purpose of the word "all" (*sarva*) is the same as before.
And for those who maintain that validity depends upon persons, it is already established that invalidity likewise depends upon them. // 29 //
[264] Furthermore, in that same way, it is observed that when something has a certain cause, its opposite occurs through the reversal of that cause;
for example, coldness in water, which has fire as its cause, occurs when that [fire] is reversed. The same applies to the validity of verbal testimony as well.

A reversal is observed due to the reversal of the speaker’s qualities; therefore, this [validity] also has that as its cause. Alternatively, whatever does not have something as its cause does not undergo a reversal upon the reversal of that [cause], just as a jar does not [undergo a reversal] upon the reversal of light. And yet, validity does not fail to undergo a reversal when there is a reversal of the speaker’s qualities.

Therefore, keeping in mind the applications of both the *vīta* (direct) and *avīta* (indirect) syllogisms, he says: "it would not exist. It should be understood that this succession of formal arguments was composed by the author of the Vārttika in order to please the minds of logicians. Furthermore, since the commentary (*bhāṣya*) beginning with "But surely, it is not so" provides a clear explanation for the meaning of these arguments in every instance, I have not explained each individual argument here. // 30 //

If, however, the Mīmāṃsaka—having had his own position refuted—should assert that the authority of the Veda is established independently of any person, he must be told: it is not established in this way. For the existence of the speaker’s virtues is established only when [the speaker] is well-known. And there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of virtues in the author of the Vedas, because of the absence of perception and the other [means of knowledge]. Furthermore, since a scripture composed by such an author would lack authority regarding the existence of those virtues, [the Veda] cannot possess eternal authority.
And because this has been refuted immediately [in the preceding section], he says—referring to all of this with the intention of [addressing] the objection "Is it not so?"—"Thus it stands. (31)

[265] Having thus stated the intention of the introductory objection (*ākṣepabhāṣya*), he now raises an objection while intending to explain the intention of the response (*parihārabhāṣya*)—beginning with the word "therein" (*tatra*). For the author of the Commentary has said: "This which is being stated is contradictory; it both asserts and [denies]."
And [the claim] that it is false is also incorrect;

for a cognition does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) merely by virtue of having arisen. If that were the case, then even regarding the words of the Buddha—which the Mīmāṃsaka has taken as the subject of the thesis because they are false—it would be possible to say this: [it is] contradictory.

"This is being stated, and yet it speaks falsely"—thus [the opponent might argue], and therein the Mīmāṃsakas would be thwarted. Therefore, this is a *jātyuttara* (a futile rejoinder). A *jāti* is that which, when a proponent has stated a reason for establishing his position, is an objection incapable of refuting it;
yet some consider it valid in certain specific cases. For they say: "When a faulty means of proof is employed, a faulty reply should be given. But that is incorrect.

Because two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) would result. For one who, without stating an existing fault, utters another that is non-existent, would incur two points of defeat known as "overlooking the censurable" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) and "censuring the uncensurable" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). Therefore, this is simply no answer at all. // 32 //
[266] *dhāsa* (KHA) [267] *tuḥ sā jātiḥ jā* (KHA, GA).

Here, having for the moment set aside the resolution of the objection raised in the commentary (*bhāṣya*), he introduces a preliminary discussion (*aupoddhātikī kathā*) with the words "all cognition" (*sarvavijñānam*). He thinks as follows: for when all cognitions...

It will be established that validity is inherent (*autsargika*), while invalidity depends upon sublation, causal factors, or defects; and since both of these are absent in the Veda— which is not of human origin—
and because it makes known its object without doubt, its validity being established, one could at most suspect its falsity on the grounds of the non-arising of cognition.

In this regard, one might argue that the statement "it produces knowledge, yet it does not produce false knowledge" will constitute a perfectly consistent reply. [But] surely, even so, since the validity of verbal testimony was previously challenged on the grounds that it is dependent upon something else, it would be more appropriate to establish the final position (*siddhānta*) by demonstrating the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of that very [testimony].

What is the use of this investigation into the great scope [of the topic]? It is said: all that has been stated is incidental. Furthermore, as long as validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not established in a general sense as being necessarily concomitant with the very nature of cognition (*jñānasvabhāva*), then even if validity were established in some particular instance, it could still be subverted by the argument: "Verbal cognition is not intrinsically valid, because it is a cognition, like other cognitions. For whatever form is invariably concomitant with a certain class of things does not deviate from that same class even when it occurs in another instance.

Just as heat is inherent to the nature of fire, so too, if extrinsic validity is invariably connected to the nature of cognition, how could it possibly transcend even verbal testimony? And it has been said: [268] ...will [be explained].
[269] Whatever power, following upon the universal, has been determined to exist,
the particular entity endowed with that [power] also participates in its designation by means of that [universal].

Thus, it has been established that while the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) inherent in all cognitions may be sublated by adventitious invalidity (*āgantukāprāmāṇya*), the authority of the Vedas will be established as being beyond such sublation; therefore, every word [of the author] is well-spoken. And here is the inquiry: are both validity and invalidity self-established?

Alternatively, by refuting the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) that invalidity is intrinsic (svataḥ) and validity is extrinsic (parataḥ), or the opposite, and by adopting the final position, the established conclusion (siddhānta) will be reached. // 33 //
[270] Therefore, validity is either extrinsic (*parataḥ*) or intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
[271] Thus, having become doubtful due to the conflicting views of the disputants, he adopts the first position— that they are non-existent by themselves (*svataḥ*).

For the proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādins*), who maintain that every class of effect arises as something already existent, have established that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*). They reason as follows: that which is non-existent by itself cannot be produced, just like a rabbit’s horn; yet jars and other such things are not unproduced; therefore, they must exist intrinsically—this is their *āvīta* (reductio ad absurdum) argument.

Moreover, because we observe the restriction of material causes (*upādāna*), a certain restriction is indeed seen regarding a particular transformation such as a jar, wherein only clay and the like serve as its material cause. This would be untenable if production were from the non-existent; for if non-existence were indistinguishable, everything could arise from everything, and there would be no restriction of material causes—such that clay alone is the cause of a jar.

"Vīraṇa grass is for a mat. In that case, one who desires anything would proceed toward everything, since there is no distinction. If it is argued that the restriction is according to capacity, we say no, because there is still no distinction. In this regard, it might be thought: having ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) which causal capacity a given entity possesses, one who desires a particular thing takes up that [entity] for that purpose. But that...

But this is not so, because there is no distinction. For we say that the modification exists in the material cause in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*); you also maintain that the power to produce the modification exists in the material cause. Thus, in this matter, only the phrasing differs, and no difference in meaning whatsoever is perceived. Moreover:

Indeed, according to your view, an effect arises from three causes: the material cause (*upādāna*), the efficient cause (*nimitta*), and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyin*). Yet that effect does not exist within those three [causes]. Having arisen as something previously non-existent, how can there be this restriction regarding the types of causes—distinguishing "this is the material cause" from "this is not"? If you argue that "that in which the effect resides is the material cause," [we reply:]...

The cause for the restriction of occurrence (*vṛttiniyama*) must be stated. Since that [effect] indeed arises from everything as something non-existent, by what is the restriction of its occurrence determined?

If it is argued that there is some specific excellence (*atiśayaviśeṣa*) in the material cause (*upādāna*) such that the effect occurs only therein, then that distinction of power (*śaktibheda*) must be explained. Neither an efficient cause (*nimitta*) nor an inherent cause (*asamavāyin*) is acceptable, as neither is admitted [by you].

For it is your established tenet that the staff and so forth are the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of the jar, while the specific conjunction of the parts of the clay is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). If you claim that this [conjunction] is the material cause (*upādāna*), we say no, because the dilemma of its being either distinct or non-distinct from the material cause cannot be logically sustained. It might be argued: "The material cause is a particular power (*śaktibheda*). This is not so; for that [power] would have to be either distinct from the material cause, or...

Or rather, it is not so. If there were a distinction [between the effect and the material cause], then because the material cause would exist as before, it would lack the status of being a material cause; furthermore, it would be difficult to maintain that even that [cause], being distinct from the effect, possesses its true nature. If, however, there were no distinction, then the material cause would be a mere entity without any specific excellence; consequently, since there would be no difference in their being entities, the absurdity would follow that everything could serve as a material cause. Therefore, [one must admit] a power for the production of modifications within material causes.

Those who maintain [this view] assert that it is precisely the modifications (*vikāra*) that exist in their causal material (*upādāna*) in the form of potentiality (*śakti*). We too maintain that the modifications in their causal materials are indeed unmanifest (*avyakta*), not gross; thus, there is no difference between us.

Thus [it is said]. If it is argued that the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) is purposeless because [the effect] already exists, we say no; for its result is manifestation (*abhivyakti*). In this regard, the following might be thought:

if modifications (*vikāra*) already exist within their material causes (*upādāna*), then the operation of causal factors by those seeking them would be purposeless, since they would merely be producing what already exists.

[They] do not approach [the object]. Therefore, modifications (*vikāra*) are non-existent. But that is not so, because [their existence] has manifestation as its result. For even though modifications exist, they were previously unmanifest and are manifested through the operations of causal factors (*kāraka*). Thus, the operations of causal factors possess purposefulness. If it is argued that the word "origination" (*utpatti*) is redundant in the case of manifestation—

No, because there is a difference in manifestation. In this regard, it might be argued: if jars and other objects already existing within clay and so forth are merely manifested by the activities of the potter and others—just as lamps and such manifest objects already present inside a house—then what is the distinction between saying "the lamp manifests the jar" and "the potter produces it"? But that is not the case.

Because of the difference in manifestation (*abhivyakti*). Manifestation is indeed twofold. One is the removal of that which obstructs the state of being the cause for the cognition of an object whose form is unobstructed, such as the removal of darkness from a jar hidden by it; this is manifestation. The other, however, is the removal of the obstruction to the form of an object whose form is currently obstructed; for example, in clay, the form of a jar is obstructed by its prior form, and the removal of that prior form is the manifestation of the jar. This word "origination" (*utpatti*) is merely a specific kind of manifestation.

It is faultless to say that the application of terms such as "Kaṭha" and so forth is like the designation of a specific type of Brahmin. It might be thought that because manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is an existent entity, the objection [regarding the futility of causal activity] is not avoided. This is not so, because it is non-existent. One who might think: "For a proponent of the theory that the effect exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*), since manifestation is also existent—just like other entities—the objection regarding the futility of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*) is difficult to avoid," should be told this: [The response follows: Manifestation is not something distinct from the object itself; rather, it is simply the object's own state of being perceived by the senses. Therefore, there is no futility in the operation of causal factors. Furthermore, even if one were to grant that manifestation is a distinct entity, its existence would still depend upon the object, and thus the same logic would apply. Consequently, the objection does not hold.

This fault would arise if manifestation were held to be existent, like a jar or other objects. But since it is non-existent and brought into being by the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*), what is there that is untenable? If it is argued that its non-existence leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), we say no; for the same consequence applies to your position. In this regard, one might think: "If indeed a non-existent manifestation is produced by a potter..."
"What offense has the jar committed that it should not be produced? But that is not so;

this undesirable consequence (atiprasaṅga) is equal for both of us. For you too, the established doctrine (siddhānta) is that when a jar hidden by darkness is manifested, the manifestation is non-existent while the jar itself is indeed existent. In that case, it could be urged as a consequence that, like the manifestation, the jar would also be something produced.

In the same way, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) might also be existent; thus, by virtue of this commonality of the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*), neither [the proponent nor the opponent] is to be questioned. Therefore, it is established that all entities already exist within their material causes (*upādāna*) and are merely manifested through the operations of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*). Furthermore, validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) are themselves inherently existent (*svataḥ-sat*). This is the established tenet (*siddhānta*) of the proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*). He now introduces another view.

"—the other [author] says: for he thinks thus—indeed, every effect, whose acquisition of its own nature is dependent upon a cause, becomes pure or impure through the qualities and defects of that cause. Therefore, as long as the quality and defect produced by the power of the causes of cognition, such as the sense organs, are not determined as belonging to the cognition itself,"
First of all, neither validity nor invalidity is ascertained;

nor do these two, when unascertained, serve as factors for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), and it is for that purpose that one pursues the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the connection [of the verse] is as follows: "They say there are two [types of cognition] precisely because of the determination of the excellences (*guṇa*) and defects (*doṣa*) produced by their causes. // 34 //
[272] Seeds (KA) [273] mine [274] was indeed so.
[275] First, he refutes the view that "the two [existence and non-existence] exist by themselves" with the words "by themselves. He states the reason: "because of contradiction.

The underlying intention here is as follows: first, regarding what was stated—that the property of being a probandum (*sādhyatva*), which is observed in a jar, is excluded from non-existent things such as a rabbit's horn—
"It makes the existence [of the effect] known"—this is incorrect, because it contradicts non-existence. For inference has as its object an entity that is not present to the senses;

how then could it take as its object a jar whose existence has been negated by the non-perception of something capable [of being perceived] in the clay? However, the restriction regarding the material cause is indeed established through a difference in capacities; for only certain materials, such as clay or thread, serve to produce specific effects, such as a jar or a cloth.
It is not the case that everything is capable for everyone;

rather, what is not plausible? That whoever desires a certain thing takes up that very thing. If it is thought that we do not perceive any further power (*śakti*) situated between cause and effect, we reply: no, we shall establish the existence of power in the section on presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). As for what was said—that only the modifications (*vikāra*) exist in the form of power—[that is incorrect].

If you argue that there is no difference between our two positions because the capacity for that [effect] to arise exists within the material causes (*upādāna*), that is not so. There is a great difference:

while non-existence (*abhāva*) subverts the existence of a transformation (*vikāra*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) establishes a subtle capacity (*śakti*). If you say, "Since those [effects] also exist in the form of capacity, they cannot be refuted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*)," [we reply:]...

What is this nature of being a potency (*śaktyātmatā*)? If you say it is that from which those [effects], though non-existent, will be produced, then that is accepted. If you say it is "non-manifestation," no; for even the eye is not perceived in the light. But surely, even in the light, what is covered is not perceived. Is the jar then covered in the clay? True. By what? Not by the material cause (*upādāna*), because that would entail the consequence of the effect being eternally covered. If you say the form of the clay (*mṛdākāra*) covers it, what is this "form of the clay"? If it is the universal (*jāti*) of that [clay],...

Since it would continue even above, it follows that there would be a constant enclosure. If you argue that it is the prior configuration of the lump of clay, then why would that not also exist above, such that it does not enclose the jar? Alas, for that too is accepted by those who maintain the doctrine of non-existence characterized by non-arising and non-destruction.

The constant obscuration [of the effect] is indeed unavoidable. Furthermore, the claim that subtle and delicate arrangements of parts are incapable of covering a large jar is trivial. As for the question: "If existence arises from all three causes, what determines the specific manifestation?"—this is determined solely by the difference in their potencies (*śakti*). Only a certain thing is capable of being manifested in such a way.
That which undergoes a state of modification [is the material cause], while something else, existing externally, exerts itself toward its production.

And this distinction of powers (*śaktibheda*) is indeed to be understood through the observation of the effect; thus, it is not without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Furthermore, since neither absolute difference nor absolute non-difference exists anywhere, there is no occurrence of either an over-narrow definition (*aprasaṅga*) or an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). As for what was asked regarding the material, efficient, and inherent causes...
"Power" (*śakti*)—this is extremely far-fetched and corrupted. For power is indeed power alone;
it is not the cause, because the substance (*dravya*) possessing that [power] is the cause. And like the cause itself, the causal power also pursues the accomplishment of the effect.
It will be established by the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the futility of the operation of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*) is indeed difficult to avoid.
As for the claim that "the operation is for the sake of manifestation," the fault already stated applies here. Moreover, whether manifestation exists or does not exist, its futility remains the same.
And if it does not exist, one can infer the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) in all cases: for everything that is a subject of dispute is an effect that is non-existent.

Because it is an effect, like manifestation (*abhivyakti*). And because it comes into being after not having existed, it is an effect in that very same way; for, while being capable of perception, it is not perceived, just like manifestation. As for what was said regarding the undesirable consequence concerning manifestation—that is incorrect; for recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is a powerful proof that prevents the notion that the jar has newly appeared where it did not exist before.

And since that [position] is the opposite of what is held by the proponents of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), what is the use of this excessive insistence on such deluded speech?
Furthermore, because there is a contradiction in the present context, how could validity and invalidity both belong to a single cognition as its inherent properties?
For the penetration of contradictory attributes is the basis for difference. Therefore, just as a single fire cannot possess both coldness and heat, [so it is with validity and invalidity].

Thus, there is neither validity nor invalidity of cognition. This contradiction regarding the scope of the relevant and irrelevant [topics] in the treatise (*tantra*) is to be explained by way of a double entendre (*tantra*). The duality consisting of validity and invalidity does not exist because of a contradiction in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, the duality consisting of cause and effect is not established intrinsically, because the existence of an effect is contradictory to its non-existence. To refute the view that this duality is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), he says: "extrinsic... (*parataḥ*).

Thus [he says]. He states the reason: "the absence of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). In this way, the proponent of dependence on both must be asked: "Does cognition not arise at all prior to the ascertainment of the merits and defects produced by its causes, or does it arise but remain in another form? It is not the case that cognition [does not arise at all].
Because it contradicts cognition. Once produced, by what nature would it abide? For there is no other category apart from these two categories by which it might abide.

If it is argued that what has arisen possesses the nature of one or the other [category], but its being such was not determined previously and is only determined later—this is not so, because you admit that the ascertainment [of the object] depends upon the ascertainment of its qualities. This is because of that ascertainment.

There was no certainty at all regarding the object. How, then, can it be said that there was validity? If, on the other hand, the cognition already had a determined form even previously, what is the use of ascertaining the presence of excellences (*guṇa*)? It would be more logical for one who does not suspect defects to strive solely for their refutation; and this will indeed be explained later. Thus, it is well said that [the cognition] is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
[276] Or rather, the eastern [GA] [277] "tum" means that [278] it is the locus of servitude.
[279] The state of lacking intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva);
[280] even from that, two (dva); [281] or its own-form (svarūpa).
[282] This has indeed been stated [previously].
And as for what was said— that it cannot be both by itself because of contradiction— [283] that too has already been explained.

He explains this with respect to the subject at hand: "How so? We have already stated that it is impossible for validity and invalidity—two mutually contradictory natures—to coexist or be present within a single class of cognition. However, one nature may become obscured through the proximity of another limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Just as coldness [is perceived] in water when there is contact with fire, and the delusion of heat regarding that same water depends upon that [contact], so too for one who maintains that both [heat and cold] are intrinsic, it is impossible for a cognition that is independent of anything else to possess a dual nature. He explains this—namely, that "neither duality exists from another [cause], because that would entail the consequence of being devoid of intrinsic nature"—by asking, "Of what nature [would it be]? For the entire world can be subsumed within two categories.
"Valid cognition and invalid cognition"—in this regard, for one who maintains that [cognition] is dependent on both, by what form is knowledge, which is devoid of both forms, to be defined? // 36 //

Regarding the statement "the two do not [arise] from themselves due to contradiction," someone raises a certain objection: "vijñāna... (consciousness...). He thinks as follows: if this difference in intrinsic nature were admitted to belong to the very genus (*jāti*) of cognition, or even to a single individual instance (*vyakti*) of cognition, then indeed there would be a contradiction.

However, when one admits a distinction between individual instances of valid and invalid cognition—just as water and fire possess the respective natures of cold and heat—[then there is no contradiction].

"In that case, since the two [terms] have different loci (*vyadhikaraṇa*), what is in contradiction with what? He answers: "Even so. This is the intended meaning: for it is logical that there should be a difference in nature between water and fire, which belong to different classes (*jāti*). Cognitions (*jñāna*), however, belong to a single class. In that regard, a difference in nature based on their class is not at all tenable for these [cognitions]. Rather, it would have to be based on the individual instances (*vyakti*).

However, it is reasonable to say that [validity] arises from that cause. But if there were no dependence on that, it would be difficult to determine which of the two—validity or invalidity—would apply to what, since both possess the same nature of being cognition. Furthermore, if both were inherent, there would be no need for external signs; thus, the distinction between the valid and the invalid would be impossible to state. This has been well said.

"The two [validity and invalidity] do not exist inherently because they are contradictory. But what is it that obstructs the authority of the *codanā*—whether it be its dependence on something else or its inherent nature—that you strive so hard to refute? One might object: even so, the validity of the *codanās* will be intrinsic according to the first position; and even in the second case, since there is no fault in either [position regarding] dependence on another, the non-human Vedas are authoritative.

Thus, what is the point of refuting both? It is precisely this [position]—that invalidity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) and validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*)—that is an obstacle to the authority of the Veda;

therefore, it is appropriate to refute that. And that will indeed be refuted. True. Even in the first two positions, invalidity necessarily follows. For instance, if both were inherent, there would have to be some external cause for determining one or the other.

For those who do not perceive [the truth], there can be no confidence even in a single instance. Furthermore, the pursuit of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*); and since such activity is absent when there is no confidence, it follows that [the cognition] is effectively non-valid. Thus, even though both [confidence and the cause of validity] are dependent on external factors, if the cause of validity is absent—even if the cause of invalidity is also absent—the practical application of that [cognition] does not arise; therefore, it is non-valid.
Thus, it is well said that both [extremes] are effectively refuted. // 37 //
[284] Therefore, that is not so; [285] it has been stated; [286] it is difficult to obtain; obtained.

Thus, having refuted both [theories]—that [validity] arises from itself or from another—the author states another prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) with the words "Therefore" up to "are capable. For those cognitions, non-validity is intrinsic, while validity is dependent upon something else. And this is the intended meaning here: for it is observed that even when a cognition has arisen, one does not engage in activity free from doubt until the fact that the instruments such as the sense organs possess excellence or that there is correspondence is perceived. Furthermore, validity has practical efficacy (vyavahāra) as its result.

Therefore, validity is inherently non-authoritative and depends upon something else for its authority. He says "here" because this is the reasoning stated here regarding the inherent lack of authority and the extrinsic nature of authority.

[287] Thus, he first demonstrates the reasoning (*nyāya*) regarding the lack of intrinsic validity (*aprāmāṇya*): "Lack of validity. *Nyāya* means logical argumentation (*tarka*), and that is inference (*anumāna*). And the formal application (*prayoga*) here is as follows: Lack of validity is not possessed of a cause, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*). Whatever is a non-entity is not possessed of a cause, just like a rabbit's horn.

Regarding the phrase "due to defects in the cause" (*kāraṇadoṣataḥ*), this is stated because others maintain that defects in the cause alone are the reason for invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). That which the Mīmāṃsakas believe—namely, that invalidity arises from defects in the cause—is not so; for [invalidity] is not a real entity (*avastu*) and thus lacks a cause. Regarding the claim that "validity (*prāmāṇya*) is dependent on something else," he states the formal argument (*prayoga*): "because it is a real entity" (*vastutvāt*). For them...

The meaning is that validity is produced by the qualities of the causes. And there is a formal argument: validity possesses causes because it is a real entity (*vastu*), like a jar. Furthermore, for the Buddhists, there is no such thing as a real entity that is not an effect, which would render the reason inconclusive; for even space (*nabhas*) is not a real entity, being merely the absence of obstruction. [This is so] "by the qualities."

And this is merely a restatement. For they consider that the qualities of the causes (*kāraṇaguṇa*) are the cause of validity (*prāmāṇya*). However, these [qualities] need not be included within the [definition of] pervasion (*vyāpti*). But what are these so-called "qualities" that are the cause of validity? Indeed, no qualities whatsoever are perceived apart from the sense faculties and so forth. If it is thought:

The claim that "qualities (*guṇa*) are specific excellences produced by various medicinal treatments" is incorrect. For if it were so, validity would not arise for those [cognitions] in which no such specific excellence has been produced by them. Therefore, the qualities must be explained; they are stated as follows: the meaning of the term "quality" is the purity of the sense faculties and so forth, which is to say, the equilibrium of the humors (*dhātu*) such as wind (*vāta*). For when these [humors] exist in a state of equilibrium within the sense faculties, they are called "qualities."

Remaining in such a state, they produce validity (*prāmāṇya*). However, when the elements (*dhātu*) are in a diseased state, defects such as cataracts arise, originating from those [elemental] disorders. In the case of speech as well, the purity of the speaker’s intention is a quality (*guṇa*), while intentions to deceive and so forth are defects (*doṣa*). Since these [defects] lack the nature of validity, it is impossible for them to be the cause of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) with respect to a non-existent object.

Invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is produced by that [defect]. Validity (*prāmāṇya*), however, is the ascertainment of the object and consists of the nature of the thing itself; thus it is logical that it is both produced and known from excellences (*guṇa*). At the time of its arising, every cognition is indeed invalid, being non-ascertaining in nature, until the emergence of a cognition of excellence or a corroborative cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*);
but subsequently, by virtue of those, validity is produced for it. [Objection: But now, the cognition that has already passed away is simply non-existent.
Thus, what will serve as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? At the time when that [cognition] occurred, it was then overwhelmed by innate invalidity;
and since it is non-existent at a later time, how could there be validity from anything else? This is true.

However, there is indeed another means of valid cognition that arises subsequent to the knowledge of the correspondence of excellences (*guṇa*). For once an object has been understood, one who previously observed deviation [in other cases]—

One who has not gained confidence through the observation of the intrinsic nature of cognition does not engage in worldly activity free from doubt until one determines the excellence of the sense organs and other factors and concludes, "This is exactly so. Once the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that [cognition] has arisen and been understood—either through the determination of its excellence or through a corroborating cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*)—worldly activities proceed. Furthermore, even for that [corroborating cognition], validity is not established by the observation of its own intrinsic nature.

Because that [intrinsic] form is obstructed by invalidity; rather, it is established solely through the ascertainment of excellences (*guṇa*). Therefore, it is well said that validity is produced by excellences.

As they say: "The production of validity, which consists of certainty, is determined for itself as an effect of the cognition of excellences—which are the causes of correspondence—because it is the nature of a real entity (*vastu*); therefore, that alone is accepted. // 39 //
[288] Those who are awake; [289] not those who are lying down; [290] but that is not the authority. (KHA)
[291] Yourself [292] not [293] speak (KA) [293] bad (GA)

Furthermore, for this reason as well, validity is not intrinsic; thus he says: "For validity... The meaning is this: if validity were inherent and naturally bound to the very nature of cognition, then, since the absence of validity (invalidity) is a non-entity and therefore uncreated, it could not be dependent on anything else. Consequently, it would follow that all cognitions—even those such as dreams—are valid, because there is no difference in their being cognitions, and because validity is bound solely to that [nature of cognition]. Moreover, invalidity, being a non-entity, cannot be produced. // 40 //

[294] Since it is established that [the Veda] is not produced by human agency, [295] how then could its lack of authority be anything other than artificial? For its existence [as unauthoritative] depends upon the presence of defects.

And its absence is observed when that [defect] is absent. One perceives a conch shell as yellow when one has jaundice (*kāmalā*), but as white when that [jaundice] is removed. Therefore, we know that the non-validity (*aprāmāṇya*) which arises through the presence of defects is its effect; hence he says, "In my view. This is the intended meaning: here, non-validity is not produced by defects. When [the defects] exist...
However, since non-existent qualities within defects do not produce their own effect—namely validity—there is no fault of implying that the non-entity of invalidity would possess a cause. // 41 //
[296] In the absence of that [cause], what indeed is the cause of validity, by whose absence there is the non-arising of that [validity]?

Therefore, he says: "The sense organs, etc., up to the cause. By the word "etc.," objects, the person (*puruṣa*), and so forth are included. The qualities (*guṇa*) of the sense organs and the person have already been explained. Furthermore, for the object as well, qualities such as grossness and so forth are [the causes of validity], while defects (*doṣa*) such as subtlety and so forth are [the causes of invalidity]. Thus, it has been established that the qualities of the sense organs and the other factors [contribute] to validity.
"Because it is the cause. But how is there an absence of that?

To this he says: "That is non-existent. He demonstrates those very [causes] by showing their deficiency: "Because they are defective. For adventitious defects drive out the qualities (*guṇas*). In the absence of any one of the sense organs and so forth, the qualities, being without a substrate, do not exist.
Just as, for those who maintain that the Vedas are eternal, [the Vedas] possess those qualities even though there is no author. // 42 //

[297] Why is this so? It is precisely because virtues are set aside by defects that the Mīmāṃsakas hold this delusion: namely, that the cognition of falsity is produced by defects. But in the ultimate sense (paramārthataḥ), however—

Defects, which are opposed to excellences, exclude those very excellences. Therefore, due to the absence of a cause, when validity is absent, non-validity remains inherent; thus he says: "For this very reason. (43)

Therefore, it is established that validity depends upon the ascertainment of qualities that are synonyms for purity. By their very nature, cognitions are non-valid; they are characterized as such through the absence of purity. For when purity is absent, non-validity—which is not set aside by a validity that has been excluded due to the absence of its causes—is what is characterized. He concludes with "tasmāt" (therefore): [298] taḥ śu (KHA).

Furthermore, he states that invalidity does not arise from defects (*doṣa*) by saying "anvaya... (in the verse). Its meaning is as follows: invalidity is threefold, consisting of non-cognition (*ajñāna*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and error (*viparyaya*). Among these, first, invalidity in the form of non-cognition is to be understood as being produced solely by the absence of causes;

it must be admitted by the Mīmāṃsakas that it does not depend upon defects. Therefore, since invalidity is observed even in the absence of defects when there is merely the presence of the absence of causes, invalidity does not arise from defects.

And thus, since validity is accepted as dependent upon qualities, for those who maintain that the Veda is eternal, there is an absence of a person [to provide such qualities], and consequently, qualities cannot exist without a substratum;
whereas even for those who maintain that the Veda has an author, [validity depends] upon the qualities of that author.

89} Since the qualities of an agent, which lack a foundation in reality due to the impossibility of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), cannot be established, the authority of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) is not tenable; thus he says: "And therefore... (verse 46).

[299] Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) has been established by means of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*). Now he begins the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*). He states the reason with "for not" (*na hi*). This is the intended meaning: first of all, it is not from the cognition of excellences (*guṇajñāna*) or from the cognition of correspondence (*saṃvādajñāna*)...

Alternatively, knowledge does not arise at all beforehand. Nor does what has newly arisen appear as being of the nature of doubt; for we do not perceive a jar in contact with the sense organ thinking, "Is it a jar or is it not? rather, a cognition arises that is precisely of the nature of certainty, namely, "This is indeed a jar. Therefore, from the very arising of knowledge...

Immediately thereafter, the engagement in worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) is observed by all cognizers. For even that which is silver known through an erroneous cognition is seen to be effective for practical action (*arthakriyā*), just like the cognition of real silver. Therefore, it is not tenable for one who is in doubt; hence, certainty has arisen. What else could constitute its validity (*prāmāṇya*), even if there were correspondence (*saṃvāda*)?
Or, if the very essence of validity consists merely in the cognition of qualities and nothing more, what is the use of disregarding that [cognition]?
If it is argued that there is dependence on something else because such [validity] is subject to deviation, we say no; for even so, the cognition remains independent.

Even for one who has been previously deceived, a cognition that is determinate and entirely independent [of external confirmation] arises. However, because of its similarity to the cognition of the deceiver, the knower suspects its truthfulness.

Even for one who is thus suspecting, the capacity for validity does not fail, since—as before—the object of cognition is determined. For the knower, however, the suspicion arises from the observation of defects; it ceases once there is a determination of either the presence or absence of those defects.

It does not depend upon corroborative cognition (*saṃvādajñāna*). For while the cognition of a jar already exists, what would one who has conceived a doubt achieve by means of another cognition of the jar? Indeed, that [other cognition] is not its remover, because it occurs only when the former is already present. Therefore, the nature of all cognitions is inherently determinate (*niścayātmaka*). Even if a doubt should ever arise, even then, for the sake of its removal, one must investigate the presence or absence of an exception (*apavāda*).

Nor [is validity established] by the cognition of the quality of correspondence (*saṃvādaguṇajñāna*). For if that were disregarded, validity itself would not be established. The same applies to the cognitions of the quality and of correspondence; because they too would be dependent, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) regarding the inability to instill the capacity for validity in the first cognition. This will be explained in detail later. Thus, the intended meaning of the present context has been explained. Furthermore, {1, ...}

Furthermore, the capacity of all entities to produce their own effects, being non-existent [prior to manifestation], cannot be produced by anything else, because [the cause] merely brings about its manifestation.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a sick person whose power has been taken away by disease, the capacity for eating and so forth—which was indeed non-existent—is bestowed by various medicines. [Reply: Not so; this is merely the manifestation of what was concealed. Otherwise, one would have to resort to the postulation of the destruction of a prior capacity and the production of a new capacity.
There would be excessive gravity [of the fault]. For this very reason, there can be no remedy even through various medicines for those whose power has been destroyed;
for if their power were non-existent, it would certainly be produced [again], since there is no distinction [between them and others]. Therefore, all...

Entities, having arisen from their own causes as possessing capacities, have those capacities obscured by some adventitious cause; they then initiate an effect once their capacities are manifested by specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). However, such dependence on manifestation is not possible in the case of cognition, because [cognition] consists of the apprehension of an object.
Because cognition cannot be determined apart from its own form, the determination of the object necessarily occurs at the very moment of its arising. // 47 //
[300] Knowledge (jñāna) is immeasurable (apramāṇa); [301] because it does not exist as a [separate] entity, that [knowledge] is such.
[303] da (GA) [304] na (KA) [305] vyava (KHA)

[306] Furthermore, even by one who maintains that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇyavādin*), it must be admitted that the arising of valid cognition is caused precisely by such factors as sense faculties endowed with excellence (*guṇavat*). Thus, if excellences are the cause for the arising of valid cognition, then, this being the case, the determination of the object— which is its effect— must likewise be dependent upon them.
[This is] appropriate, because the validity [of the cognition] is dependent upon that [absence of defects];

therefore, he says: "the acquisition of its own nature. This is the intended meaning: even in the production of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), excellences (*guṇa*) are not required merely as "excellences" per se; rather, they are required as a means for the removal of defects (*doṣa*). For defects obstruct the production of valid knowledge; these [defects] are driven away by the excellences.

"They are not able to subvert it. For this very reason, even when the qualities of the speaker—such as compassion and so forth—are absent, validity is established in the Veda solely from the absence of defects. Furthermore, a "cause" is indeed a quality with respect to the production of valid cognition;

however, it is not on that account reasonable for there to be a dependence upon it even for the determination of the object, which is the effect of valid cognition. For entities depend upon causes only for their own origination.

Not for the accomplishment of an effect. For it is not observed that once a jar has come into being in dependence upon causes such as a lump of clay and a staff, it still requires those same things for the purpose of carrying water. Rather, its activity once its own nature has been acquired is understood to proceed entirely independently of causes.
Therefore, it is established that in every respect, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is independent of anything else in the determination of an object. // 48 //

He elaborates on the statement that "a capacity which does not exist inherently cannot be produced by another" through three verses beginning with *jāte 'pi*. The intended meaning is as follows: independence from anything else is indeed the very basis of validity (*prāmāṇya*). If, even when a cognition has arisen, its validity were dependent upon the ascertainment of the excellence of its causes, then the production of a cognition of purity would have to await some other cause. [And] of that purity, if it remains unascertained...

Because it is equal to the non-existent, even that cognition of purity possesses validity only when there is purity in its cause and when there is a cognition of that purity. In this very way, since the cognition of the purity of the root cause would require further and further cognitions of purity, it would result in an infinite regress; thus, it cannot in any way attain the status of being a valid means of knowledge. // 49–51 //
