He states that there is no infinite regress if validity is intrinsic, saying "when. He states the reason, saying "it ceases. This is the intended meaning: first of all, the ascertainment of the object is established from the very nature of the cognition itself. Furthermore, the suspicion of falsity ceases without effort simply through the non-cognition of the defects that cause it. For the non-cognition of defects—that is, their prior absence—is not something to be achieved through effort. [Objection: But surely, it is not from mere non-cognition...
Non-existence is established because [the cognition] exists even when that [defect] is present. Nor is validity established without the ascertainment of the absence of defects. True;
however, even that is indeed accomplished without effort.

Generally speaking, for cognizers, empirical activity is observed to proceed entirely without doubt regarding the arising of cognition. Even for one who has developed doubt, the well-known means for dispelling that doubt—such as burning and cutting in the case of gold—are sufficient; since certainty is produced by this much alone, there is no need to go further. And this will indeed be explained below. // 52 //
[307] Furthermore, because that [invalidity] does not exist in that [cognition], he concludes:

"Therefore," meaning that the validity of cognitions, which is inherent to their nature as consciousness, is set aside by two factors: the defect in the cause (*kāraṇadoṣa*) and the cognition of the object being otherwise (*arthānyathātvajñāna*). And the cognition of the object being otherwise is twofold: either by subverting the previously apprehended form, as in "this is not so," or...

Or [it is established] by the manifestation of reality (*tattvaprakāśana*). The causes of cognitions are the sense organs and so forth. Regarding these, defects such as cataracts (*timira*) arising from wind (*vāta*) and other humors, which—by their very nature—obstruct the validity that would otherwise generally apply to those cognitions, are removed by the knowledge of them.

As for the statement that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is not produced by causes because it is a non-entity (*avastutva*), he refutes that with the words "invalidity. Even if invalidity is indeed divided into three types, what follows from that?

Therefore, he says: "Because it is a real entity" (*vastutvāt*). This is the intended meaning: invalidity is indeed threefold, consisting of the absence of cognition (*jñānābhāva*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and error (*viparyaya*).

In that regard, with respect to doubt and error, the reason "because it is not a real entity" (*avastutvāt*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), because those two are real entities insofar as they consist of cognition (*jñānātmaka*). // 54 //
The prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge, however, is established precisely because it is a non-entity (*avastu*). Nor is this [non-existence] produced by defects for us either;

for, as you have stated, its establishment follows simply from the absence of the causes of knowledge. Therefore, with the intention that if such a causeless state were being proved, it would merely be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), he says:

"in the absence of cognition" (*avijñāne*). Furthermore, one cannot infer that doubt and error are likewise causeless merely on the basis of their being denotable by the term "invalidity" (*aprāmāṇya*).
Just as in the case of ignorance, speech too would result in having horns, because it is denotable by the word "cow. // 55 //
[308] Because it would follow that there must be another means of cognition (anumāna).
[309] Surely this infinite regress (anavasthā) occurs just as much when invalidity (aprāmāṇya), like validity (prāmāṇya), is held to depend upon something else.

For dependence (pāratantrya) leads to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Therefore, what is the distinction? To this he says: "due to defects" (doṣataḥ). The meaning of this is as follows: for the Mīmāṃsakas who maintain that validity is intrinsic (svataḥ-prāmāṇya), there is no infinite regress when invalidity arises from defects. This is because, even when the defects must be known, an infinite regress is not incurred, just as it was avoided in the case of the knowledge of excellences (guṇa-jñāna). // 56 //

The seed for avoiding the charge of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has been stated by those who maintain that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇyavādin*); he now clarifies it with the words "directly" (*sākṣāt*). This is the intended meaning: for an infinite regress occurs only when there is a dependence on a member of the same class, as was said regarding the dependence of validity upon another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is not [established] by a means of knowledge through itself.

Thus, when a matter is understood directly through a cognition that is itself non-erroneous, it is grasped with extreme ease; therefore, the mere fact of its dependence on another does not lead to an infinite regress. [Objection:
But if validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), then since the preceding cognition has also arisen without doubt, how could it ever be invalid?
"Why is it that the latter is not sublated by that very same former [cognition] which previously sublated it?
To this he says: "The former," etc. The intention is as follows: True;

although the validity of the former is established by default, it becomes invalid when sublated by the latter, which serves as its exception. As for the question, "Why is the latter not sublated by that very same former one?"—[the answer follows].
That is not so;

for the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is not established by mere wishful thinking. Rather, that which appears as the sublator of something is designated as its sublator. And the former [cognition] does not appear in the form of a subsequent sublator that has not yet arisen.

He will explain this very point later when he says, "and not by the sublation of a future [cognition]. However, for a subsequent [cognition], its very arising is impossible without the sublation of the preceding cognition. And that [subsequent cognition] has already arisen; therefore, it alone is the sublater of the preceding one. Since that [subsequent cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by its own nature, there is no infinite regress whatsoever. // 57 //
[310] Regarding the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa),
[311] indeed, let it be that the former is sublated by the subsequent contrary cognition directly.

Because both [cognitions] arise with respect to the same object. However, where the subsequent [cognition] has the defect of the cause as its object, then because of the difference in objects, sublation (*bādha*) is not logical; thus, the claim that "validity is set aside by the cognition of a defect arising from the cause" is poorly stated.
Therefore, he says: "By the words 'defective' up to 'sublation'... The intended meaning is this: even though there is a cognition of a defective cause...
In cases of error such as a yellow conch-shell and the like, there is a difference in the object;

nevertheless, by implication, it attains the status of having the same object, and sublation indeed occurs. For when it is known that "the conch is yellow," and subsequently the defect in the cause of the cognition is understood, the yellowness of the conch is effectively rejected. This is because whatever effect derives its very existence from a particular cause [is negated when that cause is found to be defective].

That [cognition] is corrupted by that specific defect. And this is the defect of cognition: the manifestation of something as other than it actually exists. Therefore, when a defect in the cause is understood, the fact that the object is otherwise [than it appears] is necessarily understood.
And thus, there is a direct equivalence with erroneous cognition. On this very point, he cites a Vedic principle: "as in the case of the *godohana* vessel," and so forth.

Thus it is said. When the fetching of water (*praṇayana*) by means of a *camasa* cup for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) has been prescribed in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there occurs another injunction regarding the connection between a subordinate factor and its fruit (*guṇaphala-sambandha-vidhi*).
For example: "One desiring cattle should fetch [water] by means of a *godohana* vessel. The meaning of this is: "One should bring about cattle by means of the *godohana*.
Thus, this *godohana* vessel, being for the sake of cattle which are desired by the person, is indeed for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*).
The *camasa* vessel, which serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), is held to be superseded [by the *godohana*]. In that case as well, the difference in their respective domains is clear.

For while the benefit to the sacrifice is what is to be accomplished by the *camasa*, cattle are the result of the *godohana* by virtue of its very nature; thus, due to the identity of their purpose, supersession will also be stated there.
For the *godohana* is a substance (*dravya*); it is not capable of producing a result while remaining indifferent, unattached to an action.

Since it grasps the fetching of water—which is proximate and subserves the sacrifice—as the basis for any action one intends to perform, the meaning of the scripture is established as: "By means of that [action] based upon it, cattle are to be brought about. And thus, since the fetching of water for the sake of the sacrifice is accomplished by that very [action], the *camasa* (wooden cup) is set aside. But how can this be, given that it is already enjoined within the sacrifice?

By its abandonment, the benefit to the sacrifice (*kratūpakāra*) is produced through the *godohana* vessel. True. However, in the performance [of the rite] by one desiring cattle, the sacrifice itself authorizes the *godohana* as the means for achieving its own benefit. For interest in one's own quality is for the sake of the task to be accomplished, not out of a sense of ownership. And since that task is already secured from the *godohana* by the sacrifice precisely because it serves the purpose of the fruit, what need is there for concern regarding one's own quality? As it has been said:
[312] Or rather, [313] it is for the sake of the effect that everyone indeed takes care to perceive their own qualities.
But when the effect is accomplished through the quality of another object, what is the use of its own quality?

Thus, just as here the cup for the sacrifice (camasa), though having a different scope, is set aside by virtue of its purpose for the person (puruṣārtha) because they are effectively equal in purpose, so it is here as well; therefore, there is no fault. // 58 //

Is this the general rule—that in all cases the subsequent [cognition] sublates the prior? No, he says: "In that case. If, in that situation, when there is the cognition of a defective cause, or when there is a contrary [cognition], or when there is no sublating cognition of the subsequent kind, or when there is knowledge of a defect in the cause, then the sublation of the prior occurs; but not otherwise. Now, if both arise simultaneously, what indeed will happen?

Therefore he says: "When that [sublation] has arisen. At that time, when the sublater is itself subject to exception, the [cognition] obtains its original, general validity (prāmāṇya) immediately, free from exception. // 59 //

[Objection: But surely it is by a third valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that the sublater is sublated. How, then, is that [third cognition] itself a valid cognition? To this he says: "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*). Indeed, every cognition that has arisen is intrinsically a valid cognition so long as no defect is perceived.

This applies equally to the third [cognition]. Therefore, when that [third cognition] effects the sublation of the sublater, the validity of the first [cognition] is established. [Objection: But if [defects] do not exist...
Just as the apprehension of defects regarding defects arises in the first [moment], so too does it arise in the last; thus, validity is not established.

Therefore, he says: "regarding defects. This is the intended meaning: when the cognition of a defect has arisen, the suspected defects obstruct validity. However, in the third [moment], the cognition of a defect has not yet arisen; rather, there is only suspicion.
It is not proper to act based on mere non-perception,
because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly transactions. [314] Śāśa.
For this very reason, Nārāyaṇa said to Nara in the Gītā:
"O son of Kuntī, neither this world nor the next exists for one whose mind is full of doubt."

Thus [it is said]. However, for one in whom a cognition of defect or a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) arises regarding the third cognition, their ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) concludes with the fourth cognition. But this is not always the case;
for generally, an uncontradicted ascertainment is observed at the very moment the first cognition arises. In some instances, however, it concludes with a subverting cognition.

The arising of the third cognition is also not very common, much less the birth of the fourth cognition. Nevertheless, even if that [fourth cognition] exists, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is not impaired; it is for this reason alone that we have stated this [in our commentary]. And since the author of the *Vārttika* will likewise say, "the determination arises from the fourth cognition," or "from the production of three or four cognitions," it is for this very reason [that we have spoken thus]. What [more is there to say]?

Furthermore, the reason why one should not suspect [the absence of] a defect when no such cognition has arisen is that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not conform to a purpose. For if a cognizer who has observed deviation were to lack confidence even in a single instance, and if, consequently, worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) were to be cut off—since those transactions are established through means of valid cognition, and not the means of valid cognition through them—it is said: "it is without a means of valid cognition" (*niṣpramāṇikā*).

This is the intended meaning: for as long as the absence of defects (*doṣa*) is not ascertained, there remains a valid suspicion on the part of one who perceives properties common to both means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their opposites. However, once the ascertainment of the absence of defects has occurred, for one who would suspect them [defects], there is a direct contradiction with that very absence. For the object, the sense faculties, and so forth, are the causes of cognition; therefore, their defects...
[Causes such as] distance, cataracts, and so forth. For example, trees standing at a distance are apprehended as having a single form, [being perceived as] "a forest";
yet when one approaches them, they are seen to be manifold. In that case, it is determined that the cognition of oneness arose due to the defect of distance.
However, since no defect whatsoever is observed in the cognition of manifoldness, how can it be suspected [that this cognition is erroneous]?

In this way, the same fault applies when there is darkness or a confusion regarding a cow or a horse; however, since no fault whatsoever can be suspected in the cognition of a cow during the daytime, that [cognition] is valid. Likewise, when the absence of defects in the eyes and other sense organs—such as cataracts—is understood, any suspicion of a defect is itself without foundation. Even in cases where object-defects such as similarity or motion are the causes of error, [the validity remains intact once those are accounted for].

In that case as well, once the distinguishing property has been determined and its immutability understood, there is no suspicion of any defect; thus, there is no lack of validity for the cognition occurring at that time. // 60 //
[315] What, then, is *nirṇaya*?
[316] (KA) It is the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*) from doubt (*nāda*). (KHA)
[317] Dependent on what?
[318] On the self (ātman).
Thus, since the absence of defects is established by only three or four cognitions, no further cognition beyond those need be sought for the establishment of validity.

[Otherwise] there would be an infinite regress. However, as soon as the third or fourth cognition has arisen, one [cognition], whether preceding or succeeding, attains its own intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) without exception; thus he says: "In this way" (evam). // 61 //

It has been established, first of all, that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), while their invalidity is due to defects (*doṣa*). Now, the primary subject at hand—the validity of the Vedas—must be demonstrated in such a way that it is proven. To that end, he says "the word" (*śabda*), meaning that defects in a verbal expression depend solely upon the speaker and are not inherent (*svābhāvika*). This is the intended sense: when [defects] depend upon the speaker...
It has been established that defects reside in the speaker;

therefore, since there is no speaker in the case of the Veda, defects—which require a locus—cannot exist, and thus the validity of the Vedas is established as being beyond reproach. And it remains a settled principle that a defect in a word is dependent upon something else [namely, the speaker].

For it has already been established that [the word] does not actually touch upon the object. It is the person alone who, wandering in delusion, perceives one thing as another and, communicating it to another exactly in that way, vitiates the word. And in some cases, having understood it otherwise, he speaks otherwise out of a desire to deceive.

Even in that case, the perception of defects in the word is entirely dependent upon that [external factor]. A word is perceived as being corrupted by defects such as those arising from the vocal organs (*sthāna*) or the articulatory efforts (*karaṇa*), or by defects such as being *kalā*, *ādhmāta*, *ambūkṛta*, or *eṇīkṛta*. In every respect, [the defect] is dependent on something else; it is not, however, intrinsically defective by its own nature (*svabhāva*) like a foul odor. Now, since this defect dependent on the speaker does not exist in a sentence composed by a person when uttered by a virtuous speaker, he says: "In the absence of that" (verse 62).
[319] Having arisen (KA),
[320] while uttering the sound (KHA, GA): {1,97} Is it not the case that the qualities of the speaker remove the defects from the speaker himself?

How does the word become faultless when those [faults] are removed? To this he says: "by its qualities" (*tadguṇaiḥ*). It has been stated that only the faults of the speaker (*vaktṛdoṣa*) corrupt the word. If the fault is driven out by the qualities, what possibility is there for faults to reside in the word? For it is not possible for faults that do not even reside in the speaker to be transferred to the word; thus, the expression "transfer" is used only figuratively (*phalataḥ*). Or rather, because of the absence of a speaker, the faults remain without a substratum.

He says "or else" (yad vā) because they are unable to be eternal Vedic statements. The implication is that the intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of the Vedas is not undermined by the absence of defects. // 63 //

But surely you yourself have admitted that in human statements, the absence of defects follows from the presence of excellences (*guṇa*). And if this is so, how is this distinction established—that excellences function only to eliminate defects and not toward the validity (*prāmāṇya*) itself? To this he says: "In the case of human [statements]. This is the meaning: it is true that in human statements both [factors]—the absence of defects and the nature of excellences—are indeed observed. However, as to how validity does not arise from excellences, that has already been stated previously regarding the infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
For it would be so; therefore, qualities are useful merely for the absence of defects, and they are not utilized for validity in their own right. // 64 //

He concludes this very point with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). For there are two causes of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*): either the cognition of defects in the cause or a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). And when defects have been eliminated by excellences (*guṇa*) in the case of human statements, neither of these two is possible.
Indeed, non-existent defects cannot be apprehended; nor can there be a subverter of a cognition produced from a cause that is free from defects.
It remains established. Therefore, because those two causes of invalidity are absent, validity is by default not sublated. // 65 //

And since there is no denial [of truth], the validity that belongs to human statements by virtue of their generally producing cognition is not removed; thus he says: "The production of cognition. Here, an objection is raised: "The absence of defects" (verse 98). If, in the case of the words of a reliable person (*āpta*), the absence of defects is based on excellences (*guṇa*), then, insofar as validity would depend upon the knowledge of those excellences, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). What indeed is the distinction here?

Alternatively, validity might depend upon the cognition of excellences (*guṇa*), or the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) might depend upon that [cognition of excellences]. For if the cognition of excellences is required in order to apprehend the absence of defects, then the absence of defects for that very [cognition] depends upon the cognition of excellences;
and since the same would apply to that [subsequent cognition] as well, there is the aforementioned infinite regress (*anavasthā*). And thus, there is the uprooting of validity. // 66 //
He refutes this with the words "tadā" (then).

This is the intended meaning: if the excellences (*guṇas*) were to dispel the defects (*doṣas*) only after they themselves had been known, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). But this is not the case. How, then, do they function? To this he says: "in the absence of defects" (*doṣābhāve*).

Thus, by virtue of being pure existence (*sanmātratā*), the excellences (*guṇa*) dispel the defects (*doṣa*). Therefore, since the non-existent defects are not perceived, intrinsic validity (*sahaja-prāmāṇya*) remains established. // 67 //

[321] Thus, first of all, it has been explained how defects are avoided even in the case of human statements, despite the presence of qualities that might otherwise render them faulty. However, in the case of the Veda, which was not composed by an author, defects have no basis to exist and therefore cannot even be suspected; thus, there is no possibility whatsoever of doubting its authority. [322] Indeed, there is no doubt regarding its lack of validity.

He says: "In that regard. The meaning is that while validity is the default state and invalidity is its exception, the removal of that [invalidity] is simpler in the case of the Veda; it is not as cumbersome as in the case of human speech, which depends upon [the presence of] excellences (*guṇa*). // 68 //
[322] Thus,
[323] because even in the case of human statements, validity does not depend upon qualities (*guṇa*).

Therefore, the validity of words does not depend on the speaker; rather, it would depend on him only if there were a dependence upon his qualities. But this is not the case, as has already been explained. Consequently, the practice of the Naiyāyikas and others of postulating a speaker for the Veda in order to establish its authority—specifically their reliance on the claim that the Vedas were composed by Maheśvara—is untenable.

With the intention that their intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) is established precisely because of the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) up to the end of verse 99. He states "the postulation of an author" (*kartṛkalpanā*)—which gives rise to the suspicion of defects—is indeed conducive to invalidity (*apramāṇatva*), as expressed in the phrase beginning with "invalidity" (*apramāṇatva*). // 69 //

For this very reason, even the objection raised by the nihilists—that the Veda lacks authority because it was not composed by a reliable person (*āpta*)—does not constitute a fault in the case of the eternal Veda; thus he says, "And therefore" (*tataśca*). This is the intended meaning:

a human statement is vitiated by the fact that it was not composed by a reliable person. For if it were not composed by such a person, it would, by implication, have been composed by one who is unreliable.

It would follow that it is tainted by those defects and thus lacks authority (*apramāṇa*). However, even if it were eternal and not composed by a reliable person (*āpta*), it would still be free from defects; therefore, its authority is not undermined by the fact that it was not composed by a reliable person. For even a human composition is not invalid because it was not composed by a reliable person, but rather because it was composed by an unreliable one (*anāpta*). Since that [reliance on an unreliable author] does not exist in the case of what is eternal, how could it become invalid? But surely, by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*)...

The lack of authority [of the Veda] has been established by others through the example of the speech of children and the like, on the grounds that it was not composed by a reliable person (*āpta*). Therefore, let only logical fallacies such as the contradictory (*viruddha*) and the unestablished (*asiddha*) be stated. What is the use of this statement which merely follows its own lineage?
To this, he says: "Of the formulations" (*prayogāṇām*). It is not only of this particular formulation.

We shall indeed state the counter-arguments for all these applications later on, beginning with the words "the cognition produced by an injunction" (*codanājanitā buddhiḥ*). Therefore, the reasons for non-validity—which are contradicted by counter-reasons—do not determine non-validity through the production of doubt if they are of equal strength. However, if the reasons for validity are stronger, [they do determine it].
Consequently, being thus sublated, those factors that cause invalidity can no longer affect the self [of the cognition]. // 70 //
[324] Regarding the word "those" (ta):
how, then, is it that being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) is not a defect?

For a trustworthy person, having ascertained an object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), composes a statement; and that [statement] is [valid] precisely because of its correspondence with other means of valid cognition.

For [only] that which is composed by a reliable person (*āpta*) becomes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How could that which is not composed by a reliable person—being another means of cognition whose root is non-existent—be a means of valid cognition?

Therefore, he says: "composed by a person" (*pauruṣeya*). This is the intended meaning: a Vedic sentence is a means of valid cognition regarding its own object precisely without depending on any other root; what need has it for another means of cognition? But in the case of human speech, another means of cognition is the root cause; thus, in the absence of that [other means], it becomes defective. // 71 //
[325] As for the objection that those [cognitions] which lack a real basis and whose corroboration is impossible cannot possess validity—
that is incorrect. For by the very same reason that injunctions (*codanā*) do not have other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as their basis, [they are self-validating].

Therefore, this very lack of consistency with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is itself the primary cause of their authority. For this reason, he will state: "when the object is not [already] perceived," and "the scripture is purposeful when it concerns what has not been reached. If these were rooted in other means of valid cognition, they would necessarily result in being mere restatements (*anuvāda*).
It is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For we do not intend to say that the mere goer is the means of valid cognition; thus he says: "by that" (tena). // 72 //
[326] Even in the case of human speech regarding an object already apprehended by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
corroboration is not the cause of its validity; how much less so, then, for Vedic sentences whose objects lie beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition?

With this intention, he says: "of another as well. The meaning is that even that [other cognition] is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely by itself. Now, one and the same object is understood from multiple authoritative statements (*āptavākya*), and all of those are means of valid knowledge. For example: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age," and "One should perform the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception."
And as for the word "or" (*vā*). Therefore, how can it be said that being an object not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the sole cause of validity?

To this he says: "Of those having the same object. For it will be stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) among rice and other grains that fall upon the same purpose: "But those having the same purpose may be optional" (12.3.10).

Thus, even here, because of the difference between cognizers (*pramātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are established as being merely optional (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*), like the optionality regarding [the cutting of] branches and so forth. Mutual corroboration (*anyonya-saṃvāda*), however, is not the cause of their validity. For instance, the *Gautamīya* and *Gobhilīya* [Smṛtis] are the means of knowledge for the *Chandogas*, while the *Yājñavalkīya* is the means of knowledge for the *Vājasaneyins*, due to their being subject to optionality. Because each individual scriptural statement of Smṛti is to be treated as optional, it serves to inform each respective cognizer; validity does not arise from mutual corroboration.

Even for those who study the *Dharmadraṇa*, mutual corroboration is not the cause of its authority. For when one person has known that object, another's statement is merely a repetition; rather, it is the other [original source] alone that is the means of valid cognition. This should be demonstrated in the same way regarding medical sciences as well. // 73 //
[328] This is the reason for the invalidity of perception.

[Objection: But what happens in a case where various cognitions of a single object arise for a single knower through multiple means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For example, suppose someone first understands a fire located at a distance through the words of a reliable person (*āpta*).

Furthermore, approaching [the fire] from smoke, one infers it; then, drawing even closer, one perceives it directly. For in that case, all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have mutually consistent objects. Therefore, how could non-contradiction (*saṃvāda*) not be a cause for validity? To this, he says: "Even where... The intention is as follows: if, first of all, [the subsequent cognitions] do not have an object exceeding [that of the first],...

Thus, all of these [means of knowledge] are such that, among them, only the first is the primary means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The others, however, are of the nature of restatements (*anuvāda*). Yet these do not have non-superadded objects; for this object is not apprehended by the preceding means of knowledge in the same way as it is by each subsequent one, due to the addition of the connection with successive points in time. Furthermore, from the statement of a reliable person (*āptavākya*), it is understood in a general sense that "the mountain possesses fire."

Furthermore, specific details of that [fire] are understood through the inference from smoke; and by the perception of the unique smoke, [the fire] is distinguished by its various components such as wood and so forth.
Moreover, when all its particulars are fully disclosed by direct perception, it is determined with extreme clarity as "this is it," being immediately present.
Thus, there is no validity [of cognition] based on corroboration regarding objects of increasingly greater detail. // 74 //
[329] Gone; [330] he followed; [331] approved.
[332] Furthermore, if validity were based on correspondence (*saṃvāda*), an infinite regress would result; thus he says: "By means of consistency" (*saṅgatyā*). // 75 //

Now, if non-contradictory cognition is valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and non-contradiction is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*), then once that purposeful action has arisen, what need is there for another means of knowledge? As they say: "Valid knowledge is non-contradictory cognition; non-contradiction is the stability of purposeful action."

Thus, having asserted that there are only two means of valid cognition—perception and inference—and having stated that "one who acts after determining an object by means of these two is not deceived regarding purposeful action," it follows that the status of a means of valid cognition is determined solely by the culmination in purposeful action; therefore, there is no infinite regress in the requirement for another cognition. To this he says: "Of what? The intention is as follows: [the question concerns] the cognition of purposeful action.

The statement "it is sufficient" [to stop at the first cognition] is for the sake of establishing its validity; however, by pursuing successive purposeful actions, there would indeed be an infinite regress. If, on the other hand, that [second cognition] were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even without depending on another subsequent cognition, then why is it not accepted that the very first cognition of the object is a valid means of knowledge without such dependence? For no distinction whatsoever is observed between these two in terms of their nature as cognitions or their being free from doubt. Furthermore, regarding the object by means of a valid means of knowledge...

One who acts after having made a determination considers there to be non-contradiction regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Since non-contradiction is not understood prior to the establishment of that purposeful action, there can be no certainty of validity; thus, how could there be any activity? Or, for one who does not act, how could there be the establishment of purposeful action? Therefore, in this case, both factors being mutually dependent, the fault of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśrayatva*) is unavoidable.

Now, if one who has already acted out of doubt alone perceives non-contradiction through the persistence of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and thereby considers there to be validity (*prāmāṇya*), then enough with this "validity. For it is sought precisely for the sake of purposeful action; if that [action] has arisen from doubt alone, then that [doubt] itself is superior, because it alone is useful for worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, as for what was said regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful...

The claim that "the formulation of the determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is for the sake of instructing the ignorant, since [the practice of] rules is invariably preceded by right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)," is also untenable. This is because those two (rules and practice) are not preceded by that [right knowledge]. Furthermore, according to this view, in the case of entities such as lightning that arise and perish instantaneously, no purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) occurs; therefore, the cognition of them would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is argued that even in that case there is the application of words...

If it is said that "purposeful action" (*arthakriyā*) [is non-discrepancy], then it would follow that indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) lacks validity. Therefore, we indeed maintain that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is non-discrepant. However, we do not accept that the stability of purposeful action is itself non-discrepancy, because [non-discrepancy] consists in the absence of both the knowledge of a cause for the object being otherwise than it appears and the knowledge of defects [in the causes of cognition].

Thus, there is non-correspondence (visaṃvāda) of a cognition that has arisen; and due to the absence of that [non-correspondence], there is correspondence (avisaṃvāda). It is established by this much alone that validity (prāmāṇya) exists; therefore, validity does not depend upon correspondence. // 76 //
[333] Furthermore, even that which is non-cognition is not a means of valid cognition regarding an object.
[334] [335] It is not another means of valid cognition. (GA) [335] (KA)
[336] or [337] and (KHA) [338] or indeed (GA)

[339] Furthermore, regarding the view that validity depends upon correspondence (*saṃvāda*), he states "śrotra... [in the verse], pointing out that auditory cognition would result in invalidity because it lacks correspondence with cognitions produced by other sense organs. However, if its validity is instead maintained solely on the basis of correspondence with another auditory cognition, [then... [340]

This being the case, since a cognition following upon the utterance of each respective sentence arises even in the Veda a hundred times over, that too would not be invalid; thus he says: "If it were so" (*syāc cet*).

However, it has already been stated that a corroborative cognition produced by another means of knowledge does not exist merely in the case of the Veda, but is absent even in the case of auditory perception and direct perception; thus he says: "By a means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). // 78 //

[340] Thus, this being the case, if it is argued that the auditory sense (*śrotra*) is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its cognition accords with that which depends on a single sense-organ; then, since this is so, the validity of the Veda would also be unavoidable, because its cognition accords with the cognitions produced by those various sentences. To this he says: "Just as... Some, however, consider the repetition here to be due to lack of attention. [341] Thus ends the section.
Why [is this] by means of that objection and its refutation? // 79 //
[341] Or rather (KA): since these are defects regarding validity that depends upon corroboration,

therefore, setting aside the requirement for corroboration, that cognition which has arisen— being firm, free from doubt, and not contradicted by another cognition such that "this is not so"— is a specific object-cognition (*viśiṣṭaviṣaya-jñāna*).

"Having a greater object" means having an additional object. By this, he excludes recollection (*smaraṇa*); for that [recollection] is not distinct from previous cognition because it does not have an additional object. He states that "only that [cognition] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)" with the words "Therefore...
(verse 80).

Furthermore, where has a statement whose meaning is not connected with other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) ever been seen to be a valid authority, such that the authority of Vedic sentences could be relied upon? For indeed, all human [statements] have their objects already established by other means of valid cognition;
therefore, he says: "And not... The intention here is this: it is not the case that means of valid cognition have their own validity to be established by inference (anumāna).

We must inquire: "By whom was it seen where? For in inference, there is a dependence upon an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, since the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of means of knowledge is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), their validity need not be established by inference. Moreover, if validity were established by inference, and that inference in turn required another inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); thus he says: "of all" [verse 81].

[342] Regarding the meaning of the "sphere" (gocara), [343] someone here objects—starting with "But surely" (nanu). The intention is as follows: just as that which is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa) is not determined as such independently, but rather depends on another, [344] so too is this case.

In this way, even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) does not manifest as a means of valid cognition; thus, it too becomes dependent upon something else. For perception and the other [means of knowledge], if not apprehended as being means of valid cognition, are not fit for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). And the pursuit of means of valid cognition is for that purpose, not out of mere habit. // 82 //

[344] It does not avoid being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is the intended meaning: just as the sense organs, such as the eye, even when their own nature and power are unknown, perform their respective functions independently of anything else, so too—by the principle that the effect would otherwise be inexplicable (*kāryānyathānupapatti*)—[the means of knowledge are established].
They are determined only afterwards,

and their cognition is not utilized for the production of the effect, because that [effect] is accomplished by the sense organs themselves independently. In the same way, even a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, [is established] through the apprehension of another cognition.

Previously, while established in its own function—the determination of the object—it remained entirely independent; it might even be grasped at some later time by its very own nature if one so desires. However, the apprehension of that [nature] is not useful for its status as a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*). For in whatever form this [cognition] is to be grasped by another cognition, it already existed in that very same form previously.

Indeed, through the direct perception of a jar, the jar is made known with a determined form, namely, "this is a jar. Its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists precisely in that much;
even by another means of cognition, it is to be made known only as "the jar has been delimited by this [first cognition]."

Since there is nothing further [to be known], even that which arises is merely instrumental; thus, it is indeed another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, he will state later that in the case of what is not a valid cognition, another cognition is purposeful for the sake of knowing a form not previously apprehended. By the word "established" (*saṃsthita*), he shows the culmination of the means of valid cognition. For a means of valid cognition is established through the accomplishment of its specific effect; and once it is established, another cognition is useless. // 83 //
[346] It was not grasped by you; [347] its form is... [348] ...the making known.
And since a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is determined by other cognitions through its own nature,
and that nature has already been previously apprehended,
therefore the fact that this means of valid cognition is known by another cognition does not constitute [its] validity.

It is employed [in this way]. For its validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in the illumination of its own object, and since that is obtained from its own preceding [moment] alone, a subsequent cognition would be useless; thus, in order to clarify the point already stated, he says: "by that" (*tena*). // 84 //

"But in the case of invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), another condition (*pratyaya*) is meaningful; therefore, dependence upon that [condition] there is indeed logical," he says: "Invalid cognition" (*apramāṇam*). This is the meaning: for invalid cognition grasps the object by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*). That is to say, it superimposes upon the object exactly the same form as the nature of the cognition itself. For instance, in the case of "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl, [it appears] in the form of silver.

It apprehends that [object] as well as being immeasurable (*apramāṇa*) by way of having that very form. And for this very reason, it is false. Since this falsity itself has not been cognized by its own nature, dependence on another is indeed appropriate for the cognition of it. For if there were no other cognition (*pratyaya*) that apprehends its falsity, the superimposition of the nature of knowledge upon its own object would not cease. And in the absence of that cessation, [the error persists].
The conventional usage of validity would thus proceed from invalidity alone. Therefore, to exclude that [invalidity], another cognition is purposeful. // 85 //
[349] The end of pride.
[350] As for "apra" [351], it means "pure."

But why does falsity (*mithyātva*), when not apprehended by other conditions, not cease? To this he says: "For it is not... That which is the non-correspondence of the object—namely, that the cognition is not of such a nature as the object—is not grasped by the preceding invalid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). This means, in effect, that it has not been determined [as such]. For it is only by a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that correspondence (*tathātva*) is established.

For its being such (tathātva) is the effect of the object, and since that is revealed by that very [cognition], there is no dependence on another in that regard. However, the object's being otherwise (anyathātva) is not established by the means of knowledge [itself]; thus, another means of knowledge has scope in that case. He says:
"Let falsity be extrinsic (parataḥ)."
Even so, there is no validity for the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*), because their falsity is understood through inference. For it has been said:
[352]. Let it be so. (KA)
"Vedic injunctions concerning the relationship between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth, are false.

To this he says: "In that case also. The intended meaning is this: falsity does not arise from just any external cause; rather, even in that case, if the object does not exist as it appears, then falsity consists precisely in its being otherwise than what it seems.

The cognition that "this is not silver" or "this is mother-of-pearl" is the cause [of sublation], or else it has a defective instrument as its object. As he will state: "For whomsoever the instrument is defective, and for whomsoever there arises the cognition 'it is false'... (86).
Is this a mantra? [The opponent might argue: "Even if falsity is determined through inference, it never constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

To this, he says: "To that extent" (*tāvatā*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. This is not a mantra; rather, it is simply impossible to understand falsity through inference, because inferences are contradicted by counter-inferences (*pratihetu*), and because it would follow that even for nihilists (*nāstika*), their own accepted scriptures would lose their authority.

Furthermore, it is indeed possible to infer the falsity of those [non-Vedic] scriptures on the grounds that they are composed of sentences and so forth. Moreover, since the reasons [adduced by opponents] are contradicted by the non-doubtful and non-erroneous knowledge produced by Vedic injunctions (*codanā*), they are not capable of subverting the authority of those injunctions; thus, falsity is apprehended solely through these two causes, and not by the collection of ill-conceived arguments put forward by others. Now, as for that cognition of the contrary nature of the object or the cognition of a defective cause— [End of excerpt]

Even that [subsequent cognition] does not establish falsity without being itself a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And since its own validity is difficult to determine due to its contradiction with the preceding cognition, how can the falsity of the former be established? To this he says: "at the stage of its arising.
This twofold cognition grasping falsity is measured as a valid means of knowledge while it remains at the stage of its arising. Just as...

It is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is measured by that very nature; this is the meaning. Since it has indeed reached the stage of its arising, it is not first overcome by invalidity characterized by non-arising. And because its essence consists of certainty, it is not of the nature of doubt.
Furthermore, since no other sublater (*bādhaka*) is perceived for it, it is indeed a means of valid cognition. Therefore, by means of it, the falsity of the former [cognition] can be established.

To establish this, it has already been stated that even for such [a cognition], the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge arises upon the occurrence of a sublation; thus, it is well said that falsity is indeed twofold. // 87 //
[353] And since falsity is understood in only two ways, and not by means of another pramāṇa, [354] na pa (KA).

Therefore, one who wishes to establish the falsity of another's [position] as well should appropriately state these very two reasons for falsity; however, it is not sufficient to employ merely the similarity to what lacks valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa-sādharmya-mātra*), as has been done by others. Thus he says: "Therefore" (ataḥ). // 88 //

And [the author] says "codanā" to show that there is a contradiction with scripture for those who seek to establish the lack of authority [of the Veda] by means of inference. This is the intended meaning:
it is established that the knowledge produced by *codanā* is devoid of the three kinds of invalidity and is intrinsically authoritative (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*).

Therefore, the proposition of its lack of authority is sublated by that very [knowledge]. While that [knowledge] stands as an obstacle, [the reasonings such as] "because it is a sentence" and so forth cannot [establish] its lack of authority.
Only the relationship itself can be apprehended. // 89 //

[355] Here, someone raises a certain objection: "Because that is false. The intention is this: valid cognition, which is the knowledge produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), sublates inference. But how can that very [inference], being itself sublated and thus false, serve to invalidate it?

"It prevails. He refutes this, saying: "It has been attained. This is the intended meaning: an inference is not sublated by a false cognition of an injunction (*codanājñāna*). Rather, it is made false by that inference which, being unsublated, has established its footing. Therefore, because of that [injunction's] falsity, the validity of the inference is maintained; and because of the validity of that [inference], the falsity of the [injunction] is established.

"Thus, there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If there were some other sublater of the cognition of the Vedic injunction (*codanājñāna*), then that falsity produced by it would not be capable of sublatting the inference, and mutual dependence would not be suspected. However, there is no sublater whatsoever other than the inference stated by you;
thus he says: "No. (90)

[Objection: Since the meaning of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is not grasped by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the falsity of the knowledge produced by the injunction is established precisely because of the absence of corroboration (*saṃvāda*). Therefore, there is no circular reasoning (*itaretarāśraya*). To this, he says: "And not... It has been stated that validity is not based on corroboration; let it be so, lest the non-existence of taste and the like follow from the invalidity of the cognition of taste and so forth. But how [is their existence known]?

If validity were based on corroboration (*saṃvāda*), then taste and the other [objects] would be non-existent; therefore, he says "of these" (*teṣām*). The apprehension of these—taste and the rest—is restricted to the tongue and so forth respectively. Consequently, due to the absence of corroboration by another sense organ, if the cognition of taste were invalid, it would follow that taste and the others do not exist. // 91 //

[356] If, however, the cognition of taste is accepted as valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of its corroboration by another subsequent cognition of the same kind, then in the case of *dharma* as well, such corroboration by a cognition produced from the Veda is possible; thus he says: "For that... (*taddhiya*).

This was previously stated for the purpose of refuting validity on the grounds of contradiction (*saṃvāda*). Now, however, it is stated for the purpose of demonstrating a circular dependency (*itaretarāśraya*);
thus, because the intended meanings differ, there is no redundancy. If, on the other hand, it is argued: "The validity of our Vedic injunctions is simply unestablished;
how then can that [injunction] refute the position of invalidity?"—that is incorrect. For indeed, [validity] does arise for those who hear the words of the Veda.

Even for atheists, there is an understanding regarding the specific nature of dharma and adharma; nor do they doubt whether heaven results from the Agnihotra sacrifice or not, nor do they hold a contrary view. Thus, this knowledge produced by the Vedic injunction (codanā) is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even for them.

Furthermore, the denial of such knowledge is utterly improper for those who speak the truth, for it is impossible that one who has understood the relationship between words and their meanings [should deny it].

"One does not understand the meaning from the injunctive sentence. However, those who speak what is false, thereby transgressing the prohibition "one should not speak falsely," would incur great misfortune. Therefore, it is not proper to state [the reason] as unestablished merely out of malice;
this is what he says with the words "of mine" (*mama*). But as for the one who says: "True knowledge indeed arises..."

We declare that very [alleged] non-authoritativeness to be due solely to hatred. For logicians, whose doctrines are generally mutually contradictory, mostly maintain that something is non-authoritative out of hatred alone, and that "this view of ours" is authoritative out of attachment alone. Therefore, the authoritativeness of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) is sublated by hatred; and because there is no determination [of truth] from any other source.

Regarding the claim that there is no mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), he replies with the words "from hatred" (*dveṣāt*) and so forth. The connection is with the phrase "not invalidity. Invalidity is not established by hatred alone; for in that case, nothing at all could be conceived as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For all disputants [establish] their respective tenets (*siddhānta*) through mutual [contradiction].

They are seen censuring [it]. In that case, what is determined by way of being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Therefore, everything that possesses the characteristics as previously described is indeed a valid means of cognition. It might be thought: "Let there be no invalidity due to aversion; however, as long as there is no mutual agreement or consensus between the proponent and the opponent, validity does not become established. And that which has an unestablished validity..."

A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is capable of subverting another [opposing] [cognition]. However, since there is no mutual agreement regarding the validity of my own *codanā* (Vedic injunction), how could there be a subversion by inference? To this he says: "Because it is not accepted" (*asammatatvāt*). This is the same logical connection (*anvaya*). The rest is as before. // 93 //
[357] Thus, just as invalidity does not arise from hatred or disagreement, so too validity does not arise from one's own desire or permission;
with the intention that, in either case, the Veda alone is sublated by an inference of invalidity based on what is commonly recognized as valid, he says:

"—and not. For the nihilists (nāstika) maintain that the inference [establishing] invalidity possesses validity. Indeed, by this, the doctrine of the Vedic proponents—which holds that the Vedas, being non-authoritative, consist mostly of suffering—is avoided. Furthermore, due to the support of merit from previous lives, they have this concession: "The assertions of the non-authority of the Vedas are authoritative. And neither of these two [positions] is...

The cause of validity has indeed already been stated there. To show that invalidity does not arise from aversion, he provides an example: "fire," etc. If invalidity were due to aversion, then the pain of being burned by fire and so forth would not be perceptible; for that cognition would be non-perceptual, and what has a non-perceptual object is designated by the term "non-perceptual. Yet this non-perceptibility of the pain of burning is not accepted by anyone. However, [if it were] due to aversion...
Otherwise, that [undesirable consequence] would follow regarding invalidity. // 94 //
[358] Knowledge, or [359] speech,
[360] this is not to be led.

He demonstrates that validity does not depend on one's own desire with the words "na ca" (and not). For everyone desires the validity of a cognition that accords with their longing; if that were the case, then everyone would be satisfied even by imaginary sweetmeats. However, no one accepts its validity. Therefore, it is established that the inference of invalidity contradicts the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).

He concludes that [the Veda] is authoritative with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*), ending with the suffix *-tavyam*. Now, one might object: "In that case, Buddhists and others too could stand their ground by taking hold of their own scriptures.

To this he says: "of the Buddhist, etc. The meaning is that the distinction (*antara*)—that is, the difference—between the Vedas and the scriptures of the Buddhists and others will be stated. // 95 //

[361] He indicates the very interval that is about to be explained by means of the principle of looking forward (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*)—namely, "puruṣa" and so forth. In the scriptures of the Buddhists and others, the possibility of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises as a refutation of their authority (*prāmāṇya*), because humans lack the capacity to perceive supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*). Furthermore, realizing that they themselves have admitted the human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) of their own scriptures...
How could they now transgress what they themselves have surrendered? Furthermore, we shall explain in the *Vedādhikaraṇa* that the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

Consequently, because there is an absence of defects, the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of the Veda is established in the manner described; thus, there is a difference between the scriptures of the Buddhists and others and the Veda, regarding whether they are of human origin or not. // 96 //

Thus, it has been stated that the Vedas are eternal and inherently authoritative because they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*). However, those such as the Naiyāyikas who postulate that the Vedas have an author in order to establish their authority, and those proponents of falsity who do so for the sake of establishing that very falsity—for them, the postulation of an author who is not remembered is not supported by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even the postulation of many unseen entities would follow without justification; thus he says, ending with "kartṛmatve" (if there were an author).
First, those who speak correctly [assert] that God is the creator,
and that his qualities include unimpeded knowledge and so forth:
"The knowledge of the Lord of the World is unimpeded, as is his dispassion."
Sovereignty and righteousness—this fourfold set is accomplished simultaneously.

Thus they have been postulated. Furthermore, no more convincing reasoning is seen for such a postulation, as we shall explain in the section on the refutation of the relationship [between word and meaning]. In this way, the postulation of a faulty author by those who maintain the falsity [of the Veda] is likewise entirely without proof.
For if that were the case, the tradition of the Veda would not have continued up to the present day; indeed, it has been maintained through great effort via the succession of disciples and teachers.

They are seen upholding the Vedas and practicing their meaning; this would be impossible if they were composed by untrustworthy persons, for in that case, they would have been abandoned long ago by those who perceived their contradictions. Therefore, from this acceptance by the great multitude, we understand [the Vedas to be authoritative].

The Vedas have no authors, and even less, therefore, do they have authors possessed of faults. For the Mīmāṃsakas, nothing more than what is perceived is accepted; for the Vedas are seen now as handed down through a continuous succession of pupils and teachers. The Mīmāṃsakas accept that they have been exactly like this at all times. Therefore, there is no postulation of anything unperceived on the part of the Mīmāṃsakas; thus he says: "by the Mīmāṃsakas. // 98 //
And when it does not conform to the facts, for such an eternal Veda that produces knowledge, "error" consists in its being contrary to its own nature.

And since doubt has been clearly refuted by the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself, he says: "of such a kind. This is the intended meaning: validity consists precisely in this—that a cognition which has arisen is neither doubted nor sublated by another cognition. The cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) has indeed arisen; furthermore, both doubt and error have been [refuted] by the author of the *Bhāṣya* regarding this.
They have been refuted. For it has been said: "From the injunction 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' it is not understood in a doubtful manner as to whether heaven exists or not.
Nor does this [injunction] ever prove false at another time, in another place, for another person, or in another state.
Therefore, it is non-false. Thus, because of the absence of the three kinds of invalidity, the validity of the cognitions produced by the Vedic injunctions (codanā) is established. // 99 //
[364] That which has been stated is indeed [365] the means of valid cognition [366] for me.
"But even so, if there is a suspicion of defects in the cause, would there not still be a lack of authority? To this he says: "He will ward it off," ending with the word *abhāvataḥ*.

For it has been stated that defects in words reside in persons; and those [defects] will indeed be refuted in the section on the Veda (*vedādhikaraṇa*) by the very demonstration of its non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*). That [demonstration] was indicated by the phrase "of such a kind" (*tac caivambhūtasya*) and is explained here. What is about to be said...

It should be understood that this very point was stated previously by the term *evambhūta* (of such a nature). And thus, even though doubt and error have not directly arisen [in the case of the Veda], they should not be suspected in the Veda even on account of a suspicion regarding defects in its cause; this is what he says with the words "by that" (*tena*). 100.

[367] Having thus set aside the commentary (*bhāṣya*) that was introduced, and having established the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) which serves as its introduction, it was concluded that the Vedas are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, he states the intended meaning of the commentary beginning with "But as for what he says..."—namely, "In that way" (*tathā*). This is the intention of the commentary: by means of a proposition (*pratijñā*) stating that things are not as they appear, the invalidity of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) is established. And it has been stated that this [invalidity] is of three kinds. [368] {1}

112} First of all, we shall explain immediately hereafter that invalidity characterized by doubt and error does not exist [in this case]. Consequently, it follows that invalidity must be understood as being characterized solely by the non-arising of cognition, and thus the thesis of "not being so" (atathābhāva) is established. To this, the following reply is given: "This which is stated is contradictory; one says [something] and yet it is false," and so forth.

It is said that "he speaks" that which he intends to make known. If it is the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) that speaks, how could it be overcome by falsity, which consists in ignorance? And if this is explained in such a manner, there is no consequence of invalidity for the words of the Buddha. For the validity of knowledge does not arise from its mere production, such that this criticism would apply. For even though knowledge has arisen from those [Buddhist scriptures], it would be invalid due to the suspicion of defects in the cause, since it is produced by human speech. But here, it is not so.

Because its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) will be explained [later], and because here too the word "he speaks" (*bravīti*) indicates the independence of the injunction (*codanā*) through the use of the agentive case; for the intention is that the injunction alone expresses the matter independently, and no person does so by means of it. // 101 //
[368] But as for "and" (ca), [369] furthermore, if that other worldly statement is from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses;

That is indeed not false. Now, regarding the commentary which states that what originates from the intellect of a person who is not trustworthy, or that which concerns an object beyond the senses, is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*):
here, he first explains the word "trustworthy" (*pratyayita*) with the words "tathā" (thus). This is the meaning: in this commentary, by the word "trustworthy"...

"It is stated that [the Buddha] speaks of things as they have been perceived. However, by the phrase "or the object of the senses," the very existence of the source for that [knowledge] is established; thus he says, "by the senses. This, then, is the meaning of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) here: as for the human statement that was cited, an objection is stated there after having analyzed it. For a human statement is of two kinds: the statement of a trustworthy person...

And there is the speech of one who is untrustworthy, and the speech of one who is trustworthy. The speech of the trustworthy is twofold: that which is rooted in valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and that which is rooted in error (*bhrānti*).

For the learned remember the word *pratyayita*—derived from the root *it* according to the *tārakādi* list of suffixes—in the sense "one in whom trust (*pratyaya*) has arisen. And trust is twofold: valid and invalid. Thus, it is only this much [that is being discussed].
He remains in a state of being trustworthy; whatever he says, confidence necessarily arises regarding that. This means, in short, that he speaks of things exactly as they have been perceived.
For this very reason, the qualification "or the object of the senses" becomes meaningful through the possibility of both inclusion and exclusion.
Furthermore, by the word "senses," he indicates all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, it refers to the objects of the means of valid cognition.

Thus, this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound with the middle term elided (*luptamadhyamapada*), like the word "camel-faced" (*uṣṭramukha*). Now, if the example is the statement of a reliable person (*āptavacaḥ*) whose object is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then it is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because it is not false. On the other hand, if it is a statement of an unreliable person (*anāptavākya*) that is not rooted in a means of valid cognition, then even if...
That which is corrupted by the defects of a speaker is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*);
however, the Vedic statement is not rendered false by that [same] analogy, because the defect of a person—the cause of falsity—is impossible therein.
The phrase "originating from human intellect" is stated as the seed of invalidity; for it is indeed produced from human intellect. Therefore...
Whatever a person perceives, he does not employ speech corresponding to that perception, whether because he is unreliable or because he wishes to deceive.

For his intention is indeed one of deception. Even in the case of a reliable person, there may be error. Furthermore, the speech of an unreliable person is not a means of valid cognition for the listener, even if it is rooted in a means of valid cognition for the speaker.

Because of the abundance of contradictions and the resulting lack of reliability, we have not demonstrated its two-fold nature even though it exists. This is because the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*) lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*), even if it conforms to one of the two modes [of existence]. For this very reason, he will state later: "Even regarding what is possible, if it is untrue, it is false. (102)
[370] That [371] also is twofold:
(KHA) [372] that (GA)
[373] Others, however, say that being a witness and being truthful constitute the meaning of the term "trustworthy person" (*pratyayita*); thus he says: "being a witness," etc.
A person who perceives an object as it actually exists and speaks of the object exactly as it was perceived is designated by the word "trustworthy."

And thus, since for one who is trusted there is no possibility of non-authoritative knowledge, the qualification "or the object of the senses" is useless; it was employed solely for the purpose of qualifying the statement of one who is not trusted. Consequently, this is the meaning that results: even the speech of an untrustworthy person may be true if that untrustworthy person speaks of an object that is being perceived. Thus he says: "dṛśyamāna" (being perceived). // 103 //
[374] Or rather, he says "thus" (*evam*) because this explanation is untenable. This is the meaning:

for here, in the case of non-falsity, the statement of a trustworthy person regarding an object of the senses has been cited as an example for the other. As they say: "The word of a trustworthy person."

And that which is preceded by another non-deviant means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and has an object currently being perceived [is the definition of perception]; this applies to one who is not an authority (*anāpta*). In this regard, regarding the counter-example where the trustworthy person and the sensory object are absent, the status of the counter-example—due to the deficiency of one factor—would occur merely through the absence of either "being from an authority" or "being sensory. However, if both were absent, the counter-example would result in being deficient in two factors. // 104 //

If the counter-example were given merely upon the absence of each [condition] individually, what would follow? To this he says: "from one who is not trustworthy" (*apratyayita*). The meaning of this is as follows: when the counter-example for "one who is trustworthy" (*pratyayita*) is stated as "but from one who is not trustworthy," the counter-example should be provided merely by the absence of trustworthiness. In that case, regarding an object that is perceptible—that is, an object within the range of the senses—[the following applies].

The sentence that provides [the proof] would also be unreal. For unreality is to be demonstrated merely by the absence of a trustworthy person (*pratyayita*). Furthermore, even regarding an object of the senses, the statement of one who is untrustworthy is indeed a non-trustworthy statement; so why would it not be unreal? If, however, only a non-trustworthy statement concerning something beyond the reach of the senses is cited as a counter-example, [then the argument holds].
That is not so. For the phrase "or [a statement concerning] an object of the senses" is already countered by the phrase "or [a statement concerning] what is not an object of the senses";

furthermore, if both were to be countered, it would result in the deficiency of two essential factors. Likewise, when countering the case of an object of the senses with the phrase "or [a statement concerning] what is not an object of the senses," one must demonstrate its unreliability by the mere absence of being an object of the senses. In that context, there is the speech of a trustworthy person.

Furthermore, one may encounter such a thing that is both real and unreal, because even that is not an object of the sense faculties (*anindriyaviṣaya*). If it is said that even for an untrustworthy person [the statement] is "not an object of the sense faculties," then, as before, there is a deficiency of two factors. Regarding the position that it is "not a sense faculty" (*anindriyatva*): when the statement of a trustworthy person is itself a non-sense-faculty, it becomes an object of what is not a sense faculty.
The meaning is that, in that case, its [the opponent's argument] too would result in being unreal. // 105 //
[375] If this is not accepted, what follows?

If it is so, he says: "contradictory" (*vyāhata*). This is the meaning: for in this way, by stating matters that are mutually inconsistent in the earlier and later parts, the treatise becomes contradictory. For at the time of providing an example, the statement of a trustworthy person is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the listener, even though it is not based on the senses.

It was stated [previously] that [a statement] originates from a trustworthy person (*āpta*). Now, however, by way of a counter-example regarding the objects of the senses, it is said to be non-authoritative;

thus, there is a contradiction. Similarly, it was stated that even the speech of an untrustworthy person is true when it concerns an object of the listener's senses, by relying on the listener's own cognition. Yet, by way of a counter-example to that very trustworthiness, it is now said to be false; therefore, there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

This leads to the consequence that [the word *pratyayita*] would lack any formal connection (*agranthatā*). Furthermore, this is the intended meaning of the author of the *Vārttika*: first of all, the word *pratyayita* does not denote "one who perceives such-and-such an object. For this is an etymological (*yaugika*) term, not a conventional (*sāṃvijñāyika*) one; there is no reason to abandon the connection with the meanings of its recognized constituent parts. Indeed, the learned remember the division of base and suffix as "one to whom conviction (*pratyaya*) has arisen. [The suffix -ita is applied] in two ways...
And a witness is either correct or incorrect.

Therefore, one who is "credible" (*pratyayita*) is not one who sees things as they truly are, but rather one who speaks of things as they have been seen—meaning, one who speaks the truth. For this alone is truthfulness: the absence of discrepancy between speech and mind.
Precisely for this reason, when witnesses are bound by an oath of truth...
A witness who speaks the truth when giving testimony attains abundant worlds. [376] pīndri (KA) [377] vāditva (GA) [378] lokān āpnoti puṣkalān.
[378] Having thus shown the result with the word "kṣi," the *mānavas* recite [the following verse], showing the fault in the contrary case:
"A witness who speaks falsely in an assembly of noble men regarding what has been seen or heard [shall incur the following]."
After death, he falls headlong into hell and is deprived of heaven.

Thus, in this context, it is understood that what is stated regarding what has been seen or heard is true, while anything else is untrue. Therefore, by the term *pratyayita* (trustworthy), only the quality of being a speaker of truth is expressed, not the quality of being a correct observer; for the qualification "or the object of the senses" applies to that [trustworthy person] alone, and not to the speech of one who is untrustworthy.

Therefore, even that which has the sense organs as its object is indeed invalid. Nor is this [statement] intended merely to demonstrate non-falsity, because it is intended to demonstrate the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) in the example for the inference of invalidity; and because it is impossible to do so without establishing its validity. For this very reason, at the end of the *Bhāṣya*, it is stated: "That [inference] is invalid, as it originates from human intellect."

Thus he said. For it is only in this way that it is logically consistent: if it were previously stated that [scripture] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the speech of an unreliable person—even if its meaning is consistent with other means of valid cognition—would not be a means of valid cognition for the listener because of the lack of prior certainty; and subsequently, due to being a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), even the speech of a reliable person would not be a means of valid cognition regarding the object. If this is argued, [then the following applies].
This is another fault of his: no human statement is ever an authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Where, then, could the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) be established? Furthermore, we do not perceive anything else in this commentary that is more charming than the refutation of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, in this way, the word *pratyayita* is not [used] in the sense of a "seer of what is correct" (*sādhudraṣṭṛ*) by virtue of a collective power (*samudāyaśakti*).
It has been stated that [he] "acts. This might be the case: one who has produced a cognition is indeed "trustworthy" (*pratyayita*).

However, it is not the case that cognition itself never deviates from correctness, because all cognitions are in accordance with reality; therefore, only one whose cognition is in accordance with reality is trustworthy. That is not so, for it will be stated later:

The distinction between correct and incorrect cognition according to the *Vārttika* on the text of the *Vṛttikāra*. Thus, first of all, following the meaning of the word *pratyayita*, this is not the intended sense of the *Bhāṣya*. However, if it is explained in this way solely because the word *vā* (or) cannot be taken as expressing an alternative (*vikalpa*), thinking that "if *pratyayita* were a qualifier, then in the phrase 'whether it be an object of the senses' (*indriyaviṣayaṃ vā*), the word *vā* would have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*)," that is not so.

Because particles have multiple meanings. For it is observed that particles possess multiple meanings; however, the word *pratyayita* does not denote one who shows what is correct. Moreover, this objection is common to both of us, for in your case as well, the word *vā* occurring in the counter-example has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
116} Indeed, it is not the case that merely the statement of an untrustworthy person, or merely that which is beyond the range of the senses, is false;
