for in your own system, you accept the validity of both the statements of trustworthy persons regarding objects beyond the senses and those regarding objects within the range of the senses.
Therefore, there is no distinction [between our positions]. Those who speak in this manner have accepted nothing more than a mere internal contradiction between what precedes and what follows. If...
It is not being said that the counter-example is one from a trustworthy person;

rather, it has been stated that the statement of a trustworthy person is an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas the other is dependent upon its own [corresponding] means of valid cognition.

But [the opponent claims] that "that very same [word], when not having the senses as its object, is a non-means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)," and this is stated by the passage beginning with "from one who is untrustworthy" (*athāpratyayitāt*). That is incorrect. For at the very moment when a statement from an unreliable person (*anāpta*) having the senses as its object is a means of valid cognition, it follows by implication that its opposite is a non-means of valid cognition;
so what is the point of demonstrating that? However, for one who has employed two qualifiers in the example of a means of valid cognition, [this demonstration is necessary].

Only when there is the absence of that very person [who is trustworthy] is it meaningful to state that [the testimony] lacks authority. For, in the case of one who is untrustworthy—being determined to be a speaker whose assertions have not been previously verified—there arises either a misconception, such as "this is not so," or at least a doubt. In both cases, there is indeed a lack of authority. And even though, in this instance, the word itself is not by its own power a cause for doubt, [it still results in uncertainty].
Nevertheless, because deviation is observed in some speakers, doubt and error arise accordingly.

To that extent, the speech of an unreliable person is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). However, for a trustworthy person, even that which concerns objects beyond the senses is indeed a means of valid cognition.
For his speech, which produces certainty, possesses intrinsic validity; it becomes non-valid only upon the observation of a sublation (*apavāda*).
And thus, the justification for both counter-examples is established. Therefore, it is well said that in the opinion of the opponent, there is a contradiction within the text.
Since this explanation is untenable, he says "Therefore" (*tasmāt*), indicating that the previous explanation is superior. Its meaning is as follows:

by the former [statement], namely "if [the matter] has been confirmed by a trustworthy person" (*pratyayitāt*), the truthfulness of the statement of a trustworthy person is expressed; but by the latter...

By the phrase "or [the object] of the senses," the existence of the source is shown. The meaning is that for a trustworthy person, the word of the speaker itself is the authoritative source (*pramāṇamūla*), and not the object of the listener's senses, because otherwise it would follow that it is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*). // 106 //
[379] Vānte (KA) [380] Ata eva ta (KHA) [381] Di vi (KA, GA)
[382] That too is not so, because [383] this [384] is unestablished.
[385] Indeed, because of speaking truthfully (KHA),
indeed because of being trustworthy (GA)—
surely, by thus stating that validity arises from trustworthiness, the author of the Bhāṣya has declared that validity stems precisely from excellence (guṇa).

[It] exists. For reliability (*pratyayitatva*) is indeed a quality (*guṇa*); therefore, he says: "not from authority" (*aprāmāṇya*). Here, by the mention of reliability, it is described as the mere absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*), and not that authority arises from a quality itself.
Why is it explained in this way?
Therefore, he says: "from the excellence" (*guṇāt*). It has already been explained that excellences (*guṇas*) are merely conducive to the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*);

they are not, by virtue of being excellences, the cause of validity (*prāmāṇya*), because that would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, it is appropriate to explain the Bhāṣya in accordance with that very [point]. // 108 //

Now, if being an object of the senses (*indriyaviṣayatva*) is indeed a qualification only for the statement of a reliable person (*pratyayitavākya*) and not for the other category, then how can the word "or" (*vā*), which expresses an alternative (*vikalpa*), be used?
To this he replies with the words "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) up to the end of the previous [verse]. First of all, the word "or" has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

But the latter [example] is for the sake of providing an alternative; thus he says, "in the latter case. He shows that both—the qualifier of the trustworthy person and the qualifier of the object of the sense organ—are presented as counter-examples by way of an alternative. // 109 //

He shows these very points in the counter-example: "Even in the case of what is possible" [386]. This means that when a person is untruthful and speaks untruths, even if the matter is possible—that is, even if the object is perceptible (*dṛṣṭārtha*)—one is able to grasp the falsity of his statement; thus, "possible" refers to an object that is not beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, even one who is trustworthy and has been seen to speak the truth may become incapable.
That is to say, he lacks the capacity to grasp the meaning being communicated. In that case, even his own statement is false;

how much more so would a trustworthy person compose a statement regarding such a matter? Certainly, this occurs when one is deluded—just as the author of a Smṛti compendium is when his established doctrine is sublated by a contradiction with the Śruti.

And just as an authoritative person (*āpta*), when engaging in the conventional usage of objects already perceived, might compose some statement based on a certain cause of error— that speech becomes false because it lacks the possibility of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, a desire to deceive (*vipralipsā*) is not possible for him, nor is it the case that there is no error at all.

"Even for the Brahman-sages, error is suspected; how much more so, then, for those authorities who are more recent? Regarding this, there is another commentary: "For that [dharma] cannot be known by a person without [the aid of] verbal testimony. In this regard, we do not know what "that" refers to in that passage. For it is the *vākya* (sentence) that is the subject under discussion.

It is not impossible to know that [object], because it is easily known. However, since the object (*viṣaya*) is contained within a compound, it cannot at that time be extracted and referred to by the pronoun; moreover, because their genders differ. For the word *viṣaya* is masculine, and it is not fit to be referred to by the neuter pronoun *tat*. Therefore, this must be explained. It is said as follows: by the word "to be known" (*jñātum*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*)—which is presented through its general connection with the act of knowing—is indicated by the word "that" (*tat*). This is what is meant:

—that object of knowledge which is beyond the scope of the senses cannot be known by a person except through verbal testimony; thus, the very meaning of "object" (viṣaya), extracted from its compound, is referred to as being that which is to be known. And this has been explained by some as being intended for the refutation of an omniscient being.

He refutes that [objection] with the words "not by this. His intention is as follows: first of all, the word "all" (sarva) is not heard here in the sense that "all objects cannot be known. Nor is the refutation of an omniscient being of any use here, because the thesis—"the Veda alone [is the source of dharma]"—is established merely by the negation of knowledge regarding dharma and adharma. // 110 //
[386] For one who speaks untruth, [387] there is no (KA) [388] wealth. (GA)
[389] or [390] having known this (KA) [391] without dancing.

[392] Having stated that even this cannot be known, the author of the Bhāṣya further resorts to the refutation that it is "unreliable because it is based on verbal testimony. From this it is understood that the author of the Bhāṣya is precluding only supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*), and not omniscience (*sarvajñāna*) in general. For, with the intention that what is supersensuous cannot be known without verbal testimony, he says: "from verbal testimony" (*vacanāt*).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, since the prior portion of the world—which consists of both existence and non-existence—is understood through the means of valid cognition for existence (*bhāva-pramāṇa*), while its latter portion is understood through the means of valid cognition for non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), all objects of knowledge (*prameya*), divided into six categories by the six means of valid cognition, are indeed understood. Therefore, such an omniscient being is not at all to be rejected; thus he says, "If... [yadīti]. Now, it has already been understood that an omniscient being is not refuted by this.

Thus [it is asked]: what indeed is being accomplished by this? First, by the preceding [passage], the presence or absence of a reason for the falsity of human and non-human statements was shown, as well as the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavikalatā*) in one part [of the example]. Since the matter is concluded by just that much, it is not understood why [the author], having raised the doubt with the words "What is impossible? and so forth, proceeds to refute it. It is said in reply: a statement from a trustworthy person (*pratyayita*) concerning an object beyond the senses (*atīndriyaviṣaya*) is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

Thus it has been said. In this regard, the following objection is raised: "Is this statement of a trustworthy person (*āpta*) concerning an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)? For a trustworthy person is precisely one whose power of vision is unimpeded;
indeed, he, having reached the ultimate limit of the excellence of knowledge, perceives even merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) directly (*aparokṣa*).

Consequently, the restrictive determination that "only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)" [is the source] is not tenable. To this, the following reply is given: "For it is impossible," and so forth. This is not...

The excellence of a certain person consists in this: that he is able to perceive an object beyond the senses even without [the aid of] verbal testimony. And this, which will be stated by the author of the Sūtras themselves in the definition of perception (pratyakṣa-sūtra), was mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya by looking ahead to what follows, for the purpose of supporting his initial thesis.
However, since that alone is the field for rational discourse, we shall refute the omniscient one in detail precisely therein. // 111 //
[393] By this,
[394] her [395] ear-ornament,
like the Dharma, is rendered empty. (KHA)

"Granted, one might be omniscient by knowing the six objects of cognition through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, the claim that knowledge whose entire range is not [limited] to a single object is produced by the eye alone must be refuted;

therefore, he says: 'by one' (*ekena*). This is the intended meaning: those who say that the Buddha knows everything with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) surely perceive tastes and so forth with their own eyes as well. Otherwise, how could they [account for] the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*)?

Knowing that the range of the Buddha’s eye encompasses all objects, they maintain [that everything is known by it]. [The opponent] objects: "In that case, let all cognitions be self-evident (*svasaṃvedana*) by themselves; what is the use of relying on the authority of another? By this reproach, he shows that because this position is so utterly trivial, it does not even merit refutation. And thus, under the guise of non-refutation, the author of the *Vārttika* has actually demonstrated the path of refutation for his students.
This is for the purpose of providing an exposition; otherwise, if it were composed in any other way, it would indeed be incoherent. // 112 //
He says: "Even if the eye of modern people does not have everything as its object, nevertheless, it is not unreasonable that the Buddha’s eye was superhuman, divine, and had everything as its object.

To this he replies: "By those of such a kind," etc. The meaning of this is: for it is observed in the present day that by means of instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) belonging to the same class as the eye and so forth, there is the perception of a connection belonging to the same class as form and so forth, and existing in the present.

Therefore, it is logical that it was exactly the same even at other times. For in this way, the hypothesis is made to follow what is observed. And the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: "The Buddha's eye does not have the past and so forth as its object, because it is an eye, like our own eyes; or else, it is not an eye, because it has the past and so forth as its object, like sound. // 113 //

Now, it has indeed been understood that because of the difference in perceivers, the eye illuminates what is distant and even more distant; therefore, having reached its ultimate excellence, it will illuminate everything. Furthermore, a progressive superiority in knowledge is observed. Thus, having attained supreme excellence in some substratum, it will become universal in its range. And in this regard, something possessing excellence is known to reach its ultimate limit, as is the case with magnitude in the sky. It is something possessing excellence...

And there is knowledge. Therefore, even that [knowledge] must reach its final culmination in some substratum. And this culmination of knowledge is its state of having all things as its object, because through its great scope it attains excellence further and further; hence he says, "Even where... up to the end of the section on capacity (*sāmarthya*). This is the intended meaning: it is true that there is excellence both of the eye and of knowledge.

But it does not exceed its own proper object (*svārtha*). For even though, for one whose eyes are open, many forms (*rūpa*)—distinguished by differences such as blue, yellow, and so forth—appear, the eye does not [grasp] a single form; nor does it [grasp] through location or dimension, because it discerns objects that have various locations and dimensions. Nevertheless, there is a rule that nothing whatsoever is manifested by the eye beyond its own proper object. And what is it that is in contact with this [eye]? Just as a material thing (*rūpin*) is [in contact] with a form (*rūpa*) and with those things that are inherent in the same object as the form. First, it is in contact with a substance (*dravya*) that possesses form.

For it will be stated in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* that "that which is derived from the elements (bhautika) is indeed conjoined [with the sense organ]. Furthermore, the contact [of the sense organ] with color and its inherent properties is through "conjunction-with-inherence" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*). Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence [of perceiving] taste and so forth; for it will be stated in that very same place that contact is "attainment accompanied by capability" (*yogyatā*). And this capability is determined in accordance with the observation of the effect.

It functions according to its specific effect. For this very reason, even objects situated at an extreme distance are not the proper objects of the eye. The same applies to things that are unborn, those that have already passed away, and so forth. Thus, the eye may attain excellence regarding these very objects that are its own proper domain, but not regarding other objects such as sound. This should also be demonstrated in the case of the ear. And it is observed that the scope of the senses is limited to their own proper objects to this extent.

Excellence (*prakarṣa*) consists in the manifestation of extremely subtle objects that are not too distant. Since this [manifestation] does not deviate from its own object, it is understood here that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is restricted precisely by that [excellence]; therefore, it is not capable of establishing an inference for the manifestation of all objects. A counter-reason (*pratihetu*) has already been described. Furthermore, this "own object" (*svārtha*) of cognition is that wherein its cause exists. And the sixfold cause of valid cognitive knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*) has been analyzed; wherever that [cause] exists, [the excellence follows].

In that regard, knowledge certainly becomes more excellent through the force of practice according to its respective object, and this is indeed accepted. It has already been stated that the Omniscient One is one who perceives everything in brief by means of the six instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, as for the claim that all objects are perceived directly (*pratyakṣa*) in detail, this is not an excellence of knowledge itself;

for there is a restriction regarding the excellence of the manifestation of their own objects on the part of the causes of direct perception. Since knowledge is dependent upon those [causes], its restriction follows precisely from that restriction.

Therefore, it is not possible for the capacity of perception to transcend its own proper object. The mention of "future" is an illustration; it applies equally to the future, the past, and the present. Indeed, regarding the manifold variety of entities that depend upon the entire world with all its distinctions, there is certainly no vessel capable of such a degree of excellence as that which [is attributed] to the mere body hairs of some single individual.
One might as well be able to count atoms; how much more so, then, [the whole]?
For indeed, even that which is not present is manifested by the eye in error, as in the case of "this is silver. And yet, that is not a memory.

Because [the cognition] depends on an external sense faculty, it is not reasonable to say that only the mother-of-pearl is manifested there, since the manifestation of one thing does not have another as its object; otherwise, there would be a lack of certainty. Therefore, everything—such as non-arising and so forth—will be manifested by the eye alone when it has attained excellence in a certain respect. Or, let there be contact with all objects through "contact-with-the-contacted" (saṃyukta-saṃyoga).

For whatever indeed comes into contact with the eye, everything connected to it through that very same channel is necessarily in contact [with the sense organ], just as in the case of things inhering in what is already conjoined. This is not so; for if this were the case, no one would be non-omniscient, since such a contact would invariably apply to everything. As for the claim that even what is not present is an object of the eye—

That is not so. For in the case of an error, the object of the eye is indeed the mother-of-pearl itself, because the sense organ functions by reaching its object, and it is impossible for it to reach silver that is not present. Otherwise, errors such as the perception of non-present silver would occur independently of any actual object. But this is not the case, since no error is observed that lacks a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhāna*). How then does one with cataracts perceive hair?

For that [cognition] does not depend upon any external object of apprehension, since it proceeds from the superimposition of non-existent hair. No; for even in that case, portions of light appear in such a manner, and because they are so subtle, one thing is perceived as having the form of another, and thus it is not noticed. But how can there be a cognition of something in the form of another? The Commentator will say: "It is due to defects. This applies equally to the other case as well. For you too, non-existent silver is understood as being present; thus the objection is the same. If...

What fault is there in the experience of silver regarding mother-of-pearl? If you say that the mother-of-pearl itself is the fault of the experience of silver, then alas, in this way the dependence upon an external object is established. Furthermore, we consider it correct that the subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*)—in the form "this is not silver"—functions by negating the superimposed identity that had been presented. Thus, what is present is indeed present as silver, appearing as present. Therefore, it is established that the eye, having as its object only what is proximate and present, manifests silver and the like; hence, it is not a visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*).

It might be argued: "Let there be a restriction of objects for the eye because it functions by reaching its object; but why is the mind not accepted as having all objects—past, future, and so forth—as its domain?
Thus, entities such as those yet to come will become objects of mental perception.

This is not so, because the mind lacks independence with respect to external objects. Otherwise, it would follow that there could be no such thing as a blind person, since the mind exists even in such individuals.

How then is there the perception of a second moment following the operation of the sense faculty that causes the cessation of the first cognition, if the mind is not independent with respect to external objects? No, for even in that case, because the operation of the sense faculty has not ceased, it is logical that its cognition does not cease either. What need is there to mention the dream state? For in that state, the mind indeed displays various associations as if they were present. No.

Because it is memory (*smṛti*). And because the lack of independence of the mind (*manas*) in that regard will be explained [later]. How then can there be an appearance of the present? It is due to a defect (*doṣa*). And sleep (*nidrā*) is a manifest defect, as he will say: "Sleep is the cause of false cognition.

If it is asked, "How can there be memory regarding what has not been experienced?", he will say: "In this very life, in one instance. But is it not understood that [this occurs] in intuitive flashes (*pratibhāsu*)?

The independence of the mind—of whom? If it refers to those of the present day, it is not so, because their [insights] arise from fallacious signs and the like. For intuition (*pratibhā*) is generally influenced by the clarity or agitation of the heart associated with [past experiences], and is not based on an absolute cause. For this very reason, it is a cognition whose nature is indecisive. Now, if it refers to those who have transcended the world (*lokottara*), [then it is independent].

No. We shall explain that those [cognitions] do not transcend the nature of appearances as they manifest to people like us. Furthermore, the state of being supramundane (*lokottaratva*), which is the subject of dispute, will never be accepted by people like us as a basis for any [cognition]. Moreover, if all cognition were dependent solely on the mind (*manomātra*) while the mind operates externally, independent of external signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, then everyone’s cognition—being devoid of any other means (*upāya*)—would result in such a consequence; by what, then, could this be overturned?

It is possible [to argue as follows]. If it is claimed that external functioning is accepted because of a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*) that does not depend on signs (*liṅga*) and so forth, we say no. For that would render the commencement of other sense organs useless; since all cognition would be established from that very [unseen force] itself, through the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those respective specific unseen forces. Or else, even that [external functioning] is useless, because the act of cognition would be accomplished for the self—which is not an instrument—by the specific unseen force alone. Furthermore, an unseen force cannot be something that lacks a means (*anupāya*).

"It accomplishes [its task]," lest the initiation of the body be rendered purposeless. If that is so, then since the mind has never been observed to function anywhere independently of the subtle body (*liṅga*) and other factors, let it too be dependent on external things.
Therefore, it is established that even mental perception is not capable at the very beginning [of creation].

We shall also refute that which arises from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the context of the rejection of omniscience, because cultivation has for its object what has already been understood. This being so, cultivation would be useless, and nothing more than that [already known] would be established by it. Furthermore, does that which arises from the power of cultivation originate from the senses (*akṣaja*)?

Or rather, it is not so. First of all, it is not born of the senses, as has already been stated, since the exhaustion of the power of all the senses was mentioned immediately prior. Nor is that which is not born of the senses perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the word *pratyakṣa* is etymologically significant. For this very reason, he says "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) to show that the capacity of perception is not observed in regard to the future; for perception does not have the future as its object.
The intention is that its object is not perceptible.

This same portion should also be explained in the refutation of perception produced by the external and internal organs. The meaning is that neither visual nor mental [perception] has the capacity regarding the future and so forth. Furthermore, everything within the range of the knowledge of yogins—

If it is accepted [by the opponent], it must be explained how everything is experienced by the yogi. If you say that even the past and so forth are determined by yogis as being present, then in that case, the yogi’s cognition is false, because it is the apprehension of something as what it is not (*atasmin tadgraha*). Alternatively, if it is said that everything is experienced by the yogi exactly as it exists [in its own time], then...

In that case, it would not be tenable for an object such as the past to be a matter of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because this would lead to the same consequence for inference (*anumāna*) as well. Furthermore, the claim that "direct perception is knowledge whose object is both present and non-present" is a partial contradiction. It might be argued: "Direct perception consists in the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); the cognition of a yogin regarding objects such as the past is also devoid of that [construction], and is therefore direct perception. To this [we reply]:

No, because it is impossible for a conceptual cognition (*avikalpa*) to grasp the relation between prior and posterior time. And what is this conceptualization? If it is a cognition associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī pratītiḥ*), then auditory perception would not be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Alternatively, if it is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpasaṃsargayogyapratibhāsā pratītiḥ*), [then the same follows].

The self-awareness of a conceptual universal would not be perception. As for what they say—that this [cognition] does not associate it with a verbal expression because such association is contradictory to its nature—that is incorrect. For even in the absence of an association with a verbal expression, the universal aspect, which is capable of being associated with one, appears therein.

To that extent, since the nature of conceptual construction (kalpanā) has not been eliminated, the quality of being "free from conceptual construction" (kalpanāpoḍha) is untenable. Alternatively, if conceptual construction is defined as the superimposition of another form, then even the cognition of a yogi would not be free from conceptual construction, because it functions precisely by superimposing a present form upon things such as those yet to arise.
Furthermore, since it appears otherwise than how things actually exist, the cognition of a yogi is indeed erroneous; thus, it is excluded by the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta).

How is it direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? For just as the cognition of hair produced through the influence of defects such as cataracts is erroneous and is excluded by the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*), so too, the cognition of yogins—which has the appearance of everything as present—would not be direct perception if it were excluded by the term "non-erroneous," since it would be nothing but erroneous. Furthermore, directness (*sākṣātkāritā*) is not possible for a cognition that is not born of the senses; thus, [the definition] in the *Pratyakṣasūtra* [is formulated].

We shall explain this further. Moreover, how can perception—whether it be the cognition of a yogin arising from the power of an object, or that which arises from non-existent or unborn objects—be considered direct perception? All of this has already been demonstrated by the very demonstration of their future existence; thus it should be understood. Not our own.
[402] Thus is the fault; [403] it is the activity of non-arising, the practice of non-arising.
[404] Even so, this [cognition] which is incapable of an external object [405] (KHA),
then this too (KA).
[407] Thus, from the root *bhā*.
[408] *Bhā* means "incapable" (*asamartha*). [409] (KHA)
[410] Not from non-perception (ṇapra); [411] from fear (hād mi); [412] patience is not direct perception (kṣam apratyakṣam).
[413] Grasped. [414] Just as it proceeds (thāpravṛ). [415] Precisely by that.
[416] It might be thought by one proficient in the six types of knowledge [417]: "All perception indeed has as its manifestation that which is not present."

Because cognition and its object do not exist simultaneously due to their relationship as cause and effect, the cognition of a yogin is not thereby undermined. If this is so, then what is it that appears? It is simply the form of the cognition itself, impressed by the object. The very nature of an object’s status as a "grasped" entity consists solely in its being the cause for imparting its form to the cognition. If this is the case, then even a single part of an object is not apprehended; how much more so, then, the knowledge of all things?

124} Now, if it is argued that there is no loss of the object because the determination (*adhyavasāna*) of the perception of the object occurs precisely through the perception of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra*), then how can there be a determination of the perception of one thing based on the perception of another? If you say "by means of ignorance (*avidyā*)," then oh, what a great-souled omniscient being he must be, whose ignorance has such a vast scope! It would be better for those who perceive only a single part; even their ignorance is at least more limited. Furthermore, [the text continues:]
All this is apprehended either successively or simultaneously;

first, it cannot be the former alternative. This is because it is impossible to experience successively those infinite things that possess origination and are devoid of prior or posterior limits. For this very reason, simultaneity is also not possible, since simultaneity is impossible for infinite things—whether they are yet to arise, have already ceased, or are presently existing. Furthermore, what exactly is this "all" that, when known, makes one omniscient?

Rice and other such things are well known to be denotable by the word "all" when delimited by some particular limiting condition (*upādhi*). However, objects such as the "unborn" (*ajāta*) are not like this; how then can they be the referents of the word "all"? If it is argued that "allness" consists in infinity, [we reply]: surely this is nothing but the absence of a determination of limit;
how then can one who knows such [a thing] be omniscient? Therefore, it is established that no perception whatsoever has everything as its object.

Thus it is said. As for the claim that those things which possess excellence are understood to reach a limit—just as the measurement of space reaches its limit in the sky—and therefore knowledge too, having reached its culmination somewhere, becomes omniscient: that is incorrect. For we maintain that excellence indeed ceases upon reaching a certain limit; it is impossible for it to reach a further state beyond that.

However, the reason "the ultimate limit" (*kāṣṭhā*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For indeed, an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*) such as a jar or a water-pot, even when known to possess a superior dimension (*sātiśayaparimāṇa*), does not experience this state [of infinite expansion], because its greatness is simply impossible beyond that point. Thus, by that very fact, since it completely fills the interior of the entire universe (*brahmāṇḍa*), there is no room for anything else. Now, if it is argued that this is merely a property of a quality (*guṇadharma*), [we reply:]...

That is not so; for even in this way, the previous fault has not been avoided. Weight (*garimā*) is indeed a quality (*guṇa*), yet we do not perceive in it such an excellence that nothing further could possibly exist beyond it. Indeed, if some single effect were to be commenced by all heavy things acting together, then this might be possible.

And this is not the case. As for the measurement shown in space, that is also untenable. Measurement is, by definition, limitation. Even if such a thing exists in space, it would still not be in an impossible or ultimate state; thus, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). Alternatively, if space is indeed infinite, how then can measurement be demonstrated therein?

Its infinity consists precisely in the absence of any measure. Therefore, it will be rightly said that this is a contradiction—to claim something is both limited and infinite—and thus perception is incapable [of apprehending it]. Here, in the first part, the excellence of the sense faculties in terms of having all things as their objects was refuted; in the latter part, the excellence of perceptual cognition itself is refuted—this is the distinction. Since perception has no scope regarding the future and so forth, it is impossible to observe a probans (*liṅga*) pervaded by that [object] in any such case.

Inference, too, is not possible. Since there is no perception of an object that cannot otherwise be accounted for by similarity, neither comparison nor presumption is possible. Non-existence, moreover, is understood only with respect to some particular thing, for non-existence consists in the non-perception of what is perceptible; however, everything is never perceptible. With the intention of showing that even through verbal testimony it is impossible to ascertain all objects in detail, he says: "not from inference and the rest."
Thus [ends verse] 115.
[418] Farther away [419] among those things possessing origination [420] in the wind (KHA).
[421] Yakapa (KA, KHA) [422] Va Bra (KA) [423] Itara (GA)

On this point, others have said: "But surely this impossibility is the same even if one accepts the eternity of the Veda. For it is not possible for there to be such a thing as an unauthored sentence, since all scriptures are understood to be produced. Thus, the proponents of the Veda undertake their work for the sake of worldly prosperity and the supreme good by relying on this impossible eternity of scripture."

Thus, there is no distinction regarding the other [arguments] as well, since they too depend on the authority of an omniscient being who has never been seen before. Therefore, he says: "Omniscient" (*sarvajña*). This is the intended meaning: what has been stated by the opponents is true; however, this must be carefully considered—namely, whether these two conceptual constructions are equal or not. By that very reason for which equality was established by the opponents, this [is shown].
We must deliberate whether there is equality or not. // 116 //

He now introduces that very deliberation with the words, "The omniscient one. This is the intended meaning: equality indeed occurs when the proving and refuting means of knowledge are equal; but that is not the case here. For an omniscient being is not perceived by people such as ourselves, and for that very reason, neither by those of our kind.

This is due to the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*). It is with this very intention that the word "etc. (*ādi*) was employed. The underlying meaning is that for others like us—those who are not omniscient—it is impossible to possess knowledge of everything. This will indeed be explained further below.
Furthermore, no author of the Vedas is observed in the present age.

Because its prior limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is not understood, and it cannot even be conceived, since its object is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). This will be stated [in the sūtra] "because of the restriction to what exists in the world" (1.1.26). Nor is it inferred.

Because of the contradiction with non-existence. For inference has as its object an entity not present to the senses; and in the case of the Vedas, which were produced for the sake of unseen purposes, the creator would necessarily have been remembered. Therefore, since the creator is determined to be non-existent due to his not being seen and not being remembered, an inference of a creator is impossible. And this very absence of a creator is what constitutes the authorlessness of the Vedas. Consequently, the assumption of the eternity of the Vedas is supported by valid means of knowledge. [The same applies to] the assumption of an omniscient being.

"But it is not so," [you might say], "because there is an absence of equality between the proof and the refutation; how then can there be equality? Now, non-existence is not established by mere non-perception, because of the inconclusiveness [of that reason], since [non-perception] is possible even when things are remote. Furthermore, since the cessation of the pervader is necessarily concomitant with the cessation of the pervaded, the cessation of the pervaded should likewise be ascertained. Objects are the pervaders of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not a pervader (*vyāpaka*) of objects, because it lacks causality (*ahetutva*) and lacks identity with them (*atādātmya*). Therefore, the non-existence of an omniscient being cannot be established merely by the absence of a means of valid cognition. Hence he says: "as in the case of refutation" (*nirākaraṇavat*). This is the intended meaning: the determination of real entities depends upon the means of valid cognition. At present, an omniscient being is not apprehended by any means of valid cognition whatsoever. Not...

And it cannot be postulated that [the omniscient being] existed at another time, because it can be refuted by inference— on the grounds of being a point in time, like the present time. Furthermore, since the absence of a cause is invariably concomitant with the absence of its effect, the absence of the effect, which is knowledge of that object, is inferred from the absence of the causes of all cognition.

Furthermore, since the absence of the causes for knowledge was stated immediately prior, it is therefore impossible to show even a doubt regarding an omniscient being based on the cessation of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is because the non-existence [of such a being] is understood through the superior force of the reasons for its refutation.
It might be argued: "The non-existence of an omniscient being is not understood through scripture, precisely because it contradicts that [scripture].
To this he says: "And not... Why is it not understood through scripture? To this he says: "His own... For either scripture is his own, or it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding him.

Or [it might be] composed by another person. First, it cannot be his [the Buddha's own work], because that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): for the scripture of the Buddha would be authoritative only once the Buddha’s omniscience is established, and the establishment of that [omniscience] would depend upon the authority of that very scripture. However, a work composed by another person is not even accepted as being authoritative; thus he says: "by another person" (*narāntara*). // 118 //

It might be argued: "The omniscient one is indeed accessible only through eternal scripture (*nityāgama*), for it is heard [in scripture] that he is all-knowing and the creator of all. To this, he says: "And not... The intention here is as follows: a word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only when there is an intended meaning (*tātparya*).
And yet, such an eternal scripture (*nityāgama*) cannot be found elsewhere. What, then, is this "other" [scripture]?

He says: "If it were eternal. The intention is as follows: whatever portion of the Veda is seen to be a restatement of established facts (*siddhānuvāda*), that is for the sake of another injunction (*vidhyantara*); this will be explained in the section on *arthavāda*. Therefore, since this [text concerning the self] is also merely a supplement to the injunction for the knowledge of the Self, what fault is there in its intended meaning being that it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the [Self's] own nature?

Therefore, he says: "one who has that as his supreme goal" (*tatpara*). For the eternal Veda cannot possibly establish an impermanent omniscient being who possesses a human form, due to the contradiction between the eternal and the non-eternal. Thus, such a person must be one whose supreme goal is that [Veda], and would therefore necessarily be impermanent. // 119 //
And this is the fault in the view that [the Veda] is cognizable through an eternal scripture; thus he says: "of the scripture. If an eternal scripture is accepted, [then...]

"What is the use of postulating an omniscient being? He states the reason for its futility with the words "since" (*yataḥ*). [The opponent might argue: "The eternal scripture itself will serve as the authority regarding Dharma;

what is the point of resorting to the further assumption of an omniscient being? However, this refutation of the idea that Dharma is accessible through an eternal scripture is intended solely to dispel the delusion of the Vedavādins.
The nihilist does not accept an omniscient being who is to be known through the Vedas. // 120 //

But as for one who says: "What is the use of our grasping at [Buddha’s] omniscience? For what we must establish is the truth of the Buddha’s scripture (*āgama*). And that is indeed established even in this way, since it is observed that the Buddha is a speaker of truth regarding matters such as the objects of sensory contact, as well as regarding the momentariness of cognition and so forth. Therefore, by that very same example, the truth of the Buddha’s word is established even with respect to objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) that are to be accepted on faith."
It is inferred. And thus, the fact that even acts such as the veneration of a *caitya* constitute Dharma is established;
this he introduces with the words "yo 'pi" (even that which...). 121.

He refutes this as well with the words "by that" [tena]. For it is observed that in the case of objects connected to the senses and so forth, truthfulness exists through dependence on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); thus, by the force of the universal concomitance (*vyāpti*), even regarding supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*), there occurs validity through dependence. He states the reason for this dependence: "validity" (*prāmāṇyam*). This is the intended meaning: in the case of an object connected to the senses and so forth, there is truthfulness...

By saying this, it is effectively stated that validity depends on the authority of the sense faculties and so forth. For if validity were intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), such dependence would be useless. What is meant is this: here, the truth of the Buddha’s word alone is not understood by setting aside other means of valid cognition (*mānāntara*).
Because dependence on another means of valid cognition is never absent anywhere, it follows that the status of being a valid cognition is never established independently. // 122 //
[426] Thus, he explains dependence itself—starting with "just as. This, then, is a reason that contradicts a specific property of the subject (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*). // 123 //

He states "And just as... because this reason is not only contradictory to a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣaviruddha*), but is also a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*). For it can be argued: "The word of the Buddha is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding supersensible (*atīndriya*) objects that are not understood by others, because it is the word of the Buddha, just like statements concerning momentariness (*kṣaṇika*) and so forth. For those [statements concerning momentariness, etc. are indeed not valid means of knowledge regarding supersensible objects.

And since this single reason alone does not deviate from two contradictory meanings, this very case is the illustration for the term *viruddhāvyabhicārin* (non-deviating contradiction) ending in the singular number.

We shall explain in the section on inference that two reasons cannot be expressed by a word ending in the singular number. Nor should it be said that our position is established because this reason also proves truthfulness; for mere truthfulness is not what you intend to prove.
Because the truthfulness of a trustworthy matter is what is to be established. For this very reason it was said: "One should also postulate [it] regarding a trustworthy matter. (124)
Those who have not understood that very same [thing].
[430] Or rather, [431] (KA): this person, by establishing truth in what is untrustworthy and untruth in what is trustworthy, is not capable of proving what you desire.

However, with the intention that this reason is appropriate for proving the unreality of the Buddha’s word—despite our own desire to establish its credibility—he says, "untrustworthy" (*aśraddheya*). He explains the aforementioned contradiction of the specific (*viśeṣaviruddhatā*) by saying, "prior," etc. For a reason becomes a means of cognition only in accordance with an example; in that regard, [your reason] merely restates a prior cognition of yours.

Since that [perception] is subject to error, even the word of the Buddha—which has a trustworthy meaning—would merely establish itself as a reiteration of prior knowledge. Furthermore, independence would contradict the specific characteristic of being a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). // 125 //

[432] Furthermore, whatever heterodox teacher outside the Veda might wish to establish the truth of human-authored scriptures by means of this very reason, for him this reason becomes one that possesses a counter-argument (*sapratipakṣa*) through the presentation of a reciprocal example (*anyonyadṛṣṭānta*). Thus he says: "Furthermore... The word of the Buddha, concerning objects beyond the senses (*atīndriyārtha*), is false.

If [the opponent's scripture] has a non-worldly meaning, then because it is a human composition, it is false like the Āgama of the Digambaras; and that too is false for that very same reason, like the Āgama of the Buddha—thus there is mutual sapakṣatā (similarity of class). // 126 //

Or rather, he says "dharma" because it would follow that validity would apply to objects other than dharma and adharma by the reason of being a human statement (*puruṣavākya*) without any qualification. And here, the probandum is precisely the absence of validity regarding dharma and adharma; it is not the validity regarding an object distinct from them, since that [distinctness] is already established. As for the statement "momentary, etc. (*kṣaṇikādi*) which was mentioned as an example, [it serves as such].

He states that even this [argument] is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyavikala*) while opposing schools such as the Sāṃkhya remain alive—namely, "among the Sāṃkhyas and others. For the Sāṃkhyas are proponents of the eternal nature of all things. As long as they have not been defeated, how can the doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) be presented as true? And how this [doctrine] is untenable, we shall explain in the section on *śabda* (the *Śabdādhikaraṇa*). // 127 //

He says "alaukika" (supramundane) to show that the quality of speaking about supramundane matters, when qualified by the fact of being the word of a person, subverts the inference of truth precisely through the example of mutually opposed scriptures; this constitutes a case of "exclusion" (*atireka*) due to the reversal of the qualifier and the qualified. // 128 //

[433] Now, following the discussion regarding the two types of fallacies (*pratihetu*), that inference which has been stated by others for the purpose of establishing an omniscient being is as follows:
"That which was said by the Buddha, 'I am omniscient,' is indeed true, because it was spoken by him, just as it is the case that fire is hot and water is liquid."

"That too is contradicted by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*)," thus he says "he would speak," having arrived at the very refutation of the omniscient one. Whatever argument the disputant, having previously approached in a disconnected manner, speaks—namely, that which is about to be stated—this very argument about to be stated becomes for you, without doubt, a reason similar to the reason stated by you. This is the initial connection.
It is for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion of inconclusiveness (anaikāntika), for one who has been associated with [another] for a long time might occasionally speak falsely. // 129 //
He demonstrates this very counter-reason through its formal application: "of the Buddhas and others," etc. (130).

But how is this person free from doubt? To this he says: "It is directly perceived. That my statement "Buddha is not omniscient" is indeed established by direct perception and is beyond doubt. And in the case of the example—the statement regarding the heat of fire—that too is established by direct perception; thus it is well said that there is no doubt.

Thus, it is not possible to determine whether the statement "I am omniscient" was spoken by the Buddha or not. Indeed, we do not believe that a person acting with foresight would utter such an excessively arrogant falsehood. Therefore, since the fact that this statement and its illustrative examples—the propositions concerning momentariness and so forth—were spoken by the Buddha has not yet been established, [the opponent] says that it must be established by the Buddhist himself: "By you..."

"Regarding the word 'sādhya'": what follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "by that. This is the intended meaning: these two reasons do not function as causes of doubt due to their being equal; rather, our own reason is self-established and possesses a well-known pervasion (*prasiddhavyāptika*).

Furthermore, since the example is not deficient in its logical reason (*hetu*), our position is established. For you, however, the reason is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*), and the example has a presence of the reason that is itself doubtful; thus, your inference—lacking a proven constituent—is incapable of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*). This constitutes the distinction between us.
Moreover, this doctrine of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) is exceedingly crude.

He says "pratyakṣa... because [the opponent's position] can be refuted even by reasons such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*), which are extremely well-established. For properties such as being an object of cognition, when established in relation to the intellect (*buddhi*) and not contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), are capable of precluding its omniscience.

Nor should it be argued that the pervasion (*vyāpti*) here is unestablished due to the absence of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); for [omniscience] is impossible due to the absence of any cause for all-encompassing knowledge.
Because it has been stated that an omniscient being is impossible. // 132 //
[434] Furthermore, regarding the state of being omniscient, does not this firm memory— long established— that "the Buddha is omniscient" exist for everyone? Therefore,
it is from this very cognition...
On the basis of its firmness, we shall infer the authority of an omniscient being;
therefore, he says "not" (na ca). Why is it not inferred?

To this he says "because of contradiction" (vigānāt). For a tradition that is not contradicted establishes a source [of authority], whereas atheists [contradict] the tradition regarding an omniscient being.

Thus they mutually disparage one another, relying on various types of all-knowing ones. However, the proponents of the Vedas utterly reject the existence of an omniscient being. [Objection: But is this same disparagement not also present regarding the Smṛtis of Manu and others?
For even those [Smṛtis] are disparaged by atheists.

Therefore, he says: "severed" (*chinna*). This is the intended meaning: memory, being understood as the effect of a prior cognition, leads to the inference of that prior cognition which serves as its cause. For inference has as its object an entity not present to the senses. In this case, however, because there is an absence of any cause for all cognitions, the prior cognition is severed and cannot be conceived as the root of memory; thus, due to the determination of the opposite [of what was expected], there is no room for inference.

However, since the connection with the Vedas is possible for members of the three higher castes, it can be postulated that [the Smṛtis] have the Smṛtis of Manu and others as their source. He explains the contradiction with the words "by some. This is a statement made on a provisional basis (*anvāruhyavacana*). For if there were no contradiction at all, even such a postulation might be possible. But this is not the case.
Because omniscience has been embraced by certain individuals who constitute a portion of the great multitude, such as the Buddha and others. // 133 //
[435] They;
[436] that;

[438] By the word "or" (*vā*), [the author] explains the lack of a severed root [for the opponent's position] through [the following] refutation— namely, that he is omniscient. For it must be postulated that an omniscient being was known by at least one person on the basis of the firmness of their memory.

Only he who knows everything that is to be known is capable of knowing the Omniscient One. For as long as it is not established that "the Buddha knows all this [that exists]," one cannot determine that he is omniscient. Furthermore, there is no one posterior to the Buddha who is all-knowing; thus, he lacks the cause for knowledge of everything. Nor is it possible to remember what has not been previously cognized. Therefore, such a memory, whose very source is impossible, is simply not a valid means of knowledge. // 134 //

If, however, it is claimed that there was someone other than the Buddha who was omniscient, and that having learned from him that "the Buddha is omniscient," this tradition of memory (*smṛti-paramparā*) proceeded—this being the case, since that omniscience cannot be understood without [another] omniscient person, there would be an infinite regress of omniscient beings; thus he says, "[They] must be postulated. He states the reason for this here: "Whosoever... (v. 135).

Thus far, it has been stated that omniscience is difficult to know. Furthermore, if that [omniscience] is not understood, the authority of the scripture of the Omniscient One cannot be established; thus he says: "The Omniscient One. For if [the existence of] the Omniscient One is not understood, the authority of the scripture of the Omniscient One cannot be determined—as one might with the words of just any ordinary person. // 136 //

He states another objection: "From passion, etc. This is the intended meaning: for the composition of scripture is possible either out of passion to favor someone or out of hatred to suppress someone. But since the Buddha has destroyed all passion and hatred, no cause whatsoever is found for his composition of scripture; therefore, the teaching of the Dharma must have been composed by another.

The connection is with what is about to be said. Now, one might object: since this [Lord] is supremely compassionate, is it not entirely appropriate that, upon seeing living beings overwhelmed by suffering, his mind is deeply pained and he composes instructions on the means for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful?
To this, he says: "inactive" (*nirvyāpāra*). The intention is as follows: for that [knowledge] of the yogin is directly perceived and has all things as its object.

Knowledge is intended [as the means]. And that is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Therefore, when one remains beholding the entire world without conceptualization, with eyes stilled by meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), then for such a person—who has no recollection of the connection with words and the like—there is no possibility whatsoever of the desire to speak, of effort, or of the activity of the palate and other articulatory organs; thus, [verbal expression does not arise].

Furthermore, since it would be possible for him to deliver a teaching even without mindfulness, a compassionate one might simply remain indifferent, and thus the teaching would be composed by another. Moreover, as long as he does not examine [the matter], thinking, "This will endure," [he would not teach].

First of all, scripture cannot be composed; nor is this even possible for one who has not emerged from meditative equipoise. With this intention, he says: "In truth. Thus, it should be understood that these three reasons have been stated here regarding the fact that the teachings were not composed by another.
This might be the case: [he will teach] after having emerged [from meditation].
That is not so; for if the verbal cognition of one who has emerged from meditative absorption were an error, then the speech of such an erroneous person would be invalid. // 137 //
[440] Even for one who has arisen from that attachment,
[441] this might occur: "By the power of the Buddha, even though no specific effort is present, the teaching and instruction of the Dharma proceed even from walls and other such things."

"They go forth"—this we Vedavādins do not believe with conviction. For we, not overstepping the nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), admit the establishment of whatever kind of thing is established from whatever source. Furthermore, it is understood that the composition of a literary work is preceded solely by the intention to speak, effort, the movement of air, and the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs; therefore, [the production of sound does not occur] due to the proximity of a yogi whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is stilled in meditation.
We consider that this is established in this very way. He says this in the verse beginning with "sānnidhya" (along with its half-verse). (The meaning is: how could this be for one who lacks faith?

Furthermore, since one determines words by following the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*), there would be no confidence in teachings issued from walls and such; thus he says "kuḍyādi" (walls, etc.). // 139 //
[442] He has indeed come;

furthermore, even if [the teachings] were composed by the Buddha, there would still be no confidence. Thus we have doubt: are these teachings issued through the power of the Buddha, or were they uttered by evil-souled beings such as *piśācas* who are invisible? To this he says: "But rather... [referring to those] with invisible, subtle (*ativāhika*), and non-maternal bodies.

"It is sung in the Purāṇas that they are Piśācas. This was stated according to that [Puranic] view. And thus, the meaning is that teachings given to those who harbor such doubts would not constitute valid authority (pramāṇa). // 140 //

[443] Another view is that of the Vāṇī: the *puruṣa*, whose nature is consciousness, being under the influence of the body, senses, and so forth acquired through karma from previous existences, knows only certain things in certain places. However, when all residual karmic impressions (*karmāśaya*) have been completely eliminated, the manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of the instruments and the physical body has dissolved away.

One who has become *kevalin* perceives the entire universe—distinguished by divisions such as the subtle (*sūkṣma*), the transcendent (*atīta*), and so forth—as directly present before him. And that which arises in the isolated soul (*kevale jīve*) is called "perfect knowledge" (*kevalajñāna*). Those who maintain this view have relied upon the notion that liberated souls alone possess knowledge that encompasses all objects;
he introduces this [position] with the words "In this way" (*evam*). 141.

[444] He refutes this very notion of "isolated knowledge" (*kaivalyajñāna*) with the words "the dancer," etc. The intended meaning is as follows: it is well said that the liberated one knows the universe; however, such a state indeed belongs to individual souls (*jīvas*), and it is not this [liberation you describe], because it occurs precisely through the dissolution of the entire manifold of difference (*bhedaprapañca*) by means of the realization "not this, not this" (*neti neti*).
Since it is only thus that [omniscience] is found in the Vedāntas, and since there is no object of knowledge to be known beyond that—such as the past and so forth—how can there be omniscience?

If, however, disregarding the Vedāntas, one maintains such a form of knowledge for the liberated by relying on the authority of one's own scripture (*āgama*), that cannot be established unless the authority of the scripture is accepted. Furthermore, a scripture composed by one who is not omniscient cannot possibly be authoritative; therefore, the authority of the scripture is established only upon the proof of an omniscient being.

And since the establishment of that [omniscience] would depend on the establishment of the omniscient one, there would be a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, if a logical mark (*liṅga*) pervaded by such knowledge were perceived somewhere, then through inference the establishment of that knowledge would occur, and the fault of mutual dependence would be avoided. But no instance of such knowledge exists in the world; thus he says: "The example" (verse 142).

[445] This being so, we have thus replied to those who, relying on a superior person (*puruṣātiśaya*), maintain that the authority of scripture (*āgama*) is based upon him. Now, as for those who say: "This scripture is indeed eternal; it simply becomes understood by someone at first through primordial knowledge (*ārṣajñāna*)," [we respond as follows].

He replies to them: "The eternal scripture" (*nityāgama*). But why is this very doctrine of the eternal scripture being refuted? For even here, dharma and adharma have nothing but the Word (*śabda*) as their means of valid cognition. However, this much is the distinction: for a certain seer alone, whose every impurity has vanished and whose impressions from previous births remain unimpaired, the Vedas manifest at the very beginning.

And these [Vedas] are transmitted by him to others, and by them to yet others; thus, through the succession of disciples and teachers, they endure until the dissolution of all beings (*ābhūtasaṃplava*). In the same way, even during a new creation, the practical application of the Veda proceeds solely through the vision of the seers (*ārṣadarśana*); thus, there is no difference whatsoever. Therefore, the intention behind the refutation must be stated. That is now stated: "That indeed..."

At the beginning of creation, the sage’s knowledge is either a perception (*grahaṇa*) or a recollection (*smaraṇa*). As for perception, is it a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) or an invalid one? An ascertainment of the true nature of an object cannot arise from what is invalid. Since a perceptual [knowledge] other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not possible, what is the point of refuting it? However, if this [knowledge] of the sages is held to be a direct, intuitive perception (*sākṣātkāri-pratyakṣa*), [then it is valid].

This being the case, since one hears sounds that have not been uttered, it follows that there is indeed perception of objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). For this very reason, they say: "Who is able to surpass the words of those who, by means of the vision of the sages (*ārṣa-cakṣus*), perceive entities that are beyond the senses and imperceptible?"
Thus, this established doctrine (siddhānta) must indeed be rejected. For, by the same logic, someone might likewise perceive merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*);

consequently, the proposition that "only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) [is the source of dharma]" would be abandoned. It is for this reason that it was said: "by this direction. This means: by the direction [of the argument] used to refute the omniscient being (*sarvajña*).

By this, he shows the similarity between these two [cases], implying that this [doctrine regarding merit and demerit] is also an obstacle to the established doctrine. As for memory (*smaraṇa*), however, [it will be discussed] later.

"It will be refuted. Furthermore, since this vision of the Ṛṣis even gives rise to the suspicion that [the world] is created, he says "for not... (na hi) [in verse 143], stating that it must be refuted.
[446] "But surely, certainty will arise from that very statement;
therefore, he says: 'at all times. For it is indeed heard that speech can be a speaker of falsehood. Jaimini also [acknowledges] the tendency toward speaking untruth."
He will speak of speech in the passage beginning with "prāyāt. Therefore, because of the abundance of speakers of falsehood in the present day, there is a lack of trust even in other times. // 144 //
Furthermore, one might also say that this spontaneous intuition (*pratibhāna*) is an error, like a dream;

thus he says "dreams and so forth. The inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*) is because the appearance of an object is also suspected [to be false] by the same logic. The meaning is that for those who harbor such doubts, validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not tenable. // 145 //

[447] Furthermore, [448] this is another defect in this view; thus he says: "puruṣa... and so on. First of all, the power of the person (*puruṣa*) to perceive that which is beyond the senses is indeed admitted, namely, the apprehension of words that have not been uttered.

It has been accepted. If that is accepted, what is the point of insisting on the eternality of the scripture? For it would be better to rely on that which was stated by others—that the authority of scripture derives solely from trust in the person—rather than this [position]. Thus, the view that one perceives words that have not been uttered has been refuted. Now, as for memory:

He refutes this, saying "imagined. This mere imagination—that this eminent person’s recollection of the Vedas at the beginning of creation is based on knowledge from a previous birth, which was never previously observed in his present cognitions—is not authoritative. The meaning is that its cause (nibandhana) is rooted in another birth. But what is the fault here in the claim that the Vedas experienced in a previous birth are being remembered? For [recollection] is indeed...
It is not possible for that which is beyond the range of unuttered words to exist [as such],

yet memory is not [impossible]. For even in the present day, memory is observed regarding objects experienced long ago, which have been obscured by a succession of various intervening obstacles, even in those whose minds are deeply tormented by manifold and diverse painful sensations.

What is impossible regarding the recollection of another existence? If it is argued that mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) cannot persist once the body has perished, we say no, because they do not have that [body] as their substrate. On this point, one might think: "If bodies are no longer maintained, what substrates do the impressions have, or do they exist at all? How then can they be capable of producing a fruit in another existence? That is not so.

Because it does not have that [the body] as its substratum. Furthermore, the seed of cultivation (bhāvanā-bīja), which is produced by the influence of an exceptionally intense experience from another life, does not have the body as its locus such that it would perish upon the destruction of the body. This is because the self (ātman) is co-located with cognition; since the self is the substratum of cognition, even when it has taken up another body, it remains that very same self. Thus, there is no logical impossibility regarding its substratum. Moreover, even now, one may remember a previous birth.

No one at all is found who can establish the account of the secret conduct belonging to another existence. Furthermore, since the destruction of the latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*) follows from the destruction of the body, such an account is untenable.
Moreover, old age, death, dwelling in the womb, birth, and painful sensations—which are the causes for the cessation of those very dispositions—are exactly the same for him as well. Therefore...

"By the grace of some merit from a previous birth, he must necessarily have relied upon a certain [virtue]; for he is indeed a vessel of excellence who remembers everything known here or in the hereafter. Moreover, the accounts of history, the Purāṇas, and the Vedic injunctions are also authorities for the existence of the recollection of past births (*jātismaraṇa*). For there is a statement by Vāsudeva in the Gītā:"
[449] That which has meaning,
[450] Dṛbha, and [451] Śa are thorough knowledge.
[452] Even though I am without distinction [from the unmanifest], many births of mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna. I know them all, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
Thus say even the Paurāṇikas:
"First, the Purāṇa was remembered by Brahmā as the source of all scriptures;
immediately thereafter, the Vedas issued forth from his mouths."

[453] They recite "rga" (KA). This emergence from the Vedas found in the Purāṇas has the intention of mere remembrance, because it is not accepted that they were composed by them. And there are Vedic declarations regarding the time of attaining another body: "Knowledge and action..."
"And both former wisdom and [the impressions of past lives] attend one. In the *Mānava* as well, the recollection of births is shown to be the specific fruit of particular karma. For it is recorded:
Through constant study of the Vedas, through truth, through austerity,
and through non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.

Thus it is said. In this regard, it might be argued as follows: because it is determined to have another purpose through its association with the study of the Vedas and so forth, this [passage concerning the *parṇamayī* fuel-stick] is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise), like the *arthavādas* regarding the fruits of the *parṇamayī* stick, and it is not capable of establishing a [separate] result. For instance, the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*) is for the sake of retention alone, since what is being repeatedly recited is clearly not lost from memory. Furthermore, there is the injunction for the *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman) which is accompanied by specific procedural requirements (*itikartavyatā*), namely: "Every day, one's own portion of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) should be studied."

That [obligatory rite] as well, like the injunctions for the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, *agnihotra*, and so forth, has as its sole purpose the destruction of accumulated demerit and the avoidance of the transgression caused by non-performance; thus, it does not experience a connection with any other unintended fruit. Even though [the obligatory rite] is understood to have a great fruit such as heaven—which is distinct from the literal meaning of the words—it is not connected with another fruit. Austerities (*tapas*) likewise serve the purpose of destroying various kinds of sins.

Furthermore, since practices such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* have been determined to be for the sake of other goals, such as heaven and the like, they are independent [of the memory of past lives] and thus do not result in the recollection of previous births (*jātismaraṇa*). Non-malice (*adroha*)—that is, non-violence toward living beings—is also prescribed for the sake of specific results according to the distinctions of time; whether it be a vow (*vrata*) or a prohibition (*niṣedha*), for whom would the memory of past births be the fruit? Therefore, [the memory of past births does not arise] from the study of the Vedas and so forth.

It is argued that the mention of a fruit is merely an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise) and is not an authoritative means for postulating a result. This is not so; for while other distinct results are understood for each individual practice such as Vedic study, they are not understood when combined. However, in this case—just as with the red color (*aruṇa*) and other factors in the purchase—since truthfulness (*satya*) and the rest are enjoined toward a single result, their joint operation (*sāhitya*) is intended; thus, there is no connection with a separate result for them taken collectively.

This is not tenable. For this very reason, the statement regarding their collective recollection becomes logical. It might be argued: "The Vedas, when remembered by a single person, would give rise to the suspicion that they were composed. That is not so; for even among many sages such as Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, who possess such extraordinary powers, the possibility of mutual corroboration eliminates any such suspicion. Nor does this same logic apply to the meaning of the Vedas, because it is beyond the reach of the senses and could not have been experienced in another birth, making its recollection impossible. It might be argued: "In the case of remembering what was experienced in another birth..."

Those who have performed actions in other births and obtain their results in this life might come to know the connection between action and its fruit through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) alone; consequently, the principle that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the sole means of valid knowledge would be contradicted. This, however, is incorrect. For in the beginningless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there are infinite actions belonging to the infinite number of agents who revolve therein; even one who remembers their past births (*jātismara*) would not be able to discern such a vast amount [of causal relations].

"One is capable of knowing that 'this is the fruit of such-and-such an action. However, for transmigrating beings, the experience of the fruits of actions performed only in the immediately preceding existence is not necessarily the case;

because the fruits of good and evil deeds accumulated over various births are infinite and their measure is undetermined, the discernment of the connection between specific actions and their fruits is difficult to grasp. Therefore, no contradiction is observed between this and the traditional scripture (āgama) or memory; so what is the point of refuting it?"

To this it is replied: Even if, by relying on the authority of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, some maintain that certain sages in the various ages beginning with the Kṛta-yuga remember the Vedas while possessing bodies not born from a womb—let that be so. Even this does not cause any loss to our established doctrine (siddhānta), for we are refuting the memory of only a single individual.
For that indeed brings about the state of being artificial. Therefore, he will say: "the intuition of one.

Here too, by the use of the singular "of this" (*asya*), he refutes the recollection of only one [person]. It is simply impossible to establish that there are many non-womb-born bodies who could be the rememberers. Indeed, a non-womb-born body is not possible for human beings.

Because there would be no contradiction regarding the restriction of intrinsic nature; for if there were contradiction, it would follow that all worldly conventions concerning both the seen and the unseen would be utterly destroyed. As for those born from a womb, even if they possess extraordinary qualities, we do not believe that they could remember the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (*aṅga*). For birth, old age, death, suffering, and humiliation are a great cause for the destruction of mental formations (*saṃskāra*); how then could such a person [retain such knowledge]?

A textual composition, neither deficient nor excessive by even a single syllable, might be remembered by someone; furthermore, it is observed that some people do remember certain events from other lives—let it be so according to what is seen that one is a "rememberer of births" (*jātismara*).

Alternatively, let a specific assumption of a non-womb-born body be postulated on the strength of the fact that the Vedic texts concerning the memory of past births, which are inferred from human experience, would otherwise be inexplicable.

It is like the assumption of uncommon, extraordinary bodies, sense organs, and so forth for sages such as Bhṛgu and others, which is postulated because the Vedic injunctions regarding the desire for heaven would otherwise be inexplicable.

For we, being established in the scriptures, rely upon them according to the scriptures. Furthermore, an excellence that has arrived through the power of the scriptures cannot be refuted by inference, precisely because it would contradict scripture. Moreover, what was experienced in another birth is not remembered.

Let it be that this [scripture] indeed has as its intended object supersensible matters (*atīndriyārtha*). In any case, it is established that the hypothesis of a single person possessing both scripture and memory is not tenable. // 146 //
[455] From you,
[456] there is the extraction of the meaning-bearing and non-different [element], [457] namely *sva* (KA).
[458] And those which have other meanings; [459] the meaning of "etc.";
[460] but the bodies.

[461] Once again, returning to the very position of apprehension (*grahaṇapakṣa*), he states the refutation [beginning with the words] "in being an object of apprehension" (*grāhyatve*). [The opponent objects: "But surely it is the supersensible object (*atīndriyo 'rthaḥ*) of scripture that is supersensible, not scripture itself; so how can there be parity? To this he replies: "For that which... For scripture (*āgama*) when unuttered is indeed supersensible.
Such is the intended meaning. // 147 //
