[462] The opponent says: "But surely, even though they are equal, we and others have relied upon the acceptance of scripture (*āgama*). What is the fault? To this he replies:
"First, the person... The intention here is this: there is no equality in this case. For when it comes to the manifestation of meaning, the person is independent.

Because the determination of the meaning follows that [scripture]. However, in the case of a person who relies on scripture, the person is dependent upon the scripture regarding the meaning; and the scripture, too, for its own establishment, is dependent upon that [person]. Thus, because of this mutual dependence, both lack authority. // 148 //

[463] But surely, this dependence upon scripture (*āgama-pāratantrya*) is equally common to you as well. For its true nature cannot be trusted without relying on the authority of a person (*puruṣa-pratyaya*);
therefore, he says: "by many" (*aneka*). The intention is this: dependence upon a single person leads to error.

Because it gives rise to manifold doubts. For in such a case, doubt arises as follows: "Has this person seen or composed this scripture? And even if he has seen it, is it exactly as it stands or otherwise? Those who are thus beset by doubt would find no confidence anywhere. However, regarding the Veda, which rests upon many persons, there will be neither suspicion that it was composed nor any suspicion of its being otherwise; this the author will state later. Therefore, the Veda attains authority with its independence unimpaired. Furthermore, as for this postulation of a memory, without exception, of things experienced in one life within another life—
That too indeed establishes the dependence of the Vedas.

For it is suspected there: "How indeed has this great composition of texts been remembered by him after being interrupted by death, which cuts away all residual impressions (*saṃskāra*)? Therefore, he must surely have composed it himself with the desire to deceive us."
He cites the traditional scripture (āgama) as being remembered. Thinking in this way, they would not determine the authority of scripture independently.
However, for us, because perception and memory arise within a single lifetime, this fault does not occur; thus he says: "In one [lifetime]. (149)
[464] They would pant.
(GA) [465] Thus, what is the advantage in its being situated within many persons?

Therefore he says: "Otherwise. For when there are many transmitters of the tradition, the suspicion that the Veda might have been altered is removed. Indeed, if the Veda were destroyed by one person, another would prevent it by saying, "It is not thus," and would show it otherwise. Thus, through the consensus of many, the determination of the Veda’s true nature as it actually exists occurs. [In contrast,] the intuition of a single individual—
However, this does not differ from the hypothesis that [the self] is both produced and a cognizer, because in both cases the lack of trust is equal; thus he says: "Of one... (verse 150).

[466] Therefore, just as there is not a single author of the Vedas, so too there is not a single person who initiates the tradition; thus he concludes with the words "ataś ca" (and therefore). As in the present day...

But he says "many" to show that even in the past there were many men who were dependent on their religious studentship and so forth; and this should be demonstrated by means of formal argumentation. // 151 //

Thus, it has been established that the postulation of a superior person (puruṣātiśaya) is not equivalent to the postulation of [the Veda] being authorless (apauruṣeya). Therefore, as for the claim made by others that these two postulations are equal, he says with derision—beginning with "If this were so"—that such equality holds only insofar as one must either abandon or accept the very same thing that is to be postulated. // 152 //

He clarifies this very point with the words "na hi" (for not). Jaimini’s view is that the Vedic usage has been extended in exactly the same manner as it is today; and since this follows what is observed, Jaimini has not postulated anything supernatural, such as a superhuman being who was never before seen by others. Furthermore, the refutation of the inference for human authorship has already been stated previously.
However, for those who maintain that the Vedas lack authority, there is both the abandonment of what is observed and the postulation of what is unobserved; thus he says, "By [claiming] non-authority.

For a defect is the cause of non-authority, and such a defect, being unobserved in the authorless Veda, must be postulated. Furthermore, the observed authority of a cognition that is free from the three kinds of non-authority would have to be abandoned. Now, one might object: is not this subversion of what is observed common even to the case of errors?

Now, if it is argued that there is a reversal [of the cognition] there due to the force of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), then that too would be inferential in this case; therefore, he says: "arisen" (*utpanna*). This is the intended meaning: it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya* that "this cognition has arisen because it is free from correctness, doubt, and error. Furthermore, even inferences may contradict scripture (*āgama*).
And it has already been stated that there is a contradiction with a counter-reason (*pratihetu*). Therefore, this sublation (*bādha*) is postulated even without a cause.
But in the case of an error (*bhrānti*), this is not so; thus, the reversal is clear. // 154 //
And it is seen, having been seen, indeed seen.
Thus. u.
[470] As for what was said— that verbal testimony cannot be a means of valid cognition because it does not accord with one's own or another's perception—

that is incorrect. For when we shall demonstrate that the Vedas are authorless (*apauruṣeya*), then this cognition arising from the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) will [be established] by means of perception.

We do not perceive any distinction [between the two], because both arise from causes that are free from defects. Therefore, he says "it is established" (*sādhita*) to address the question: "What is the use of corroboration by perception (*pratyakṣasaṃvāda*) here? The meaning is: it is both faultless and the arising of that cognition. // 155 //

{1,142} Here is another commentary: "But surely, instruction for those who lack knowledge is not possible," and so forth. He states its intended meaning: "Instruction. This is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) stated by the author of the Bhāṣya. For instruction is observed in the case of Buddhas, Anantas, and others. And this instruction is not logically possible for those who do not know the subject matter. Therefore, the object of the instruction is perceived.

"It is postulated that [this] meaning was [stated] by Manu and others. The mention of Manu and others is for the sake of persuasion (*prarocanā*). For he thinks thus: 'This Mīmāṃsaka indeed accepts the truth of the scriptures of Manu and others; therefore, I shall first cause him to accept this very point by pointing to Manu and others, namely, that there exists a seer of supersensible objects (*atīndriya-artha*). And from that, I shall easily establish that the Buddha also possesses the vision of the objects of his own scripture.'"
And whatever is the nature of existence,
who is it that does not possess limbs?

[474] He states that the Veda is a commentary intended as an inference from external scripture with the words "Or rather" (*yad vā*). For the status of being an instruction (*upadeśitva*) is understood to be pervaded by having a perceptible object as its antecedent, as seen in the instructions of physicians and the like. That same status is understood even when its scope concerns objects beyond the senses (*atīndriya-artha*), and thus it leads one to infer that [the Veda] possesses such a nature.

But is it not the case that the author of the *Bhāṣya* has not stated here that "being a teacher" (*upadeśitva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*), but rather that "the impossibility of instruction for those who do not know"? Therefore, how can this be described as having the intention of an inference? To this he says: "by way of negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*). This is the intended meaning: according to the view of one who holds that negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is primary, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated here that the logical reason functions as a means of cognition by way of negative concomitance. For whoever...

"He does not know it, therefore he does not teach it," as is the case with a physician regarding dharma and adharma. But Manu and others did not fail to teach matters that transcend the senses. Therefore, the fact of being a teacher—distinguished from those who are ignorant—infers their state of being wise. Having thus stated the intention behind the twofold objection, he states the intention of the explanatory passage (*bhāṣya*) which provides the refutation: "Otherwise... (anyathā).

Being challenged with the intention of [proving] presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), the refutation of that [implication] is stated by this commentary (*bhāṣya*) through the demonstration of an alternative explanation: "For instruction can indeed arise even from delusion. Since the occurrence of instruction is possible even through delusion, it is not possible to postulate [the existence of] supersensuous knowledge (*atīndriyajñāna*).
And this is observed even today.

143} For those who are deluded, there is the instruction on the meaning of the treatise in a contrary manner and the composition of works by authors. But when the challenge is intended as an inference, then he says "of the mark" (liṅgasya), meaning that the fault of the inference—the deviation (vyabhicāra) of the logical mark—is being stated by this. "A child" means one who is ignorant. Even for such a person, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika) because instruction is observed [to be given] even to them. // 158 //

Furthermore, regarding the *Bhāṣya* statement, "Also, when there is no delusion, [the truth is known] even from the Veda," he explains that up to the words "from the Veda. This is the intended meaning: this is precisely a refutation of inference.
First, it was stated that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); now, however, it is said that it proves what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

As for this inference of knowledge from instruction that has been stated, it is here established as something already proven. True. Instruction regarding objects beyond the senses belongs to those who have known them through the Veda. For in this way, the Veda alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding supersensible matters, and not the person by his own power. But how is it a case of proving what is already established? It is because the knowledge of supersensible matters on the part of the Buddha and others does not arise from the Veda; indeed, they are not to be informed by means of the Veda.
Because there is no study [of the Veda] in their proximity. Therefore, for those who do not know the nature of the Veda, instruction based on knowing it from the Veda is not possible;

hence he says, "of Manu and others. This is the intended meaning: it is true that this is not stated as a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) with respect to the intention of the Buddha and others;

however, by saying "Manu and others have given instruction," Manu and others are pointed out. And it will be explained in the section on *Smṛti* (*Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*) that their instruction was indeed based on knowing it from the Veda itself. Just as...
He will say:
"The object is cognized by one who is meditating."

[477] Sacrifices [are not authoritative], because they are subject to error, because they are based on personal experience, and because they originate from human speech which is prone to deception; [478] nor from the Veda (ka), because it is subject to error and because it is based on personal experience, and also because of the possibility of deception through human speech.
Because it is established through conformity with what is perceived, the Vedic injunction alone is the most parsimonious means.

Thus [it is said]. However, for those who propound meanings contrary to the Veda, instruction from the Veda is simply impossible; as he will state: "But in case of contradiction, it should be disregarded. This is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), meaning that [the authority] is accepted even in relation to Manu and others. Furthermore, there is another commentary intended to explain the distinction between the human and the non-human: "Moreover, from the human..."

From the mere statement [of a person], the cognition arises: "This person knows thus," but not [the cognition] "The object is thus. Furthermore, a cognition indeed fails due to some statement made by a human being; however, there is no means of valid knowledge whatsoever for the falsity of the Vedic statement. The meaning of this is: previously, indeed... [1]
144} By means of the analogy of human speech, beginning with the words "nanu atathābhūtam" and so forth, the falsity of the Vedic statements was established.

Therein, following the lineage of the Mīmāṃsā school, the final conclusion (siddhānta) was set forth by means of the passage beginning with "vipratiṣiddham," while maintaining that validity is intrinsic (svataḥprāmāṇya).

Furthermore, by means of the section on "trustworthy persons" (pratyayita), it was shown that in one part there is a deficiency of the probandum (sādhyavaikalya) in the example, and in another part [the falsity] is dependent upon other causes.

The falsity [of perception] has been stated as a refutation of inference. In the interim, a digression occurred. Now, that very distinction between worldly and Vedic sentences is being explained, by which the Vedic sentence is indeed an independent authority, whereas the human-made [sentence] is dependent and some is simply non-authoritative. And thus, as for that dependence on other cognitions which was implicitly included in the thesis regarding the nature of things—that all sentences possess authority [only through such dependence].

And that which was explained by the author of the *Vārttika* with the words "for [a cognition] seen through another means of knowledge," etc., is thereby refuted. Furthermore, it is shown that the internalized reason for falsity—namely, "being a sentence"—is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) when falsity is the property to be proven. And although that [cognition] originating from human intellect is invalid, [the argument remains sound].
Thus, in this context, it has been stated that invalidity depends upon the defects of the person;

nevertheless, that was merely asserted as a proposition and not yet demonstrated. Now, however, a doubt arises: how is it to be understood that invalidity is dependent on the person and not an inherent consequence of the nature of the sentence? To this, the following [is said]:

It is said: even the statement of a person (*puruṣavākya*), although it does not directly produce certainty regarding an object—provided that all suspicion of defects in it has been dispelled by the ascertainment of the speaker’s authority—is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of that [ascertainment]. As it has been said: "Thus he knows this;

the meaning is not otherwise. This means that the certainty regarding the object is mediated by the speaker’s authority and is not independent. This applies to that which is invariably connected to the very nature of the sentence.

If there were no invalidity [in human speech], no human statement whatsoever would be authoritative. Therefore, we understand that a sentence is inherently authoritative and becomes non-authoritative only due to defects in the person. This is what was meant by the statement, "it indeed falters. A cognition arising from the speech of an unreliable person falters; it falters in various ways.

"Thus" means "is of the nature of doubt," that is to say, "it is not thus. Or, "it errs. Thus, it has been shown that the inherent validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*) of statements is set aside by defects. Furthermore, it has been stated that the qualities of the speaker are not the cause of validity here, because their function consists solely in the removal of defects; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, how could the cognition produced from the Vedic word—which is by nature free from defects—[be otherwise]?

"It becomes non-authoritative. This very point was already set forth in its entirety by the author of the *Vārttika* regarding this [Vedic word] itself, with the words beginning "the arising of defects in the word," and so on.

Therefore, it was said: "but not of the Vedic statement. Thus, the summary of the meaning is as follows: this dependence upon other means of cognition is indeed appropriate for human statements, whose ascertainment is contingent upon those [other means].

And let it be granted that the lack of authority [of human speech] arises from the speaker’s dependence on authority for the determination of meaning, due to his defects; however, the cognition of the sentence-meaning arising from Vedic sentences—being produced by the inherent capacity of the word-meanings themselves—is independent and does not depend on another cognition, nor is it unauthoritative. // 159 //

Explaining the meaning of this very commentary, he first states an objection with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*). That determination of an object from human statements which was said to be preceded by the speaker’s knowledge is untenable, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining that knowledge. For a human statement is not necessarily a cognition whose object is its own referent without deviation, such that it could be understood [as such]. Indeed, an unreliable person (*anāpta*), knowing one thing, may intend to express another; and the production of a sentence is dependent upon the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). Therefore, by the force of that intention, the sentence is produced in quite a different way.
And since it is known otherwise as well, the inference of knowledge from a sentence is not absolute. // 160 //

Let alone the inference of knowledge from speech; even the mere intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) cannot be understood from it. Thus he says: "of one who is deluded. For the intention to speak is indeed extremely closely connected to the composition of a sentence. Even when that intention exists, a person who is deluded might sometimes construct a sentence otherwise.

It is observed [that this occurs]. Therefore, even according to one's intention (*vivakṣā*), a sentence does not necessarily proceed. If it is asked, "How can there be the composition of a sentence in the absence of an intention?", we say: no, because another intention is possible. If it is asked, "How can the intention for one thing be the cause for the production of another?", what is the fault? For an intention is the cause for the production of a sentence by way of effort (*prayatna*), not by means of some invisible form (*adṛṣṭa*). And that [sentence] was produced precisely by one impelled by a different intention; due to some deficiency, it did not turn out correctly.

It is established. Therefore, something else entirely has arisen, produced by incapacity—just as someone who intends to fall on dry ground falls instead into mud. However, the existence of a subtle intention (*vivakṣā*) is perceived only by those with subtle vision.
For intention is the desire to speak; and if that [desire] is a distinct quality of the self (*ātman*), [then it follows...]

In that case, how can it be asserted that [the intention] exists while remaining unknown, like pleasure and other such states which are known through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*)? Or, if it consists of a cognition in the form of desire (*abhilāṣa*), even so, how can it be inferred that there is a desire to speak of something else when another sentence is being manifested? Thus, this [argument] is trivial.

[479] Because of its existence, the commentary (*bhāṣya*), having been thus challenged, provides the following resolution: "the speaker’s cognition" (*vaktṛdhīḥ*). This is the intended meaning: for there are two kinds of speakers—the authoritative (*āpta*) and the non-authoritative (*anāpta*). Among these, it is one who is determined as follows: "This person does not speak otherwise than what he has known," which is to say, an authoritative person (*āpta*).

From that very statement, the speaker’s cognition is understood as "it is known thus. However, in other cases—namely, in the case of the speech of an unreliable person—it is subject to distortion; this is what was stated by the words "it is distorted" and so forth. In this regard, the following is said: when, first of all, a cognition has arisen from the speech of a reliable person without any doubt, and practical activity has been undertaken, and no contradiction is observed;

In that case, it is indeed auspicious. Even for a speaker who has become apprehensive, by recollecting the reliability (*āptatva*) of the speaker, a certain determination regarding the object arises preceded by that [reliable person's] knowledge. Furthermore, error on the part of a reliable person is not even suspected; for he is so exceedingly skillful that he generally does not err. Nor would such an effort as this—namely, his acting for the sake of another’s understanding—occur if he had not correctly understood the matter himself.
He utters a statement. Nevertheless, for one who is doubtful, certainty regarding that means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises precisely from questioning him.

If, when pressed, he teaches his own knowledge to the extent of three or four [instances], by that much alone the accomplishment of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), which is free from suspicion like his own means of valid cognition, is established. And the subversion [of truth] arises from the speech of an unreliable person in various ways.
"It has already been explained. Thus, first of all, the two types of distortion regarding cognition and its conditions have been explained by means of the determination of their objects.

Now, he demonstrates the intended meaning of the commentary with the words "by that" (*tena*). Regarding the fact that the nature of being a sentence was stated as a reason for [the object] not being as it appears, its lack of logical necessity (*aprayojakatva*) is asserted by this [statement]. For in the case of the statements of authoritative persons (*āpta*), truthfulness exists by general rule (*utsarga*), since defects have been eliminated by their excellences (*guṇa*).
It has been observed. For this very reason, the determination of an object follows that cognition; otherwise, even that [cognition] would be false.

However, in the case of the words of an unreliable person (*anāpta*), there is invalidity due to the sublation caused by those defects. Thus, the inherent power of correct discernment is attributed here to the word as speech. Furthermore, falsity is adventitious and does not function by virtue of being a sentence, for that [falsity] depends upon a pervasion (*vyāpti*) employed by another.

For it is as if the state of being unrighteousness (adharma) is caused by the fact of being prohibited, just as the state of being violence (hiṃsātva) [is caused by the fact of being prohibited]. // 162 //
In this regard, it has been stated: "In the case of the words of a reliable person, the speaker's cognition is understood. [481]

Regarding this, he states the reason: "padārtha... (concerning word-meanings). For when the speaker has composed the word-meanings for the listener, the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises. And the speaker’s mode of composition is preceded by the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*). Since that [intention] cannot exist in one who is not authoritative (*āpta*) without prior knowledge, it requires previous cognition. Therefore, by the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), prior knowledge [is inferred] from the statement of an authoritative person.
It is understood. // 163 //

Therefore, he demonstrates that the composition depends solely on the speaker's intention, stating: "by another intention. When, through the arrival of a different intention, a different composition is observed—characterized by the removal or addition of preceding or subsequent words—it is understood from this that the composition is dependent upon intention. // 164 //

And thus, since the composition [of a sentence] depends upon the speaker’s intention, and that [intention] is preceded by knowledge, for that reason, even when the hearer has produced a cognition of the meaning from the sentence, the thought arises regarding the speaker’s knowledge: "Surely this meaning was known by the speaker. He says "by that" (tena) because it is preceded by the speaker’s means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The sense is that one is not independent in composition; certainty does not arise from the mere knowledge of the meaning. Thus, in the passage "Therefore, here, by means of both the general rule and the exception," the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya is stated as being that the capacity of speech is innate. From the words "dependent upon the arrangement of word-meanings" up to "by that [arrangement] there is the cognition of the object," it is shown that the words of authoritative persons depend upon other means of cognition.
It should be understood that the intended meaning of the commentary has thus been elucidated. // 165 //

[483] Regarding the meaning of this: [484] Since authoritative speech (*āptavākya*) is understood here to be dependent upon the knowledge of that [object], he says: "The word of an authority" (*āptokti*). When one person practices an object that has been stated by an authority, and another questions him: "What is this for you?"...

When one says, "This is a valid means of knowledge," then that person, acting upon the words of a trustworthy authority, shows that very authority as the root source for that [knowledge], thinking: "He who speaks thus is the trustworthy authority; he knows this, not I. For if it were independent, the manifestation of that knowledge would be purposeless. // 166 //
[485] He asks: "Is the word of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) then not at all a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its object?

[486] It is not so; rather, for one who has conceived doubt because the reliability of the speaking person has not been ascertained, the word remains indifferent [as to whether it produces certainty]. For when the sense organs and other factors that constitute the cause of the speaker's cognition are ascertained to be unimpaired, [the word leads to certainty].
At that time, by dispelling the suspicion of defects, validity itself is established.

Here, the validity of words—which was introduced as being based on their being the cause of comprehension—was weakened by the suspicion of invalidity; now, once the defects have been refuted by the determination of the speaker’s own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says this [verse] for the sake of strengthening it: "Because it is mediated by the knowledge of that" (*tajjñāna-antaritatvāt*), i.e., because it is mediated by the speaker’s knowledge. This refers to the production of certainty.

The meaning is "of the word. By the word "for now" (*tāvat*), he refutes absolute invalidity; rather, validity is established even after some delay. But if certainty thus follows the authority of the speaker, then the word is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*); since it was not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) prior to that certainty, when is it a means of valid cognition? This has been stated: it is a means of valid cognition precisely at its own time.

The function of the speaker’s cognition consists solely in the removal of doubts regarding defects. For the listener first understands a meaning that was previously unknown; when a doubt arises due to the observation of deviation in some cases, its validity is established by removing that doubt. It is for this very reason that it is called "establishment" (sthāpana). // 167 //
[486] But even if this were not so, how could words first become indifferent? For has that object already been communicated by the word, or not?
If he says "no," then how is the speaker’s cognition inferred in this way? For the word *evam* has the sense of "in such a manner. [487]

Furthermore, a cognition that is formless (*nirākāra*) could not possess a mode [of appearance] by its own nature when it is not embraced by an object. Nor does an object that has not entered into the hearer’s intellect qualify the speaker’s knowledge as being of such a nature. If, however, the cognition of the object is understood even prior [to the speaker’s knowledge], then the reason for its dependence must be stated. For, since the determination of its own object is accomplished by that [cognition] at the very moment it arises, what else would it require? It is for the sake of certainty that there is a dependence upon the speaker’s means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
No, because indeterminate knowledge (*aniścayajñāna*) is impossible. For knowledge is indeed certainty (*niścaya*);

if that exists, how can it be said that there is no certainty? Therefore, this claim—that the speaker’s cognition is understood solely through the cognition of the object and that its validity is the cause—is untenable. To this, he says: "The object... regarding what was previously stated concerning the uncomprehended.

Regarding the point that "an object does not exist in such a manner," the reply is simply by way of admission: it is true that the object was previously indeed cognized. As for the objection that "uncertainty regarding a cognized object is impossible," that is not so;
for such uncertainty is possible for one in whom a doubt has arisen. Even if there is no doubt arising from the word itself, [it remains possible].

Nevertheless, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed, doubt (*saṃśaya*) certainly arises. As for the claim that there is no such thing as knowledge whose nature is non-ascertainment (*aniścayātmaka*), and that upon the arising of knowledge, ascertainment (*niścaya*) alone must arise—that is not correct; for even doubt is a form of knowledge.

Therefore, even when knowledge has arisen, if doubt arises due to some cause, then because [the speaker's] authority (*prāmāṇya*) depends on the speaker, ascertainment is attained through the cognition of the object (*arthajñāna*).

That very cognition of the speaker becomes the prior constituent in the validity of the preceding cognition; thus, when the suspicion of defects has been dispelled by it, there is the ascertainment of validity. // 168 //
[487] By those,
[488] wisdom (prajñā) is also understood (vijñāta).

[490] Thus, it has been stated that in the case of human statements, validity depends upon another cognition, and in some instances, invalidity is adventitious (aupādhika). However, in the case of Vedic statements, because the word possesses by its very nature the power to determine the correct meaning, [there is no such dependence].
It has been stated that the possibility of falsehood applies to human speech but not to the words of the Veda;

this is what he expresses with the word "ataḥ" (therefore). Granted that the lack of authority in human statements may arise from the suspicion of defects in the speaker, the Vedic word, being inherently free from defects, cannot possibly possess such a nature. // 169 //

[491] Since there is no intervention between the cognition of the speaker and the cognition of the listener even in the case of the Veda, the meaning of the sentence is understood through the word-meanings alone, which are eternal and faultless; thus he says: "tadbuddhi" (the cognition of that). Therefore, it is established that in the Veda there is no dependence upon another cognition.
"And it is not the case that [cognition] is non-correspondent with reality. He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "therefore" (ataḥ). // 170 //

Otherwise, he states the intention of the Commentary (*bhāṣya*) with the words "by being non-authoritative" (*apramāṇatve*). Whatever common worldly statement was cited as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*) for the purpose of establishing the non-authoritativeness of the Vedas, by this passage it is stated that the example lacks connection with the probandum (*sādhyānāsaṅgitā*), meaning it is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). // 171 //

[492] How is it that the probandum is not attached [to the example]? To this he says: "of those" (*teṣām*). This is the intended meaning: this was stated by the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) against opponents according to their own [philosophical] view. For instance, when—{1,}

150} Such is the position and the formal argument (*prayoga*) of the Lokāyatas: "Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is false, because its object is not apprehended by perception and other means of knowledge, like the words of the Buddha and others. This is stated from the perspective of the Buddhists. In that view, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is irrelevant to the probandum (*sādhya*). For in their system, speech is not a valid means of knowledge regarding an object. To explain: first, words merely cause the recollection of an object; they do not, in any case, bring about or remove anything. Furthermore, even a sentence is not a valid means of knowledge regarding an object, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed.
Therefore, how could that [external object] be established by it? Rather, it is the speaker’s intention alone that is understood through words by virtue of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*).

As they have said: "But the establishment of the [external] object does not follow from these [words], because no necessary connection is established between them and that [object]; rather, they would indicate the speaker’s intention. Therefore, as for what was stated regarding the effect to be communicated by the words of the Buddha and others—

In that regard, their correctness alone is established because it is non-deviant. However, their operation with respect to an external object is not admitted at all. Therefore, as previously demonstrated, there is no cause whatsoever for the falsity of Vedic statements. // 172 //

[493] Regarding the statement, "The meaning is dependent on the word-meaning," and so forth—by which it was said that the inference of the speaker’s cognition from the sentence occurs through the force of the connection (*pratibandha*). [494] KA: GA.

He shows this [with the words] "tad darśayati. If it is argued that wherever a speaker's statement functions, it refers to the object itself—distinct from the speaker's cognition—as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then that would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). To this he says: "svavyāpāra... (by its own operation). Even for the Vedas, falsity is admitted as being distinct from their own objects, because the opponent accepts their falsity for the sake of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Regarding this, there is another commentary: "But surely, there will be an inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam anumānam*)."
"Having observed that human speech is false, one infers that Vedic speech is also false because it shares the common property of being speech.

He states the intention behind this [inference] with the words beginning "without knowing" and ending with "is seen. This is the intention of the author of the Bhāṣya: that the property of being a sentence (*vākyatva*) is not a probans for falsity.

Not understanding that the Commentator had merely stated the mere words regarding the presence or absence of defects—which are the causes of truth or falsity in the statements of reliable and unreliable persons—the opponent, acting from a position of ignorance, said, "But [it is] an inference based on general observation," and so forth. Therefore, one should not raise the objection:
"How can there be a counter-argument using that very same reason when the lack of probative force of the reason has already been stated?"
151} Because of the objection raised by one who has not grasped the intended meaning. For he thinks as follows: "Let the falsity of human statements be whatever it may be;

even so, because the connection is established, the reason is indeed indicative. Thus, for both artificial and non-artificial statements, there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) known as "the generally observed" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). To this, the explanatory response (*parihārabhāṣya*) is:
"No, because they are different."

He anticipates that objection with the words, "not because of its being different. To the question, "How is it not a flaw? he replies, "from this [it follows]. When the falsity of Vedic statements is to be proven, a human statement is cited as an example. In that case, what fault is there in this so-called "difference"? On the contrary, this is indeed a merit. For it is precisely because of its difference that something serves as an example; otherwise, if it were non-different, it would result in the fallacy of the example being equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*). Indeed, the subject (*pakṣa*) itself cannot be the corroborative instance (*sapakṣa*), because the subject is that which is yet to be proven.
Because the similar instance (sapakṣa) is already established, and because there is a contradiction between an established entity and that which is to be proven being one and the same. // 174 //

[495] In this regard, setting aside for the moment the detailed commentary on the text, he says "therefore" (*tasmāt*) to state the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. He describes that very intention with the words ending in "having admitted" (*abhyupetya*). This is the meaning:

In the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "even according to the intention of the ultimate [view]," it was stated that the sentence is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) only with respect to the speaker’s knowledge, but it has no operation regarding the object itself. We accept that. Let it be that a human sentence is a means of valid cognition only with respect to an external object, and not with respect to the speaker’s knowledge. Furthermore, let the example for those who argue that [human speech] lacks validity be based precisely on its dependence upon an external object.

[This is] the name [of the fallacy]. Nevertheless, the refutation is stated as "even when there is an intervention. Even though a human statement is indeed non-authoritative regarding an object that is mediated by cognition, we nevertheless say that the reason (*hetu*)—namely, "being a statement"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of its commonality with the case where one accepts the authority of that very object; for even in the case of truthful statements by reliable persons (*āpta*), the property of being a statement is observed. This is the refutation here of the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*).
This turns over in the mind of the author of the *Bhāṣya*. The sense is that the *Bhāṣya* itself must be understood according to this very intention. [Objection:

Even though the object is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), we shall qualify [the reason] by saying "because it is a sentence" (*vākyatvāt*). Since every human statement whose object is beyond the senses is invalid, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) [of the reason]. To this, he says: "beyond the senses" (*atīndriya*). Even in the case of that which is beyond the senses...
For when someone, by chance, composes a statement regarding an object never before seen—
just as one says "Indra exists" while another says "He does not exist"— then, between those two, one of the statements must necessarily be true. Thus, for that single statement...

Regarding truthfulness: neither the existence nor the non-existence of Indra has been ascertained by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, even the speech of an unreliable person, when uttered by chance regarding a supersensible object (*atīndriyārtha*), is seen to be true;
thus, even with this specific reason, there remains the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). // 178 //

Having thus stated the intention of the author of the *Bhāṣya*, he applies the *Bhāṣya* to that very point with the words "nānyatvāt" up to the end of the section on "ābhāsa. This is the meaning: that which is called "fallacious" (*tadābhāsa*) by the opponents—the Naiyāyikas—because it possesses an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetuka*), is different from [valid] inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*). Therefore, the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established from this fallacy of inference based on general observation, because this fallacy is distinct from valid inference based on general observation.

Thus, he states another interpretation of the meaning of the commentary, beginning with the words "the counter-example" (*vipakṣam*). This is the intended sense: since the reason "being a statement" (*vākyatva*) is observed even in the case of true statements by authoritative persons (*āpta*), it occurs in the counter-example (*vipakṣavṛtti*); therefore, it does not establish the probandum (*sādhya*). That very point remains the refutation; however, the formulation (*yojanā*) differs. The point is that when falsity (*mithyātva*) is the probandum, truth (*satyatva*) constitutes the counter-example, as it is other than that [falsity], and because the reason resides in that [truth]. // 179 //

He explains otherwise, beginning with "Or rather" (*yad vā*). That which was shown in the Bhāṣya as the non-probative nature of being a sentence (*vākyatva*), starting with "api ca," and which the opponent had stated without realizing—that very point has been exposed by the author of the Bhāṣya with the words "not because it is different" (*na anyatvāt*). For indeed, the cause that renders [cognition] invalid is discordance (*visaṃvāda*), not the state of being a sentence; and this [discordance] is not possible in the case of the Veda.

Because [the Veda] is not of human origin, and because defects reside in persons; and because it is impossible for a cognition produced by non-defective causes to be non-correspondent (visaṃvāda). How could there be a reversal of conviction—namely, the notion "this is not so"—which constitutes non-correspondence, in a case arising from non-defective causes? This is because the cause of falsity is something else. Such is the interpretation of the *Bhāṣya*.

He states another explanation: "Of the object" (*viṣayasya*). For it was previously stated that, according to the opinion of others, the example is not connected to the probandum (*sādhyānāsaṅgī*). This very same lack of connection with the probandum is now stated on account of the difference in the object (*viṣayānyatvāt*). For the object of a human statement (*puṃvākya*) is the intention of the speaker (*vaktrabhiprāya*), and falsity does not apply there because [the speaker's intention] is never deviant (*avyabhicārāt*). Previously, however, [it was argued that falsity applies to] the operation directed toward the object as a thing (*arthaviṣayavyāpāra*).

Having previously stated [the argument] by assuming a difference [between the two], now, however, remaining within the opponent's own position, it is stated that [the reason] is not connected with the probandum. // 180 //

Furthermore, the *Bhāṣya* states: "For it is not the case that because one thing is false, another thing must also be false. He shows the meaning of this with the words "For it is not... By the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "For it is not because of one," it is stated that the falsity of one thing does not result in the falsity of another when that other is otherwise. He explains this very point with the word "intention" (*vivakṣā*). For the intention of the speaker in that case has as its object something that is not in accordance with reality.

The [word] has a false meaning, but it is not the sentence, because the validity of that [sentence] consists merely in its conveying that [meaning], and because that [meaning] is established from it by the force of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). Therefore, since the sentence does not have a false meaning, it is established that the probans is not concomitant with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*). This is also the case in the first position (*pakṣa*).

The commentary beginning with "na hi" (for not... must be explained as follows: it is not the case that because one person's untrustworthy statement has a false meaning, another person's trustworthy statement would also have that [same] meaning. Since the property of being a human statement (*puruṣavākyatva*) exists even in the case of true statements—which serve as the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). In this very same way, when the falsity of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) is to be proven in the second and third [arguments], the falsity of the other [property], namely "being a statement" (*vākyatva*), is what is to be proven.
It should be explained as "it is not possible. However, in the fourth [case], the explanation is found in the Vārttika. // 181 //
[496] Thus, in this regard, [497] there is also another passage from the Bhāṣya beginning with "For Devadatta’s dark complexion... and so forth.

He states his intention [regarding this] with the words "in the case of dark complexion. Just as when "dark complexion" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), "masculinity" is an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) because it is absent in fair-skinned people and so forth, so too "being a statement" (*vākyatva*) is common to both true statements by a reliable person and others; thus, this example is given for the purpose of demonstrating such commonality (*sādhāraṇya*). Others, however, thinking that when a faulty means of proof is employed, a faulty rejoinder (*uttara*) must be given, consider this to be the "balancing of the alternative" (*vikalpasamā*).

The commentator has stated that this is merely a "name" (nāmajāti) and not something else, as in [NS 5.1.4]: "Because it is not different" (*nānyatvāt*). Thus he says: "From the opponent's statement. *Vikalpasama* (balancing the alternative) consists in introducing an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by means of an alternative regarding another property (*dharmāntara*). This is to be illustrated as follows: "Is a certain sentence observed to be other than a human sentence? Just as...

A Vedic statement is in some respects non-different from that [reality], just as it is that very thing. Thus, because there is an alternative between being different and non-different, there will likewise be an alternative between truth and falsity, since there is no distinction in their status as statements. Therefore, falsity is not necessarily established merely by virtue of being a statement.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this [position] was presented according to the opponent's view precisely as something "inexpressible," because it would result in two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): either failing to state what ought to be stated, or stating the opposite of what ought to be stated.
"The reply is equal to the conceptual construction. // 182 //
[498] Because of the fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*).

[499] Thus, it has been stated that this is a statement of refutation based on the argument that "it is not so because of difference. Now, however, this is indeed a statement of proof (*sādhana-vacana*).

Thus he states another interpretation, beginning with "Or else" (*yad vā*). For when the opponent has established falsity (*mithyātva*), the proponent establishes truth (*satyatva*) by means of another reason. The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is inference (*anumāna*); this will be explained further below. To the question, "What kind of proof is that? he replies, "Contradictory" (*viruddha*). If there were equality of strength (*tulyabalatva*),...

The "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is a cause for doubt. Now, if the reason for the established tenet (*siddhāntahetu*) is more powerful, then there is sublation by inference (*anumānabādha*). In this case, there is indeed sublation by inference, because the reason for truth is more powerful than the reasons for untruth due to its being distinct [from them]; such is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. // 183 //

[500] He presents that very same [Vedic injunction] as the means of valid cognition for its truth—namely, "the Vedic injunction" (codanā). And this inference, which possesses an exclusive reason (ekāntika-hetu), is stronger than an inference based on general observation (sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa) which possesses a non-exclusive reason (anaikāntika-hetu). Furthermore, the non-exclusivity belongs to the [reason] when it is unqualified, whereas it does not exist when it is qualified.
And the reason has already been stated. Therefore, by this very powerful [reason], the inference of falsity is sublated. // 184 //

[501] While this very correctness (*samyaktva*) is to be established, he shows another two reasons by means of the illustration of the statement of a reliable person (*āptokti*), beginning with "likewise" (*tathā*). The logical connection (*anvaya*) is: "because there is an absence of sublation (*bādhavarjana*) despite differences in place, time, and so forth. In this context, since the reason is "due to the absence of sublation," it is indeed possible for both inferential signs (*liṅga*) and sensory cognitions (*akṣabuddhi*) to serve as examples; however, the cognition based on the statement of a reliable person has been presented as the illustration because it is common to both cases. // 185 //

"But is it not the case that this 'being produced by non-defective causes' and 'being generated by speech not uttered by an untrustworthy person' are unestablished (*asiddha*), since all sentences are products? To this he says: 'Because of being authorless. For the authorlessness of the Vedas will indeed be established; therefore, the reason is not unestablished. The Commentator stated this distinction with the intention of inferring truth based on such [reasons]; thus he says: 'In this way,' etc. By the word 'etcetera' (*ādi*), the reasons mentioned in the critique of the relationship [between word and meaning] are included."
[502] Its non-artificiality and the various options for explaining the commentary have been composed like the first six chapters of the original text. // 186 //

In this regard, there is another commentary (*bhāṣya*) intended to demonstrate the sublation of inference by scripture (*āgama*) through the "inference based on general observation" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*): "Furthermore, because it shares the same nature as human speech, the Vedic word is false;

however, the cognition regarding the Vedic word is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*). If this refers to the cognition whose object is the sentence (*vākya*), then that is incorrect, because the same would apply to the speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*). Even the cognition of its own nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed perceptual. It is not...
This is false. However, it will be stated in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra* that the meaning (*artha*) of Vedic sentences is beyond the reach of the senses;

therefore, this [statement] does not intend to refer to the meaning. If, on the other hand, "perceptibility" (*pratyakṣatā*) is asserted with reference to the nature of the cognition (*pratyaya*) itself, that too is incorrect, because in the *Śūnyavāda*, even that will be stated to be inferable (*anumeya*). Therefore, it must be explained [otherwise].

Therefore, he says: "perceptual" (*pratyakṣa*). This is the intended meaning: since primary perceptuality is impossible, the word "perceptual" is used in a figurative sense. For that which is firm and first is intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), whereas that which is contradicted by something else is invalid (*apramāṇa*). Thus, the word "perceptual" is applied to the cognition derived from scripture (*āgamika*) with the intention of attributing one of these four qualities; and that [scriptural cognition] too is firm.

Because it is free from doubt and error; because it arises swiftly, lacking dependence on examples and the like due to the absence of any inference for falsity; and because the falsity of what has arisen is established by inference.
It has been proven that for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), validity and invalidity reside respectively in themselves and in others. Therefore, it is equal to perception (*pratyakṣa*).
"How can this condition be otherwise? This contradicts the thesis that the meaning [of the Veda] is contrary [to reality].

Nor is it possible to object here by claiming that the authority of the Veda is unestablished for us; for even for atheists, there is no difference in the production of certain and non-erroneous cognition upon hearing it, and because the consciousness produced by the eternal scripture [is likewise certain]."

Because it is impossible for [the Vedic scripture] to be produced by a defective cause. However, those who maintain that scripture is of human origin argue that it was composed and handed down by the Self (Ātman) Himself;

thus, they are not able to raise the objection of contradiction with scripture against those who seek to prove the falsity of others, since their own scriptures have been tainted by the suspicion of defects inherent in human authors. And all of this has already been set forth by the author of the Vārttika, having been previously extracted from what was stated in the Bhāṣya.
One should connect this with the passage beginning "the alteration of the meaning of the injunction" (codanārthānyathābhāvam), and so forth. // 187 //
[503] Therefore, it is not false (KA); [504] precisely because of that,
[505] by means of that very knowledge (GA).

[506] Or rather, the word *pratyakṣa* (perception) in those scriptural passages should be explained in its primary sense alone; thus he says: "And [it is] the absence of cognition. In this way, the proponent of falsity (*mithyātvavādī*) should be addressed: "Falsity is indeed threefold. And here, neither doubt nor error exists," so states the Bhāṣya.

Thus it has been said. Therefore, if you seek to prove that falsity (*mithyātva*) is simply the absence of knowledge, you contradict your own perception (*pratyakṣa*). For in your own system, knowledge is indeed perception itself. If, according to your desire, the reality of this Vedic scholar is to be inferred, then how can you assert that falsity—which consists in the absence of knowledge—applies to him when he is clearly observing the very knowledge produced by hearing the Vedic words through direct perception? // 188 //

[507] From this supreme [GA] [508] that which is thus; first, it has been explained that by this commentary a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) has been stated. Now, another intended meaning (*tātparya*) of this very [text]:

He demonstrates this with the words "just as" (*yathaiva*). This is the meaning: by this commentary, it is stated that you establish falsity on the grounds of its similarity to human speech. Just as this falsity is observed [in human speech], so too must the Vedic statement be false. And that falsity is observed to be dependent upon sublation (*bādhaka*).

Thus, it would be exactly the same in the case of the Veda as well. And it has already been established that such a thing is not possible. Therefore, the conviction regarding the words of the Veda is indeed firm and perceptible; it is never sublated. Consequently, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is contradicted by a specific instance (viśeṣaviruddha). // 189 //

[509] Having thus established that the nature of being characterized by injunction (*codanālakṣaṇatva*) applies even to the eternal, the author of the Bhāṣya concludes: "Therefore, that which is characterized by injunction is the producer of the highest good (*śreyaskara*). Regarding this, although one ought to conclude exactly according to the Sūtra, there is a specific intention behind the employment of the term "producer of the highest good."

He says: "Dharma. The word *śreyaskara* (conducive to the highest good) is employed precisely to explain the meaning of the term *dharma*. For by its use, it is communicated—through a sequence of objections and their refutations—that dharma is that which conduces to the highest good. // 190 //
In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya, following an objection—"In that case, then, that which brings about the highest good (śreyaskara) must be investigated"—stated:

"That alone which brings about the highest good is denoted by the word *dharma*. In that context, it is not known by what means the nature of *dharma* is stated here; therefore, for the sake of distinguishing that, he says: "The highest good (*śreyaḥ*). This word *śreyaḥ* is well-known to mean human pleasure (*puruṣaprīti*).

And their causes—substance, quality, and action—are understood through the force of the Vedic injunction (codanā). Therefore, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that dharma-ness resides in those very things by virtue of their being conducive to the highest good (śreyaskara). // 191 //
Regarding this, there is another commentary: "For those who perform a sacrifice are called 'righteous' (dhārmika). Its meaning is as follows:

Dharma is that which brings about the highest good (śreyas), because worldly people apply the term "righteous" metaphorically to one who performs sacrifices and the like, whose status as bringing about the highest good is determined by Vedic injunction (codanā). Thus, it is logically established that sacrifice and the like constitute Dharma.

For whoever practices *dharma* is a practitioner of *dharma* (*dhārmika*). Therefore, sacrifice (*yāga*) and the like possess the nature of *dharma*. It is for this very reason that the application of the term "practitioner of *dharma*" is appropriate for one who performs them, and not otherwise. This is incorrect. This usage does not necessarily imply that sacrifice and the like alone constitute *dharma*, since it is also logically consistent for human qualities, the unseen force (*apūrva*), and so forth to be *dharma*. For even the unseen force (*apūrva*) and the rest produce their effects through sacrifice and the like. So how is this distinction made: that "this person is a practitioner of *dharma* because he practices sacrifice," and not because he practices the unseen force and the rest?

Therefore, he says: "something else. This is the intended meaning: it is true that the establishment of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) is a byproduct of sacrifices and the like; however, that *apūrva*, being the goal of the sacrifice and so forth, is not pointed out by the performers [as the cause of their status]. This is because it exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), and potentiality is beyond the reach of the senses. Consequently, it is not tenable to apply the term "righteous person" (*dhārmika*) to one who practices such acts merely on the basis of perceiving that [invisible result]. Therefore, it is certain that the designation "righteousness" arises precisely from the connection with sacrifices and other such acts.

Furthermore, is it the very nature (*svarūpa*) of sacrifices and the like that constitutes *dharma*? If this were so, there would be a contradiction between what was stated previously and what follows. For, first, it was stated previously that its status as *dharma* consists in its being of such a nature (*tādrūpyeṇa*).

And by the latter [statement], it is said that at that time [of performance], it does not exist in the form of a means for accomplishing a result (*phalasādhanarūpeṇa*), because at that moment it does not exist.

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, that form of sacrifice and so forth, being beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), is not visible through perception and other means of knowledge like the *apūrva*. If, however, one were to assert the essential nature of sacrifice and so forth [as the meaning of "dharma"], then an infinite number of potencies would have to be postulated for the single word *dharma*. How indeed could this [word] function with respect to substances, qualities, and actions of various classes by means of a single potency alone? It might be argued: "[It does so] because it expresses the state of being a means to pleasure (*prīti*) which is common to all [of them]."

"It is not a fault," [you might say]. No; for it has already been stated that this too is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of denoting the qualifier alone.
For it is impossible to denote the means of pleasure (*prītisādhana*) without having first denoted the pleasure itself; thus, that [pleasure] would have to be denoted first.
And in such a case, if the function of denotation were exhausted by that alone, the successful denotation of the qualified entity (*tadviśiṣṭa*) could not be established.

It is like the words "cow" and so forth, and like the word "sāman. For it is established that where a qualified entity is made known by an indivisible word, the denotation (*vācya*) of that word is the qualifier itself. Therefore, the author will state that the word *sāman* denotes only the melody (*gīti*) and does not denote the specific melody [of a particular verse]. The Vārttikakāra also, while refuting the view that Dharma is an action qualified by the *apūrva*, stated:
If those [past actions], distinguished by their residual karma and the unseen force (*apūrva*), are designated as "dharma," [then this is the case].
The denotative power being exhausted in the qualifier, the word cannot reach the qualified object.

Thus it is said. This same [argument] applies even when the result is specified as qualified [by the action]. It might be thought that the object of duty (*dharma*) is that which is to be enjoined. That is not so. For if that were the case, the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) itself—being extremely proximate to the injunction—would attain the status of being denoted by the word *dharma* as the object to be enjoined. For it is an established tenet that this [efficient force], consisting of three parts, is what is enjoined. Therefore, it is better that the term *dharma* denotes the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality) alone.

This is because the term *dharma* follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [apūrva]. For instance, at the time of the fruit's attainment, even though the ritual act no longer exists, people are seen to employ the figurative expression "this person possesses *dharma*" solely on account of the existence of the *apūrva*. Conversely, even when sacrifices and other rites have been performed, if they are defective and the production of the *apūrva* has not been achieved, people are not seen to employ the term *dharma*. Therefore, the referent of the term *dharma* must be explained.
It is said: this word *dharma* functions, like the word *pācaka* and others, as a term whose meaning is restricted (*sabhāga*) to the instrument of support (*dhṛti-sādhana*).

And *dhṛti* is a synonym for joy (*prīti*). Furthermore, this [word] is included among those taught in the *Pṛṣodarādi* list; it is to be derived by inferring the division between root and suffix. Thus, here, from the root *dhṛ*, we have *dhṛti*.

And by means of the suffix *manin*, its accomplishment (*sādhana*) is denoted. Nor does this lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that it would apply to food, recreation, and so forth, because we accept a conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) based on etymological derivation (*yoga*), as in the case of words like *paṅkaja* ("lotus"). This is because the term denotes only that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaskara*) as characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). Furthermore, the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*) of the word is not independent of its etymological derivation, such that it would result in the application [of the term] to the mere qualifier alone. Nor does it lead to the undesirable consequence that it applies to the mental realization (*bhāvanā*).

Because that [word "dharma"] does not denote those [sacrifices and so forth], since it is established by the authority of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) that sacrifices and the like alone are the means to achieve the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). One must accept that the two designations [of "dharma" for sacrifices and for pleasure] are based solely on conventional usage (*rūḍhi*): the term "dharma" is applied metaphorically (*upacāra*) to that which is a means to pleasure and to that which is enjoined, because of its application to both the means of achieving pleasure and to what is prescribed.
Furthermore, the designation of a mere attribute for that which is indivisible is only figurative; however, in the absence of any other recourse, there must be a designation of the whole.
And here, since joy and its means are understood to be enjoined by the word *dharma* in the same manner [as the goal], why should they not be expressed by the word itself?
As for the claim that this form is also invisible, that is not so.

[This is] because of understanding from the Veda. We observe that even those who have understood only this much—that sacrifice is the means for attaining prosperity (*abhyudaya*)—use the word "virtuous" (*dhārmika*) with reference to the performers of sacrifices and so forth, without having reckoned with the *apūrva*. Therefore, they are determined to be "dharma" by virtue of that very nature alone. Thus, it is established that the meaning of the term "dharma" is a prescribed means for attaining prosperity. As for what was said:

"It is not the case that sacrifice and the like are *dharma* because they do not exist when [the constituent factors] are deficient. This is not so. Since such a [deficient] act lacks the capacity to be a means to prosperity (*abhyudaya*), and since it is therefore *adharma*, how could the word *dharma* be applied to it? However, the application of the term *dharma* at the time of the fruit is intended solely in reference to that which is the means to prosperity. For even at that time, that [efficacy] still exists, persisting in the form of a latent potency (*śakti*).
In its own nature. And how the *apūrva* is not denotable by the word "dharma" will be explained precisely [in the following section]. // 192 //
[513] Joy (*prīti*).

The meaning is as follows: Animals and the like are well known to be the fruits of *dharma*. Therefore, the thought arises that whatever has these as its fruits is itself *dharma*. Furthermore, since it is understood from the scriptures (*śāstra*) that these [animals] are the fruits of the *citrayajña* and other such rites, he concludes that the *citrayajña* and others are *dharma*—this is expressed by the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is not only so in common worldly usage; even in the Veda, the term *dharma* is well established specifically for sacrifices and the like.

By demonstrating this, the author of the Bhāṣya has shown that [the passage] "The gods sacrificed with sacrifice; those were the dharmas" means that the word *dharma* here is in grammatical apposition with "sacrifice" (*yajña*), and is thus determined to denote that very thing. But how can the word *dharma*, which differs in gender and number, stand in apposition with "sacrifice"? [The answer follows: It is through its being in apposition with "sacrifice."

It is being pointed out [as follows]: for if it were in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word "sacrifice"], it would have to be "that dharma. Since only a single sacrifice is under discussion (*prakṛta*), and since that [sacrifice] is masculine, [the author] says: "regarding gender" (*liṅga*). Here, the author of the Commentary has shown that the word *dharma* itself is intended, having abandoned specific gender and number, because a term functioning as a generic class name (*jātiśabda*) grasps whatever is under discussion.

Furthermore, because there is no other context [for it], it is determined that the word *dharma* is in grammatical apposition with "sacrifice" (*yajña*). The intention is that the discrepancy in gender and number is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*). Moreover, the first occurrence of the word *yajña* here has the sense of indicating the means for performing a sacrifice, while the other has its literal, primary meaning. // 194 //
[Kha] Thus, first of all, the category of *dharma* has been explained according to the Bhāṣyakāra. Now, other views will be presented.

He rejects [the view], saying "by the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇa*), as it is not seen by the end [of the verse]. For the Sāṅkhyas rely on dharma as a specific modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ, namely the mind (*manas*). The Śākyas, however, [rely on] a pure latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced within one consciousness by another consciousness.
The Ārhatas, moreover, declare dharma to be subtle, corporeal *pudgalas* that initiate effects. The word *pudgala*...
But by the Ārhata [Jainas], it is designated as such in relation to those very things. The Vaiśeṣikas, however, maintain that *dharma* refers to the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self.

A certain school of Mīmāṃsakas, on the other hand, applies the term *dharma* specifically to the production of the *apūrva*. Their intention has already been described. Furthermore, the etymological definition of the word *apūrva* is "that which has no prior birth" (*na pūrvaṃ janma asya*); this is its meaning.

For that [result] certainly does not arise prior to the action, since it is accomplished only when the action has been performed. Furthermore, the use of the word *dharma* is not observed in common worldly usage with respect to any of these things. And worldly usage is the root for determining the meaning of a word. Therefore, those are not *dharmas*. But how [could they be] the function of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*)?

The status of being *dharma* is being refuted. Even the Mīmāṃsakas indeed accept that [status], since they admit that only mental volitions (*saṅkalpa*)—such as those regarding sacrifice and the vow not to look at the rising sun—are *dharma*.
This is not so; the volitions are not merely mental.

Because the Self is the agent, as is seen in the Upaniṣads. For it is heard [in scripture]: "The Self which is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, without hunger or thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"; and likewise, "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere resolve the fathers arise for him. Here, the suffix *kṛt* (the suffix *-ka*) denotes the agent according to its grammatical definition.
The genitive case indicates that the intention (*saṅkalpa*) has the self as its agent; thus, it is not a property (*dharma*) of a mental modification (*manovṛtti*).

Furthermore, the impossibility of the relationship between the perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfumer (*vāsaka*) among momentary and simultaneous minds will be explained precisely in the Vijñānavāda section.

Therefore, setting that aside for now, it was stated that mental perfuming (*cittavāsanā*) is not a *dharma* because there is no [logical] application [of such a relationship]. As for the statement "meritorious persons" (*puṇyāḥ pudgalāḥ*), if these refer to atoms (*aṇu*), [the following applies]:

The application of the word *dharma* to those [entities] is not observed in the world. If, on the other hand, they are something else, then since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for them, how could they be established? And all the more so, how could the word *dharma* be applied to them when their existence has not been established? As for the quality of the person (*puṃguṇa*), it must be either eternal, like omnipresence (*vaibhava*) and so forth, or produced, like pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth. If it were eternal, ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*) would be useless. If it were produced, it could not be any one of the categories such as the "unseen force" (*apūrva*).

We perceive a specific quality inherent in the self. However, it has already been stated how the *apūrva* is not a *dharma*, and he will further state that it is "because it is not [the result of] performance. Furthermore, as for the definition of *dharma* that was stated—that it is a quality of the self produced by conjunction, which bestows the fruit upon the agent and is opposed by its effect—[that too is incorrect].

That is incorrect, because it would entail the commonality of non-dharma (*adharma*) and the commonality of the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) that cause memory; for those two as well would result in being *dharma* by virtue of having such characteristics. Furthermore, [the definition] "that which bestows the fruit upon the agent" is too narrow (*avyāpaka*), since it is heard in scripture that at a *śrāddha* ceremony, the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and others who are not the agents receive the fruit of satisfaction, and likewise in the case of the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice.

Furthermore, it is your established doctrine that the fruit of a rite performed by the father accrues only to the son. For, having prescribed the injunction, "One should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara when a son is born," the scripture declares: "When a son is born, he who performs this sacrifice becomes pure, resplendent, an eater of food, endowed with sensory power, and possessed of cattle. [This is because] "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer" (Jaimini Sūtra 3.7.18).

Thus, the general rule that [the fruit] goes to the father is set aside by the scriptural statement that the fruit goes to the son. Therefore, it is established that internal organ modifications (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) and so forth are not *dharma*. Now, you yourself accept that the term *dharma* is applied to that which brings about the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Since these [modifications] are means to the highest good, why is it said that the word *dharma* is not seen to be applied to them? To this he says:

"Not so," he says. First of all, the fact that these [mantras] are means for accomplishing a result is not cognizable through perception and the other means of knowledge, because they are beyond the senses. Nor are they cognizable through Vedic injunction (codanā), since by that [injunction] one understands that the means for accomplishing the result are only sacrifices and the like. // 196 //

[516] He said: "Let it be that the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and so forth are not *dharma*, because they are not understood as being the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). However, the *apūrva* is indeed the means for attaining bliss, because the fruit is accomplished from that alone once the ritual act has passed. For even those who maintain that the sacrifice itself is the means [to the fruit] [must admit] that 'having produced the *apūrva*...'"

Those who explain [the matter] include the *apūrva* (the unseen force) within [the definition of Dharma]. It has also been stated by others: "Heaven results from the undertaking [of action], and the undertaking results from ritual action (*karman*).
By "undertaking," they mean precisely the *apūrva*, for it is that which is undertaken. Therefore, they consider it logically correct that Dharma is indeed the *apūrva*.

Therefore, he says: "And not... The intention here is as follows: What is this so-called *apūrva* (the unseen force)? If it is either the power of the ritual act (*karma-śakti*) or the power of the fruit (*phala-śakti*), it is neither a means (*sādhana*) nor an end to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is because a power is not an agent (*akārakatvāt*), and because it is established as being merely incidental to the fruit desired by the person. If, on the other hand, *apūrva* is said to be a distinct entity altogether, [then...]

That too is incorrect, because it is impossible to cognize that [word-meaning] as it does not enter into either of the two forms of the probandum or the probans. For we do not understand from the word itself that it is the means for attaining heaven or the end to be attained by the sacrifice; nor from any other means of valid cognition, since it is admitted that such things are not known through them. Precisely for this reason, it is not known from the word.

Because there is no linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) regarding that which is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and because that which is not the meaning of a word cannot be the object of a sentence. Therefore, apart from the relationship between the probandum and the probans, an *apūrva* (unprecedented force) that is a distinct entity cannot be understood through any other means of valid cognition; for it is impossible to demonstrate that [entity], which lacks these two forms, by means of any other form. // 197 //
[517] Regarding the end of the section on types (KA):
[518] Furthermore, if it is maintained that something unprecedented (*apūrva*) is the object to be accomplished by the sacrifice and the means for attaining heaven;

Therefore, he says "the abandonment of what is heard and the fabrication of what is not heard" (*śrutahānir aśrutakalpanā ca*), referring to the phrase "the means [of accomplishment] as heard" (*śrutasādhaneti*). The meaning of the sentence is that the nature of the object and the mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) thereof constitute the sentence-meaning. And since that cultivation depends upon both the end to be achieved (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*), it will be explained in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* how it grasps only heaven and sacrifice, as will also be discussed here in the section on the "Cage of Cultivation" (*bhāvanāpañjara*). Consequently, that which is not heard must first be discarded. [This applies to] a non-entity (*avastu*) that is beyond the senses.

"Since that which resembles a sky-flower and the like must be conceived as having the nature of both the probandum and the probans, this is an 'inference of what has not been heard' (*aśrutakalpanā*). With the intention that if neither of these two forms is admitted, there would be a total non-existence of that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he says: 'But in the case of difference, there is formlessness. (198)
This was stated for the purpose of demonstrating boldness; it does not mean that something devoid of these two forms cannot be denoted by the word *dharma*.

Therefore, the *apūrva* is not a distinct ontological entity. Rather, it is merely the power (*śakti*) of the sacrifice and so forth when they have set out to produce a result, or the mere power of the animal and so forth when they have set out to arise—this subtle state is the *apūrva*.

It is not a different reality. Nor is the potency of the action itself the means of accomplishing the fruit, because the action is the intermediate operation.
