[The merit] arises for the donor who has bestowed that [gift] upon a worthy recipient; according to the scriptures, it is understood that for as many years as there are hairs on the body of a cow with its calf, he dwells in heaven. However, in some cases, it is stated that the fruits are equal, double, a thousandfold, or infinite for non-Brahmins, Brahmins, learned Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), and those who have mastered the Vedas (*vedapāraga*) respectively;

thus, the example is deficient in its probandum (*sādhyahīna*). Furthermore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the subject (*pakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) occurs through the very same term expressing the probandum.

It is said: here, in the example of giving (*dāna*), the meaning of the word "object" (*viṣaya*) is the recipient (*sampradāna*); however, in the case of injury (*hiṃsana*), it is the victim that is the object (*karman*). With the intention that this is not tenable, he says—up to the end of the section on the discrepancy—"the recipient.
If, however, for the sake of avoiding this discrepancy, the meaning of the word "object" were to be the recipient alone even in the [other] case, [then...]

Therefore, he states "in the case of the recipient" (*sampradāne*) because the thesis would be contradictory due to its being the opposite of the intended object to be established. He clarifies this very contradiction with the words "is pleased" (*prīyate*). For the animal sacrifice has Agni and Soma as its recipients;
and in that context, since the deities Agni and Soma are pleased, there is a promise of a result corresponding to the object [of the ritual] for the one who performs the act of violence.

It would follow that even violence is something that causes pleasure; and in this way, the fact that it produces harm is not established, because it is impossible for the fruit of pleasure to be harmful. Therefore, the thesis would be contradictory. But what is intended here by this "possession of a body contrary to the [conclusions of the] Devatādhikaraṇa"? Why is it said that "the deity is pleased," even though a recipient (*sampradāna*) consists essentially in not being rejected?
Nevertheless, that [deity] does not derive pleasure from these actions, because they consist merely of the hearing [of the words]. Therefore, he says: "Thus it stands for you. True;
this is not our established conclusion (siddhānta). But for you, the Sāṅkhya, this remains fixed: that the deity derives pleasure. Consequently, your position is contradictory. // 240 //
[561] those [562] which [563] they (feminine plural)

[564] End (GA) [565] This (KA). First, the fault regarding the meaning of the word *viṣaya* as the recipient (*sampradāna*) in both cases has been stated. He states the fault in the case where it signifies the object (*karman*)—namely, "in the example. For if the object of giving were indeed the object (*viṣaya*), [then the following would occur].

The intention is that, since there is no fruit whatsoever from giving away cows and the like, it is not logical for such acts to be a means for achieving a corresponding result. Furthermore, this reason is a "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*); thus he says: "recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth. For specific actions such as recitation do not operate toward the harming or favoring of others; rather, they [are considered meritorious] merely by virtue of being enjoined.

[The means] are understood as being for the sake of a purpose (*artha*). Therefore, by that very same example, it is possible to establish that violence (*hiṃsā*) enjoined [by the Veda] is indeed for the sake of a purpose.

Consequently, there is the fallacy of "contradictory non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritā*). Nor can it be said here that this result conforms to its object (*viṣaya*), because no such result is observed in the case of the object. If, first of all, the object of *japa* (muttering) is the mantra being muttered...

What is its fruit? For no one else are injury or favor observed [to result]. Therefore it has been said: "Because of the avoidance of injury to others, etc. Having established such an example, the status of being a reason (*hetu*) for that which is enjoined becomes possible; thus, it constitutes a "reason that is non-deviant yet contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*). And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "The slaughter of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*) is purposeful..."
Because it is prescribed, like the recitation of mantras and so forth. // 241 //

[566] However, the introduction of inference regarding dharma and adharma, which are established by the means of valid cognition consisting of injunctions and prohibitions, is utterly misplaced; thus he says: "vihiteta" (242).

Moreover, one who maintains that the fruit corresponds to the object must rely on the fact that dharma and adharma are based on harm and benefit respectively. And in this case, since one or the other would be absent in both the recitation of mantras (*japa*) and the drinking of spirits (*śīdhu*), there would be no mutual benefit;
thus he says: "Because of benefit" (verse 243).
{1,186} And for those who approach the wife of a guru, great merit arises precisely from the favor shown to another; thus he says, "crying out" (*krośata*).

For the heart of one who approaches the wife of a guru, being filled with trepidation, seems as if it were crying out; hence the word "crying out" is used. If one should say: "For in the case of one who approaches the wife of a guru, a crying out of the heart is observed, just as in one who kills a Brahmin"; [this is] violence (*hiṃsā*).

And it is established that [an action] is harmful because it yields a result corresponding to its object. Therefore, since the heart’s reproach is experienced only by those who perform actions that have harmful results, it is understood that even one who approaches the wife of a teacher incurs demerit (*adharma*).
To this, the following reply is given: "Even with a heart that reproaches. For he thinks thus: if the fruit of actions corresponds to their object, [then...]

This being the case, even one who approaches the wife of his teacher would be righteous, since he produces a great benefit for the woman of the realm, even if his heart cries out. If it is argued that unrighteousness is also inferred for him because of the crying of his heart,
then [the result] would not correspond to the object [of the action].

The pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the [proposed] actions is unestablished; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, when two reasons with contradictory meanings coincide, there would arise a doubt regarding whether something is merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*). Consequently, being merit or demerit is not based on causing harm or benefit. // 244 //
[567] From the approach of passion;
[568] from understanding through tranquility;
[569] and from the letter *dha* (GA).

Furthermore, we find no reason for this proponent, who relies primarily on inference and disregards the scriptures of prohibition, to feel remorse in his heart. For such remorse arises from the thought that one is practicing unrighteousness (*adharma*). However, for one who maintains that dharma and adharma are determined by inference, there is no basis whatsoever for the notion that it is unrighteousness. Indeed, their determination follows the scriptures; [this action] is contrary to the scriptures.

As he proceeds, no trembling of the heart arises at the thought, "I am practicing unrighteousness. On the contrary, because this heart is intent on benefiting others, only serenity arises; thus he says: "By inference... (verse 245).

Now, surely that which, when performed upon oneself or another, brings about suffering is precisely what constitutes unrighteousness (*adharma*). For this very reason, even self-harm is unrighteousness. Thus, in this case, even if assistance to others is observed, if suffering is experienced due to a pang in the heart, it possesses the nature of unrighteousness. And so, its status as unrighteousness is established by the occurrence of suffering.

To this he says: "Because of pain" (*pīḍātaḥ*). For one who has not yet relied upon the scripture, since there is no prior cause for the arising of the knowledge of unrighteousness (*adharma*), it must be stated what causes the pain. If it is argued that it is caused by the cognition of its being unrighteous, then what is the cause of that very cognition? If it is argued that the pain itself is the cause for its being unrighteous, [then...]

Therefore, since neither of these two—suffering nor being a property [of suffering]—can have any other basis here, an irresolvable circularity (itaretarāśraya) results for one who does not rely on the scripture. // 246 //

Furthermore, [570] if approaching the wife of one's guru is unrighteous (*adharma*) because distress is observed in the agent despite the fact that it benefits others, then for one such as a barbarian (*mleccha*) for whom no such distress arises from this act, there would be no production of demerit. To address this, he says: "In such cases," and so forth. Distress that conforms to the scriptures arises only for one who knows the scriptures; for one ignorant of them, since that [distress] is absent, it lacks authoritative basis.
"Regarding the phrase 'the yoga of the Dharma' // 247 //"

And therefore, having excluded both benefit (*anugraha*) and harm (*pīḍā*), as well as their absence, those who seek knowledge of dharma and adharma must follow only injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*niṣedha*).
He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the meaning: neither benefit is the cause for being dharma, nor is harm the cause for being adharma.
Or rather, the nature of dharma and adharma consists in the absence of benefit or the mere absence of harm. // 248 //

On this point, they say: the unrighteousness (*adharma*) of killing and other such acts is not established by inference; rather, it is established solely in accordance with scripture (*śāstra*). For through the prohibitory scripture, the capacity of killing to produce demerit (*pratyavāya*) is understood. Indeed, every instance of killing, whether occurring at a sacred site (*tīrtha*) or a non-sacred site, is simply killing. Therefore, how could any act that is killing fail to produce demerit? For the injunction for the killing of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*) is not capable of removing the inherent power of a thing, because it merely teaches the existence of the power residing in the substance, its qualities, and so forth.

Regarding the scriptures: these [scriptures] do not function by adding or subtracting capacities [to things]. Therefore, it is precisely by following the scripture that the unrighteousness of acts such as killing is postulated—namely, that the very same act [of killing] which is taught in the scripture as a cause for sin (*pratyavāya*) applies to the ritual killing of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*). He introduces this point as follows:

—By the triad beginning with "in some cases" (kvacid). The connection is as follows: in some cases, because external injury is prohibited, it is understood that the capacity of injury to be a cause of demerit does not depart even due to [its] injunction. // 251 //

[571] Having thus introduced [the objection], he refutes it with two verses beginning with "evam" (thus). For one who speaks in such a manner [would contradict] the prohibitory scripture stating, "One should not drink liquor."

Since the capacity for demerit (*pratyavāya*) inherent in drinking liquor is understood [from scripture], even a Śūdra, by drinking it, would incur that demerit. Similarly, since the attainment of prosperity through the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice is shown to be established by the rule for a Vaiśya sacrificer, that same fruit would accrue to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas as well, according to the capacity of the Vaiśyastoma; yet this is not accepted. Likewise, there is a difference in capacity due to the difference in time.

It is observed that for the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there is capacity on the festival day (*parvan*), whereas there is incapacity on the fifth day; likewise, for the *agnihotra*, which is performed in the evening and morning, it serves as a means to the fruit [of the sacrifice], but at midday it does not. Therefore, the actual existence of capacity must be accepted exactly as prescribed by the scriptures. // 253 //
Therefore, he concludes that the potency of the fruits of actions must be accepted solely in accordance with the scriptures: "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 254 //

Thus, regarding violence—which is distinct from the two parts consisting of the means and the goal—the knowledge that it is a cause of demerit (*pratyavāya*) arises from the prohibition "one shall not kill. This [prohibition] is set aside in other ritual contexts by injunctions such as "he who is initiated" or "he should sacrifice the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Thus he says: "Violence... (verse 255).
As for what was stated—that the scripture does not function with respect to the addition or removal of the inherent power of things—[that remains true].

That is indeed accepted. However, according to the scriptures alone, powers are understood as being established through the distinctions of their respective functions. Therefore, with the intention that there is no over-extension [of the principle], he says:

"If it is asked how one and the same action can possess both the presence and absence of power, let your honors examine worldly actions. For instance, even a single act of eating is seen to possess different powers depending on whether the agent is healthy or ill."
For when that [action] is performed by one who is healthy, it increases the body through a successive transformation of chyle, blood, and flesh.

But when performed by one who is ill, it causes emaciation because of the improper transformation of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). With the intention that the same will apply even to actions whose results are unseen (*adṛṣṭārtha*), he says: "The established rule" (*vyavasthā*). // 257 //

Just as, despite there being no difference in the nature of food, a difference in potency is established therein by relying on a difference between individuals—based on the distinction between the healthy person and the sick person—so too here, although there is no difference in the nature of violence (*hiṃsātva*), a difference in potency is logical because one perceives a difference between individuals, such that "this is limb-violence" and "this is external-violence. With this intention, he says: "because of the non-difference of form" (verse 258).

[573] Regarding the distinction in established status (vyavasthābheda): if, however, one does not admit internal differences and instead maintains that there is a single result based merely on the non-difference of their nature (*rūpa*), then it would follow that all worldly and Vedic actions have a single result simply because they share the common property of being "actions" (*kriyātva*). In that case, this [Vedic action] would have heaven as its result.

With the intention that the non-confusion [of results]—such as "this is the fruit of the Putrakāmeṣṭi"—would not be established, he says: "Even so" (*tathāpi*). Let it be for now that confusion of results occurs because of oneness through the great universal (*mahāsāmānya*); however, even due to the non-difference of subordinate universals (*avāntarasāmānya*) such as "having sacrificed" (*yajitva*), there would be an equality of results for rituals like the Citrā sacrifice.
Thus he says: "Having sacrificed" (*yajitvā*). // 259 //

If it is argued that in that case [the prohibition] refers to a specific distinction within the established rule, then here too it is the same; thus he says: "Because of the difference. Now, it may be objected: "The injury to animals is indeed enjoined as a subsidiary part [of the sacrifice]. Even so, why is it not an evil (anartha)? There can be no injunction whose fruit is evil; such is the royal decree. To this he replies: "Of the injunctions... This...

The intention is as follows: this is not a royal decree; it is simply the power of the word itself. For an injunction (*vidhi*) is the cause of the cognition that something ought to be done (*kartavyatā*).

And the world understands that which is a means to a desired end (*iṣṭābhyupāya*) as something that ought to be done. Therefore, whether directly or even mediately, it is necessarily determined that the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) is the fruit of the things enjoined. [This applies] directly to the primary [acts].

[The prohibition] is separated from the subsidiaries. Therefore, it is not concluded from this that the injunction results in an undesirable consequence (*anartha*). He says that the fruit of injunctions is understood through the force of the injunction itself. Furthermore, the claim that "the injury to the subsidiary is an undesirable effect" is not something perceived in this world (*sāndṛṣṭika*). Nor is its connection with an undesirable result heard in the scripture.

Thus, he asks how it could be a means to an undesirable end, and replies: "Nor in these [cases]... [Objection: Even if it is not explicitly heard, it will be inferred, just as in the case of eating *kalañja* and so forth.

Therefore, he says: "Because of negation. In that context, negation is the cause for conceptual construction; however, it is not possible here. This is because one observes only the positive injunction, precisely due to the absence [of negation]. // 261 //

[574] Furthermore, even if it were established that the injuries to the sacrificial components (*aṅga-hiṃsā*) serve a human purpose (*puruṣārthatva*), one might occasionally assume that harm (*anartha*) is their result. However, those [injuries] do not have a human purpose as their result, because they are recited within the context (*prakaraṇa*). This is because, through application by virtue of the injunction of the context, they serve the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvarthatva*).
With this intention, he says: "And not... What indeed is that which is to be postulated? To this he replies: "The assistance to the ritual act (*karmopakāra*).

For that which resides within the context of a specific rite, only assistance to the primary ritual act is postulated, whether it be visible (*dṛṣṭa*) or invisible (*adṛṣṭa*). As, for example, the husking of rice grains (*vrīhīṇāṃ vituṣībhāvaḥ*), required by the injunction, is a visible result; or as the invisible result produced by the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
Thus [ends the verse]. 262.

[575] Therefore, there is no occasion here for the postulation of a purposeless result; thus he says: "postulation" (*kalpanā*). The meaning is that no fruit is expected from the injury to the animal parts, because [the sacrifice] has no further expectancy once it has been fulfilled by its assistance to the ritual (*kratu*). Furthermore, even regarding what is for the sake of the ritual, this distinction holds: namely, that this is merely a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the animal.

However, the injury to the animal is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) that provides assistance from a distance (*ārāt*), like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, because it is preceded by the performance of purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as immolation. For this very reason, in the act of quieting (*saṃjñapana*), the animal is heard in scripture as the primary object, as in the injunction: "one quiets the animal," just like the rice-grains. This is what [the author] expresses by saying: "it is for the sake of the sacrifice" (*kratvartha*). By demonstrating that it is a directly contributing auxiliary (*sannipatyopakāra*), its status as being for the sake of the sacrifice is established.

It is thus shown that [the latter] is more powerful. Even if there were as much affliction as there would be in the case of being a remote benefactor, such [affliction] does not exist here at all. // 263 //

Even though this [cutting] is indeed a *saṃskāra* (purificatory rite), it has this distinction: like threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth, it serves a visible purpose; however, unlike sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and so forth, it does not serve an invisible purpose, because it results in the production of the eleven portions required by the sacrifice. For in the case of the animal dedicated to Dakṣa (*daikṣa-paśu*), one first cuts a portion from the heart. Then...

[The text continues with] "of the tongue," "then of the chest," and so forth, by which the sacrifice accomplished through eleven portions (*avadāna*) is described. Now, in the absence of a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) involving injury, the production of the eleven portions from the animal would not be possible. Therefore, since the injury to the limbs serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), there is no occasion for postulating that it is harmful;
with this intention, he says: "visible" (*dṛṣṭa*). Thus, first of all, the injury situated within the constituent parts of the means to the Jyotiṣṭoma is not unrighteousness (*adharma*).

It has been stated. Regarding those sacrifices of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) such as the *śyena* and others, since these one-day rites (*ekāha*) have the *jyotiṣṭoma* as their archetype (*prakṛti*), the injury to living beings that is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) is not unrighteousness (*adharma*). Thus he says: "Malevolent magic" (*abhicāra*). (264)

And therefore, he concludes that this status of being an evil (*anarthatva*) applies only to that violence which, though not a constituent part of the rite itself, resides within the portion of the result— by the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). But how can it be that even violence residing in the portion of the result, when enjoined with reference to the *śyena* sacrifice and the like, [is considered an evil]?
Because it is a harmful purpose, he says: "from the mention [of the Śyena]. This is the intended meaning: here, the result is not enjoined with reference to the Śyena sacrifice;

for it is violence itself that is mentioned as the result. Indeed, it is the means that is enjoined with reference to the result, but not the reverse. Now, one might object: even though they are objects of mention, there is an injunction regarding place and time.

This is indeed accepted. It is true that those two [prohibitions] are not obtained from any other source. However, it has already been stated that a person who is impelled toward a result by passion is not impelled by an injunction. // 265 //
[578] Having paid homage, [the author asks:

how, moreover, can a distinction between what is to be performed and what is not to be performed be stated regarding the prescription for the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the three aspects? For this very reason, the objection that it is purposeless because it is included within cultivation was raised. To that, he states the reply: "Cultivation" (*bhāvanā*).

This is the intended meaning: for an injunction (*vidhi*), like a swan extracting milk from water, grasps what has not been previously obtained by avoiding what has already been obtained. And so it will be stated: "But its qualities should be enjoined, because they are not [otherwise] distinguished, provided they have not been taught by another [injunction] whose purpose is enjoining" (1.4.9).

Thus, even in the case of an injunction for a specific meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because it is concerned solely with the means (*sādhana*) and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), it excludes the portion consisting of the fruit (*phala*).

Therefore, it is established that the Śyena sacrifice is neither *dharma* by its own nature, nor is it *adharma*. However, because the fruit itself is connected with what is harmful (*anartha*), it is metaphorically designated as "harmful" by way of that fruit. He concludes [this point] with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*). // 266 //
[579] To perform (GA); [580] the implication of the object was shown (KA) in the case of a non-existent object.

But surely, since injunctions have human goals as their fruit, and since the Śyena sacrifice is the object of an injunction, why is another result consisting of a worldly purpose not postulated by the force of that injunction—just as in the case of the Viśvajit and other sacrifices? Therefore, [the opponent] says "of that which has no further expectancy" [in response to the claim] that it will be dharma by its very nature. This is the meaning: [the Śyena is performed] by means of the single act of slaying one's enemy, which is dearer even than heaven.

For a *śyena* sacrifice that is already free of expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), the postulation of another result is not possible. For the seed of such a postulation is the expectancy of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). And since a single efficient force is satisfied by a single object to be accomplished (*bhāvya*), it does not admit a connection with another object to be accomplished. As he will state: "Or rather, [the *śyena* is a name] because there is a single injunction" (4.3.14).

Thus, it is established that that which has an undesirable result is itself an evil (anartha) by way of that result; hence he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). But what is the reason that the *śyena* sacrifice is not *dharma*, given that it is connected with an undesirable result? To this he says, "By way of its result" (*phalataḥ*). For in the world, the word *dharma* is well-known to apply to such actions. // 268 //
[582] This is the sense.

Here, an objection is raised: "But surely," etc. The intention is as follows: what, then, is the reason that the *śyena* sacrifice and others are neither inherently *dharma* nor *adharma*? For *dharma* is defined by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) as a means to a desired end. Thus, in the case of the *śyena*, since its fruit is connected with an undesirable consequence...

Therefore, this [term] must be stated simply as *dharma*. Here, intending that the *śyena* sacrifice is devoid of both forms [of dharma and adharma], he introduces the deliberation with the words "the result. It is established, for now, that the result of the *śyena* is violence (*hiṃsā*), and that violence is not *dharma*. Now, we shall determine the essential nature of the *śyena* and other such sacrifices in accordance with worldly convention: [it is] *dharma*...
"Or it is dharma. // 269 //

In that regard, he presents two positions in order to determine one of them, using the pair beginning with "yadi" (if). For us, worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is the root for determining the meaning of all words; therefore, that very consensus must be examined. In this context, if it is said by the world that "Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) and consists of a means to what is desired, provided it is free from undesirable consequences," [then...]

Consequently, the *śyena* sacrifice and others are to be avoided because they are unrighteous (*adharma*), as they lead indirectly to undesirable consequences (*anartha*). However, if worldly people, disregarding such indirect connection to undesirable consequences, were to apply the term "dharma" directly to that which has pleasure as its fruit and is understood through Vedic injunction (*codanā*), then the *śyena* would also be considered dharma, since it too is of that nature. Regarding the phrase "without regard for what is to be done or not to be done": for the discerning understand that whatever is connected solely with pleasure is indeed what ought to be done (*kārya*).

The sense is that what is contrary [to common consensus] is not to be performed. By the very explanation of the division of common consensus (*prasiddhi*), the determination here has been stated. It is established that, for the time being, the word *dharma* must be accepted according to common consensus. And since the scope of the word *dharma* according to common consensus is exclusively that which does not entail undesirable consequences and which is a means to achieve what is desired, it follows that the exclusion of the Śyena sacrifice and others is precisely what is determined. // 271 //
"But in that case, the Śyena sacrifice would indeed be unrighteousness (adharma) by way of its result, because it is connected with what is undesirable.

To this he says: "If... The intention here is as follows: even the application of the term "unrighteousness" by worldly people must be examined as to its specific object. Therefore, if even that which is the meaning of a Vedic injunction (codanārtha) is well-known to be unrighteousness—whether directly or through mediation—as a cause of displeasure, [then the objection holds].

In that case, the Śyena sacrifice would also be unrighteous (adharma). Now, if it is argued that people use the word "unrighteous" for what is enjoined by the Veda—even if it causes displeasure—due to traditional usage, then it is not unrighteous. And since the usage of the word "unrighteous" by worldly people is never observed to refer to what is enjoined by the Veda, the point is that the Śyena and other such sacrifices are not unrighteous by their very nature. // 272 //

But as for the one who says: "Indeed, the violence enjoined pertains to two parts [of the sacrifice]; nevertheless, by means of the observation of a counter-indicative mark (*pratibaddhaliṅga*), we shall infer its status as a cause of misfortune (*anarthahetutva*). For instance, the property of being violence (*hiṃsātva*) is known to be invariably concomitant with being a cause of misfortune in the case of external acts of violence; that same property, being observed even in enjoined [violence], leads to the inference of its being a cause of misfortune. Having set forth this view, he refutes it with the words "But as for the one who says" (*yas tv iti*). And this sublation by scripture (*āgamabādha*) will be elaborated upon in the discussion on inference.
Thus [ends the verse] // 273 //
He says "that" (tam) [in verse 274] because, if there were no regard for scripture, there would be an infinite regress.
But surely, according to scripture (*āgama*), even those acts of violence occurring within a sacrifice (*kratu*) are understood to be unrighteous (*adharma*).

For instance, there exist certain mantra-explanations (*arthavāda*), historical narratives (*itihāsa*), and so forth, which censure even that violence which exists within a sacrifice. As, for example, in the *Japastuti*: "Those who... [and so on].

"The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is superior to the ritual sacrifice (vidhiyajña) by tenfold qualities"—thus, the ritual sacrifice is censured precisely because it involves the element of violence (hiṃsā). Therefore, he says: "In the Gītā. The meaning of this is: here there is a direct contradiction with Śruti, since the injunction is seen to apply to the ritual sacrifice, whereas elsewhere...
And from the Vedic revelation: "From the sacred fords" (tīrthebhyaḥ). [586] [585] Regarding its state as possessing form (sākāratve), [586] it is recorded in the Smṛti (smṛ). [KA]
Sacrificial animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
for sacrifice leads to the prosperity of the world, therefore, killing in sacrifice is no killing at all.

And thus, this should be explained as a commendatory statement (arthavāda) intended for another purpose. As he will say: "For a censure does not aim to censure that which is censured; rather, it aims to praise something other than the censured. // 275 //
[587] Thus.

(KA) Here, there is another commentary: "Is it not the case that this sūtra is incapable of expressing these two meanings—that dharma is characterized by injunction (*codanā*) and not characterized by the senses and so forth, and that dharma is a beneficial purpose (*artha*) and not a harmful one? For in that case, the sentence would be split. Such is the objection regarding the splitting of the sentence.
Having formulated this objection, he says: "It is replied. This applies only where the meaning is understood from the sentence itself;
however, that is not the case with the Vedic sūtras. Since the meaning is already known from other sources, it must be understood that the sūtra serves to clarify that very meaning.

He anticipates this objection with the words "to the students" (*śiṣyān*). The meaning of this is: the sūtras [are intended] for those who desire to know and who have already learned the meaning of the Vedas from other sources.

They were not composed by Jaimini. Therefore, they are equal to Vedic statements for those [opponents]; yet both—the Vedas and the Sūtras—are incapable due to defects such as syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). And that which is incapable of conveying meaning is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, there is no distinction whatsoever between the Vedas and the Sūtras; thus, the statement in the Bhāṣya, "not in the Sūtras," is not a satisfactory answer. // 276 //

Regarding this, he states the rebuttal: "As previously stated," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: True, it is the case that due to the division of sentences and other such factors, the Sūtras themselves lack the capacity [to provide a definitive answer], and there is no distinction [in this regard] for the students. However, the result of that previously mentioned restrictive rule (*parisaṃkhyā*)—"provided it is possible"—is what is being demonstrated here by the author of the Bhāṣya. For in this way, the students who were deluded by fallacious arguments are [corrected] by the author of the Bhāṣya.
It has been taught that when the intended meaning cannot be established [otherwise], the sūtras must be interpreted even by means of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and other methods.
This very point is demonstrated here in the *Codanā-sūtra* itself, namely, that the meaning of the *Codanā-sūtra* is understood even through the splitting of the sentence.

"By this" means: by the reasoning stated in the Bhāṣya, which consists in the fact that [the Veda] has as its object a matter already apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). "This" refers to...

Moreover, the very method for resolving syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) as stated in the *Bhāṣya* is being recalled. As it says: "These two are merely parts of two distinct sentences. By this, it is shown that although there is no difference [in the subject matter] for the students, the commentator has explained the specific manner of exposition used by commentators themselves. For commentators are capable of recollecting the entirety of the established principles (*nyāya*) with which they have long been familiar.
They explain the sūtras by means of logical reasoning, as well as through methods such as splitting the sentence (vākyabheda) and so forth. // 277 //

Since comprehension of the sūtras is possible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), even by means of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*) and so forth, he says "therefore" to indicate that this sūtra should be explained either by repetition (*āvṛtti*) or by a single simultaneous application (*tantra*). Regarding repetition first, the entire sūtra must be recited twice. In that case, for one [recitation], it is as follows: "Dharma is characterized by an injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*)."

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Regarding the statement "the meaning of the other [Veda] is Dharma," if the focus were on something else, the connection with either one [of the two] would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). However, since both are established through the division of the Sūtras, the justification for restating both is valid. Furthermore, "tantra" refers to any one of the three [criteria], beginning with "defined by Vedic injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*); this will be explained later. On that view, there is no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). For it is thus:
This sūtra consists of three words. The meaning of the sentence is the meaning of these three words as they are mutually connected.

In that case, if one were to repeat [the word] for the purpose of connecting all three, that would indeed split the sentence. However, when there is a connection with both through *tantra* (simultaneous application), there is no splitting of the sentence, because it is uttered only once; for that which is stated once may, by its very fitness, be connected with both.

Because of the distinction in capacity (*śakti*). Thus, here the middle term *dharma*—when uttered within the compound—is connected with both [the preceding and following terms]. And both are established: "Dharma is that which is characterized by an injunction" and "The object is Dharma. Or, the middle term is connected with the first and the last. In this way as well, the desired meaning is established: "That object which is Dharma is characterized by an injunction. Or, the first term alone is connected with the two subsequent ones: "That which is characterized by an injunction..."

"That very object is itself the dharma. It should be understood that this single sentence has two meanings because it connects with both through *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions). And it is said: "[588] For the purpose of connection..."
When "codanālakṣaṇa" and the others are combined through the method of *tantra* (simultaneous application) with a single [word],
that one [word] will have two meanings because it expresses the meaning of both together.
Thus [ends the verse]. 278.

By stating that these two are merely parts of two distinct sentences, the Commentator has shown that this consists of exactly two sūtras. He introduces them as follows: "ekadeśa... (the part). One sūtra is "Dharma is the object," and the other is "That which is characterized by Vedic injunction. Thus, there is one [sūtra] consisting of the word *dharma* from the immediately following sūtra, inferred through its connection with the part "characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*).

"It is established that Dharma is characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). This is what has been stated: "Because it is an inference from a single part. Now, [one might object]: since the statement "Dharma is the object" does not specify whether it is that which is characterized by injunction or that which is not characterized by injunction, when there is a need for such specification, who can prevent that which is not characterized by injunction from also presenting itself? In this way, even in the case of the definition "Dharma is characterized by injunction," the consequence follows that it would include what is harmful (*anartha*).

It must be shown [how this is so]. Therefore, he says: "mutually" (*itaretara*). These two very words, *codanā-lakṣaṇa* and *artha*, due to their mutual proximity, are conceived as qualifiers and as supplements to the sentence within both sūtras respectively. Consequently, there is no assumption of parts that are non-*codanā*-defined or non-objects (*anartha*). Furthermore, as a restatement (*anuvāda*), the connection of the parts of *codanā-lakṣaṇa* and *artha* with the two distinct sūtras must be demonstrated here.

That which was stated by the single aphorism "Dharma is that for the sake of which [the Veda exists]" is [defined as] "that which is characterized by injunction" (codanā-lakṣaṇa); and that which was stated here as "Dharma is that which is characterized by injunction" is [explained as] "for the sake of that. // 279 //

[590] Furthermore, the commentary states that "the nature of dharma belongs to that which is an object characterized by injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇa*)—that is, they have the same meaning. He objects to this with the words ending in "viśiṣṭa": [it would mean] the prescription of dharma by way of restating an injunction characterized by the qualification of the object.

This has been shown. Even so, the sentence is indeed split by virtue of its being directed toward both the qualifier and the qualified, just as in the injunction for washing (*sammārga*) which is based on a reference (*anuvāda*) to a ladle (*graha*) qualified by singularity. Therefore, with what distinction was the alternative resolution (*parihārāntara*) stated [with the words] "or rather" (*athavā*)? Since this is not a valid resolution, he states that the previously mentioned dependence upon three words (*padatrayatantratva*) is the answer to the objection regarding the split of the sentence—this is the meaning up to the end of the word *artha*.

And this triad of treatises has already been explained. By the word *saṃjñā*, the term *dharma* is expressed. For that [term] is a technical designation (*alaukikī saṃjñā*) for an object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), just as the word *dhātu* is for roots such as *bhū* and so forth. This was stated according to the opinion of the ancient teachers. If it is absolutely necessary to avoid the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākyabheda*), then one sentence with two meanings must be explained through the method of *tantra*. And it is not possible to avoid the objection regarding the splitting of the sentence by any other means. // 281 //
[591] It would indeed be perceived;
[592] not by means of the suffix *ṇa*;
[593] it belongs to you. For that is indeed *co* (KA).

[594] Now the following must be stated: [595] "Dharma" is what is to be discussed here. To this, an objection is raised: "This is the intended meaning—there are indeed two ways of interpreting the statement here, by way of restating that which is characterized by *codanā* (Vedic injunction)."

Or [it may mean] a contrary prescription of dharma. Regarding the first of these positions, since the characteristic of being defined by Vedic injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇatva*) does not invariably entail being for a purpose (*arthatva*), the qualification is indeed appropriate. However, when this [sūtra] states the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of restating dharma as already established in a general sense, then being for a purpose is already established.

Because it is well-established that *dharma* is precisely that object which is the means for achieving the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). For all proponents of philosophical systems are in agreement on this point—that *dharma* is the means for producing pleasure;

their dispute concerns only its specific varieties. Thus, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that *dharma* consists in sacrifices (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*), while the Buddhists hold it to consist in prostrations to the Saṅgha and so forth. However, the general definition of *dharma* as the nature of that which produces pleasure is established without dispute among all disputants. This very [definition]...

Furthermore, the establishment of the general [definition] has already been stated. For this very reason, when there is a desire to know the establishment of the specific [details], the application of specific means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is prescribed, because their establishment follows from that alone. For instance, when the Vedic tradition is the authority, sacrifices and the like are *dharma*; but when the Buddhist tradition is the authority, the veneration of caityas and the like are [dharma].
Even in the question "What is *dharma*?", the inquiry is made precisely out of a desire to know the specific details. And he will state later: "And there is a desire to know the specific."

Therefore, this alone is the primary mode of expression here. For this very reason, since perception and other means of knowledge were refuted first by the *satsūtra* (the sutra beginning with "sat"), it is evident that this is the mode of expression intended by the author of the sutras. When it is asserted as a proposition that "whatever is dharma is characterized by injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*), the subsequent refutation of other definitions becomes logically consistent.

It cannot be otherwise. Therefore, this alone is the correct mode of expression here. And since there is no deviation from the meaning in this [mode], the qualification of the object is redundant. // 282 //

[596] He refutes [the objection] that [it is] merely a request (prārthanāmātra): "An injunction" (codanā). This is the intended meaning: True, this indeed is the grammatical construction here. However, this very [construction] is not established unless there is a qualification of the object; therefore, the mention of the word "object" (artha) is for the purpose of including that which possesses a result (phalavat). For if that [term "artha"] were absent, there would likely be much doubt regarding other possible word-interpretations (*vacanavyakti*). For in that case, it might be conceived thus:

"That which is characterized by an injunction (*codanā*) is Dharma. But here, the fault that will be stated later [would apply]. However, when the term *artha* is understood as a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*), such a word-interpretation is not possible, because the inclusion of the term *artha* cannot function either as an injunction (*vidhi*) or as a restatement (*anuvāda*). First of all, it is impossible for it to be an injunction, because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Furthermore, it cannot be a restatement (*anuvāda*), because such a restatement is not established here. For that which is characterized by an injunction (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*) does not fail to relate to a purposeful object (*artha*), since even that which is purposeless is nonetheless characterized by it. Therefore, it is not a restatement. Nor can this [sentence] have the status of a sentence-meaning (*vākyārthatva*) by abandoning this [purpose], because a portion of a sentence would then be meaningless. Consequently, whichever of the two positions allows for the syntactical connection with the word "purpose" (*artha-pada*)—[that is the one to be accepted].

Therefore, that alternative (pakṣa) would have to be accepted. Since it is possible for there to be an injunction regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by way of a restatement of the object (*dharma*), the view that the word "object" (*artha*) is a mere restatement of what is already established is determined as the correct position. Consequently, the word "object" is intended solely to indicate the distinction between injunction and restatement; it is not a qualifier. Furthermore, he will demonstrate that even without a qualifier, this very [interpretation] is clearly the meaning of the Sūtra. // 283 //
[598] This might be argued: "What is the fault in adopting the interpretation of the sentence that has been considered?

To this, he says: "In the same way. By restating the definition of *codanā* (Vedic injunction), when there is an injunction regarding *dharma*, even *adharma*s are established as means to what is harmful (*anartha*) through the injunction of their prohibition. [599]

If acts such as the killing of a Brahmin were characterized [as dharma], they would possess the nature of dharma because they are defined by Vedic injunction (*codanālakṣaṇa*). But this is not accepted.

Therefore, even for the sake of what is to be enjoined, the inclusion of the word "artha" (purpose/benefit) in the phrase "the fruit of the injunction is purposeful" (*vidhiphalam arthavat*) is not meaningful. Consequently, this interpretation of the sentence is not the most sound. // 284 //

[599] Since the meaning is [already established], one should here resort to a figurative expression (*vacobhaṅgī*) by setting aside that [literal sense]. [600-601] Therefore, its name must be adopted here through a shift in phrasing.
That [sentence] in which the purpose (*artha*) is not abandoned by virtue of its being the nature of the dharma (*dharmatā*),
and in which there is a single sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), is a rule of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇavidhi*) through the restatement of the dharma;
for in such a case, because the purpose does not deviate from being the nature of the dharma, the purpose is not abandoned, and there is indeed only a single sentence-meaning.

Because the meaning is indicated by implication (*sāmarthya*). And this [implication] is established precisely through the restatement of the meaning (*arthānuvāda*), and not otherwise; as has already been stated, he says: "Therefore" (verse 285).
[601] Only the means of proof [602], and not anything else (GA),
if this indeed is the mode of expression here.

How then does the author of the *Bhāṣya* demonstrate that the word *artha* functions as a qualifier [of *dharma*] through the passage beginning with "both here" (*ubhayam iha*)? For it is stated there quite clearly: "The mention of the word *artha* is for this purpose, so that what is not beneficial (*anartha*) might not be called *dharma*. Furthermore, regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "or rather" (*athavā*) which was raised as an objection, we have found no resolution for it up to the present day.

Therefore, he says: "Because of the qualification. By this, both [objections regarding] the two commentaries are resolved. As for what was stated here as "both," that was explained by the author of the commentary as being produced solely by the force of the meaning (*arthasāmarthyakārita*), even without an explicit qualification of the meaning. What is this "produced by the force of the meaning"? This is what is meant: because the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are prescribed by way of restating a property (*dharmānuvāda*), [the exclusion] of non-meanings follows from that very fact.

Since violence and the like are to be avoided because they constitute non-dharma (*adharma*), if one were to enjoin dharma by restating what is already established through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), those [acts] would also result in being dharma. Therefore, the word "beneficial" (*artha*) is employed to ensure that what is harmful (*anartha*) is not here designated as dharma; thus, the word "beneficial" serves to adopt a specific interpretation of the sentence structure.

Thus it has been shown. This very same passage is also to be explained as the resolution of the objection raised in the Bhāṣya. This answer provided by the author of the Bhāṣya is not one produced by the force of the word "or" (*atha vā*); for in that case, there would be a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*).

Here, however, even without a specific qualification, this is stated as being produced solely by the force of the meaning. And that [meaning] is established by resorting to a particular mode of expression (*vacana-vyakti*).

This has been shown. Furthermore, a meaning that follows by implication does not cause a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), because such a split is not based on verbal authority (*aśabdapramāṇaka*) and because a syntactical split is a defect of the words themselves. Therefore, by the phrase "or else" (*athavā*) and so forth, the author of the Bhāṣya has demonstrated here that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are prescribed with reference to *dharma*. In that case, since the word "meaning" (*artha*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), the syntactical split is indeed easily avoided.

The meaning is this: the avoidance of harmful acts such as violence, which is expressed through the statement prescribing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by way of restating dharma, is said by the author of the Bhāṣya to be the result produced by the force of the meaning itself. // 286 //
[603] *dhāv anarthā* (GA) [604] *dakatvā* (KA),
thus in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by Upādhyāya Sucarita Miśra.

The *Codanāsūtra* is completed. [Next is] the *Nimittasūtra*: "The investigation of its cause" (*tasya nimittaparīṣṭiḥ*). This is its meaning: that which is the cause of that *dharma*, namely the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) designated as *codanā*.

"An investigation (*parīṣṭi*) must be performed. Furthermore, the grammatical derivation of the word *parīṣṭi* is optional. For it is traditionally taught that from the root *iṣ* (meaning "to go"), when the suffix *yuc* is prescribed by the rule *iṣer anicchārthasya*, there is an option regarding the suffixes *ktin* and *yuc* by the rule *parer vā*. Consequently, when *yuc* is applied, the form is *paryeṣaṇā*; however, when *ktin* is applied, it is *parīṣṭi*. Regarding this, they say:

Why is this proposal for an investigation made at such an inappropriate time? For it was previously proposed that "Dharma is a matter characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanālakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*).
Therefore, when the occasion has arrived to state the reasons capable of establishing that [proposition], why is another investigation—concerning the cause (*nimitta*)—being proposed?
Indeed, the Naiyāyikas do not, having merely proposed that "sound is impermanent," introduce an investigation by saying, "Now we shall investigate this."

Nevertheless, they state the reason "because it is produced" all at once. Therefore, here too, for the sake of establishing the two-fold restriction promised in the *Codanāsūtra*, it is appropriate to state the reason through the two subsequent sūtras (*Satsūtra* and *Autpattikasūtra*). What is the point of stating the thesis (*pratijñā*) for examination in the interim?
If it is thought that this is the rule for theses intended for others—that the reason must be stated immediately after the thesis—then [the objection stands].

"But in one's own realization (*svapratipatti*), the properties of the reason (*hetudharma*) need not be applied. This is not so. For even Jaimini did not compose the treatise for his own realization;

rather, having already known the meaning of the Vedas from other sources, he composed the *sūtras* for the benefit of his disciples. Therefore, here too, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is solely for the sake of others (*parārtha*). Now, it might be argued: "The 'other' is indeed twofold, due to the distinction between those who have risen [from confusion] and those who have not. In the case of instructing those who have risen, the reason is stated immediately after the proposition."
This is logical. As for the subsequent [categories], however, they are established by stating the reasons only after an examination;

this is not so. For the same consequence would apply to other definitions as well. Even regarding the definitions of "difference" and so forth, one would have to undertake an examination after first asserting their respective objects; yet such is not observed. And what logic is there in this, that for one who is in disagreement...

The reason (*hetu*) is stated immediately after the proposition (*pratijñā*), and not for the sake of the students. On the contrary, it is more appropriate to state the reason immediately after the proposition for their own convenience; what is the point of inserting an intervening proposition that causes distraction? This is trivial. Therefore, this [is the case] here.

Samādhi: Here, by the first aphorism, the purpose of the treatise is proposed; by the second, the proposal of a summary of the entire meaning of the Tantra to be explained hereafter; and by this [third], however, the proposal of the subject matter of the first chapter is made for the sake of easy comprehension. *athātaḥ śeṣalakṣaṇam* (3.1.1).
*atha viśeṣalakṣaṇam* (8.1.1).
Thus it was composed by the Sage.

This is what is meant: "In this chapter, we shall examine the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding dharma. Although, in the *Codanā-sūtra*, while providing a summary of the entire system's meaning, it was also asserted as part of the definition of the means of valid knowledge that "codanā alone is the means of valid knowledge," [it is here specifically examined].

Nevertheless, although the proposition was stated in a composite form, the meaning of the first chapter is now being restated by extracting it from that. For if it were not extracted, then due to the confusion of the propositions, it would not be known which portion of the proposition the reason is being stated for by means of the *Samanvaya* and *Autpattika* sūtras. Much...

For indeed, the nature of the Dharma and so forth were promised there; therefore, someone might be deluded into thinking that this [following] statement of a reason also pertains to that context. To dispel such a delusion, he himself demonstrates the determination: "This meaning of the treatise which has been briefly promised by us," [is as follows].

While that [Dharma] is being explained, the examination of its means (*nimitta*) alone shall proceed in this chapter, because the establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is preceded by the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, first of all, a fourfold examination will be conducted: whether there is a restriction (*niyama*) such that "is it the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone, or something else?", or an alternative (*vikalpa*) such as "is it the Vedic injunction or something else? [and so forth].
"Or both" means a conjunction; "not both" means the denial of both. And it is said:
[605] tro (GA)
[606] He who. (KA) [607] The syllable *m*. (GA) [608] Not in *re*. (GA)
And here, the investigation of the sign (nimitta) will be conducted in exactly four ways:
[the inquiry] whether it is "only the injunction" or "something else," or whether it is "something else" or "also the injunction."
Alternatively: "And [the object] is neither different from the injunction (*codanā*) nor is it not different from the injunction.

Thus, there are four positions based on restriction (*niyama*), option (*vikalpa*), combination (*samuccaya*), and the denial of both (*ubhayāpalāpa*). And there occurs an option regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vikalpa*); for instance, one sometimes cognizes a fire situated at a distance through an inferential mark (*liṅga*), and sometimes through the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta-upadeśa*).
Nor is either [of the two means] redundant in the case of their conjunction;
for the great sages perceive *dharma* through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), while others do so through scripture (*āgama*). Thus, because of the difference among cognizers, both are established.
However, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra) has shown this merely for the sake of illustration, asking whether it is *codanā* alone or something else as well, for one who is investigating.

For indeed, a counter-argument (*pratibhā*) arises in only four ways. Thus, here in the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*, by means of the negation of perception and so forth, the [fourfold] alternatives—namely, contradiction (*prati-pakṣa*), restriction (*niyama*), option (*vikalpa*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*)—have been refuted. As for the denial of both [perception and scripture], it will be rejected in the *Autpattika-sūtra* through the establishment of the authority of Vedic injunction (*codanā-prāmāṇya*), on the grounds that "it is a valid means of knowledge because it is independent" (*tat pramāṇam anapekṣatvāt*). Therefore, this is the summary of the examination of the causes [of knowledge].
By the exclusion of perception and other means of knowledge, it is established through the restrictive determination that "only *codanā* [is the source]";

by the refutation of the suspicion regarding non-existence, it is established as "indeed a valid means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*); and by the demonstration that the relationship between word and meaning and the composition of sentences are not of human origin, there is the exclusion of invalidity that might be suspected due to the involvement of a person.
Furthermore, there is the establishment of the basis for the cognition of the meaning of sentences;
subsequently, the explanation of the manner in which the authority of mantras and arthavādas is established;

and by means of the Smṛti-pāda, the demonstration of the existence of a foundational Veda for those ritual items—such as the Kāṣṭhā festival and the Holākā rite—which are recorded in the remembered traditions of authoritative figures like Manu and others, yet whose specific causal origins are not perceived.

Furthermore, by means of the section on names (*nāmadheya-pāda*), it is explained that names such as *udbhid* and others—which appear to refer to qualities—are actually employed in ritual action solely by virtue of being names. Thus, it is well said that this entire chapter constitutes an investigation into the grounds (*nimitta*) of Dharma; hence [Jaimini] stated, "An inquiry into its grounds" (*tasya nimitta-parīṣṭiḥ*). Regarding this, the Bhāṣya says: "We have already stated that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the ground for the knowledge of Dharma; that was stated merely as a proposition," and so forth. That is incorrect.

Because he has stated his thesis along with its supporting proof (*sopapattika*). For instance, by the passage beginning "The Vedic injunction (*codanā*) indeed [concerns] what is existent," etc., the establishment of the validity of the injunction has already been stated;

and by the statement "there is no other sense-organ," the establishment of the invalidity of others has been stated. Therefore, how can it be said that this was stated merely as a thesis? To this, he says: "The thesis... (in the verse) and the following half-verse. Its meaning is as follows: although the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakāra*), by looking ahead (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*), has [already] indicated the reasoning for his own position—which is distinct from the mere thesis—by means of the two sūtras concerning the "Eternality" (*autpattika*) and the "Injunction" (*codanā*) which are to be explained later...
Nevertheless, since no formal argument has been stated by the author of the Sūtra, this is merely the statement of a proposition according to his view. // 1 //

He states another justification, saying "the author of the Vṛtti. Its meaning is as follows: that capacity of the *codanā* to illuminate matters such as past events, which was established by the passage beginning with "for [it is] *codanā*," was stated merely as a gateway to its authority (*prāmāṇya*). The ultimate reasoning will be stated later by the author of the Sūtras himself.
Therefore, what was mentioned there was merely a possibility of its authority, exceeding nothing more than the reasoning yet to be stated. [Thus, it is] rendered probable.

For, in a formal proposition (*pratijñā*), it is the thesis (*pakṣa*) that is established by the reason (*hetu*), and not something impossible; thus, even according to one's own intention, the mere statement of a proposition is logically justified. // 2 //
Thus ends the *Nimitta-sūtra*, the fourth [chapter], the *Pratyakṣa-sūtra*, in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.

{1,204} Immediately following this, in order to introduce the examination of the cause (*nimitta-parīkṣā*) promised in the *Parīṣṭi-sūtra*, the Sūtra states: "When there is contact of a person's sense organs with what exists, the arising of cognition is perception; it is not a [valid] means [of knowing Dharma], because it is the apprehension of what is already present. This [Sūtra passage], having been separated from the word "animittāt" (from the non-cause) in other commentaries, is intended as a definition ending with "tat pratyakṣam" (that is perception).

This has been explained. Having introduced this point, he refutes it with the words "it is described" (*varṇyate*). The meaning of this is as follows: it was indeed promised that "the cause of Dharma must be examined. Yet, the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) being stated immediately thereafter does not cohere with that prior promise. // 1 //

"It is not a supreme consistency, nor even a useful application," he says with the words "of the definition" (*lakṣaṇasya*). The sense is: for a Mīmāṃsaka who deals with the conventions of means of knowledge well-established in the world, what is the use of formulating such a definition? For the initial thesis consists of two parts: "only *codanā* is the means of knowledge" and "it is a means of knowledge."

"Thus, 'codanā' is the formal proposition summarizing the meaning of the system (*tantra*). Furthermore, by means of the *parīṣṭi* sūtra, it is extracted as having for its object the definition of the first [means of knowledge].

Nor is the statement of a definition useful merely by establishing one part [of the subject matter]. However, if one were to formulate a definition of perception following the method of the Naiyāyikas and others—"

For in that very same way, since he states "inference is of three kinds preceded by that," the formulation of a definition for inference and so forth would also follow as a consequence; thus he asks: "For what purpose? (2)

It might be argued as follows: "Inference and the other means of knowledge are indeed invalid because they are different from perception, just like fallacious perceptions; therefore, their definitions need not be stated. This is incorrect, as he says: "Not at all," etc. The intended meaning is this: whatever proof is adduced to establish the invalidity of those [other means], that very proof is sublated by that [invalidity] itself. Furthermore, inference...

To establish the lack of validity [of perception], an inference is not being presented; thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words. Therefore, enough of this heretical prattle that "non-perceptual [means] are not valid. It might be argued: "Just as with probability (*sambhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*), since inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*) are included within perception, the definitions of the others are not stated. That is not so. He says, ending with the words "nor also," that this is because of the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It might be argued: "The very difference in defining characteristics is unproven."

[The opponent argues: "Because [all cognitions] arise only when there is contact between a sense-faculty and its object. That is not so. For one who infers fire upon perceiving smoke—even though that smoke is in contact with the eye—does not perceive it if the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unknown or not remembered. Therefore, the very absence of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that could otherwise establish a cognition through sense-faculties, logical marks (*liṅga*), words, or similarity, constitutes the respective arising of the means of knowledge such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others.
Regarding the term "means" (*sādhana*): since there is a difference in characteristics due to the diversity of means, it is not possible for them to be mutually inclusive.
This is what he states with the words "And not... (verse 3).

Nor should it be argued that because the definition of perception is stated at the very beginning, the other [means of knowledge] are defined by virtue of being preceded by that [perception], and thus their definitions need not be stated separately;

for since memory and so forth—which are preceded by that [perception]—are seen to be invalid, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion with fallacious cognitions (*ābhāsa*). Thus he says: "And also not... (4).

Furthermore, unlike the definition of the extension of general properties (*sāmānyātideśa*), the statement of the definition of perception does not imply the ultimate definition of inference and the other means of knowledge, for those are established even without it. However, a general property cannot attain its own nature without implying various particular instances; thus, it implies specific objects. This is what he says: "perception... (verse 5).
Furthermore, by accepting the premise that [perception] is preceded by that [non-apprehension], we previously stated that there is a deviation (vyabhicāra) due to memory.

That [premise] also does not hold, because the definition of perception lacks the quality of being established otherwise (ananyathāsiddhi); thus he says: "That and not-that" (*tadatad*). "That and not-that" means both that and not-that. The term "that-and-not-that-prior" (*tadatad-pūrva*) is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that which has those as its antecedents. This is the meaning: either that [perception] itself, or...
Nor can it be understood from the definition of perception that "something else" [i.e., inference and the rest] comes first; for that is not known from the definition of perception itself.

If, however, one were to assume that the others are preceded by perception even without a reason, simply because of the mention of the definition of perception, then alas, one could just as easily assume on the basis of mere words that they are *not* preceded by it. Thus he says: "Because of the mention of that. The analysis of the compound should be shown as: "that of which this is the non-precedent. // 6 //

Dream-cognition is independent of the operation of the external sense-faculties and so forth; if one were to exclude only that [dream-cognition], then everything would result in being [considered] perception (*pratyakṣa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), recollection (*smṛti*)—which has as its cause a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) awakened by nothing other than the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)—is intended. Therefore, since the complete definition of perception is not included here, it cannot be established.

He says "therefore" (tasmāt) to show that it is possible to restate [the definition]. That which is perception has such-and-such a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)—this is the formulation of the definition (*lakṣaṇavidhi*). That which has such-and-such a characteristic is perception—this is the restatement of the definition (*lakṣaṇānuvāda*). Furthermore, a meaning that has not been previously stated cannot stand in the relation of being the object of a formulation or a restatement.
Because the designation is common to both as well. // 16 //

Having thus rejected the view that the sūtra is intended to provide a definition, and having preceded this with the refutation of an undesirable interpretation of the words, he states the intended syntactical construction of the sūtra with the two verses beginning with "tena. This is what is meant: it is not the meaning of the sūtra that "that which has such a characteristic is perception. What then? [It is] that which is well-known in the world as perception—of that...

There exists a property called "arising from contact with the existent. Because it possesses that property, there is the state of perceiving what is present. Consequently, when the object (dharma) is not yet present—that is, in the future—it would follow that [the cognition] lacks a causal basis (animittatā). // 18 //

But is it not the case that even in the *Śābara-bhāṣya* it is stated that perception is not a means [of knowing Dharma], because it is defined as having such characteristics? Since it would be untenable for the Sūtra to have the purpose of defining that [perception] as lacking those characteristics, he says:
"In this way. This is the intended meaning: even the followers of Śabara, by restating the definition well-known in the world, [establish its] non-authoritativeness.

We do not tolerate even those [interpretations], because the Sūtra is incapable of expressing a complete definition. Therefore, the statement of the definition here is intended solely as an indicator (liṅga). Just as smoke is the indicator of fire, so too is "perceptibility when present" the indicator of "not being a means of valid knowledge. For it is the intention of the Commentator that "it is indicated by that"—this is what is meant. // 19 //

{1,210} It reveals both that which is the mark (*liṅga*) and that which possesses it—this is indicated by the word "since" (*yataḥ*). The property known as "being perceived while existing" (*vidyamānopalambhanatva*) is the mark; however, "not being a cause [of knowledge]" (*animittatā*) is that which possesses the mark. If someone were to argue that this mark is unestablished (*asiddha*), then for that person, the lack of causality is to be understood through that very mark, which is well-known by means of another reason, namely "being born from the contact with an existent object" (*satsamprayogajatva*); thus, the word "well-known" (*prasiddhena*) is used. // 20 //

How, then, is another reason established? To this he says: "Because it is perception. This is what is meant: these are the three formal arguments—perception is not a means [of knowing dharma], because it is the apprehension of that which is present; and its being the apprehension of that which is present is because it arises from contact with what exists.

And the state of being born from the contact with the existent [is established] because of its being perception (*pratyakṣatva*). In this context, it should be understood that the status of the cause for "apprehending what is present" (*vidyamānopalambhanatva*) is explicitly expressed by the fifth case (*pañcamī*), whereas the causality of the other two [characteristics] is indicated by their very mention. Furthermore, this should be understood as an elaboration of the statement: "That which is established among people as perception. For instance:
In that very context, its lack of a [distinctive] cause (*animittatva*) is due to its being the apprehension of what is present (*vidyamānopalambhanatvāt*);
likewise, its being the apprehension of what is present is due to its being born from a contact with existing things as characterized by such properties (*evaṃdharmakatvopāttasatsamprayogajatvāt*).

And its being "that which produces perception" (*pratyakṣaṃ yajjanaḥ*) is stated because it possesses such properties simply by virtue of being perception (*pratyakṣatvāt*). This, indeed, is the intended meaning (*ākūtam*) there.
"Direct perception is thus characterized by existence. However, this must be addressed here: what is the purpose of this elaborate construction of formal arguments?
For the desired conclusion is indeed established even by this much: "That which is the object of dispute is not a cause [of its own cognition], because it is a direct perception.
