For they might think that [the Veda] was declared to be non-authoritative merely because of the commonality of the word "śruti. Yet, total similarity does not arise from the mere sameness of the term "śruti" alone; for instance, the word *pada* (foot) or *vāk* (speech) is not possessed of horns. Furthermore, the claim that [the Veda] is non-authoritative because it perceives only what is already existent (*vidyamānopalambhana*) strengthens their conviction. And how could that which perceives only the existent be an authority regarding the future?

There is a sign. And how is it that what is born from contact with the existent is a perception of what is non-existent? For that which is born from contact with the present is designated as "born from contact with the existent," because the word *sat* (existent) denotes the present. And a contact with a future dharma is not possible for something that is present.

For a relation is that which subsists in two related entities; it is not logical to assert that such a relation exists when it does not subsist in either one of them. Likewise, the word *pratyakṣa* (perception), whose application depends upon the contact of a present sense organ with its object, ought not to apply to that which arises from a non-existent contact; thus, the sequential explanation is appropriate. Furthermore, since the Mīmāṃsakas are fond of elaborate exposition, this [detailed treatment] is fitting.
The designation of conceptual proliferation.

[615] Indeed, this must be stated: the quality of being born from the contact of the senses with what is existent (*satsamprayogajatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding the perception of what is currently existing (*vidyamānopalambhana*).
For even when there is contact with the eye and the swelling of a river, there arises a cognition of past rain; [and likewise for] the present.

And thus, the contact between the eye and a cloud produces a cognition whose object is a future rain. Therefore, it is not an absolute rule that knowledge arising from actual contact perceives only what is presently existing. Moreover, even a cognition that appears as immediate is seen to arise from present contact while having a non-existent object; for this occurs when there is present contact between the eye and mother-of-pearl.

[The definition of perception as] "the apprehension of silver [as it actually exists], even when that silver is past, future, or spatially remote" is flawed. For you yourselves, on the occasion of refuting Bhavadāsa, stated that the quality of being produced by the contact of a real object (*satsamprayogajatva*) is common to all cognitions, whether they be valid (*pramāṇa*) or invalid (*apramāṇa*). It might be argued: "Inference, which has the past and future as its objects, is certainly not produced by the contact of a real object."

Because there is no absence of the pervasion of what has been known and remembered. For even in that case, there is indeed a sensory contact between the eye and the flood of water in the river; yet, there is no cognition of past or future rain. Even in the perception of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, the cause is simply the sensory contact with the substance present before one. However, the experience of silver arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a previous cognition, aided by a defect (*doṣa*).

For the reason that the sense organ is indeed brought into proximity with various objects, and it does not produce the manifestation of something non-existent when defects are absent; therefore, errors—which follow the positive and negative concomitance of defects in the object and so forth—make that very [object] the cause within themselves. This is not so, because even the cause of a cause does not lose its status as a cause. [The case of] the contact between the eye and mother-of-pearl...

For indeed, in the case of error, the cause for the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is [the contact]; and in inference, it is the contact with the logical mark (*liṅga*) and the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

Therefore, it can be said that both of these are, by way of a causal chain, born from the contact with the existent (*satsamprayogaja*). And here, the mere quality of being "born from contact with the existent" has been stated as the reason without further qualification. Consequently, the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of such a reason is difficult to avoid.

[616] Regarding this, it is said: [617] It has already been stated that this is the characteristic of perception as established in common worldly usage, namely, that it arises from the contact of the senses with an existing object.

Thus, the reason for establishing that [perception] apprehends what is presently existing has been stated. And it is established in the world that perception occurs only when there is contact with the very object to be grasped; for it is never observed that something is perceived by an eye in contact with one thing while perceiving another.

Therefore, in this context, the fact that it arises from contact with a present object through the very thing to be grasped is stated as the reason for its being an apprehension of what is presently existing.

And that [definition] is not possible in the case of inference and the like; for in those cases, there is no sensory contact with the object of apprehension, such as rain and so forth. However, according to the position that defines perception by its characteristics (*lakṣaṇapakṣa*), since it would depend solely on whatever is heard [in the definition], even error and the like would necessarily result in being considered perception. Furthermore, if in that case too one were to depend upon worldly consensus, then the formulation of a definition would be in vain. [Objection: But is it not the case that perception is not an authoritative means [of knowledge]?
Regarding the statement "because [the object] is perceived while existing," what is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*)?

If it is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, that is not so; for it would result in no distinction between the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the corroborating instance (*sapakṣa*). And that is improper, because there is a distinction between that which is already established and that which is yet to be proven (*sādhyo*).

For the subject (*pakṣa*) is established, and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is also established. And it is not logically tenable that a single thing should possess both an established and a yet-to-be-proved nature.
Furthermore, the fact that perception is not a means of knowing *dharma* for people like us is already established;
what, then, is the point of proving it? Therefore, he says: "for people like us. The intention here is [to refer to] a specific kind of perception.

Having made one perception the subject (*pakṣa*), another perception is made the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); thus, there is no identity between the subject and the similar instance, nor is there the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). // 21 //
[618] One is associated, the other is the application; thus it is said there. [619] It is that.
[620] Therein, it is that.
Having thus explained the Sūtra according to his own view, he now addresses and refutes the objections raised by opposing schools with the words "by what is under discussion" (*prakṛtena*).

For it was stated that in the opposing view there is a lack of connection with the subject at hand; that [fault] does not exist here. Indeed, it was asserted that "injunction alone is the means of valid knowledge" (*codanāiva pramāṇam*).

And that [assertion] has its form established by demonstrating that perception is not the cause [of knowledge regarding Dharma], and by showing the lack of authority in the remaining means—such as inference and the rest.
"It is established. But how is it that, if perception is not the means [of knowing dharma], inference and the others are also not the means?

For it is not the case that because perception is incapable regarding the future and the past, inference must likewise be so. Otherwise, there would follow the absurdity that rain—whether future or past—could not be inferred from the rising of clouds or the swelling of a river. Therefore, he says: "That..."

Thus [it is said]. This is the intended meaning: since the arising of inference is dependent upon the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and since the cognition of pervasion is impossible with respect to *dharma*, which is eternally beyond the senses, there is an absence of the emergence of inference. Nor does this entail an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to rain and the like;
for in those cases, the cognition of pervasion is possible because they have been previously perceived. By the word "and the like" (*ādi*), the similarity to *dharma* is included. This...
This will indeed be explained in detail further below. // 22 //
[621] Not so (KA).
[622] Even if that were the case (GA), why are the other [means of knowledge], like perception, not likewise established as non-authoritative by means of the Sūtras? Therefore—

He says: "It is possible. For if one were to establish the definition of only one [means of knowledge], the definitions of all others would remain unestablished; thus, the task of defining them all would have been necessitated. However, since it has been stated that perception is not a means [to the knowledge of Dharma], and because the others are preceded by it, their non-authoritativeness can also be understood; therefore, they are not defined separately. As he will say: "Because they function through the door of perception, inference and the other means are also not causes [of that knowledge]. Even if the definitions are of no use...
He says "and not" (na ca) because even the objection that was raised does not apply here, precisely because a definition is not admitted. // 23 //

[623] Furthermore, because it does not include the qualification of the object to be apprehended (*grāhya-viśeṣaṇa*) [as "non-erroneous"], and because it fails to encompass inference and other means of valid cognition, the definition is deficient. [624] Even by [the opponent's] own [admission], it is thus deficient due to the non-inclusion of inference and so forth, as well as the failure to employ the qualification of the object to be apprehended.

Regarding what was also stated—that because all cognitions are non-deviant when there is contact with an existent object (*satsamprayoga*), the mention of "contact with an existent" (*satsamprayoga-nirdeśa*) is redundant—that too is not to be suspected here; thus he says, "And not... For defects such as deficiency or redundancy apply to the formulation of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), not to that which is not a definition. Indeed, this is what must be established here in every respect: that which is well-known in the world.

"That very [cognition] has such a nature" means that the complete definition of perception need not be stated by this [sūtra], nor need it be avoided; we have no concern with that. And because the sūtra is intent upon something else, the status of perception—which was attributed to cognitions of mirages and the like under the view that the sūtra provides a formal definition—is not incurred. Thus he says: "In every way. (25)

Now, if it is argued that if the mere state of being non-causal (*animittatva*) is to be proven here by demonstrating the nature of dharma as established in common worldly experience, then one should simply say: "Perception is not a means [of knowing dharma], because it apprehends only what is present. What is the point of adducing [reasons] such as its arising from contact with existing objects? To this, he says [the following] in two and a half verses beginning with *atīta*. The meaning is this: it is true that by this much alone the state of being non-causal is indeed established. However—

However, for those who maintain that the quality of "perceiving only what is present" (*vidyamānopalambhanatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*)— because knowledge regarding objects such as the past and future arises even in yogis and liberated souls (*muktātman*)—
another reason, namely "being born from the contact with the existent" (*satsamprayogajatva*), has been presented in order to establish the reason for them,
and not with the intention of defining the essential nature of perception itself. Thus, by stating the reason "because it is the perception of what is present,"...

The reason implicitly contained [in the definition]—that a future object which does not exist cannot be experienced through perception precisely because it is future—is stated [by the author] so that this [definition] may not be subject to deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by way of the objects of yogis and those who have attained self-mastery, which are other things that are future. For this purpose, too, the phrase "born from contact with what exists" (*satsamprayogaja*) is employed. By this, the following is expressed: every perception arises only when there is actual contact between the sense organ and its object; therefore, nothing [else]...

Since it refers to a future object, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra). The dual number is employed so that both "unestablishedness" (asiddhatā) and "deviation" might not occur together. That is how it is. What?
[626] There is no such dharma;

however, this must be stated here: that which has been refuted is indeed impossible for a person to know without verbal testimony—this refers to the fact that the direct perception of yogins has future things and so forth as its objects. What, then, is the point of raising this objection again? Regarding this, some say:

They say: "For in that case [the Sūtra], the capacity of persons to experience supersensuous objects was refuted without recourse to verbal testimony. Here, however, by means of verbal testimony alone, it is established that merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) will become perceptible to one who contemplates them for a long time; thus, the objection is refuted. This is incorrect, for all of that was stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya and Vārttika with a view toward the future.

For this has been stated right here by the author of the Sūtra himself. Nor is it the established tenet (siddhānta) of others that objects—whether subtle, concealed, distant, or otherwise—past, future, or present, manifest directly to the Buddha or to anyone else who has ascended to that level without any external cause. Rather, [they manifest] through scripture alone, after having long known those phenomena (dharmas) in a general way.

"For one who meditates, [objects] appear clearly and non-conceptually. It is precisely the knowledge born from the power of meditation that is called the "divine eye" (*divya-cakṣus*). As for the claim that everything is made directly perceptible by means of the physical eye alone—that is utterly preposterous. They said this merely for the sake of displaying their boldness. Even such a view must be refuted right here.

This is because it has already been refuted right here by the author of the Sūtra. Therefore, it has already been stated that what was said there was intended precisely for this context, by way of looking ahead. Now, one might object: "The demonstration of each subsequent reason is due to the suspicion that each preceding reason might be unestablished;
since it was stated [in the previous section] with the words 'Because this property exists there' up to 'pratyakṣatvam ado hetuḥ,' this [present passage] is redundant."

[627] To this, it is said: the seed of the opponents' counter-argument is now stated. For they maintain that the perception of yogins is indeed the apprehension of what is non-existent, by the power of the dharma born of yoga. Therefore, regarding the past and the future...

By the words "even in that case" (*apy arthe*) and so forth, the seed of the reason's lack of establishment (*hetvasiddhi*) has been shown. Previously, however, it was only stated that the sequence of reasons was adopted due to the suspicion of non-establishment; nothing was said there as to *how* there is non-establishment. Regarding the statement "it is expressed for the sake of what is possible," the specific excellence (*atiśayaviśeṣa*) of the yogins is also implicitly included therein. That very [excellence] is made manifest by the passage beginning with "past and future" (*atītānāgata*). Who...?
Furthermore, regarding the view that perception has objects such as the past and the future, their intention is as follows: Listen.
For they think thus: "Let it be granted that Dharma is not perceived by the perception of people like us, which apprehends only what is presently existing;

however, why should it not be perceived by that [perception] arising from the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which has as its objects all things—past, future, and so forth? Since that [cultivated perception] is unestablished..."

If it is argued that this is untenable, we say no; for it is established through inference. In this regard, one might think: "There is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of such a perception born from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), which has never been observed among people like us. But that is not so, because it is established in this way through inference. For when objects are cultivated while avoiding obstacles of a different nature, there arises a clarity of wisdom (*prajñā-prasāda*).

A distinction is observed. For instance—what else could it be? Here indeed, certain fortunate ones behold with extreme clarity the Self itself—which is otherwise exceedingly difficult to attain—as one from which all stains and disturbances caused by the body and the senses have been shaken off, and from which the grasping of the distinctions between the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge has entirely dissolved, as "I. Thus say the proponents of Vedānta. For that is certainly not an object of knowledge for people like us.
"No," [they reply], "for even yogins do not perceive it; or rather, we too understand it to be so. And there is a reason for this:

indeed, an excellence in the cause is observed to be pervaded by an excellence in the effect, just as the excellence of a craftsman such as a painter is pervaded by the excellence of his work, such as a painting.
Furthermore, the cause of the direct perception arising from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in a certain yogin is itself excellent; this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Now, it might be asked: "From what cause is the excellence [of the result] understood? It is from the very nature of the reason (*svabhāvahetu*). Whoever, being intent upon something, practices it, reaches the pinnacle of its excellence, just as an artist reaches the perfection of his craft. And since someone, being attentive, practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), this demonstrates a reason that is concomitant with the probandum (*sādhyānvita-hetu*).

Therefore, from the excellence of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), there follows the excellence of the knowledge that arises through its power. And what other excellence of knowledge could there be than this clear, non-conceptual manifestation? As they have said:
[629] Proposition (KA) [630] Whatever— whether real or unreal— is intensely meditated upon, from that [arises the result]. (GA)
When the power of cultivation is perfected, its fruit is a cognition that is vivid and free from conceptual construction.

Thus it is said. Now, one might object: while it is appropriate for artisans to practice their craft for the sake of livelihood, there is no basis whatsoever for the practice of meditation. How can there be no basis? Compassion (*karuṇā*) is indeed the basis for the practice of meditation. For someone indeed becomes compassionate due to formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*) from a previous existence.

He becomes intent upon compassion alone, and through the excellence of his practice, that compassion reaches its highest degree for him. Having reached this peak of intensity, he sees those wandering in saṃsāra overwhelmed by suffering; with a mind deeply pained, he reflects, "How might I deliver them? Thereupon, seeking the means to accomplish the goal of human endeavor, he applies himself to meditation.
He exerts himself. Then, through long-term practice, having perfected his meditation (*dhyāna*), he perceives even dharma and adharma directly.

Another opinion holds: for transmigrating beings, the arising of knowledge is dependent upon the sense faculties; for they possess bodies and sense faculties acquired through the karma of previous lives. Therefore, it is logical that their cognitions conform to the state of the body and sense faculties. However, when these [beings], through the practice of yoga...

When they have thus completely exhausted all latent impressions of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karmāśaya*), they are then liberated from the body and the senses. At that time, due to the absence of a governing agent and because their own nature is self-luminous, they perceive everything, including the past and so forth. Therefore, with respect to them, the condition of being perceived by a presently existing [perceiver] is unestablished; hence, for the purpose of awakening them to this fact:

"Jaimini says that 'existent' and so forth are well-known in the world. He now informs those [opponents] that [this is not the case]: "It is not distinct from the world. The meaning is this: even their perception cannot be something transcendent of the world. // 28 //

[631] Here he states the reason: "by virtue of being perception" (*pratyakṣatvena*). This is the intended meaning: Is that cognition of the yogis perceptual or not? If it is not perceptual, then it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because no means of valid cognition other than perception and inference is admitted, and because it lacks the defining characteristics of inference. And what is not a means of valid cognition is incapable of establishing an object. Therefore, what is the point of admitting it? Or else—

Since the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is etymologically significant, it must necessarily be produced by the sense organs. For no common usage among people is observed where that which is not produced by the sense organs is called "perception.
[Objection: But is being produced by the sense organs not the definition of perception?
Rather, [it is as follows:]

"Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). Conceptual construction is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being associated with verbal expression. Perception is that knowledge which is devoid of such [construction], which is non-erroneous—meaning it is not affected by delusions caused by cataracts, rapid spinning, traveling in a boat, or physical agitation—and thus free from error. Furthermore, this definition certainly encompasses the knowledge of yogins as well, for that too is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).

It is non-erroneous. For this very reason, they divide direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) into four types; that fourfold [perception] consists of: that which is born of the sense faculties (*indriyajam*), that which arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) born of the sense faculties (i.e., mental perception), the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), and the cognition of the yogis (*yogijñāna*). For if the definition of direct perception were merely "being born of the sense faculties,"...

The triad [of object, sense-organ, and contact] would not be perceptible. Furthermore, even the Mīmāṃsakas accept that mental [cognition] is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, it is determined that the word *pratyakṣa* denotes merely the state of appearing as non-mediately-present (*aparokṣāvabhāsitva*) common to all [perceptions]. Just as the word *go*—derived from the root *gam* with the suffix *ḍoḥ* (Pāṇini 4.1.41)—is determined to denote merely the universal *gotva* common to all [beings], because it is seen in usage even for those who do not move (*agacchat*), so too the word *pratyakṣa*, whose etymological analysis of its constituent parts has ceased to function, operates solely through a conventional power (*samudāyaśakti*) toward that which appears non-mediately.

This is not so, because there is no deviation in the concomitance of the constituent parts (*avayava*). For it is only when there is a deviation in the concomitance of the constituent parts that the power of the whole (*samudāya-śakti*) acquires its own nature. And the concomitance with the sense organ (*indriya*), which is denoted by the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), does not deviate. If it is argued that there is a deviation in the case of mental [perception] (*mānasa*), we say no; for the mind (*manas*) is also a sense organ. Or, if you claim that there is no such thing as a sense organ called the "mind," [we respond:]...

However, it is said that among the continuous stream of cognitions (*dhārāvāhika*) produced by the sense organs, the mind (*manas*) is the cause of the cognition that grasps the subsequent moment; thus, the subsequent [cognition] is called "mental" (*mānasa*). That is incorrect. For when the sense-born cognition of a preceding moment has passed, the subsequent moment is experienced. How could that [subsequent moment] be made manifest by that [preceding cognition] which is no longer connected [to it]? If you argue that it is like the sense organ (*akṣavat*), [we reply: no.

No, for it will be stated right here that the sense organs function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). Therefore, even the apprehension in the second moment is produced by the sense organ alone;

thus, there is no deviation [from the rule]. This is because that [second-moment cognition] also conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the sense organ. Indeed, a cognition of form persisting in one whose eyes are closed is never observed. Consequently, since there is no deviation regarding the positive concomitance of the parts (*avayava*), the power of the whole (*samudāya*) does not acquire its own nature [as a causal agent].

Therefore, the cognition of yogins or liberated souls (muktātman), which is not born of the sense faculties, is not perception (*pratyakṣa*). Perception is restricted to the apprehension of what is presently existing;
as for non-perception, it is already rejected by the very fact that [the Buddhist] does not accept it as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[632] Or even [633] in the case of a practitioner [634].

[635] Furthermore, as for the claim that the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is the cause for the arising of a yogi’s cognition—that is not so, because cultivation has as its object that which has already been cognized. Nor is it possible for a cognition to arise from nothing at all, since everything that comes into existence possesses a cause. If, on the other hand, it is argued that what is cultivated is something already cognized through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
What is the use of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), since that [result] is established from that very [source]? Furthermore, what is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

It is certainly not inference (*anumāna*), because, due to the prior non-apprehension of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), there is no perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*) pervaded by them. Nor is it presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the diversity of the world...
It is merely inferred that there exists some cause, but no specific detail is provided. Furthermore, meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) does not occur with respect to an unspecified object.
Even in the Yoga treatises, only specific objects are taught as the focus of meditation—for instance:
"The Self is the object of meditation; it is the Lord who resides in the heart like a lamp."

[This is established] by such statements as these. [Objection: "In that case, what has been understood from scripture will be cultivated through meditative realization (*bhāvanā*). [Response: If it is understood from a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since it is already understood from that very source, what is the use of cultivation? For an object is investigated for the purpose of its rejection or acquisition; and since those two are already accomplished by that [means of cognition] alone, cultivation is useless. Even a compassionate person would simply explain the scriptures on Dharma to his disciples with great effort.

One should not experience weariness with meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Now, if one—doubting whether scripture (*āgama*) is a valid authority because scriptures abound in contradictions—seeks to know [the truth] through meditative cultivation, that is not correct;
for even by that means, it remains unestablished. Even knowledge perfected through the power of meditative cultivation has as its object only that which is not to be trusted.

Because even that which is non-existent, when being meditated upon, appears as if it were directly perceived. Thus it has been said by those very [masters]: "Therefore, whether it be real or unreal... [636] ...not [is there] of this [GA] ...of this [KA].

Furthermore, that which arises from the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is not a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it apprehends what has already been apprehended. For exactly as much as has been previously apprehended is made an object by cultivation; however, cultivation does not take as its range even a fraction more than that. Indeed, what is called "cultivation" is simply memory, caused by the proficiency of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced through the practice of yoga. And it is already established that this [memory] is not a valid means of cognition. Nor is it...

There is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the claim that a direct perceptual knowledge arises at a time subsequent to that [initial cognition], because a direct perception of an object is never observed to occur in the absence of sensory contact. In this regard, there is the following formal argument: yogins do not possess a cognition that manifests the dharma and adharma as directly perceived, because of the absence of sensory contact.

It is like ourselves and others. Furthermore, that which was stated—that there is an excellence of the effect due to an excellence of the cause—is incorrect, because an excellence of the cause is impossible. Moreover, the impossibility of an excellence of cultivation has already been described, owing to the absence of a purpose, the lack of an object, and the fact that there is no further object to be attained. Nor is there any observation today of anyone possessing such an excellence.

It would have to be accepted because it has been seen [by someone]. However, regarding the excellence of Brahman, which is established by the authority of the eternal and faultless Vedānta, nothing is untenable. Even in that case, perception not born of the senses is not possible; for that state is one in which the entire manifold of cognizer, object, and means of cognition has been completely severed. And even where excellence is observed through practice, it is memory alone that is being perfected.

Furthermore, through repeated practice, even an object not in contact with the sense faculties does not become non-mediately perceived (*aparokṣa*). For it is impossible even to imagine that for one who is non-erroneous, something that is not present and not occurring would appear as if standing before them; so enough of this. Thus it is sung. [638] ti gīya (GA).

[639] But surely, it was previously stated that "being perceptible" (*pratyakṣatva*) is the reason for establishing the remaining reasons. How, then, is "the state of apprehending what is present" (*vidyamānopalambhanatva*) established by that?
To this he says: "[640] 'Being born from contact with what exists' (*satsamprayogajatvam*). This is the intended meaning: this is not the sequence of reasons prescribed by the treatise (*śāstra*).

Since a fault would arise from its transgression, it is possible for this [reason] to establish both [properties]—just like the perception of people such as ourselves—by virtue of its pervasion; thus, there is no restriction on how one chooses to express it. // 29 //

Regarding the phrase "satsam" (KA), here the author of the Sūtras, by accepting [the validity of] perception while demonstrating that the perception of yogins is not a means [of valid knowledge], has effectively indicated that if one were to accept its status as a means, it would not be perception.

He demonstrates this through two formal arguments (prayoga) using the two lines beginning with "teṣām" and "tatas tv eva. This is because [yogic perception] has as its object that which is not present.

This is the meaning. However, if the Buddhist, whose own position has been refuted, should claim that this other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is indeed denotable by the term "non-perceptual" (*apratyakṣa*), then for that purpose, the refutation of its status as a *pramāṇa* is undertaken. And this [refutation] was already included by the author of the Sūtras through the very force of the inclusion of the term "contact with the existent" (*satsamprayoga*); thus it is said that it is expressed by the word "existent" (*sat*).
Another view is this: indeed, for the perfected ones (*siddhas*), a direct intuition (*pratibhā*) regarding objects such as the future arises by virtue of their conformity with the Dharma.
And even today, this occurs in some cases among people like us—for instance, [the thought] "my brother will come tomorrow.
However, since such knowledge generally arises for the seers (*ṛṣis*), it is called "seer-like" (*ārṣa*). As they say: "Seer-like [knowledge] is the vision of the perfected ones."

And [the phrase] "from the dharmas" is refuted by the word "worldly. This is the meaning: the intuition (*pratibhā*) of yogins or sages is not capable of determining an object, because it is an intuition, like the intuition of people such as ourselves. For in the case of people like us, intuition is observed to be mostly inconsistent (*visaṃvādabhūyiṣṭhā*). // 32 //

Thus, having first raised the objection that the reason (*hetu*) "being perceived while existing" (*vidyamānopalambhanatva*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), what was stated—"because it arises from contact with the existent" (*satsamprayogajatvāt*)—has been explained. Now, he explains what was stated for the purpose of dispelling the suspicion that the reason "being future" (*bhaviṣyattva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*): "of that which is non-existent" (*avidyamāna*). This is the meaning: if it were not said that perception arises from contact with the existent, [then the reason would be inconclusive].

Therefore, since perception arises for yogins in some cases even when a conjunction is absent, its capacity with respect to a future dharma would remain unobstructed. Consequently, the reason "being future" would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Thus, Jaimini stated [the verse beginning with] "existent" (*sat*) and so forth. // 33 //

[641] Regarding the phrase "you might be": surely it is said that a phenomenon (*dharma*) is not perceptible because it is yet to come into being; thus, when it is future, let it indeed not be perceptible. But when it actually occurs, why then is it not experienced through perception?

Therefore, he says: "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*). This is the intended meaning: for it is for the sake of performance that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought. That [means of cognition] must be sought precisely before that performance. And since dharma does not exist prior to its performance, how could it be perceptible? [Objection: Is dharma then perceptible when it exists as performed by another? [Reply: No; he says: ...dharma is not perceptible when it exists as performed by another. He says: no. He says: no. "Performed. The connection is "it is not perceived. Here he states the reason: "by way of being a means to the result.

This would be so if substances and the like were *dharma* by their own nature; however, these are *dharma* by way of being means to a result, and their status as *dharma* consists precisely in that form. And that form does not exist at the time of performance.

Because there is no fruit here in the case of fruits belonging to the next world; and even in the case of fruits belonging to this life, it occurs after a long time. For when the goal and the means are in immediate succession, the means is perceived directly, as in the case of the pleasure of massaging. But here, at the time of the fruit, the means has long since passed away, and at the time of the means, the fruit has not yet arisen; thus, the means to the fruit is not perceived. Furthermore, the potency (*śakti*) of all entities is eternally beyond perception. Therefore, Dharma, as qualified by that [potency], is not perceptible.

[642] Having established the point at hand, he now concludes that perception is not a means of knowing *dharma* because it apprehends only what is presently existing—this is indicated by the words "asmad... and ending with "...dharmam. The perception of those in meditative absorption (*dhyāyin*), being existent and apprehending what is present, does not apply to *dharma*.

"It is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), like our own perception. The word "and" (*ca*) refers to the reasons that will be stated later. It is connected with what follows, namely, "it is not accepted. Furthermore, by stating the sequence of logical arguments (*upapatti-krama*), the author of the Sūtras has shown the sequence of reasons (*hetu-krama*) in order to cultivate the minds of all [disciples]. Since it is possible to establish its lack of causal basis (*animittatā*) by the mere fact of its being a perception, he says: "Because it is a perception" (35).
[643] Just as in the case of our own perception,
[644] having thus explained the purport of the Sūtra, he now examines the constituent parts. Therein also—

At the outset, one considers the word "existent" (*sat*). Regarding this, a monk has said: "The qualification 'existent' is purposeless, because there is no possibility of association with the non-existent, and thus [the term] is not subject to deviation. As it has been stated:
"'Existent' is for the purpose of excluding the non-existent; it is not understood through mandatory application."
For association occurs necessarily only for that which exists.

Thus [it is said]. Having rejected this by not accepting it, he demonstrates that it is indeed a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, "avidyamāna" (non-existent). Its meaning is as follows: the meaning of the sūtra is not that "contact with the existent" (*satsamprayoga*) means contact with something that exists. What then? This is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "that which is both existent and contact. And the word "sat" (*sat-śabda*) signifies that which is present (*vidyamāna*). That...

The meaning is this: perception is that which arises from contact with something presently existing (*vidyamāna*). Consequently, the refutation of the perceptual nature of the yogis’ cognition—which was stated by them [in the Sautrāntika critique] beginning with "if [perception were] in regard to a non-existent object" (*avidyamāne 'rthe*)—is established in this way. For the word *sat* (existent), which denotes a present object, excludes what is non-existent (*asat*). How could that exclusion be established if such an object did not exist? And this is the meaning of the Sūtra.
It should be understood that this was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya while explaining the phrase "when there is a connection between the sense-faculties and their objects. // 36 //
[645] That is the clarification.

Surely this meaning is obtained here by the locative case used in the sense of "cause" (*nimitta-saptamī*) alone; for non-existent contact cannot be a cause. Therefore, he says: "by means of the locative. The intention is this: it is true that non-occurrent contact does not exist in sensory cognition (*akṣaja-jñāna*).

[Objection: It is not the cause; however, some consider even that [past object] to be a cause. Thus, when only the word "conjunction" (samprayoga) is heard here, they might imagine it to refer to either a future or a past object as they please. Therefore, in order to refute such imagination, Jaimini has explicitly employed the qualification "existent" (sat). // 37 //

The word *sat* has been explained. Now he examines the word *sam*: "properly" (*samyak*). Proper application is "correct application" (*samprayoga*). By this, improper application (*duṣprayoga*) is excluded. He says: "You will distinguish the correct application"; first, however, you should explain the application itself. Therefore, he says: "application. They call the activity of the sense organs—which is to be inferred from the effect, namely the cognition of form and so forth—the "application," which is a synonym for "operation."
Thus [ends the thirty-eighth].
[646] First, what is the faulty application (*duṣprayoga*) here that is excluded by the word "proper" (*saṃ*)?
To this he says: "Because it is faulty. But how is it faulty? For [faults such as] excessive proximity (*atyāsatti*) and so forth belong to the application (*prayoga*).

[The opponent claims: "These are defects (*doṣa*). And those defects do not belong to one whose eye is in contact with the mother-of-pearl and who is thus erring. Rather, it is the object itself, conditioned by similarity, that is the cause of the erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*) there. Therefore, he says: "Because of the perception of silver. The intended meaning is this:
conjunction (*samprayoga*) is indeed the cause of cognition; when that [conjunction] is defective, it causes one thing to appear as another.

Because the defect of the effect is inseparable from the defect of the cause, that which is free from defects produces correct knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Its correctness arises from the absence of all defects in its causes. When, however, either the sense organ or the object is defective, then the contact (*saṃyoga*) dependent upon them also becomes defective. Therefore, the inherent defects of contact are excessive proximity (*atyāsatti*) and so forth.

Furthermore, defects of the object (*viṣayadoṣa*), such as similarity and the like, act as corrupting factors. Thus, in this case, when mother-of-pearl is perceived as silver, it is understood from the defect of the effect that the connection with the mother-of-pearl is corrupted. Therefore, this [connection] is excluded by the prefix *sam*, which signifies "correctness. And so, when this analysis of the word's components is adopted, the injunction regarding its being non-causal (*animittatva*) is established even by way of restating a definition already well-known in the world.
He says "it is not faulty" with the word "thus" (evam). // 39 //

Likewise, as for what was stated by the Buddhists—that the definition [of perception] is non-pervasive because the ear and the eye function without reaching their objects, since they take the word "application" (*prayoga*) to mean "attainment" (*prāpti*)—that too has been refuted by us by explaining that the word "application" denotes merely an operation (*vyāpāra*). Thus he says: "And therefore... The connection with what follows is that it is not contradictory because it expresses merely an operation. // 40 //
He states the Buddhists' position regarding the fact that the ear and the eye function without reaching their objects—ending with the words "not by reaching" (*prāpya*). For they have stated:
"If there were apprehension by reaching, there would be no perception of distance, nor of something larger [than the sense organ].
This means: if the eye and the ear were to grasp their object only after reaching it, [the aforementioned defects would follow].

This [perception]—namely, the apprehension of distance as in "the sound is far" or "the object is far," and the apprehension of objects such as the earth or mountains which are vastly larger than their physical bases—would, they claim, not occur at all; for such properties are not observed in the case of the skin and other senses that function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārin*). What is meant by this is: that which functions by reaching its object does not perceive what is distant or what is larger.

"Just as the body is not so [oriented], the ear and eye are not either"—this is the *āvīta* reason (*āvītahetu*). The word "kila" (it is said) is used in the context of the objection, because both [the alternatives] will be resolved later. Or, he says "yadi vā" (or rather), intending that "conjunction" (*samprayoga*) is understood as abiding in a straight position (*ārjavāvasthāna*). For it is when [the sense organ] is situated straightly that the cognition of form and so forth arises; it is precisely in that case that the term "conjunction" is applied figuratively (*upacāra*), as in the case of the skin and other [senses].

The meaning of the term "conjunction" (samprayoga) is understood as a cause of cognition. This state of rectitude (ārjava), being likewise a cause thereof, is designated in that same way. The same should be shown regarding functional activity (vyāpāra) as well. // 41-42 //

Alternatively, he says "yogyatā" (capacity), referring to that relationship characterized by a capacity indicated by its effect, which exists between the word and its meaning just as it exists between form and the eye, etc., and is termed *samprayoga* (contact). Or rather, let the relationship be simply one of "attainment" (*prāpti*) as established in the systems of the Sāṅkhyas and others;
nothing is faulty here either, so he says "Sāṅkhyādīn" (the Sāṅkhyas and others). For, having defeated the Sāṅkhyas and others, the position of attainment [is established].

This is refuted here: "And they cannot be conquered [by you]. For, on the view that [the sense organ] acts without reaching [its object], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving subtle, obstructed, distant, and other such objects, since there is no distinction in their being equally un-reached. This is the intended meaning. // 43 //

He states that the fact that the ear and the eye function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*) is also understood through inference, saying: "Of those two. This means: of the ear and the eye. [The inference is: "The eye and the ear function by reaching their objects, because they are external sense organs, like the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*). Now, one might object: the ear-cavity and the eyeball are perceived as being situated within the body; how then can it be said that they function by reaching [their objects]? To this, [the author replies] regarding these Sāṅkhyas who maintain that [the senses] function by reaching their objects:

He settles the matter by citing the opinion of "some": for the Sāṅkhyas think as follows—the activity (*vṛtti*) of the ear and the eye, which are derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*), extends outside the body and reaches the location of the object. And that activity is inferred from the observation of its effects; it persists according to the nature of those effects. (44)

Is it not the case that the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is indeed the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), since we observe the faculty’s suppression or enhancement through the removal or restoration of that basis? Otherwise, such [suppression or enhancement] would be impossible. For if the sense-organ were something distinct from its basis, then the refinement of the basis would be purposeless.

Therefore he says: "medical treatment, etc. This is the intended meaning: if the sense organ were not connected to its substrate (adhiṣṭhāna), then the refinement of the substrate would not be beneficial to it. However, that [organ] has the substrate as its support. Therefore, the refinement of that very substrate, which serves as the support, will be beneficial to the supported sense organ, just as the refinement of the saddle on an elephant or a horse is beneficial to the rider. // 45 //

But even so, let it be that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the eyeball (*golaka*) alone is what assists [the cognition]; however, for that part which is unconnected with the eyeball, the refinement of the eyeball would not be an assistance. And there is no purpose in refining that [unconnected part], because it is already attained and thus serves as a manifestor (*prakāśaka*). Therefore, that which is the manifestor...

It is impossible to refine [the object], because there is no connection; and that which is possible to refine has no utility for the purpose at hand, since it is impossible to manifest a part that is unconnected. Therefore, he says: "in its own location" (*taddeśe*). This is the intended meaning: the single activity of the sense organ, having a connection with the location of the underlying substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that pervades [it], reaches as far as the location of the object.

Therefore, the refinement (saṃskāra) will be beneficial to all precisely where it is located; just as a refinement applied to the feet will be beneficial even to the eye, though it is situated at a distance.

Therefore, it is not an absolute rule that the sense organ functions only at the location of its substrate because of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) there; thus he says, "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). He establishes the apprehension of [objects] beyond the immediate vicinity with the passage ending in "it would be external" (*bahiḥ syāt*). For the functioning [of the sense organ], being postulated on the strength of the observation of its effects, remains in accordance with those effects.

Thus it has been said. Therefore, because one perceives objects with a magnitude greater than that of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the [visual] faculty will be conceived as having a broad tip (*pṛthvagra*). And because one perceives them without interval, it is continuous (*santata*). Consequently, whatever degree of width (*pārthava*) exists in the portion of the activity (*vṛtti*) in a given place, a corresponding object—such as a mountain—is perceived as being larger than its substratum. Although the activity itself is formless (*amūrta*), its [perceived size] is adventitious (*aupādhika*).

The designation of parts is like that of space. Whatever is manifested by it receives the designation of parts only through its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Nor should it be asked: "If the function (*vṛtti*) manifests the object as having the nature of sound (*gatvārtha*), why does it not manifest entities located at an extremely great distance? For only to such a distance as the effect is perceived does [the function] extend.
He says—“even at a distance”—to show that this should be understood as having an excessive range of vision, since it is said that "this one creeps along."
Now, even if objects are indeed manifested by the functioning of the senses, that function must then have gone out [from the body]; why then do objects not appear even to one whose eyes are closed?

To this he says: "Like the light of a lamp. It is not necessarily the case that there is a functioning of the sense for one whose eyes are closed; rather, because its effect is absent, it is inferred to have perished—just as the light of a lamp perishes when the lamp is extinguished—even for one who is closing his eyes. // 49
Or let there be a functioning even when the substratum is covered; nevertheless, that [functioning], supported by the effort of the self, brings the object to the self.

For, since the self’s effort is interrupted when the substratum is covered, an object not brought forth by that [functioning] which is unsupported by effort is not experienced by the self; thus he says: "adhiṣṭhāna... (50).

He now establishes the cognition of disjunction—stating "it is disjoined" (*vicchinna*). Although the self (*ātman*) is all-pervading (*vibhu*), the body is the locus of all enjoyments acquired through the karma of a previous birth; with respect to that [body], there arises the cognition of disjunction. However, since there is no disjunction from the body in the case of the sense-organ (*kāyendriya*), a cognition of non-disjunction is appropriate. But as for sound, the cognition of a disjunction exceeding [the reality] is merely an error; so what is the point of establishing that? Thus:

For indeed, sound is manifested by the auditory organ in its own location alone; how then could there be any spatial separation of it? And how could there be increase or decrease for that which is all-pervading and formless? To this he says: "But in the case of sound... This, however, has been stated according to his own view. According to the Sāṅkhya view, the function (*vṛtti*) of the auditory organ actually goes to the location of the sound. In that case, the perception of spatial separation must be explained solely with reference to the body.
And we shall explain its impossibility in the section concerning sound. [647] No. [648] Not so. [649] Self. (KA)
Regarding the word "śabda" (KA):

this position of the movement of the function (*vṛttigamana*), established as a tenet of the Sāṅkhya school, was mentioned by the author of the *Vārttika* merely because it shares the commonality of reaching [the object], but it was not his own intended view. For no such thing as the "function of the sense-organ" (*indriyavṛtti*) is apprehended through any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: the followers of Kapila maintain that the sense-organs are derived from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkārika*). As they say: [text continues]
"The group of eleven [senses] proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (transformative) *ahaṅkāra* as *sāttvika*.
Now, what is this *ahaṅkāra*? If it is that which illuminates the self (*ātman*), then it is knowledge (*jñāna*);
how then can it be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of the sense organs? Knowledge is internal and has the self as its substrate.

How could the external sense organs be produced by that [ego]? Now, if it is thought that the ego is a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*), that is not so, because there is a lack of valid proof (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even as a distinct principle, that [ego] is asserted by the followers of Kapila to be all-pervasive (*vibhu*). Consequently, the sense organs, being composed of that, would also have to be all-pervasive. And the functioning (*vṛtti*) of all-pervasive entities is not logically possible. Functioning...

[The opponent claims: "There is an 'going forth' (*nirgamana*), but that is not possible for all-pervading (*vibhu*) things. It might be thought: we do not say that the all-pervading sense organs go forth; what then? It is their function (*vṛtti*) based upon them [that goes]. [Reply: It must be stated what this function is. If it is the capacity of the ear and so on to grasp sound and so on, then how could that formless power (*śakti*) go? Moreover, there are three internal organs: the Great One (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*)."

Thus the followers of Kapila maintain. Furthermore, it is not logically tenable that an instrument (*karaṇa*) should be the material cause (*prakṛti*) of other instruments, because it is itself an instrument, just like the mind (*manas*). Therefore, the sense organs do not originate from the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*). Nor is there any valid evidence for the hypothesis that their activity (*vṛtti*), being immaterial, reaches its object. Likewise, in the section concerning sound (*śabdādhikaraṇa*), he will state the refutation of the movement of the activity in the context of the position that the ear travels [to the object].
Therefore, it must be stated that the sense organs are indeed material (*bhautika*) and function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakārin*).

What, then, is the proof for the material nature of the sense organs? It is conformity with what is observed. For instance, it is observed that only external elements possess the capacity to manifest color and other qualities as appropriate; for example, light manifests color.

By means of a lamp [color is manifested]. Taste [is manifested] by water. Even in dry substances, although taste exists, it is not perceived as clearly as it is in moist ones. Yet, it is not that taste is absent in dry things, because it persists as long as the substance exists. Therefore, taste is manifested by water. And there is a certain substance consisting of earth...
An expresser of fragrance is observed, such as neem bark for the fragrance of sandalwood; for when sandalwood is sprinkled with its decoction, its fragrance is manifested more clearly.
Nor is this [fragrance] manifested by water alone, because water by itself lacks the power of manifestation. Furthermore, the manifestation of external touch is perceived through the wind.

Just as in the winter and early spring, when the water particles spread through the atmosphere are so subtle that they are imperceptible, yet their cold touch is perceived in the wind—and this [coldness] does not belong to the wind itself, because the touch of the wind is neither hot nor cold—therefore, the eye, which manifests visible form, is composed of fire (*taijasa*); the tongue, which manifests taste, is composed of water (*āpya*); and the nose, which manifests odor, is composed of earth (*pārthiva*).

The tactile faculty is composed of air for the perception of touch. Now, what is the nature of the auditory faculty? It too is elemental, because it is a sense faculty. What, then, is its constituent element? We say it is space (*ākāśa*). For instance, the effect of all elements is twofold: the body and the sense faculty. Since space also assists the body by providing room, it is likewise [an element].

There is a relationship of cause and effect. Therefore, that [space] must also have the sense organ as its effect. In this regard, since the other elements serve as the material causes (*prakṛti*) for the other sense organs, it is determined that space alone is the material cause of the auditory organ. Furthermore, the other elements manifest only their own respective qualities;
and sound is not a quality belonging to them.

Because it is a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*). Therefore, it is logical that space alone is its manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*). In this way, a hypothesis is made that follows what is observed. For there exist portions of the elements such as earth (*pṛthivyādi*) within bodies, which possess the established power to manifest odor and so forth externally; thus, it is logical to infer that those very [elements] existing within the body are the manifestors. And so, in this manner...
The [quality of] reaching [the object] (*prāpti*) is also desired [as a condition for perception].

For the skin, nose, and tongue possess the property of acting by reaching the object as a matter of course. As for the ear, too, it manifests the all-pervading sound right at its own location—that is, the space delimited by the ear-cavity which is sustained by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).

It is precisely its mode of reaching [the object] (*prāpyakāritva*). For it is entirely logical that the eye—being of the nature of light (*tejas*) and thus possessing the inherent quality of radiating—goes forth and reaches the location of the object. Furthermore, because its form (*rūpa*) is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*), there is no perception of its own form. For this very reason, the conceptualization of the fire-element of the eye as having a broad tip and so forth is made in accordance with the observation of its effects.

Because it possesses corporeality, [the theory of contact] is logically tenable. Furthermore, it must be demonstrated that the connection between the sense organ and its object is "contact" (prāpti), which is accompanied by a capacity (yogyatā) corresponding to the observation of the effect in every case. Therefore, no over-extension (atiprasakti) need be alleged, as he will state:
"Contact is indeed mere reaching. Thus, it is established that the sense organs are material (bhautika) and function by reaching their objects (prāpyakārīṇi). // 51 //

[650] Thus, the terms *sat-samprayoga* and so forth have been explained. Hereafter, we shall follow the syntactical connection of the words. In this context, it is indeed said that the "contact" (*samprayoga*) of a person with the sense-faculties is the "arising of cognition" (*buddhi-janman*).
But that is incorrect.
Because for the omnipresent Puruṣa, since his conjunction with all states of being is invariable, it would be pointless to employ qualifiers [such as "possessing eyes"].
Furthermore, the sense organs, being composed of material elements, are insentient. For all people in the world and the investigators alike consider that intellect (*buddhi*) is indeed consciousness;
they do not, however, consider that intellect is the operation of the sense organs. For the Sāṅkhyas apply the term "intellect" to the functioning of the sense organs.
They apply [these terms] figuratively; in that case, for them, it is merely a verbal designation. Therefore, it must be stated here what kind of word-connection (*padānvaya*) exists in this context;

hence he says: "the words *puruṣa* and *indriya*. This is the intended meaning: what is there to be said here? The author of the Bhāṣya has explained the words *puruṣa* and *indriya* by means of an interrupted construction (*vyavahitakalpanā*), since he says this while the connection between the sense organ and its object is actually present.

"That cognition which arises for a person (puruṣa) is perception. But who is this "person" with whom the arising of cognition is connected? To this he says: "the person. There is no intention here [to define the person], because the aphorism is devoted to another purpose. In the ultimate sense, however, the "person" intended here is the Self (ātman), which will be established in the doctrine of the Self. It is not the body, because, being composed of the elements, it is insentient. // 52 //

But even so, that which the Mīmāṃsakas consider to be the eternal self would not be established; for since it would undergo modification upon the arising of cognition, it would follow that it is impermanent, like a hide. Alternatively, if it were not modified by the arising of cognition, it would follow that it is not a knower, remaining as it was in its prior state. To this he says: "Modification. For they think thus: a thing is not destroyed merely by undergoing some modification.

Because of the recognition of that [same person]. This will be stated by the Commentator precisely within the doctrine of the self (ātmavāda). Therefore, what has been poorly stated by others is refuted: "If there is a modification of the person upon the arising of cognition, then there is impermanence; if, on the other hand, this self is unmodified, it is not logical that it be the cognizer."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the arising of cognition (*buddhi*) is called perception (*pratyakṣa*). What is the meaning of this? Is the arising of cognition something distinct from cognition, or non-distinct?

If it is distinct, it must be stated what kind of thing it is. Furthermore, the nature of "arising" has not been explained according to our own school’s position. If "arising" is defined—as the Vaiśeṣikas say—as inherence (*samavāya*) in its own cause, then because that [inherence] is eternal, it would not depend on the sense organs; consequently, it would be untenable for it to be denoted by the term "perception. On the other hand, if it is non-distinct, the fault is simply tautology.

Therefore, he says: "the birth of cognition" (*buddhijanma*). This is the meaning: this is not a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning "the birth of cognition"; rather, it is a descriptive compound (*karmadhāraya*) consisting of "cognition" (*buddhi*) and "birth" (*janman*). Furthermore, the word *janman* ends in the suffix *manin* used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).
Thus, it refers to cognition as that which is being born (*jāyamānā buddhiḥ*).

It is thus stated that [inherence] is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, we do not describe it as being eternal or absolutely distinct [from its relata], as the Vaiśeṣikas and others do. Rather, it is said that the very specific state of the cause is itself the arising of the effect. This [inherence] is not entirely separate from the effect and the cause. Therefore, what is the use of pointing out further faults? // 53 //

He states the purpose for employing the qualification "being born" (*jāyamāna*) as follows: "The operation (*vyāpāra*). Other causal factors (*kāraka*) are observed to persist for some time after being produced before engaging in their own effects. Therefore, the author of the Sūtra has made the intention to express "birth" (*janman*) so that [the definition] may not apply to cognition (*buddhi*) when it is considered a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
But what is faulty about [the cognition] sharing the same nature as other causal factors?

To this he says: "For not... The intended meaning is this: nothing is faulty. However, unlike the sense organs and so forth, once it has arisen, the cognition does not remain even for a single moment. Therefore, how could it proceed by remaining [stable] in that very manner?
It does not remain indifferent merely after having been born, but even while being born, it does not remain indifferent. For it arises only by manifesting its own object as it is produced;
thus, it does not wait for another moment. Indeed, no form of cognition is perceived other than the manifestation of the object.

Thus he says: "It is born. By demonstrating its dissimilarity to other types of causal factors (*kāraka*), the proponent of eternal cognition is refuted here, and the non-permanent nature of cognition is stated. In this regard, the reason is as follows: since this [cognition] possesses origination, it must necessarily be subject to destruction.
Furthermore, destruction cannot occur without a cause.

Precisely because it possesses an origin. Nor is a blow or the like a cause for its destruction, since it is formless (*amūrta*). Therefore, it is destroyed either by another cognition or by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [cognition]. And both of these are accomplished simultaneously. For there exists [the causal complex] consisting of the sense faculties and so forth.

The causal complex is unimpeded. Why then does it not produce another cognition? Furthermore, since the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of memory is produced by this very [cognition] as soon as it arises, it is logical that the destruction of the intellect is immediate, due to its opposition to its own effect—just like an action (*karman*). Moreover, there is no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the intellect such that "it is that very same one. Nor [can it be established] merely from the non-apprehension of difference.

The proof of [the mind's] unity is as follows: moreover, when a different object is perceived, the destruction of the cognition is clearly immediate; and thus, even when a single established object is being perceived, its inference [of destruction] occurs in exactly the same way. Furthermore, in that case as well, the cognition ceases when the object is obstructed; this would be impossible if it were to endure for a long time. For if it were so, perceptual cognition would continue with respect to an obstructed jar. But this is not the case; rather, memory is observed later. That [memory] would be impossible if it were pervaded by perceptual cognition.

It could not be so, because there is a contradiction between the perceptible and the imperceptible when they occupy the same object at the same time. It might be argued that this indistinct apprehension occurs due to the non-duration [of the cognition], like the indistinct apprehension of form during a flash of lightning. This is not so, because it would imply an admission of the very thing to be denied. If you think that because the light [of cognition] is fleeting, it does not persist for long after the intellect [has arisen], as in the case of a flash of lightning—
"Objects would not be manifested clearly;

therefore, cognition is not something that perishes very rapidly. This is not so, because you are conceding the very thing you intend to deny. For, by asserting that cognition—which produces an indistinct awareness from the flash of lightning—perishes as soon as it arises, you are in fact conceding its non-rapid destruction, which is precisely what you seek to refute. Furthermore...

Furthermore, when specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are not apprehended, the apprehension of the mere universal (*sāmānyamātra*) is what constitutes "indistinct apprehension" (*avyaktagrahaṇa*). However, there is nothing whatsoever that is indistinct within its own sphere of operation, because apprehensions conform to the nature of their objects. Moreover, the non-apprehension of specific qualities occurs solely due to the absence of the causes for such apprehension, and not because of instability in the cognition (*buddhi*). This is true even in the case of a flash of lightning, as long as it is extremely rapid in its destruction.
That which is made an object by the cognition is indeed manifest. However, the particulars therein remain ungrasped due to the absence of a cause for their apprehension;

they are not, however, determined as "unmanifest. For it is impossible for something already grasped to be called "unmanifest"; thus, even if cognitions are not stable, there is no consequence of an unmanifest apprehension. And this is the intention [of the author] regarding those who maintain the existence of an eternal intellect, as discussed in the *Śabdādhikaraṇa*.
The author of the Bhāṣya will state this. // 55 //
[651] It would be [652] however [653] in the case of a vowel following *ud*.
[654] Thus.

[655] Viśeṣya: Is it not the case that what is called a "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is a specific kind of causal factor (*kāraka*)? And a causal factor does not exist without performing an action. If, however, the intellect (*buddhi*), having been produced, does not exert itself, [it cannot be a means of valid cognition].
How is it that this [cognition] is designated by the two terms "agent" (*kāraka*) and "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), both of which are general and specific words?
To this he says: "By that. It is true that there can be no status as an agent without a connection to an operation (*vyāpāra*). However, the very arising (*janma*) of the cognition is its operation.

Because no other operation is possible, that very [cognition] is metaphorically designated as "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) by virtue of the speaker's intention. For its status as a means of valid cognition arises through its birth.

Thus, by that same action, the term "instrument" (kāraka) and the term "means of valid cognition"—the general and the specific—are established as designations. By the word "and" (ca), the meaning is "and it is a means of valid cognition. // 56 //

And this position that [cognition] is non-different from its birth was described by the Commentator himself when he said, "the cognition which is born"; thus he says, "and 'birth'. He also states another purpose for employing the qualification "in the state of being born": "and that. If it were merely stated that "cognition is the means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇa*), some might imagine that even a cognition that has already occurred or one yet to occur is the means of valid knowledge, as was explained in the case of the qualification "existent" (*sat*). Therefore, in order to dispel that doubt, the qualification "being born" is employed; [otherwise], there would be the inclusion of pastness, futurity, and so forth.
The fifth case ending is used in the sense of "causing that to fall" (tyāpādane). // 57 //
[656] Not so.
[657] Or let it be that birth (*janman*) is indeed something distinct, consisting in the inherence (*samavāya*) of the effect in its own cause, as established in the Vaiśeṣika system.

Nevertheless, nothing is thereby impaired; thus he says: "But when... Indeed, although that [Self] is eternal, its manifestation is dependent upon the sense organs; therefore, it requires perception. // 58 //

In this regard, the author of the Bhāṣya has shown the lack of restriction regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by stating, "either the cognition or the birth [of the cognition]," and so forth. Regarding that, he states the intended meaning: "But the relationship between the means of valid cognition and its fruit... This is the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra: this single sūtra is not capable of performing both functions—that is, establishing what the means of valid cognition is and simultaneously prescribing the state of being non-causal (*animittatā*). For in that case, the sentence would be split. Therefore, in this context, it is merely the state of being non-causal that is intended.

What is to be established is [the fact that the object] is apprehended while existing. As for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), however, it will be one among [the group] beginning with cognition (*buddhi*), according to the speaker's intention. For the means of valid cognition is an instrument (*karaṇa*), and an instrument is that which is the most effective means of accomplishment (*sādhakatama*).

And the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) depends upon the speaker’s intention. Therefore, whatever is intended as being proximate to the result in relation to the external object will be the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and what follows that may be designated as the "result" by virtue of the intention to emphasize its importance. // 59 //

He shows precisely this conceptualization with the words "or else" (*yadvā*). Since knowledge does not arise when the sense organ is absent, that [organ] itself is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, even if the sense organ exists, it does not produce knowledge if it is not in contact with the object; therefore, its contact with the object (*arthasaṅgati*) is the means of valid cognition.

Moreover, even if the sense organ is connected with the object, it is not a means of valid cognition if it is not presided over by the mind (*manas*); thus, its conjunction with the mind (*manassaṃyoga*) [is the means of valid cognition].

It is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since knowledge does not arise even when there is a contact between the self, the mind, and a real object, that [contact] is the means of valid cognition.

Alternatively, since knowledge is not produced even if any one of all [the factors] is absent, the contact as a whole is the means of valid cognition. Or rather, it should be construed as "the contact of the mind with the self. // 60 //

He shows the result (*phala*) in these cases of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "then" (*tadā*). The meaning is that, in the view where the sense organs and so forth are the *pramāṇa*, knowledge (*jñāna*) is the result. Now, an objection: if the sense organs and so forth are the *pramāṇa*, then knowledge must necessarily be produced by them at all times. But that is not the case;

for indeed, one whose eyes are covered still possesses the visual organ, yet it does not cause [knowledge] to be known. If it is argued that it causes what is in contact [with it] to be known, [the response follows:]

No, because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Indeed, the visual light of this [organ] comes into contact with various objects, yet it causes only some of them to be known. Therefore, due to this deviation, the sense organ and so forth are not the cause for the arising of cognition;

thus he says: "In that case. We have already stated that the word *prayoga* signifies an operation (*vyāpāra*), and that operation is to be inferred from its result (*phala*). Consequently, since they possess an operation precisely where the result is perceived, they possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in those very instances.
Thus, since no result arises in the absence of an operation, there is no over-extension [of the definition]; so he says: "The operation... (verse 61).

Granted, the avoidance of over-extension may be achieved under the view that the word *prayoga* denotes an activity (*vyāpāra*). However, if it denotes "attainment" (*prāpti*), the over-extension is difficult to avoid. For the ocular light is indeed in contact with various objects, yet it does not make all of them known; rather, it makes only some known at certain times. Furthermore, what is this "attainment"? If it is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), [then the same problem remains].

And since that [contact] would consist of the substance alone, there would be no cognition of color (rūpa). If it is argued that contact exists even through that [substance] by way of inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya), then that [same relation] is common to taste and so forth as well; thus, those too would be perceived by the eye. This addresses what has been stated by others regarding the position that conjunction with the sense organ is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—namely, that there would be a perception of objects consisting of all [qualities]: "And not... (na ca) // 62 //

Furthermore, what is the intention of one who says that there is no connection whatsoever? If [the opponent means] that conjunction with the qualities is not possible in the case of taste and so forth, then it would likewise not exist for color either, since there is no difference in their being qualities (*guṇatva*). Moreover, it has already been stated that "inherence in that which is conjoined" (*saṃyukta-samavāya*) is the same for all [qualities].
Therefore, he says:

"attainment" (*prāpti*). This is the intended meaning: this fault would arise if the relation between the sense organ and its object were taken as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in the sense of mere attainment alone. However, it is [the relation] accompanied by fitness (*yogyatā*). And fitness is to be inferred from the observation of the effect.
Therefore, the capacity for contact with that [object] belongs only to that which is experienced immediately after contact with a particular sense organ, and not to anything else,

due to the absence of evidence. For this very reason, why is it not accepted that the undesirable consequence of perceiving subtle forms and so forth— which one does not wish to grasp— is also to be avoided?

Therefore he says: "Let it not be so. This is the intended meaning: for even one who, accepting cognition as the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), maintains that contact with an existing object (*satsamprayoga*) is the cause of the means of valid knowledge rather than the means itself—by him too, lest there be the determination of color by the skin due to the lack of distinction in "reaching" (*prāpti*), mere reaching must not be accepted as the relation. // 63 //
