But if it is maintained that, in the production of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), "attainment" (*prāpti*) accompanied by "capacity" (*yogyatā*) is required, then the same could be said regarding the production of the result (*phala*); thus, since the avoidance of the resulting fault is equal in both cases, neither party should be subject to censure. With this in mind, he says: "Just as... For the contact of the eye and other [senses] with their respective objects, such as color-form (*rūpa*), is indeed restricted to a specific [instance].
"Because of its suitability" means: because it is suitable for the observation of the effect in that very [place]. // 64 //

Thus far, the avoidance of the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) has been stated regarding the position that the contact between the sense-organ and the object is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Now, he addresses the objection: "How is conjunction (yoga), which depends on two [factors], designated by the sense-organ alone?"—with the words "of conjunction" (yogasya).
The meaning of this is: it is not an unprecedented thing that even when connected with many, something is designated by one alone.
For it is indeed the case that the mother of Ḍittha and Ḍavittha is designated as "Ḍittha’s mother. He says: "Let the designation be based on either one;
however, in this case, the designation is observed to be by means of the sense-organ (*akṣa*) alone and not by the object (*artha*). But the mother is sometimes designated even by means of Ḍavittha;
therefore he says: 'Or rather' (*athavā*). For a designation occurs by means of what is unique [to the subject].

The sense organ is the specific cause of cognition, because the organs are produced solely for that purpose. The object, however, is common to other effects; therefore, it is not the basis for the designation [of the cognition]. // 65 //

In this regard, under the view that the contact between the sense faculty and its object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is indeed no difference in the object (*viṣaya*) between the means of cognition and its result, because the contact has the object as its locus and the cognition likewise has that same object. One might then raise the objection: "Under the view that the contact between the self and the mind is the means of valid cognition, however, there would be a difference in the object; for that [contact] has the self and the mind as its locus, whereas the cognition has the external object as its object. Thus he suspects.

Up to the point where it says "But in the case of conjunction" [658], ending with "of the two results," he provides the rebuttal: "No. He states the reason: "For in the object... The meaning of this is as follows: although the connection between the self and the mind does not reside in the object, nevertheless, it operates upon the object. Since cognition also arises having that very object as its domain, there is identity of object by virtue of their operation. // 66 //
[658] Thus (GA).

Furthermore, if the basis (*āśraya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) are intended [as the two factors], then since both reside within the self (*ātman*), they are all the more identical in their object; thus he says: "But even so... (verse 67).

"This very conjunction of the self and the mind, being proximate to the arising of knowledge, is distinguished from other causal factors; therefore, this alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," he says: "Because it is the most excellent instrument" (sūtra 68). Even in the view that all conjunctions are the means of valid cognition, one should keep in mind the resolution of all the previously mentioned objections; thus he says: "The means of valid cognition. Furthermore, even in the view that the sense organ is the means of valid cognition, because of its attainment of the object and because the knowledge has that [object] as its domain...
He states clearly that there is equality regarding the object: "the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa). // 69 //

Thus far, the identity of object between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) has been explained under the view that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and so forth constitute the means of valid cognition. Now, it must be shown that this is exactly the same even under the view that cognition (*jñāna*) constitutes the means of valid cognition; thus he says: "The means of valid cognition... {1, 235}. All determinate cognitions (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) are preceded by the cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa-jñāna*), as in: "This is a man with a staff," "This is a cow," "This is white," "This is walking," "This is Ḍittha. Therefore, in this case, the cognition of the qualifier...

The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is the cognition of the qualificandum, and the result (phala) is the same. This is because the cognition of the qualifier exists for the sake of establishing the cognition of the qualificandum.
In that case as well, there is identity of object by virtue of the operation. // 70 //

But when it is the qualifier itself that is to be understood and desired to be known, then what is the distinction between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), or how can there be identity of object? To this he says: "But in the case of the qualifier. The intention here is as follows: even in that case...

Two cognitions are perceived. For among them, the cognition of mere observation (ālocanājñāna) produces a determination regarding the qualifier; and because it is for the sake of that [determination], they share the same object—this is the distinction. // 71 //
"In that case, what is the distinction [of *viveka*] if it culminates merely in the knowledge of initial perception (*ālocanājñāna*)?

To this he says: 'ascertainment' (*niścaya*). The intention is as follows: even in the knowledge of initial perception, there certainly exists another form of knowledge—consisting of recognition such as 'this is that,' or consisting of ascertainment such as 'it is of this kind'—which is devoid of the association with words."
Just as in the case of animals or others who do not understand words, they apprehend a unique object devoid of any expressive term.

Therefore, because two types of cognition are demonstrated, there is indeed a distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*). However, when no ascertainment arises regarding the object that has been perceived, then it lacks the status of a means of valid cognition at all; thus he says: "This [is not so]," because the status of being a means of valid cognition consists in having the determination of the object as its result.
And because that [cause] does not exist at that time. // 72 //

Now, what is the status regarding the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*)? It cannot be non-valid, for that would lead to an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in all cases. Nor can its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be established when there is no fruit (*phala*). If it is maintained that this very [cognition] is both the means of valid cognition and the fruit—thus possessing a dual nature—then let there likewise be a dual nature even in the case of the cognition of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth.

What is the use of proposing this distinction? This is indeed appropriate. For in this way, the absolute proximity between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is maintained, and that alone is logically consistent. Indeed, it is never observed that the instrument of proof (*sādhana*) resides in one place while the object to be proven (*sādhya*) resides in another; for when the axe has reached the *khadira* tree, the cutting does not occur in the *palāśa* tree.
Therefore, he says: "abandonment, etc. The intention is as follows: regarding this identity of the means of valid cognition and its result due to an excessive thirst for proximity—

We shall refute that very point immediately thereafter. As for the claim that no other fruit of the cognition of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is observed, that is not so; for even in that case, there exists a fruit such as avoidance (*hāna*) occurring at a subsequent time. Now, if you think that the fruit of a cognition is simply [another] cognition, and thus here too the cognition of avoidance and so forth will be the fruit; or if you think that the cognition of avoidance and so forth is not the fruit because it is mediated by the recollection of assistance (*upakāra*) and the like—what do you consider?
"In that case, let this very recollection of benefit and so forth be the result"; thus he says: "Benefit and so forth" (upakārādi). // 73 //

But as for the claim that the identity of the means of knowledge and its result is maintained by one who desires the identity of their objects—that is both unconventional and illogical—as he says: "The object... (verse 74).

As for what was said—that when the axe rests upon the *khadira* wood, no cutting is seen in the *palāśa* wood—is this indeed what is observed: that there is identity between the axe and the act of cutting? Therefore, wherever the instrument operates, there the result is produced;
and this has already been established previously.
But with the intention that the means itself is not the result, he says: "in cutting," etc. (75).

If, however, it is argued: "A difference in objects between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is not observed, and they are one and the same; therefore, since one or the other must be accepted, we prefer the non-difference of the object," that is not so. For this can be said by the opponent as well. Thus, he says with derision: "Of yours" (*bhavataḥ*). 76. GA. 2.659. Do. dṛ. (GA)

If, however, it is argued: "The status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) for knowledge itself, which is the result, is somehow imagined as figurative (aupacārika), but not as ultimate (pāramārthika). For it is impossible for a single entity to possess two forms in an ultimate sense. Therefore, by relying on that figurative instrumentality, we shall establish both [the means and the result]. If that is so, then the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its result (phala) would indeed be distinct.
"Why is it not assumed that there is some kind of identity between the object [of cognition] and the cognition itself?

If that were the case, both would be ultimately real. To this he replies: "By being the instrument," and so forth. That aforementioned "some kind of identity between the object" has already been explained. The phrase "by others" refers to the Buddhists, for the word "other" (para) is used here with respect to one's own self (svātman). // 77 //

Now he concludes the current discussion on the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) with the words "pariccheda" (delimitation). When the result is the delimitation of an object, the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*), etc., is considered the means of valid cognition because it is intended as the immediate antecedent. And when cognition itself is the means of valid cognition, the prior cognition such as indeterminate perception (*ālocana*) is the means of valid cognition, while the subsequent cognition of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), etc., is the result; such is the meaning of this section. And all of this is thus.
It should be understood that this was stated by relying on the position that [the text] is a restatement of what is already established (saty-anuvādatva). // 78 //
But if it is argued: "This is not a figurative instrumentality;

rather, cognition is a single entity possessing two forms—namely, self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) and the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*). In this regard, self-cognition is the result (*phala*), and the form of the object is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As they have said:
The very form of the object is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for by it the object is measured;
self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the fruit (*phala*) here, for the ascertainment of the object has that [self-awareness] as its nature.

Thus [it is said]. Having set forth the Sautrāntika position—that the objective form is not intrinsic to consciousness itself, which is inherently formless, but is imparted solely by the object—he refutes it with the words "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvitti*). A cognition capable of experiencing an external object such as "this is blue" is not capable of experiencing its own nature.

"We shall explain in the section on the Vijñānavāda that there is a contradiction of action upon itself. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that is not so, because there is no proof (*pramāṇa*).
It is not our proof that the knowledge is produced by the object through the name "form of the object."

Because the diversity of cognitions dependent upon that [object] would otherwise be untenable. However, if this objective form resides solely within the object, then in that case, the fact that the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) and its result have different objects becomes unavoidable; thus he says: "In the means of knowledge... (79).

[660] We have no other view: cognition, which is by nature clear, grasps itself by itself as having a manifold form such as blue, which has been superimposed by beginningless habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Of this [cognition], its own form is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the form of the object is the object of cognition (*prameya*).
"Self-awareness is the fruit. As they say:

"That which appears is the object of cognition; the means of cognition and its fruit, moreover, are the form of the grasper and self-awareness. Therefore, these three are not made separate from one another."
Thus [it is said]. Having introduced this point, he refutes it with the words "and its own form" (*svākāra*). It has already been stated that self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is what is to be negated.
Furthermore, this "own form" which is postulated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not perceived as anything other than self-awareness.

The very nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatā*) is the own form of knowledge. And since that is precisely the result (*phala*), what else could there be that constitutes the means of valid cognition?

The meaning is that the form of the object, being established by a cognition whose form is uncontradicted as being external, cannot possibly experience an internal occurrence; thus, even in this way, it is impossible to establish that they have the same object. // 80 //

[661] Or let it be that the self-aspect (*svākāra*) is distinct from self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*). Is that [aspect] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is determined (*paricchinna*), or because it is undetermined?
First of all, it cannot be undetermined, because what is undetermined cannot coherently exist as a reality. Furthermore, determination cannot belong to that very same thing by itself.

He says "of its own form" (*svākārasya*) because there would be the consequence of an infinity of forms if one were to postulate ever-new forms. He says "and not" (*na ca*) because the existence of an unperceived own-form is not established. This has indeed been stated by us previously, looking toward what follows. Furthermore, this form of the object which is imagined to be non-different from cognition and [thus] the apprehended (*grāhya*), [is untenable].

Since that [object] also cannot be grasped by cognition due to the contradiction of a thing acting upon itself, and because no other grasper is perceived, it would follow that it does not exist; with this intention, he says: "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). Thus, in the position of the opponent, there is indeed only a triad consisting of the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the result.
It has been shown that [the object] is being destroyed. // 82 //

But surely, even on your own position, one must admit that in the direct perceptions of pleasure and so forth, self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) alone is the result, because pleasure and the like cannot exist apart from cognition. These too have causes identical to those of cognition; for cognition arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) aided by latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Pleasure and the like are likewise produced from cognitions of form and so forth, aided by latent impressions.
Therefore, that too is indeed cognition, because a difference in effect is impossible when there is no difference in cause. As they have said:
"Entities possessing such-and-such a nature are born from causes possessing such-and-such a nature."
Is that pleasure and so forth ignorance, since it is produced from causes non-different from those of consciousness?
[662] Regarding the word "ka" (GA): since there is no other object to be grasped when cognitions exist in this manner, they possess the nature of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) alone;
therefore, he says, "and of the mind. This is the intended meaning: even the cognitions of pleasure and so forth do not follow the rule of being [perceived by] another cognition.

They pass away. Even those [objects], when conjoined with the internal organ—the mind as a sense-organ—are apprehended by the Self as being included within its own qualities. Therefore, even in that case, the divisions of the object (*meya*), the means of knowledge (*māna*), and the knower (*miti*) are distinct. As for what was stated regarding "the nature of cognition" (*jñānatva*) by virtue of being the cause of cognition:
in that regard, is cognition the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*) of pleasure, or rather the instrumental cause (*nimitta*)? It cannot be the former alternative.

Because those [faculties] inhere in the self just as cognition does, their status as instrumental causes (nimittatva) in all purposeful activities is no different from that of cognition; consequently, it would follow that they too possess the nature of cognition. Therefore, there is nothing whatsoever that is self-cognizing. As for what has been stated by others—that the self-cognition of all minds and mental factors is perception—[that is untenable].
That has been answered. // 83 //
But surely, you have presented this entire elaboration of the means and results of valid cognition by accepting their definitions.

Therefore, it is also appropriate here to show the specific object [of each], just as others, having stated the definition of perception as "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," have shown that its object is the particular (svalakṣaṇa). To this, he says: "connected" (sambaddham).

Thus [it is said]. This is the intended meaning: let him indeed demonstrate an object for whom there is something to be excluded, such as the universal (*sāmānya*) for the Buddhist alone. For us, however, perception has as its object that which is connected and present.
Since neither the universal nor the particular is to be excluded, what is the purpose of specifying the object? // 84 //

[663] (KA) But surely, the author of the Bhāṣya has stated here: "Perception is not the means [of knowing dharma], for it is characterized in such a way. Therefore, let that which is characterized by such a definition be called "not a means" (animitta).

Anticipating the objection as to why that which is characterized by the Buddhists and others does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*nimitta*), he says: "the definition" (*lakṣaṇam*). He thinks as follows: if even that which is defined by the criteria of the Buddhists and others is worldly perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*), then it necessarily apprehends what is presently existing (*vidyamānopalambhana*). If it were not so, it would not be perception at all; thus, it is established that everything [defined by them] is not a valid means of knowledge. // 85 //
And as for those Buddhists who maintain that perception is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), for them it is all the more impossible for perception to be a means of knowing *dharma*;

thus he says: "non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpaka*). He states the reason for this here: "the relation between the goal and the means" (*sādhyasādhana*). *Dharma* is precisely the relationship between the goal and the means, such as heaven and sacrifice;
this cannot be grasped without conceptualization (*vikalpa*). // 86 //

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya, having established that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a means [of knowing Dharma], stated that inference (*anumāna*) and the other means are also not means because they are preceded by that [perception]. He raises an objection regarding the impossibility of their being preceded by that, asking: "How so?
To the question, "Why is it not so?", he replies: "When... He thinks as follows: [Perception] arises solely from the capacity of the sense organs and their objects.

For perception is indeed cognition (*dhī*), and it is free from conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding name, genus, quality, substance, and action, which are projected by memory. Neither the sense organs nor the object are capable of remembering;

as they say: "The sense organ is not capable of performing so many operations, because it arises through the power of a present object. Therefore, it is not tenable that inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by such a [non-conceptual] perception. // 87 //
Now, one might ask: why is it that inference and the other means of knowledge do not have non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) as their antecedent?
To this, he says: "And not... The intention here is as follows: inference and the rest are preceded by conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) of the logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth.

It is not possible for them to obtain their very existence (*ātmalābha*) from non-conceptual perception alone. Furthermore, cognitions that are intermingled with conceptualization cannot be considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

This is untenable. Because the operation of the sense organ toward its object is interrupted by the recollection of the meanings of the qualifiers and the qualified that occurs in the interval, there is no evidence that the sense organ, having been engaged in the arising of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), is again engaged in the production of determinate perception (*savikalpaka*).

Since determinate perception—which arises immediately after the recollection of the qualifiers and so forth—occurs only when those [recollections] are present, it must have them as its cause. Furthermore, if that sense organ were again engaged in the production of determinate perception...

Furthermore, since that cause existed previously as well, why would it not produce conceptual cognitions (*savikalpakapratyaya*) all at once? Therefore, conceptual cognitions are not produced by the causal capacity of the sense-faculties and their objects; thus, they are not perception (*pratyakṣa*). If, however, something were considered perception merely because of the absence of sensory activity, [the following would ensue].

Even for one with eyes closed, conceptual construction would become perception. Furthermore, that which is non-conceptual perception does not involve conceptual construction of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth; thus, inference and the other means of knowledge cannot in any way be preceded by perception. As for analogy (*upamāna*), when a person living in the forest sees a *gavaya* and recalls a cow seen in the city, there occurs a grasping of similarity [between the two].
That too does not occur without conceptualization; such is the connection. // 88 //
[664] A cover; [665] memory like that of Yaśas; [666] this is to be seen. (GA) (KA)

Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also capable [of functioning] only with respect to objects that transcend the senses; it does not operate toward things such as the auditory organ (*śrotra*) which have never before been perceived by perception or by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). How then could it be preceded by perception? To this he says: "Presumption. In some cases, it operates even toward something previously perceived, provided it is qualified by a specific configuration (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*).
As it has been stated: "Just as for a person like Devadatta who perceives the absence from the house, there is the comprehension of his presence outside.

Now, let it be granted that presumption (*arthāpatti*) has supersensuous objects as its domain; however, that which proceeds upon perceiving something as logically untenable (*anupapadyamāna*) will be preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*). To this, he says: "It proceeds... [1]

And thus: even that which serves as the basis for the presumption (*arthāpatti*) of [the existence of] power (*śakti*) and so forth—namely, burning and the like—is not a basis for presumption as long as one has not deliberated: "How is it that this effect has arisen at some time without a cause? // 89 //

Moreover, in a case where the means of motion (gatisādhana) is inferred as the probandum (liṅgin) by inferring the motion of the sun through its arrival at another location, how can there be "having perception as its antecedent" (pratyakṣapūrvakatva)? To this he says: "And where... The connection is that the probans (liṅga) is the motion of the sun and so forth; however, the probandum (liṅgin), which is the means of motion, must be shown here.

Furthermore, if [inference and other means of knowledge] were preceded by perception, they would result in being invalid because they would apprehend what has already been apprehended; thus he says: "By perception... [and so on]. Now, one might object: "Perception is a valid means of knowledge at one time, while inference and the others will be valid means of knowledge at another time. To this he replies: "When by them... If perception does not operate at the time when inference and the other means are active, then that object is not within the range of the sense organ; how, then, could there be the state of being preceded by perception? And as for the time of the comprehension through perception, it has already been stated that [inference and the rest] are invalid because they apprehend what has already been apprehended.

Now, it might be argued: "We do not say that the object of inference and the other means of knowledge is grasped by perception itself—that is what constitutes being preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvakatva*). Rather, it is because one of the factors, such as the *liṅga* (the inferential mark), is first known through perception. He anticipates this objection with the words, "Now, for someone... For indeed, for every person as soon as they are born, there is first some perception, and thereafter inference and so forth; thus, its being preceded by that [perception] is analogous. He refutes even this with the words, "In that case... For here:

Furthermore, since this object will exist but does not exist at the time of cognition, it has been stated that its future state is the cause for its not being known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). That [reason] does not apply; such is the meaning. // 92 //

"Why should this not be so? To this he says: "The present [object]. He thinks as follows: it is for the sake of establishing that [dharma] is not cognizable by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that its perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) is denied; however, there is no purpose in denying it merely by way of perception alone. For even by that much, the thesis that "only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) [is the source of dharma]" remains unestablished. Therefore, if inference and the other means of knowledge were to operate only upon something already grasped by perception in some particular case...
Such is the dependence of inference and the other means of knowledge upon perception:

at that time, when an object is known by perception as being present in some respect, a property (*dharma*) that is not yet present is understood through inference; the same applies to other means of knowledge as well. Consequently, the fact that perception does not grasp [the property] because it is yet to come is irrelevant.

It would be so. If that "being preceded by perception" (tatpūrvakatva) consists in their functioning only with respect to the objects of perception, then they too do not function with respect to what is not an object of perception; thus, the fact that [Dharma] is not cognizable by other means of knowledge is established. And this confirms the thesis that "only the Vedic injunction" (codanā) [is the source]. The phrase "from a mark" (liṅgāt) is merely an illustration;
the meaning is "by those [means], namely inference and the rest. // 93 //
If [the opponent argues that] such "being preceded by that" (tatpūrvakatva) would be a subverter of what is desired, he says: "By perception," etc. (94).

Having thus refuted [the opponent's position] according to the opinion of others, he establishes [his own view] with the words "some [say]... To the question "What indeed is this?", he replies: "preceded by that" (*tatpūrva*). For he thinks as follows: it is not here that being preceded by that (*tatpūrvakatva*) is stated as the reason for the other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) not being the cause [of Dharma]; rather, once the fact that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not the cause has been established, there remains the possibility of validity for inference and the rest based on their being preceded by that [perception].
Thus, by this commentary, it has been stated that "that [object] does not exist at all. // 95 //

Not being satisfied here because no reason has been stated for the fact that inference and the other means of knowledge lack a basis [in perception], he states another solution: "By perception" (*pratyakṣeṇa*). This is the intended meaning: inference and the others have as their objects only those things perceived through direct perception. For instance, as long as fire has not been grasped, it is impossible to determine the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke by it; therefore, even upon seeing smoke, fire is not inferred at all. As long as [the fire] is not in the city...

As long as the cow is not determined through direct perception, even one who sees a gavaya in the forest cannot perform an analogy. Therefore, if dharma were also determined through direct perception,
it might at some point be inferred from the observation of a logical mark (liṅga) pervaded by it.

Or it might be compared [to something else]. However, it has been established that this [object] is never perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And this point was demonstrated by the author of the *Vārttika* when he employed the word "mark" (*liṅga*): for smoke does not become a mark of fire unless there is a perception of its pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor...

And there is no observation of pervasion when there is no cognition of fire. This should likewise be demonstrated in the case of analogy (*upamāna*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the term "similar" (*sadṛśa*) is included. // 96 //

Furthermore, that which was stated—that inference based on an inferred [reason] (*anumitānumāna*) is not preceded by perception—is also incorrect. For even in that case, as long as the relationship between the movement and its means is not apprehended through perception, inference does not proceed;

for the sign (*liṅga*), namely the sun's arrival at another location currently being observed, is the means for understanding the possessor of the sign (*liṅgin*), i.e., the movement. Thus he says: "Inference... (verse 97).

In every inference, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by a property (*dharma*), not the mere existence of a thing. However, in the case of inferring a property, it would follow that the mere existence of a property—that "the property exists"—is what is being inferred. And that is not tenable; thus he says: "And [if] existence... If, on the other hand, even here some single locus qualified by a property were to be inferred, [then the fault would not apply].

Anticipating the objection that this is incorrect because the qualification of that property (*dharma*) is unestablished, he says together with [the verse], "By means of the property" (*dharmeṇa*). // 98 //
He demonstrates, by means of a formal argument, that the state of not being inferable has been thus established: "Therefore," etc. (99).
He states the formal argument (*prayoga*) even regarding the fact that the property (*dharma*) is incomparable: "not being perceived," and so forth. For that which possesses similarity is similar;

and similarity consists in the persistence of commonality among the constituent parts (*avayava-sāmānya-anuvṛtti*) with respect to the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*). Now, the persistence of commonality is not possible for that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
To explain: its very uniqueness [precludes it].
It would not be so.

Thus, there is this single formal argument (*prayoga*): A phenomenon (*dharma*) is not comparable, because its similarity is unperceived, like that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*). Or likewise, it is neither inferred nor compared, because it is itself unperceived, like a sky-flower;
thus it should be inferred. // 100 //

He says: "Let it be granted that comparison and inference are not the means [of knowing Dharma]. However, since presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is generally seen to have as its object things beyond the senses, Dharma will be understood by that very means, which is produced by the observation of the diversity of the world. To this he replies with "But surely" (*nanu*). He demonstrates the very diversity of the world with the words "happy," etc. For [the world] is divided by the distinctions of happiness and suffering, through the differences such as being a lord or a pauper.

The world is perceived. Thus, this manifold variety of the world, being untenable in the absence of a cause, leads one to infer a cause; and that cause is merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). Now, it may be argued: "In the case of pleasure and pain, that which immediately precedes their manifestation is itself the cause. Since in those cases too, only something already perceived was present, what is the use of postulating an unperceived [cause]?"

Therefore, he says: "of what is seen. And even when that which is seen exists, [the effect] does not occur. Furthermore, for those who know causes, a cause is held to be one that is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). Therefore, the implication is that only the postulation of an unseen factor (*adṛṣṭa*) remains.

Not only does it not occur when the seen exists, it certainly occurs even when it does not exist. Whatever occurs when something else is absent does not have that as its cause, just as a jar does not have a hare's horn as its cause.
Thus he says: "the absence of that. He elaborates upon the very [charge of] deviation: "in the case of the equality of service and study. // 102 //
He refutes this very point with the words "it might be so. Once the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavāda*) has been refuted, it is possible to postulate the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*).
However, the doctrine of intrinsic nature cannot itself be refuted; for its necessity must be accepted in order to establish the diversity of the potency of karma.
Thus he says: "of the potency of karma. Indeed, for the sake of establishing the diversity of results, a distinction in the potencies of actions must necessarily be admitted.
This must be accepted; for in that case, it is not even possible to conceive of a cause other than intrinsic nature (svabhāva). // 103 //

Now, if it is maintained that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause in this case, then let that [intrinsic nature] alone suffice for the sake of the world's diversity. What is the use of the useless postulation of the power of karma? This is what he says: "And just as... (verse 104).

[667] For even that has been stated: "Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is something that does not depart, just as coldness and heat belong to water and fire respectively. [668] But in this case, one who was wealthy suddenly becomes poor; therefore, it is not tenable that this is due to intrinsic nature. Thus, it must be postulated that this is due to the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).

"Because of its destruction, the destruction of this [wealth] occurs. Let it be, then, that the establishment of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) is of an undetermined nature; what is the use of such excessive insistence? As for this distinction—that "this is the fruit of merit" and "this is the fruit of demerit"—it cannot be understood. Nor is there any reason why knowledge would be of any use in a matter that remains uncomprehended. To this he says: "Demerit" (verse 105).

[668] *Soḥ*. *i* (GA). He elaborates on this very point with the words "What indeed... It is not only that the distinction between the fruits of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) is not established; it is also not established what kind of specific action brings about the attainment of the fruits of merit, such as heaven, sons, and so forth.
He says that it is known [from the following]: "heaven, sons, and so forth. // 106 //

Nor should it be said that one need not know the distinction between action and its fruit, for there is at least the knowledge of the general cause; and since activity does not occur by that much alone, he says "iti" (thus). Furthermore, those who seek abandonment and acquisition examine the root of that knowledge which is a factor for activity; thus he says "pravṛtti" (activity). // 107 //

He concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The author of the Sūtras has also proposed the desire to know the particular (*viśeṣajijñāsā*) alone, because it is precisely the particulars that are to be investigated in what follows. And he says—referring to the phrase "of the particular" (*viśeṣasya*)—that this particularity has been stated to have no other means of valid cognition (*ananyapramāṇaka*). // 108 //

The followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśe�ṣikas), however, maintain that because the diversity of the world establishes [the existence of God] in a general sense, He is understood in His specific nature through scripture (*āgama*); thus, they say that He is fully established by these two means of valid cognition alone. To this, he replies: "being understood" (*gamyamāna*). He thinks as follows: when there is a general understanding, a specific detail is not determined here because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). But a specific entity being established is established only as something not divorced from its general character; so what is the point of treating it separately?
[This is] due to [the object's] being well-established. Therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a cause for the establishment of a universal. // 109 //

However, those who say: "This is not presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), but rather this is inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*); because the generality of effects is pervaded by the generality of causes, this is therefore simply an inference, just like that of those who argue for the world's diversity through presumptive testimony"—they too are refuted by the very refutation of presumptive testimony. Thus he says: "Just as... This...

The meaning is as follows: regarding the analogy made for inference—that inference proceeds like presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*)—those who claim that this analogy is not intended, will not be inferred, and will not be compared merely because presumptive reasoning has been refuted, for them the negation does not apply to the analogy itself. However, if it is argued that even inference depends upon scripture (*śāstra*) for the determination of specific details, [then the following applies].
In that case, it would follow that the means of valid cognition for both the universal and the particular is likewise independent; thus he says: "And if [it were] scripture... (110).

Thus far, it has been stated that inference and the other means of knowledge proceed by first apprehending one of the signs (*liṅga*) and so forth through perception; therefore, they are said to be "preceded by perception" (*pratyakṣapūrvaka*). Now, however, he restates the objection—which was previously raised that the perception of the sign and so forth does not constitute [valid] perception because the apprehension of the sign and such is conceptual (*savikalpaka*)—in order to refute it: "Perception... Having thus restated it, he refutes it: "That is not so. He states the reason: "Because it is accepted. This...

The intention [of the author] is this: it is not the case that perception is exclusively non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). For we shall explain in detail later on that what is experienced as the form of an object—assisted by conceptualization and with the operation of the sense organs still unceased at a time subsequent to that [initial moment]—is also perception. Therefore, it is logically established that inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by conceptual perception (*savikalpakapratyakṣa*). // 111 //

Here, someone who cannot tolerate the word "even" (api) objects. He thinks as follows: every cognition is indeed conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because it is a consciousness permeated by the form of speech. Indeed, no such cognition is observed in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words. And a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is employed for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, there is no practical activity whatsoever by means of a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition.

Because all worldly transactions depend upon the determination of specific distinctions, and because such determination does not exist without conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If it is argued that infants and animals possess cognition and transaction devoid of conceptual construction, that is not so; for even in them, subtle speech is established. For they divide speech into three types: *vaikharī*, *madhyamā*, and *sūkṣmā*. As it has been said:
For them, the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman) alone is indeed the transforming primordial matter (pradhāna),
through its division into the states of speech as the gross (vaikharī), the intermediate (madhyamā), and the subtle (sūkṣmā).

Thus [it is said]. But what, then, is the proof for the existence of subtle sound in infants? It is their very nature as cognizers (*pratyayatva*). For how could these cognitions be devoid of sound, just like the cognitions of people such as ourselves? If it is asked, "How do infants, who have not yet acquired linguistic proficiency, associate meaning with sound?", the answer is:
no, because this is possible through the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of sound from previous lives. Indeed, they possess the latent impressions of sound belonging to other existences.

Being manifested by the power of similarity, it brings about the recollection of the word; thereafter, even children comprehend the object as permeated by the subtle word. Therefore, the word "also" (api) in the phrase "even for conceptualization" is inappropriate.
To this he says: "It exists. The intention is this: this too is an inconclusive [reason], namely, that perception is exclusively determinate (*savikalpaka*).

The knowledge of observation (*ālocanājñāna*) also exists as something distinct from conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). Indeed, we perceive with wide-open eyes a suddenly appearing, indistinct, ultimate reality possessing two forms, which later investigators divide into the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). If, however, it is argued that non-conceptual cognition does not arise at the outset, [we reply:]...

Consequently, how does even conceptual cognition (savikalpaka) come into being? For that [conceptual cognition] is preceded by the recollection of words and so forth existing at the time of linguistic convention. Nor does such recollection appear spontaneously; rather, it is logical that conceptual cognitions arise when they obtain their own nature. Furthermore, as for the claim that non-conceptual cognition (nirvikalpaka) is not a factor in linguistic practice (*vyavahāra*), that is incorrect. For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not resorted to solely for the sake of linguistic practice; indeed, equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the fruit of valid cognition.

This is indeed accepted. Moreover, there are certain practical activities that arise from non-conceptual cognition alone, such as the sudden retreat of one being burned by fire. For that [action] is observed to occur instantaneously, without depending on reflective deliberation (*parāmarśa*).
Furthermore, all the practical activities of animals and infants occur through non-conceptual cognition alone; nor is there, for them, the presence of subtle linguistic expression.

There is no valid means of knowledge [for this]. Because the property of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to our own self-cognized non-conceptual cognitions (*svasaṃvedya-avikalpaka-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, how could those [beings] who have not grasped the relationship [between word and meaning] have a cognition of an object associated with words? As for what was said previously—that the explanation [is possible] by virtue of impressions (*vāsanā*) from a former life—that is not so; for that [impression] is generally destroyed by death. Or, if there were recollection of experiences from another existence, then even subsequently the grasping of the relationship would be useless. For one who, as soon as born, [acts] while lying on the birth-stool...
A young child lying in bed remembers his previous existence;

how then could he not remember what is above him? If it is thought that his mental formations (*saṃskāra*) perish later on, that is not so. For one whose formations are destroyed by birth and the pressure of the womb, how could the destruction of those formations occur all of a sudden after only two or three years? Therefore, infants possess non-conceptual cognition (*avikalpa-pratyaya*).
And since linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is rooted in that [conceptualization], it is established that even non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) exists.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the cognition of newborns, the deaf, and animals is included. // 112 //

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) arises solely from the capacity of the object and the sense organ? In that [cognition], neither continuity (*anuvṛtti*) nor exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) appears; and these two do not manifest without the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, how can that [cognition] have them as its objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Not the particular," and so forth. He thinks as follows: It is true that the non-conceptual [cognition] arising at the first moment...

"It does not manifest the universal and the particular. What undesirable consequence has been brought about here? [The opponent asks: "But if the universal and the particular are not cognized, what indeed is there to be understood by that? For there is no entity existing apart from those two. To this he replies: "Of those two," etc. The intention is as follows: non-conceptual cognition has the mere individual (*vyakti*) as its object. Or, is there an individual distinct from the particular? Certainly.

That object which is the locus of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particulars (*viśeṣa*) is the individual (*vyakti*). What, then, are these particulars? They are [individuals] such as Khaṇḍa and others, by which individuals are distinguished from one another. The universal, however, is self-luminous. And this non-apprehension of the universal and the particular by means of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) is [the basis for the claim that] "this is the universal..."

And it was stated [earlier] because there is no apprehension of them after having distinguished that "this is the particularity. However, even in those two cases, their own essential nature (svarūpa) certainly shines forth.
We shall explain this further below. // 113 //
The proponents of non-dualism (advaitavādinaḥ), however, declare that indeterminate perception has pure existence (sanmātra) as its object;

he introduces this very point with the words "the great universal" (mahāsāmānyam). For they think as follows: indeterminate perception establishes the intrinsic nature of a thing, but does not differentiate it from other things. Indeed, it manifests as "this," but not...

Furthermore, [it is argued] that this is not so; for when a distinction (*viveka*) is not manifest, specific features (*viśeṣa*) do not appear. Moreover, the distinction between a cow and a horse consists in their mutual exclusion (*itaretaravyavaccheda*). Therefore, in this case, does the affirmation of one presuppose the exclusion of the other, or does the exclusion of the other presuppose the affirmation of one?

Now, as for the simultaneous [application] of both: first of all, an affirmation preceded by exclusion is not possible, because an exclusion without a substratum is untenable. That which has its own nature already known is excluded from something else; but when it is not cognized, what is excluded from what? For this very reason, simultaneity is also untenable. However, [an affirmation] preceded by affirmation...

Exclusion is not possible when cognition does not persist for another moment. For that [cognition], having established one [object] and being suddenly ceased, is not able to exclude another in a subsequent moment. Moreover, mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is a particularity (*viśeṣa*);
how could that be an object of direct perception?

Because it has as its object the sixth category [of existence], perception therefore grasps only "Being" (sanmātra). This is the meaning: others claim that the "Great Universal" (mahāsāmānya), which is denoted by synonyms such as "substance" (dravya) and "Being" (sat), is what is grasped by perception.
Thus, he says "sāmānya... [verse 114] to show that they maintain this view that perception has a universal as its object.

[Objection: But even so, since particulars do not appear [in cognition], they do not exist at all; how then will the universal be established? To this he says: "But the particulars... Particulars are manifested by cognitions possessing various conceptual constructions (vikalpa) that are projected by beginningless latencies (vāsanā). Therefore, the conventional usage of the universal occurs based upon them. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), it does not.

That is the universal. However, the knowers of the Vedānta maintain that reality is one alone, in which the entire manifold of universals, particulars, and so forth has subsided. Accordingly, the subsumption of all particulars is stated [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone; there was nothing whatsoever here that was manifold."

What, then, are those specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) that are perceived by conceptual cognitions? He demonstrates their nature with the words "And those... Specific qualities are indeed of two kinds: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Common ones are, for example, substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth.
In that case, earth and the others are called "specific qualities" because they are distinguished from other existing things, namely from qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*).
But those very [qualities] are said to be "resorted to in many" [ways]. // 115 //

[669] Śe said: "For substantiality (*dravyatva*) resides in the nine [substances], earth and so forth; however, those which are specific (*asādhāraṇa*) are distinct for each individual substance. But what are they? If you mean things such as [specific pieces of] sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*) and the like," [670]...
That is not so, because those too are common. For even among things such as the "mutilated" or the "crested," there are distinct individual instances (*vyakti*).

This should be demonstrated for color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] as well. Therefore, no so-called "particulars" (*viśeṣa*) that are exclusively unique (*asādhāraṇa*) are apprehended.
As for those ultimate particulars (*antya-viśeṣa*) which reside in eternal substances—

Some have stated that because they are the cause of the very cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), they are indeed particulars (*viśeṣas*). That is incorrect, due to a lack of evidence (*pramāṇa*). To explain: first of all, those [particulars] are not objects of cognition for those of us who perceive only the near side; and as for the claim that yogis perceive them, no proof (*pramāṇa*) is available to us. Nor can anything [be established] on the basis of things never before seen by them.
The inferential mark (*liṅga*) must have its relationship [to the object] known; therefore, it should be stated that there exist specific qualities residing in each individual substance.

These are now described: it is true that when considered individually, color and the other [sensory qualities] are not unique; however, that collection of properties such as quality-universals (*guṇajāti*) by which each individual instance is distinguished from other instances is indeed unique. For even though many things may be common, that which—

In whichever individual something is either deficient or excessive, by that very thing it receives its specific designation. And this the author of the Vārttika will state during the explanation in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* [the section on form], at the occasion of defining the individual as "that which possesses unique particulars. These [individuals], which exist in the nature of both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*), are of neither kind [taken alone].
Nor did he imagine any distinctions. Perception arising with regard to either a cow or a horse is not differentiated; for a distinction in cognition is dependent upon a distinction in its object.

If no distinction in the object appears, the distinction in the cognition is difficult to ascertain. Therefore, it is established that perceptual cognition has only "pure being" (*sanmātra*) as its domain. This is what he says: "those... [116]. Even those who hold the view that... (GA)
[672] t. na (KA) [673] tīti ta [674] tā (GA)

He refutes this, saying: "That is incorrect. The intended meaning is as follows: Is the cognition of one who has opened their eyes and perceives various objects distinguished [from that of one with eyes closed], or not?
If he says "no," then what is the use of his subsequent argument? But if it is distinguished, [then...]

In that case, that very cognition which has arisen with a distinct form, being free from doubt even when there is a difference of place and so forth, establishes multiplicity just as it establishes unity, since no distinction [between them] has arisen. For how could both multiplicity and unity be objects of a single cognition, such that one is real and the other false? As for perception, it establishes the intrinsic nature of the object.
It was said that [the cognition] does not negate; this is true. However, while enjoining this, it enjoins only that which is distinct, because it is perceived as such.

[Objection: But surely, without the negation of the other, it is impossible to enjoin what is distinct. [Reply: Not so. For this is not distinct from the object by virtue of the negation of the other; rather, it is distinct by its own nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, it manifests. To say that "the distinct does not manifest" is difficult to maintain. Hence...

As for what was said—that there would be the consequence of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) being perceptible—that too has been refuted. For mutual non-existence is not to be grasped by means of grasping a distinct [entity]. Let that [distinction] exist there for now; however, it is not determined by perception. Rather, it is subsequently determined through a conceptualization of existence (*bhāvavikalpa*), preceded by the recollection of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) and so forth. This also applies to the two cases of affirmation (*vidhi*) and exclusion (*vyavaccheda*).

The conceptualization of succession and simultaneity is likewise devoid of objective reality. For at the moment of the arising of non-conceptual [cognition], there is no comprehension of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*). What, then, is the point of questioning its succession and so forth? Only the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the object is manifest, and that occurs solely through the force of direct experience (*anubhava*).

It has been stated that [the universal] is "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*). Now, one might object: if the entity is distinct by its very nature (*svarūpa*), what is the use of particularities (*viśeṣa*)? It is not the case that an entity is resorted to on account of some purpose; rather, it is on account of cognition (*saṃvit*). And since that cognition is no different with respect to the particulars, why should the particulars not be resorted to? Furthermore, if the particulars did not exist, that distinct nature itself would not even come into being—just as, for example, if the variegated parts such as blue and so forth did not exist.
It has a variegated form (*citrarūpa*). Yet, it does not become something distinct from those [parts] merely by that much; nor is it perceived apart from the perception of them.

In the same way, the distinct form of a substance, which is manifested precisely through the influence of its specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), is experienced at the very same time as the perception of those [qualities].

Therefore, the objection that there would be the consequence of perceiving it independently of them should not be raised. And all of this is established by us solely on the strength of consciousness (*saṃvidbalāt*).

It is so designated; however, nothing supramundane is being postulated. It is with this very intention that it was said: "because of the perception of a distinct form. What is meant by this? That which is distinct is simply a form (*rūpa*). Therefore, it is logical that it is determined by perception independently of any cognition such as the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*). He asks: "In that case, let that form be defined—what is its name?"
Therefore he says: "Not indeed. This is the intended meaning: existence is not the cause for the reality of an object that is not verbally expressible (*anupākhyavastu*);

rather, it is manifestation (*prakhyā*). And it has been shown that even in the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), there is a consciousness of a distinct entity whose object possesses a differentiated form.
And that form which appears in non-conceptual cognition can indeed later be shown to others as well, by means of two or three qualifiers, without being at a great distance [from them]. // 117 //
Is non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) now restricted solely to objects whose forms are excluded [from others]?

No; he says so with the words ending in "grahaṇam" in the verse beginning with "nirvikalpaketi. The meaning is that there is a grasping even of an object consisting of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*). For instance: when one perceives at once several individual cows (*gopiṇḍa*) which possess diverse natures, then suddenly a cognition possessing two forms (*dvyākārā mati*) appears through non-conceptual perception. This form indeed manifests even when there is the awareness of a single individual (*ekavyakti*), for that is the very nature (*rūpa*) of the individual.

How could it not be manifest when that [universal] is manifest? Likewise, upon seeing another individual after having seen one, the recognition "this is that very same cow" arises; and this is not possible with respect to something previously unseen. And it has been said:
"[The cognition] has as its object-form precisely that..."
In that case, it is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) that "this was seen before";
for indeed, recognition is impossible regarding an object never seen before.

Thus [it is said]. Now, an objection is raised: "It has been stated that neither the particular (*viśeṣa*) nor the universal (*sāmānya*) is perceived by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). How, then, can it be said that there is a grasping of an object consisting of both? To this, he says: "This is what is called its definition. The meaning is as follows: this nature of indeterminate cognition, which consists of the object characterized as both universal and particular, is [perceived] by indeterminate cognition.

"It is made an object" means that this is described by investigators who define perception as being free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). However, the cognizer perceives the thing in a completely indistinct form, devoid of discrimination such as "this is a universal" or "this is a particular.
"Pure" means that it is apprehended as being devoid of reflection upon its inclusion (*anuvṛtti*) or exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). [The phrase] "born from a pure thing" [is used].
Thus, in this case as well, this very meaning should be understood for the word "pure" (śuddha). // 118 //

He elaborates on this very point, stating "it is not," with the intention as follows: the universal and the particular are apprehended by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) solely in their own essential nature (*svarūpamātra*), and not as the unique particularity (*asādhāraṇatā*) or as the universal (*sāmānyatā*), because there is an absence of conceptualization regarding exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or inclusion (*anugama*). Now, one might ask: what is that other essential nature of the particular and the universal, distinct from exclusion and inclusion, which is said to be apprehended? That very thing is their essence (*ātman*). How so?

"In that case, their non-apprehension [when there is no apprehension of the object] will be logically established. Oh, what skill in discernment on the part of your honors! To say that the universal and the particular possess the properties of persistence and exclusion, but that they are not themselves persistence and exclusion—this is quite trivial. 119 //

[676] Having thus explained non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the author now intends to demonstrate that conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*), which arises by the force of the former, possesses the status of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
To begin with, he states its status as direct perception, saying: "Thereafter" (*tataḥ param*). The meaning of this is: from that non-conceptual [perception].
Furthermore, that cognition by which an object is grasped through the conceptualization of genus, quality, and action— such as "this is a cow," "this is white," or "this is Ditttha"—
is also accepted as being direct perception (pratyakṣa). // 120 //

Now, it has been stated that perception is knowledge arising solely from the capacity of the sense-faculties and their objects, whereas conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arise through the power of all names, universals (jāti), and so forth, which are drawn forth by memory. Furthermore, since neither the sense-faculties nor the object possess the capacity for recollection, conceptual cognition is not perception. To this, he says: "And the instrument... The meaning is as follows: if we were to say that the sense-faculties, having recalled [the name], then conceptualize the object, [then the objection would hold].

Thus, we might be reproached for saying that [the self] is unable to remember those [past experiences]. But this is not so, because the sense organs are instruments (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, since memory inheres in the agent, which is the self (*ātman*), the inability to remember those [experiences] is not a fault at all. // 121 //

[677] Then, what is that cognition supported by? To this he says: "In the self alone. For it is the self that perceives; and it cognizes, remembers, and synthesizes the object brought forward by the senses acquired through the merit (dharma) earned in a previous birth. Thus, nothing is untenable. // 122 //

[Objection: But has it not been stated that, in this way, because the contact of the sense organ is mediated by the recollection of sound and so forth, it would result in [the cognition] being non-perceptual?
To this he says: "By that" (*tena*). This is the intended meaning: here the connection between the sense organ and the object is not severed.

And while that connection exists, even one who is recollecting sound and so forth possesses perception with respect to that [object] which he grasps by conceptualizing the thing through its genus and other qualifiers.
The person indeed remains [the same]; the meaning is that this is because the sense faculties have not been impaired by the act of recollection. // 123 //

Now, it is said that perception is produced by the sense-faculties alone. In that case, since the sense-faculties have the recollection of words and so forth as their concomitants, how can they be designated by the term "perception"? To this, he says: "And this [is as follows]. Knowledge dependent upon the sense-faculties is called perception. This is the case for one whose sensory activity has not ceased, regarding the knowledge that appears directly as "this is a cow."
The point is that [a cognition] being born is necessarily dependent upon the sense faculties, and is therefore designated by those very sense faculties,

because even when memory assists them, those [faculties] alone are the cause. As for those conceptual constructions of recollection, such as "this is a cow," which do not depend on the operation of the senses at all— we ourselves do not accept these as perception, since they have memory alone as their cause.
Thus he says: "Because of its lack of connection with that" (tadasambandhāt). // 124 //

However, since there are many conceptual constructions (vikalpa) that follow upon the connection with the sense faculties and are indeed denotable by the term "perception" (pratyakṣa), he says: "Furthermore... (punar). 125.
As for what was said—that if the sense faculties are the cause for the arising of conceptual construction, why do they not produce it immediately?
To that he replies: "Not indeed," [verse 126].
Now, if it is argued that there exists a sensory cognition (*aindriyaka-jñāna*) produced by the first impact which has an indistinct appearance,
he says "just as" (*yathā*) to show that this is the same in the present case as well. 127.

As for what was said—that for one who has seen something, even when the eyes are closed, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would become a perception (*pratyakṣa*) merely by the absence of sensory activity—that is not so. He says "yadi tu" (but if), precisely because that is not accepted. The intention is this: the mere absence of sensory activity is not the cause for something being sensory (*aindriyika*).

What then? It is the non-cessation of the operation of the sense faculties. Therefore, because there is an absence of following the connection with the sense faculties, there would be no status as perception (*pratyakṣatā*) in that case. // 128 //

But surely, since conceptual cognition has multiple causes such as the self and the sense organs, why is it designated by the sense organ alone? To this he says: "because of the lack of connection" (*asambandha*). This is the meaning: for that which is unique [to a specific cognition] is the cause for the application of a word. And while the self and other factors are causes, they do not apply to conceptual cognitions regarding objects that are not connected to the sense organs.

This is the same in the case of recollection, inference, and so forth. However, because the sense organ alone is the uncommon cause for the arising of a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*) that appears as immediate (*aparokṣāvabhāsin*), it is designated by that very term. "Conceptualization" (*kalpanā*) means determinate cognition (*savikalpakajñāna*). [The word *saṃbandha* refers to the connection...]

[679] [680] This objection is equally applicable even to those who maintain that perception is non-conceptual; thus he says: "Non-conceptual... If, however, this [conceptualization] were to arise immediately after the non-conceptual [perception] born of the senses...
That [conceptual cognition] has precisely that [non-conceptual perception] as its cause;
however, it is said that the sense faculty has its function exhausted at the very production of the non-conceptual [perception].
Nevertheless, because the sense faculty is an indirect cause, it will be designated as "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), just as a flower is called a "lotus" (*paṅkaja*).

Thus, it is not born from mud; rather, it arises solely from a bulb that grows in the mud. Since this state of being non-sensory (non-born from the senses) through a causal chain is common to inference and the other means of knowledge, we shall also seek a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) for them in order to exclude their designation by the term "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). This is just as the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") [is used], despite its etymological connection (*yoga*) being mediated, because it applies commonly to the fragrant water-lily (*saugandhika*) and others.
Conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is accepted as that which determines [the meaning]. This very thing is called "convention based on etymology" (*yogarūḍhi*) by the followers of the Vārttikakāra.
He states this as follows: "that tradition," and so forth. However, this must be addressed here: if convention is resorted to, what is the point of accepting etymology?
For by the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*) alone, a word will function only in certain cases—such as *aśvakarṇa* and the like—and not in others; so why [accept etymology]?
257} We do not resort to yoga out of addiction, nor out of a habituated passion for it;

rather, we are unable to abandon a well-established yoga, just as one cannot avoid threshing grain once it has been seen [as necessary]. Just as in that very case, the postulation of an unseen result (adṛṣṭa) follows from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the restrictive rule (niyama), so too here, why would it be untenable to postulate a collective power (samudāya-śakti) for the sake of the restrictive rule of application? [Objection: But surely [it is untenable] because of non-application...

"Thus there will be non-application elsewhere. What does this "non-application due to non-application" mean? If it means that because earlier speakers did not apply [the word], later speakers do not apply it either, that is incorrect, because there is no such thing as non-application [of the constituent parts]. For it is merely the application [of the parts] that serves as the cause for its occurrence; indeed, the application of the two members in their own respective senses is clearly observed. But the whole (*samudāya*) is nothing other than those [parts]; therefore, there can be no non-application of it.

It can be said [that there is no such thing as a "whole" (samudāya)]. This is because we do not accept the existence of a power residing in a whole; rather, words such as *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") function solely through their conventional usage.

For the word *paṅka* is used in the sense of "mud," and the root *jan* in the sense of "manifestation. Apart from these, there is no such entity as a "whole" at all. It must be stated: of what [entity] is there non-usage? Indeed, the connection of meaning (*arthānvaya*) is the cause for such usage, and that [connection] exists in the case of fragrant lotuses (*saugandhika*) and the like.

Since the [etymological] derivation is the same, the application of the word *paṅkaja* occurs even in those [other cases]. Therefore, in order to prevent its use elsewhere, one must necessarily resort to conventional usage (*rūḍhi*). As for what was said—that the non-application elsewhere brings about conventional usage—that is indeed accepted. It has also been stated that the etymological derivation (*yoga*) is observed and cannot be abandoned. However, in the case of words such as *aśvakarṇa*, because there is no correspondence between the parts [of the compound and their meanings], [conventional usage is required].
Conventional usage (rūḍhi) establishes itself only in certain instances. Therefore, this is neither purely conventional nor purely etymological (yoga);
the elders consider it to be "etymological-conventional" (yogarūḍhi).
[681] ṇam i [682] ja e (KA) [683] ya śa

Now, if you think that because of the intervention [of conceptualization] it is not the cause [of the word "perception"], even so, the word *pratyakṣa* will apply to the determinate [cognition] (*savikalpaka*) by usage alone. For it is there, in the majority of cases, that worldly people employ the word *pratyakṣa*. [The author] says that the indeterminate [cognition] (*nirvikalpaka*) is rare:
"It is indeed without a [conventional] cause" (verse 131).

If it is argued that while the elders indeed employ [the term] "truth," the authors of the definitions maintain that perception is strictly non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), as they say: "Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*)," then he replies with the two verses beginning with "vṛddhaprayoga. This is the intended meaning: for the worldly referent of a word...

This is the connection. Therefore, even by investigators, one must proceed exactly according to worldly convention. If they act otherwise, they will certainly encounter contradiction from the world. // 133 //

Moreover, even for those who maintain that [perception] is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), conceptual cognition is indeed accepted as being perceptual with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). As they have said:
"Conceptualization is also accepted in its own awareness, but not with respect to the object, because it is a mental construction.
For they think thus: conceptualization does not conceptually construct itself when it is self-aware.

Because it appears as a conceptual construction of an external object, and because even that which is of the nature of a conceptual construction—being unique—is itself the locus of conceptualization. Regarding this, they also say: "This [consciousness] does not associate with verbal expression, because such an association would be contradictory to its own nature.
Therefore, for them, self-awareness is not accompanied by verbal expression.

And thus, this perception consisting of the self-awareness of conceptual construction would not be tenable. For that too has its sensory operation mediated by a non-conceptual cognition. If it is argued that the word "perception" (pratyakṣa) is applied there by conventional usage, then the same applies to the manifestation of external objects such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth.

With the intention that [cognition] does not exist solely in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), he says: "conceptualization" (*kalpanā*). If it is thought that there exists therein sense-born non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and that this very thing is called the mind (*manas*), as they say:
"And that is fourfold, [namely] sense-born... [and so forth].

[The opponent argues: "That which is born from the sense-faculties (*indriya*) is mental (*mānasa*), arising from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Since the mind (*manas*) is also a sense-faculty, perception will be dependent upon the mind. This is equally true even in the case of the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. Even in that cognition, we certainly maintain that there is an operation of the mind; however, we disagree regarding the nature of that mind. To the point that it is indeed something distinct [from the senses], he says: "the mind" (*manaḥ*). (134)
[Objection: But how can the internal mind function toward the cognition of external objects?
He raises this doubt with the words "in its own self-awareness. He refutes it with the word "the world. The intention is as follows:
It is true that you maintain that conceptual cognition is perceptual (*pratyakṣa*) in its own self-awareness; however, [this is not so] for ordinary people.

They consider this to be a misconception. Ordinary people regard the conceptual determination of another's form, such as "This is a cow," as being determinative (savikalpaka), but they do not regard the self-determination "I am a cow" as such. As for the claim that the mind does not operate with respect to external objects: that is true;

it does not function independently of the external senses. However, properties such as "cowness" are brought into contact with the eye through the relation of inherence in what is conjoined (saṃyuktasamavāya).
The meaning is that because there is a mental operation (*manovyāpāra*) directed toward them, they receive the designation "sense-faculty" (*akṣa*) based upon that.

Therefore, those who claim that perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of conceptual cognition (*kalpanāpratyaya*) within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) must necessarily accept either the mind as a sense-faculty, or [the term] "sense-faculty" as a conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), or as a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*). With the intention of showing that we too are able to offer a counter-argument in every respect, he says:
"Therefore," [it is said]. // 135 //

Even in the case of the self-awareness of pleasure and so forth, you have maintained that the mind alone is the sense organ (akṣa) relied upon. He says "But of the mind... [verse 136] to show that in this case as well, there will be a conceptual construction regarding the genus (jāti).

Now, even though [the status of] being dependent on the mind is equal [to other types of cognition], only a certain [cognition] is accepted as perception in accordance with the definition of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*).

If such an arrangement were to be made according to mere whim, we too would state whatever we desired as perception according to our own inclination; thus he says: "Because it is dependent on that" (tadadhīnatva). // 137 //

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is also logical that this conceptual cognition (*savikalpakabuddhi*) is included within perception; thus he says: "from signs, etc. [Verse 138]. Now, elimination occurs when validity is established, but this [conceptual cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore he says: "because there is no sublation" (*bādhaka*). // 138 //

But this must be said here: it is true that this [cognition] is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*), because—like the cognition of a mirage and the like—it does not contradict worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Nor is it a means of valid knowledge because its object is non-existent.
