It is designated as "recollection" (*smṛti*) because it brings about the attainment of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which was previously inundated by non-conceptual [perception]. And since recollection is not a means of valid knowledge, he says: "And not... [referring to the cognition] whose object is a thing previously seen.

Recollection occurs. Nor can there be a perception of a universal by means of non-conceptual [cognition], because according to your own tenet, that [universal] is not an object of perception. For us as well, the commingling with other particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) was previously unperceived. Furthermore, it is not the case that [the cognition] has a non-existent object, because universals and so forth will be established later by the reasoning to be stated. Therefore, there is no lack of validity due to apprehending what was not previously apprehended, nor is there any lack of validity due to having a non-existent object.
Therefore, being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is included within perception by the method of elimination; thus he concludes with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Even you [the opponents] declare this cognition to be invalid solely on account of a discrepancy between speech and thought. He says "in practical activity" (*vyavahāre*) because all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are dependent upon conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*). // 139 //

Now, one might object: "Why is it not logical that this [conceptual cognition] lacks validity? For conceptual constructions (vikalpa) apprehend a qualified [object], and the qualifier is distinct from the qualificand; for if there were no distinction, the relationship between qualifier and qualificand would be impossible. Therefore, when a thing is grasped as qualified by universals (jāti) and so forth—which are entities separate from it—conceptual cognition is nothing but an error, because it apprehends that [qualifier] in what is not that."
He says: "Birth and so forth. (140)

He refutes this, saying: "This is not so. He states the reason: "Because it is established [as such]. For when one thing is characterized by means of another's form, an error occurs. And there is no "otherness of form" (pārarūpya) regarding universals (jāti) and the like, because they are not distinct from one another; this is the intended meaning. // 141 //
Now, was it not stated that the relationship of qualifier and qualified is untenable in the case of non-difference?

To this he says: "yadi hi" (if indeed). The meaning is that the qualifier—such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth—is not absolutely distinct from the qualified, because its form is always cognized as being identical with it. // 142 //
"But surely, it is observed that even a substance such as crystal, which is absolutely distinct [from the object], is perceived as qualified by the form of lac-dye and the like;
likewise, a cognition qualified by a universal (*jāti*) and so forth, being of that very nature, would be false.
To this he replies: "In the case of crystal and the like. This is the intended meaning: we have already stated [this].
An object is always perceived as qualified by its genus and other attributes, because for anyone at any time, there is no cognition of their distinction [from those attributes].
Therefore, how could it be false? However, only someone who is untrained and lacks the realization of their distinction perceives a crystal stained with lac as "red";
thus, that cognition is an error. For at that very moment, others who have seen the distinction [between the crystal and the lac] perceive it correctly.

They know that "this is not red," [realizing] that this appearance of redness is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Even one who is unlearned knows as soon as the adventitious condition is removed that "this is not red. Therefore, it is logical that it is an error (*bhrānti*), because sublation (*bādha*) arises. // 143 //

However, the mutual distinction between the universal (jāti) and so forth and their possessors has never before been observed. Therefore, it is not logical that [the cognition] be erroneous; thus he says: "For not... Now, let this be the case regarding the universal—for indeed, no object ever perceived is devoid of it. But as for qualities and actions, the cognition of an object separated from them is certainly observed; for even while the substance persists, [the cognition arises] from some cause...
Because of a cause, the destruction of a previous quality and the arising of another quality are observed. This should be shown to apply to action (*karman*) as well.
Therefore, how can there be non-difference between the two?
To this he says: "by its release from that" (*tadvimokena*). The intention is this: although the object is seen as released from that [action], [the action is not distinct].

But those [qualities], once released from that [substance], are never perceived. For when something is distinct from another, even if it is released from it, it may sometimes still be perceived—as the incidental redness of a gem [is perceived even when separated from the sun]. But this is not the case here. Therefore, by the cessation of the pervader, there is the cessation of the pervaded, namely absolute difference. How then can there be the destruction of the preceding quality and action and the production of the subsequent ones?

For it is the substance (*dravya*) that is recognized as "this is that very same thing," whereas the quality (*guṇa*) and the action (*karman*) have perished. This [recognition] would not be possible if there were no identity [between the former and the latter]. It is not the case that it is not possible; for we shall explain in the discussion of the example of the golden ornament (*rucaka*) and so forth that, for us, a real entity (*vastu*) consists precisely of persistence, origination, and destruction. Therefore, in this context, even the entity itself perishes when the quality and the action perish, for that is the very nature of the entity.

How can it be said that [the universal] does not perish when those [particulars] perish? For even in their case, there is no absolute destruction, because they continue to exist in the form of entities. This same reasoning applies to the genus (*jāti*) as well; for even there, persistence, origination, and destruction are indeed observed. Furthermore, cognition dissociated [from a particular] is also observed; for indeed, a cognition dissociated from one destroyed individual is seen in another individual.

The universal (*jāti*). How could that be different from them? Now, if one were to somehow rely on a difference there and apply this same solution [of non-perception], then why not also speak of it regarding qualities and actions? By what distinction, then, did they describe a difference between qualities and actions while relying on the non-difference of the universal? Therefore, when universals and so forth are perceived, they are understood as being non-different from the individual object (*piṇḍa*); thus, they too possess non-difference. As for whatever logical inconsistency is alleged, it does not apply to those who maintain the doctrine of non-exclusivity (*anekāntavāda*); let this matter rest for now.
Thus [ends section] 144.

[684] If, however, cognitions of redness and so forth were to occur even in the case of a crystal and the like, following the rules for the cognition of genus and so forth, who could then prevent their validity? To this he says: [685] "In that case also... (tatrāpi). // 145 //
[685] (GA) Having thus established the non-difference of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, he now addresses the followers of Kaṇāda, who maintain an absolute difference, saying:
"Nor even... For they think as follows: the relationship characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) exists only between the distinct genus and its possessor (*tadvat*).

Thus they recite: "Inherence is that relation which is the cause of the notion of 'here' among things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*) and stand in the relationship of substratum and superstratum. This is untenable because a relation between two inseparably established things is impossible. To the question, "How, then, is the relatedness of inseparably established things untenable? he says:

"—there is no relation for that which is unestablished. This is the intended meaning: what is this "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhi*)? Is it merely the absence of separable establishment (*yutasiddhi*), or is it separate establishment (*pṛthaksiddhi*)? If it were the absence of separable establishment, then by what could there be a relation of what? For a relation occurs only between two related entities that are already established.

"Not of two things that are unestablished. Now, if you mean "non-separate establishment," the same answer applies there as well: "there is no relation for that which is not established. The sense is that identity exists between two things that are established non-separately. If, in order to avoid this fault, separate establishment is accepted, then it follows that they are actually established apart; thus he says: "In the case of establishment... (146).
[686] You do not exist; [687] if you [688] were to arise... please ask.

But what undesirable consequence has been brought about? Is it not indeed accepted that there is some slight temporal difference between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*), even though they are unconnected? And since yogis perceive that state of theirs, one must say that their relation—like that of a rope and a jar—is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*), given that they are established separately (*yutasiddha*). For us, "established separately" is not defined by being located in different substrata or having separate movements; rather, it is [defined by] having different substrata or possessing separate motion.

Furthermore, *yutasiddhi* (separate existence) belongs to two things or to either one of them; the absence of that is *ayutasiddhi*. Now, since neither of those two [conditions] exists for a genus (*jāti*), the relation between two things that are *ayutasiddha* must necessarily be inherence (*samavāya*).
To this he says: "And such being the case. The intended meaning is as follows: we do not [accept] the genus and the individual as being separately established (*pṛthaksiddha*).

We perceive [them]. Furthermore, a moment devoid of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which is accessible only to yogins, is indeed difficult to establish. Even granting that it exists, we say: there would be no relation due to the absence of a cause. For, unlike a rope and a jar, no unifying agent is observed for Devadatta and the like, who are respectively the genus and the individual (*vyakti*), as they are established separately. Moreover, inherence (*samavāya*) cannot be the cause of the relation.

Because the nature of a relation is admitted. Even if it were its cause, even so, it does not relate when there is separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*). But has it not been stated that there is no separate establishment for a universal (*jāti*), because of the absence of inherence in different substrata and because of not having a distinct mode of movement? No;
for the word "separate establishment" denotes merely the state of being established separately.

By the negative particle (*nañ*), mere non-existence is expressed; inseparability (*ayutasiddhi*) is what is being described. If that [non-existence] is a state of separate existence (*pṛthaksiddhi*), how can there be inseparability? Furthermore, even if the term "inseparability" is technical, since an individual (*vyakti*) inheres in its own parts and a universal (*jāti*) resides in the individual, they possess the property of residing in different substrata; thus, the consequence of separate existence (*yutasiddhi*) follows. Moreover, inherence (*samavāya*) is not the cause for a relationship of separate existence, nor is there any other cause.

"It is well said that 'even if [it] exists,' there is no cause for a relation. Because of the absence of a cause for a relation, all six categories—substance and the rest—would become unrelated; thus he says: "Of the six... (147).

[689] Furthermore, this inherence (samavāya), when connecting the two related entities, does so either by being connected itself or without being connected. It cannot be without being connected, for a cause of connection is never observed to exist while it remains unconnected. Moreover, a connection is not possible without another cause of connection.

And that [inherence] is not perceived. Therefore, because of the separation and dissociation of inherence from its inherent substrates (samavāyin), there would also be a mutual dissociation among the inherent substrates themselves; thus he says: "Because of inherence" (samavāya). Furthermore, he says: "In the postulation of that" (tatkḷptau), meaning that if one were to postulate yet another cause for the relationship, there would be an infinite regress (avyavasthā). // 148 //

If, however, it is argued that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the two inherent entities (*samavāyin*) is itself inherence (*samavāya*), and thus it does not need to be related by another [relation], then in that case, the doctrine of non-difference (*abhedavāda*) has been accepted; let the very nature of the attribute (*dharma*) and the substrate (*dharmī*) be inherence itself, if there is necessarily a purpose for the name "inherence. Why then resort to the apprehension of a further inherence? Thus he says: "Now" (*atha*). 149.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "For not... It has been stated that if one accepts another cause for the relation of a distinct entity, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, in the case of non-difference, one must simply accept the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), both of which are established for both disputants. What is the use of postulating *samavāya*? // 150 //

"Let it be granted, then, that there is no difference among properties such as genus (*jāti*) and the like; however, the substratum (*dharmin*) itself, which is distinct [from them] and which is made an object by conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), is not perceived.
He introduces this point with the word "nanu" (surely). For they think thus: "This substratum is not something over and above its properties."

It is perceived like the thumb from among the fingers; yet perception does not operate toward its determination, because perception is born of the senses, and the five senses are restricted to the five [objects] such as form, while the sixth, the mind, lacks the independent capacity to determine external objects. As they have said:
The eye and the other [senses] are exhausted within the five [objects] such as form;
no sixth sense exists externally that could be its perceiver.
Thus, it is only a mere aggregate of form and so forth that is perceived externally, and not a separate reality, just as the cognition of a "forest" arises from an aggregate of trees. // 151 //

To this, he states the refutation: "By means of manifestation," ending with the word *dharmyanta*. This is the intended meaning: we indeed perceive, with eyes wide open, a single substance just like color and other qualities, and that [substance] does not undergo reversal;
how then could it be otherwise? As for the claim that it is not perceived as non-different [from its qualities], that is true;

but by whom is an absolute difference of the substratum (*dharmin*) from its attributes (*dharma*) accepted? However, the absence of a perceiver [of such a difference] is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just as in the case of color and the rest.

This [objection] must be refuted by demonstrating the efficacy of perception and touch alone. Furthermore, if the substratum (*dharmin*) were not distinct from its attributes (*dharma*), what would it be that is recognized as persisting through the visible forms (*rūpa*) and other qualities which possess the nature of manifestation and disappearance?
For we do indeed recognize: "This is that very same [object], whose former color has been displaced by contact with fire and in which another color has arisen."

One says "the jar" [referring to] the jar. And that [designation] is not tenable if there were absolute non-difference, because it would follow that persistence, origination, and destruction would occur simultaneously in one and the same thing.

Therefore, there exists a substratum (dharmin) distinct from its attributes (dharmas), which persists through them; it is by virtue of this very [substratum] that such a distinction [between the jar and its states] is possible. Furthermore, in the case of the position of absolute non-difference, without the apprehension of the attributes...

The substratum (dharmin) would not be known at all. Yet, it is observed that the cognition of the substratum exists even prior to the apprehension of its properties (dharma), such as existence and so forth;
thus he says: "Or where... Therefore, it is established that the substratum exists and that the properties, such as genus (jāti) and the rest, are not distinct from it. // 152 //

[690] He states that because there is no determination of another form (*pararūpa*) in the cognition of that qualified object, conceptual cognitions (*savikalpakajñāna*) do not lack validity—thus he says "therefore" (*ataḥ*). // 153 //

Or, even if there were an absolute difference [between the two], it would still not be false; thus he says with the two verses beginning "yasyāpi" (even for whom...). This is the intended meaning: falsity does not consist merely in being cognized under another form, but rather in being cognized otherwise—that is to say, by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). And in this case, since the cognition always possesses that very form for everyone, there is a cognition qualified by the meaning of the verbal root, just as in the case of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
It is not false. // 155 //

Now, if this were so, the subject (*dharmī*)—the object-field of the body and the eye—would be distinct due to the difference in the perceivers, just like color-form (*rūpa*) and other objects. Or else, those [objects] would not be distinct even when there is a difference in the perceivers, just as existence (*sattva*), which is perceived by multiple sense-faculties, is seen not to be distinct. If you say this, we reply: no. Because conceptual form (*vikalparūpa*) is not apprehended by the sense-faculties. Furthermore, if the sense-faculties had overlapping objects, the multiplicity of sense-faculties would be useless.
Moreover, since that single sense organ alone would distinguish various objects, what is the use of a plurality of sense organs? As it has been said:
"What being is not manifold? Or is the non-difference of form and so forth not observed? If you say it is, it is not by means of the sense organ."

Regarding the statement, "The multiplicity of the sense organs would be useless, for [the cognition] possesses the capacity [to perceive] even when its own object is distinct" (PS 1.21c–22d), he says here: "And not by multiplicity. As for what was previously stated—that there is a distinction [of the self] because of the distinction of the perceivers—that is incorrect;
for the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the eye situated in different bodies perceives an object that is non-distinct. // 156 //

If, however, it is argued that because they are one in their nature as "eye," there is no distinction of sense-faculties (*indriya*) therein, then here too it is the same in their nature as "sense-faculty. Therefore, with the intention that the distinction is based solely on the difference in cognitions (*buddhi*) and not on a difference in the apprehending subjects, he says: "because there is no difference in genus" (*jātyabhedāt*). For this very reason, even *sattā* (existence), though apprehended by different sense-faculties, [is considered one] because it is the object of a single cognition.
He says that it is not divided: "equal," etc. The sense is that there is indeed cognition of existence (sattā) and quality-ness (guṇatva) by means of all the sense-faculties. // 157 //

Regarding what was stated—that there is no difference between color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth—he replies: "Because of the difference in cognition" (*buddhibhedāt*). Or, he states that both applications [of the argument] suffer from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*): "As one... The meaning is that color-form and the rest are one in their nature as *sat* (existence), whereas the substratum (*dharmin*) is manifold in its form as color-form and so forth. // 158 //

He states the rebuttal to the objection that there would be either multiplicity or uselessness of the sense organs with the words "kvacic ca" ("and in some cases"). The meaning is that since no confusion between the skin and the eye has ever been observed in any single substratum (*dharmī*), it is logical that there is only one sense organ. He states the reason for this with the word "dārḍhya" ("firmness"):
for if unity were to be assumed based on the observation of such confusion, [it would lead to absurdity].
Otherwise, the distinction based on the strength or weakness of those [faculties] would not be tenable. For when the eye is strong and the ear is weak, color is perceived;

likewise, when the ear is strong and the eye is weak, sound is heard. This established distinction between the objects of the eye and the ear would not be possible if the sense-faculties were one. // 159 //

But surely this restriction is untenable, because it would apply everywhere. For if one sense-organ does not function with respect to the object of another sense-organ, it would not function with respect to anything at all. Or, if it were to function, it would function everywhere without restriction, since we observe instances of such transgression.

Therefore, he says with the two verses beginning "Just as...": this is not being proposed as a position without an illustrative example, namely that there is order in some cases and confusion in others. For the mind is indeed confused with the eyes and other senses in the cognition of form and so forth, yet it remains restricted in the experience of pleasure and so forth. Thus, order and confusion, which follow from the observation of effects, are not untenable; however, [it is not the case that...]
Because a fixed rule is observed in one instance, confusion is excluded everywhere; or, because it is observed in some cases, it would follow that it must apply everywhere. [160]

What, then, is the cause for this distinction and non-confusion regarding the mind? To this he says: "Of the ear and so forth. Even one whose ears and other senses are impaired remembers sound and the like; therefore, while the mind is occupied with internal objects such as memory and pleasure, it does not perceive external forms and the like. Thus, in that case, the mind depends upon external causes. Consequently, the established rule—that there is confusion in some instances and non-confusion in others—is proven. 162. [692] Not where... (KA)

Having thus established the distinction and non-confusion [of functions] through the determination of their respective effects, he now states the fault in the case of the unity of the sense organ: "One" (*ekam*). [Objection: Even if there is unity, the distinction [of functions] will be established through a difference in capacities (*śakti*);

therefore, let it be postulated that the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) is one and all-pervading throughout the body, while its capacities are distinct in the various parts of the body—what is the need for a plurality of sense organs? To this, he says: "It is postulated" (*kalpyate*). Whether a difference in capacities is postulated or a difference in sense organs, what is the distinction? Indeed...

Furthermore, one must also postulate another distinction for the possessor of the power (*śaktimat*), which results in conceptual complexity (*gaurava*). Or, let it be granted that even very many unseen things are to be postulated provided they are supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇavat*);
it has already been explained that there exist within bodies portions of the elements such as earth, etc., which possess the established powers of manifesting fragrance and so forth.
As for the postulation of a single tactile organ (*tvagindriya*) of a wind-nature that pervades the entire body and possesses the power to manifest color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest—

The meaning is that this [object] is absolutely unperceived and lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). "It would be a sense-faculty" means that a potency (*śakti*) would have to be postulated as occupying the place of a sense-faculty. // 163 //

Having thus established the determination of functions through the distinction between strength and weakness, the multiplicity of the sense organs has been supported. Now, he states the fault that would arise if this determination were not accepted—beginning with the words "he would hear. If the sense organs did not have fixed objects, then even a deaf person who possesses sight would hear sound, because the eye would also be operating upon that [sound] as its object. Therefore, they are not restricted to a single [object].

Based on the observation of confusion (*saṅkara*), one must assume its existence everywhere. This [statement], "due to the distinction between strength and weakness," is precisely the demonstration of the contrapositive (*vyatireka*). A systematic order (*vyavasthā*) is indeed observed; however, if there were confusion everywhere, this fault would arise. Now, regarding the mind, by means of the phrase "just as in the case of the mind," the systematic order and the confusion previously illustrated are [discussed].
Wishing to demonstrate the fault in the negation of what has been stated, he first speaks regarding the negation of *saṅkara* (intermixture), saying: "Or [if it were] the mind.

This is the meaning: if the mind were independent in the perception of external objects, then this very same fault would apply there as well—that a deaf person would hear sound—because that mind would also exist [in the deaf person]. And this...

By the phrase "and because of the ignorance of the present," the exclusion (*vyatireka*) is shown of that confusion (*saṅkara*) of the mind which was demonstrated [to exist] in the perception of external objects. // 164 //

Regarding the independence of the mind (*manas*) that has been stated in its perception of internal objects, he states the fault in its absence with the words "it would not remember. For if the mind, even regarding internal objects, were dependent on the external just like the perception of external objects, then a deaf person would not remember a sound because of the absence of the ear. Now, if [one argues that memory occurs] even when the cause is absent—

Memory would [persist], and likewise, there would be perception of the present as well. This [point] constitutes the negative concomitance (vyatireka) with respect to the internal state of the mind, which was stated by the phrase "even when there is impairment of the ear and so forth. // 165 //
The dependent nature (*paratantra*) is said to be the mind (*manas*) in the perception of external objects. But what is the reason that the mind is active in the cognition of the external?

Since the eyes and so forth are themselves the causes therein, he says: "And memory," up to the end [of the verse]. This is the intended meaning: by one who speaks thus, the mind itself is implied. And in that regard, this much must first be stated.

"The non-existence and existence of cognition when there is contact between the self, the sense organs, and their objects is the mark of the mind. Indeed, the self exists. And the visual light is in contact with various objects; yet only some [of them] are known, not all. For what reason? Because it is observed that an effect is obstructed by a deficiency in its causes, just as a cloth [is not produced] even when the threads exist.

It does not arise because of the absence of the conjunction of threads. Likewise, here too, there exists another cause of cognition, in the non-operation of which cognition does not arise, and in the operation of which it does arise; and that is called the mind (*manas*). Furthermore, at the time of perceiving sound and so forth by means of the ear and other senses, if the mind were not operative, [cognition would not occur].

How else could recollection at a later time be possible? For the mind (*manas*) is the cause for the arising of memory. If, therefore, the mind was occupied at the time of perceiving sound and so forth, then it follows that this object was previously illuminated by the mind and can thus be remembered later. However, if prior cognition were caused by the external sense-faculties alone, there would be no operation of those faculties toward the production of memory.

Memory would not exist; for the arising of cognition cannot possibly occur without a cause. Therefore, there is an operation of the mind (*manas*) in the perception of external objects. Furthermore, the experience of pleasure and so forth would not be possible if the mind were non-existent. Moreover, if the mind were non-existent, this fact—that there is no recollection of all things previously experienced—would not be tenable; rather, only certain things are recollected at certain times.

It is observed that someone remembers; this is possible only if there exists some internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), for memory is determined by a specific conjunction of that [organ] with the self. Nor can the determination [of memory] be based on the awakening or non-awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). For a latent impression is an auxiliary to the instruments [of cognition], not an independent instrument. Otherwise, however, that...
He says "and not" (na ca) to show that [the self] would thus become the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). // 166 //

[694] Now, if one were to say: "This discrimination between the external and internal organs will be accomplished; but what is the cause for the very existence of these organs? [695] [The answer is: MA. MA says: KA. [695] MA says: "This discrimination between the external and internal organs will be accomplished. But what is the reason for the very existence of the organs?"

For the person (*puruṣa*) has consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*bodhasvabhāva*). Therefore, this [person] would perceive sound and so forth independently of anything else; hence he says "consciousness" (*bodha*). For if this person, having consciousness as its intrinsic nature, were to cognize independently of anything else, it would know the entire universe simultaneously. Consequently, one must necessarily admit that there are restrictive causes for this [cognition]. // 167 //

Having described the non-confusion of the established order through the two powers of the grasped and the grasper by means of their own nature and their other primordial state, he now concludes with the words "Therefore": for it is by way of their effects that the powers of the grasped and the grasper exist; from these, the establishment of the non-confusion of the order is proven. // 168 //
[697] Regarding the grasping subject (grāhaka): surely, if the diversity of the sense-faculties is described according to their effects, then—
given that there are multiple perceptions distinguished by differences such as blue and so forth— an inference of sense-faculties following those [perceptions] would certainly not be determinate.

Therefore, he says: "the eye, visible form, and so forth. For although visible form is of many kinds, those with wide-open eyes perceive it; thus, disregarding internal subdivisions, it is determined that the eye is simply the illuminator of visible form in general. The same should be shown regarding the ear. Consequently, there is no infinity of sense organs. [The phrase] "the eye, visible form, and so forth" means that the distinctions among the eye and the others are due to the distinctions among visible form and the others. This is the function of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*).
The connection is with each [term] individually. // 169 //

Now, for the sake of easy comprehension, he briefly demonstrates the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) and the non-confusion (*asaṅkara*) [of categories] with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Form (*mūrti*) is the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of a substance possessing touch; or rather, it is the dimension of a non-omnipresent substance.
Substances characterized by that—namely earth, water, and fire—are perceived by two means: sight and touch.

Likewise, the pentad beginning with color (*rūpa*) is perceived individually by the eye and the other sense organs. Thus it is also for other substances, other qualities, actions, and universals (*jāti*).
And the systematic arrangement and the confusion [of categories] should be understood according to how they appear. // 170 //

Thus far, it has been stated that there exists a substratum (*dharmin*) which remains undifferentiated despite the diversity of its apprehenders, and that properties such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth are not distinct from it; therefore, because there is no determination of an extraneous form (*pararūpa*), conceptual cognitions (*savikalpakajñāna*) are not false.

Now, however, there are those who argue that since entities—which are themselves non-verbal in nature—are determined within conceptual cognitions by way of a verbal form, they do indeed possess an extraneous form.

He sets forth their view with the words "nanu" (but surely). This is the meaning: even if the substratum (*dharmin*) consists of universals (*jāti*) and so forth, nevertheless, since those [universals] themselves do not exist apart from the word, when the entity is determined in its form as such, it results in being determined solely through the nature of the word.
Consequently, for things that do not have the word as their essence, to be determined through the essence of the word is once again to be determined by another's form (*pārarūpyam*).
If [the object] were something already attained, then like the cognition of a mirage and so forth, the five types of conceptual construction would be false. // 171 //

He refutes this, saying "not by means of a word. He states the reason, saying "prior [to that]. The intended meaning is that here there is no cognition at all that possesses the form of a word. // 172 //
Here he raises an objection with the two verses beginning "nanu" (but surely). This is the meaning: what is this that is called "the cognition as it was prior to the word"?

For indeed, prior to the knowledge of the relationship between word and object, there do not arise cognitions having as their objects entities such as the form of a cow or whiteness in the form of "cowness," "whiteness," and so forth.
It is only at a time subsequent to the connection with a word that a cognition of that nature arises. Therefore, if...

If universals (jāti) and the like existed as entities distinct from words, and if they possessed that very form [of being denotable], then even one who does not know the word would perceive that form prior to the connection with the word. Yet, he does not so perceive it. Therefore, because it follows the positive and negative concomitance of the word, it is determined that the word itself possesses that form. // 174 //

He refutes [the objection] with the words "just as" (*yathā*). For just as color, taste, smell, touch, and sound appear distinctly in sensory cognition even without a word, so too do universals such as "cowness" and actions such as "going" be perceived even prior to words, by means of a non-conceptualizing [cognition] in their own distinct forms. However, subsequent to the grasping of the relationship [between word and object], there occurs merely the grasping of the relationship between the name and the named.
There is nothing further or additional beyond this. However, if it is said that sound and the other [objects] do not exist, it must be stated of what there is superimposition. // 175 //

Even the identity of [universals] with sound would be established if universals such as "cowness" were not perceived at all prior to their commingling with sound; however, this is not the case, because the cognition of them arises even for one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and object]. Thus he says: "And not... (verse 176).

He states that even beyond this, there is no figurative application of non-difference, using the words "śruti" (scriptural authority). He provides the reason with the word "vivekāt" (due to discrimination). The meaning is that by two sense organs, two objects—namely, sound and [the rest]—are perceived.
However, the function of the word consists merely in extracting the property of one or the other from those two.
He says "ananta" (infinite) to show that there is no superimposition of its own nature. // 178 //

It might be argued: "The word is a means for the cognition of the object; and properties belonging to a means are seen to be superimposed upon the goal, just as the properties of a mirror and so forth are [superimposed] upon the face and so forth. To this he says: "And not... The intention is that the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (anaikāntika). // 179 //

On this point, others say: "We do not deny universals (*jāti*) and the like. What then? We maintain that because cognition is permeated by the form of the word through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as 'this is a cow,' we speak of a superimposition of form. To them, he replies: "Always" (*nityam*). The intended meaning is this: if the cognition of cowness and so forth were always permeated solely by the form of the word, [then the following would ensue].
But no other form of these [objects] has ever been perceived;
how, then, can a difference in their forms be established from the nature of the word?
If there is no difference, upon what could anything be superimposed? // 180 //
And since there is no "other-naturedness" (*pārarūpya*) when non-difference is admitted, conceptual cognitions do not possess falsity; thus he says:
"If [there were] non-difference. But if one admits a difference of intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) on the ultimate level, the verbal formulation of superimposition (*adhyāropa*) is purposeless.
For an entity whose own-being is unmixed cannot be superimposed by those free from delusion as having the nature of another entity.
Furthermore, error is not possible for everyone at all times;
thus he says: "If there were difference. Therefore, he states that this conceptualization of superimposition belongs to those who advocate it solely on the basis of error: "by error. // 181 //
He states the seed of the error: "by means of the word. The sense is that an object once apprehended cannot be designated without a word.
Nevertheless, he asks what follows from this and replies: "the cow. The designation for all three—the denoted, the denoter, and the cognition—is identical:
"cow" as the word, "cow" as the object, and "cow" as the cognition. And that [object] is both the denoted and the cognition.
And [this applies to] the denotata and the cognitions thereof. The meaning is that for those persons who speak of them, a common designation, namely "cow," is perceived. // 182 //

[699] Even so, what has occurred regarding the meaning of "cow" (*go*)? To this he says: "In the instruction," etc. This is the meaning: the listener indeed conceptualizes in this way because this speaker employs the same word for all three;
thus, his experience is likewise identical across all three. And for that reason, it is itself an object of knowledge (*prameya*) for conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*).

Understanding the object, one determines that the cognition of the threefold domain has the nature of the speaker. That is to say, one understands it exactly as it was apprehended by the speaker. Thus, because subsequent listeners share a common designation in accordance with each preceding speaker, there arises the delusion of superimposition (adhyāsa). // 183 //

If it is argued that there is a delusion due to the commonality of the designation, why is the superimposition of the object itself not explained as occurring in the word and the cognition? For the seed of delusion is indeed the same; therefore, he says:
"Delusion. For the means [of cognition], namely thought and hearing, belong to the object which is insentient by nature and lacks self-luminosity; they are preceded by the means [of apprehension].

Thinking that "the state of being a *copeya* (a type of bird)" refers to something prior [to the word], they imagine it to be superimposed upon that [object]. Furthermore, the term *śruti* is defined as that which is heard, namely the word (*śabda*). Although the superimposition of cognition (*mati-adhyāsa*) was not previously introduced, it has been adopted by some;
and since it will be refuted by the very same reasoning used to refute the superimposition of sound (*śabda-adhyāsa*), it is presented here [alongside it]. Thus...

The Buddhist grammarians maintain that the referent—such as a universal (*jāti*) and so forth—is incapable of being defined because it is removed from the conceptual alternatives of being either distinct or non-distinct [from the individual]. However, since an external object is impossible in cases such as the arising of an empty sprout, it cannot be accepted;

therefore, the referent is nothing other than the form of cognition itself. But even that [position is untenable], because the form of the object is perceived prior to the cognition itself, and thus [the cognition] must be understood precisely through that [object].

It should be understood that [the objection] has been refuted by the determination of knowledge (*jñānāvadhāraṇa*). However, the avoidance of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) will be explained in the section on "Form" (*ākṛti*).
But in the case of the "void" (*śūnya*) and so forth, the possibility of an external object constitutes the doctrine of baselessness (*nirālambanavāda*). // 184 //

[700] Indeed, for those who contemplate the meaning skillfully, a cognition characterized by a distinct nature arises even with respect to the three; thus he says: "in 'cowness'. The meaning is that the cognition of both is inferred to be formless (anākāra). // 185 //
He states that this is another defect in the superimposition of the word: "And if... and so forth. The meaning is: "by way of non-difference from the word.

When the word is superimposed upon the die and other such objects, because of the oneness of the word and because the object—such as the die—would possess that same form, it would follow as a logical consequence that the die and so forth are also one. // 186 //
[Objection: "But surely there is indeed a unity among the three [words] through the exclusion of non-eyes; [Reply:

No, because it is not apprehended prior to the word, and because a word whose relation [to its meaning] has not been grasped does not convey meaning. Anticipating this objection, he says: "It might be so. The proponent of superimposition (adhyāsavādī) raises an objection according to his own intention: "In the case of 'cow' and so forth..."

The other [author] offers a reply from his own perspective, saying "No. He states the reason: "Because of oneness. For it has already been stated previously that even by means of non-conceptual [cognition], a single form is seen as persisting through words. // 187 //

[702] Since there is no conformity to a single form among the *vibhītaka* and other such things if they were real entities, he says: "The three. Here, it is the word alone that is common, being distinct from words denoting universals such as "cow" and so forth; it is not the object. // 188 //

But why, in this case as well, is the connection with a single property not accepted on the basis of being denotable by a single word, as in the case of a *śābaleya* cow and others? To this he says: "mutually... Furthermore, this cognition of distinct forms is not tenable under the theory of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), because there would be no differentiation of the form of the word;
thus he says: "that superimposition... (verse 189).

But is it not the case that the phoneme (*varṇa*) is not the word? What then? It is the *sphoṭa*. Therefore, one might suspect here that the *sphoṭa* is indeed distinct, as it is determined by the cognition of distinct meanings—this is what is meant by "they would be distinct. To this, he states the refutation: "No. He states the reason: "Because of the meaning. For doubt arises when a word has been uttered regarding its meaning; that [doubt] would not occur if there were a difference in the word itself.

[The opponent says: "There is doubt. [The author asks: "If there is doubt, what of it? To this he replies: "Not from the universal" (*na sāmānyāt*). For doubt is based on the perception of a commonality (*sāmānya*); that [doubt] is untenable when there is a difference in words. [The opponent suggests: "In that case, the doubt will arise from the similarity of sounds.

To this he replies: "Because there is no difference in form" (*rūpābheda*). This is the intended meaning: we shall explain later that there is no word-sphoṭa distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*). For the word is nothing other than the phonemes themselves.
And those [atoms] are perceived as having an undifferentiated form. // 190 //
He states another objection—that the distinction between words is difficult to articulate—with the words "in the case of *bhavati* and so forth. (191)

And he states that there is this further fault, ending with the words "How [could] the word...": for the completed form of the word is indeed non-different in both nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). And he says, "How so?", because this is not tenable. What, then, is the embodied object?

It cannot be the universal (*jāti*), because it is incorporeal (*amūrta*). As for the individual (*vyakti*), however, it is certainly not denied even by those who maintain the theory of superimposition (*adhyāsa*); and that [individual] is indeed embodied.

What is the fault? It is true. However, this is a refutation directed against those who maintain the theories of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and manifestation (*vivarta*). For the proponents of transformation believe that speech itself transforms into the form of objects; they are thus reproached: how can there be a material transformation of that which is immaterial? For only in the case of material things, such as clay and the like, is there a material transformation, such as a jar and so forth.

This is logical. The same should be said regarding the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). For it is logical that a material object, such as a face, should appear manifested in a mirror since it is perceived as material. But in the case of the manifestation of the immaterial, how can there be a cognition appearing as something material? // 192 //

Likewise, the classification that "cow," "horse," and so forth are genus-words (*jātiśabda*), while "white" and so forth are quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), would not be tenable if one disregarded the nature of the denotatum; thus he says: "Cow, horse," etc.
He states that even the relationship between qualifier and qualified does not hold without depending on external objects: "tree, *plakṣa*, etc. (verse 194).

Furthermore, since grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—as seen in cases such as "blue lotus"—is possible for both words and cognitions, it is not tenable that it arises from superimposition (*adhyāsa*) even in the case of the cognitions of objects; thus he says, "grammatical coreferentiality. Moreover, when two cognitions are unified upon a single locus, they become coreferential. Therefore, according to those who maintain the theory of superimposition, it must be stated where this unification occurs in this case. It cannot occur in the unique [particular], because that too would have to be postulated; thus he says, "upon a single [locus]. In our view, however, there is unification upon a single locus by way of the entry into the denotative part (*vācyabhāga*); this is how it should be distinguished. // 195 //

If, however, it is maintained that the synthesis has as its object only the unique particularity (*asādhāraṇa*) while having the generality of "being an entity" (*vastutva-sāmānya*) as its scope, then—since all words such as "cow" and "horse" would equally have "the entity" as their object—they would necessarily result in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Thus he says: "in the mere entity. Here, the author of the *Vārttika* [introduces this] even without establishing the acceptance of "being an entity," because of the abundance of faults [in the alternative view].
Thus, an over-extension [of the argument] has been stated. // 196 //

Even granting the restriction to unique particulars, the word "blue stone" (nīlopalapada) would not be applicable because of the infinity of individuals; yet it is observed to be used. Thus, he states another refutation: "And not... (na ca). // 197 //

Furthermore, you do not accept a universal "blue-lotus-ness" (*nīlotpalatva-jāti*) that is common to multiple individual blue lotuses, wherein the word could reside; thus he says, "And not... It is not merely that such a thing is not accepted, but there is also no logical justification for its admission; thus he says, "Of the word and the object... For two [aspects] are here superimposed upon the word "blue lotus. Therefore, following the parts of the word as they are heard, only two objects consisting of the superimposition of the word are understood.
For indeed, when there is a superimposition of two words, the unity of the object to be conveyed is not possible. // 198 //

If it is argued that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) results merely from simultaneous usage, then since the use of synonymous terms (*paryāyaśabda*) is sometimes observed when the meaning is not yet understood, those two would also possess coreferentiality; thus he says: "of the two words" (verse 199).
Furthermore, a word does not convey its meaning unless its relationship [to that meaning] has been apprehended, nor can a relationship be apprehended when the referent is not yet understood.
It cannot be experienced. Therefore, regarding this theory of superimposition (adhyāsa), it must be stated what kind of object is to be cognized at the time of experiencing the relationship;
thus he says: "And not... The sense is that it cannot be cognized in any form whatsoever. // 200 //
Why is it not possible?
To this he says: "At that time. For an object has the nature of a word; and one who has not mastered the linguistic convention is not capable of determining its identity with that [word].

Thus, in this case, the cognition of the relationship arises from superimposition, and from that [cognition] arises superimposition; the point is that there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) here.

Furthermore, one should not even suspect that the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] occurs through what is unique [to a single instance], because that would entail the consequence of the word never being used again with respect to another individual object; thus he says: "And not... (201).

Thus, it now follows by force that a word, independent of any relationship, possesses the power to superimpose its own form [onto an object]; and in that case, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even a first-time hearer would understand the object in that form. To this, he says: "In that regard" (tatra).

Nor can you say: "Even for you, the word is eternally connected with its meaning; why then does it not produce remembrance [of that meaning]? For in my view, there exists a denotable object distinct [from the word], and one who has apprehended the relationship between the denoted and the denoter remembers the meaning upon seeing the word. But for one who does not know "this is its denotable object," there is no remembrance of the meaning; thus, nothing is inconsistent. So he says: "In my [view]... (mama).

But for you, since there is no form of the denotable object (vācya) distinct from the form of the denoter (vācaka), even upon the first hearing, there would be the state of being superimposed; thus he says "for you" to connect with what preceded. // 203 //
He shows by way of a negative instance that this is not the case, with the words "just as" (yathā). // 204 //

And since even one who has grasped the word does not thereby comprehend the object, it follows that the denotable is not at all dependent upon the denoter; thus he says, "Therefore. However, because the Veda merely causes the recollection of an object already apprehended through other means of valid cognition, its dependence on those [other means] is logical;
thus he says, "Because it is a reminder. // 205 //
He summarizes: "By that," [verse 206].

Regarding the instructions for engagement and withdrawal—such as "one should act" or "one should not act"—it is argued that because the word itself is not of the nature of the object, the cognition of an object possessing that nature would be untenable; to this he says: *pravṛttau* (verse 207).
Furthermore, since there is a difference between synonymous words, it would follow that there is a difference in their meanings; to this he says: *karahastādi* (verse 208).

Moreover, this superimposition occurs either through similarity, as silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl, or through coloring, as the redness of a hibiscus flower [colors] a gem. Neither of these two, however, is possible in the case of the superimposition of a word. This is because, for one standing at a distance, neither coloring nor the perception of similarity is possible. He states this very point in the verse beginning with "the superimposition of the Self" (and its half).

As for the objection raised by the proponents of the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavādin*), who claim that just as the moon and other objects are perceived in water even though they are far away—as an illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)—so too will sound be perceived [in the ear], that is incorrect. Because a reflection is impossible for that which lacks form (*arūpa*), he says: "Even though far away... (verse 210).

Now, as for what was said—that because of being situated at a distance, coloring by the word is not possible—that is incorrect, because the word, by virtue of its all-pervasive nature (*vaibhava*), is present everywhere. To this he says: "The word...

Furthermore, this coloring is observed only with that which is perceptible by the same sense organ; just as the redness of a gem perceived by the eye is colored only by redness perceived by the eye. For when a crystal is being experienced by the sense of touch, the visual redness does not color it.
In this way, he states that an auditory sound is not able to color a visual object, saying: "And not... (na ca). // 292 //

Thus, first of all, that which was stated regarding the falsity of conceptual cognitions (*savikalpaka-jñāna*)—by way of the consequence of their having an extrinsic nature (*pārarūpya*) when they perceive what is non-sonorous as being of the nature of sound—that has been refuted. However, for those who maintain the theory of superimposition (*adhyāsa*), the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of inference and other means of knowledge is difficult to establish because conceptual cognitions are false; thus he says: "Inference... It is not only that the validity of inference and the rest is not established, [but...]

However, since all determinations depend upon conceptual construction (vikalpa), there would follow the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all worldly and Vedic transactions; thus he says: "of determination" (nirūpaṇasya). Determination (nirūpaṇa) means ascertainment (nirṇaya). // 213 //
[Objection: Is it not the case that everything other than speech is indeed false, because the entire universe consists of speech?

For the Śruti declares: "Just as all leaves are pierced by a single pin, so too all speech is pierced by the syllable *oṃ*; the syllable *oṃ* is indeed all this; speech alone gave birth to all the worlds. To this, he says: "Let it be so."
If everything were false, the very thesis itself would be false; therefore, the falsity of everything is not established. // 214 //

Moreover, this denial of the external world—also known by the name "superimposition" (adhyāsa)—is the Mahāyāna position. And that must be refuted precisely by means of the critique of the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyavāda); thus he says, "by the doctrine of emptiness. The mention of "intellect" (buddhi) is for the purpose of refuting the superimposition upon the intellect.
This has also been explained previously. // 215 //

He concludes the meaning of the section with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). "By cognitions of difference and identity, etc. means by cognitions of inclusion and exclusion (*anugata-vyāvṛtti*). // 216 //

Thus far, it has been stated that while verbal testimony has as its object a thing already apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the nature of that object does not depend upon the word itself. Now, however, although an object whose means of access is the word is not cognized in the absence of the word, nevertheless, there is no destruction of its own essential form (*svarūpa*). For it is not the case that because the pentad of objects beginning with visible form (*rūpa*) is not perceived in the absence of the eye and other [senses], they thereby become non-existent. This very point he expresses in two verses beginning with "śabdābhyupāyaka. And here, by virtue of its dependence on a means of access, the [objection of] non-existence is refuted.
For it has been stated that the reason [adduced] in the passage "not indeed [due to] the lamp, the sense-faculties, etc. is inconclusive; such is the distinction. // 217-218 //
[Objection: Let it be granted that the form of the object is distinct from the word. However, prior to the apprehension of the relationship, that [form] was not cognized in the form of the word;
but at a later time, it is cognized in that form. Thus, because there is a cognition of a form belonging to one thing (the object) as having the form of another (the word), it is false.
To this, he says: "Of the relationship... For the relationship between the signified and the signifier is eternal; therefore, even previously, the capacity to be signified by that word [was present].
It certainly existed; however, it was later manifested.

And even at that time, its nature as having the form of a word (*śabdākāratva*) did not constitute its identity with the word itself (*tadātmatā*). Therefore, since that which does not have that form is not perceived as having that form, how could there be any illusion? Furthermore, this "nature as having the form of a word" is spoken of merely by virtue of its connection with the word, but not because it has the word as its essence.

The distinction here is that in the passage beginning "If [the universal] such as 'cowness' were eternal," the erroneous nature [of the cognition] was refuted by accepting its nature as being of the essence of the word (*śabdātmakatva*). "Formlessness" (*arūpatā*) means the absence of the form of a word. But how is it understood that this [universal] existed in that form even prior to the apprehension of the relationship?

To this, he says: "simultaneously. For it is not the case that all people simultaneously perceive an object unmixed with the form of words. Indeed, at the very moment one person perceives an object as having no verbal form, another who is linguistically trained conceptualizes it as "this is a cow. Therefore, there is no apprehension of an object that does not possess a certain form as possessing that form. // 219 //
Here he raises an objection: "Regarding its form.
For just as that which does not have that form is not apprehended by everyone, so too that which does have that form is not [apprehended] by everyone; how then can it be so?
Thus [it is said]. He provides the rebuttal: "When there is a pair. He shows the nature of the investigation: "Is it rather... (220).
He states the conclusion: "Regarding existence and non-existence. It is not tenable that the state of having that form (tadākāratva) both exists and does not exist;

rather, for that which is present, perception and non-perception are logical due to the distinction between capacity and incapacity. Furthermore, the existence and non-existence of that capacity are themselves established by the difference in their substrata. Thus, the state of having that form is indeed present, but it is simply not experienced by those who lack the capacity.
Thus is the conclusion. // 221 //

Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration with the word "yathā" (just as). The meaning is: just as there is the capacity or incapacity [to perceive] color due to the difference between perceivers.

And since this will be explained in the section on the refutation of the relation (*sambandhaparihāra*), he says: "ity abhidhāsyate" (it will be explained). The particle *iti* here has the sense of "this.
He analyzes the capacity and incapacity with the word "tena" (by that): by which this... [1]

Since the establishment [of the distinction] according to capacity is logical, the discrimination is as follows: for a grasper who employs words as a means, there is a cognition with the form of the word, but not for another. // 222 //

Here he raises an objection: "Devadatta, etc. The word *tu* (but) serves to set aside what was previously stated, as in the phrase "it might be eternal. That which was said earlier—that this object is merely the form of the word—is not universally applicable (*avyāpaka*), because such a thing is impossible in the case of Devadatta and others; for in their case, the relationship [between name and object] has a beginning, and the object, Devadatta and so forth, is also impermanent. Therefore, regarding the two extremes [the past and the future],...

Through thorough discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), it is understood that the conformity to that [object], namely the nature of sound (*śabdarūpatva*), is impermanent. Therefore, since that which does not possess the form of the object is necessarily imagined there as having that form, it is false (*mithyātva*). // 223 //

He refutes [this objection] with the words "tatrāpi" (even there). The word *devadatta* also expresses its meaning—namely, that "the gods should give him"—by its own inherent power (*nijayā śaktyā*) through the medium of a benediction (*āśis*). Likewise, words such as *caitra* and others, which are based on [the conjunction of] lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), planets (*graha*), and so forth, possess an eternal relationship (*nityasaṃbandha*) just like words for "cow," "horse," and so on. Therefore, just as in those cases, there is no lack of conformity to that form; rather, the object which is given by the gods (*devair dattaḥ*) is the very thing that produces the cognition of that specific form.

The meaning of this is as follows: therefore, with respect to the cognition of that object's form, there exists an innate capacity (*autpattikī śakti*) between the apprehended and the apprehender, or between the signified and the signifier.

However, the mere application (*niyoga*) [of a word] to a newly formed individual is what is non-eternal. And it is not because of that non-eternality that the relationship between word and meaning becomes non-eternal, because the word does not have that [individual] as its meaning. // 224 //

In that case, how can there be truthfulness regarding those objects where words such as "Devadatta" and so forth function by mere convention (*niyoga*) without being etymologically meaningful (*anvartha*), and where words such as "Dittha" and so forth are devoid of any underlying correspondence?
For in those instances, the object is conceptualized solely through the nature of the word itself, and there exists no qualifying attribute inherent in the object.

And that very [conceptualization] is called "the conceptualization of names" (*nāmakalpanā*). However, if the term were to be taken according to its literal meaning (*anvarthatva*), then one would have to demonstrate only the conceptualization of action (*karman*) and so forth, as the case may be. Consequently, it would again follow that the conceptualization of names is false. To this, he provides an answer by accepting the view of certain [teachers], saying: "In that regard" (*tatra*). // 225 //

He states the rebuttal according to his own view: "But when... It is true that even subsequently this lump [of clay] is not apprehended as having the form of the word, being indeed devoid of that form. Rather, the name remains in that very same state;

it is the cause for the recollection of that very object exactly as it was previously understood. Therefore, since one thing is not apprehended under the form of another, how could there be falsity? But how is it that, in the conceptualization of a name, there arises the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "This is *Ḍittha*"?

For grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is observed in cases such as "blue lotus" through a qualifier that is inherent in the object. However, it must be explained how there can be coreferentiality between the word, the object, and the cognition when their domains are entirely distinct. Therefore, this [notion of coreferentiality] is merely an illusion. Not so. For it has been stated: "In this case, no entity possessing the form of the word appears. The meaning of the statement "This is *Ḍittha*" is not that [the word itself is the object].
"This [person] consists of the word 'Ḍittha'. For such a cognition does not occur; rather, it occurs as "this person has the name 'Ḍittha'.
Therefore, the conceptualization of a name is not an error. // 226 //

Another opinion holds that even prior to the application of a name, the object possessed the capacity to be apprehended in the form of that name; for it is impossible to conceive of something as being absolutely non-existent, like a flower in the sky. However, once the application of the name is made, that capacity is merely manifested. Therefore, since there is evidence for the existence of that form even prior [to the application], there is no "other-naturedness" (pārarūpya).
This is what he says: "By means of an injunction" (niyogāt). // 227 //

He elaborates on this very point with the words "sarvākāra" (of all forms): for an object indeed possesses the capacity to be delimited by every word. For when one or another word—such as *ḍittha* or *ḍavittha*—is applied to it, that very word causes it to be understood. Likewise, a word too is capable of bringing about the cognition of an object in all its aspects; wherever it is applied, it causes only that [object] to be understood. Therefore...
Thus, when the contingency of non-restriction arises, a mere restriction is established by the appointing agent, such as a father or other authority. // 228 //

[703] Thus, first, the argument for the transformation into another form (*pārarūpya*) has been refuted in every respect. Now, he dispels the possibility of invalidity due to the confusion of memory, by means of the following one and a half verses: "In that case," etc., [referring to] the cognition which arises even for a cognizer who is recollecting the relationship between a word and its object.
This [cognition] is not non-perceptual;

for when a cognition arises regarding an object in contact with the eye, that is perception, and at that time as well, the contact with the eye has indeed not ceased. Likewise, even though it arises from the recollection of what was previously apprehended—as in "this is that very same cow"—this too is not non-perceptual.

Because the eye, which is the cause of perception, has not ceased [to function]. Therefore, in this case, the status of being perception is not precluded by the prior recollection of the relationship between word and object and the subsequent synthesis of what was previously grasped; this will be demonstrated later than the initial thesis. Nor is this point already covered by the statement "nor is there here a connection between that [synthesis] and the sense-object," for in that context, it was merely asserted as a thesis that "even while recollecting, a person who conceptualizes according to his own mental properties possesses perception."

However, this has not yet been established. In the preceding section, up to the refutation of the superimposition of words (*śabdādhyāsa*), the conceptualization of its own properties (*svadharmavikalpa*) was demonstrated.

Now, however, the meaning of the phrase "even though remembering" (*smarann api*) is being elaborated upon. Therefore, that [preceding] is the introductory statement (*grahaṇakavākya*), while the subsequent portion is its detailed exposition (*tatprapañca*); thus, there is no fault. Furthermore, this [exposition] delights the minds of those who are inattentive, but not others.
But how is it that [cognition] lacks authority due to the intrusion of memory? To this he says: "They are indeed distinct. (230)

He demonstrates this very distinction by saying, "they are remembered. For it is the word and its relation that are remembered; therefore, those two are not perceptible, but the perceptibility of the object itself cannot be denied.

[Objection: But surely an object is apprehended only as it was previously apprehended; it is then recognized as "this is that very same [object]. Therefore, how can it be a case of perception? To this he replies: "Even though it has been apprehended. The meaning is: "by way of distinction," that is, by way of something additional. // 232 //

He demonstrates this very superiority [of perception] with the words "vyakti" (individual instance), etc. For a universal (*jāti*) previously apprehended in one individual instance is now apprehended in another individual instance; likewise, what was apprehended on the previous day is apprehended on the following day, and what was apprehended at the moment of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) is apprehended at the moment of determinate perception (*savikalpaka*).
Thus, because there is an additional object of determination, there is scope for valid cognition (*mīti*).
Furthermore, when time is understood as being within the range of an object connected with a sense faculty, it is understood by a perception produced by that very sense faculty;

thus, the perceptibility of its connection is established. For those who maintain that time is not perceptible, however, cognitions such as "slow" or "quick" would be without an objective basis (*anālambana*). [Objection: Let these very cognitions be the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of time; however, their object must be specified. If you say it is substance and so forth, we say no.

Because [time] does not arise as a mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), and because it is impossible to infer time if it were the object of that [cognition], and because the position that [cognition] terminates in its own part (*svāṃśa*) will be refuted in the Vijñānavāda section, it cannot have its own part as its objective support (*ālambana*). Therefore, that which is their objective support is indeed determined through perception (*pratyakṣa*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the distinction of states (*avasthābheda*) is included. But is it not the case that...?
One might object: "If only something more is being cognized, and not something previously already known, then how can there be validity?

To this he says: "That which was previously... For in the case of a verbal cognition accompanied by recollection, the nature of the word, the object, their relationship, and the temporal relation all manifest. Among these, since parts such as the word and so forth are objects of memory, let them indeed not be objects of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, the existence of the thing at the present time [is what constitutes the object of the new cognition].

Since it was not previously determined [by another means], there is an occasion for a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in that regard; thus, its validity is established. Furthermore, because it conforms to the operation of the sense faculties, it is perception (pratyakṣa). And this single means of valid cognition, designated as recognition (pratyabhijñāna), should be understood as being of the nature of both apprehension and recollection, having as its causes the mental impressions (saṃskāra) produced by prior cognitions and the present sense faculties and so forth. // 233 //
[Objection: But surely this [cognition] has an excessive object;

since it occurs after the time of recollection, how can it be perception? For this characteristic is not observed in non-conceptual perception. To this, he says: "For not... For being prior to recollection is not the definition of perception; rather, it is the state of being born from the sense faculties (*indriyajatatva*).
The meaning is that this [point] is no different here as well. // 234 //

If the very operation of the sense faculty were prevented by memory, then it would be sublated; consequently, the conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) that arises at a subsequent time might indeed occur. But this is not the case, as he says: "And not... (v. 235).

Since memory neither contradicts nor corrupts the sense faculty, therefore, whatever cognition arises from the contact between a sense faculty and its object—whether prior to or subsequent to that memory—all of that must be accepted as perception; thus he says, "Therefore" (tena). // 236 //

[Objection: Surely, even when the connection between the sense organ and its object exists, only some individuals conceptualize that object through universals (*jāti*) and so forth, while others do not. Therefore, since there is a lack of some specific factor within the causal complex itself that acts as a non-obstructing cause, conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-pratyaya*) is nothing but an error (*bhrānti*). To this, he replies with the two verses beginning with "vimanaskāḥ. This is the intended meaning: [The author’s response: It is not the case that all people conceptualize the object in the same way. For some, due to the influence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), conceptualization arises; for others, it does not. Furthermore, even among those who possess the complete causal complex, conceptualization occurs only when the mind is directed toward the object, not otherwise. Thus, the difference in conceptualization is due to the presence or absence of mental attention (*manaskāra*), which serves as a specific auxiliary cause. It is not that conceptual cognition is inherently erroneous. This is what is expressed by the two verses. The underlying intention is as follows: [text continues]
Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*) does not arise from mere linguistic proficiency or the contact of the sense organs [with their objects] alone;

even that depends upon the attention of the mind (*manas-praṇidhāna*) and other factors common to all [cognitions]. Therefore, even if for someone whose mind is distracted or who is deluded due to defects in the object—such as distance, subtlety, or similarity—the appearance "this is so-and-so" does not occur with extreme clarity, [it is still conceptual].
It is not reasonable to claim that, on this account, there must necessarily be an error even for one who is skilled in discerning subtle similarities and the like regarding the wholesome. // 238 //
Right here he states an illustration with the two verses beginning "Just as ṣaḍja, etc. The phrase "refined by that" means refined by the practice of ṣaḍja and the other notes. // 240 //

Just as even one unskilled in [the musical notes] such as *ṣaḍja* has a cognition of their distinct forms without the employment of words like "ṣaḍja," so too is "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like perceived as distinct by those who do not know or remember the words for them; thus he says: "For those... (verse 241).

However, that [object], though mixed with various universals (jāti), qualities (guṇa), and so forth, appears to one who does not know the word as distinct from heterogeneous individuals. But for those whose mental impressions are refined by the recollection of the word, only the universal and so forth, distinguished from the individual, appear;
thus he says: "mixed" (saṅkīrṇam). // 242 //

Since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are dependent upon memory, therefore, when the memory of a particular word manifests, by that very [memory] is the object then conceptualized. Just as form and so forth are perceived by one who possesses sight and the like, but not by another;

and even by one who possesses sight, if he is deaf, only form is perceived and not sound, because [sound] lacks the necessary means [of perception]. All of this is stated in the two verses beginning with "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is: "of the words which are the causes of discrimination."

Therefore, it is established that even determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is [a form of] direct perception. However, as long as words—which are the means for discrimination—have not become manifest to the intellect, perception remains indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*); yet this does not mean that [determinate perception] is not perception at all. Thus he says: "by that" (*tena*).

Therefore, we agree with what has been stated by the Buddhists—that even conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is accepted [as existing] in self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), but not in regard to an object because of its being a conceptualization—only in the case of conceptualizing the properties of another; we do not agree regarding conceptualizations of one's own properties, such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
Thus he says: "Therefore" (verse 246).

Therefore, since the universal of the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin), as well as their relationship, are known through determinate perception (savikalpaka-pratyakṣa), it is established that inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by perception; thus he says: "The state of being perceptible" (pratyakṣatva).

But why strive to establish that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is perception? For even by means of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), the practical application of inference and so forth will be possible for Buddhists and others, just as it is. To this he says: "And all..."—meaning that inference and the rest do not acquire their own nature without being preceded by non-conceptual cognition.
This will be explained in the inference of that [object]. // 248 //

Here he raises an objection: "But surely, in this way...
