Now, it might be argued: "Both of these cognitions, because the distinction between them is not grasped, do not appear as distinct from the cognition of real silver; and since that [cognition of real silver] is known to be the cause of practical activity, one acts here [toward the shell] as well."

Ah, this proposed solution is difficult to comprehend. To this we reply: does the distinction between the cognition of real silver and [the cognition of the shell] not appear here, or does their non-difference appear? In the former case, there would be no inclination toward action as in the previous instance. In the latter case, it would be the doctrine of erroneous cognition (*viparītakhyāti*).

There is no distinction [between the two cases] in that both consciousnesses appear as distinct and non-distinct objects. Now, if you consider that [the cognition] is not the reality because it is equivalent to the cognition of real silver, then there can be no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding its existence as such. For one who knows a *gavaya* to be similar to a cow does not employ the linguistic usage "this is a cow. And when there is a discrepancy in linguistic usage due to a cause of error, there is an absence of error for one who does not seek that object, since there is an absence of linguistic usage [regarding it].

If it is argued that even in this case there is the employment of words, we say no; for such usage is not observed in non-conceptual error. Furthermore, how could silver, which is remembered independently [of the present perception] and has not been presented [to consciousness], be negated in relation to the mother-of-pearl by the words "this is not"? For a negation must be preceded by a prior apprehension. How could that [negation] occur in the absence of such [apprehension]?

Upon attainment, one acquires the Self. But surely nothing here is sublated; rather, a distinction previously uncomprehended is now understood, as in "this is not silver. What is the meaning? That the silver is distinct from the mother-of-pearl. Oh, what skill in exposition this is on the part of your honors, that even consciousness, established in one way, is explained in another! If it is argued that the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding silver is sublated—

No; for it has already been stated that even that [subsequent cognition] does not apply [to the object]. For there would follow the consequence that a linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) that has not applied would lack sublation (*bādha*). Nor is the sublation of a linguistic usage due to a royal decree; rather, it occurs by way of precluding the application of a certain form (*tādrūpya*) to what was previously applied. Therefore, it is correct to say that one thing, having been applied under the form of another, is sublated. Furthermore, the application of that form has been made explicit in the cognition "this is silver. [Objection: But then it follows that [the cognition] is without an objective basis (*anālambana*).

It has been said: "True. That which perceives something as being otherwise than it actually is, that is accepted as cognition without an objective basis (*nirālambana-jñāna*). What is so wonderful about this? For it is precisely the lack of an external objective basis that we must refute with effort, since we admit that in all cases there is an external objective basis located in another place and so forth. How does [cognition] produce a cognition of what is not present?"

[Objection: Is this property of perception being superimposed upon all cognitions? For perception has as its object that which is present and immediate, whereas other cognitions do not. Moreover, this [cognition] is not perception, because it is a mere appearance (*ābhāsa*). As for what was said—"How can a sense organ connected with one thing be the cause of a cognition having the form of another?"—the answer to this is stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "The fault belongs to false cognition."
It is the cause; for when that [defect] exists, false cognition arises, whereas in its absence, there is the vision of right cognition.
But surely defects only obstruct an effect and do not produce another effect? No; for in a dream, due to a defect of the mind, even that which is not present appears as if it were present.

For an effect, whose acquisition of its own nature depends upon its causes, becomes defective when those causes are defective; thus, this is not untenable. And this is the defect of cognition: that which has one object as its domain possesses the form of another. Therefore, a cognition produced by defective causes apprehends what is present under the form of silver that is not present; thus, for a cognition that has both [the shell and the silver] as its objects, there is an objective basis. [The contact of] the self, the sense organ, the mind, and the object...

For [the absence of defects] is the cause of knowledge. When defects are absent, it is the cause of correct knowledge; when they are present, however, it is the cause of erroneous knowledge. Thus, the distinction between knowledge that accords with reality and knowledge that does not is well-stated. But what is the definition of perception by which it is [considered] in accordance with reality? To this he says: "that which has the appearance... [meaning] knowledge that has such-and-such a form.

Therefore, that arising of cognition in a person which occurs through the conjunction of the sense-faculties is accepted as perception (*pratyakṣa*). How could that be non-correspondent with reality? (19)

[Objection: But was it not already stated that if the sūtra were intended as a definition (lakṣaṇa), there would be over-extension? Furthermore, by one who says that perception is not defined by this sūtra, how can the sūtra now be described as having the purpose of providing a definition? To this he replies: "In its complete form. As the sūtra stands, it is not a definition because of the confusion of appearances; however, according to the view of the author of the Vṛtti, it is capable [of defining] when its words are rearranged.
Regarding the phrase "in order to characterize the definition":

how then is it complete? To this he says, "of *tat* and *sat*. For, according to the literal reading of the Sūtra, the definition of perception would be merely "that which is born from the contact of the sense organs"; and since that [contact] is no different even in the case of a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). But when [the words] are transposed, then...

In the *Upaskāra*, it is stated that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is that cognition which arises when there is contact between the sense organ and the appearing form, due to the mental apprehension of the form of the cognition;

thus, in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, because there is no contact with the sense organ regarding the appearing [silver], the over-extension [of the definition] does not apply.
He states the meaning of the preeminent word "good" (*sat*) as "having the sense of excellence. Now, previously... [2, ...]

The word *sat* has been explained as qualifying "conjunction" (*samprayoga*) by virtue of its having a present object. How, then, is it said to have the sense of "excellent"? And it is appropriate that it qualifies conjunction; for, as was stated previously, if that [qualification] were not specified, the yogic perception arising from conjunction with future objects and so forth would remain unexcluded. This is also [the case] because of its occurrence [in the compound], even though it is read separated [from the term it qualifies].

The compound is even more difficult to justify. Furthermore, since there is indeed a dependence on that which is such [i.e., correct perception]—namely, that "this is a correct perception"—being dissatisfied with this alternative formulation, he states another way: "Or else" (*yadvā*). Here, both *tat* and *sat* are to be supplied (*adhyāhāra*). Among them, the supplied word *tat* is for the purpose of referring to the appearing form (*bhāsamānākāra*), while the other (*sat*) is for the purpose of referring to the nature of perception (*pratyakṣarūpa*).

However, it should be discerned that the word *sat*, being recited in proximity to *samprayoga*, has precisely that [contact] as its specific meaning; whereas the word [implied by] *adhyāhṛta* has "excellence" (*śobhana*) as its meaning. // 20 //
But surely, since the definition of a semblance (*ābhāsa*) has not been stated, it is not possible to demonstrate the distinction between direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and its semblance;

therefore, he says: "by implication" (*arthāpattyā*). When it is said that "direct perception is of such a kind," it follows by implication that what is not of such a kind is a semblance. Here, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, having raised the doubt as to how the distinction between being produced from contact with that [object] and not being so produced can be understood, stated the subverting factor (*bādhaka*).
For where a cognition arises that "this is not so," it occurs upon contact with something other than that; whereas a contrary [cognition] occurs upon contact with that very thing.

This is incorrect. What is the reason that the former is sublated by the latter, rather than it being logical that the later, inferior [cognition] is sublated by the former? To this he says: "The sublating... For that is indeed the sublater.

That which does not subvert anything else cannot even establish itself; thus it is said in reply: "Therefore, it is logical that the former subverts the latter. It will be stated in the sixth [book] that even a later rule is stronger when it is independent of the former. However, where the later rule depends upon the former, there the former is stronger, as was stated in the third [book]. // 21 //

Furthermore, does the sublation of the prior [cognition] by the subsequent one consist in the falsity of the existent [prior cognition], or in the invalidation of its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? If it were the invalidation of its status as a *pramāṇa*, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). However, falsity is not established without sublation;

and since sublation is dependent upon that [falsity], there is a circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, he says: "And that... Indeed, the arising of the subsequent [cognition] does not depend on the ascertainment of the falsity of the prior; rather, the subsequent [cognition] arises from its own causes independently of that. Thus, there is no dependence on another regarding its production.

Nor is there any need for a causal construction [of the cognition], because cognition is of the nature of awareness (*avabodha*), and because that [awareness] does not depend on anything else for the illumination of its own object.

Therefore, there is no mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*). If, then, the subsequent [cognition] is independent of the preceding one and thus sublates it, what does the preceding [cognition] depend upon that it should be sublated?
For that [subsequent cognition] is also indeed independent;

therefore, he says "and not" (na ca). Even though it is independent of what follows it, nevertheless, because it does not appear as having the nature of a sublater of a future [cognition], it is not a sublater. // 22 //

In that case, however, where there is no emergence of a sublation such as "this is not so," but rather a cognition of a defect in the cause (*nimitta*), there the circularity (*itaretarāśraya*) is unavoidable. The sublation is to be produced there by the defect in the cause; and that [sublation] can be produced only if the prior [cognition] lacks validity.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that [the cognition] is invalid because it is subsequently sublated;

therefore, he says: "on account of the cause" (*nimitta*). For generally, errors such as [perceiving] yellow in conch shells and the like, which arise from defects such as bile, are later sublated. Indeed, a correct realization occurs: "This is not yellow; this is white. Therefore, it is not [invalid].

In that case, falsity arises merely from the awareness of a defect in the cause (*nimitta*). However, where even when a defect in the cause is known, there is no subsequent sublation because the cognition of that form persists—just as the disorientation of one who is lost does not cease even though he knows the cause of his confusion—it is not a case of mutual dependence, since the determination [of truth] occurs through the correction provided by another person. // 23

"In that case, how is it [uncontradicted] where there is no subversion, as in the cognition of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, among other people and the like? And that [cognition of genus] is not real, because it cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of being either distinct or non-distinct [from the individual]. To this he says: 'of all' (*sarveṣām*). For that which does not undergo subversion in other places and so forth is uncontradicted and is indeed correct. [Objection: "But even in that case, a sublating cognition must be produced on account of its logical inconsistency."

How is this correctness established? To this he says: "For not... Indeed, for one whose sense organs are unimpaired, there is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consisting of the recognition of a prior form in other individual bodies. How could that be sublated by a logical contradiction (*bādhana*)? For when the mouth of one who is unlearned is forcibly closed by a stronger person, it does not find its own [expression]. And it has been said even by those of our own school: "Not..."
Inference whose object is a cause contradicted by perception does not attain validity, just as the inference of coldness in fire [does not]. // 24 //

He states that this is a clear instance of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) in the phrase "in the case of universals and so forth" (*jātyādiṣu*). For here, the sublation-cognition (*bādhakabuddhi*) arises because the cognitions of universals and so forth are false;

and their falsity [is established] upon the arising of that sublation-cognition. However, there is no sublation-cognition arising from a particular (*vyakta*)—as there is in cases such as the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

23} If, then, falsity is not understood through the mere defect of the cause in the absence of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*), how can it be said [in the Nyāya-sūtra] with a distinction: "that whose instrument is defective" and "where there is a cognition that it is false"? For in that case, the cognition of falsity itself would have been stated as the cause for incorrectness. Therefore, the object [of the two cases] must be specified.

It is explained as follows: Suppose a person previously ascertained that there was one moon, but now, with his eyes pressed by a finger, he sees two. For him, who has developed doubt based on his prior cognition and has now clearly perceived a defect in the cause, a definitive conclusion arises: "The previous cognition was produced from non-defective causes, whereas this [present cognition] originates from a defect in its cause, which has been clearly identified."

And the defect of the effect is necessarily determined by the defect of the cause; therefore, it is incorrect [to claim otherwise]. Thus, in this case, the prior experience is the cause for the arising of doubt.

The determination of falsity occurs precisely through the ascertainment of a defect in the cause. In the same way, the falsity of external scriptures is also ascertained solely through the ascertainment of a defect in their cause; for their contents are not directly sublated, since they are of human origin and thus subject to the suspicion of defects in their causes.
Thus, it is entirely logical that there are two types [of wrong view]. // 25 //

[Objection: Let it be granted that the cognition of birth and so forth does not invalidate [the self]. But how can that [cognition] possess validity? For the nature of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) is common to both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*). Therefore, because deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed, doubt is appropriate. Furthermore, the various conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) such as "subsistence" (*vṛtti*) and so forth, even if they do not themselves induce invalidity, likewise obstruct validity. To this he says: "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*). If...

Since validity and invalidity are both invariably connected with the nature of cognition (*jñānatva*), there might indeed be uncertainty; however, it has been established that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Therefore, a determination that is not sublated by the cognition of the existence of universals (*jāti*) and so forth is logical. And this cognition is not ours alone;
even those who deny universals and the like [must admit it].
It exists for them as well; for they too, without denying the cognition of that [object], cannot possibly deny birth and the other [characteristics]. // 26 //
Thus ends the commentary on the work of the Vṛttikāra in the Kāśikā-ṭīkā composed by the Preceptor Sucarita Miśra.

{2,24} Here, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), following the objection that "surely every cognition is without an external object, like a dream," establishes the existence of external objects by stating, "For how could the well-ascertained intellect of one who is awake be erroneous? He demonstrates the utility of this [establishment] for the present inquiry into the meaning of the Veda with the four verses beginning with "pramāṇatve... For indeed, everyone...

This entire elaboration of the Mīmāṃsā system is based solely upon external objects. For instance, it was asserted in the *Codanā-sūtra* that "only the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is the means of valid cognition regarding dharma; the perception of yogis, the Buddha’s scriptures, and so forth, are not valid means of cognition. This [assertion] would be untenable if the referent of the term "injunction" were not an external object. By the very presentation of its status as a valid means of cognition, there is included the acceptance of the following: the inherent nature of the relationship between word and meaning discussed in the first quarter of the second chapter (*adhyāya*), the eternality of words, the existence of the basis for the comprehension of sentence-meaning, and the composition of Vedic sentences which are not of human origin.
Furthermore, by the presentation of [the Veda's] lack of authority, it should be shown that the reasons for non-authority indicated in the *Pratyakṣasūtra* are being adopted.

Likewise, even that which was asserted in the *Codanāsūtra* itself regarding the nature of dharma and adharma— otherwise known as merit and demerit— by means of both the verbal testimony and the sense of the passage, [is here addressed].

Even that cannot be demonstrated if there is no external object. For it has been described therein that the nature of merit and demerit is established by the authority of injunctions (*codanā*) consisting of prescriptions and prohibitions. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one includes the turning away from unwholesome acts, which is devoid of the nature of both merit and demerit. Whatever thing is the means for achieving an end, or its opposite, that is [the referent] of the terms "merit" and "demerit."
"Groundless. However, turning away from the inauspicious results neither in pleasure nor in pain; thus, it is devoid of both forms.

This too has been established by the word "object" (*artha*) found in the *Codanāsūtra*. And by the phrase "its fruit," one takes up the fruit consisting of the desirable and the undesirable for the threefold object of Vedic cognition—namely, merit, demerit, and that which is neutral. This also is included within the very definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*).

For it is not possible to experience the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *dharma* and so forth without its connection to a result being established. Thus, in this way, there is a complete utility for the first chapter (*prathama-pāda*) in establishing external objects; likewise, there will also be utility for what is to be stated [in subsequent chapters]. For the meanings of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras consist of the relationship between the goal and the means, the injunction itself, the object to be enjoined, the praise, and the recollection (*smṛti*) of that which has been enjoined.

The scope of the *arthavāda* (explanatory passages) is established even without an external object. For, as will be stated in the section on the *audumbara* [wood], in the case of the passage "The sacrificial post is made of *audumbara* wood, for the sake of attaining strength," since there is no injunctive force (*vidhi*), the connection of the quality of being *audumbara* with a fruit is not established. Likewise, in the section on *arthavādas*, the utility of *arthavādas* for the purpose of praise (*stuti*) has been demonstrated. For it is said there:

"Because the Veda has action as its purpose, those [parts] that do not have that as their purpose are useless" (1.2.1). The meaning of this is as follows: the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) maintains that only those [Vedic passages] which teach an action or something connected to an action may be authoritative; however, those which do not have action as their purpose—such as "He wept" and "Because he wept"—do not establish any dharma. Thus the objection is raised.
It has been stated [in the sūtra]: "But because they form a single syntactical unit with the injunctions, they would serve the purpose of praising those injunctions" (1.2.7).

This is its meaning: the *arthavādas* would be authoritative by virtue of their meaning being in the form of praise for that which is to be enjoined. But how can they have the purpose of praise? For it cannot be the case that praise is not required as the meaning of the *arthavādas*. It is not so.
Because it is required. Indeed, praise is required by the injunction, which is also known by the name *śabdabhāvanā*.

For that [injunction], while impelling a person toward action, requires the knowledge of the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the object of that activity. And the *arthavādas*, having been studied through the force of the injunction for Vedic study (*svādhyāyavidhi*), do not reach their conclusion as long as they lack a purpose; thus, when the requirement arises as to "what is to be done in this regard," [the *arthavādas* fulfill that need].

When the capacity [of the explanatory passages] is being determined, once a certain degree of interest has somehow been generated in the mind through the process beginning with the grasping of the syllables,
it is ascertained that the explanatory passages (arthavādas) serve as the purpose for that [injunction]. For an injunction requires such interest,
and since those [explanatory passages] are able to produce it to some extent, they— revolving in the mind as having no other purpose— are thus established.

Thus, they are determined to have that as their purpose. Therefore, this is the meaning of the treatise: it is by means of the *arthavādas* alone that an action, having been made attractive, conduces to prosperity (*abhyudaya*). And since the nature of an injunction (*vidhi*) has already been explained previously, it will not be elaborated upon here. The meaning of the mantras will also be discussed in the section on mantras (*mantrādhikaraṇa*). In that context, after citing mantras such as "I cut the grass, the seat of the gods" (*barhir devasadanaṃ dāmi*), an investigation was conducted.

— Are these [mantras] for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*) merely by virtue of being uttered, or are they for the purpose of manifesting a meaning? In this regard, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was established as having an unseen purpose through arguments such as "because of an injunction for that purpose" (1.2.31), even though it is precisely the meaning which the mantra manifests.

In that very context, this [mantra] is seen being employed by the Brahmana, just as the first mantra, "Spread yourself wide" (*uru prathasva*), is used to spread out the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). If this mantra were intended solely for its meaning, then since its employment would already be established by its own indicative power (*liṅga*), its explicit mention in the injunction would be redundant. Therefore, when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was raised that "mantras do not have their words intended to convey meaning," it was replied: "But [the meaning] is not distinct... (*aviśiṣṭas tu...*) [Mīmāṃsāsūtra 1.2.40].

Thus it is. For just as the meaning of Brāhmaṇa passages, when being perceived, is not unintended, so too it is with the mantras. Since they too reveal a meaning that is useful for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), how could these mantras have words that are unintended? For at the time of performance, rites such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa cannot be performed if they are not remembered.

[Mantras] depend upon the cause for the recollection of their own designated meanings. And mantras, like explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), linger while awaiting [an application], wondering "What indeed should be done by us?", because they possess a connection with the refinement of study acquired through the force of the injunction to study one's own Veda (*svādhyāyādhyayana-vidhi*). Since an application is impossible for that which lacks efficacy, when examining its capacity, they are determined to have the purpose of effecting a prescribed recollection that is required by the sacrifice and not accomplished by any other means. As they say:
The recollection of the constituent elements of the ritual, which necessarily occurs during performance,
is regulated by mantras that have no other means of accomplishment and no other purpose.

Thus it is said. As for the objection that the application [of the mantra] would be purposeless, that is not so; for the sentence serves as an *arthavāda* (explanatory praise). For "spreading" (*prathana*) is heard there [in the text]. The meaning is: "This kind of spreading is praiseworthy, namely, that which is performed with this mantra. This, then, is the relationship between injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory praises (*arthavāda*), and mantras.

The meaning [of the Veda] is not established if there is no external object. Thus, taking as an example the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*," it was deliberated whether this is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). Having raised this doubt, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) was proposed that it is an injunction of a quality because it effects a specific mode of activity; for those who enjoin a quality effect a specific mode of activity.

Otherwise, the mere name would be meaningless. Since these words are capable of denoting some instrument such as a spade by virtue of their connection with the action of breaking open, it follows that they are injunctions of accessory materials (*guṇavidhi*). To this, it is replied: they are not injunctions of accessory materials. For these are in grammatical apposition with the object (*karman*), because of the use of the instrumental case. Indeed, in this context, the object is expressed as the means for the production of cattle in the statement, "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the *udbhid*. What has been said? [That the word denotes the instrument.]

"One should bring about the sacrificial animals by means of the sacrifice. Therefore, in the case of "by means of the *udbhid* sacrifice," the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is indeed explicit. However, if it were an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*), since the sacrifice itself lacks the nature of being the *udbhid*, there would have to be coreferentiality through the figurative indication of possession (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*), namely, "by means of a sacrifice possessing the *udbhid*. And in that case, the figurative indication itself would be a fault. [Objection: But if this is so, then even in cases such as "one should sacrifice with rice-grains" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), [the coreferentiality] would be with the instrument of the productive operation (*bhāvanā*).

Words such as *vrīhi* (rice) and others, when uttered in conjunction with the word *yajati* (he sacrifices), would come to be the names of rituals. This is not so, because their meanings are already well-established (*nirūḍha*). For the meaning of a word whose sense is unknown or doubtful is determined precisely through its well-known grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with another term; however, a word whose meaning is firmly established cannot be displaced from its own primary sense. And it has been said:

A word whose meaning is unknown or doubtful is determined by its non-differentiation in usage from well-known words; however, a word that is firmly established in its conventional sense is not displaced from its own primary meaning.

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, because the breaking forth—that is, the manifestation—of cattle is performed by means of this rite, the word *udbhid* denotes the rite through its connection [to that result]. Since there is utility even for those [words] mentioned as injunctions of a relationship between a quality and a fruit, they are not purposeless.
Consequently, it is established that words of this class serve a function in the rite precisely as names of the action. This applies to words such as *citrayā* and so forth.

The reasons for [the terms] being names (*nāmadheya*) are not enumerated here for fear of prolixity. In some cases, because there is no other word that can bring about the ritual action (*karman*), the term must indeed be an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). For example, in the case of "the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni" (*āgneyo ’ṣṭākapālaḥ*), the word *āgneya* is an injunction of a ritual action accompanied by a quality.

This is because, prior to the injunction of the connection between the substance and the deity, the form of the ritual action is not understood, such that the word *āgneya* could function as its name.

The phrase "it would be a name" (*nāmadheyaṃ bhavet*) and so forth—stated in the section on Names (*nāmadheyapāda*)—is to be understood as having been introduced by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) and continuing until the end of the chapter.
Furthermore, the subject matter stated in the section on Tradition (*smṛtipāda*) is also to be understood as ending with what has not yet been mentioned here.

And in the course of demonstrating the utility of direct Vedic revelation (*pratyakṣaveda*), the meaning of the section on Names follows immediately after the utility of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the rest.

...is enumerated. Therein, by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the subject matter of the *Smṛti-pāda* is enumerated. For instance—having cited the *Aṣṭakā* rites and others whose Vedic basis is not heard, when there arises a doubt as to whether they constitute *dharma* or *adharma*, [the Sūtra states]:
"Since *dharma* has its root in the Word (*śabda*), that which lacks a scriptural basis (*aśabda*) should be disregarded" (1.3.1).

Having thus adopted this position, it was established on the basis that the Veda is their root: for all Smṛtis cannot establish themselves unless there is prior knowledge (*pūrvajñāna*). And this foundational prior knowledge must be either an error, a direct perceptual experience, or produced by a human-authored scripture (*pauruṣeyāgama*).

[The source of the Smṛti] must be either delusion or that which is produced by an [erroneous] injunction. In that regard, it is first of all improper for authoritative persons such as Manu and others—who are themselves subject to error—to compose the foundational texts of the Smṛti.
For it is already difficult to assert that those sages were indeed subject to error; and as for the composition of a great literary work by those who are erring, [that is even more impossible].

Furthermore, it is impossible even to imagine that this [tradition] has been grasped by the Noble Ones (ārya) who perceive [reality], based on memories passed down from the beginning of time. Moreover, the notion that experience can have a supersensible object was refuted in the *Pratyakṣasūtra*.
Even the word of a person, lacking a possible basis, is simply not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). Deception, like error, must also be rejected.

However, since the injunction (*codanā*) serves as the basis for the Smṛti of the three castes who possess a connection with the Veda, it is simpler to merely postulate that [Vedic] injunction itself. But one might object: "In that case, why are injunctions such as those for the Aṣṭakā rites not perceived, just like the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites? This is not untenable; for the Vedic revelations (*śrutis*), resting upon many scattered branches (*śākhās*), are intermingled with instructions concerning both ritual sacrifices (*kratu*) and human goals (*puruṣārtha*).

Is it not possible that those who are negligent today do not perceive [the Vedic source] through discrimination? Therefore, it is established that even though it is not currently heard, the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) is the cause of the *aṣṭakā* and other such duties; thus, the *aṣṭakā* and others are indeed *dharma*. In this way, there is an inference of a Vedic text (*śruti*) from texts that are not in conflict with directly perceived *śruti*. However, when there is a contradiction with directly perceived *śruti*, a *śruti* cannot be inferred; this is the point of the section on "Contradiction" (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).

It has been stated. Furthermore, it must be shown later on that the authority of *ācāra* (customary practice) and the examination of the relative strength (*balābala*) between it and *smṛti* (tradition), and so forth. Moreover, in all cases characterized by difference (*bheda*) and the like, [such difference] is not possible through their own sets of means of proof, such as "difference of words" (*śabdāntara*) and so on, if an external object does not exist. It will be explained that the difference among the productive forces (*bhāvanā*) of sacrifice (*yāga*), oblation (*homa*), and giving (*dāna*) arises precisely from the difference of words, as in: "One should sacrifice with *soma*," "He offers the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*)," and "He gives gold to the son of Atri. And likewise, [the difference] of the *samidh* [offerings]...

In the case of the five *prayāja* offerings beginning with "he sacrifices" (*yajati*), although there is no difference in the words themselves, their distinction is shown because otherwise the repetition would be purposeless. In the statement "he offers three oblations," the distinction between the oblations is shown because the number resides in their separateness.

Furthermore, in the case of "Now this is the *Jyotis*; one should sacrifice with it," there is a distinction of rites due to the different name, *Jyotis*, from the *Jyotiṣṭoma*. [And] in the *vaiśvadevī*...

And because of the lack of contradiction with the *ikṣu* (molasses) enjoined as the primary element in the originative injunction, "Molasses for the Vājins," the *vājina* (whey), failing to find a place within the Vaiśvadeva rite, necessitates the assumption of another sacrifice as its own locus. This is the distinction based on the quality (*guṇa*) of the *vājina*.

In the case of the Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana, the statement "He performs the Agnihotra for a month" [constitutes a separate rite] from the regular Agnihotra due to the difference in context (*prakaraṇāntara*).

There is a distinction regarding the Kauṇḍapāyina-homa sacrifice. Thus, in the second [book], the sixfold differentiation of action (*karmabheda*) has been explained through various means such as the introductory discussion (*upoddhāta*). In the third [book], however, the accomplishment of application (*viniyoga*) for the sixfold nature of subsidiarity (*śeṣatva*), characterized by being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*), has been stated. For instance, once it is understood in a general sense through the direct statement of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā-śruti*) that redness (*aruṇimā*) is an auxiliary to the action, the specific action—namely, "one buys with the red one" (*aruṇayā krīṇāti*)—is obtained from the syntactical connection (*vākya*).

As for application by indicative power (*liṅga-viniyoga*): it is the application of the *barhis*-mantra—whose status as a general auxiliary has been determined by the force of its recitation within the context—to the cutting of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), based on its *liṅga*, which is synonymous with "capacity" (*sāmarthya*). As for application by context (*prakaraṇa-viniyoga*):

it is the connection of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, which are recited within the context of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice and require an objective to be accomplished, with that [context] which requires an assistance; this is characterized by the mutual requirement of both.

For we explain *prakaraṇa* (context) in this very way. As for *krama-viniyoga* (application by order), however, it concerns those subsidiary elements (*aṅga*) recited in proximity to a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) that has no further expectancy for the assistance provided by the archetypal sacrifice (*prakṛta*). For in that case, application by context is not possible; for context consists of an expectancy that extends to both [the archetype and the ectype], whereas here the modified sacrifice is devoid of such expectancy, being already embraced by the ritual items obtained through the medium of the archetypal assistance.

However, because the recitation of the subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) in close proximity [to the main rite] would otherwise be purposeless, their application (*viniyoga*) therein is determined precisely by that proximate recitation. As for application by name (*samākhyā-viniyoga*), it is as follows: regarding those items designated by the name *ādhvaryava* (pertaining to the Adhvaryu), [it is understood that] "these must be performed by the Adhvaryu by means of this [text]."

In the fourth [book] as well, it will be explained that the relationship of the employed and the employer (*prayojya-prayojakatva*) belongs to items such as the fetching of curd and the *āmikṣā* offering, whose status as subordinate (*aṅga*) and principal (*aṅgin*) has been determined by direct statement (*śruti*) and other means. For it has been established that whatever is understood through direct statement and other means to be a subsidiary (*śeṣa*) to something else is employed by that thing. Therefore, even here in the definition of employment (*prayukti-lakṣaṇa*), the collection of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-gaṇa*) consists precisely of direct statement and the rest.

Even in the case of the definition of subsidiary elements (*śeṣa*), the restriction of sequence for the subsidiaries, the principals (*śeṣin*), or both, is established solely by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other criteria, distinguished by slight differences. For instance, in the rule "The Adhvaryu, having initiated the Gṛhapati, initiates the Brahman," the restriction of sequence is established by the direct scriptural statement of the suffix *-ktvā*. Similarly, although a different order might be understood from the textual recitation (*pāṭha*) in the case of "He offers the Agnihotra; he cooks the gruel," [the sequence is fixed by other means].
This means that there is a reversal of the fixed order of sequence. For if the cooking were performed after the oblation, it would be purposeless.

Furthermore, since the oblation cannot proceed in the absence of the sacrificial material (*havis*), it is established by implication that the cooking must indeed take place prior to the oblation. Thus, this is simply an *liṅga* (an indicative mark), differing from it in name alone.

For it is determined that capacity alone is the mark (*liṅga*) of entities. Here too, the determination of the rule of sequence occurs precisely through the observation of the capacities of substances and actions. However, the rule of sequence for the five [fore-sacrifices], such as *samidho yajati* and so forth, arises from their textual recitation (*pāṭha*). For since many ritual items cannot possibly be performed simultaneously by a single agent, a sequence is necessarily required.

Since performance depends upon comprehension, when [the elements] are stated in a sequence, they are understood in that very same way; thus, when there is a requirement for a sequence in the performance, that very sequence is determined. This is because it is untenable to abandon what has been perceived and adopt what has not been perceived. This rule of sequence is also established by *sthāna*—which is another name for *pāṭha* (textual order). An example of the determination of sequence from *sthāna* is found in the *Sādyaska* sacrifice.

Regarding the injunction, "In the ritual action, one sacrifices the animals together," when it is enjoined that the Agniṣomīya, Savanīya, and Anubandhya animals are to be sacrificed together at the place of the Savanīya, there arises the expectation: "Which one should be performed first? In response to this, the Savanīya—being understood through its position (*sthāna*)—is determined to be performed first. Its place of performance is that [very spot]. This is the sequence characterized by proximity of performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*). Previously...
However, [the order] characterized by proximity in location (*sādeśya*) is twofold; thus the third [type of] sequence is divided into two. As it has been said:
"In that regard, sequence is held to be of only two kinds, characterized by proximity in location;
due to proximity in recitation (*pāṭha*) and proximity in performance (*anuṣṭhāna*), it is the cause for application (*viniyoga*)."

Thus, there is a restriction of sequence by way of initial performance (*pravṛtti*). For example, when it is enjoined, "One sacrifices seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati," regarding these animals, a doubt arises as to whether—when the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and other rites obtained through the *codaka* (transfer rule) are to be performed on any one of them—the second and subsequent animals follow the very same initial performance, or if there is no such restriction. In this case, since there is no cause for restriction, [the view is] that of the initial performance.
Having adopted the position that there is no fixed order because there is no inherent necessity for one, the rule [of order] is actually demonstrated by the very first performance.

For, by the force of the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), the simultaneity of the animal sacrifices is established; and since this cannot be avoided due to unavoidable delays, it does not permit any further interval between the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). This is because the animals, together with their subsidiaries, must be performed simultaneously.

Even if urged by the Lord, since it is impossible for Him to bring about [the result] in such a manner, the intervention of unavoidable obstacles is permitted by the Ordainer (vidhi). And in that case, because there is no cause for inequality, the intervention of auxiliary factors (aṅga) is exactly the same for all. When the first ritual act has been performed by the agent, immediately thereafter, for the sake of performing the other auxiliaries—

When the agent is impelled by that very primary [act], and is drawn toward other animals by the force of simultaneity based on the authority of the injunction for performance (*prayogavacana*), that animal awaits the performance of its own constituent parts (*padārtha*) in the other animals. And at the end of that, it draws the agent toward the performance of the second constituent part. In this way, among the seventeen animals, by means of sixteen...

The absence of an interval between each [action] is prescribed and permitted. However, because no specific distinction [in the interval] is perceived, it is impossible to rely upon any particular interval.
Therefore, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that the performance of the second and subsequent actions also begins from that very point, there is a fixed order (*kramaniyama*).

Furthermore, this [order] is indeed included within the context (*prakaraṇa*), as it is based solely on the single means of knowledge that is expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*); thus, even each individual animal is [to be treated] without an interval.

It implies the performance of the constituent elements (*padārtha*). And the performance of those elements occurs in proximity to themselves. Therefore, the determination of sequence (*krama-niyama*) arising from the mutual requirement (*ubhayākāṅkṣā*) becomes contextual (*prākaraṇika*). Furthermore, the determination of sequence for the constituent parts follows the order of the principal acts (*mukhya-krama*), as in the case of the two rites dedicated to the female and male deities Sarasvatī and Sarasvant, which arise simultaneously; in their performance, the sequence follows the order of the *yājyā* verses.

When the sequence among the subsidiaries is required, that sequence is regulated precisely by the order of the principal acts. For there is no existence of the subsidiaries outside the time of the principal; as it will be stated later, "The principal together with its subsidiaries [constitutes a single unit] because of being enjoined by a single word. Thus, this regulation of sequence is indeed by means of the sentence (*vākya*). For the principal, together with its subsidiaries, is enjoined by a single sentence and possesses a single beginning and end; therefore, the sequence of the subsidiaries follows the very order of the principal.
The rule of sequence arises. Here too, the group of means of proof consists of direct statement (*śruti*) and so forth.

Likewise, in the discussion concerning qualification (*adhikāra*) and other matters, since they serve the purpose of elaborating upon the relationship between the subordinate and the principal (*śeṣa-śeṣi*), one must demonstrate that the very same means of proof—direct statement and so forth—as described in the definition of the subordinate are the grounds for establishing the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). For instance, in the very first [sūtra], "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*).

In the inquiry as to which of the sacrifice and heaven is the subordinate (*śeṣa*) and which is the principal (*śeṣin*), the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is adopted on the basis of the force of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) that "substances, when connected with an action, are related as subordinate qualities" (PMS 6.1.1); thus, heaven is taken to be subordinate to the sacrifice. For it is the capacity of an existing substance that brings about the action to be accomplished; and heaven is indeed a substance.

Just as in the case of garlands, sandalwood, and garments, because of the application [of the term "heaven"] to them, fine garments are considered heaven; therefore, it is the substance itself that serves the purpose of the ritual action.

Furthermore, the connection with the word *kāma* (desire) must be shown as referring to the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For one who desires a certain end necessarily desires the means to that end as well. Having thus presented the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) on the strength of such indicative marks (*liṅga*), the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) is established by the force of the injunctive scripture (*vidhiśruti*). The injunction...

For [injunction] consists in the impelling of volition, and it is not possible to impel a person toward what is harmful; thus, the ritual action becomes a means for attaining heaven for the sake of the sacrifice. As it has been said: "But it is not a means [to heaven] because it exists for that purpose" (6.1.2).
Therefore, lest the power of the injunction to impel be contradicted, the ritual action itself must be for the sake of heaven.

And heaven is not a substance (*dravya*). This is because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood to be a word denoting pleasure (*prīti*). For we do not observe people metaphorically applying the word "heaven" to a substance that causes displeasure; rather, since the word "heaven" follows the presence and absence of pleasure, it is determined to be a term for that [pleasure]. Furthermore, pleasure that is most desired by everyone is not for the sake of producing something else.
This is correct. Therefore, whatever is expressed in conjunction with "pleasure" (prīti) is for that purpose alone;

thus, even the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is contrary [to the opponent's view]. Consequently, it is established that the sacrifice is for the sake of heaven, and it is established that there is a qualification (*adhikāra*). Furthermore, later on, it will be shown that the qualification belongs only to the agent who has become a subordinate element (*śeṣa*); thus, the definition of qualification is established by the very force of direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest.
This is also the established position of the Siddhānta.

Regarding the latter six [chapters], however, it must be determined—on the strength of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) and other means—whether the remaining [elements] are connected with everything solely by virtue of being taught, or whether they are restricted according to their respective archetypes (*prakṛti*). For when the connection with ritual properties (*dharma*) is based on explicit instruction (*aupadeśika*), extension (*atideśa*) is not established.

For in that case, the ritual properties (*dharma*) would become promiscuous (*pāriplava*). Thus, in the first section of the seventh book, by way of an introductory digression (*upoddhāta*) on extension (*atideśa*), it was deliberated whether the properties are prompted by the *apūrva* of the sacrifice. Since the properties are enjoined with reference to the sacrifice (*yajati*), and since the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is a term of general application, it follows that they apply everywhere;
nor does the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* serve as a restrictive factor.

Since it might be argued that, due to the enumeration and the specific restatement of the qualified [act] by means of a specific reference, [the subsidiaries are enjoined], the following is established: here, in the injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," the subsidiaries are not enjoined with reference to the sacrifice;

rather, only the apūrva-efficient-force (bhāvanā) qualified by both the subsidiary and the primary act is enjoined. Subsequently, however, for the subsidiaries which are subsumed within that single efficient-force—

Furthermore, the mutual connection of principal elements is established—just as in the case of the *aruṇā* (red) and the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow). Moreover, since a distinct *apūrva-bhāvanā* (unprecedented efficient force) is differentiated in each ritual context by means of synonyms and other criteria, how could there be a confusion of ritual duties (*dharma-saṅkara*)? This systematic arrangement is established precisely through the consideration of the application (*viniyoga*) based on the authoritative means of knowledge such as direct statement (*śruti*). For it is established that the application of ritual duties is inherently connected to the *apūrva-bhāvanā*, and not merely with reference to the sacrifice in general.

Then the systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is established. Through that establishment, in the case of rites such as the *saurya* sacrifice where the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not explicitly heard, there arises a dependence on the extension of the ritual details (*vidhyanta*). Once the general extension (*sāmānyātideśa*) is established, the specific extension (*viśeṣātideśa*) is established by means of the abundance of commonalities—such as direct scriptural statement, name, unmanifest injunction (*avyakta-codanā*), and the commonality of substance and deity found in its constituent parts. For example, in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, the statement "the rest is the same as the *śyena*" is a scriptural declaration (*vācanika*) regarding the specific features of the *śyena*.

This is *atideśa* (extended application). In the statement "He performs the *agnihotra* for a month" (*māsam agnihotraṃ juhoti*) within the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana* sacrifice, there is an extended application of the ritual details (*dharma*) of the permanent *agnihotra* by virtue of the name "oblation" (*homa*).

Furthermore, because the *ekāha*, *ahīna*, and *satra* sacrifices are enjoined by unmanifest injunctions (*avyakta-codanā*) and thus resemble the *Soma* sacrifice, there is an extended application of its ritual details; such cases are to be demonstrated.

And all this *atideśa* is established for the subsidiary elements solely in accordance with the application (*viniyoga*) indicated by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*); therefore, it is brought about by the collection of those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Likewise, modification (*ūha*) is also divided into six types. Since it is established for mantras and the like solely by following the instruction regarding the archetypal form (*prakṛti*), it too is based on the means of valid cognition such as direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). For that too is the application of dharma to a new matter (*apūrvārtha*); thus, it will be established once [the general principle] is established.

For this very reason, the application [of dharma] to the *apūrva* was proven in the first [chapter]. Sublation (*bādha*) also occurs solely by following the means of valid cognition such as direct Vedic statement; in that case as well—

When the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is established through the extension of the archetypal rules (*prakṛti-śāstra-atideśa*) such that all [archetypal] performances apply, it will be explained that—because the extension primarily concerns the benefit (*upakāra*)—there is either an annulment (*bādha*) due to the absence of that benefit, or because it is obtained from another source, or by means of a prohibition. For example, this should be illustrated by the case of the threshing (*avaghāta*) in the *kṛṣṇala* sacrifice, and by the post (*yūpa*) and sacrificial grass (*barhis*) being replaced by the *khalevālī* and the *śara* grass, respectively, and so forth. This too [is to be understood].

It is determined that in the *prakṛti* (archetype), the application [of elements] is based on the scriptural injunctions (*śruti*) and so forth, which extend up to the [postulation of] the benefit (*upakāra*).

This much, however, is the distinction: in the *prakṛti*, the postulation of the benefit is preceded by the inclusion of the constituent items (*padārtha*), because those items are not yet established prior to it. In the *vikṛti* (ectype), however, the inclusion of the constituent items is preceded by the inclusion of the benefit, through the observation of the benefit already postulated for the *prakṛti*. For it is that very benefit which is required by the injunction; and that...

Even though [an element] is not established in the archetype (*prakṛti*), it is grasped after being conceptualized; and in the ectype (*vikṛti*), that which is already established in the archetype is simply adopted. For this very reason, there is no extension (*atideśa*) of either the scripture or the categories [of the archetype], because those two are not required by the injunction. Furthermore, even in the definition of *tantra* (simultaneous performance) and *āvāpa* (repetition), only the specific [auxiliaries] of the principal acts are what provide assistance through *tantra*.

Furthermore, since it is precisely the remaining cases that are being investigated by the phrase "or by way of reversion" (*utāvṛttyā*), the determination following the group of means of proof (*pramāṇa*) must be demonstrated there.

For in that case, the connection of place, time, fruit, and so forth with the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) will be the reason for the performance of the *prayāja* and other rites as a *tantra* with respect to the *āgneya* and other sacrifices. And since that [connection] is based solely on the means of proof such as direct statement (*śruti*) and the rest, the same group of means of proof applies there as well. This is the definition of *prasaṅga*.

Furthermore, the fact that the remnants of the *prayāja* and other offerings performed for the sake of the animal sacrifice assist the *puroḍāśa* (cake) offering—which occurs within the same ritual procedure (*tantra*) as the animal sacrifice—is based precisely on the commonality of place and other factors; thus, the collection of means of proof is the same as in the previous case. For this very reason, the Commentator employed the term "characteristics of the subsidiary" (*śeṣalakṣaṇa*) in the first sūtra specifically regarding the tenth chapter. As for the distinction between the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) based on different modes of verbal expression:

For example, regarding the statement "one who desires heaven should sacrifice," the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*) is that "one who desires heaven should perform the sacrifice," while the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that "one should produce heaven by means of the sacrifice.

This [distinction] also cannot be established in the case of cognitions devoid of external objects. Furthermore, the connection between rituals such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *kārīrī* and their results—such as heaven in the next world or rain in this world—is based upon external reality.

Because, in its absence, a twofold division would be untenable; therefore, if this entire [system] were to result in being illogical due to the non-establishment of external objects, the Mīmāṃsakas, who seek dharma, must exert effort to establish the existence or non-existence of the object through means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) such as perception (pratyakṣa) that are well-known in the world, by distinguishing between the prima facie (pūrva-pakṣa) and the final (uttara-pakṣa) positions. [This is] purified by the prima facie position...

For it is the intellect that establishes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Therefore, having first formulated the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) through inference that denies external objects, the establishment of their existence must be demonstrated through perception. And all this effort is for the sake of establishing them with respect to every worldly and Vedic activity; otherwise, there would be the cessation of all purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*). Thus, the demonstration of external objects is purposeful. However, as for that which is not a factor in activity, even if it were demonstrated...
It is indeed logical that one understands the action as "mine" (mama). Thus ends the fourth [verse].

Here he raises an objection: "When... and so forth. For, according to the position that [the world] consists of cognition alone, this entire conventional practice of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the like is indeed established, just as it is for the Buddhists. They indeed say:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) in the world and the truth in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*)."
Thus, since conventional usage is established in that very manner, what is the point of this obsession with establishing ultimate reality? // 5 //
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Of the conventional" (*saṃvṛteḥ*). True. All of this is indeed relied upon by the Buddhists on the basis of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

However, this is not tenable, because a distinction between truths is logically untenable. For this distinction between truths relied upon by the Buddhists—namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)—is itself problematic.

This is not tenable. Because conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) lacks the nature of truth; for the word "conventional" (*saṃvṛti*) is a synonym for "false. How, then, could it be used in conjunction with the word "truth"? For this word "truth" is not common to both the conventional and the ultimate (as the word "akṣa" is common to the *vibhītaka* tree and others); therefore, a distinction between types of truth is untenable. He clarifies this very contradiction: "If it were true... (verse 6).
Furthermore, precisely because of the contradiction between the false and the ultimate, even "truth" (*satyatva*) cannot be accepted as a commonality (*sāmānya*).

A commonality is the state (*bhāva*) of things that are similar. How could there be room for such a thing in the case of two contradictory entities? For it does not happen that "dharma-ness" or "adharma-ness" is a commonality shared by both dharma and adharma; thus he says, ending with the word "contradiction," "truth" (*satyatva*). [This applies] to two things that are merely different from one another.

Furthermore, because there is no such comprehensive apprehension [of a commonality], it is difficult to establish a universal (*sāmānya*) between a tree and a lion, just as "treeness" is not shared between them. But how could there be one between two contradictory things?

To this he says: "For not... (2.34). Here, one should distinguish that while previously the word *satya* was refuted as being a common term like *akṣa* and so on, here it is treated as a universal term like *go* (cow) and so on. // 7 //

Therefore, he says—from "tulyārthatve" up to "saṃvṛtiḥ"—that even though the word *saṃvṛti* is a synonym for falsity (*mithyā*), it is employed by the learned Buddhists when they intend to express falsity itself, because it does not cause distress; this is done out of a desire to avoid their own appearance as nihilists, just as the term *vaktrāsava* (mouth-nectar) is used for saliva. This [term] is to be connected with the particle *iti* which will be mentioned later.

He says, "And [the phrase] 'even the employment of words based on conceptual construction,'" meaning that even the resort to such verbal formulations by them is solely for the purpose of avoiding their own nihilism. Furthermore, the claim that "all worldly transaction proceeds by means of an external world constructed as mere conceptual construction" is difficult to maintain; for in a world devoid of reality (*nirvastuka*), it is impossible to differentiate the non-dual pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) through conceptual construction. For [differentiation] occurs only in some cases where there is something distinct.

In this way, some other form becomes the locus of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), just as the form of silver [is superimposed] upon mother-of-pearl. But for that which has no distinct [form at all], by what form could it be conceptually constructed? This is what he says: "Conceptual construction also... (verse 9).

Now, one might object: "We divide reality into exactly three categories: the real, the unreal, and conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*). For the conventional is not absolutely non-existent, because it is non-contradictory in terms of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*); nor is it simply existent, because that would contradict other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like [the existence of] a universal (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, conventional reality is neither a valid cognition nor an invalid cognition; thus it is a distinct category."
Since the conventional usage [of the form] "this is that" is justified by its dependence upon that [object], he says: "Therefore.

For indeed, since conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is false cognition and is not capable of establishing a real entity, therefore that which is determined to be non-existent from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) cannot, by way of convention, possess that nature. That simply does not exist. However, that which is non-contradictory to conventional usage does exist.

For it is not possible for that which is non-existent to always function as a cause for conventional discourse. Moreover, your own established tenet is that only that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*) is ultimately real (*paramārthasat*). Therefore, how can universals (*jāti*) and the like be unreal even while they possess causal efficacy? Consequently, if the external object exists as a constituent of conventional discourse, [it must be real].
Therefore, that alone exists from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

That alone is called "truth" (*satya*); anything else, however, is conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and false. Thus, it does not admit of a conceptualization consisting of two truths. By means of the elliptical construction (*tantra*), the term occurring therein is connected with both the preceding and the following; and thus, [the phrase] "from the perspective of ultimate reality" implies "it does not exist."
It is connected with what precedes. // 10 //

Moreover, even objects perceived in dreams are seen to be causes for worldly transactions such as grief and joy; therefore, these too are merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Likewise, if external objects were admitted, the experience of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma would be exactly like the enjoyment [of objects] in dreams and so forth.

Thus, in order to exclude that [consequence], one strives for the existence of external objects within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); this is what he says with the words "dreams and so forth. (11)

What, then, is the fault in its being like a dream? To this he says: "For not... Why does one not engage [in it]? To this he says: "Because it is accidental" (*yādṛcchikatvāt*). For the wise do not exert themselves with the thought, "May dream-pleasure come to me. For dream-pleasure is indeed accidental, having no regard for causes pertaining either to the next world or to this life.
Having understood that "it does not come to pass for one who exerts effort," the wise should remain silent and indifferent; the meaning is that no effort whatsoever should be made. // 12 //

Therefore, those who necessarily desire the attainment of the ultimate fruit must establish, through reasoning, the realization that has external objects as its domain; thus he concludes that there is a purpose for investigation:
"paramārtha... (verse 13).

In this context, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) has established the existence of external objects by means of a preliminary prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), but he has not [established] the existence of cognition. For what reason? Because there is indeed a disagreement regarding its existence as well; for the Mādhyamikas deny even cognition. Therefore, its refutation was also appropriate.
Yet, setting that aside, the denial of external objects is now being refuted.

The reason for this must be stated; therefore, he says "therein" by means of these three [verses]. The meaning is as follows: the Yogācāras indeed consider cognition alone, devoid of objects, to be ultimately real. The Mādhyamikas, however, because there is no object of knowledge (*jñeya*), maintain that since cognition without an object cannot arise, cognition itself is non-existent. In that regard, the emptiness of external objects is common to both disputants.
Since the cessation of cognition is dependent upon the cessation of the object, the denial of external objects is common to both [positions]. Therefore, that [denial] alone is refuted;
moreover, the denial of cognition is rooted in it. Consequently, once that has been refuted, [the other] is indeed refuted as well.
Thus, the author of the Bhāṣya has exerted effort in distinguishing between the prima facie and final positions regarding the existence of external objects. The first...

The word *tatra* is for the purpose of introducing the sentence; the second [instance of] *tatra*, however, is for the purpose of referring back to the previously mentioned difference of views (*darśanabheda*). Thus, the meaning is "in that difference of opinion" (*matabhede*). // 16 //

Now, is it not the case that the Buddhists have resorted to two ways of denying external objects: by way of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and by way of the object of valid cognition (*prameya*)? For instance, they have stated as follows: "First of all, atoms, being beyond the senses, are not objects of the means of valid cognition.

Nor is their aggregate [the object], because there is no such thing as an aggregate distinct from them. Nor is there a composite whole (*avayavin*), because it is not perceived apart from its parts. If it were not distinct [from the parts]..."

And because that [whole] would collapse into its mere constituent parts (*tanmātra*). Thus, having analyzed it by means of its ultimate constituents, the composite whole (*avayavin*) must be rejected. But those [ultimates] are indeed beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Therefore, nothing remains as an object of apprehension. What, then, is the reason for abandoning this [position], such that the denial of the external world is both proposed and refuted solely on the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says, with the half-verse beginning "bāhyārtha": the meaning is this—even though the denial of the external object is twofold...

Although it is resorted to by the Buddhists, it is nevertheless examined here precisely because it is based on valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since that is the foundation. For the establishment of the object of cognition (*prameya*) is rooted in valid cognition. Therefore, if valid cognition is favorable [to our position], what is the use of conceptual constructions regarding the nature of things? It is not by the force of such constructions that an object is established after having set aside its logical inconsistency. But if, however—

The means of valid cognition itself refutes the object; what is the use of futile conceptualizations regarding the objects of cognition? This is in the Śabara system. Now, at this juncture, the denial of external objects is being investigated precisely from the standpoint of the means of valid cognition. // 17 //

Now, if that which is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be investigated, then since direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is primary, it is logical that the investigation should follow it alone. For even the Buddhists have relied upon a single reality solely on the strength of direct perception; for when a single form appears, duality cannot establish itself.
[The opponents] think thus: "But since inference has already been refuted for one who is deluded, why is it being brought forward again?

To this he says: "In the present context. He thinks as follows: although the determination of the capacity of perception alone is primary regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects, nevertheless, others have also presented inference as a means for the denial of the external; therefore, that too must be refuted. For [the opponent's position] remains unrefuted...
For indeed, some might still maintain their adherence to that very [position] therein. And in this case, this sequence of presentation is appropriate:
first, an inference is presented;
then, its sublation by perception is presented; and once that has been stated, the proponent and opponent again engage in debate regarding the capacity of perception.
Thus, once the determination has been made through the examination of the power of perception, the introduction of inference would indeed be out of place. // 18 //
He introduces the *Anumāna-bhāṣya* with the words "Now, therein... up to "...end," in order to demonstrate its connection to the subject at hand.

He states the connection with the words "...of this" up to "...difficult to obtain. This is the meaning: the connection occurs precisely through the objection to that which was stated by the author of the Sūtras—that perception is produced by the conjunction of those [two]. For this conjunction of sense-organ and object is indeed conceptual (*kālpānika*).

Because of the absence of the sense organs and so forth, and because that which is conceptual is common to all false cognitions, the distinction between what arises from contact with that [object] and what does not is not tenable; this is the objection stated in the Sūtra. // 21 //

Alternatively, he states "falsity" (*mithyātva*) to show the connection [of this verse] by way of an objection to his own previous statement. That which was stated at the end of the commentator’s (*vṛttikāra*) work—namely, "that cognition alone is incorrect for which the instrument is defective and for which there is the conviction that 'it is false,' and not any other"—is what is being challenged here: [the objection being] that if everything were false, the employment of qualifiers would be meaningless. // 22 //

He now presents the inference, which was obscured in the commentary, clearly: "The cognition of a pillar," and so forth. "The cognition of a pillar" is the statement of the subject (*dharmin*). "Is false" is the statement of the property (*dharma*).
"Because it is a cognition" is the logical reason (*hetu*). "For instance" is the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). // 23 //

Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Every cognition is indeed without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), like a dream. This establishes the lack of an objective basis for all cognitions exactly as it was heard [in the text]. However, in that respect, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*), because delusive cognitions are already admitted to be without an objective basis. For a cognition that perceives an object as being otherwise than it actually exists is precisely what is intended to be without an objective basis. Furthermore, if "everything" is made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*), then since dream-cognition is also included therein, there is no example (*dṛṣṭānta*) available.

Furthermore, the use of the particle *eva* in the phrase "all indeed" (*sarva eva*) would be inappropriate. For that particle is seen used in the negation of a prior distinction; as for example, when there is a statement regarding a division such as "this for the gods, this for the Brahmins," one says, "all this indeed for the Brahmins.

In that case, the particle *eva* is observed to serve the purpose of negating the division. However, if [the opponent's] position were that [the term] refers to the whole, he should have simply said "all" (*sarva*).

One should not employ the particle *eva* [in that way]. Therefore, he says—using the half-verse beginning with "siddhasādhana"—that the commentary must be explained solely with the intention of referring to the waking state of consciousness (*jāgradbuddhi*). [Objection: Even so, if one adopts "lack of an external object" (*nirālambanatva*) without qualification, there is a contradiction with what you yourself accept;
for Buddhists certainly maintain that cognitions have their own parts (*svāṃśa*) as their objects. To this he replies with the word "svāṃśa. For this very reason...
The meaning is that what must be proven is the state of being without an objective support (anālambanatva) as qualified by external qualifiers. // 25 //

There is another commentary as well: "For the nature of a cognition (*pratyaya*) being without an objective basis (*nirālambanatā*) is observed in a dream. Even for one who is awake, there occurs a cognition such as ‘a pillar’ or ‘a wall’;

therefore, that too is without an objective basis. He states its meaning with the words "of a cognition" (*pratyayasya*). By this much—that the nature of a cognition being without an objective basis is observed in a dream—the state of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) is pervaded by the probandum, which is the absence of an objective basis.

The reason (*hetu*) is being pointed out, namely, "the statement of the example" (*dṛṣṭāntavacana*). But surely the reason "because it is a condition" (*pratyayatvāt*) was not explicitly stated; of what, then, is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) being pointed out? To this he says: "And the reason. Although the status of the reason as a fifth-case [ablative] term was not explicitly stated for "being a condition," nevertheless, by means of the member of the proof-statement called the application (*upanaya*), namely the phrase "even while awake," etc., the reason has indeed been demonstrated. For at that very moment, "being a condition," which was previously shown to be conjoined with the probandum (*sādhya*), is again—

When the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is brought forward [into the context], it is precisely at that moment shown that "this is the reason (*hetu*) here," because only that which resides in the subject (*pakṣa*) and is concomitant with the probandum (*sādhya*) functions as the reason. But what is this application (*upanaya*)? It is a specific member of the syllogistic argument (*sādhanavākya*). For [the argument] consists of five members.

The statement of proof consists of the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the indication of that which is to be proven is the proposition; for example, "Sound is impermanent. "Because it possesses the property of arising" is the reason. "A substance such as a pot, which possesses the property of arising, is seen to be impermanent" is the example. "And likewise, sound possesses the property of arising" is the [application].

The application (*upanaya*). For it has been described as the application of the probandum (*sādhya*), which is a restatement—either "it is so" or "it is not so"—in dependence upon the example (*udāharaṇa*). What is meant by this? The reason (*hetu*) establishes the probandum in two ways: either through similarity to the example (*sādharmya*) or through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Among these, similarity has already been demonstrated. As for dissimilarity, however, it is as follows—in that very same [context]:

In that very proposition, when the reason "because it has the property of arising" is employed, substances such as the self (*ātman*) are observed to be eternal because they lack the property of arising; yet sound is not likewise devoid of the property of arising. In this context, the *upanaya* (application) is the statement that summarizes the property of having the nature of arising—which belongs to the probandum, sound—as being connected to it, depending on the two kinds of examples: "so it is" when the example is based on similarity (*sādharmya*), and "it is not so" when the example is based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

And that [application] depends precisely upon the example. It is from the duality of the examples alone that the duality of its application arises.
