By means of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), there is an application of the reason as being connected with the probandum through the exclusion of the contradictory; for instance: "The self and so forth are substances, eternal, and characterized by non-origination, but sound is not like that"—here, by the negation of the property of non-origination, the property of having the nature of origination is applied. But in the present case, regarding the example based on similarity (*sādharmya*)...

In the same way, the application (*upanaya*) is to be understood as the conclusion based on the reason (*hetu*). The conclusion (*nigamana*), however, is the restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason; for example: "Therefore, because it possesses the property of being produced, sound is impermanent.

It is called *nigamana* because by means of it the proposition, the reason, the example, and the application are brought together (*nigamyante*) into a single meaning; that is, they are rendered effective (*samarthyante*) and connected.

Up to this point: for if that [conclusion] were absent, there would be no capacity to convey meaning for those whose relationship [with the other members] is unmanifest. But when it is present, because the intended purport (*tātparya*) of all the members is seen, their mutual connection becomes clear.
"Nigamana" means bringing together, connecting; that is to say, up to this point. // 26 //

[Objection: Surely a logical reason (*hetu*) does not exist unless it is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*); therefore, its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must be demonstrated by showing its dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Yet, it has not been shown here in that manner, because only a statement of similarity (*sādharmya*) has been made. To this, he says: "In the case of the counter-example... For when "being without an object" (*nirālambanatva*) is what is to be proven (*sādhya*), "having an object" (*sālambanatva*) is the counter-example. And for one who asserts that everything is without an object, that [counter-example] does not exist; so what is the use of demonstrating its exclusion?

[Objection: But if the cognition (*pratyaya*) itself is made the subject (*pakṣa*), then the reason (*hetu*) would be a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśa*). To this he says: "of the universal" (*sāmānyasya*). For cognitions consist of both the universal and the particular. In that case, when the particular is made the subject, the universal serves as the reason; thus, there is no [fallacy of] being a part of the meaning of the proposition. // 27 //

In this regard, the Siddhānta-bhāṣya states: "For how could the cognition of one who is awake, being perfectly certain, ever be erroneous? By this, it is indeed intended to establish that waking cognitions possess an objective basis (*sālambanatva*) on account of their perfect certainty. However, this perfect certainty as being connected to an external object is not established for others [the opponents]. Therefore, by means of this unestablished member (*asiddhāvayava*), the inference that [waking cognitions] are without an objective basis (*anālambana*) is not refuted.
Or rather, [the opponent's argument] possesses a counter-proof (*sapratisādhana*), because its members are established for both parties, whereas this [other argument] is the opposite of that.
Therefore, he objects that this very [argument] presented by the author of the *Bhāṣya* is merely a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) by means of the two verses beginning with "jāgrajjñāne.

We shall explain the nature of the "balancing the heterogeneity" (*vaidharmyasama*) and "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasama*) fallacies under the section on words. This is because, while the status of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) remains the same, there is a distinction based on whether other properties are well-ascertained or not well-ascertained.

"Equivalence through conceptualization" (*vikalpasamatā*) occurs by introducing a conceptual alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). Likewise, when a similarity (*sādharmya*) has been adduced by the proponent, "equivalence through dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasamatā*) occurs by means of an opposition based on dissimilarity:

namely, that while dream-cognitions, being without external objects, are seen to be not well-ascertained, waking cognitions—the very things to be proven—are well-ascertained due to their dissimilarity [to dreams]. It has already been stated that the elaboration of these points will follow later. // 28–29 //
Thus, he resolves the objection raised by one opinion with the words "because it is faulty. For they think as follows: when a faulty means of proof is employed, a faulty reply must be given;
for in this way the proponent is enlightened, thinking: "Just as you consider my refutation to be faulty, so too do I consider your proof."

"Therefore, he turns away from his own proof"—this justification, however, is not tenable. For it entails two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Such a speaker would incur both points of defeat consisting of "neglecting what is to be censured" (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) and "censuring what is not to be censured" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), since he fails to state an existing fault while prattling about another non-existent one. Furthermore, for a speaker who argues in this manner, there is no comprehension of the refutation of his own proof.

It is so; however, he rebukes [the opponent] by employing a flawed refutation. Therefore, he offers another resolution—stating "the proposition" (*pratijñā*)—to show that this [objection] is of the same nature as the *Pāśupatottara* and must be rejected. By this, an inference is not being introduced;

rather, the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*) of the inference stated by the opponent is being described. Inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object that is not present to the senses.
In this case, however, because the external world— whose existence has been ascertained by well-determined waking cognitions— is rejected,

the inference [of its non-existence] simply does not arise due to the obstruction of perception, just as the inference of coldness in fire is impossible. At best, the statement of the proof regarding the external world would merely amount to a formal application (*prayoga*).

Even for one who is inferring, a clear cognition of an external object certainly arises. If such a cognition were false, what confidence could there be? [Objection: In that case, inference would indeed be untrustworthy.
[Reply: No, because it does not exist [in that sense].

This has been stated: when perception stands as an obstacle, inference—which is its opposite—cannot establish itself, just as an inferential [application] cannot prevail against a Vedic application (*viniyoga*). However, in a syllogistic argument (*sādhana-vākya*), because of the proximity of words whose connection is impossible, the cognition of a relation is merely an error, like the sentence "the son of a barren woman. No inferential cognition of absence regarding pillars and the like ever arises for anyone.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the state of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) is pervaded by the absence of an object (*anālambanatva*), and that for one who has known the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, the knowledge of the pervader does not arise? Thus, this [position] is merely a dogmatic assertion. [Reply: No, because that would entail the collapse of the pervasion (*vyāpti*). For, while cognizing the pervasion through uncontradicted perception occurring across all places and times, one determines that falsity is not caused by the state of being a cognition, but rather is caused by the two previously mentioned reasons. This is what was stated: "But the falsity of the dream-cognition is understood from another source, namely from its non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*). (Verse 30)
[704] Whose is this opinion?
[705] (KHA) Furthermore, how is there sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) in this case? For perception, not finding its own self without an object to be grasped, [does not arise].
It establishes only that [internal] measure and not the external. For what is not established for it without the external?

And the fact that the apprehended portion is a part of itself (*svāṃśa*) is indeed accepted by the Buddhists. Therefore, there is no contradiction with its being perceptible and so forth even when the external is denied.
Thus he says, "We shall be able," in two verses. This is the intended meaning: for in the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*), perception has as its object only its own part (*svāṃśa*).

We shall indeed refute that [position]. And in its refutation, the inclusion of the qualification "external" (bāhya) is entirely purposeless, because no other object of cognition (grāhya) distinct from that [self-aspect] is possible. Therefore, the position of being without an objective support (anālambanapakṣa) results in the negation of the object of cognition alone. Since perception and the other means of knowledge are refuted as having their own parts [as objects], only the external object remains. Thus, even without the qualification "external," there occurs the denial of the mere object of cognition.

There is a sublation of the thesis by means of perception and the other [means of valid cognition]. Even if an external qualification were somehow attached, since perception and the others also have external objects as their specific domain, the proponent who negates them would suffer a sublation of the thesis by those very perceptions and so forth. However, the prior mention of "perception" is for the sake of illustration; indeed, there is a contradiction with all [means of valid cognition], such as perception and the rest, for an inference that lacks an objective basis (*anālambana*).
"It should be shown," [he said]. // 32 //

As for the objection that the connection with an external object is well-established through firm certainty, and therefore asks what is the point of introducing that [certainty], he replies: “By firm certainty. We have already stated that this is not a formal syllogism (*anumānaprayoga*);

rather, the mention of "firm certainty" is intended to demonstrate the difference between those cognitions for one who considers waking perceptions to be of the same nature as dream-cognitions. These [waking cognitions] are firmly certain.
The conditions (pratyaya) are more powerful; inference finds no footing among these obstacles. The meaning is: "from this inference. // 33 //

He elaborates on this very point with the words "by faulty cognition" (*duṣṭajñāna*). An object apprehended by a faulty—that is, an indeterminate—cognition is subject to negation, but not any other. However, if there were a sublation of everything merely apprehended, many defects of the proof (*sādhanadoṣa*) would be implied by the Commentator. Intending to demonstrate those, he first states the absence of a thesis (*pakṣābhāva*) with the words "apprehended" (*gṛhīta*). If it is said that everything merely apprehended is false, [then the following ensues].

In that case, even this own-position (*svapakṣa*) of yours—that "cognitions are without an objective basis" (*nirālambana*)—would be false because it has been apprehended. Therefore, it can be said that in this proof of yours, there is no thesis (*pakṣa*) at all.

Furthermore, cognitions qualified by "being without an objective basis" are what are being proven. Here, since the apprehension of the distinction between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is also false, the differentiation between the qualifier and the qualificand is not established.

And because of that absence, it is impossible to state that the thesis has an unestablished qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), an unestablished qualificand (*viśeṣya*), or that one or the other is unestablished. This is what he says with the words "and because of its being ungraspable. The meaning is that the non-establishment of one or the other must be stated.

He states another refutation with the words "of the speaker and the listener. Self-contradiction (*svavāgvirodha*) is fivefold, occurring through the expression of the denotation, the utterance, the property (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), or both.

Thus, by stating both [of these], there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavāgvirodha*). For the cognition that arises in the speaker and the listener regarding both the qualifier and the qualified—as well as the cognitions of those two cognitions themselves—is also without an objective basis (*anālambana*) because it is a cognition; therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) is not established.

And since that [reason] would be inconclusive if it were to have an object, cognitions could not be without objects. Thus, by stating both [possibilities], there is a contradiction with one's own words. // 36 //

He states another refutation: "And there is no possibility," etc. For it must be analyzed in this way: Is the state of being without an object (nirālambanatva) different from or non-different from the subject (dharmin)? It cannot first be non-different, for it would not then be capable of functioning as a qualifier. Nor can it be said that it is capable of qualifying because the cognition grasping the difference is false. He concludes: "Therefore," etc. (37).

He states the Buddhists' counter-argument: "The state of being without an objective support" (*nirālambanatā*). For they think thus: "A conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) such as 'exclusion' (*vyatireka*) and so forth is appropriate regarding a real entity (*vastu*), not regarding a non-entity. As they have said: 'This conceptual construction would apply to a real entity. And since there is no negation of the objective support as a real entity, what is the point of questioning its exclusion and so forth? (38)

He states another refutation with the words beginning "yadi" and ending with "tvam": If, first of all, it is a non-entity (*avastu*), how can you have the desire to inform us of it, or how can there be a cognition regarding it? For a non-entity cannot be an object of cognition; if it were such an object, it would follow that it possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), since the defining characteristic of a real entity is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

And [this applies] to the existence of that [object]. For the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*) is characterized by that [existence]. If, however, it is argued: "Even though that which is called 'objectlessness' does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, having imagined its existence, the conventional usage of inference is carried out—just as one performs the conventions of worship and so forth toward a deity in an image"—that is incorrect, because it is impossible to imagine what is non-existent.

For it is appropriate that deities such as Viṣṇu and others, whose existence is well-established elsewhere, should be postulated in another context; however, non-objectivity, whose existence is absolutely unestablished, cannot be the object of conceptual construction, just like a sky-flower and the like. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The imagined... (verse 39).
[706] Nam ā [707] kta (KHA) {2,45}. Furthermore, what is this conceptual construction? If it is cognition, [then...]

What is known by that? If it is objectlessness (*nirālambanatva*), then how can conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), which is active in the production of cognition, be a non-entity (*avastu*)? For being an entity consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and the production of cognition is itself a form of causal efficiency; with this intention, he says: "in the postulation" (*kḷptau*). Here, an objection is raised: "How so? If it is a non-entity, it cannot be something to be established.
"But how is it that for you as well, the absence of rain is established by means of the absence of clouds? He replies: "A real entity (*vastu*).
This would indeed be so if non-existence were not a real entity. That non-existence is a real entity will be explained in the section on the determination of non-existence (*abhāvapariccheda*).
And although non-existence is not denotable by the word "real entity" because that would contradict common worldly usage, [it is nonetheless a real entity].

Nevertheless, it is not devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For it appears in a form that is distinct from [mere] existence and is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). Therefore, it will simply be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); thus, nothing is untenable. // 40 //

Furthermore, this must also be examined here: as for this word *pratyaya* which denotes the substratum (*dharmin*), is it derived in the sense of existence (*bhāva*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the instrument (*karaṇa*), or is it derived in the sense of the object (*karman*)? In the previously mentioned alternatives, there is a contradiction, because a cognition devoid of an object is impossible. For it is not possible that there be a cognition while there is nothing to be cognized. [If it were so,] that which is not grasped by it...

Because that form [of the agent] is not manifested. The same must be said for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*). Even if cognition itself is metaphorically designated as the agent or intended as the instrument in the manifestation of an object or its production—since this depends on the speaker’s intention—even so, those two are untenable without the object (*karman*), which is the factor to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*). This is a contradiction with one's own words. As soon as the word "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is uttered, by reflecting upon its very nature, the absence of anything to be cognized is negated, just as when one says, "My mother is barren," the status of being a mother is contradicted.

[The consequence would be] barrenness [of the argument]. Therefore, when the cognition (*pratyaya*) is made the subject (*pakṣa*), it is impossible to prove its lack of a real objective basis (*nirālambanatva*). If the term is derived in the sense of an object (*karman*), it is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). He states all of this with the words "tathā" (so).

He explains the point of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with the words "of that which is to be made known" (*pratyāyyasya*). For indeed, an insentient object such as color and so forth does not fail to serve as a support for something. // 42 //

{2,46} But in the case where [the cognition] is taken as the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), there is this further fault: that even the two words expressing the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) would have to be admitted to be without a basis (*nirālambana*). For a cognition arises only when an agent or an instrument is perceived. And just as the states of being an agent or an instrument occur in relation to cognition by virtue of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣāvaśāt*), so too [would it be here].
"Likewise, the word [is the agent]. For this very reason, he will say:

"The status of words as either instruments (karaṇa) or agents (kartṛ) has been established. Furthermore, this lack of an objective basis (anālambanatva) for the two words is not due to anything other than the absence of a denotable object (abhidheya). And in the absence of that [object], the consequence would be the non-existence of the subject of the proposition (pakṣa); thus he says: "As the agent," etc. (verse 43).

He explains what was stated—that there would be a contradiction regarding the state of being [the agent] and so forth—with the words "and by the object to be conveyed" (*pratyāyyena*). For the state of being the agent and so forth is not possible without a distinction in the object to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*). Consequently, there is a self-contradiction (*svavacanavirodha*) in the word *pratyaya* when it is used as the basis for its own application (*tatpravṛttinimitta*). This very point has already been explained by us previously. The word "or" (*vā*) is used in reference to the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of "object" (*karman*) that was just explained. // 44 //
If, however, the word "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is taken in its conventional sense as an undivided whole,

and its referent is made the subject of the thesis, even so, since for us in reality only that which grasps another entity is established as a cognition, there would be a direct contradiction with one's own words.

This is what he says: "Even so" (*athāpi*) and "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*). The connection with the preceding [argument] is that "even so, there is a contradiction with one's own words. How is there a contradiction with one's own words? To this he says: "The grasper" (*grāhakam*). For it is well known to us that the grasper of an object (*grāhya*) which is indeed a distinct entity is itself an entity called a "property of the self" (*ātmadharma*), which is the cognition (*pratyaya*). Therefore, how can there be an establishment of that [cognition] when the object is non-existent? He states another refutation: "Having accepted that" (*tam abhyupetya*).

Thus, this proponent of a non-proof (asādhanavādī) should be addressed as follows: "Do you accept and take as your subject (pakṣīkriyate) that very kind of cognition which we intend to establish, or not? In the first case, if you do accept it, there is a contradiction with what you have already admitted. Moreover, if this were so, your thesis would have an unestablished subject (aprasiddhaviśeṣya)."

He says "of the qualificand" because, in your view, you do not accept a cognition that apprehends an external object. However, regarding your own intended position which is not like that, he says "for us," meaning that for us, the subject (pakṣa) would have a qualificand that is unestablished. // 46 //

Furthermore, whatever kind of self-property (*ātmadharma*) we accept as the probans (*pratyaya*), that subject (*pakṣa*) may be one accepted by you or independent. In the former case, there is for you the fallacy of an unestablished substratum (*aprasiddhaviśeṣyatā*);
in the latter case, it is for us, as shown previously. Thus he says: "self-property" (*ātmadharma*). If...

If it is argued that "mere cognition," whose specific characteristics have not been determined, is being made the subject of the thesis (pakṣa), that is not so; for such a thing cannot be defined. Thus he says: "And not... (na ca). 47.

But surely, this could also be said regarding other things that have been made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), as follows: "Is sound a quality of space, or an independent substance, or is that which is called 'pudgala' being made the subject by virtue of its permanence? If it is then argued that in those cases the subject is the form characterized by the general nature of the word-meaning, with its specific distinctions left unexpressed; [then we reply:]

Since this is the same here as well, he says: "Regarding the word," and so forth. Just as for others there is a definition of other positions by way of the universal form of the word and its referent (*śabdārtha-sāmānya-rūpeṇa*), such a thing is not possible here for you. This is because for you, a denotable object (*vācya*) consisting of a universal that is distinct from the unique particular form (*asādhāraṇa-rūpa*) is not accepted. // 48 //

Thus, first the subject (*dharmin*) has been refuted through its conceptualization. Now, he refutes the property (*dharma*), namely "objectlessness" (*nirālambanatva*), by means of conceptualization—starting with the words "objectlessness. If "objectlessness in every respect" is what is to be proven, the thesis (*pakṣa*) becomes one whose qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
For there is no such thing as "objectlessness in every respect."

[The opponent's position] exists, because it is accepted that in all cases there is an external objective support (*ālambana*) situated in another place or time. Furthermore, as for the dream-cognition which was stated as an example, even that is not entirely without an objective support; for it will be explained later that an objective support is established in every case in some way or another. Therefore, if this were so, the very absence of an example would result.

However, if it is not being argued that there is no object of cognition whatsoever, but rather that even for that which possesses an object, there is a state of being objectless in some particular manner, then—since cognitions of taste and so forth are already established as being devoid of objects such as form—the argument would result in proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhana*). To this, he says: "in some [particular] way" (*kenacid*). 50.

"Now, we shall prove that whatever form a cognition has, it does not take that as its object, so this will not be a case of proving what is already established. Anticipating this, he says: "Now... He refutes this as well with: "of its own form... For you have indeed accepted that the cognition's own form is its object, by asserting that "the object of cognition is that which appears [in consciousness]. Therefore, the absence of such an object [is untenable].
It is contradicted by what has already been accepted. // 51 //

[708] [Objection: But surely, having accepted [the existence of external objects], why do you raise this objection? For our position is that there is no external object of apprehension (*anālambanatva*). This has indeed been explained in the *Bhāṣyopaskāra*. Therefore, there is no contradiction with what has been admitted (*abhyupetabādha*). To this he says: "External... The intended meaning is as follows: it must be analyzed (*vikalpanīyam*).

This refers to the state of not having an external object as its support (*anālambanatva*). Is it being established by this form that "it does not take an external object as its support," or rather that "in reality it does not take an external object as its support"? In the former case, it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). In the latter case, the fault will be stated later. For cognitions of pillars and so forth take their own objects precisely as having the form of pillars and so forth, and not as being external. // 52 //

But if it is being proven that the pillar is simply not an object of cognition, then, since the awareness of its form is actually perceived, there would be a contradiction with experience; thus he says: "In that case... (tathā). 53.

Here he raises an objection: "In the case of the double moon and so forth. For they think as follows: this same contradiction with conscious experience (*saṃvid-virodha*) applies equally to cognitions such as that of a double moon, which are intended to be without an objective basis (*anālambana*). In those cases too, two moons indeed appear. To deny that [appearance] would be a blatant contradiction with conscious experience. Therefore, by what means could these [cognitions] be without an objective basis?

He refutes this, saying: "Not by the sense-faculty. This is the intended meaning: if we were to claim that there is a difference [between the object and its cognition] due to a distortion of appearance (*pratibhāsa-viparyāsa*), then we might be criticized in such a manner. But we do not do so. Our established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that whatever consciousness makes manifest an object not reached by the sense-faculty is without an objective basis (*anālambana*). And such is the case with the cognition of two moons and the like. Therefore, it is without an objective basis.
It is said: however, this is not by way of denying the appearance of a double moon and so forth;
therefore, there is no contradiction with our consciousness, nor is the lack of an objective support (anālambanatva) unestablished for us. // 54 //

[Objection: But if, in this way, cognition is not denied and the object exists according to its appearance, then there would be no distinction between the existent and the non-existent; therefore, he says: "In all cases. The meaning of this is as follows: it is not the case that "this is an existent object of apprehension" and "this is a non-existent object of apprehension" means "this manifests this object" and "this does not [manifest it]. What then? It is simply that, at the very moment it arises, [cognition] has the object as its domain.

This distinction [between real and unreal objects] is based on the presence or absence of the contact between the sense organ and the object within cognition. That which manifests an object conjoined with a sense organ is a real apprehended object; the opposite is otherwise. Furthermore, the existence of an object does not correspond to its appearance, because sublation is observed. Therefore, that which apprehends an object situated in another location and not reached by the sense organ is an unreal apprehended object.
It is said that its object does not exist. For in some cases something is negated; nothing is negated by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*).

This [cognition] "this is silver" does not mean that "silver does not exist," for it exists in other places and so forth. However, it means "it does not exist here," where it is not reached by the sense organ.

Even the expression "this exists" refers only to that which is actually apprehended by a sense faculty. Here, there is the cognition "the jar exists," but not [merely] the verbal assertion "the jar exists. (55)

And this distinction is not possible for the Buddhist; thus he says: "of yours. Furthermore, the Buddhist has no sense organs and so forth, such that the two—namely, the prohibition of [contact with] external objects and the taking of them as objects of cognition—could be logically established on the basis of whether there is contact or non-contact. // 56 //

He states another objection with the words beginning "bahirbhāva" and ending with "sādhyatvena. For those who maintain that cognition is without an objective basis (*anālambana*), no such thing as an "external existence" is established, by means of which a specific lack of objective basis for cognition could be proven. Why is it not so proven? To this he replies: "This is not [the case]. For the statement of a proof (*sādhana*) is indeed for the purpose of making known the subject (*pakṣa*).
And a thesis characterized by an unestablished category cannot be made known. // 57 //

But why is it that the subject (*pakṣa*) is not known? When both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*) are unknown, the qualified entity as such is not known. Since both of these are indeed well-known, what is the point of the non-establishment of the qualifier of the qualifier? To this he says: "Just as... What follows from the non-establishment of the qualifier alone? It is not the establishment of the subject itself. If it is argued that such a [subject] cannot be made known by another, [the author replies:]...
This [objection] is the same even when that qualification is unestablished; thus it is well said that "if that qualification is unestablished, the subject (pakṣa) is not known. // 58 //

He elaborates on this very point: "Not [if] unestablished. For the meaning of the thesis-statement depends upon the meanings of its constituent words; therefore, if external objects and so forth are not established, the subject (pakṣa) is not established. // 59 //
He states another refutation: "In the case of a paryudāsa [exclusion]," [it is argued that] a cognition does not have a non-distinct object;
[that is, it does not take a distinct thing as its object].

For thus two meanings are possible through the two types of negation: exclusion (*paryudāsa*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). For in the case of exclusion, because of its connection with a noun, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is that the cognition has a non-distinct object. But in the case of prohibition, because of its connection with a verb, it does not have a distinct object. For in both ways, there is the proving of what is already established; for by [the property of] being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), and so forth, the world [is already established].

We do not maintain that there is a difference [between them]. Therefore, from the cognition of a pillar and so forth, it is non-different by virtue of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and the like.
Precisely because of this non-difference, it is also not different; thus, [your argument] results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). // 60 //

Furthermore, this too must be considered here: is the state of being without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*) established by means of a pillar or the like that is absolutely distinct [from consciousness], or by means of something distinct in some way? Regarding the first alternative, it is merely proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*); thus he says, "If... The phrase "proving what is already established" is to be connected with what precedes. However, when the state of being without an objective basis is being established by means of something distinct in some way...

There is a contradiction with the previously established position (*pakṣavirodha*). For you also accept that an external object of cognition (*ālambana*), though in some way merely imagined through conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*), exists. Therefore, in its negation, there occurs a sublation of the position by what was previously established. This is what he says:
"in some way" (*kathañcit*). // 61 //

He shows that otherwise there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with the words "the entity" (*vastu*). For it is already established that cognition, being insentient in nature, does not take anything as its objective support (*ālambana*) when appearing in the form of an entity and so forth. However, by means of its uncommon nature as luminosity (*prakāśātman*), it does take the external as its objective support. In this context, since no qualification has been specified [in the opponent's argument], it is possible to show the fallacy of proving the already established. [The opponent objects: "But surely our thesis here is that the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is non-different from the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*); why then these various conceptual distinctions? To this he replies: "From the subject of apprehension... [and so on]. First of all, cognitions are not without an objective support (*nirālambana*).

The meaning is this: the object of cognition (*grāhya*) is non-different from the subject of cognition (*grāhaka*). Even if this were so, it would contradict the accepted view that cognition possesses a dual capacity—that is, that cognition has both the capacity of being the object and the capacity of being the subject—because the object is thereby denied. Although the Buddhists do not accept a capacity that exists apart from its substratum, [the contradiction remains].
Nevertheless, it should be understood that [the author] demonstrates precisely this dual nature by means of a distinction in capacities. // 62 //

If, however, you seek to establish merely the arising of a cognition devoid of an object because every other possibility is impossible, even in that case it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). For when it is said that "cognitions arise without an object," the very cognition of their being objectless arises. Yet this [cognition] is not capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) because it lacks a real object;
with this intention, he says: "without an object" (*nirālambana*). // 63 //
Nor should it be said that its lack of referential objectivity (*anarthakatva*) is not established; for if that were true, it would follow that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Therefore, this cognition must be admitted to terminate in itself, just like the cognition of a mirage and the like. Since we also establish the falsity of the cognition that grasps the falsity of all things, there is no dispute between us; thus, the fact that cognition is without an objective support (*anālambana*) is proven.
He says that [the opponent's position] is meaningless: "It is correctness" (samyaktvam). // 64 //

And thus, even when a cognition devoid of an object—which terminates in the aspect of the self (ātmaṃśa) and lacks an external referent—has arisen, the lack of an object (*nirālambanatā*) is not apprehended as a property (*dharmatā*) of the cognitions of Caitra and others that have been made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*), by means of the cognition produced by the proof (*sādhana*). This is because they have different objects; therefore, [the subject] is not refuted by its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), namely, the lack of an object.

53} Furthermore, who could prevent the attainment of an objective support (*ālambana*) through the thorough investigation of the actual nature of Caitra and others? For the relationship of sublated and sublator exists between two cognitions that fall upon the same object and have contradictory referents, such as "this is silver" and "this is not silver. But it is not so here. Cognitions of Caitra and others establish their own objects, and the cognition that [allegedly] lacks an objective support does not refute them, because there is no object [for it to refute]. For that [cognition of non-existence] has its own part as its range; therefore, its own part is its object. And this is the case for the cognitions of Caitra and others as well.

Since the objects [of cognition] are clearly distinct—as in the case of Caitra and others—what could possibly sublate what? This is stated by the pair of verses beginning with "Caitra and so forth" (vv. 65–66).
Furthermore, regarding what was previously stated— that in the capacity of an agent or an instrument, even a word is denotable by the term "condition" (*pratyaya*)—
if that very term *pratyaya* is here likewise taken as a condition by virtue of being the agent or instrument of cognition,
then the status of Caitra and others as the objective support (*ālambana*) for that cognition would be precluded.

"Caitra and others do not become the objective supports (ālambana) for the cognition of the word [‘consciousness’]. Therefore, because it is insentient, Caitra and others lack the status of being the objective support for that cognition; thus, in one respect, this is merely proving what is already established. To this, he says: "If... (verse 67).

Now, if it is argued that its lack of an object (*anālambanatva*) consists in its being devoid of the capacity to produce a cognition—that is, the word "cognition" (*pratyaya*) is without an object—what has been stated? It means that no cognition capable of producing a [specific] object can be generated. Consequently, since that which is incapable does not illuminate the thesis (*pakṣa*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established. To this he says: "buddhyutpādana... (in the phrase *buddhyutpādana-sāmarthyarahitatvāt*). [This refers to] the non-establishment of the probandum.
He states the reason: "of the means" (sādhanasya).

{2,54} He states with three [verses] beginning with "And not" that this position is also contradicted by one's own prior admission: first of all, a sentence of proof cannot be employed in words that do not denote anything; nor is denotation possible for words without a relation to an object;
nor is a relation possible without difference; and difference is not possible without a cognition that makes known the difference residing in both word and object.
It is possible. Therefore, one employing a proof (*sādhana*) here must admit that word and meaning are distinct.

This being so, the judges, the members of the assembly, and the proponent and opponent grasp the constituent parts of the proof-statement as separate—the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). As long as this is not established, there can be no instruction for one who has risen [from the debate].

The application of the proof occurs as follows. And all of this constitutes a contradiction with what was previously accepted, provided that one accepts [the opponent's position] and then attempts to prove that [cognition] is without an objective basis (nirālambanatva). // 69–71 //

He says—ending with the word *bheda* in the verse beginning with *dharma*—that this position is even contrary to the intention of the Buddha, who is considered the most authoritative (*āptatama*). For as long as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are not established as distinct ultimate realities, and as long as there is no disciple to be instructed and no self to be the instructor, the instruction regarding merit and demerit is not possible. And yet, practices such as the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*) have been taught to disciples.

By the Buddhas, [the world] is [seen] as having the nature of *dharmatā*. Therefore, by observing their conduct, it is inferred that everything is approved by the Buddhas; thus, their intention is deduced. Consequently, when there is a statement contrary to that, it constitutes a contradiction with their intended meaning.
Furthermore, in certain specific sūtras, external objects (*bāhyārtha*) were clearly accepted by them, relying upon which the Sautrāntika maintains the existence of external objects.
Therefore, he says "clearly" (sphuṭam) [in verse 73] to show that this position is also contradicted by his own scripture.

Likewise, because he negates the earth, mountains, and oceans that are well-known to the entire world, [the opponent's position] is also contradicted by common worldly experience; thus he says "all" (*sarva*).

Furthermore, if all cognitions were without an objective basis (*anālambana*), then since the cognition of the entire proof would be false, one could either establish the absence of all means of proof or, as desired, establish a deficiency in the thesis and other members of the argument; thus he says "entire" (*kṛtsna*). However, if it is not...

It is said that the knowledge of the means of proof is false; therefore, the reason is inconclusive precisely because of the cognitions of the thesis and so forth. To this he says: "Of those... (vv. 74–75).

If it is asserted that only those cognitions distinct from the apprehension of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), then it follows that the cognition which apprehends their distinction from those [subject and so forth] would be false, because its object—the subject and so forth—is not included within the thesis;

thus he says: "of that which is other than that" (*tadanyasya*). He states the fault in accepting this position: "that is false" (*tanmithyā*). This refers to the falsity of the cognition of that which is other than those [subject and so forth].
For if that which was apprehended by that [cognition]—which grasps the exclusion of the cognitions of the subject and so forth—is false, then it follows that everything is false. // 76 //

[709] Why is it not established? To this he says: "The pillar," etc. For if the cognition apprehending the distinction [between the subject and the means of proof] were false, there would be no difference whatsoever between the cognitions of the pillar and so forth and the cognition of the means of proof (*sādhana*). Indeed, in that very same way, the cognition of the means of proof would also be false.
However, in order to avoid this fault, if only those cognitions distinct from the cognition grasping the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are made the subject of the thesis, then,

since there would follow the falsity of the cognition grasping the negative concomitance of that [subject] due to its own exclusion [from the class of non-cognitions], all the preceding [arguments] would fail to be established.

Furthermore, there would be an infinite regress in qualifying that [other] as well. However, since the opponent must eventually rest upon something somewhere, one must demonstrate the absence of each preceding [position] due to its falsity; thus he says "as far as" (*yāvat*). Moreover, these positions shown by the propositions regarding "other than that" (*tadanya*) and so forth, starting from the first position—

Regarding all of those, he states that there is either "contradictory non-deviation" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*) or "contradiction with inference" (*anumānavirodha*), saying: "Contradictory... (vv. 77–78).

To the question "How is this both?", he says: "In this way. "In this way" means by the manner that is about to be described. Here, a counter-argument must be stated; he demonstrates that very counter-argument with the words "external," etc. The cognition whose object is an external thing is the subject (*dharmin*). "Correctly" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*).

Because it possesses a cognition free from sublation, like the cognition that sublates dream-knowledge and the like. And since this [cognition] has well-known constituent parts, it is stronger than the inference of "lack of objective support" (*nirālambana*); thus, there is sublation of that [latter] by inference. If one considers them to be of equal strength, then they constitute a case of "non-deviant contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*); such a distinction must be demonstrated. (Is it not the case that [the former] is for one's own sake?)

But if one were to say that even the cognition which sublates dreams and the like is itself false, then, because those [dreams] would remain unsublated, there would be no illustrative example for their unreality; thus he says: "That too... (vv. 79–80).

Furthermore, regarding those cognitions which hold that "distinct cognition alone is momentary"—whether these be correct or false—if they are true, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) [in the reason]; thus he says: "vijñāna... (verse 82).

But if their falsity is admitted, then because there is an absence of the cognition that was made the subject (*pakṣa*) by its specific qualification, there is a sublation of the subject (*pakṣabādha*); thus he says: "tanmithyā... (verse 82).

And this being so, if there were no knowledge of emptiness as an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), who would be bound and who would be liberated? He says "thus" (*tathā*) to address this. Since this is the case, even the ascetic practices such as renunciation (*pravrajyā*) that aim at liberation would be fruitless for the practitioners; thus he says "therefore" (*tataḥ*). // 83 //

If, however, it is argued that the position that [the world] is mere cognition is established by conceptual knowledge (*savikalpaka-jñāna*), because all conceptual constructions are false, whereas [the ultimate nature] attains itself through non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka*), that is incorrect. For the universe as mere cognition, or the fact that "all things are momentary," and so forth, does not appear to anyone through non-conceptual knowledge. Rather, such matters are [established] by means of inference (*anumāna*).

They are established; and since that [establishment] is false due to its conceptual nature (*savikalpatvāt*), the position that knowledge exists and so forth is difficult to maintain. Therefore, he states with the verse beginning "vikalpa" that the effort toward liberation is rightly fruitless. Furthermore, it must be said here that if non-conceptual cognition were real, then cognitions of pillars and the like—which are likewise non-conceptual—would also have to be real, and thus the non-existence of external objects would not be proven.
Having disregarded that [objection], another refutation has been stated on account of the subsequent manifestation. // 84 //
Moreover, for those inferior to yogins— such as ourselves and others— all cognition whatsoever is based on conceptual construction and is therefore nothing but false knowledge.

Indeed, no distinction whatsoever is observed between cognitions such as "the Pradhāna is the cause of the world" or "there are twenty-five principles," and cognitions such as "the world is mere consciousness" or "all entities are momentary."

Since everything is admitted to be false because it is conceptual in nature, there is no reason to be found for this partiality toward the Buddhist doctrine alone— setting aside the systems of the Sāṃkhya and others— among the various doctrines of the non-Buddhist teachers regarding the objects being apprehended. Nor can it be argued that, despite the lack of difference in their status as objects of conceptual construction, there is a distinction based on the existence or non-existence of the object.

Whether correctness or falsity arises based on the proximity or distance of the sense faculties is impossible, because all conceptual constructions have unreal objects, and because, when all external things are denied, this distinction becomes difficult to establish. This is what he states with the two lines beginning "And all... (verse 86).
[710] Furthermore, you yourself have observed that the falsity of cognitions is pervaded by sublation, as seen in the case of cognitions such as those of a mirage;
yet waking cognitions are not sublated. Therefore, with the intention of showing that the pervaded is negated by the negation of the pervader, he says:
"Falsity" [is the term]. // 87 //

If one were to accept falsity even in the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), there would be a lack of determinacy because cognitions such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) would themselves be false; thus he says: "Because of sublation" (*bādhāt*). Furthermore, "correct" (*samyak*) and "false" (*mithyā*) are dependent upon their counter-correlates (*pratiyogi*). For something becomes false only in relation to something else that is correct, and something else becomes true only in relation to something that is false. But for you, who accept the falsity of everything, by what would this distinction be established?
The distinction between the correct and the false: for us, however, it is logical that waking cognition alone is true, while dream-cognition and the like are false in relation to their counterpart;
this is what he states—“perception” (pratīti). // 88 //

Not only is the falsity of cognitions such as dreams not established due to the absence of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), but the falsity of waking cognitions is also not established due to the absence of a counter-correlate consisting of a beautiful designation and truth; thus he says: "And not... (verse 89).

{2,59} In his own system, the falsity of cognitions such as dreams has been stated in relation to their opposites, namely waking cognitions. He states the justification for that very point in the verse beginning with "svapna" (dream). For waking cognitions are indeed distinct from the cognitions of dreams and the like; they are well-established for all people, whereas a dream occurs only to someone whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is overcome by sleep. Therefore, just as [the dream] is sublated by that [waking cognition]...

Since the condition [of being a cognition] is universal across the world, dream-cognitions and others possess the status of being counter-correlates (pratiyogitva) to waking cognitions such as that of a pillar; and in relation to those waking cognitions, dream-cognitions and the like are considered false. // 90 //
Here he raises an objection: "Of the yogins. It is true that falsity is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*);
however, even the cognitions of those in the waking state will be false in relation to the knowledge of a counter-correlate produced by the power of intense contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

For that [contemplative cognition] arises for one whose every impurity has vanished as a clear, non-conceptual manifestation. Therefore, it is logical [to consider waking cognitions false] in relation to that.
The falsity of worldly cognitions. // 91 //

Now, one might object: "Surely it is only for some yogi who has reached the pinnacle of the excellence of meditative cultivation that a cognition arises which opposes waking consciousness. And it has been stated that those [cognitions] are indeed well-known to all the world. Therefore, how can cognitions belonging to everyone in the world be sublated by a cognition that arises only for a particular individual?"

Therefore, he says: "of those who have attained. This is the intended meaning: transmigrating beings do not consider [the world] to be sublated only so long as they have not ascended to the stage of a Buddha; however, once that stage has been attained, all living beings indeed consider it to be sublated. Consequently, it is established that there is no distinction based on the greater or lesser extent of the object, because the cognition of the yogi serves as its counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
The falsity of those whose intellects are awake. // 92 //
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "In this case," etc. (93).

{2,60} For the time being, we do not perceive any cognition that contradicts the waking consciousness of anyone. However, as for whether such a thing might exist for a yogin, no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) applies to us.

Yet, if one were to assert a contradictory cognition regarding the knowledge of a yogin even without such a means of valid cognition, it would be possible for us to say the same: "The contradictory [cognition] of our own yogins is [exactly] as you have described."
Or else, there will be a contrary cognition of sublation, because in the case of arbitrary action there is a lack of a regulating factor; thus he says: "of the yogins. (94)

[711] Now, by demonstrating various objects that are properties not belonging to the position of mere cognition as taught by the Buddhists, it is either directly rejected by its counter-correlate through the statement "it is not thus," or it is shown to be contrary to its own object. Nor does this imply that there is no distinction between our two positions.

It must be said: it is by means of inference that we establish such a nature of the cognitions of yogins. For, by using as an example any given cognizer whose [cognition] has been apprehended, the cognition of external objects by yogins is likewise inferred, because every present cognizer possesses a cognition of external objects. However, the claim that yogins perceive mere consciousness (*jñānamātra*) entirely devoid of all distinctions such as "blue" and so forth is without an example.
This is what he says: "of such a nature. And here there is the following formal argument (*prayoga*):
Yogis possess cognitions contrary to those described by you, because they are cognizers, like present-day cognizers. // 95 //
As for what was said—that there is no proof for the claim that a cognition arises for yogins which serves as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to waking cognitions—that is incorrect.

How can it be asserted that such [a cognition] lacks authority while inference remains alive? For in this case, the following inference is established: waking cognitions possess counter-correlates or are sublated, because they are cognitions, like the cognitions of a mirage and the like.
This is what he says with the word "atha" (now): since the nature of being a counter-correlative and the nature of being sublated have already been explained [previously]. // 96 //
[Kha] This also refutes what was stated up to the words "it is accepted" (*iṣṭam*)— namely, that [the dream cognition] is sublated (*bādhya*).
It is true that for those cognitions occurring during the waking state, the cognitions of a mirage and the like are indeed their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*).
Since their status as true is understood in relation to this [ultimate reality], there is the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*);
moreover, their sublation is also established. For even those cognitions regarded as true do not differ from false cognitions insofar as they consist of the nature of cognition (*buddhi*).

Therefore, when those [objects] are sublated, they too become sublated; such is the operation of speech. Otherwise, he demonstrates the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) with the words "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). For those whose cognitions are true, the object of apprehension is one thing, while for those whose cognitions are false, it is another;

when that [latter] is sublated, because there is no difference in their being objects of apprehension for everyone, even the object of apprehension of true cognitions becomes sublated as well. Furthermore, those very cognitions of the yogins which are held to be the sublaters of waking cognitions—

He states that for this very reason the probans is inconclusive by saying "by subverting [factors]. Furthermore, if one were to include the qualification "other than those," an infinite regress would have to be mentioned as before; thus he says "in being other than those. // 98 //

And this reason is "contradictory by way of a specific property" (*viśeṣaviruddha*); thus he says with the half-verse beginning *mithyā*: "For the cognitions of dreams and so forth are seen to have as their counter-correlates (*pratiyogin*) the cognitions of transmigrating beings which are false; therefore, by the force of the logical connection (*pratibandha*), through the reason of being a cognition (*buddhitva*), it is established that waking cognitions are indeed counter-correlatives to false cognitions. In that case, the 'specific property' (*viśeṣa*) desired for those cognitions which are the counter-correlatives is their reality (*satyatva*)."

That [reason] is sublated. Thus, since the realization of yogins has the destruction of passion and so forth as its cause, there is a sublation of every specific quality that is desired for the yogic cognition in contrast to [ordinary] cognition; therefore, the reason becomes one that contradicts the specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*). Furthermore, this contradiction should be understood as arising from the sublation of a specific property of the subject (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*). // 99 //
He states another refutation: "of the great multitude," and so forth. This is the intended meaning: it is indeed possible to state a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*), namely:
"The cognitions of waking people are real, because they are not sublated at present by the great multitude, just like the yogis' sublated cognitions admitted by the opponent.

And if this [counter-argument] is of equal strength to the inference based on sublation (*bādhyatva-anumāna*), then it constitutes a counter-argument (*sapratisādhana*). However, if [the original argument] possesses well-known logical members (*avayava*)...

It has already been stated previously that there is a sublation by inference (*anumāna*) which is more powerful; however, the intent here is simply that, in every respect, one must obstruct the opponent's proof.
He says "now" so that the reason (*hetu*) does not become unestablished (*asiddhi*) due to sublation by the cognition of a yogi. [This refers to] the sublating cognition of yogis.
Even in the case of a future [time], the pervasion is established by means of the affliction experienced by the great multitude. // 100 //

And as for the faults mentioned in the *Mūlasādhana* regarding [the argument] through conceptualizations such as "dharma" and so forth, those too should be applied here to this inference; thus he says, "pūrva... (beginning with the previous). Having again established that introductory transition (*pātanikā*), he states another refutation regarding that very point: "tasya ca... (and of that). And of that previous proof, there is now another fault.

We reply: having conceptualized the property and the locus (*dharmin*), they have been refuted. Furthermore, there is no reason (*hetu*) established for both [parties] regarding that [subject], because it is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*). For this very cognition which is the probandum cannot be stated as the reason itself, since it would constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*). Therefore, the proof is devoid of a reason. [Objection: But surely, by virtue of being a universal (*sāmānya*), the reason would not be a part of the subject (*pakṣa*)?
To refute this, he says: "The universal. We have already stated that there is no reason (hetu) established for both [parties].
For you, the nature of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) as being both different and non-different is unestablished;
and for us, there is nothing whatsoever that is absolutely non-different. Thus it is established that there is no reason established for both. // 102 //

However, he states "sārūpya... [in verse 103], because he will refute later on the view that the universal has the nature of the exclusion of what is other than those possessing similarity (sārūpya-anyanivṛtti-rūpa).
He concludes: "Therefore. But if it is argued that there should be no universal (*sāmānya*), and that the particular (*viśeṣa*) alone is stated to be the cause;

That is incorrect. He says, "Because it is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) and because there is an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*)," referring to the phrase "of the two particulars" (*viśeṣayoḥ*). Here, two particulars are at play: the subject (*pakṣa*) and its counterpart, the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), which is also called *tattulya*. In the former case, there is an absence of positive concomitance for the reason; in the latter, there is the fault of not being a property of the subject. Previously, when the particular itself was proposed as the reason, it was stated that it cannot be expressed because it is non-different from the probandum (*sādhya*). Now, having raised an alternative, another refutation is being stated.
Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Let it be that the reason (*hetu*) does not consist of both the universal and the particular;

rather, a cognition devoid of an external object (*arthaśūnyā*) shall be the reason. For when we say, 'It arises because it is a cognition,' some cognition indeed occurs that is devoid of an object. This entire conventional usage regarding reasons and so forth is produced by cognition alone."
The followers of Sugata (Buddhists) hold this view; therefore, he says: "And not... (105).

For this very reason, due to these two faults, a cognition devoid of an object cannot be the logical reason (*hetu*). For that [cognition] is not a property (*dharma*) of another cognition; nor is a momentary thing capable of serving as a locus for positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum. Thus, this reason has an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), because its substratum—the cognition grasping the qualified—is itself unestablished due to its being without an objective support (*nirālambana*). Therefore, he says: "The locus... We ourselves, in fact, describe the thesis (*pakṣa*) as having an unestablished qualified element.

The meaning is that the reason's [hetu] lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) is also essentially already stated. Likewise, if "objectlessness" (*nirālambanatā*) is here being proven in every respect, then by that very conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*) made for the sake of establishing the unestablished qualifier, two things are indicated: the contradiction of the reason (*viruddhatva*) and the absence of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*) in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is because [the reason would apply to] total objectlessness.

For, since nothing of that kind is established in the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) proves something entirely contradictory to "being objectless in every respect" for one who wishes to establish objectlessness in some way or other by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

This is because even cognitions such as those in dreams lack objectlessness in every respect; thus, the example is devoid of the probandum. He states this with the word "tathā" (so). He elaborates on the deficiency of the probandum with the words "svapna... (in dreams...).
"Why is this not accepted?
To this he replies: "In all cases. For indeed, in all cognitions, there exists an objective support (*ālambana*) located in another place and so forth.

For that very thing which was seen in a certain place or time is what is perceived in another place and so on; this is precisely what constitutes the state of being without an objective support (*anālambanatva*).

"But it is not that there is an absolute absence of an object of apprehension. [Objection: "But even that which has never been experienced before in any place or time appears in dream-cognition. Therefore, how can it have an external support located in another place and so forth?
To this he says: "In [another] birth. This is the intended meaning: dream-memory indeed has as its domain what was previously experienced, with the mind alone as its companion.
And due to the influence of defects, there is cognition of the present. Furthermore, there is no fixed rule here that only what was experienced in one particular life is determined in a dream;
for even what was experienced in another life is quite capable of appearing in the mind, revolving there due to some unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
It is the object-domain of cognitions such as those of dreams. Therefore, there exists, at least in some way, an external objective support for even delusive cognitions;
that is to say, [it exists] at another time within even a single lifetime. // 108 //

Thus, the objective support for the delusion of dreaming, which arises from the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), has been explained. Now, he shows the external objective support for those delusions arising from the external senses, ending with the verse beginning "alāta" (the fire-brand). In the cognition of a circle of fire-balls (*alātacakra*), the very fire-brand, corrupted by rapid whirling, is the objective support. In the delusion of a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*), however, it is the clouds situated in a particular configuration [that are the support].

Thus, due to distance, they are apprehended by means of the previously perceived form of a house. Therefore, in this case, the houses seen previously and the clouds are the objects of apprehension through the delusion of their specific arrangement. Thus, here, the defect of the object is twofold and serves as the cause of the error. In the cognition of water in a mirage, both the previously experienced water and the saline soil heated by the sun's rays are the objects of apprehension; for indeed, both [are present].

Delusion gains its own existence by plunging [into the substrate], for it would cease to exist if either of those two were absent. In this case, error arises from both defects of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the object. For one whose internal organ is afflicted by thirst, a saline wasteland heated by the sun's rays appears as if it were water; however, the cognition of a hare’s horn arises solely from the mind.

Thus, [the notion] arising from some cause of error has as its causes the horn existing in another substance such as a cow and the self of the hare, because it occurs when both are present and ceases even when either one is absent. But surely, for the cognition that "there is no hare's horn," there is no objective referent whatsoever?

Neither the rabbit, nor the horn, nor their conjunction can be the objective support (*ālambana*) of this [cognition]. Because it is of the nature of a negation, it is not a non-existent thing (*abhāva*), since it does not appear as something independent (*svatantra*).

For instance, when it is said, "The rabbit's horn does not exist," we do not understand an independent non-existence. Therefore, it must necessarily be stated that this cognition "it does not exist" has only the self (*ātman*) as its objective support.

Therefore, he says: "shaving" (*mauṇḍyam*). In the negation of this horn, the shaving of the hare's head is the cause. This is what is meant: although an independent non-existence (*abhāva*) is not perceived, it is indeed perceived as having existence as its locus. Therefore, the parts situated on the head of the hare, which diminish further and further and have undergone a transformation into a long and firm configuration—known by the name "shaving"—are known in the form of the absence of a horn. For whatever appears in a certain manner [is understood accordingly].
That [object] is indeed the objective support (*ālambana*). Even non-existence (*abhāva*), when experienced as being dependent on something else, will likewise be the objective support.

But consciousness (*jñāna*), being of a positive nature (*sadrūpa*), cannot be the objective support for the cognition "it does not exist. And it has been said: "How can consciousness, which is of a positive nature, be said to be 'non-existent'?"

Thus [it is said]. If, then, a cognition arises from the word "void" (śūnya) that has no objective referent, it would be without an object (anālambana), because it is impossible to cognize a total non-existence and because there is no manifestation of any particularity. Therefore, he says: "a thing" (vastu). The intention is this: the cognition of the void is not independent.

For something arises by means of something else, and that which is empty is determined [by it]. A house is [determined as empty] by Caitra, while the world is [determined as empty] by the son of a barren woman.

Therefore, the cognition of emptiness has only the house and so forth as its objective support; it does not have [the cognition itself] as its objective support, nor does it have its own part (svāṃśa) as its objective support. // 112 //

Thus, he states that even for those verbal delusions produced by sentences such as "the finger [is the moon]," it is precisely the word-meanings corrupted by the defect of proximity (*sannidhi*) that are the cause—this is expressed by the words "kāraṇatvam" (the state of being a cause). Now, regarding an object such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) which has never been experienced before and is merely imagined by the intellect of the Sāṃkhyas and others—in that case, no objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition is actually perceived. For while things like horns may not be seen in one place, they are seen elsewhere.

It is logical that it is perceived. But how or where could there be a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) of something that does not exist in its own right? To this, he says: "absolutely," and so forth.

For earth and the other elements are indeed conceived by them as being subtle *pradhāna*. Indeed, the production of the gross world cannot be accounted for without a cause; thus, *pradhāna* is postulated. And it is not possible for that [gross world] to arise from anything other than atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Thus, in some way, it is the very elements such as earth and the rest, existing in a subtle form, that are grasped by the notion of "Pradhāna. This is an error regarding Pradhāna because, due to their subtle nature, they are not perceived as such; yet, in ultimate reality, the object of that [notion] is merely postulated through the conceptual construction of Pradhāna in their place. Therefore, the subject under discussion has been transformed.
"The conceptualization of that" is what is being referred to. // 113 //
But has it not been stated in this very context that "an object that is indeed non-existent is made an object by the intellect"? That is incorrect;

for how can there be a non-existent objective support (*ālambana*) for an existent cognition? Indeed, a present cognition of a jar is never observed to have a non-existent jar as its object. To this, he says: "This..."—namely, that very state of having a present object.

And [the definition] "having as its object a thing in contact with the sense-faculties" is a characteristic of the means of valid cognition that is perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), and not of other types of knowledge. However, errors (*vibhrama*) are not perception, because they are mere semblances thereof (*tad-ābhāsatvāt*). // 114 //

Now, one might ask: "What is this so-called 'property of perception' (*pratyakṣadharma*)? For there is no Vedic injunction here stating that perception must necessarily possess such a property. Just as [perception] is incapable of producing knowledge of what is not present, and thus perception has a present object, so too should its appearance (*ābhāsa*) be of the same nature. For how could knowledge be produced therein by means of something that is not present?
It is possible [for the past and future to be objects], because it is impossible for that which is non-existent to function as a cause. He first raises this objection with the words, "How?

and answers it with, "Why? For it is observed that what is not present is incapable of other causal operations, yet [the cognition] certainly produces knowledge; this is because even past and future rains serve as causes for the arising of inference.

Perception, however, conforms to the contact of the sense organs with its object. Since the sense organ cannot come into contact with that which is not present here, perception has the present as its object. But it is not untenable that, when the sense organs are aided by defects, that which is actually not present appears as if it were present, due to the force of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior experiences. Now, was it not stated that it is impossible for what is non-existent to be a cause?

Thus [it is said]. For a cause must possess power (*śaktimat*). And the inherence of power in that which is non-existent is not possible. No, because it exists. If that [silver] were absolutely non-existent, it would not produce cognition. Since that silver exists in other places and so forth, its inherence of power is not untenable.

However, because it lacks presence (*sannidhāna*), it is described as not occurring in any particular place. But then, how can that which does not exist at all by way of its own nature—such as rain and so forth—be a causal factor for cognition, whether past or future? Even in that case, [it is known] through inference based on a universal (*sāmānya*) by means of that [past or future] form.

Only that which exists can be an agent (*kāraka*). Alternatively, when it existed—that is, when knowledge was produced in the self by that [object] which had become an agent through its possession of power (*śaktimat*), and by that [knowledge] a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) was produced—then, in this way, the power of the object is transmitted to the self through a succession. And since that self is eternal, [the impression] has an eternal substratum.

Power initiates effects. And by that very power inherent in itself, when cognitions such as memory arise, past and future objects are said to be their cause, just as a sacrifice, though already perished, acts through the medium of a power. Let this be granted for the case of remembering the past; [but what of] the future?

But how is it with respect to awakening (*bodha*)? In that case as well, since it is impossible to infer [the object] without grasping the relationship for something not previously apprehended, a prior experience must necessarily be admitted. Therefore, even there, its status as a causal factor (*kārakatva*) is established through the successive transfer of causal capacity. [Objection: But surely the specific feature (*viśeṣa*) previously experienced was one thing, and this which is about to occur now is another.

It is known by that [cognition]. Therefore, how can one thing be the causal agent (*kāraka*) of another through a power deposited in it? No, because there is oneness in its universal nature (*sāmānyātman*), and because it is precisely that form which is the object of inference. // 115 //

But even so, you have not yet accepted an object exactly as it appears. For the object of appearance is that which is present, and yet you do not accept it as such. We see no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for accepting an entity that contradicts its appearance; for if that were the case, one would have to choose between the imagined state of having one's own part as the objective support (*svāṃśālambanatva*) or having an external object as the objective support (*bāhyālambanatva*).

Or rather, there is no distinction whatsoever; therefore, he says: "external," etc. This is the intended meaning: our dispute concerns whether or not external objects exist as the domain of cognition. And even in the case of erroneous cognitions, there is no discrepancy between the appearance and the [actual] external existence.
Objects appear only as external. The cognition of a mirage, "This is water," is not [the same as] "I am water. And that [water] exists in another location.

For even by a sublater cognition (*bādhaka*), the existence of water known externally is not sublated. Indeed, the thought does not arise, "That water does not exist"; rather, it is "This is not water. What is being said? It means, "There is no water here. That...

In this case, the conjunction with water in a particular location is what is being negated, not the water itself. Therefore, when the proximity is sublated, what contradiction is there to the appearance?
[Objection: Even so, the cognition of proximity would itself be without an objective basis (nirālambana), since its support would be a non-existent proximity. [Reply: No;
by "proximity" here, the conjunction of the water with saline soil (ūṣara) is designated, and that too, being well-established in some cases, is what is negated in this instance.

Thus, nothing whatsoever is without an objective support (*anālambana*). Therefore, since all this has been shown exactly as it appears, there is no contradiction with the appearance anywhere. // 116 //
[714] (KHA) What now is this so-called "without an object"?
For you, it is nothing at all.

If this is so, then the distinction between truth and falsity is denied. To this he says: "Therefore" up to the end of the word "knowledge. We declare that even external [objects], though existing otherwise, are apprehended otherwise; thus, knowledge is without a [corresponding] objective support (*anālambana*). It is not the case that a non-existent thing is the grasped object. That is how it is called "false. [Objection: Then what is the objective support for a cognition that has non-existence as its support?

It is not, first of all, an existent entity (*bhāva*), because that would involve a contradiction. Nor is it a non-existent entity (*abhāva*), because such a thing does not appear as something separate from existence and lacking independence. Therefore, by necessity, it follows that it is indeed without an objective support (*anālambana*); thus he says: "non-existence" (*abhāva*). // 117 //
Regarding this, he states the reason: "bhāva" [and so forth]. It is true that non-existence (*abhāva*) is not apprehended independently;

for it is a property of existence (*bhāvadharma*). How, then, could it be removed as something independent?
