Therefore, precisely because of the aforementioned impossibility of defining independence, the cognition that arises with respect to a cow or the like—which exists as a positive entity—with respect to the nature of the non-existence of another object, is said to have non-existence as its objective support (*abhāvālambana*).

The distinction is that this was stated previously and is now established. For the Buddhists, however, because all cognitions terminate in the self (*ātman*) and because there is no distinction caused by the presence or absence of an object, both—being without an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) and having non-existence as their support (*abhāvālambanatva*)—are difficult to define, since the two causes [for such definitions] are absent. Indeed, only when a cause exists can something be defined as being "with a cause" (*sahetuka*).
But this is not the case, as he says: "bhavatām" (of yours). The meaning is: "in your view. // 118 //

{2,69} Thus, first, the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyahīnatā*) in the example has been explained. Now, he states another refutation, namely that the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), beginning with the words "the proposition" (*pratijñā*). Just as the defect of the proposition and so forth was previously stated—namely, that because the cognitions apprehending the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmī*) are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), neither the property, nor the substratum, nor both exist—[so too is the reason here contradictory].

Likewise, by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*), both collectively and individually, even that which contradicts their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its specific qualities (*svaviśeṣa*) is a reason (*hetu*) for the cognition [of the object]. // 119 //

The example is not merely deficient in the probandum (*sādhyahīna*); rather, all possible defects of an example—from the absence of its statement onwards—must be applied here. For in the case of a single entity consisting of mere cognition, there is no objective basis for the probandum-part (*sādhyāṃśa*), which is "being without an external object" (*nirālambanatva*), nor for the probans-part (*hetvaṃśa*), which is "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*).

Furthermore, its pervasion by the insuperable portion [of the probandum], as well as the status of the example-subject and its properties for both the probandum and the probans—all this is established. Therefore, with the intention that one may state the deficiency of the example in whatever way one pleases through various statements and so forth, he says: "the example," etc. (120).

Some raise the objection that this formal argument (prayoga) is deficient in its example of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta); thus he says, "some. For there are two ways of stating an example. Some maintain that even when the positive concomitance (sādharmya) has been stated with universal pervasion (vyāpti), the statement of dissimilarity must also be made. It is with reference to the opinion of these "some" that the objection was raised; hence the phrase "some" was used.

Now, it might be argued that the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is intended to exclude the reason from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), yet here the presence of the reason in the counter-example is not possible. This is because, without such a statement, the exclusion of the reason from the counter-example cannot be established through the formulation of the proof (*sādhana*). Others, however, maintain that the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum (*sādhya*). If that is so, and if the pervasion is correctly understood from the statement of similarity (*sādharmya*) alone, [then the example is redundant].

It has been explained during the commentary on the *Sādhanabhāṣya* that [the reason] is neither mere coexistence nor a reversed positive concomitance; so what is the purpose of stating the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*)? And it has also been stated by others: "Or rather, because of its absence there, it does not occur in that case. Therefore...

There is no fault in the non-statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Therefore, he says: "In the absence of that... This statement of yours, namely that "there is no occurrence in the absence of that," finds no occasion here in the present proof; how then can it be said to have no occasion? To this he replies: "In the form of a positive injunction (*vidhirūpa*). The meaning of what was stated—"in the absence of that, there is no occurrence"—is as follows: when a positive entity is proposed as the thesis (*pratijñā*), its absence constitutes the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). And in the absence of that [positive entity], it is the counter-example.

"Because an entity lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), the operation of a reason is not possible; therefore, a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) cannot be made. Even this the Buddhists are simply unable to say. For among them, nowhere does a reason function as a manifestor in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) like perception. Indeed, they are proponents for whom the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is primary; for in all cases, their cognition of the reason is associated with the probandum (*sādhyānvita*).

Because it is difficult to find [such examples], the capacity of a reason to prove its conclusion is everywhere based solely on its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, when the statement of dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) is absent, the exclusion from the counter-example cannot be demonstrated. Therefore, according to your own view, a dissimilar example must be stated in every case. Even accepting this for the sake of argument, it is said: let it be that [the thesis] has the nature of a positive formulation (*vidhirūpa*).

Because it is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), [the reason] does not occur there due to its absence. However, when the thesis (*pratijñā*) is stated such that the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is a real entity (*vastu*) characterized by being without an objective support (*nirālambana*), then the counter-example is precisely a real entity that *does* have an objective support (*sālambana*). Since the occurrence of the reason within that [counter-example] is possible, it is indeed appropriate to state the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). Therefore, it is well said that there is a deficiency in the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-nyūnatā*). // 122 //

[715] Even in a thesis formulated in the form of a positive concomitance (*vidhirūpa*), there is merely an absence of purpose for the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*). However, in the case of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) that consists of a non-entity (*avastu*), the employment of the dissimilar instance is indeed possible; and it is so employed by those skilled in inference. Therefore, the dissimilar instance must necessarily be stated.

To the objection that what is not stated is improper, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). By the word *tat*, the thesis (*pratijñā*) in its positive form is referred to. The particle *hi* indicates a reason. Since the application [of the reason] is possible when there is no non-entity as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), therefore a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) must be stated in every instance. Thus, having stated the thesis here out of place, he demonstrates the very possibility of the formal argument by means of two reasons expressed through the two halves of the subsequent verse and the two occurrences of the particle *hi*: "In which... (*yasmin*).

When it is stated, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced," the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is indeed possible: "Whatever is not impermanent is also not a product, like a sky-flower.

This is because the absence of all [properties] can be demonstrated in a non-entity (*avastu*), whereas a positive entity (*bhāva*) cannot be demonstrated there. Furthermore, impermanence is a universal characterized by the activity called "destruction"; thus, the thesis is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*).

Thus, first of all, it has been shown that the formulation of the logical reason (*prayoga*) is possible even when the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is a non-entity (*avastu*). In this case, however, within the proof under consideration (*prakṛtasādhana*), the probandum (*sādhya*) is the absence of an object (*ālambanābhāva*) for the entity, while the counter-example is the entity that possesses an object (*sālambana*). Since the presence of the reason (*hetuvṛtti*) is possible in an entity, its exclusion from the counter-example (*vyatireka*) must indeed be stated because it serves a purpose; thus he says: "In this case..."

The word "tu" (but) is to be connected with the end [of the sentence]. However, whoever demonstrates a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) even here must necessarily accept that by means of the two negations inherent in the particle *nañ*—namely, "that which is not without an objective support"—there is actually a positive injunction of having an objective support (*sālambana-vidhi*).
And it is impossible to state a positive injunction of an objective support with respect to a non-existent entity in every respect. Thus, this is a "noose from both sides" (*ubhayataḥpāśā*).

[The opponent says: "It is a rope. [We reply: In stating a dissimilarity (vaidharmya), there would be the consequence of it being a real entity (vastutva); or, if it were not stated, there would be a failure to state what ought to be stated. This very point is expressed by the verse ending with the word *cit*: "And he who... [125]

[Kha] If it is argued that there must be a total dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) [between the subject and the example], then what would be the status regarding the negation of an omniscient being? For even in that case, when a non-entity is the probandum (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) must be excluded from the entity-nature of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—namely, the omniscient being. And in that way, the consequence of admitting such [an omniscient being] would follow.

Therefore, he says: "In this way. For in that case, it is established as follows: the direct perception of a Buddha does not have all things as its object, because it is a direct perception, like our own direct perception; however, that which has all things as its object is not a direct perception, like sound. Thus far, the objection has been shown against those who consider the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) to be pervasive.
But we do not think in this way, for he will say:
And when the positive concomitance (sādharmya) has been stated through pervasion (vyāpti), the negative concomitance (vaidharmya) is not required. // 126 //

The purpose of stating that [reason] is to eliminate the suspicion of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). However, since there is no counter-example (*vipakṣa*) here, such a suspicion cannot possibly arise; so what is the point of stating it? To this he replies: "By way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmya*). "This" refers to the probans under discussion. "Not a fault" (*adūṣaṇa*) means that no fault exists. // 127 //

"In that case, it follows that the proof is successful; agreement itself is the answer. To this he says: "In every respect" (*sarvathā*). For those who possess other means for establishing the probandum—namely, the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—are authorized in the paths of debate. But the followers of the Sugata (*saugatas*) do not [possess these] in the three types of discourse. Therefore, the deficiency of not stating a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is indeed not a fault. For how can there be the establishment of a probandum for one who lacks the means? We, however, establish the probandum through similarity (*sādharmya*).

Considering this, we do not take account of the difference [in terminology]. However, one who denies everything is simply not entitled to engage in formal debate (*vāda*). The mention of "debate" (*vāda*) is merely illustrative; for there are indeed three types of discourse: *vāda*, *jalpa*, and *vitaṇḍā*. *Vāda* concerns the student;
whereas *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* are employed to establish a point for a student who has become obstinate. Of these two, [the latter] lacks the establishment of one's own position.
Speech [that is merely] cavil. Therefore, in all three of these cases, the proponents of emptiness are not qualified [to participate]. // 128 //

Now, having avoided all the aforementioned faults, the Buddhist replies with "But surely" (*nanu*). This proof is intended to awaken you, who maintain that [cognition] has an objective support (*sālambanavādin*). Therefore, since you understand the probandum through well-known reasons (*hetu*) and so forth, why do you direct such manifold refutations against me by formulating alternatives regarding the thesis (*pratijñā*) and other members? // 129 //

The Mīmāṃsaka, having destroyed the entire web of fallacious arguments, mocks the one who speaks thus: "You are a deceiver. Surely you are a knower of logic (*nyāyavid*). Why do you speak in such a way merely to deceive us? Have you perhaps never heard that even in formal debates (*kathā*), only that which is established for both parties can serve as a proof? // 130 //

[Objection: But surely, a reason that is unestablished for the opponent is seen to be employed, as in: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product. For the Mīmāṃsaka, the fact that sound is a product is not established. If it is argued that even what is unestablished is proven by means such as the observation of its appearance immediately after an operation, etc., [we reply:]...
Even if [the reason] is not established for oneself, what fault is there in proceeding in that manner?
To this he says with the two verses beginning "yo 'pi": For when something is unestablished for the opponent but established for oneself, a formal proof serves as a remedy;
but when it is unestablished for oneself, there is no remedy at all. If one were to attempt to prove such a thing, it would result in a contradiction with one's own prior commitment.
But that which is unestablished and non-existent cannot establish the probandum. // 132 //

Here he raises an objection: "But [the opponent] says... For the statement of a proof is indeed for the purpose of making another understand. And that other person cannot be made to understand by means of what is unestablished for him. Therefore, it is logical that what is unestablished for the opponent is not a proof. However, we do not know on what basis the status of being a non-proof is attributed to that which is unestablished for oneself. // 133 //
And since it is not established, [the objection] "Is it not the case that the reason must be established for both parties?"—even by your own elders—that has been abandoned.

Therefore, he says: "Of both. This instruction from the elders is not for the sake of something unseen; rather, following what is observed, it is determined that its purpose is solely to refute what is not established for the opponent. Thus he says: "They will accept..."

Thus: since the opponent cannot establish the probandum by means of reasons (*hetu*) and so forth that are unestablished for himself, how could the speaker [the proponent] be able to do so? To this he says: "he should state" (verse 135).

For when a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*) is employed by a speaker, it is based on what has been directly perceived; through that perception, one may conceive of some capacity for its employment. What is the point of determining its specific details? For you, however, who do not seek to establish a thesis (*apratijñārthin*), it is more appropriate to examine the power of the proof itself—namely, "How was this proof employed by the speaker?"—rather than this [investigation]. This is so because...
He elaborates on this very point: "It is apprehended. (136)

[718] Since wisdom (*prajñā*) depends on the person for its determination, and because one follows that conviction, it is appropriate to investigate the cause of that knowledge when seeking a definitive conclusion;
it is not by means of inference (*anumāna*). Thus he says: "Where... (verse 137).

But even here, since the determination depends on the person, the determination would follow from the mere thesis alone; there would be no need for a proof. Thus he says: "And if it were so," etc. (138).

He shows by way of contrast that this is not the case with the words "But since... (*yatas tu*). The meaning is: "of this very means" (*asyaiva sādhana-syaiva*). One might ask: "Is the sentence then devoid of purpose?
He says, "No," with the words "Therefore, [the mention of] the Smṛti...
(*tat-smṛti*); the sentence is intended solely for the purpose of recalling the means.
Therefore, it is that very capacity alone which should be investigated; what is the use of defining the person? For this certainty does not follow from the pursuit of unattained conditions. // 139 //

Therefore, just as in inference for oneself one does not depend upon a speaker, so too here you should not depend [upon one]; thus he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is: because the statement is merely a reminder (*smārakam*). // 140 //

If, however, you maintain that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) depend upon a person, then that [dependence] would apply to one who perceives an object through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Yet, neither the reasoning established by me nor the probandum (*sādhya*) which is determined by direct perception exists there;
for instance, in this case, you desire the establishment of the reason "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) for the probandum "the lack of an external basis" (*nirālambanatva*).
He says: "And that which... (verse 141).

Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), [intending to show] that the comprehension of the object to be proven is not an act of rashness, even when [the reason] is established for oneself but not for the other. // 142 //

He refutes [this objection] with the two words "It is true. This is the intended meaning: this might be so if the statement of the proof had as its sole fruit the mere understanding on my part. For instance, would the statement of the proof merely instruct: "Understand the capacity to ascertain"?

Furthermore, once it has been established by you that the world is mere cognition, if you are then questioned as to how this was understood, the reply "you yourself know" is not at all a valid response. // 144 //

How is it not tenable? To this he says: "by himself" (*svayam*). When one is questioned regarding the cause of knowledge, that very [cause] must be stated, not my own established view (*matprasiddhi*). For a statement based on my established view would be tenable only if you yourself had personally realized this probandum by means of a reason that was either ungrasped or established for me alone. The word "pratipanna" is in the active sense (the agent). It is not [the case that the reason is established for me].
But both of these indeed exist. // 145 //

Furthermore, even according to your own definition of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), the statement of the proof (*sādhana*) has as its sole fruit the manifestation of one's own realization; it is for this reason that [Dignāga] stated [the verse]. However, inference for others is the manifestation of an object perceived by oneself; therefore, with the intention that the cause of one's own knowledge must necessarily be established, he says: "And not... The statement of the proof is not extended toward the judges (*prāśnika*) or the members of the assembly (*sabhyā*) other than for the purpose of communicating the cause of one's own certainty. For they...

These are the points to be established. However, if the opponent, out of insolence, does not understand what has been demonstrated even though it has been presented, what can be done in this case? Since the truth is determined by the questions of the judges, he disregarded the opponent and employed the term "judges" [to settle the matter]. // 146 //
Moreover, since the cognition of another is not perceptible, it is indeed difficult for you to establish that it is "well-known to me" (matprasiddhatva);

thus he says: "matprasiddhatvam. Furthermore, a statement of proof (*sādhanavākya*) is employed with the intention (*vivakṣā*) of communicating an object previously known; but for you, who do not know [the opponent's mind], by what would such an intention be produced? Nor is the production of a sentence possible without being preceded by that [intention].

He asks: "How so? [The opponent replies: "Even though I am desirous of knowing. First of all, I am not one who is desirous of knowing, because I have risen from that state. Therefore, your refutation alone must be applied to me in every respect. Even if I were desirous of knowing, nevertheless, the cause for your desire to speak is not perceived, due to the absence of prior knowledge. Precisely because it is impossible to state what is unestablished for oneself, [the objection does not apply].

For this very reason, your own [teachers] have stated that even in the case of *vṛddhi*, the reason is one established for both parties, and not merely for the sake of what is established for the opponent; thus he says: "iti" (148).
If, however, the status of being a reason were to occur merely by virtue of my own acceptance,

then just as you wish to produce in me a cognition of the probandum by means of a reason accepted by me, so too would I [produce a cognition] by means of these very reasons and so forth— which, though accepted by me, are unaccepted by you— by pointing out their respective deficiencies.
"I wish to establish your ignorance through various kinds of refutations. Even though reasons (*hetu*) and so forth are well-known to me, they are unestablished for you;
thus, this constitutes a refutation for you.

What is the distinction [in this case] such that a means of proof (*sādhana*) which is itself unestablished is called a "refutation" (*dūṣaṇa*)? Therefore, with the intention that the employment of inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is impossible for one who is ignorant [of these conventions], he says: "By that... (*tena*).

Furthermore, this "delicate hope" of yours—that I must understand the probandum by means of reasons (*hetu*) and so forth that are themselves unestablished—is also untenable. For it is you alone who fail to establish them; if I were to understand the probandum [by such means], I too would be subject to contradiction, since there is a mutual contradiction between the probandum and the proof. Thus he says with four verses beginning with "Just as... These verses are self-explanatory. // 153 //

He states, "And because it is clear," that one also falls into the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "contradiction between the reason and the thesis" (*hetupratijñāvirodha*). Akṣapāda has stated that contradiction between the reason and the thesis is a point of defeat, and he provided an example:

"Sound is eternal, because everything is non-eternal. For if sound were eternal, there would be no such thing as the non-eternality of everything; or, if everything were non-eternal, then that which is included within "everything" could not be eternal. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction between the reason and the thesis.

Regarding the "point of defeat" (*nigrahādhikaraṇa*), this has been refuted by the Bhikṣu. And it was said: "This is not a valid reason, because it is a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). As he stated: [719] dhe (GA).

"For this example has been stated by the unlearned in terms of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For a reason (*hetu*) is that which is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). And since not all impermanence is a property of sound, how could it be the reason? This [example], however, is one of dissimilarity for permanence; for there is nothing other than that which constitutes the side opposed to the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*)."

It is so. Here, permanence (*nityatā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), and its opposite is impermanence (*anityatā*). Therefore, it is correct that all of this constitutes a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). The underlying intention here is as follows: "Whatever is not permanent is non-all; this [sound] is not non-all; therefore, because it is not non-all, sound is permanent. Thus, "non-all-ness" (*asarvatva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*).

Therefore, since the non-eternality of everything is not the reason, there is no contradiction between the reason and the probandum. Furthermore, it has been stated: "This statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is also not correct, because it is the reverse of the rule of non-existence. For here, while 'everything' is the absence of the reason, the demonstration made is of the absence of the probandum, namely non-eternality. However, in a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the absence of the reason must be shown when the probandum is absent; for in inference, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through its contrapositive."

Because it will be stated later. Here, although one should have said "because of the non-eternality of everything," the statement "because everything is non-eternal" is due to his being well-trained in stating the dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*). This is incorrect;

for when this reason was intended by Akṣapāda, he stated a contradiction between the reason and the probandum (*sādhya*). As for the claim that it is not a reason because it does not reside in the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), [that too is incorrect].
That will be another refutation. Or how can "non-universality" (asarvatva) be a reason?

That too is unestablished (asiddha) here, because it is included within "all. Therefore, the Naiyāyikas have stated this—namely, that there is a contradiction between the reason and the thesis—merely by way of a hypothetical consideration regarding this intended reason. Or, let that example not be [discussed] here. In this case:

However, there is a clear contradiction here, which others—the Buddhists—have failed to see when they stated that "contradiction between the thesis and the reason" is not a valid refutation. The word *kila* expresses disapproval. This is because the contradiction in this case is so manifest that it requires no further illustration.

Here he raises an objection: "But surely... The conventional practice of inference and the object of inference exists during the state of saṃsāra. And in this context, the reasons (*hetu*) and so forth are indeed well-known in the world. By "the world," he refers to the worldly conventional truth (*laukika-saṃvṛti-satya*). Therefore, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of a reason and so forth established through conventional truth certainly occurred previously.
But in the state of ultimate reality, we declare that everything is non-existent; thus, there is no fault because of the distinction between these states.

He refutes [the objection] with the words "yo 'dhunā" (as for that which is now). For if it is said that [the object] does not exist by the force of its sublation (*bādhaka*), then it did not exist even previously. By means of the sublater, it was rejected even before; like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, from the very moment of the cognition [of the shell]. Therefore, how can that which is non-existent even previously possess the status of a means (*sādhana*)?

Or, if its status as a means were admitted previously, it would follow that it exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*). To this he says: "sādhaneti. He states the reason: "siddhir iti" (establishment). // 159 //

Why would this not be logical? To this he says: "It is not seen. This implies the following inference: the status of being a means (sādhanatva) is never observed for that which is absolutely non-existent, such as a rabbit's horn.

Furthermore, even a form that is observed in one place may, when metaphorically attributed elsewhere, lack the status of being a means to ultimate reality; how much more so, then, for causes and the like that are absolutely non-existent? Thus he says: "by means of vapor and so forth. // 158 //
He concludes: "Therefore," [verse 159].

[Objection: But surely, even though lines and the like are unreal in their nature as [the letters themselves], they are seen to be means for reaching the ultimate reality of the letters; therefore, unreality is not an inconclusive reason [for proving that cognition is false]. To this he says: "Even those... For a reason that occurs in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is inconclusive. And in the case of lines and so forth, which are means to the ultimate reality, there is no unreality, because they possess reality in their own form (*svarūpa*). For it is in that form that they serve as the means for the cognition of the letters; for one who perceives them and recalls the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), the letters arise in the intellect. // 160 //

[Objection: Let it be that they exist as their own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). However, insofar as they consist of phonemes (*varṇa*), they are indeed unreal. To this he says: "The phoneme... For all entities exist by way of their own nature but do not exist by way of another's nature. By some particular [criterion], the example of the line is given. // 161 //
And this mode is not possible for causes and so forth that are absolutely non-existent; thus he says: "In its own nature.

Even that which is unreal exists as something real in one form while being [unreal] in another form. For it has been stated that there is neither a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) nor a state of unreality. // 162 //

He clarifies this very point with the words "of the reasons and so forth. Here, the status of being a means (*upāyatva*) for the reasons and so forth toward [the goal], such as fire, is like that of steam and so forth toward fire;

however, it is not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthena*), but rather like a drawing. Thus he says, "by that. This is intended primarily to demonstrate the absence of the status of being a reason (*hetutvābhāva*). // 163 //

Here he raises an objection: "Of the means" (upāyānām). Does this [thesis] entail that the means are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*)? For they consist of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), and as such, they truly exist in that form. // 164 //
He refutes this by saying "by way of conventional reality" (saṃvṛtyā). For form that exists merely conventionally is constructed by words alone;
it does not serve as a means for the ultimate truth (paramārtha). // 165 //

Furthermore, there is no reason for a distinction between the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) of the world, because even the cognition that apprehends such a distinction is false; thus he says: "the ultimate reality... Moreover, if the ultimate reality were also accessible through worldly means, then it would not be the ultimate reality.

He says "laukika" (worldly) because [Brahman] is accessible through worldly means, just as fire is understood through steam and the like. Furthermore, the distinction between the two truths was previously refuted; now, however, the distinction is that the conventional is the means to the ultimate. But surely, the knowers of the Vedānta maintain that Brahman—which consists in the dissolution of the manifold—is described precisely by means of the unreal manifold of scripture and so forth? As they say:
{2,81} And the definition [of Brahman] is by way of the dissolution of the manifold of difference.
Thus: "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he attains immortality through knowledge."

Thus it is said. What has been stated? Brahman is of the nature of knowledge (*vidyā*), and the Vedas and other scriptures are of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*). He who knows both of these together, having crossed over death characterized by ignorance, attains the bliss of Brahman characterized by knowledge. Therefore, it is from ignorance alone that [this occurs].

"It is held that the attainment of knowledge [is required]. What offense have we committed by saying this? It is not our established tenet (*siddhānta*) that the manifold of scripture and the like, being non-existent, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman. For even those [scriptures] cannot be denied, as they are established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Just as the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is established by direct perception through the recognition "This is he,"...

"In the same way," they say, "those [means] ought to be correct in that very manner. And for him—whose enjoyments and the bases of enjoyment have dissolved through the cessation of prior karma and the non-arising of subsequent karma—there is isolation (*kaivalya*), which is liberation, not the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Passages from the Vedānta such as "one only, without a second" must somehow be interpreted as being devoted to establishing detachment from sense objects, like other types of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). This very [Self], by means of the formula "not this, not this," clearly [negates] the existence of external objects.

It demonstrates this. The phrase "this" merely describes the distinction of the object of Brahman, which is indicated as being non-remote; it does not state its non-existence. Furthermore, the discourse on ignorance (*avidyā*) in the Śrutis and other texts is for the purpose of praising Brahman, just as the term "non-animals" is applied to other animals in the statement, "Others than cows, horses, and elephants are non-animals. Therefore, in no case is that which is not ultimately real a means to the ultimately real. Let it be so.

Or rather, [we understand] Brahman as non-manifestation, established by the eternally faultless Vedānta; we do not, however, perceive through any means of valid cognition a duality consisting of a stream of momentary consciousness. This is so even on the basis of this [objection]. // 166 //

Now he presents another counter-argument from the Buddhist side, beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*). For they think as follows: even though an external object such as a logical reason (*hetu*) does not exist, nevertheless, the conventional practice of inference and the object of inference (*anumeya*) will be established by means of a reason and so forth that have ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*). Indeed, the various conceptual distinctions (*vikalpa*) regarding reasons, examples, and so on—such as "this is the reason," "this is the example," and so forth—are produced by the influence of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Thus ends the section on "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*).

We call this conceptual cognition (*savikalpikā buddhi*). Therefore, it is stated that from the difference in latent impressions (*vāsanā*) comes the difference in cognition, and from that difference comes the difference in the [logical] reasons and so forth. Furthermore, you too must necessarily accept this: that the distinction between the subject (*dharmin*) and other factors is dependent upon cognition. For it is not the case that "sound is impermanent because it is produced" [is established independently of such conceptualization].
There is no cognition of two distinct properties or of two distinct subjects and predicates as being separate from one another.
Therefore, the conventional usage of "difference" here is based solely on the difference between cognitions. And in every case, cognition alone is the basis for difference.

Even if one pursues the matter to its furthest extent through logical reasoning, difference ultimately resolves into cognition itself. Therefore, let it be that this [conventional usage] is based precisely upon that.

In every case there is difference. For even one who asserts difference on the basis of differences in place and so forth, when questioned regarding that difference, resorts only to a difference in cognition. Since conventional practice is established by that much alone, why pursue difference through any other mode? In this regard as well—such as in the case of fire and smoke, or producedness and impermanence—a clear apprehension of difference occurs, characterized by distinct features. Even there, it is not a difference in genus (*jāti*).

Or rather, it must be said that [the distinction] is based on a conceptual construction (*nibandhana*). And even that is produced solely by the words "fire" and "smoke. Indeed, we do not perceive any differentiation of universals (*jāti*) through any mode other than the conceptualization of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). Therefore, when there is a difference in words, [universals] such as "fire-ness" and so forth are merely the playful manifestations of conceptual constructions regarding objects.
Furthermore, this was stated with a lack of conviction, being intended to refute the existence of external objects; for even the difference in words does not [arise] from a difference in cognitions.

It occurs without [external causes]; that too is manifested by cognition alone, and it was stated [in that way] merely for the sake of distinguishing the conceptual divisions of external causes and so forth. // 167 //

He states that "this alone is the established doctrine of our own Tantric authors" by saying, "by those who know the logic. For this was said by the masters such as Ācārya Dignāga, who are knowers of logic: "This entire conventional practice of inference and the object of inference, according to the principle of the property (dharma) and the locus of the property (dharmin) as they appear in the intellect, does not depend upon external existence or non-existence. // 168 //

He refutes this as well with the words "astīti" (it exists). It has been wrongly stated by others that the linguistic usage of inference and the object of inference is based on what is mentally constructed (*buddhyārūḍha*), for no distinction based on words or based on the cognition produced by them is observed in the case of non-existent things such as a hare's horn. // 169 //

Furthermore, let it be granted that the distinction between the reasons (*hetu*) and so forth is based on the distinction between cognition (*buddhi*) and words (*śabda*); however, how could those two themselves arise without a cause? For the production of an effect without a cause is impossible. Nor can a cause for those two even be imagined within a void world; thus he says: "devoid of a real object" (*nirvastuka*). And as for this distinction of words which has been described as the cause for the distinction between reasons and so forth—
Since that [inference] is also untenable due to the absence of that [linguistic convention], he says: "The word," etc. (verse 170).

Furthermore, if a distinction such as that between the probandum (*sādhya*) and so forth—which does not exist at all but is merely imagined by the intellect—is postulated for the sake of the practice of inference, then the practice of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) would likewise be of that same nature. For indeed, in this case of proof, the notion of refutation arises from the mere statement of a deficiency in the reason (*hetu*) and other factors. Thus he says with the two verses beginning "Or if":
even in this way, it can be said that this entire practice of the refuted and the refuter proceeds by means of the logic of the refuted and the refuter as they have ascended into the intellect.
He says "and that which... [verse 173] to show that it does not depend on the external existence or non-existence [of an object].
"Even so, there is indeed no distinction between us two;
for just as our knowledge of the refutation has arisen, so too has your knowledge of the proof. Therefore, how do you achieve victory?
To this he replies: "By the intellect," and so forth. This is the distinction between us: for you, who operate solely by means of the intellect, my stated refutation [is not perceived].

"Since it is unestablished (*asiddha*), your position is not proven. Furthermore, the proof (*sādhana*) stated by you is unestablished for us; therefore, we do not accept the probandum (*sādhya*). // 174 //

How is the proof unestablished? To this he says: "External," etc. For we are those who deal with external objects, unlike you, who take refuge in cognition alone. In that case, how can we perceive [an object] when no external [object] exists? // 175 //
{2,84} Again, another objects: "But surely" (nanu). For just as my proof (*sādhana*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), so too is the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*); thus, the proof is not defective. // 176 //

But the Mīmāṃsaka says with derision: "Now, this Pāśupata speaks thus, that by abandoning the proof, because of its absence, even the refutation is non-defective"—this is what he means by "not now. (177)

Furthermore, the distinction among conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that was described as being based on a distinction among latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is also untenable because the cause for that distinction is absent; thus he says, "And not... [in the verse]. Now, one might object: "Surely the distinction among latent impressions will arise simply from the distinction among cognitions;
how can there be an absence of a cause? No.

Since that very distinction [of cognitions] would be without a cause, whereas if the distinction were based on latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*), he says "jñāna... along with this apprehension. Now, one might object: cognition itself will be inherently distinct and thus the basis for the distinction in latent impressions; how then could there be mutual dependence? To this he says: "of the clear... For the nature of cognition itself is clear.

The Buddhists have maintained that for that which has no perceivable difference, the cause of its apparent differentiation is precisely its being clouded by forms such as blue, which are projected by beginningless latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
therefore, this results in an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśraya*). // 179 //

"Surely, because they are beginningless, just like the seed and the sprout, the fault of mutual dependence will be avoided; therefore, he says: 'There is no proof. For in the case of the seed and the sprout, whose natures are well-established, the avoidance of this fault occurs due to their beginninglessness. But as for the impression (*vāsanā*), which is distinct [from the object], no proof whatsoever applies to it. For whoever..."

If one disregards an object of perception connected with the external world, how can one admit the existence of *vāsanā* (latent impressions)? Or, if such [a *vāsanā*] is admitted, what wrong have other entities done? Furthermore, we define *vāsanā* as the very *saṃskāra* (impression) which is the cause of memory and is produced by a prior experience. Therefore, if that [memory] exists...
Furthermore, it is cognition itself that constructs various apprehending subjects. As for why diverse external entities appear, it is not understood; thus he says: "it would produce... (verse 180).

Regarding the point that habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not the cause for the diversity of objects of apprehension, he states the logical proof with the words "by means of cognition" (*saṃvittyā*). Habitual tendencies are indeed the cause of memory; and memory does not perceive even slightly more than what was previously experienced. Furthermore, external entities that are absolutely non-existent have never been perceived anywhere before, so habitual tendencies are not capable of causing them to be remembered. Moreover:

And for this reason, the impression (*vāsanā*) is not tenable; because cognitions are momentary, perish without leaving a trace, and are not connected with one another—as he says: "In the case of momentary [cognitions]. Just as there can be no impression for things that are momentary and perish without leaving a trace, so he will explain further below. // 181 //

He elaborates on the very point already stated—that there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) due to a lack of coexistence—by saying "the previous," etc. Even if coexistence were admitted, a latent impression would not be possible because of the absence of any relation characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) or any other such category. For smoke from black aloe-wood does not perfume a house if it is unrelated; thus he says, "coexistence," etc. (verse 183).
It was stated that there is no *vāsanā* (impression) because of momentariness;

here he states the reason for this: "because of momentariness. For the relationship between the impressed (*vāsya*) and the impressioner (*vāsaka*) is based on causal activity (*vyāpāra*), since that [relationship] is a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka*).

And it is not possible for a momentary entity—whether preceding or succeeding—to engage in such activity toward those very two [entities]. Now, is it not the case that the very arising of cognition... [2]
It was stated that there is an operation (*vyāpāra*) in the determination of an object;
the same will apply to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) as well. No, because the reasoning is flawed. For indeed, it is observed that [the object] arises...

Nor is it the case that cognition determines its object; for it does not remain idle even for a moment, nor is it logical to claim that it exerts itself anywhere other than in the determination of the object. Since being an agent consists in the very act of arising, and no cognition is observed to arise while infusing another cognition with a latent impression (*vāsanā*), how can there be causality toward a latent impression by virtue of its arising?
Furthermore, the Buddhists do not admit any such thing as "arising" (*janman*) upon which the status of being a cause could depend. For us [the Naiyāyikas], however...

However, it is held that the "birth" of an effect is a particular state of its inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). And since that [state] is not absolutely different from the thing being born, it is logical that there exists a relationship of action and agent.
It was stated that there is no latent impression (*vāsanā*) because of the nature of destruction without residue; regarding that, he states the reason: "while perishing..."

Thus, for that which has ceased in its very own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and does not persist in any form whatsoever, it is impossible for it to be perfumed by that [perfuming agent], nor can it be said to possess that form. Likewise, as for the perfumer, how can that which has perished without any continuity (*niranvaya-vinaṣṭa*) perfume another? For only entities that remain stable, such as houses and the like, are perfumed by stable things such as the smoke of agarwood and so forth.
Thus it has been observed; and this *avīta* reason is to be inferred. // 184 //

Here he raises an objection: "If it is 'persisting' (*avasthita*). For that which possesses states (*avasthāvān*) and is non-different from them, persistence is untenable because of the destruction and arising [of those states] through the production and disappearance of different states. Or, if it were to persist, then, just as in the prior state, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no latent impression (*avāsanā*) in the subsequent state as well. In our view, however, both the subsequent and the prior cognition are transitory (*bhaṅgura*).

There is no single, stable cognizer whose prior form remains unaltered. Therefore, in this view where things are subject to destruction, it is logical that a latent impression (*vāsanā*) belongs to a subsequent [moment] which, though distinct from the prior one, resembles it. This very resemblance of the subsequent to the prior is what constitutes the latent impression.
Just as when a citron flower is sprinkled with lac-dye, the fruit that arises in its likeness is considered to be permeated by that essence.

It is said in reply: as for the claim that [the preceding moment] lacks the status of a causal factor (*kāraka*) due to the absence of activity (*vyāpāra*), that is incorrect. The status of being a causal factor does not arise from activity;

rather, it arises from prior existence. This is because an activity distinct from the entity itself is logically untenable. Furthermore, this very fact that the preceding [moment] is the cause of the succeeding one is precisely what constitutes its "informative" (*vāsaka*) nature, whereby the preceding [moment] [conditions] the succeeding one.

"87} It is perfumed (vāsyate). What is the meaning? That its own nature (svarūpa) is produced. Therefore, he says—referring to the phrase "bhaṅgura"—that the theory of perfuming (vāsanā) is logically tenable only for those who maintain that things are transitory (bhaṅgura), and not for those who maintain that they are stable (sthira). Setting aside the proof of one's own position for the moment, the refutation of the opponent's view is stated here. For once that [opponent's view] has been refuted, the established doctrine (siddhānta) can be easily set forth. In this regard, as for what was first stated—that perfuming is simply the capacity to produce a cognition whose form is existent (sadrūpa)—[the following refutation follows].
That is incorrect. For if a preceding cognition were the producer of a subsequent one, it would produce either a similar or a dissimilar [cognition];

however, it is not the producer of that subsequent one, because it is impossible for what has not yet arisen—that is, what is non-existent—to be a producer. The same applies to what has already perished.

Because there is no great difference between that which has not yet arisen and that which has already passed away, and because there is no persistence of a completed thing for even a single moment, the question "when will it produce? is untenable; thus, the production of a corresponding [effect] is cast far aside. For nothing at all can be possible as a correspondence for that which has perished without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vinaṣṭa*).

For "conformity" (*ānurūpya*) consists in the continuity of dharmas. There is no continuity of preceding dharmas in a subsequent cognition, because if that were admitted, it would contradict the principle of destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*). Nor is there any manner by which conformity could occur in the absence of a commonality of dharmas. He states all of this in the verse beginning with "This is not so," consisting of two and a half lines. [Objection: But surely it is simply the state of having been previously produced...

It has been stated that [an entity] possesses causal agency (*kārakatva*); what need is there for it to persist into another moment? Nor is there a relationship of activity and cause such that persistence into another moment would be required for the sake of that connection; this has already been explained as being non-existent. Do not say so. For we do not maintain that causality consists merely in prior existence. Otherwise, the relationship of cause and effect would obtain even between a cow and a horse simply by virtue of their temporal sequence. Therefore, there must be a necessary restriction (*niyama*) regarding that sequence.

[However,] there is the relationship of cause and effect. And this [relationship] is not possible among momentary things. But since activity (vyāpāra) is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception, it cannot be denied. // 189 //

[720] He states another refutation regarding the nature of *ṇaka* (the suffix -ana): "If... and so forth, in one and a half verses. For although it is said that a latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from a corresponding [cognition], when a cognition of an elephant arises immediately after a cognition of a cow, then in that very case, because of the dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*), there can be no latent impression.

It would not be so; even beyond that, the cognition of a cow would not be possible without a seed. And since the cognitions of a cow and an elephant were mentioned merely for the sake of illustration, he says "all" to indicate that no cognition of a dissimilar object could arise from a dissimilar [object]. // 191 //

Thus, for now, the position that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is of a corresponding nature has been refuted. Now, returning once more to the position that the latent impression is distinct from cognition, he states another refutation: "bāhya... (external...). For according to those who maintain the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), the latent impressions residing in the self, produced by prior cognitions, generate their effect only when they have attained awakening in dependence upon certain similar perceptions and so forth.

It is logical that [cognitions arise] in succession. However, for one who maintains the doctrine of cognition-only (*vijñaptimātra*), there is nothing that assists the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in producing their effects such that they would delay; therefore, all [impressions] would simultaneously initiate all effects, and cognitions would not be perceived in succession. Since the cognition of the entire universe would have arisen at once, nothing whatsoever would exist in the subsequent moment.

It might be so. However, there is no persisting form (*rūpa*) among these [impressions] that could produce an effect again. Because they perish without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśitva*), the impressions cannot serve the purpose of another (*pārārthya*) anywhere else, as they do in our own system within the self (*ātman*), since there is no other entity to be refined (*saṃskārya*). Therefore, because there is no subordination through serving the purpose of another, sequential order is not tenable. Through serving the purpose of another...
For [the opponent], just as for us, there might even be a sequence of cognitions depending on the attention of a cognizer, similar to the sequence of memories;
however, since none of this exists [for the opponent], the sequence of effects is untenable. // 192 //

Furthermore, are these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dependent upon something or not? If they are dependent, then since no [permanent] substratum exists, it must be stated what they depend upon. In that case, when a single cognition perishes, all the latent impressions supported by it would perish as well; for your established doctrine is that an effect begins precisely through the destruction of its cause, as any other mode of causality is untenable. For it is only while in the very process of perishing that a cause produces its effect; thus, [if the support were a single cognition], they would perish simultaneously.

If the omniscience of all aspects were produced by the latent impressions (vāsanās) all at once, and remained so, yet perished in that very same single moment, then nothing would exist in any subsequent moment. To this he says, with the two verses beginning "destruction" (vināśa): // 194 //

If, however, it is argued that even when the cognition which serves as the substratum perishes, the capacity—that is, the latent impression (vāsanā)—does not perish, then the established doctrine of momentariness (kṣaṇikatva) is abandoned. Furthermore, since for a permanent entity causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is untenable through either succession or simultaneity, it would follow that no effect could ever be initiated; thus he says: "If... (yadīti). // 195 //

But if it is argued that the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) proceed independently, just like cognitions, then the relationship of mutual cause and effect between cognition and latent impression would be untenable; thus he says: "The latent impression... (verse 196).

"Why might this not be so? To this he says: "They would [both] produce. For at that time, knowledge and its latent impression (*vāsanā*) would initiate their respective effects as similar counterparts—knowledge producing knowledge and the impression producing an impression—but not one from the other. Now, one might object that the production of a dissimilar effect will occur due to the intervention of a cause of a different genus; to this he says: "Not another. The implication is that there exists no entity apart from these two. // 197 //

Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), meaning that habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are imagined as if they were of the nature of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), but do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Furthermore, he says "na ca" (nor), because it has already been explained previously that such a thing is not suitable for any purposeful action (*kārya*). // 198 //

Now he establishes the theory of *vāsanā* (mental impressions) according to his own view, beginning with the words "But for one who... It is logical that a stable knower becomes the substratum of mental impressions through the practice of knowledge; however, that which is momentary cannot be impressed. Furthermore, such impressioning would not serve any purpose, as it lacks utility anywhere. Nor does that which is impressed differ absolutely from its previous state.

By which [change] one perceives difference; yet it is not undifferentiated as before, such that there would be no latent impression (*vāsanā*). Nor is it untenable for something to remain constant when another state arises, because the cognizer who persists through both the prior and subsequent states is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*). Thus, in this case, regarding the states and that which possesses those states...

When non-difference is intended to be expressed, the person alone—endowed with the impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by previous cognitions—would be the latent disposition (*vāsanā*). But when difference is intended to be expressed, it is the substratum of that [disposition]. // 199 //

As for the example of the citron flower sprinkled with lac that was described under the view of "conformable latent impressions" (*anurūpyavāsanā*), that is appropriate because of the transfer of its form [to the fruit];

however, no form whatsoever of one cognition transfers to another cognition, because [cognitions] perish without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśitva*). This has already been stated; thus he says, ending with the words "kusuma... (the flower...). He concludes the meaning of the treatise:
— thus it is called "without latent predispositions" (avāsanā). // 200 //

Furthermore, we do not believe that this *vāsanā* has been described by the Buddhists who perceive reality (*tattvadarśin*) as an actual entity. Rather, having conceptualized *vāsanā*—which is non-existent, unsupported by reason, or devoid of logic—in order to turn one away from sense objects, the negation of external objects was stated, just as the Upaniṣads state "one alone, without a second" and so forth. However, the misconception of moderns regarding that very point constitutes their grasp of the established doctrine; thus, [the author] reassures the opponent who has been refuted by saying "by reason" (*yuktyā*). // 201 //
Thus ends the "Refutation of the Non-Existent Object" (*nirālambanavāda*) in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
004. The Doctrine of Emptiness (*śūnyavāda*).

Now, regarding the doctrine of emptiness, the commentary here states: "But it is empty. How so? We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition; [this is] perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
And this is our understanding. Therefore, we see that there is no such thing as an object-form distinct from that [cognition].
In that case, because both that which is empty and that by which it is empty are not apprehended, the propositional statement "but [it is] empty" has an inconsistent meaning.
However, if—by supplying the word "cognition" (pratyaya) from the preceding proof-statement—the meaning is "cognition is empty of an object-form distinct from it," [then it is consistent].
Furthermore, according to the subsequent text, it is explained that "name" means "empty of object" (*arthena śūnya*).

If that were the case, the meaning would already have been established by that [previous statement] alone; therefore, he says "thus" (*evam*). Here, the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is that cognition is empty of an object. Nor is the meaning redundant, because there is a difference in the reasons for the counter-argument. That same nihilist (*nāstika*) who maintains the doctrine of the absence of an objective basis (*nirālambanavādin*) has his own proof vitiated by contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition.

Now, having set aside the objection, he establishes his position. For it was argued that there is a contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge by relying on a cognition that grasps external objects.
To this, it is said: cognition is not capable of operating upon an external object because of the lack of a connection;

and if there were the manifestation of what is unconnected, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, because only a single form is perceived, the existence of an object as the domain for the operation of cognition is not established.

For this "blue" that appears as "this is one blue" must logically be one [entity] alone, because it is impossible to admit a plurality when no distinction is perceived. Thus it has been said: "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and the cognition.
Therefore, this is the manifestation of all forms such as blue and so forth, which are projected by the impressions (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time; herein, nothing [external] exists.

If it were established as something external, then by its denial there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition. Therefore, this very same position has been revitalized again by avoiding the refutation [previously raised]. This was also stated previously:
"And when an objection based on perception was raised, [the response came] later from an examination of its capacity."
Thus [ends the first section]. // 1 //
{2,92} Here, intending to state the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), he introduces the examination of consciousness with the words "yat tāvad" (as for that which...).

Whatever refutation— such as contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*)— is stated by you, the Mīmāṃsaka, who considers perception to be the grasper of external objects, against the proof of the absence of a basis (*nirālambana-sādhana*):
This should now be examined. Here, by means of the examination of perception (*pratyakṣa*), the examination of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) itself is introduced;
for it is not admitted that any cognitions whatsoever possess external objects. However, the presentation of the examination of perception is made as the primary focus. // 2 //

Furthermore, as to what kind of investigation this is, he demonstrates its nature by saying "in order to function. Is this perception capable of functioning toward an external object, or does it terminate within its own constituent parts? Such is the investigation (*parīkṣā*). And investigation is defined as the determination of the strength of the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the conclusive (*uttarapakṣa*) positions after having raised a doubt. Thus, by this, the nature of the first stage of investigation has been shown.
It should be understood that this has been presented. // 3 //

He says: "You will discuss the examination of consciousness (*saṃvit*). It must be stated what its purpose (*prayojana*) is; for that which lacks a purpose, even if it be doubted, is not to be examined, like the teeth of a crow. Therefore he says: "If that... The intention is this:
this discussion arises by way of challenging everything that has preceded. And among all such challenges, the purpose belongs specifically to the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*).

As he will say: "In the case of the objection, [it concerns] the previous section. Therefore, if we are able to establish that perception grasps external objects, then, by means of establishing that refutation, we shall state that it is directed toward external objects. However, if the object of apprehension for all cognitions is only the internal aspect of the self, [then...]

Therefore, once the proof [of the external world] is established through the refutation and subversion [of the opponent's position], the nihilist’s denial of the external will be overturned. Thus, this investigation is introduced as being useful precisely for the establishment of external objects.
{2, 93} However, the proponents of a certain school of nihilism object, saying: "This investigation of the power of consciousness is without a basis.
For they, distressed by the absence of an object of apprehension, have described that even consciousnesses do not exist. Therefore...

In an empty *saṃsāra*, it is examined what is capable or incapable of proceeding, and where. Therefore, he says: "Therein. This is the intended meaning: it is not possible to assert the negation of both [the appearance and its object], because the manifestation of forms such as blue is established for all living beings without dispute. However, this must be considered: is the blueness of all cognitions merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), or is it intrinsic (*svābhāvika*)?
Regarding the phrase "of the external": in a void-like saṃsāra, an appearance without a seed is not tenable. Therefore, this must be examined:
does this very cognition, its nature obscured by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*), manifest as having the form of blue and so forth within its own domain;
or is it capable of establishing an external object that is ultimately real? If it first presents that [external object], [then it is established].

Therefore, that [momentariness] is also established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arising from the power of that [previous argument]. By presenting various forms such as blue, yellow, long, and so forth, he shows the seed of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This form—blue and so on—is not seen as having a single, fixed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because even non-fixed things like length and so forth are seen as being adventitious (*aupādhika*). Alternatively, if it were real, its lack of fixity would be untenable. And this will be made clear further below. // 5 //
"Let it be so, then—that both exist according to their appearance;
nevertheless, what occasion is there for investigation? For when both are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), investigation is not appropriate.
To this he says: "And not... The intention is this: both would be established only if there were a difference in form between the cognition and the object of cognition.

It is indeed seen. For at that time, it is impossible to deny that both [the cognition and the object] appear as distinct forms (*viviktākāra*). However, only a single form, such as blue, appears. Therefore, how could both be established beyond dispute such that they would not be examined?
This principle (*nyāya*) is indeed subtle and must be understood by the learned; by means of it, when one form is appearing in a single [cognition], [the other...]

It is established [that this is so]. This is not proven for those who lack critical investigation (*aparīkṣaka*). Thus it was stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "We do not perceive any difference in form between the object and its cognition. Therefore, the establishment of duality based on perception as the sole means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣaikapramāṇika*) must be subjected to critical examination.
Furthermore, we shall explain later how neither of the two [the object nor the cognition] is perceptible. Now, if there is no determination of a difference in form in this way...
This form should be accepted as belonging to whichever one—either cognition or the object—is perceived to possess it;

what is there to be examined in this matter? To this he says: "And not... This would indeed be so if it were more clearly understood that this form belongs to either cognition or the object. However, its being a property of either one is not evident. Therefore...
Whether it be cognition or the blue object that is the referent, the investigation is indeed appropriate. // 6 //

Now, even if there is no perception of a difference in form, one of the two is established by implication through the establishment of the other. For instance: first, since an insentient object cannot be established as manifest in the absence of another manifestation, its establishment does not proceed from itself. Furthermore, because knowledge that is not an object [of cognition] does not arise, the establishment of the knowable proceeds from knowledge. Thus, the dualist position alone is more sound; what is the use of further investigation?

He says: "Of that which is being apprehended. This is the intended meaning: the Buddhists are deluded in thinking that only that which manifests in a direct perception—such as in the apprehension "this is blue"—possesses existence, and not anything else, because what is not established by perception lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, the external object of knowledge cannot be established from internal cognition, because there is no connection between them; and if there were manifestation without a connection, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the establishment of cognition from the object of knowledge lacks any means of valid cognition.

We shall explain immediately below that the grasper lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, the acquisition of their own existence is possible only for both [the grasped and the grasper] as they appear in direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no perception of a difference in form;

thus, the establishment of duality is not evident. The point is that an investigation must be set forth to demonstrate this. And since the existence of the object being grasped [depends on the grasper],...
Therefore, this single object possessing a form is apprehended as "this is blue," and thus it remains one;
it does not draw in another reality. With this intention, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 7 //

And while others are thus wandering in error, it is impossible to provide a determination without critical examination. Therefore, if, while we are examining the matter, the justification provided by the arguments of our opponents were that cognition itself possesses a form, then perceptual valid cognition would be exhausted by that alone, and no external object could be established. But if, on the other hand, this is indeed an external thing...
It is established that [the object] possesses form in accordance with its appearance;

therefore, once it is settled that this [object] exists as something grasped by perception, then—by the very fact that its establishment would otherwise be impossible—in the manner to be described, the intellect (buddhi) is established, and with the intention that "my duality is thereby established," he says: "Therefore," in two verses. // 9 //

{2,95} Thus, having first introduced the examination of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and having stated its essential nature, purpose, commencement, objections, and resolutions, the Mīmāṃsaka—desiring to adopt the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—reflects for himself in accordance with his own school’s tradition, ending with the words "How could it be so? Now he adopts the prima facie position: "Cognition possesses a form" (*jñānam ākāravad*). But how is this [to be understood]?

Thus, with the intention of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that form-possessingness (*ākāravattva*) is predicated of the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is clearly of the nature of supreme illumination, he asks:
"Why? And this question—"How so?"—is to be explained in accordance with the inquiry in the Commentary (*bhāṣya*).

Furthermore, it is precisely with the intention of the Commentary's statement, "We do not perceive a difference in form between the object and the cognition," that [the author addresses] the form-possessingness of cognition.
He states the justification: "one. This is the intended meaning: we have indeed apprehended only a single reality in the form of blue and so forth.
Therefore, we rely on that alone;
we do not venture to rely on both. // 10 //
Now, let it be granted that one [of the two] possesses a form;

nevertheless, how is this certainty established—that it is cognition which possesses the form and not the object? To this he says: "If that... If the external object alone is held to possess the form, then, because that insentient thing cannot be self-luminous, it would follow that another grasper must be postulated for its manifestation. Cognition, however, has luminosity as its very nature.

It is not illogical that cognition manifests as a direct perception precisely without requiring another manifesting agent; therefore, the intended meaning is that cognition alone possesses the form [of the object]. // 11 //

"Is it not the case that the postulation of another apprehender, which follows from the force of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), is indeed logical? To this he says: 'By that' (*tena*). This is the intended meaning: this would be so if there were a postulation supported by valid cognition; however, since it lacks valid cognition, one would have to postulate a formless entity called 'cognition' as something possessing form, distinct from the external [object]. For the external [object] is... [The text appears to contain a corruption here. ...by that [cognition], its nature is unknown. [End of fragment.]

A relation does not, for its part, lead to that [inference], because it would entail an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, for one who maintains that cognition is eternally imperceptible, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established by means of cognition anywhere. Moreover, in the inference of an object from cognition, the logical mark (*liṅga*) must be either the object itself or a property of the object. In the former case, the reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*).

Because the object exists even when there is no cognition, and because it is impossible for that which is not cognized to function as a logical mark (*liṅga*), given the accepted principle that "it is from the perception of one part [of the whole] that [the mark is known]. Furthermore, that which is cognized cannot be a logical mark in the absence of a cognition of that cognition, since it is impossible for something to be produced without its qualifier being apprehended. Indeed, it has been stated that the logical mark is the object as it is cognized, not in its own intrinsic form, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Moreover, this state of being cognized (*jñātatva*) is nothing other than a relation to cognition; therefore, that cognition must necessarily exist.

For one who desires to know, there first occurs the experience of cognition; then, once it is known, it is determined as either knowledge or ignorance. Now, we do not say that the object is the inferential mark (*liṅga*) by its own nature, nor that it is the object qualified by cognition. Rather, the manifest object is the inferential mark. But surely that very cognition of manifestation belongs to the object;

if that [cognition] is unestablished, how can the manifest object, which has that as its limiting condition (*upādhi*), be established? If you say that the cognition of manifestation is not the essence of the object—

Is that [cognition] born from the object or not? First, it is not born from it, because it is impossible for a cognition that is unconnected [to the object] to deposit a new property (*dharma*) within it. Nor is it born from something other than that, because if it were not born from that, it could not be its mark (*liṅga*);

for when there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between the cause and its effect, there is no necessary connection (*apratibandha*). As they say: "Or is it that even though it is born from cognition, it is not [born from the object]?"

"One should lead [the cognition] to the intellect because of the absence of an obstruction. Furthermore, since it is a property of the object and is common even to one who does not know [it], being indistinguishable [from other cognitions], it would also lead to the inference of another's cognition. And it has been said: "And because the nature of the object is common, there follows the undesirable consequence of inferring the cognition of another as well. This might be argued: "This is not an inference."
As for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), it indeed arises even for one who has not grasped a [logical] relation; therefore, it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As they have said: "That correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*) is of two kinds: perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*)," because verbal testimony and the like are included within these very [two] among the means of valid cognition. Or, let it be a separate means of valid cognition. By what kind of logical inconsistency (*anupapatti*) is the object [established]?
Knowledge makes [an object] known. For that [object] has acquired its own nature from the totality of its causes. Why would that not be possible even in the absence of knowledge?

Indeed, it exists even when unknown. True; however, its "knownness" (*jñātatā*) is untenable. It has already been stated that this [knownness] is not something other than the relation with knowledge. If it were a property of the object...

Furthermore, the charge of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) has been described; it applies equally to other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For even when one person perceives a property residing in an object that is not perceived by another, the presumption (*arthāpatti*) of the other person's cognition is thereby established. Moreover, "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) is the obstruction by another means of valid cognition. In that case, by which means of valid cognition is the known object obstructed?
Whatever could be established through the conceptualization of cognition is therefore not established as being non-perceptual;

thus, cognition is not proven to be imperceptible. As for the one who says: "It is true that cognition is not established as imperceptible, but in that very same way, the object too is indeed established by perception—for in a single manifestation there is the illumination of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*pramā*), as in 'I know the blue'"; therefore, it is established by the force of perception.

Thus [is established] duality. We shall refute this later, stating that "there is no perception [of external objects]. Therefore, it is well said that if one accepts the existence of the form of the object, another entity must be postulated without any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). // 12 //
