This might be the case: one might think that regarding an object whose nature is non-luminous, there would be a postulation of another entity without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*), because otherwise the manifestation of the object would be impossible. However, we shall maintain that the object itself has the nature of luminosity, and we will not postulate another entity. To this he says: "Of that" (*tasya*). This is the intended meaning: our thesis is that a single entity alone possesses the forms of both the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*). Therefore, if the object...
Thus, such [a thing] is accepted by you;

our position is established, because the doctrine of non-duality (advaita) is proven. There would be a disagreement between us only regarding the name, not regarding the reality itself. For both of us...

[The opponent objects: "Even because they accept [the object] as a single entity. But how can there be a disagreement here over a mere designation? For the proponent of the object (*arthavādin*) admits a stable object, whereas the proponent of cognition (*jñānavādin*) admits it as momentary. [The author replies: True. However, this is the distinction: in any case, reality (*tattva*) itself remains one and the same. This alone is what must be investigated here. As for whether it is stable or unstable, that is something else entirely. (13)

He explains this very point with the words "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). Now, one might object: there is indeed this distinction that the external object is external and cognition is internal; therefore, how can there be no difference between things? To this he says: "external" (*bāhya*). The intended meaning is as follows: this distinction between the external and the internal cannot be established as ultimate if there is no difference in reality (*tattva*). For if there were a real difference, then one would be external and the other internal.

Thus, when reality is undifferentiated, in relation to what could there be anything external or internal? Therefore, this conceptual construction—this imagining—is merely false, being fashioned out of cognition alone. // 14 //

But surely, for the Buddhists as well, cognition is a single, transparent form. Therefore, how can this [cognition]—which is variegated by the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender—be determined as "this is blue" and "I know [it]," such that it appears as divided? For it is not possible for that which is transparent to possess the nature of blue and so forth; nor is it possible for a single thing to have the status of both apprehended and apprehender, as in the thought "I know this blue."

Because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, for this very reason there is no such distinction as "I know this. Therefore, the position that the object possesses its own form (*arthākāra*) in accordance with its appearance is the only logical one; hence he says, "In my view," in two and a half verses. The meaning is this: although the nature of cognition is pure and unitary, [it appears otherwise].
Nevertheless, in this beginningless saṃsāra, those very prior cognitions constitute the "progenitors"—that is, the sources—of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Because these impressions are diverse, being the causes of variegated cognitions such as blue, yellow, and so forth, there occurs an "affliction" (*upaplava*) of that pure self whose nature is cognition, in accordance with its own [past] form. An "affliction" is erroneous cognition.

What is meant by this? Whatever kind of latent impression (*vāsanā*) there is, it produces a corresponding delusion (*vibhrama*) that accords with itself. That is to say, a latent impression of blue produces blue, and a latent impression of yellow produces yellow. Thus, due to a disturbance (*upaplava*) that conforms to its own nature, the form of blue and so forth appears within the very self of cognition. And that [cognition] is variegated (*śabala*) by the forms of the grasped and the grasper precisely because of the disturbance caused by the latent impressions of those forms. By means of these variegations of the forms of the grasped and the grasper...

For indeed, by previous cognitions, latencies (*vāsanā*) bearing those very forms have been deposited. Therefore, the manifestation of those forms—just like the forms of blue and so forth—is not untenable. Furthermore, the appearance of distinct [objects] must be explained solely on the basis of the latencies for distinct forms. And thus, by the power of latencies alone, the form of blue and so forth appears, colored by the forms of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*).

It is logical that this [cognition] appears as if divided into "this is blue," and thus it does not depend upon an ultimately real external basis. For within a single reality, the triad of the result of cognition (*pramiti*), the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), and the object of cognition (*prameya*) is complete. As they have said:
"Though the nature of the intellect is undivided, it is perceived by those whose vision is distorted."
It appears as if it possesses a distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and their cognition.

Thus [it is asked]. He replies: Let it be granted for now that the various manifestations of cognitions are based upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*). But from what does their very diversity arise? If it is argued that it is because they are the causes of diverse cognitions, [we reply: no, for that would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). To explain: the distinction between cognitions arises from the distinction between latent impressions, and the distinction between latent impressions arises from the distinction between those cognitions; thus, this circularity is difficult to resolve. Therefore, he says: "mutual" (*anyonya*), etc. This is the meaning: this is not a case of mutual dependence.

This causal relationship between latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and cognition (*jñāna*) is beginningless, like that between a seed and a sprout. Here, no prior limit for either of them can be conceived. Therefore, what is untenable about the notion that from latent impression comes cognition, and from cognition comes latent impression? By the term "potency" (*śakti*), he refers to the latent impression; for it is well known as the "potency of cognition. This is the resolution of the charge of mutual dependence by means of beginninglessness.
Regarding the phrase "in beginningless saṃsāra," one should understand that what was merely indicated there has been explained here. // 17 //

{2,99} Thus far, it has been established that cognition possesses an aspect (*ākāra*). Now, he states another reason for that very point in the two verses beginning with "aneka" [v. 301-302]. The intention is this: the proponents of duality (*dvaitavādin*) fall into the fault of conceptual proliferation (*kalpanā-gaurava*), whereas we, who maintain monism (*ekatvavādin*), do not. [Objection: But even for you, there is indeed duality due to the postulation of a power (*śakti*); for if that power did not exist, the aforementioned distinction would be untenable. To this he replies: "of mere power" (*śaktimātrasya*). This is the underlying thought:

In reality, there is no such thing as "residual impression" (*vāsanā*) that exists apart from cognition and brings about duality; for it is merely constructed by conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). And a conceptually constructed entity does not bring about duality. Furthermore, even for those who maintain the existence of external objects, having accepted that [residual impression], another distinct power inherent in it must necessarily be postulated to account for the diversity of its respective effects. Therefore...

This postulation of power (*śakti*) is common [to all schools]. However, for the proponent of cognition (*jñānavādin*), there is this distinction: he postulates only the power of cognition itself. And this has been stated while accepting a real distinction between powers. But the Buddhists do not think so, because they accept that only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) is real. For this reason as well, he says that cognition possesses an aspect (*ākāra*): "Therefore..."

Thus, up to the end [of the verse], it is established for both proponents—the dualist and the non-dualist—that cognition is proven; therefore, it is logical that the conceptualization of its form belongs to that [cognition] alone, because it has a proven substratum. Consequently, the meaning is "having drawn [the form] from the distinction between real entities. But for you, since our [proposition regarding] the object is not established, the conceptualization of that form would have to be preceded by the conceptualization of another substratum; thus he says: "bhavataḥ" (for you). // 19 //

He states the reason for this: "Because [the object] would be incapable if that were unestablished. For blue and so forth are observed to be dependent upon something, as in the thought "this is blue"; this [dependence] is not possible without a substratum (*āśraya*). Thus, if it is accepted that the substratum is cognition (*jñāna*), then the substratum is established;

otherwise, it remains a substratum yet to be proven—such is the distinction. Furthermore, if one resorts to the form of the object in this way, it would follow that the form of blue and so forth is separated from that cognition.

And therefore, with the intention that there can be no manifestation [of an object] by that [consciousness], he says: "by that. By this, the reason stated by the Buddhist—"because of being a cognition"—is implicitly included. For he has stated as follows: "There is no cognition of something other than itself, just as when there is the cognition of blue, there is no cognition of yellow. But for that which has become one's own self, its manifestation is just like [the manifestation of] one's own self; thus it is not untenable. This very point is expressed in the phrase "in the case of non-difference from the object" (*anarthāntaratve*).
However, because blue and so forth are experienced, they manifest as being of the same nature [as that experience];
thus, there would be an experience of blue and so forth. "In that way" (*tathā*) means as it was stated [above], that [the object] is of the nature of cognition (*jñānātman*).
Therefore, precisely from this self-awareness (*saṃvedana*), the non-distinction between the appearing blue and so forth and the awareness of them is established. Furthermore...
He sets forth the reason stated by the Buddhists for the denial of external objects—namely, "because of the possession of the characteristic of being graspable"—by saying "it is proximate.

This is the intended meaning: for me, it is logical that blue and so forth, which are of the nature of cognition and are absolutely proximate, should attain the status of being graspable; however, for that which is unconnected, there is no possibility of possessing the characteristic of being graspable. [Objection: But is this not precisely the [definition] of an object?

The state of being an object (*grāhyatā*) consists in the arising of cognition from that [object] and its similarity to it (*sārūpya*). For cognition indeed possesses the appearance of external blue and so forth. First, its own nature arises from that [external object], because at times cognition is absent despite the presence of other causes, as has been stated: "When other causes are present and capable, the non-arising of the effect, which is cognition, indicates a deficiency in another cause. That [other cause] is the external object.

It may be so. According to the Sautrāntika school, light, the sense faculties, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth, indeed exist; and these are the causes of cognition. Yet, it is not observed that cognition arises [without them]. Therefore, since this [cognition] arises precisely from the contact with an external object, the existence of that [object] is established.
And thus, it is said that the apprehension of an object occurs solely through its arising and its conformity in form (*sārūpya*). (Or: "the objects are grasped...")

And it is said that "the object is apprehended. Therefore, since only origination (*utpatti*) and similarity (*sārūpya*) constitute the defining characteristics of the apprehended (*grāhya-lakṣaṇa*), the apprehended object cannot be denied. This is not so. If that were the case, then immediately following [the first moment], the subsequent consciousness would have to be the object of the preceding one, because it shares the same object, due to its similarity to it and its origination from it; for the arising of subsequent cognitions depends upon the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Furthermore, there is no similarity between the object and the cognition.

Because the gross form appearing in cognition does not exist within the atoms, and because this single form is situated within the cognition while the forms and other [sensory objects] are many and aggregated— how can there be a correspondence (*sārūpya*) between these two?
Furthermore, there is no single gross object as a whole (*avayavin*),
since that is not distinct from its parts.

If there were a difference [between the part and the whole], there would follow a plurality [of wholes]. Furthermore, if one part were to move, it would follow that the entire whole moves. And if one part were covered, because there is no difference [between them], the whole would either be entirely covered or not covered at all; thus, it would follow that the whole would be perceived without its parts being distinguished. It is not the case that the covering belongs to the part and not to the whole, for if there is no difference [between them], that is logically impossible. Or, if there were a difference, then even when that part is covered, the whole would remain uncovered, and it would follow that it would be seen just as before. Moreover, why would the whole—being distinct [from the part]—have a cognition dependent upon the cognition of the part?

Indeed, the cognition of a jar does not depend upon the cognition of a cloth. If it is argued that this is due to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things, we say no; for if that were so, it would follow that [the jar] could not be perceived when any one of its parts is not perceived. Furthermore, if there were perception [of the whole] upon the apprehension of a few parts, it would follow that even when only the tip of a finger is seen, the gross object would be perceived. Therefore, there is no such thing as a single, gross entity.
That which makes cognition conform to its object—now, is this conformity between cognition and the object in one respect, or in every respect?

If it were conformity in one part, then even blue would be conformable to the cognition of yellow, because both are momentary and unique; thus, that [yellow] too would become the apprehended object. And in that case, everyone would be omniscient. If it is argued that there is no apprehension because [the cognition] does not arise from that [object], then...

No. Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*), we have no proof that the cognition of blue arises from the blue object itself, being similar to both the blue object and the cognition of blue. Furthermore, we shall explain immediately below that there is likewise no proof for its arising even from the blue object. Moreover, since similarity (*sārūpya*) is equal [in both cases], there is no distinction between the apprehended object and the other. However, one who maintains that similarity exists in every respect would fall into the state of insentience (*jaḍatva*).
One might even superimpose an object onto the cognition; and in that case, the world would indeed be blind. As they say:
"If self-cognition were by way of partial similarity, then everyone would be a knower of everything."
But if there were identity in every respect, knowledge would become non-knowledge.

Thus it is said. Nor is the arising of cognition dependent upon that [external object], because the absence of the effect is established solely by the absence of a specific material cause (*upādāna*). For, on the strength of observing the effect, we declare that the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is synonymous with "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), is the cause of subsequent cognitions. Therefore, when that effect is absent, its [the external object's] existence is also absent.

We raise this objection: it is not possible for a complete cause to exist and yet its effect not to come into being. Therefore, since the material cause itself (*upādāna*)—when it has not yet reached the state of that specific name—is simply not yet functioning as an initiated effect, what is the purpose of including the term "object" (*artha*)? As it has been said:
"In whatever way one describes the form of an object belonging to that [cognition] which appears..."
I do not know how even such a grasping at objects can be true.

Thus, it is established that even when other causes are present, there is an absence of the effect. Therefore, similarity of production (*utpatti-sārūpya*) is not the defining characteristic of the apprehended object. Furthermore, since an object cannot be established if it is not being apprehended, it is proven:
"There is no other [object] to be experienced by the cognition, nor is there another experience of it."
Due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [consciousness] shines forth by itself.

Thus, because it lacks the characteristic of being an object of apprehension, there is no other experienced object; for this very reason, there is no further experience of that [cognition] either, since it is impossible for that [subsequent cognition] to grasp it. Therefore, it is established that cognition alone, being self-luminous, rejoices. As for one who maintains that an object is manifested by cognition even though it is entirely unrelated [to it], [that view is untenable].

Thus, the two reasons have been explained: that one maintains the illumination of a jar even by a lamp that is not connected [to it], and that the rule of simultaneous perception will be explained further below. // 20 //

Furthermore, he states another reason for the fact that cognition alone possesses a form—namely, "for this reason as well. For you Mīmāṃsakas, it is an established tenet that "that cognition is illuminating. Of what is it the illuminator? To this he says: "of itself. It is accepted as the means for the external object, which is insentient by nature and lacks self-illumination.
Otherwise, its manifestation would be impossible. // 21 //
What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "And not... For that which is the illuminator of something illuminates it only when it has itself been apprehended.

Therefore, if cognition is the illuminator of an object, it too would not illuminate that object if it were unapprehended. Consequently, it must necessarily be apprehended. And it is not possible to apprehend it as being devoid of form (*anākāra*).

Furthermore, no difference in form is perceived between the object and the cognition; therefore, one must necessarily accept that this form belongs to the apprehending cognition itself—this is the intended meaning of the word "sāmpratam" (fitting). Regarding the phrase "because its manifestation depends on that," the meaning is: that whose manifestation—that is, its appearance—depends upon the cognition. // 22 //

Thus far, it has been stated that the form belongs to cognition alone because it must necessarily be grasped, and that this necessity of being grasped arises from its being illuminating. He states that the other [the object] is also necessarily grasped with the following two verses beginning with "utpanneṣu": for an arisen entity is not perceived in two ways—either due to the absence of an illuminator or due to an obstruction. For example, a jar hidden by darkness [is not perceived], or [an object is not perceived] due to an obstruction such as a wall.

Or as it is in the world. And that very [object] is possible in both ways within cognition. Therefore, since there is no other cause for apprehension, it must be apprehended at the very moment it arises. And thus, it has already been stated that this results in the cognition itself possessing a form (sākāratva). // 24 //
If, however, cognition were not to arise at all prior to the manifestation of the object,

then it would not be apprehended because it is impossible to apprehend what is non-existent; yet this is not what you yourselves accept, since you admit that an object is known only when the cognition has already arisen.

Therefore, since there is no cause for the non-apprehension of that which has already arisen, its apprehension at that very moment must necessarily occur; thus he says, "And previously, with regard to the object... up to the end of the verse. However, if it were argued that although [the cognition] has arisen, it is not apprehended by anyone due to some obstruction, then it would follow that it is eternally unperceived. With the intention that in such a case the very non-existence of cognition would result, he says:
"If not," [it is said]. // 25 //

Furthermore, why is there no apprehension at another time? To this he says: "Why? For if the specific difference is not apprehended, it is untenable that there should be non-apprehension before and apprehension after. // 26 //
Now, one might ask: "Is it not possible that even a cognition that has already arisen could be apprehended in dependence upon another cognition? To this he replies with the word *jñāna*.

It is logical that an object, being non-luminous by nature, requires another cognition for its manifestation. But since cognition itself is of the very nature of luminosity, what need has it for another manifestation? Therefore, it must manifest instantaneously. [This would be the case] if there were a requirement for another cognition of the same kind.

This leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). As they say: "If [cognition] were experienced by another cognition, it would be accepted [as an infinite series]. Nor is it tenable to claim that cognition is simply not known at all, for that would entail its non-existence. Furthermore, because recollection is observed at a later time—indeed, people are seen to remember an object previously perceived together with the cognition itself, thinking, "That object was known by me"—and the recollection of a cognition that was not known is not logically possible.

And it has been stated by others: "And in that case too, there is memory. Furthermore, if there were a dependence on successive cognitions, one's lifespan would be exhausted within the cognition of a single object, and no transition to another object would occur. Yet, in that case, cognition is observed [to take place]. As they say:
"In that way, there would be no transition to another object, yet such a transition is desired."
Thus. Having intended all this, he says: "of that" (tasya) // 27 //

{2,104} Furthermore, cognition is known prior [to the object], and the form of cognition consists of blue and so forth; for we observe people remembering an object that was previously perceived and has since ceased, preceded by its cognition, thinking, "I knew that King So-and-so who passed away long ago. For if the form belonged to the object, how could the intellect be colored by it when the object no longer exists? Therefore, it is logical that cognition itself arises having projected the form of the object. And if, at a past time, the object were preceded by its cognition...

If [the object] were not perceived, how could it now be remembered in such a way? For memories grasp exactly what was previously understood; how then could they transcend even slightly that which was previously experienced? Therefore, he says "knowledge" (jñāna), meaning that the form of blue and so forth belongs to knowledge, and the experience of the object is preceded by knowledge.
By means of two [arguments]. Furthermore, these two [positions], which appear as if mutually contradictory, are both observed to be established. For instance:

on the one hand, it is characterized by the acceptance of the object, in that "the object is experienced preceded by cognition"; yet, by establishing the form of cognition, one rejects [the object], whereby its [the object's] existence is rendered false. Do not say so. For in this case, the object is not determined as being preceded by cognition.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparya*). He thinks as follows: "For now, I shall cause this Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) to accept the established nature of reality, which is preceded by experience upon experience. For this follower of the Vedas (*chāndasa*), even while considering the proof of duality to be thus flawless, first grants assent to the perception of cognition. Then, because the perception of a formless [object] is impossible and because there is the perception of a single form, [he accepts it] without effort."

And we shall explain the denial of the object in this very manner. Likewise, the author of the Bhāṣya has also shown the acceptance of the object only through a figurative device when he says: "Is it not the case that an object is said to be known only when the cognition has already arisen? The author of the Vārttika has followed him exactly in the same way.
Therefore, there is no fault. // 29 //
For this reason as well, the object conforms to cognition. To explain: there are speakers who say, "This object is blue because of the experience of that form.
This would not be possible if the determination of the object were independent of cognition. Thus he says: "There are speakers... (verse 30).
Therefore, he concludes that the cognition of an object is preceded by the cognition of the intellect (buddhi), stating "tasmāt" (therefore).

Here, some say: "Why is this undesirable consequence being urged—that cognition is itself experienced? For we perceive a triad within a single consciousness: the knower, the act of knowing, and the object of knowledge;
namely, the object of knowledge such as 'blue' with its form, the formless act of knowing, and the knower. Indeed, such is this perception: 'This is blue...'"

"I know. Herein, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the locus of the word "blue"; the cognition (*miti*) is conveyed by the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*); and the knower (*pramātṛ*) is conveyed by the first-person pronoun (*uttamapuruṣa*). What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for these three? It is perception (*pratyakṣa*). For perception is a direct realization (*sākṣātkāriṇī pratītiḥ*), and in this awareness of the object, there is the direct realization of all three. Even so, the manifestation of the knower and the object is dependent on another [the light], whereas that of the cognition is not.

Because [the self] is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśatva*). But the other two [the body and the senses] do not possess self-luminosity, because they are not perceived even when present, as in the case of dreams and so forth. Indeed, this person exists, because of the recognition [of the self] both during sleep and upon waking. The same applies to objects. Yet, at that time [during sleep], they do not manifest. For what reason is that?

If objects and the self are self-luminous, then consciousness (*saṃvit*) is non-manifest not because it is non-luminous, but simply because it is impossible for it to exist during states such as deep sleep. Furthermore, consciousness—which is the fruit and has the cognized object (*meyam*) and the cognizer (*mātṛ*) as its domain—is itself apprehended; there is no other, distinct consciousness of that [consciousness], by virtue of which this [primary] consciousness would have to depend on another for its manifestation. Therefore, in this context, consciousness is self-luminous, while the cognizer and the cognized are its objects. Even though there is no difference in their being objects of consciousness, the self does not possess the status of an object (*karmabhāva*).

Because it is logically consistent with the case of the goer. For just as, although the village and other such objects share equally with the goer in being participants in the conjunction and disjunction resulting from motion, they possess the status of the "object" (*karman*) while the goer does not; so too, despite there being no difference in the self's connection to the cognition that is the fruit of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the self possesses the status of the "agent" (*kartṛ*). Why is that? Because the status of being an "object" consists in being a participant in the fruit of an action that inheres in something else. And this is because [the object] possesses parts and is that which is to be traversed, due to the inherence of the motion in the body.

Because knowledge inheres in the self, that village is the object (*karman*) therein; and since the objects are likewise [inhering], they are thus [objects]. Therefore, consciousness, being formless yet established by its own power, also determines the knower and the known. Now, is it true, as the words of the careless suggest, that "cognition arises first, but it is not known first"? No.

Because there is the designation "cognition" (*buddhi*), and because that [designation] is inferable. Or rather, is there a distinction between cognition (*buddhi*) and awareness (*saṃvit*)? We say: there is. What, then, is cognition, and what is awareness? Cognition is the conjunction of the self and the mind. Cognition and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not different in meaning. Awareness, being the result, is the locus of terms such as "experience" (*anubhava*). And by means of that [awareness], the causal conjunction of the self and the mind is inferred. So what [of this]?

This is untenable. Because they are not far removed from one another, one term is employed for the other. But if this were so, when consciousness and the objects of consciousness are being experienced, there would be the consequence of perceiving two distinct objects of consciousness. And this is not the case, because there is a single form of cognition. It has been stated in this regard that only a single form is the object of consciousness, [and it is] formless.
"Consciousness manifests. Now, is consciousness then something that is not itself cognized? We do not say it is uncognized.

For consciousness is cognized precisely by its very nature as consciousness (*saṃvittayaiva*), and not by being an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatayā*). What kind of expression is this: "This is this, yet no state of being an object [of action] exists for it"? Because it is self-luminous (*svayamprakāśatvāt*). And thus, it is not non-consciousness.

Since the state of being an object of cognition does not have anything other than consciousness as its root, that [consciousness] is indeed the establishment of all things; and since that which is non-existent cannot be established, how could those [objects] be established either? Therefore, it is the very light of consciousness that establishes duality—so what is the point of proving what is already established? For blue and the like are mounted upon consciousness.
It brings about non-duality (*advaita*). However, since blue and other objects are distinguished from consciousness itself—which is consciousness without form—they do not conduce to non-duality;

thus it is established that there is the knower (*pramātṛ*), the act of knowing (*pramiti*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). To those [who hold this view], he replies: "Not so. This is the intended meaning:
even according to the perspective of the Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), the intellect (*buddhi*) is characterized as being inferable. For he has stated as follows:

"But when [the object] is known, one understands it through inference. As for the claim that this refers to "cognition" (*jñāna*) and not to "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), that is incorrect, because these two are synonyms. Worldly people understand that *cetana*, *buddhi*, *jñāna*, and *saṃvit* are not different things. Furthermore, the conjunction of the self and the mind is not *cetana*.

Because its qualities would be identical to those of form and so forth. Furthermore, if the mind were conscious, it would follow that consciousness belongs to the mind as well, since that [consciousness] is common to both the self and the mind. To say that "intellect (buddhi) is unconscious" is unworldly. As they have said: "Intellect is indeed perceived as being conscious.
Therefore, that very cognition (saṃvit) which you maintain to be formless is, for now, nothing other than intellect.

The statement that [the object] is inferable by the intellect (*buddhi*) is precisely with this intention in mind. However, it is not tenable to say that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is experienced directly as being without form (*anākāra*), while the intellect is inferred. Therefore, the meaning is this: that worldly intellect which is apprehended directly is not without form; consequently, for one who maintains that the intellect is perceptible, this form must reside within the cognition (*jñāna*).

This must be stated: as we have said, or according to the Vārttika, the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is that it is the object alone that is perceived, not the cognition. And in that regard, the impossibility of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for inferring cognition has already been explained. Therefore, it is unproven that consciousness itself establishes duality through the non-perception of a formless cognition. // 31 //

[722] ha [723] Even though this is being experienced (saṃvedyamāna), since there is a rule of simultaneous apprehension (sahopalambhaniyama), it follows that the three would result in non-difference; thus he says: "Because of the absence of a cognition of distinction (vivekabuddhyabhāvāt)."
And so it is said. Because there is no cognition of distinction among the three, it follows that there would be a perception of a single cognition alone as possessing a form;

this is the connection with what will be stated hereafter. The mention of "cognition" (*jñāna*) is for the sake of illustration. What is intended is that reality itself would be one and possess a form. For one who maintains the simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha*) of the object of knowledge (*meyam*), the knower (*mātṛ*), and the means of knowledge (*pramā*), there is an absence of a cognition of either one as distinct from the others.

Otherwise, the three would necessarily be non-different, because a restriction [of simultaneous perception] is impossible if they are different. For in the case of distinct things such as jars and the like, their simultaneous perception is not restricted;

indeed, they are perceived both together and separately. Therefore, since difference is pervaded by the lack of restriction, it cannot exist when there is the perception of that which is contradictory to its pervader.

It would be like smoke pervaded by fire even where there is no fire. If it is argued that there is a distinction because of a distinct appearance, we say no, because that is not invariably the case. In this regard, one might think:
"Even at one time, the triad, while being experienced, appears as distinct just like a jar, a wall, and so forth; therefore, it is distinct."

This is not so. Because the perception of difference is inconclusive regarding difference. Indeed, in the cognition of two moons and the like, the moon is perceived as non-different, yet it is not distinct from the single moon. For what reason? Precisely because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*).
For that [cognition] is necessarily perceived simultaneously with its primary object.

Therefore, it is not distinct from that. Thus, only those entities whose co-perception (*sahopalambha*) is not fixed are distinguished when they are apprehended as distinct, and not others. As they have said: "Even though there is a distinct appearance, there is no state of being a different object, because blue is experienced [as such];
for those two, there is a rule of co-perception, like the double moon. But surely, even for two distinct things, such as form and light, there is a rule of co-perception?
[Objection: It has been observed that there is no cognition of form (*rūpa-buddhi*) when light is not perceived. [Response:
That is not so, because light is sometimes seen even by itself, and because form exists among certain classes of living beings even without light.
For there are indeed some beings who perceive form only in darkness, while they are hindered by light. [This applies to] the cognitions of the mother, the means of knowledge, and the object.

Since they are always perceived together, they do not deserve to be considered distinct. For yellow is not invariably perceived together with blue as something distinct from it. Therefore, due to the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), the triad [of object, cognition, and self] must be non-different. Now, let this objection apply to certain Mīmāṃsakas who maintain the rule of simultaneous perception; however, as for those who hold that [cognition] is preceded by the awareness of the object...

Those who maintain that consciousness is perceived by the intellect (*buddhi*) find the rule of simultaneous apprehension unestablished for them; for consciousness is always apprehended only at a time subsequent to the cognition of the object. As they say:
"First the object is grasped, and afterwards the cognition [is known] by virtue of the object's cognizedness (*jñātatā*)."

Thus he replies to them with the words "That [is] it" (*seti ta iti*). This is the intended meaning: first of all, this is beyond dispute—that an object possessing form (*sākāra*) is perceived. And this perception of form does not manifest as a mere existence (*sanmātratayā*) when consciousness (*saṃvedana*) is not directly perceived, because if that were the case, it would follow that [the object] is eternally manifest. Therefore, the manifestation of the object occurs precisely through the existence of the apprehension of the object, and not through the existence of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpasattā*). Furthermore, the existence of the apprehension of the object is unestablished; it cannot serve for linguistic usage based on existence.
Therefore, its establishment must be accepted as occurring through the act of "striving" (ghaṭata). And there is no establishment of entities other than cognition;

thus, if perception is known to be unestablished, then in the absence of that [perception], the object is unestablished, whereby the entire world would vanish because that very [perception] is the establishment of it. Consequently, from this untenable observation of an object possessing form, it is understood that there is simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha*).
Otherwise, its perception would be impossible. As they have said:
"For one who does not perceive the apprehension itself, the seeing of the object is not established.

Therefore, it is proven that because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, cognition is understood as possessing a form; there is no real distinction [between the cognition and its object]. // 32 //

He says: If the object of perception is not established when the perception itself is unestablished, let the perception remain unestablished. However, [the perception] will establish the object of perception once it is established by another perception. Even so, the rule of simultaneous perception remains unestablished, because the establishment of the object of perception is preceded by the establishment of the perception. [The rule] is preceded by the establishment of the object of perception.

The proof of apprehension has been rejected, because if proof is unestablished, the probandum cannot be established. Why, then, is the establishment of the probandum not accepted as being preceded by the establishment of the proof?
Therefore, this reason is indeed unestablished; to this he says: "For not... The meaning of this is: such a conceptual construction is not possible.

That which is experienced at the outset as a formless consciousness (*nirākārā saṃvit*), and subsequently [the object] as a formed object (*sākāro 'rthaḥ*)—this conceptualization is not tenable. For it has already been stated that a cognition devoid of form is unperceived. Furthermore, for what reason could an object distinct from its own perception be perceived at the very moment when its own perception is being perceived?

For it is a most ill-spoken statement that what is not established even while being perceived would be established when not being perceived at the time of another's perception. Moreover, if cognition is perceived by another, that other is itself unestablished and thus cannot serve to establish it;
this leads to an infinite regress through mutual dependence. If one is unestablished, all are unestablished. Or else, if there were something self-luminous anywhere, others too [would be so].
Thus they would be indistinguishable. Therefore, it is established that cognition perceives both itself and the form of the object simultaneously;

this is the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*). For a single operation cannot occur sequentially. Indeed, this operation of consciousness toward its own self and toward the form of the object is of the nature of illumination; it does not occur in succession, nor is such a thing possible. // 33 //
[Objection: "Granted that there may be no perception of a formless cognition; nevertheless, that [cognition] will be perceived as possessing a form, as will the object.
Therefore, both will possess forms. Consequently, what is untenable about their being perceived?
To this, he says: "The form... The meaning of this is as follows: if this distinction between the possession of form by the cognition and the object...

If it were known, then having known it, one would also be able to speak of it—just as one distinguishes between blue and yellow. Yet, it is not possible to speak in this way: "such is the form of the cognition" and "such is the form of the object."

"Because [the object] is known merely through its form as blue and so forth. For in this way, everything becomes consistent. If the object were established as possessing a form only after the cognition has been apprehended, then—since that [object] could not otherwise be established—the cognition too might occasionally be established; thus, duality would be proven. But here, since the object is not established when the cognition is unapprehended, it was already proved in the passage "and because of the perception of the form [itself]. Therefore, with the intention that duality is not established in any way whatsoever, he says: "prior [to the apprehension of cognition]," etc. (34).

Another opinion holds: it is true that cognition possesses an aspect (*ākāra*), but this aspect is imparted to the cognition by the object. This alone constitutes the relationship of apprehended and apprehender between the object and the cognition, namely, the object’s conferral of its own aspect upon the cognition. Otherwise, how could a past object—occurring at a different time—serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for cognition, given that [the object] is momentary? As they say:

If it is asked how that which exists at a different time can be an object of cognition, those who know the logic of reasoning understand that its very nature as a cause— its capacity to impart its form to the cognition— is what constitutes its status as an object.

Thus [it is stated]. He refutes this with the words "but not. Why is it not so? To this he says: "For not... For the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is a property of the object (*arthadharma*). And a property is not capable of abandoning its own substratum or going to another substratum, because that would entail the loss of its own nature (*svarūpahāna*). // 35 //

[724] Furthermore, this might be possible if the object's possession of a form were established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, there is no proof that such a form exists as a property of the object.
As for the claim that "the non-production of an effect even when other causes are present indicates the deficiency of some other cause," that has already been refuted.

With the intention of stating that the accomplishment of the effect follows precisely from the specific nature of the appropriation (*upādāna*), he says: "In this way" (*ittham*). However, as for those who say:
"Granted that the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is not capable of abandoning the object or migrating to another substratum;
nevertheless, this is seen as a reflection of the object itself within the nature of cognition, which is as clear as a pure mirror," he addresses them by saying: "Belonging to that" (*tadīya*).
"From this very [reason]" means that there is a lack of evidence for the existence of the form of the object. // 36 //

He awakens [the student] to those very points by means of the well-known example of a reflection, beginning with "niścandra" (without the moon). By the force of the context, "tam" (it) refers back to the moon; the meaning is "in the sky and in the water.
He says "vijñāna" (consciousness) because this logical principle [of reflection] is not possible here [in the case of consciousness]. // 38 //

Furthermore, while the conception of a reflection may be possible for things possessing form (*rūpavat*), the conception of a reflection for formless things such as sound and so forth is in no way possible; thus he says "sound" (*śabda*). Moreover, cognition (*saṃvit*) is perceived in the form of blue and so on. What wrong has been done that this form is disregarded and instead accepted as a property of the object, and that its perception is said to be like a reflection? With this intention, he says "in cognition" (*jñāne*). // 39 //
But as for the one who says: "The form of the object does not transfer into cognition. Nor is a reflection residing in the object perceived.

Rather, cognition is touched by the object like an iron ball by fire; therefore, just as in iron, the form of the object appears in cognition due to delusion," he replies to him: "Externally. For [this would require] the contact of iron and fire...

It may be argued that a delusion of non-discrimination arises from ignorance; however, the external and internal regions are objects of knowledge that are not in contact with one another. Therefore, how can there be a delusion of non-discrimination between these two due to ignorance? // 40 //

Moreover, while a certain individual might be deluded, the postulation of delusion for the entire world is itself a mere delusion. Furthermore, no one is ever seen here who is not deluded, because everyone fails to perceive the distinction [between the self and the objects]. Therefore, he says "of one who is undeluded" to show that the postulation of delusion is not tenable. If, however, delusion were postulated even when the distinctness of knowledge and its object is not perceived, then it would not be restricted to those two alone. For in that case, one could simply enumerate whatever principles one desires and call that "delusion."
To the question "By what distinction? he says: "When being conceptualized," etc. (verse 41).

Another view holds: "The form of the object is not perceived in cognition due to delusion; rather, this form is adventitious (*sāṃsargika*), like the redness that arises from the mixture of lime and turmeric. This too is untenable for the very same reason—namely, because of being external and internal respectively—as he states with the word "saṃsarge" (in the mixture). He clarifies that very point with the words "deśabhedāt" (due to the difference in location). Furthermore:

Knowledge is formless, while the object is formed; how could a form, which is a property of their conjunction, arise from these two? [The author] says—“likewise, by virtue of being formed and formless”—because such a thing is not observed in cases such as a jar and space. // 42 //

[Objection: "Even if there is no spatial co-location (*ekadeśatva*), there will still be a relation (*saṃsarga*) due to their being simultaneous. To this, he says: "By the three worlds" (*trailokyena*). For if the three worlds were in contact with cognition by virtue of being simultaneous, they would appear bearing a form produced by that contact; but such is not the case. Therefore, because it overextends [to all things], there is no relation by way of simultaneity. [Objection: "But surely there is a state of direct alignment (*ārjavāvasthāna*) between cognition and its object..."

Thinking that there might be contact [between the sense organ and the object], he says "and not" (*na ca*). Because one who is not facing [the object] lacks directness (*ārjava*), the object does not abide in a state of directness relative to the cognition.

Alternatively, if it were "facing all directions" (*sarvatomukha*) due to the cognition of objects in every direction, it would follow that there is contact with all objects, resulting in the perception of all forms.
For it is not logical that something facing all directions could be directed toward any single [object]. // 43 //
Moreover, by whatever object the connection of cognition is imagined, it must be imagined as being connected with that object in every respect,

because [cognition] is partless (*nirbhāgatva*). And thus, when a single entity is experienced by the eye, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the taste and other qualities contained therein by means of that very same [eye].
And he says "in every way" (sarvathā) to indicate the perception of the subtle forms contained therein. // 44 //

[Objection: "But surely, that very state of the object as being present as the objective correlate (*viṣayatā*) toward its cognition will constitute the connection (*saṃsarga*) between these two. To this he says: "And not... He states the reason for this: "Because it is the state of being an object (*viṣayatva*). This is the intended meaning: for one who maintains that the form [of the object] exists in the connection, the connection must be asserted prior even to the perception of the form. Yet, the state of being an object does not exist prior to the perception of the form. Therefore, how could there be a form based upon that [connection]?
Consciousness arises. // 45 //
"Why might this not be so? To this he replies: "For indeed... For those who know the object (*viṣayavid*), an entity is an object only when it is being experienced.
Therefore, since the status of being an object occurs only after its apprehension, one cannot accept that the cognition of the form is based upon that [object].
However, if this were postulated, it would result in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). Thus he says: "By the status of being an object... [namely] by way of having blueness as its object.

Through association, the form of that [object] is produced; and through the production of that form, its status as an object [is established]. Thus, this mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) is difficult to resolve. // 46 //

He states another objection with the words "of the two": this is the intended meaning. If the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of both cognition and the object were understood to be devoid of form (*ākāra*), and yet at some point there were a perception of form through their being in contact, then perhaps one could imagine the form as a property of their conjunction. But we shall explain that this is not the case. // 47 //

Nor has the existence of the object as distinct from cognition ever been previously apprehended; nor is it apprehended upon cognition, such that—like the powder and the turmeric which are apprehended separately—their conjunction could be postulated. Thus he says: "And not...
He states the reason: "For not... For if the form were a property of the conjunction...

113} First, there must be an awakening to the absence of mental aspects (anākāra) regarding both [subject and object]. And it has been stated previously that there is no apprehended object (grāhya) devoid of mental aspects. // 48 //

He concludes: "Therefore. But what does it mean to say that the existence of the object has not been apprehended? For the very impossibility of the diversity of cognitions is the proof for the existence of the object. Indeed, for a cognition whose form is inherently clear, neither its connection with a form nor its diversity can be accounted for without another cause. Therefore, there must be some cause distinct from the cognition itself by which this diversity is produced.

It must be admitted that [the cognition] is produced. Nor is it logical to claim that the sense organs alone are the cause therein, because since they are uniform in nature, the diversity of the effects would be untenable. Furthermore, it is not appropriate that the perception of diverse forms arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone;
for we observe that immediately after a dissimilar condition, an entirely dissimilar cognition is indeed apprehended.

That [theory] is untenable if it were to have that as its cause. However, it is logical to postulate diverse causes according to the diversity observed in their effects. And these [causes] are what are denoted by the term "object" (*artha*). Thus, since the existence of the object is well-established and knowledge is likewise established beyond dispute, the conjunction of these two, whose existence is proven, is indeed logical.
Therefore, he says: "By the variety of cognitions" (jñānavaicitrya). // 49 //
Why is it not a conceptual construction?

To this he says: "That" (*tat*). If the diversity were known to be connected [to the object] by virtue of being dependent upon an object, then it would lead one to infer that object. However, no diversity can ever be produced by an object that has never before been perceived.

It is not logical to infer that [the object] exists simply because it is seen; for, by the power of seeing an effect, a cognition arises with a certain form from some specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This is entirely plausible. Since those specific material causes (*upādānaviśeṣa*) possess distinct potencies, nothing is faulty. Indeed, it is precisely when the determination of causes follows the observation of effects that [the system] is well-established.

The absence of form (*ākāra*) is established even in the case of the two feet, because the absence of a cause is inferred from the absence of its effect. However, even in those states, there exists a continuum of pure consciousness, as is evident from subsequent cognition and perception; for it is impossible for that [consciousness] to be without a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). If it is asked, "How can something possessing form be produced from that which is formless?"—then how can something dissimilar arise from what is dissimilar? Even in that case, the basis is simply a specific capacity (*śaktibheda*), which is to be inferred by the force of observing the effect. Indeed, here in some instances, such as at the head or at the end, there is a distinction in cognition...

There exists [a cause] which, upon the subsequent destruction of the fainting spell, produces the cognition of forms such as blue. This inconceivable power of that [cause] is to be established by the evidence of the observed effect and is not to be subjected to [further] investigation; thus it is well said that "the existence of the object was not apprehended."

Furthermore, if the object possesses a form (*sākāra*) and the diversity of cognitions is dependent upon it, then how could the form or the diversity of a subsequent series of cognitions be established by means of a final, formless cognition occurring after a state such as fainting? For neither of these two [form and diversity] can be produced by an object, since they do not exist even when that object is present. Indeed, the object was certainly present during the fainting; yet that form was not manifested by it.

Therefore, it must be admitted that the production of the diversity of forms occurs from the specific immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) alone, even though that condition is formless. And since this is so, it is appropriate to admit this in all cases; what is the use of grasping an external object?
For they recite: "How can the apprehension of an object be real? This is what he says: "by that which is formless" (verse 50).

Furthermore, while objects such as blue and so forth, which possess forms, may impart their own form to cognition, how could an object that is formless—such as a sky-flower, a rabbit's horn, or the son of a barren woman—impart a form to the intellect? For in those cases, there is no such thing as an objective form at all. One must therefore admit by necessity that in those instances, it is the cognition itself that possesses the form. Let that [cognition] be the pervasive factor; why resort to this "half-old-woman" approach? With this intention, he says:

— "From that which is formless" (*nirākārāt*). Furthermore, since there is an absence of the form of an object in the case of memories of previously experienced things—which are by nature unconnected [to the present], in dream-cognition and the like, and regarding objects such as the cutting off of one's own head which have never been experienced at all and are infinitely remote—the cognition of those who maintain that [cognition possesses an object] would result in being formless (*anākāra*). Thus he says: "In memory... (verse 51).

[725] He states the reason for sleep and so forth here with the words "for not" (*na hi*). The sense is that it is because of the existent (*satā*). How then is there a lack of connection with forms therein?

To this he says: "merely" (*kevala*). Regarding "latent impression" (*vāsanā*): it takes up only the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which has another name, namely "appropriation" (*upādāna*).

However, it should be understood that the distinction between latent impressions (*vāsanā*) was previously described according to the ancient Buddhist view, and not as something exceeding [the nature of] cognition.
And thus, even in the case of waking cognitions, it is logical to rely on the appearance of forms as being caused solely by latent impressions;
with the intention of asking why one should resort to this "half-old-woman" approach (i.e., being inconsistent), he says: "Thus... (verse 52).

Furthermore, he demonstrates through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the postulation of the form of cognition alone is more excellent—this is shown by the words "by positive and negative concomitance. The word "thus" (*evam*) introduces another argument. How is this understood? To this he says: "For not... (by the one who speaks thus). The meaning of this is: even in the absence of an external object, as in dreams and the like, since the concomitance of form is observed solely due to the positive concomitance of cognition alone, it is determined to be produced by cognition itself. However, for the proponent of an external object (*arthavādin*), it is not so, as it would be devoid of cognition.

They are capable of demonstrating the conformity of the object's form [to the cognition], because in the absence of cognition, the appearance of a form would be impossible. Therefore, it is established that this form of cognition is caused solely by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and is not a property resulting from contact with an external object. However, if one must necessarily assert that this form is produced by such contact, [then...]

But the supreme [view] is that for cognitions which are by nature devoid of form, the application of words regarding "form" is based on its connection with latent impressions (*vāsanā*); thus he says: "Therefore... (verse 54).

The position that [the cognition] possesses the property of being a composite is refuted. Another opinion is as follows: a form such as blue appears; yet this cannot be determined as residing in either the cognition or the object. Therefore, since no distinction is perceived, it is maintained that a single entity alone renders both [cognition and object] possessed of form, just as lac-dye [colors] a pair of adjacent jewels. Having set forth this view, he refutes it:

— "Of the two. How is it then not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Because of the difference in location" (*deśabhedāt*). For knowledge is internal, whereas the object is external. Since there is no contact (*sannikarṣa*) between these two, these two together cannot possibly produce a single form. However, in the case of a pair of gems, it is not untenable that a single dye of lac, being in proximity, colors them both. But [one might object]: how can there be a single cognition of two things located in different places...
One might think that there could be a subsistence in a single form for two things that are somehow conjoined; therefore, he says: "because of non-conjunction.

This has already been stated: a conjunction between these two is never perceived, because—as in the case of a gem—there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Furthermore, there could only be a common form for a pair whose existence is established separately.

But here, two [entities] with distinct forms are not perceived, because at all times only a single form is perceived. And it has been said: "We do not perceive a difference in form between the object and the cognition. This very point he states: "Of the two," etc. (55).

Another view is that both of these [the cognition and the object] indeed possess distinct forms, but because they are extremely similar, the distinction between their forms is not perceived, like that of *kādamba* birds in a grove of blue lotuses. Having presented this, he refutes it with the word "evam" (thus).

The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that there would be no non-distinction due to similarity. He states the reason with the word "bheda" (difference): [it applies] to two things whose difference is already known.

It is appropriate to speak of non-discrimination based on the similarity between a blue lotus and a kādamba flower; however, to claim non-discrimination based on the similarity of an object that has never been previously perceived as distinct—one which is like a sky-flower—is a great non-discrimination indeed. It should be understood that all these positions of certain Buddhist followers who maintain the reality of external objects have been presented and refuted. // 56 //

For this reason as well, he states that the form belongs to cognition—namely, "in the same way. In delusions such as the double moon, when the object is established as one thing, a cognition arises with a different form. And that [different form] would not be possible if the form were based on the object. For how could an object having one form produce a cognition having a different form? Therefore, [the form] must necessarily appear even when the object is non-existent.
The form must be described as belonging to cognition alone; therefore, the restriction [to cognition] is appropriate in every case—this is the intended meaning. // 57 //

Furthermore, this state of having multiple contradictory designations for a single object—as in the cases of *nakṣatra*, *tārakā*, *tiṣya*, and *dārā*—is not tenable if [the cognition] possesses the form of the object; for the superimposition of contradictory properties is based on difference, which would entail a difference in the objects themselves.
It is, however, logical that distinct cognitions of various objects arise, conditioned by diverse latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
This very point he states: "The asterism," [verse 58].

Just as in the case of a single woman’s body, there arises the conceptualization that she is a "corpse" for a wandering mendicant, a "beloved" for a lustful man, and "food" for a dog—this [distinction] would not be possible for proponents of objective reality (*arthavādin*) if the object were a single, unitary entity.
Thus he says: "The wandering mendicant... Here, the phrase "not based on the object" (*nārthanibandhanā*) should be supplied. And this is another [point]:

He says "long, etc. because [this] is not tenable for the proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*). For a single finger is perceived as both long and short in relation to the thumb and the middle finger; and this [perception], which consists of a single identity, is not tenable for those proponents of objects. Previously, consciousness was said to possess multiple forms in relation to the subject (*pramātṛ*); but here, not only do subjects who are distinct have a cognition of multiple forms regarding a single object, [but even a single subject does].
However, it has already been stated that even for a single entity, a cognition of multiple forms is observed due to the difference in its limiting adjuncts (upādhi). // 59 //

Not only is cognition manifold due to adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*), but even with respect to a single object, one observes the simultaneous conceptualization (*vikalpa*) by multiple perceivers such as "this is a jar" and "this is earthen. This would not be possible if the object existed in an ultimate sense (*pāramārthika*), because that [object] possesses a single nature (*ekātmatva*). Since an object is of a single nature, it would be apprehended by everyone in that very same way.

But this is not the case. Therefore, it is correct to conclude that this multiplicity of forms is merely a manifestation of the intellect itself. This is what he says with the words "ghaṭatva" (pot-ness) and so on. Here, one should understand that the presentation has been made in reverse order, starting from the lowest generality up to the highest generality. However, "knowability" (*jñeyatā*) is not a generality, because it is conditioned by its relation to cognition. This...

Furthermore, this was stated for the purpose of demonstrating that the mode of cognition is observed [in this way]. Even though no contradiction is seen here between "pot-ness" and so forth as there is between "longness" and so forth, nevertheless, because the nature of a single, partless object is unitary, the appearance of multiple forms is untenable; thus it has been said. // 60 //
Why should this not be so? To this he says: "No. First of all, it is not logical for a single object, which is of a unitary nature, to possess multiple forms. As they have said:
"Otherwise, how could the forms of a single entity that appears in various shapes be real? For that would entail the loss of its unity."

Thus, the occurrence of contradictory forms is even less possible; and that has already been stated previously and should be referred to. However, for the proponent of cognition (*jñānavādin*), it is logical that various cognitions arise in various ways; thus he says: "of the cognitions. But what is the cause for their being so? To this he says: "according to their capacities" (*śaktyanusārataḥ*).

By "capacity" (śakti), they point specifically to the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), because the accomplishment of the effect, which is cognition, is dependent upon that. Furthermore, a capacity distinct from that is entirely without any basis in valid cognition (apramāṇika); thus, it is certainly not accepted by the Buddhists. // 61 //
Therefore, it is established that the appearing form belongs to cognition itself and is not dependent on an object;

rather, if one wishes to accept an object that conforms to cognition in whatever way it exists by its own nature independently of an object, let it be so. However, there is no such thing as a cognition that is "in accordance with the object" (yathārtha). Thus he says: "independent" (nirapekṣam). // 62 //

"Let it be, then, that the object is merely that which conforms to cognition. No; even so, duality is not abandoned. To this he says: "In this way. This is the intended meaning: we have said "the object is thus" merely as a concession, like one with a loose tongue. However, if [the object] consists of the form of cognition, no such thing as an "object" is established at all.

Because no distinction in form is perceived, it is therefore impossible to postulate an object when [consciousness] is dependent upon cognition alone. Cognition itself, whose form is not superimposed by an object, will be employed within its own self; it illuminates only itself and not an object as its domain. If this is so, since all cognitions would be devoid of objects, what would constitute the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge? It is established by the presence or absence of a cognition that performs purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Knowing this, may you be at peace. For the conventional status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is based on the expectation of consistency with worldly practice; it is invalid when there is inconsistency with that practice. However, as for ultimate valid cognition, only certain fortunate ones, by cultivating the wisdom born of reflection, bring before them a state in which all adventitious stains such as blue and so forth have been completely shaken off.
That fourth state they call direct perception.

He now begins the presentation of his own established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "No" (na). Its meaning is as follows: your established conclusion is that cognition is indeed a single entity possessing both the grasped and the grasper; yet there is no illustrative example for a single thing having a dual nature. However, this statement appears to have been made by one who has not paid close attention to what precedes and follows it. For instance, it is not [the case] that the Buddhists [assert] that cognition possesses the forms of both the grasped and the grasper.

It is accepted [by us]. Rather, it is held that there is only pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), self-luminous, in which the grasping of the apprehended and the apprehender has dissolved. For it has been said:
"Due to the absence of the apprehended and the apprehender, that very [consciousness] shines by itself.
Even by the Mīmāṃsakas who are influenced by Buddhist views, it has been stated: "Indeed, consciousness is cognized by consciousness itself, and not..."

Because it is an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatayā*), it does not possess the status of being an action (*karmabhāva*). Furthermore, the statement regarding the absence of an example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) is also ineffective.

For the Buddhist’s counter-argument is not currently based on inference (*anumāna*), such that he could be reproached by the statement concerning the absence of an example. Now, when the sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) has been stated for the inference of the lack of an objective support (*nirālambana*), [the following applies].

Since [the opponent] has already raised an objection by means of the very examination of the capacity of direct perception—stating that cognition is not able to operate upon an external object because it lacks the characteristics of a graspable entity (*grāhya*) and so forth—why is he reproached with the statement regarding the absence of an example? To this it is replied:
He thinks as follows: "This relationship between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) must necessarily be accepted by the Buddhists in relation to consciousness."
Otherwise, how could that very [light] be established? For there is no establishment of anything that does not have apprehension as its function.
But surely light is self-luminous; what need has it for another light? What is the meaning of "self-luminous"?
It means that it shines by itself and does not depend on another light. Furthermore, does this expression "it shines" denote something other than light?

Or rather, it is not so. If [the word "manifests"] expresses a different object, then there must be another manifestation of consciousness (*saṃvid*). Otherwise, the phrase "it manifests" would be redundant and could not even be uttered, for its own nature is already grasped by the word "consciousness" itself. Therefore, the very state of being the object of cognition is what constitutes the meaning of the term "manifests" for consciousness.

It is like saying, "the jar shines. One might argue: "This is a reference to an agent; therefore, the status of being an object (*karman*) is not established by this. This is not so. Even in this case, the status of being an agent must be predicated of the referent of the word "shines" (*prakāśate*). This [status of being an agent] is not established unless there is a distinction in shining, because that which is non-dual cannot be divided. Therefore, there is no establishment of what has not been attained. Nor is there even the attainment of an object.

Since consciousness exists as a reality, its status as an object that must be reached (prāpyakarmatā) must necessarily be asserted, just as it is for other entities; there is no other way. [Objection: But surely the object is the thing, the self is the agent, and consciousness is the fruit.

How then can it be called an "action"? No; for even a result that is not itself an object of cognition cannot be established. Otherwise, since the mother [the subject] and the measure (the means of knowledge) would also necessarily be self-luminous, what would be the point of postulating consciousness (*saṃvit*) to establish them? We do not assert consciousness for the sake of some purpose.

Rather, it is from the perspective of cognition (*pratīti*). For we cognize a consciousness that has become the fruit, whose domain consists of the mother [cognition] and the object of knowledge (*meya*). We do not [cognize] another [consciousness] distinct from that; thus, we remain settled at just that much. Do not say so. This [notion] that "the cognition is perceived with various forms" has already been refuted. For for us, the manifestation of the object does not appear as something distinct from the manifestation of the consciousness itself.

Because it manifests merely as the form of blue and so forth. [Objection: Let jars and the like, whose nature is non-luminous, depend upon another luminosity; but why should consciousness, which is of that very nature, depend upon another luminosity? [Reply: No, because it is not of that nature. For even consciousness does not have the nature of being luminous in itself; rather, it is the luminosity of the object. As he will state:
Or rather, such luminosity belongs to that [object]. Therefore, a distinction between cognitions must necessarily be admitted for the sake of establishing consciousness.

Now, does consciousness establish the object of cognition while being itself unestablished, or is it established by another consciousness? The first alternative is not tenable; for it has already been stated that consciousness which is unestablished—and thus non-existent—cannot function for the sake of worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*). If [consciousness] were dependent upon another consciousness...

"But it has been stated that this leads to the consequence of a lack of fixed determination regarding its establishment. True. Consciousness does not establish the object of consciousness by means of a dependence on another consciousness;

rather, it establishes it while being real in its own nature (*svarūpasat*). If it is asked how it can be [an object] while being dependent on cognition, [the answer is: the state of being an object of cognition is not existence (*sattā*); rather, it is a universal (*sāmānya*) belonging to those things that arises at a time subsequent to their production. Therefore, like a seed covered by soil and water, its capacity remains unknown in its own nature."

Cognition establishes the object. And that object, once established, proves the cognition by placing another cognition [upon itself] when there is a desire to know it. Now, as for the objection that this establishment of cognition through the power of the object has already been refuted and that some other entity must be postulated—how this is not refuted, we shall explain immediately hereafter.
"Thus, as long as one has not attained the knowledge sought through inquiry, even the lack of a fixed determination does not arise.

For this very reason, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) stated by others is unestablished for us; because at the time of the cognition of the object, consciousness itself is not perceived. Indeed, it is only the object that appears to us in the form "this is blue."

"I am not blue. Furthermore, such manifestation would be impossible within the illumination of consciousness (*saṃvit*). For consciousness, which has itself as its object, cannot consist of the determination of another; otherwise, there would be no distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another, or between the notions of "this" (*idam*) and "I" (*aham*). This [consciousness] points to its own self as "I," and to another as "this. It does not, however, employ both the notion of "this" and the notion of "I" together in one place as non-different. Therefore, this [external object] does not exist.

In the case of the cognition "blue," the reason—that there is an apprehension of consciousness—is unestablished. However, it has already been stated that this objection applies only to those who maintain that consciousness is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*).

This might be argued: "How can a cause that makes something known (*jñāpaka-hetu*) make it known if it is itself unknown? This is not a fault, for even though the eye is unknown [as a conscious entity], [it performs its function].

Because it is perceived as the producer of knowledge. [Objection: But surely, like a seed is to a sprout, the eye is merely a producer (*kāraka*) of knowledge; thus, it is logical that it can be a generator even when it is itself unknown. [Reply: Not so. For it is precisely because something is a cause of knowledge that it receives the designation "indicator" (*jñāpaka*). Furthermore, knowledge is not an indicator-cause, because it is itself knowledge. Indeed, smoke and the like, which are the generators of knowledge, are indicators, but knowledge itself is not. How so?
The properties of a cognizer are being attributed to that which is not a cognizer. An object is established by a consciousness that exists in its own right;

however, that [consciousness] itself is later established by another cognition. But if there were no state of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*), consciousness itself would not be established.

Thus, having attributed the relationship of apprehended and apprehender, the refutation is stated regarding their identity: that [relationship] cannot be established in a single, non-dual entity. As for what...
Furthermore, it has been refuted by this very [argument] that the cognition of blue and the cognition [itself] are untenable when there is no difference [between them].
