On the contrary, it is said: "Cognition occurs in the state of oneness," because the relationship between the grasped object and the grasper is dependent upon difference.

And because self-luminosity is denied: for a single reality that is without internal division cannot exist with respect to itself, due to the contradiction of an action directed toward one's own self. Indeed, the tip of a finger does not touch itself, nor does the point of a needle pierce itself. For agents of an action are intended in both ways (as subject and object) only by resorting to a distinction between their attributes—as in the case of fields and so forth during the act of reaping—but they are never absolutely a single self. This applies even to the self’s state of being the grasped and the grasper.

It will be established immediately thereafter that for a single entity, the state of being both the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) is impossible. As for the objection that "if there is a difference [between them], the definition of the apprehended object is untenable": if this is intended in the sense of a similarity in terms of arising (*utpatti-sārūpya*), we certainly agree, precisely because such a form of apprehensibility has already been shown to be flawed. However, as for [the claim] regarding the production of cognition... [text fragment ends].

If that [object] is to be grasped, how can it be cognized when it has not become part of the self and is unconnected? For in this way, a single cognition would encompass the entire universe, since there is no difference in the lack of connection. Or rather, if there were identity (*aikātmya*), what connection could there be between the cognition of blue and [the object]? But surely that [connection] is based on difference; how then can it find a footing in a single undivided [entity]? This might be so.
[Objection: Even if there were identity (*aikātmya*), what would be the use of a relation?

For that single entity would simply be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). [Reply: Not so. For the contradiction of something acting upon itself (*svātmani vṛttivirodha*) has already been stated. Therefore, blue—which possesses the characteristic of being an object of apprehension—approaches consciousness as something entirely distinct; thus, we maintain its difference when it is apprehended. [Objection: There is non-difference (*abheda*).

Thus, in the manner just stated, there is an incompatibility with the definition of the apprehended object (*grāhyalakṣaṇāyoga*). As for the impossibility of a gross [object] (*sthūlānupapatti*)—which was brought forward through arguments such as the perception of moving and non-moving things in order to refute the similarity (*sārūpya*) between cognition and the object—we shall address that during the occasion of discussing the forest. However, since we do not maintain that an object is apprehended by virtue of similarity, we do not concern ourselves here with the proof of the gross object. Therefore, all three reasons are refuted in this single manner.

How, then, could that which is unconnected appear? Or, if it were to appear, would there not be an over-extension [of the principle]? It is not the case that what is unconnected appears; for the sense faculties are the illuminators.
And because they function by reaching [their objects], they produce within themselves a cognition whose object is the thing, being indeed connected with that thing.

And since those [objects] that are not present or not currently existing are not reached by them, there is no over-extension [of the definition]. However, cognition is not an illuminator because it is itself luminous. Furthermore, that which is an illuminator is not an illuminator if it is unconnected, like a lamp;

thus, for the sense organs which possess that mode [of being illuminators], a connection is indeed accepted. Therefore, is it the case that there is no connection at all between cognition and the object? If this is so, how [is it explained]?

The cognition of a jar is not without a relation; indeed, the subject-object relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is itself a relation, and that exists between cognition and its object. However, neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*) is accepted [as this relation]. What is the meaning of "object"? It is this state of being the objective of a cognition. For "cognition" is an action; in this action, the self is the agent, the sense organs are the instrument, and the object is the objective. Thus, this which belongs to the object—

In cognition, there is the status of being an object (*karmakārakatā*); that itself is its state of being an object (*viṣayatva*). And this nature, which did not exist prior to the cognition, must necessarily be admitted to be produced after it; otherwise, there would be no distinction between what is known and what is unknown.
That very [nature] is *jñātatā*.

The mark (*liṅga*) is the state of being known (*jñātatā*), which is the locus of the knowledge of objects. But how can that be cognized when cognition itself is not cognized? For "the state of being qualified by knowledge" is precisely what *jñātatā* is. How can that be known when the qualifier—namely, the knowledge—is unknown? An unperceived mark, or one that is logically untenable, does not lead to the cognition of the object; it cannot do so. No.

For an unperceived mark (*liṅga*) does not bring to mind the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*), nor does that which is logically impossible bring to mind its subsumer (*upapādaka*). This would involve mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because the establishment of "being known" and "the state of being known" would be dependent upon one another. It has already been stated that an object, by its mere intrinsic nature, is not a mark, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This might be so if the "known" were perceived only when the cognition itself is perceived.

But when that [cognition] arises, it is said to be "apprehended. Therefore, being established by itself, it establishes the knowledge. As for the claim that "knownness" (*jñātatā*) is the state of being qualified by knowledge—that is not so; for it has already been stated that it is indeed the state of being its object (*karmatā*). And this state of being an object for the thing cannot exist at the time of its apprehension; rather, it exists at the time of the arising of that [knowledge]. Thus, by its very arising, this [object] is something previously unobtained by the knowledge.
An object has now been reached, which brings about cognition. For prior to the arising of cognition, as in deep sleep and similar states, he was like one blind;

he knew no object whatsoever. He reflects: "What is this sudden appearance of objects? Indeed, the existence of things can never occur without a cause, for that which depends on no cause would result in being eternal, like space."

Or rather, it must be like a flower in the sky; this contact with an object, which occurs at certain times, must have some cause for its existence. For it does not exist by its own nature alone, as that would entail its being eternally so. Nor is it due to the power of the sense organs, because even when those [organs] are present, the reality of the object is not perceived during deep sleep and the like, nor is it perceived when they are not functioning during the waking state.

"Let it be then that the operation of that [sense-organ] alone is the cause for the object being such [as it is perceived]. No; because even when that [operation] exists, [the object may not be perceived]. Indeed, there is a unique operation of the sense-organs when they are in contact with various objects; yet, only a certain [object] becomes known at a certain time. It is exactly the same in the case of the self and the mind: even though they exist, one does not observe the object to be such [as it is].

[The opponent claims: "It is due to the absence of a cause [for non-perception] by way of its being such [i.e., unconnected]. But surely the mind's connection [with an object], which is non-deviant, will be the cause when that [perception] exists. [The author asks: "Of what? Of the sense-faculties or of the self? That cannot first be of the sense-faculties. For whatever external sense-faculty, such as the eye and so forth, is understood to be conjoined with the mind by virtue of the observation of its effect, only that [specific faculty] makes something known, and not any other.

Since it is logical that the state of being known (*jñātatva*) has as its cause the conjunction of the sense organ and the mind, that [conjunction of the self and the mind] is not postulated as the cause. Furthermore, even when the mind is conjoined with the self, for what reason would only some things be known and not others? If it is argued that whatever sense organ, such as the eye, comes into contact [with an object], that object becomes known through the conjunction of the self, the mind, and that [organ], then—
No, because of the previously stated deviation. For even when something is in contact with the eye, only a certain thing is known at a certain time and not another;
this would not be possible if there were no distinction [between objects].

Furthermore, it is established in the world that being the object of cognition (*jñānakarmatā*), being known (*jñātatva*), and consciousness (*cetanā*)—that is, cognition (*jñāna*)—are not different in meaning. Therefore, if the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātmamanoyoga*) were consciousness, [it would follow that the self is the object of cognition].

Because that [quality] is common to both, the consequence of [the mind itself being] consciousness has been described. If it is argued that cognition (*jñāna*) is not consciousness (*cetanā*), but rather experience (*saṃvedana*), there must indeed be some distinction between these two. But in that case, would one not employ the expressions "he cognizes blue" and "he experiences [blue]" as synonyms?

Because they are not synonyms due to a difference in meaning, the conjunction of the self and the mind is not knowledge. Therefore, the state of being known (*jñātatva*) of entities is not produced by that [conjunction]. Thus, this state of being an object of cognition (*prāpyakarmabhāva*), which would be uncaused and produced by the self, is not tenable.

This is because its inference is based on the absence of the effect, which is invariably concomitant with the absence of the cause. Consequently, this [position] results in an untenable contradiction between perception and other means of valid cognition and inference.

For those [means of cognition] bring about the attainment of the object (*artha*). And the inference based on the absence of a cause rejects that attainment. This untenability is resolved by the postulation of knowledge (*jñāna*): there exists a certain modification of action (*kriyābheda*), inherent in the self, denoted by synonymous terms such as "cognition" (*jñāna*) and "awareness" (*saṃvedana*), which takes the verbal root *jñā* as its basis, and in relation to which objects have the status of being attained as objects (*prāpyakarmatā*). But is not cognition a quality (*guṇa*)?

Because it is recited in the section on qualities (*guṇakāṇḍa*), it is not an action (*kriyā*). Therefore, how can its meaning be called "action"? For it is not possible for the all-pervading self (*ātman*) to possess the inherent nature of motion (*spanda*). Nor is action something that lacks the nature of motion, since all five types of action consist of motion. [Reply: No, because the mere meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action. As he will state:

And [it would follow that] action would be merely the meaning of the verbal root. Furthermore, from words such as "he understands" (*budhyate*), it is observed that a cognition of action itself arises, because there is an apprehension of a sequence of prior and posterior stages. Therefore, for those who maintain that objects take the form of cognition, it is indeed logical that objects are the objects of knowledge. Moreover, the attainment of previously unattained [objects] such as blue must necessarily be asserted; otherwise, [the experience of them would be impossible].
Just as before, even at a later time, if the form of the object does not appear, the world would surely be blind.
If it is argued that the form of the object appears but is not apprehended by anyone, for whom does it appear? If it is for no one, [then it does not exist].

What causes the distinction in conventional usage? For one person is seen who, having cognized blue, takes it up, while another who has likewise cognized it does not. What is the basis for this difference regarding the independent blue? Indeed, it cannot be independent, nor can it belong to anyone, being unperceived by anyone like a forest fire [occurring] elsewhere. Therefore, its occurrence must necessarily be stated to exist within some continuum (*santāna*). And thus they recite: "The object of cognition (*prameya*) is that which has the appearance [of the cognition]. Nor can it be the object of a non-valid cognition.

The status of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) is possible. This distinction between the object of cognition and so forth does exist, but it is constructed by delusion. And thus it has been said: "The nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), though undivided...

True, this has been said; however, it is untenable. For if that were so, there would be nothing whatsoever that is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), not even the state of pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*).

For it is precisely on the basis of experience that [the object] is accepted. In the same way, how could the form of the object (*viṣayākāra*), which likewise appears, be non-ultimate? Or, if it were the opposite of that, how could the nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*) itself not be subject to error?
For in both cases, no sublation (*bādhā*) is observed. Therefore, consciousness alone [perceives] an object distinct from itself.

It is established that when one points [to something] saying "this," it cannot be stated otherwise; thus, it is proven that an object well-known externally establishes the cognition by being designated as "this.
As for what was said—that a property residing in the object, even if known by another, would cause one to infer the cognition—that is incorrect.
For it has been stated that an object, when known to be otherwise inexplicable, is the cause for the postulation of a cognition; yet this is not the case for everyone.
Rather, it is a matter witnessed by experience that for whomsoever a cognition has arisen, for him alone is that object "known.
Just as it is only for one who performs the act of going that the reaching of another place occurs, even in the absence of a cognition of the motion itself. Of what nature is [this]?

Furthermore, the dharma is that which resides in the object (*artha*). It has been stated that [the dharma] is the "karmic factor" (*karmakāraka*). Now, one might ask: since the capacity of the object (*karmaśakti*) is not established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can it cause knowledge to arise? We do not postulate the cognition on the basis of the capacity of the object; rather, we do so on the basis of the object itself as the thing (*artha*), and that [object] is indeed established through direct perception. Even though its capacity is imperceptible, its perceptibility is nonetheless possible, just as in the case of other causal factors (*kāraka*).

For the capacities of other causal factors (*kāraka*) are likewise indeed imperceptible; yet, this much does not constitute their state of being imperceptible. Therefore, an object obtained through means of valid cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the cause for the conceptualization of knowledge. Some maintain that "attainment" (*prāpti*) of an object is its state of having never existed before, and that this is self-cognized by everyone. Others, however, hold that the attainment of an object is simply its fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), such as avoidance (*hāna*) and so forth.

They say: for that very [consciousness] is the state of being known; that indeed is the fruit of cognition. And the status of being an object (*karmatva*) consists in being the recipient of the fruit of an action. Thus, it is established in every way that cognition is inferred from the object as something already known. Even those who maintain that consciousness, being itself perceptible, establishes itself just as it does its object—

Even by them, it must be admitted that prior to the arising of cognition there was no distinction of properties residing in the object, which comes into being only subsequently. However, the direct perception of the object is not identical with the direct perception of the cognition.

For when one thing is directly perceived, another thing does not thereby become directly perceived, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If the direct perception of the object were indeed identical with the direct perception of consciousness, [the consequence would follow].

[Otherwise,] this would apply even to the object of inference (*anumeya*) and so forth, because inferential cognition (*anumāna-saṃvit*) would also be [nothing but] perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, one must necessarily state a distinction belonging to the cognition itself by which perception and its opposite are distinguished. Consequently, it is established that the postulation of a cognition for the sake of establishing an object of knowledge is not without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*); thus, the duality [of subject and object] is established. However, if all cognitions were devoid of objects (*anarthaka*), the recognition of the form of the object would be entirely without foundation.

For it is precisely thus that one recognizes on a later day an object seen on a previous day. It is not perceived that the mental aspect (ākāra) which has ceased along with that cognition [of the previous day] is the same as this one. Indeed, this mental aspect of today’s cognition is one thing, and that which was previously determined and has since ceased is another. Which of these two, then, do we recognize? [This is the basis for] the distinction between valid cognition and its opposite.

Furthermore, it is untenable that all cognitions are devoid of purpose. Nor is it correct to maintain that this [status of being a valid cognition] is based solely on the presence or absence of a cognition that performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*). For if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of validity even for objects perceived in dreams, since a cognition performing a causal function occasionally arises regarding such dream-objects. Yet, dream-cognition is sublated immediately thereafter.

If it is argued that [dream-cognition] is therefore not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then waking cognition is also certainly sublated during the state of deep sleep; how, then, can it be a valid means of knowledge? If you reply that it is sublated only after a long time, [we respond as follows:]

It is not by such a distinction that truth and falsity arise. For it is not the case that a cognition of illusory gold is considered valid simply because its sublation is not observed for a long time; therefore, what is valid is valid, and what is invalid is invalid—it is not possible for something to be "half-valid," like the "half-old woman" (ardhajarati). Thus, it is established that the object, which follows the definition of the apprehended, is indeed distinct from the cognition, and that it is this [object] which establishes the cognition. [This concludes] the statement regarding the absence of a supporting example.
Nor is this for the purpose of refuting inference;
rather, it is for the sake of avoiding the refutation of the inference intended by [the opponent] himself. For in this context, an inference is implicitly contained:
"The undivided is not of a dual nature, because it is undivided, like one of its own parts. And if someone were to say that [it is dual] because fire and so forth are sometimes perceived [in it]...

If he were to state that [the reason] is inconclusive, for that purpose this was said: "And there is no example for you of a single thing having such a nature. And this point will be elaborated upon later. // 64 //

[KHA] [726a] Cf. PVin 1.100,14–19: But surely, it has been observed that fire and other such things, despite having a single nature, possess the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this:

He says: "Fire," etc. This is the meaning: those things such as fire which are well-known as illuminators do not [illuminate] jars and the like by means of their own self; that is, they are not of the nature of light with respect to the essential nature which is light itself. Furthermore, why are they not illuminators of the light of their own self? For they cannot be established unless they are themselves illuminated. Nor is there a dependence on another of the same class for the sake of their establishment.
It is observed that a lamp does not depend upon another lamp; therefore, he says: "because of non-dependence.

This is the intended meaning: they do not depend upon themselves for their own illumination, because it is a contradiction for something to act upon itself, and because it is impossible for something to illuminate itself. // 65 //
Are they now manifested while previously unmanifested?

It is not so either. By what, then, are they manifested? To this he says: "the state of being an object" (*grāhyatva*). For they are grasped when manifested by ocular light. Therefore, that [light] is their cause of being made known (*grāhayitṛ*), not their grasper (*grahītṛ*), because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the sense organ itself possesses consciousness.

[Objection: But in this way, if light requires another light, there would be an infinite regress due to the requirement of a homogeneous [cause]. [Reply: Not so. It has already been stated here that the capacity of visual light to establish form is established in accordance with the observation of its effects. Since external light is observed to illuminate form, that very same [light], even when present in the body, illuminates form as well as the other elements and the luminous element itself. And it is not the case here...

There is dependence on what is of the same class, due to the distinction between intermediate species. For this very reason, lamps and the like are not objects of cognition for a blind person. Furthermore, if they were self-luminous, they would become objects of cognition even for the blind. Likewise, the sense organ is an illuminator [of its object] only through that which is conjoined with it in a single substrate—namely, color, or that which possesses color—but not of itself.

He states that at the time of its apprehension, the cognition itself is the grasper, as established by the means of knowledge known as *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability): "akṣa... (verse 66).

However, it has just been established that cognition (*buddhi*) is known by another cognition; thus he says: "In that [cognition]. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely... For since the self lacks any other grasper, one must necessarily admit that it possesses both natures (of being both subject and object).
Indeed, it is not grasped by another, because that would entail an infinite regress of graspers. Therefore, just like that [self], the nature of a single cognition—[must likewise be admitted].
Thus, the state of being the grasped and the grasper is not untenable. // 67 //
He refutes this with the words "in some way. This is the intended meaning: it is your established tenet that cognition is partless (*nirbhāga*).

And for such a thing, a dual nature is not logically possible. But why should it not be possible for the self to be the grasper by one aspect of its nature and the grasped by another aspect of its nature? For instance, [this is so] for one who possesses a conjunction of the mind with the sense organ that is itself conjoined with the object.
A so-called "cognition" (pratyaya) arises as a distinct property (dharma). And this [cognition] is somehow different from that [object] by way of its nature as a property;
by means of it, this [cognition] is the grasper (grāhaka). That which is its form as substance and so forth, common to other substances such as earth and the like, is the grasped (grāhya).
However, the Buddhists do not accept any such division within cognition itself. Therefore, how can it possess a dual nature? // 68 //

But even so, an absolute difference between the grasped and the grasper is certainly not desired, since non-difference is also accepted in the case of attributes and their substrata; therefore, he says: "But that which... For we do not accept even an absolute difference in the case of things such as jars and fire, because they are non-different in terms of their nature as substance and so forth. Therefore, in all cases, it is only between things that are different in some respect [that this relation holds].

Thus, the relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator is not untenable even for the Self. If, then, the aspect of cognition (*pratyaya*) is the object of apprehension and the aspect of substance (*dravya*) is the object of apprehension,

how is it that the Commentator [Śabara] states that "this occurs with respect to the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and not with respect to another," thereby establishing its occurrence within the inner self?

[The opponent] thinks [the self is the object]. But in that case, would not the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) have the other [person] as its object? For the other appears to the notion in the form of a substance and so forth; therefore, he says: "[Because of] proximity. This fault does not apply, because this quality of the self's being directed inwardly (pratyagātmavṛttitā) is what is manifest. For everything indeed functions toward another in a non-exclusive manner; however, the self possesses the characteristics of being both the grasper and the grasped in a state of extreme proximity.

It manifests as having the nature of the internal self (*pratyagātman*). For water and the self are extremely close to a person; therefore, that which is common to both is designated as the "grasped" and the "grasper. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever. // 69 //
Furthermore, this usage of "I" (*aham*), which is associated with the word "we" (*asmat*), is observed to give rise to a consciousness that is clearly distinct and has the self as its object;
however, cognition (*jñāna*) is never perceived arising with itself as its own object. Therefore, it is impossible to claim that cognition possesses a dual nature by using the self as an analogy.
For it is never seen arising in the form "I am blue," since [cognition] is at all times a consciousness distinct from such usage.

Therefore, it is indeed established that self-awareness has the self as its agent, and not cognition; thus he says: "intermingled with the usage of 'we' (*asmat-prayoga-sambhinna*). On this point, some who follow Kumārasvāmin say: "The self is not known by a cognition intermingled with the usage of 'we. For we do not perceive a person as 'this is I' as something distinct from the aggregate of cause and effect (the body). [Rather, it is] the experience of substances such as earth."

Thus, self-luminous consciousness establishes its own self as that which is self-luminous, as well as the self as the object of cognition and the object itself, such as substance and so forth. For if the person were not connected with the cognition of the object, no distinction could be established between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another. Therefore, objects do not appear when the cognizer does not appear; nor does the cognizer appear within them. For this very reason, upon the cessation of the cognition of objects, the self [remains] like an insentient void or the like.

They maintain that [the self] remains [in a state of void]. Indeed, when this person is liberated, with the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of all karma entirely exhausted, then—due to the absence of the sense organs and other instruments of cognition—there being no perception of objects, it remains devoid of consciousness like the sky. For they consider liberation to be characterized precisely by the total annihilation of all specific qualities (*vaiśeṣikaguṇa*) of the self. Nor does it follow from this that it is not a human goal (*apuruṣārthatva*).

For even the cessation of suffering is sought by a person. Indeed, those subject to saṃsāra, being distressed by suffering and intending its absolute eradication, are seen renouncing their homes and going forth into homelessness. But surely pleasure (*sukha*) is also a specific quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*); would it not follow that because of its cessation, there would be a lack of human purpose (*apuruṣārthatva*)? Not so. For the pleasure of one in saṃsāra is also crowded with various and manifold sufferings.

The great ones do not follow [pleasure] for too long; casting even that into the category of suffering, they rise for the sake of liberation. Therefore, when the sensation of objects ceases, a person possesses no consciousness. For this very reason, while sleeping day after day in happiness, one remains as pure existence (*sanmātra*) alone and knows nothing at all. And regarding that experience, there is subsequently a recollection of objects, just like those encountered in a dream.
[It] would [be so]. But this is not the case. Therefore, the cognizer is not manifested when objects are not manifest.

Nor is there a fusion with the use of the word "we" (*asmat-prayoga-sambheda*) in the cognition of objects; for if there were no apprehension of objects due to a lack of fusion with "we," there would be no grasping of a self. Furthermore, it is inconsistent to say that there is a fusion with the use of "we" in the cognition of objects and the grasping of a self, [and thus to claim] "fused with the use of 'we'."

Therefore, he says: "of cognition" (*jñānasya*). This is the intended meaning: is there an awareness distinct from our own application [of the senses], or not? If it does not exist, then the unsurpassed teachers have won the victory. But if it exists, one must state what its objective support (*ālambana*) is: is it the body or the sense organs? First of all, it is not the body.

Because it is the object of a knower. The notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) rests upon a knower in the form "I know. Now, the body does not cognize, because it is composed of the elements (bhautika), and because the elements themselves are insentient, and because the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their causes. For this very reason, the sense organs are not knowers. Nor is cognition itself [the knower], because of recognition (pratyabhijñāna). For one who recognizes today an object seen on the previous day possesses a single entity common to both the prior and subsequent moments.
One identifies oneself [with the thought], "I saw this. But that is untenable if [the self] were within the scope of cognition;
for he who saw it on the previous day was one, and he who sees it today is another.
Because cognitions are momentary,
that which is the object of the "I-notion" (ahaṅkāra) is distinct from the intellect, the sense organs, and the body;
since it is established by the power of consciousness itself, it does not lose its aforementioned nature.

Thus it has been said: "And [the agent] is none other than cognition itself. For this consciousness, which is inseparable from our own mental application (*prayoga*), belongs to the agent of cognition;
and it has been stated that there is no other agent of cognition. Therefore, by the very force of consciousness (*saṃvidbalāt*), the dual nature of the self is established;
yet it is not the case that the self ever knows itself as cognition.
For this [notion] that "this is blue" is always an object external [to the self].

As for the claim that we do not perceive anything distinct from the aggregate of the body and its instruments: is it then the case that the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) has the body and so forth as its objective support? That point has already been refuted. Furthermore, it cannot be without an objective support, according to our established doctrine. Therefore, this [notion], failing to find a self that is without an objective support, draws toward itself the knower who is its own object.

Thus, the person (puruṣa), whose dual nature is established by the force of experience, is not untenable; however, he is not [identical with] the body, senses, and so forth, which are merely intermingled with them.
It can be discerned by distinguishing that "this is indeed that person. Yet, it does not follow from this that [the person] has not been apprehended.

For when milk and water are mixed, it is not the case that both are unapprehended simply because they are not apprehended through distinction. Likewise here, a person of confused intellect [practices] yoga, such as withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and so forth.

By those who practice only the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika*), refraining from what is prohibited, and by whom the entire accumulation of karmic impressions (*karmāśaya*) has been exhausted through experience, this [Self] is discerned and directly realized as "I am this. However, even when an object is known, it is not discerned as "this is named so-and-so. Even for those who maintain that a person is grasped only at the very moment of perceiving an object, [the Self remains ungrasped].
Even by them, it is impossible to demonstrate the distinction of this [consciousness]. Therefore, the fault that "the distinction is not apprehended" does not apply.

However, this [distinction] is not known at the time of the cognition of the object; for, as will be stated immediately after with the words "but not here," there is no perception of anything else besides that [object] at that time. Indeed, even consciousness itself does not manifest at that moment.

It has already been stated that the distinction between entities depends precisely on the cognizer. As for the claim that there is no difference between what is known by oneself and what is known by another, that is not so. For it has already been said that objects appear only to one in whom cognition has arisen. Therefore, how could another experience what has been cognized by one who has produced cognition, or how could another know what has been known by him? Indeed, the distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another is not caused by the cognition of the subject (*boddhṛ-saṃvedana*).
On what grounds could this be so? For it is by this much alone that an object is known to one person and not to another:

namely, that a cognition has arisen in that person. This might be the case if objects were not known in the absence of a cognizer’s mental state, or if the cognition of that state itself were the knowledge of the object.

But this is not so, because [the self] is apprehended solely through its objects. For it is impossible for a cognition directed toward one object to have another as its object. And thus, the claim that "the person is not manifested when there is no cognition of the object" is also ill-stated; for in that case, liberation would be nothing but death, wherein the entire collection of the senses has ceased.

Thus, it would be permitted by another expression. Furthermore, there is indeed no difference between the existence and non-existence of the person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is consciousness. Therefore, this [person] certainly shines forth even in the state of liberation (*apavarga*). But by what is this [person] then illuminated? By nothing at all. Some say that he is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*); however, it is not so.

Because non-differentiation is established by the negation of self-luminosity, even then it must be stated that this [consciousness], by resorting to the distinction between attribute and substrate, is the grasper in the form of cognition and the grasped in the form of substance and so forth. Is there, then, at that time, a difference between attribute and substrate?
What is the fault? Contradiction with scripture. For it is heard in scripture: "One, without a second."

This is not so, because of the negation of a separate object of apprehension (*grāhya*). For otherwise, even the distinction between selves (*ātmabheda*) would not be established. Nor is such a distinction undesired, as it would lead to the collapse of the distinction between those who are liberated and those who are not. Furthermore, it has been stated in various places that such discrepancies [in cognition] are merely for the purpose of precluding the apprehension of external objects. Therefore, even in the state of liberation (*apavarga*), the self (*ātman*) consists precisely of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender. And it is heard in scripture: "This person indeed knows."

"But it must be understood that he does not know. For at that time, there is no loss of the knower's capacity for knowing. However, there is nothing else distinct [from him] by which he might know a second object. Therefore, from the use of the verb "to know" (*jānāti*), we understand that even in liberation (*mokṣa*), the person possesses the state of being an agent of action (*karmabhāva*). This is because the verb "to know," when devoid of an object, is never employed. Such, however, is the distinction.

Since this [Self], under the influence of the elements and the senses, appears as if its power of knowledge were undifferentiated because it undergoes various modifications due to the coloring by objects, its own innate power of consciousness remains directed toward itself when there is no coloring by objects. If it is asked, "How can there be the arising of knowledge without an instrument? [the answer follows].
Not so; for even then, the mind exists. Indeed, it is accepted as being eternal, like the self. And it has been said:
"One who practices yoga, such as withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and performs prescribed actions, perceives the self through direct perception by means of the instrument that is the mind."

Thus, there is no consequence of experiencing external objects, because the mind lacks independence with respect to the external world. Furthermore, since the cognitions of objects are produced by karma—given that they serve as causes for pleasure and pain—they cannot occur in the absence of karmic impressions (*saṃskāra*). And since the knowledge of the Self is not produced by karma, it belongs only to one whose entire accumulation of karmic residues has been dissolved.
It is established that even when omniscience (*kevalajñāna*) is rejected, it is only the cognitions of objects that are refuted, not the knowledge of the self. And it has been said:
"Because of its own innate consciousness, because bliss is directly perceived, and because of its eternity, omnipresence, and so forth, the self is certainly not liberated [from existence]."

Thus [it is said]. Some maintain that even in deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is indeed self-awareness (*ātma-saṃvit*). For this very reason, one who has awakened from deep sleep reconnects with the self, thinking, "I slept happily. Alternatively, because the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*) persist there, the mind (*manas*), being dependent upon them, does not manifest the self alone.

It is not so, because there is no cognition of the object [apart from itself]. Therefore, self-cognition is not simply the cognition of an object. Moreover, in this way, when both appear within a single cognition whose scope includes both the object of knowledge (*meyam*) and the knower (*mātṛ*), what would constitute their relationship as object and agent? For in that case, that cognition would possess two objects. As for what was stated—that being the recipient of the fruit of an action inherent in another constitutes the state of being an object—[that too is untenable].

That is incorrect. For that which is obtained at the moment of the arising of cognition is the object to be reached (*prāpya-karma*). And since the self (*ātman*) is likewise [obtained], how can it lack the status of being an object? Furthermore, what is this action, through the inherence (*samavāya*) of which the self possesses agency by virtue of partaking in its fruit? What, then, is it? It has been stated: "the conjunction of the self" (*ātma-yoga*). But surely, because this [conjunction] also inheres in the mind (*manas*), it would follow that the mind too is an agent. [And] its connection with the fruit...

Since there is no distinction between the two [positions], the same consequence follows. And in that regard, the undesirable consequence of the mind being conscious has already been stated; thus it is established that the triad is not established through the cognition of objects alone. Furthermore, what was said in this view—that liberation is simply the cessation of suffering—is also incorrect.

Because bliss is heard [in scripture]. For it is heard: "Consciousness, bliss is Brahman," and "Bliss is the form of Brahman," as well as "This is dearer than a son. Nor is bliss merely the cessation of suffering, for that would entail the absurdity [of bliss] existing even in stones and the like. It might be argued: "The internal state, when perceived, is happiness by way of the absence of suffering.
And since the Self does not know anything internally because it is insentient, it neither suffers nor experiences happiness. This is not so.

Even so, for an embodied being whose parts are distinct and joined together, there would not be a simultaneous experience of pleasure and pain arising from the causes of pleasure and pain; for while one part is indeed suffering, another part experiences pleasure. If that pleasure were to occur upon the cessation of suffering, it would be untenable. If it is argued that pleasure is simply the absence of suffering in another location, [the same objection applies].

No. Because the specific quality of bliss is self-evident (*svasaṃvedya*), and because there is an absence of suffering in other regions, it would follow that one would be happy in another hell simply due to the absence of suffering in that particular hell. Therefore, the cessation of suffering is what constitutes happiness. Furthermore, there is no scriptural authority for the claim that this [cessation] is bliss (*ānanda*). For if the primary meaning of the scriptural term "bliss" is accepted, nothing at all remains untenable.

Since [consciousness] is explained as being secondary (gauṇa), we therefore maintain that consciousness is blissful Brahman. However, it is established that bliss which is not consciously perceived is merely like non-existence; thus, even without the perception of an object, the Self shines forth within consciousness that is inseparable from our own cognitive activity. // 70 //

Furthermore, the self, which is cognized by a consciousness that is distinct from our own cognitive application (*prayoga*), is not of a dual nature in the same way that cognition is. For in the cognition "this is blue," no form of the instruments—the sense organs—is perceived, nor of the apprehending self, nor of the cognition itself, because there is only the manifestation of the blue. Thus, as in the previous case, even though it is non-different [from the object], the cognition of the blue is not the apprehended object (*grāhya*) for that [cognition of the blue] in the same way the self is; rather, only the blue is apprehended by it, while that [cognition] is understood from the [object] once it has been known.

This has indeed been established; thus he says: "But not... The mention of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) is for the sake of an illustration. Just as in the case of the cognition "this is blue," neither the instrument—the sense organ—nor the grasper—the person—is perceived, so too is knowledge (*jñāna*). Only the object (*karman*) is understood here. And there is no agent, instrument, or action [perceived]. // 71 //

It might be argued as follows: "This very cognition of knowledge is 'this is blue. Its taking on the form of determining the nature of another object is based upon latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For the latent impressions of those in saṃsāra are beginningless;

by their power, one determines even one's own self as if it were another, and [identifies] another's body as the self, thinking 'I am. To this he replies: 'having another form' (*anyākāra*). The intention here is this:
for us, the determination of the reality of things is grounded in consciousness."

132} This consciousness, arising as the manifestation of an external object—namely, "this"—is observed. If, however, this very [consciousness], despite having such a form, is held by you to have another [internal] cognition as its object, then why do we not likewise postulate that consciousness, which possesses the form of the cognition, has the external object as its object? Furthermore, it is not reasonable to assume that something has another thing as its domain merely because there is no sublater [of that perception], nor is it logical to claim that [the appearance of an external object] is an error. Moreover, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from a prior cognition and resides within itself [as its substrate].

It is *saṃskāra* (formative predisposition) that is so designated. This does not exist for the nihilists (*nāstika*), because of their doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*). Nor is cognition (*jñāna*) the substratum of the latent impression (*vāsanā*), because of its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Nor is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) the latent impression.

Because that [object] is not established as having such a nature. Furthermore, this [cognition], being restricted to its own object, cannot show another [object] as being the object of another, because it does not possess that form and because it is impossible for it to be produced with that nature. Otherwise, even the nature of experience would not belong to it. For it is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) that extends the form of experience to the subsequent [cognition]. Why is that? Because of the established principle that an effect must originate in conformity with its own nature.

For this very reason, it is not logically possible for the cognition "this" to arise from a subject that has the self as its object. As for the conceptualization of "I" with respect to another [person], that is indeed an error, since the *ahaṃkāra* (the sense of "I") has been stated to have the knower as its object. However, there is nothing here—in the case of cognition having an external object—that is untenable such that one must necessarily postulate that it has the self as its object; thus it is established that cognition has only an external object. // 77 //

Thus far, it has been stated that when one of the two is not apprehended, the other is not apprehended either. In the same way, he demonstrates by way of summary that there is a non-apprehension of both, saying: "And just as... The meaning of this is as follows: just as when the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is not apprehended, the subject of apprehension (*grāhaka*) is not apprehended, and when the subject of apprehension is not apprehended, the object of apprehension is not apprehended; so too, there would be a non-apprehension of both.

But it is not [the case] for the mere apprehender or the mere apprehended. Previously, by means of the example of the non-perception of one of the two, the non-perception of the other was established; now, however, it is stated by combining both together—thus there is a difference in the formal argument (prayoga). // 78 //

And he says "sa" (that), because this apprehension of the mere object, devoid of an apprehender, is stated in the Bhāṣya by the words "connected with an external location," and so forth. This is the meaning of the Bhāṣya: that very external object alone is cognized through direct perception;
it is not, however, the apprehender. // 79 //
However, in order to establish that the form of the object is directly blue and so forth, the connection with external space (*bahirdeśa*) is indicated as the cause;

we do not accept this, as he says: "the other" (*param*). For no such thing as "external space" is established for the opponent which could be put forward as the cause for the object's having a form. This is because everything is admitted to be of the nature of a cognitive form (*jñānākāra*). Therefore, [the notion of] external space...
And that connection, with respect to the Buddhist, is precisely the probandum (sādhya) and not the logical reason (hetu). // 80 //

Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore) to show that the meaning of the commentary is exactly as stated. Its meaning is as follows: in the commentary beginning with "bahir" (externally), by the word "idam" (this), there is cited as the object of cognition for the collection of means of knowledge such as perception—that which is extracted from the subjective portion, namely the mere blue and so forth residing in the conceptual construction "this is blue. What is meant is this: [perception] does not [cognize] its own objective domain...
Knowledge [is established] from external manifestation,
because of the determination by another that "this is [it]. For within its own objective domain, there would be no manifestation as "this is not."
"But I [am here]. Thus, by introducing the connection with an external location here, it is stated that consciousness indeed has an external object as its domain. // 81 //

Likewise, regarding the consciousness of the apprehender alone, he says "no" to the claim that "it is true that cognition arises first, but it is not known first. For here, by stating that although cognition has arisen previously, it is not apprehended beforehand but rather later, he has asserted that there is consciousness of the apprehender itself as being entirely devoid of the form of the apprehended. // 82 //

In order to establish that [the object] is not apprehended prior to cognition, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "For it sometimes happens that an object which has been known is said to be unknown. The meaning of this is as follows: an object previously known, when at some time not being remembered, is designated as if it were unknown; however, the mere cognition directed toward that object is remembered. For it is thus that speakers say:

"The meaning of this scripture was understood by me while it was being explained by my teacher; now, however, I have forgotten it. Yet, I remember that the knowledge regarding this subject arose previously. Furthermore, he will later state that this cognition serves as the cause for non-apprehension with respect to its result, because the description of the text is intended to convey that result.

In this regard, he says "no" [to the opponent's claim] that even from the mere recollection of the grāhaka (the subject), there will result a cognition of the grāhaka as distinct from the form of the grāhya (the object). // 83 //

But if there were no distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender, then, just as there is recollection of the apprehender, there would also be recollection of the apprehended; thus he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
This means "therefore, from the apprehender. Since, however, there occurs only the manifestation consisting of the recollection of the apprehender alone, and not that of the apprehended—

Therefore, we understand that even at the time of experience, this cognition alone is apprehended; otherwise, how could it be remembered in its solitary state? This is what [the author] expresses with the words "grāhaka... (the apprehender). Because there is a manifestation of memory regarding the apprehender alone, the meaning is that at the time of apprehending the apprehender, cognition is apprehended in its solitary state. // 84 //

Why is this so? To this he says: "That. That is, recollection. The meaning is that because of the absolute inseparability (*atyantāvinābhāva*) of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), a single form does not arise. Thus, since one part is associated with the other, the distinction between the grasped and the grasper is established through their mutual exclusion; to this he says: "In association... (verse 85).

Here he raises an objection: "The apprehended," etc. The meaning is this: that which you assert—having accepted the non-difference between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*), and then deducing the apprehension of one from the apprehension of the other—is incorrect. For it is not necessarily the case that what is not different from something else must be apprehended when that thing is apprehended. Indeed, properties such as permanence or impermanence, though non-different from sound, are not apprehended when sound is apprehended. However, even in the case of non-difference, whenever a particular aspect...

At that time, it is only that which possesses the capacity [to be grasped] that is apprehended, and not anything else; what is there that is untenable here? Furthermore, the objective aspect (grāhyāṃśa) is fit for apprehension because of the existence of the subjective aspect (grāhakāṃśa), whereas the subjective aspect is not, since there is no other subjective aspect distinct from it. Therefore, when the object is apprehended, there is no consequence of the subject also being apprehended. // 86 //

It might be argued: "The very objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) of this [cognition] will be its own subject (*grāhaka*). That is not so, because it is impossible for an object (*karman*) to have the status of an agent (*kartṛ*). With this intention, he says: "the objective," and so forth. Furthermore, even by accepting that a single cognition possesses the nature of both the grasped and the grasper, you are led to the conclusion that both are apprehended. And if the objective aspect were also the grasper...
Otherwise, duality itself would be lost, because [the object] would result in having the very same nature as the grasper; thus he says: "grāhaka... (verse 87).
Alternatively, the objective aspect (grāhyāṃśa) is indeed the object;
and if the subject (grāhaka) were also perceived, then there would be identity with the nature of the object alone. Thus he says: "the subject. And what we are saying here is far too little.

"If both are grasped, there would be a single form. But even that is not established at all. For when the object of cognition (grāhya) is absent, the subject of cognition (grāhaka) is absent; and when that [subject] is absent, the object of cognition is absent. Thus he says: "It would not exist" (na syāt). // 88 //

Thus far, it has been stated that the grasper is not apprehended because other grasping subjects are excluded. Furthermore, the emergence and suppression of entities are established as the causes for their apprehension or non-apprehension. Therefore, it is not illogical that whichever aspect of an entity emerges at a given time, that very aspect is apprehended; thus he says, "emergence" (*udbhava*). Regarding this very point, he provides an illustration with "just as" (*yathā*) // 89 //

For at night, only the form of things such as the light of a lamp is perceived, not its touch. He says "by day" because [the touch] is overwhelmed. Regarding the day and night, when both touch and form are overwhelmed, the cause is the moon's cool touch and the powerful, crossing-over light [of the sun]. Such, then, is the case regarding being overwhelmed.

It has been stated that what is overwhelmed [by other factors] is not perceived due to the proximity of other causes. Now, he demonstrates by means of an example that something is also not perceived because it is itself subtle—namely, "like a fragrance. For when minute portions of substance, being impelled by the wind, come within the range of the olfactory faculty, [they are not perceived].

Even while those [substances] are present, only the fragrance is perceived and not the substance itself, because it has been overwhelmed. Furthermore, they consider this transference of substance to be illogical. For if the substance of the *campaka* and so forth were actually to transfer into the sesame seeds and such, then when those seeds are crushed, the *campaka* fragrance would perish, just as the fragrance does when the flower itself is crushed. [This would have to occur] in the case of the *campaka* substances themselves.
When those [flowers] are crushed, the destruction of their fragrance is observed. Likewise, it would occur even when the parts of a flower situated on sesame seeds are crushed.

For how could that [fragrance] which perishes when gross flowers are crushed not perish when situated in subtle parts? Therefore, [the fragrance arises] from the proximity of the *campaka* and other such [flowers].

One might think that it is simply another odor that arises in sesame seeds and the like. In the same way, one must state that there is the acquisition of a new quality in water due to contact with fire; it is not the transfer of the fire itself, because such is not perceived. For we perceive only the touch of the fire there, not the fire itself. Furthermore, this poor fellow, by asserting the transfer of a substance, would fall into the sin of smelling liquor, [since] the particles of the liquor [would have been transferred].

[The fragrance] moves from the interior of the nose to the mouth; therefore, this transfer of substance would result only in self-destruction. To this it is replied: first of all, we do not consider it possible that a fragrance goes to another substrate by abandoning its own substrate, because qualities are not independent. For dependence upon a substrate is indeed their defining characteristic. Nor does it become another quality...

It must be said that [the fragrance] arises from contact with flowers in the presence of space, wind, and so forth, because fragrance is absolutely absent in those [elements]. Nor can it be asserted that another fragrance arises within the nose itself, because of the great distance and the lack of contact with the flower. Therefore, it is the very particles of the flower, having been perceived as connected to that fragrance, which [are carried] by the wind.

The conceptual construction that "they are perceived when, being impelled, they reach as far as the interior of the nose" is supported by valid evidence (*pramāṇavatī*). Furthermore, the claim that the fragrance is destroyed upon crushing [the flower] is also incorrect. For it is subtle particles of the flower that have transferred there; they are not crushed. Therefore, it has been stated that the fragrance is not destroyed. As for the objection that one incurs the fault of drinking liquor (*surāpāna*) by smelling the fragrance, that is not the case. For the drinking of liquor is forbidden, not the smelling of it.

However, the fault in smelling it is slight; moreover, one who smells liquor is not said to be drinking it. Therefore, it is established that there is no occurrence of the act of drinking liquor merely by the proximity of subtle particles to the nose; rather, it is simply a substance possessing fragrance that exists therein, which is not perceived due to its subtlety. // 90 //

Having thus stated that there is no apprehension of what is overwhelmed in these examples, he applies this to the subject at hand with the word "not" (*na*). Just as there is no cognition of other qualities in the light of a lamp and so forth, and just as there is none of the substance in the case of a fragrant substance, so too there will be no cognition of another form in the cognition of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) or in the cognition of the apprehending aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*). // 91 //

And he says "from the object of apprehension" (grāhyāt) to show that this other [property] is indeed non-different from the object of apprehension, yet is not apprehended: there exists some differentiation of properties which, although non-different from the sound that is the object of apprehension, is not perceived—just as eternality and so forth are not perceived when sound is being apprehended. // 92 //
But this must be considered: whose is this counter-argument, that "the apprehended aspect [is grasped] by the apprehending aspect," and so forth?

It cannot belong to the Buddhist, for he maintains the apprehension of the undivided nature of consciousness itself as differentiated by the distinctions of the apprehended, the apprehender, and self-awareness. As he has said:

Although the nature of the intellect is undivided, it is perceived here by those with perverted vision as possessing the distinction between the grasped object, the grasping subject, and consciousness itself.

Thus [it is said]. Therefore, since only cognition with three aspects (trayākāra) is experienced, how can one object by means of not apprehending one or another part? The Buddhists [assert] that the division into the apprehended (grāhya) and so forth is constructed through delusion; it is not that this division does not appear to them at all. Therefore, whose objection is this? True. The Buddhist is not the challenger here; this is the speech of a bystander. For some bystander here says: "What is this?"

By you, having indeed accepted the state of the apprehended and the apprehender, the grasping of two forms is entailed. For there exists no other apprehender of the apprehender; and if that were grasped, the possession of two forms would be lost. Since that [possession of two forms] has already been accepted, how can the Mīmāṃsaka make a statement contrary to it? Furthermore, it is observed that even when there is non-difference, the distinction between grasping and non-grasping is established by factors such as manifestation and suppression.

Now, according to the Buddhist view, he says: "non-difference" (*abhedam*). For an ultimate difference between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is certainly not admitted. Rather, it is accepted that the nature of cognition (*buddhyātman*), which is of a single form, manifests in that way. Therefore, since this very manifestation of the nature of cognition belongs to both of them, why would it not be grasped when either one of them is grasped? Moreover:

The objection raised against us by accepting non-difference—asking how the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) can exist if there is no difference—is incorrect. For how could it be possible for any part of a non-different reality (*tattva*) to remain unapprehended? However, if non-difference is not accepted, [then the following applies].
This undesirable consequence cannot be maintained; for it is precisely because they are distinct that their non-apprehension is logically established. // 93 //
He now concludes the previous objection with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). For that which is fit for apprehension is apprehended;

and that which has either the existence or the arising of an apprehender is fit for apprehension. Therefore, since only a portion of the aforementioned duality—consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender—can be apprehended and not the other, neither of the two should be urged [as an objection], due to the absence of the capacity for apprehension. // 94 //

To this, he states the rebuttal: "Why? The intention is as follows: first of all, the division into subject and so forth is not imagined through delusion (*bhrānti*), because there is no sublation (*bādha*) [of it]. Even if it were indeed a delusion, then by that same logic, it would follow that even the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) would be subject to that [delusory status], resulting in its reduction to non-existence.
Therefore, this real division of the grasped object and so forth cannot possibly exist within a single, non-dual self of knowledge; thus, first...
It was stated [by the opponent] with the words "this is not so," and so forth.

Furthermore, by the words "and when non-difference is accepted," and so forth, the consequence of perceiving both [forms] was brought forward by accepting that a single thing possesses a dual nature. In that case, this rebuttal—that "because of unsuitability or because it is overwhelmed, the other is not perceived"—is not tenable.
For indeed, within a single cognitive self, neither the distinction between suitability and unsuitability nor the nature of emergence and suppression is possible.
Therefore, if non-difference is maintained, it must necessarily follow that when either one is perceived, there must be the apprehension of both forms. // 95 //

But how is it that the nature of emergence and suppression cannot belong to a single entity? To this he says: "A single... For such is the reality designated as the grasped and the grasper. In that case, if the aspect of the grasper is suppressed, how can it be said that the aspect of the grasped, which is non-different from it, is not suppressed? Because, through the imposition of contradictory attributes, a distinction [between them] would result. And thus, if both were suppressed, even the aspect of the grasped would lack the status of being grasped; consequently, no reality whatsoever would be possible. Thus he says: "In that way..."

In this way, unfitness (*ayogyatā*) must also be examined: is both [the object and the cognition] unfit, or is only one? If both were unfit, nothing would be apprehended, and thus the consequence of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) alone would follow. However, if it is said that one is unfit while the other is not, that is not tenable in the case of a single, non-dual [reality]; thus he says: "unfitness. Furthermore, as for the examples mentioned here regarding color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth in the light of a lamp and the like—

In that case, the designation of "emergence" (*udbhava*) and "overpowering" (*abhibhava*) is appropriate, because emergence and overpowering are logically possible there through the mutual distinction between visible form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects]. For visible form is indeed distinct from touch;

thus, when visible form emerges at night, it is not illogical that touch—being overwhelmed—is not perceived. This is what he says: "The examples," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the distinction between the capable and the incapable is also included. The distinction between emergence, overpowering, and so forth, follows upon the distinction in their own essential natures (*svarūpa*).
This is the meaning. // 97 //

Is it not the case that there is no ultimate distinction between form and the other [sensory objects]? Indeed, this is a great affliction, in that their distinction is asserted to arise from the substance itself. Furthermore, their mutual distinctions are established with even greater difficulty. Therefore, it is a single entity, such as the form of a substance, which appears divided into the distinctions of form and so forth due to the difference in the perceiving subjects, just as a face [appears differently in various mirrors].

140} Some maintain that this is like [the appearance of] different reflections in mirrors. Therefore, even in that case, since the determination of arising and so forth is observed as being nothing but non-differentiation, there is no distinction whatsoever. Hence he says: "Even when... The intention is this: if our own established doctrine regarding form and so forth is adopted, then those [reflections] are indeed distinct from the substance and from one another. Or, if it is according to another school's view...

Nevertheless, even so, the emergence and suppression of a single entity are not established. Therefore, even in our view, one must accept that just as a single form of clay is differentiated by various transformations such as jars and bowls, so too a single substance-form is differentiated by various transformations such as color and so forth. As for the claim that the differentiation of a single substance-form arises from a difference in the perceiving subjects—

That is far too crude. For it is reasonable to resort to the doctrine of adventitious difference (*aupādhika-bheda*) based on the recognition [of identity] in the case of faces, by resorting to the difference in mirrors;

but here it is not so, and thus the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) alone is better. Furthermore, in that [theory], a fixed distinction between the emergence and so forth of a single entity is not observed in the world. As for this accidental transformation of form into the nature of touch, and then again that very same thing into the nature of form—

It is not appropriate to say that [the object] is signless (*nirnimitta*). Furthermore, it is untenable that a single substance possesses a single form which, being suppressed by the emergence of another quality during the day, is perceived again at night. For when there is transformation (*pariṇāma*), milk transformed into the nature of curd is never seen to transform back again into the nature of milk. Therefore, it is precisely this: that from the substance itself, and from one another, the form and other qualities are distinct.

Now, we shall set aside for the moment the point that difference is established even in the absence of a difference in location and so forth—a point which will be explained immediately hereafter—and instead address the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*): "In this way also, there can be no manifestation and disappearance of a single [entity]. (98)

Regarding this other point which was stated—that even though it is non-different from the apprehended object, something such as permanence and so forth is not experienced in the case of sound and the like—the author restates and refutes it with the words "non-different" (*abhinna*). For just as the difference among color-forms and the like is based on a difference in cognition, so too those who assert that properties such as "being produced" are distinct from sound and from other properties by virtue of a difference in cognition cannot be deterred by a mere staff. // 99 //

What, then, is the cause for their distinction? To this he says: "For not... Substances, qualities, and actions are indeed distinct; what is the reason for this other than the difference in cognition? And since this [difference in cognition] occurs even when there is no difference in properties such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), their distinction is caused by that [cognition]. Now [an objection]: [2, ...]

No difference of location or difference of form is perceived among these [entities]. Therefore, how can they be distinct? To this he says: "And not... Indeed, for us, the distinction between entities is not merely conventional. For we take consciousness alone as our refuge; and it is consciousness that, being either differentiated or undifferentiated, establishes distinction or non-distinction. It is not, however, distinction by way of location or form.
Thus, it is precisely this limitation that is defined. // 100 //

But what is this "producedness" (*kṛtakatā*), which is understood as being differentiated by various cognitions? To this he says: "of the causal factors" (*kārakāṇām*). This relation between the causal factors—such as the potter—and the effect-substances—such as pots—is what constitutes producedness. For there is a traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating: "In the case of *kṛt* affixes, *taddhita* affixes, and compounds, the expression of the relation [between the members] occurs when neither *tva* nor *tal* are used. This is that [producedness].

How can such "producedness" (kṛtakatā) be said to be non-different from the sound? For at that time, the sound consisting of the form of the letter *ga* and so forth is one thing, while this "producedness"—which is its relation to its causes—is another. However, as for impermanence (*anityatā*) in the case of composite things like jars, it consists essentially in the disintegration of their parts; thus he says: "disjunction" (vibhāga). // 101 //

However, since for partless entities such as cognition (*buddhi*) and the like, impermanence consisting of the disintegration of parts is impossible, he states that their "perishability" consists in their remaining in the form of non-modification (*apariṇāma*). He says "cognition," etc. By stating "perishability is impermanence," he shows the nature of permanence: "permanence," etc. Some maintain that there is a difference between being a real entity (*vastutva*) and existence (*sattā*).

But that [position] is not accepted; thus he says: "being a real entity" (*vastutva*). It will be stated in the *Ākṛtigraṇtha* that being a real entity is existence itself (*sattaiva*) and nothing else. // 102 //

He states that "knowability" (*prameyatā*) and "cognizability" (*jñeyatā*), which consist in the relation to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and to knowledge (*jñāna*), are indeed distinct from the word [itself]—thus he says, "pramāṇa...
Since "knowledge-ness" (*jñānatva*) is common to both valid and non-valid cognitions, "cognizability" (*jñeyatā*) is stated as being characterized by a specific relation to knowledge.
And in all these cases, even if there is no determination of a difference in place and so forth, a difference is determined by some self-cognized nature of its own.
Thus he says: "in all cases. // 103 //

Therefore, just as in our view the distinction between color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities is held to be produced solely by a difference in cognition even when there is no difference in location and so forth, he concludes that the same applies to these various distinctions of properties such as sound: "Therefore" (verse 104).

But even so, an absolute difference between these is not admitted, because they are different in some respect. Therefore, it is established that arising and so forth belong to that which is non-different. This is not established. For we do not admit absolute difference for anything, since everything is non-different in its nature as "being" (*sat*) and so on. However, there is indeed a difference in some form or other; and it is precisely by resorting to this [relative] difference that the connection with contradictory properties is possible.
It is concentrated. With the intention that this is not possible for knowledge within the Buddhist tenet-system, he says: "absolutely," etc. (verse 105).

But what is the reason that [qualities] such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*), though non-different from the word, are not apprehended by means of the word? If it is argued that this is because difference also exists, then—alas!—if non-difference is also real, why is it not apprehended when the word is apprehended?
To this he says: "And all... That collection of properties such as being produced which has been introduced is present even while there is non-difference from the word.

It is apprehended in dependence upon action, causes, and so forth. For apprehension does not occur merely because an entity exists; rather, it depends upon the procedure of apprehension (*grahaṇetikartavyatā*).

In the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*), the action is the activity of the potter and others, and its cause is the potter and so forth. Furthermore, the desire to apprehend (*jighṛkṣā*) is the cause of apprehension.

Therefore, if that [desire] is not perceived, there is no apprehension of producedness and the like, even though there is no difference [between the property and the possessor]. However, in the case of absolute non-difference, the distinction between apprehension and so forth would be impossible.
It would not be established; moreover, such a thing is not accepted by us. // 106 //

Furthermore, this distinction based on the object and its subject is not possible in the case of cognition, because cognition is non-dual. Nor is there any other factor to be depended upon—such as action, cause, and so forth—that could establish the distinction between apprehension and non-apprehension, since there exists no entity distinct from cognition. Thus he says: "In cognition. Not accepting [the claim] that it is independent of anything else, the opponent objects: "By means of one another. The intention here is as follows: first of all, the very meaning of dependence...

It is difficult to establish [this position]. When reality is undivided, what could depend upon what? Even granting [the premise], we say: whatever might be depended upon, whether it be the grasper (*grāhaka*) or the grasped (*grāhya*), that very thing would be present [simultaneously], because there is absolute non-difference between the two. Therefore, since there is no cause for the non-apprehension of either one, it follows that both aspects must be apprehended simultaneously. // 107 //

Here he raises an objection: "But surely," etc. That which you have stated, having accepted [the notion of] dependence—that [the object] is "present"—is incorrect. For in the apprehension of blue and so forth, the cognition does not arise that "this is the object" or "this is the subject.
Therefore, since they are not understood as object and subject, how can there be their presence? How can dependence be asserted?
The meaning is that the acceptance of dependence is not logical. // 108 //

He avoids [this objection] with the words "mā bhūt" (let it not be so). Even if one does not conceptualize [the distinction], thinking "this is the object of cognition" or "this is the subject of cognition," nevertheless, since a single entity is grasped in its entirety, it is entirely reasonable to say that whatever is required is precisely what is obtained. The conceptualization consisting of the verbal expression "this is the object" and "this is the subject" is something else; it is distinct [from the actual perception].

And it is of the nature of cognition. If that [cognition] is apprehended in its entirety, what else remains to be expected, such that through its non-apprehension there would be no awareness of both aspects? Even so, if it is not apprehended as having a dual nature, how will it possess a dual nature? Therefore, with the intention of establishing that cognition is not dual-natured, he says: "In this way" (evam). 109.

Thus, first, that which was stated—that although it possesses a dual nature, it is not apprehended as having a dual nature—has been refuted. Now, he introduces [the following] in order to criticize what has been asserted by the Buddhists, namely, that cognition is apprehended as having only a dual form: "uttarottara... (by each subsequent...). For the Buddhists think in this way: cognition has a twofold form, being self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*).

For that [cognition] indeed arises as "I know the jar. In this regard, "I know" is the subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*), and "the jar" is the objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*).
