Thus, although cognition possesses a dual nature even when it is self-cognized, the Buddhists maintain the presentation of successive specific cognitions for the purpose of awakening those who, being deluded, do not comprehend it. For it is thus:

They point out that one says, "I know the cognition of the jar. In this case, the objective aspect and the subjective aspect of the first [cognition] color the subjective aspect of the second cognition, which then appears as a composite manifestation. This is consistent with the first [cognition] having two forms; otherwise, the first would have to be either merely the objective aspect or merely the subjective aspect.

Consequently, even the second and subsequent [cognitions] would have that same object and that same form. In that case, if the first [cognition] consists of the mere apprehended object, then the second cognition would also arise as "the jar" alone. Therein, the designation by means of three terms—namely, "I know the cognition of the jar"—would not be possible; for indeed, there is no such thing as a meaningless designation for those who are not afflicted [by delusion]. And thus, regarding the third and subsequent cognitions...

The demonstration by means of the fourfold [reasons] and so forth should be shown. Therefore, it is understood from the successive distinctions of cognition that there is also a perception of the form of the apprehender (*grāhakākāra*). Furthermore, this other reason for the experience of two forms has been stated: "And because of memory at a later time; for this [object] is not unperceived."

Thus, just as one remembers the object of apprehension by thinking, "This is that very jar," so too does one cognize the aspect of the apprehender, which is expressed by the thought, "I knew the cognition of the jar. Furthermore, since a memory whose object was not previously experienced is impossible, there must first have been a cognition of the form of the apprehender, inferred from the memory through its connection with the prior experience.
He says that it is "conceived" because of memory. // 110 //

He elaborates on that very point with the verse beginning "of a single form" (ekākāram): this has already been explained previously. However, if it is maintained that the form of the apprehender (grāhakākāra) is itself apprehended, then the observation of an accumulation of those forms would be logical; thus he says: "the apprehender... (grāhaka...). 112 //
How is this established? To this he says: "It is born. For previously, the cognition "I know the jar" has the form of both the apprehended (grāhya) and the apprehender (grāhaka).
In that very [first cognition], which has become the object, there is the subsequent cognition "I know the cognition of the jar," and its own apprehending form as well as the two preceding ones.

The forms of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject, residing within the cognition that has reached its own objective domain, become submerged. In this way, the experience of three forms is established. // 113 //

In this very manner, through the increase of cognitive forms (*ākāra*), the distinctness of each subsequent cognition from its predecessors is established even in the case of the third and following cognitions.

Otherwise, if the preceding cognition possessed only the form of the apprehended (*grāhya*), then because it would function as an object by imparting its own form [to the next], the subsequent cognition would likewise be similar to it and consist essentially of the jar; thus, [the claim that it is a cognition of the cognition] would be untenable. The same applies if the preceding cognition possessed only the form of the apprehender (*grāhaka*).
Because of that identity of form, their distinctness would not be established.
Even in the view that [consciousness] is formless, the same consequence follows:
because the preceding and succeeding cognitions share the commonality of being formless.

With this intention, he says: "In others. Thus far, the point that [the existence of past objects] follows from the specific nature of successive cognitions has been elaborated. Now he elaborates the point that it is known through inference because of memory—namely, "the object of apprehension," etc. And this has already been explained previously. // 114 //

Regarding the accumulation of forms (*ākāra*), he states the refutation: "No. This is the meaning: forms accompanied by an accumulation are not perceived in successive cognitions, because only the forms such as blue and so forth appear. For at all times, our object alone appears externally as "this"; however, it has been described more than once that only occasionally does a formless cognition appear for one whose desire to know has arisen. Therefore, [the form] is not mounted upon the cognition.

The view that "two aspects are perceived" is based on the authority of consciousness (*saṃvit-pramāṇaka*), because there is no cognition such as "I am blue. What, then, is the meaning of "I know the jar"? The verb "to know" (*jānāti*) does not necessarily apply to the cognitions of objects, since the cognition occurs simply as "this is a jar. However, when it is the knowledge itself that is sought to be known, then knowledge [is understood] by virtue of the object's state of being known (*jñātatā*).

It might be perceived; and in that case, there would be this application of the verb *jānāti* (he knows). However, it does not follow from this that knowledge itself possesses a dual aspect (*dvayākāra*). Once the external object-aspect has been cognized, this formless knowledge (*anākārajñāna*) is indeed distinct [from the object]. If there is only the awareness of a formless knowledge, how then can there be the designation "knowledge having a blue aspect" or "knowledge having a yellow aspect"? To this he says: "By means of the object" (*viṣaya*). The intention is as follows: first of all, knowledge is not seen as possessing an aspect.

It has been stated that this is because [the cognition] perceives an external form. As for the designation "cognition having a blue form," the possession of a form by the cognition is not established thereby. For it is the object that is the locus of designations such as "blue"; and it is precisely by means of the designation of that [object] that the cognition is designated, but the cognition itself is not blue.
If one asks: for what reason is it designated by means of the designation of another?

No. Because it is impossible to designate [cognition] without that [form]. For it is not possible to define it without that designation, saying "this cognition is of such a kind," because cognitions themselves lack an intrinsic form. // 115 //

As for the claim that, under the theory of formlessness (*nirākāratva*), it would follow that all cognitions are identical, that is incorrect. Even if they are formless, the distinction [between cognitions] is established by the distinction between their objects (*grāhya*);

for the objects, which are the referents, serve as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding cognition. And since those objects are seen to be distinct, they necessarily render the cognitions themselves distinct.
"They establish [the object]"—therefore, for the sake of establishing its distinction, it is not logical to admit other forms inherent in it;
thus he says, "Therefore. The meaning is that it is based on the distinction of the apprehended object and has that as its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). // 116 //

"Let it be granted, then, that the difference in the objects of apprehension (*grāhya-bheda*) serves as the means of proof for [the difference] between cognitions. But how can the difference among those [cognitions] that are formless (*anākāra*) be established? This is indeed difficult to demonstrate; therefore, he says: 'Insofar as they are formless' (*nirākāratve*). The intention is this: what is this "formlessness" (*anākāratva*) of cognitions? If it means being devoid of intrinsic nature (*nirasvabhāvatva*), that is not accepted, because their nature is manifestation (*prakāśa*) brought forth by virtue of the object. If, on the other hand, it means the absence of forms such as blue (*nīla-ādy-ākāra-viraha*), [then...]

No. For even in the absence of such [objective] forms, a distinction is admitted in the case of space, time, the self, direction, and action. Therefore, just as entities possessing forms such as blue appear distinct from one another despite being non-distinct in their possession of form, so too cognitions—though non-distinct in their lack of form—will be distinguished by their very nature through a self that is inferred from the difference between the objects grasped. // 117 //

Regarding what was stated—that there is inference from memory—he now presents and refutes that argument with the words "smṛteḥ" (from memory). The meaning is that this which is sung by the Buddhists is indeed false. How is it false? To this he says: "tadaiva" (at that very time).

Indeed, at that very time this cognition in the form of the subject (*grāhakākāra*) is experienced. For in that case, the jar is remembered. [The inference is] based on the impossibility of that memory otherwise.

And that knowledge which serves as its cause is postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "Surely the jar was known by me; otherwise, how could it be remembered? Furthermore, regarding that very knowledge known through presumptive testimony, there is the use of the verbal form "I knew" (*ajñāsiṣam*), but it does not mean that the knowledge itself was previously apprehended. // 118 //
[727] As for what was stated previously regarding the experience of two forms— that even while admitting non-difference, one asks how it is that when one is apprehended,
the other is not apprehended— he refutes that with the words "it is apprehended" (*gṛhītam iti*). This refers to what we have said:

When questioned regarding the cause for not perceiving the two parts—namely, "Why is that which consists of both natures not perceived?"—it is not merely our intention that you should engage in such verbal activity, nor do we care whether you have stated it one way or another. Rather, you must state the actual reason for its non-perception.
It is not the case that it is not perceived as having a dual nature because of non-difference; you cannot escape us by mere verbal assertion.

"But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), it has already been stated that there is no cognition of the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender. Thus he says: "The apprehended...

This might be the case: "Let it be granted that the dual nature is not grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, we shall establish the cognition of both forms through inference (*anumāna*).
The self of the apprehender is grasped because it is non-different from the apprehended."
To this, he says: "like that [self]," etc., meaning: "perception," etc. The intention is as follows: your position is that cognition is perceptual.

And on this position, it is not logical to establish the apprehension [of the object] by means of inference. For if cognition were produced with two forms, it would manifest in exactly that way. Therefore, on the position that cognition is perceptual, this perception of two forms could not be inferential. Nor is cognition with two forms perceived by anyone through direct perception.
Thus, cognition does not possess a dual aspect. // 120 //

If, however, a dual aspect is postulated within a cognition that has only a single form, then, since there is no difference in the lack of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is a thousandfold aspect not likewise postulated? To this he says: "evam" (in this way). 121.

Here he raises an objection: "The apprehended... and so forth. This is the intended meaning: that which you have established—namely, that because of the non-difference [of the two parts], the apprehension of one part entails the apprehension of the other—is incorrect;

for this would be the case only if there were non-difference. However, there is no mutual non-difference between the apprehended and the apprehending parts. For it is the cognition (*jñāna*) that is non-different in that context.

And the two parts are indeed distinct from one another. Therefore, just as the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the various cups (grahas) dedicated to Indra-Vāyu and others do not become distinct [from the sacrifice] despite being mutually different because they are all limbs of the Jyotiṣṭoma,
so too, although knowledge is non-different in its own essence, there is no room for the objection regarding the confusion of apprehensions, because the two parts are mutually distinct.
Thus ends the rebuttal of the Buddhist who has had his own position refuted. But the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says:
"It is not possible that this Buddhist, being a proponent of an absolute view, would assert the difference between the grasped and the grasper while accepting their identity and difference;
therefore, he must certainly have asserted an absolute difference between the grasped and the grasper. Thinking thus, he says: "Siddha..."
Thus [it was said]. The other [opponent], in order to reveal his own intention, first states the refutation of the opposing position, saying: "No. He states the reason:

"Because of being cognition, due to non-difference. The meaning is this: even in this way, your position is not established, because it has already been stated that there is no difference between the two parts by virtue of their being cognition. // 122 //

Now, the opponent, seeking to demonstrate the loss of the [proponent's] own tenet, refutes that very proponent with the words "distinct" (*bhinna*). For the Sāṅkhyas, not accepting an absolute difference between the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikāra*), maintain that there is a difference within the primal nature by way of its modifications, and a non-difference of the modifications by way of that [primal nature]. Thus, according to the Sāṅkhya doctrine, a thing is postulated as being of the nature of both distinct and non-distinct.

Likewise, how is it that you, with a deluded mind, having spoken of the Buddha’s teaching, have imagined the state of being both different and non-different in a single cognitive self? For us, however, who maintain the doctrine of manifoldness (anekāntavāda), such an admission is established in the case of the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice. // 123 //

But for you, if the duality consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender were one with the nature of cognition, then the statement that they are distinct would be untenable; otherwise, there would be no unity. Thus he says: "one" (ekam). // 124 //

Thus, he says "one" (ekā), meaning that by resorting to your own position, it is possible to establish a single identity here. The apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) are of one essence, because they are non-different from the nature of cognition (*jñāna*), which is a single form. Just like that [cognition] itself, cognition would—by reason of the mutual oneness of the apprehended and the apprehending—be either of the nature of the apprehended or of the nature of the apprehending.

And in that case, when the two have attained a single nature, upon the disappearance of either the apprehended (grāhya) or the apprehender (grāhaka), the other too—which is devoid of its counterpart—cannot logically exist;
thus, there would be the non-existence of both parts of cognition. And in this way, cognition would result in being devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) and consisting of non-being (abhāvātmaka);
therefore, emptiness (śūnyatā) would apply to both the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and its object (artha). Thus he says: "In that case" (tatra). 126.

Thus far, by means of the non-difference from cognition whose nature is undivided, the non-difference of the two parts has been established. Now, [the author] demonstrates the difference of the nature of cognition from the two parts, even though they are different, on the grounds that [cognition] is not distinct from them—stating "from the two different [parts]. And with the intention that, in this way, duality is established when the apprehended and the apprehender are absolutely distinct, he says: "And therefore... (verse 127).

Thus, if it is your intention that once duality is established, the mere designation "knowledge" (jñāna) is to be applied to both the grasped and the grasper, we certainly accept that; so he says with a touch of irony, "of those two. Alternatively, what is the use of this technical term "knowledge"?
For us, just as in the case of words like "sense-organ" (akṣa), this single word "knowledge" applies commonly to both the object and the cognition through a difference in etymological derivation.

He says "or else" (athāpi vā) to indicate that [the term] occurs [in both senses]. If the word *jñāna* is taught with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of the object (*karman*), as in "that which is known is knowledge," then the object is knowledge. But if it is derived in the sense of the state (*bhāva*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in "cognition is knowledge" or "that by which something is known is knowledge," then consciousness alone is knowledge; thus, the status of being "knowledge" is established in both ways. // 128 //

For in every way, when the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is etymologically derived, a distinction between entities is indeed established. As for the word itself, let it be applied to either "knowledge" or its "object" according to one's preference; we have no disagreement on this point—thus he says, "in every way" (*sarvathā*). 129.

On this point, other Buddhists say: "It is true that there is a distinction between the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka). Nevertheless, an external object (bahir-artha) is not thereby established, because it is precisely past cognition that is grasped by a subsequent cognition. For this very reason, there is the state of 'this-ness' (idambhāva), since consciousness has another as its objective range (paragocaratva). If it is asked how a past [object] can be grasped,"

No, because it is precisely its status as a cause that constitutes being the apprehended object (*grāhya*). That which is the causality of the preceding [moment] in the production of a subsequent cognition by way of imparting its own form—that alone is its state of being the apprehended object. As they say:

"If it is asked how that which belongs to a different time can be the apprehended object, those who know the reasoning understand that the very capacity to impart the form of the cognition is what they call 'being the apprehended object'."

Thus [it is said]. This verse is common to both the Sautrāntikas and the Vaibhāṣikas. He introduces this point with the word "atha" (now). Even if the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) is distinct from the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), nevertheless, that which has passed away is merely another cognition and not an external object. He refutes this as well with the words "jñānatve" (in its being a cognition). The sense is that there is no logical justification for that cognition—which is intended to be the object of apprehension—to be a cognition [in the same sense as the subject].
But if that knowledge is intended according to the previously stated etymology of the word "karman," then we also accept it;
thus he says: "pūrva... (verse 130).

He says "knowledge" because the form that follows as "knowledge, knowledge" is not perceived as belonging to both the grasped and the grasper. We accept that [the word] is a common term like "sense-organ" (*akṣa*) and so forth, but not that it is a term for a generic form (*ākṛti*). Even granting that, we say: that universal (*sāmānya*), which persists through the preceding and succeeding instances, is either different from or non-different from those two.
Or rather, he says "distinct" (*vyatirikta*) because [the opponent] does not admit that [the universal] is different from those [particulars]. // 131 //

And he says, "In the case of difference," pointing out this further fault regarding difference: "In the case of those two, the former and the latter, the apprehended and the apprehender. If their difference from cognition in general (*jñānasāmānya*) is accepted—that is to say, if it is held that [the object] is distinct from them—then those two would not have the nature of cognition, because cognition is admitted to be characterized by that very form.

Thus [it is said]. What follows if this is so? To this he says: "tadrūpa" (having that form). Since an entity whose nature is non-cognition would be impossible if it were devoid of the nature of cognition, it follows that there would be an absolute absence of both the preceding and succeeding cognitions.

Moreover, that universal, when connected with those two [particulars], must be connected with each one either in its entirety, like the qualities of the elements and their actions, or by way of interpenetration, like the thread of a garland. In the former case, there would be a plurality [of universals]; in the latter, it would possess parts. Thus, one should apply the same critique as against the Vaiśeṣikas and others. He says this and explains "like the Vaiśeṣikas and others" with the words "just as": "Just as these faults were stated by the Buddhists themselves against the universals and so forth of the Vaiśeṣikas and others..."

In the same way, these same faults apply even to the Buddhists and others regarding the connection—that is, the relation—of a single, undifferentiated cognition-in-general with two distinct preceding and succeeding cognitions. // 134 //

If, however, a universal is asserted to be non-different from those two, then that very same differentiation which was previously established—on the grounds of its being non-different from two distinct things—is once again incurred; thus he says:
"from those two. Furthermore, one must also consider what the nature of that universal is. In this regard, if one resorts to the universal as we conceive it:

The reductio ad absurdum has thus been stated. He says "sādṛśya... [verse 135], because he will later refute the universal (sāmānya) as having the nature of similarity and the nature of exclusion (apoha).

Moreover, there is an additional fault in accepting a universal in the form of an exclusion (apoha) here; thus he says: "of another entity" (vastvantarasya). He explains this very point: "no" (na). Knowledge is to be grasped through the cessation of ignorance. But for one who maintains that there is only knowledge, there is no such thing as ignorance to be excluded. // 136 //
Moreover, even that which is absolutely non-existent cannot be the object of exclusion (*apoha*); thus he says: "exclusion" (*apoha*). This is the intended meaning:
if ignorance were merely the absence of cognition, then, being of the nature of a non-entity, how could it become the object of the act of exclusion?
Or, if one were to admit that even a non-entity is to be excluded, then [it would follow that] even a non-entity is a real thing (*vastu*).

He says that [the negation] is the attainment of another entity, namely, "another thing" (*vastvantara*). He states the reason: "And because it is a real entity (*vastu*) since it is something to be excluded (*apohya*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. // 137 //

Therefore, since the absence of knowledge cannot possibly be negated, if one desires knowledge upon the cessation of ignorance, it follows for you that ignorance must be something other than knowledge—namely, the object itself. Thus he says: "By that. Here, someone raises an objection: "It is imagined. For regarding words such as "the knowable" and so forth, it has been stated by the Buddhists:
"Having postulated the unknowable (*ajñeya*), the word 'knowable' (*jñeya*) functions.

This is the same here as well. By means of the conceptualization of non-knowledge and its exclusion (*apoha*), the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) will function. Therefore, there is neither an absence of something to be excluded (*apohya*), nor does it result in the status of being a separate entity. He refutes this as well, saying: "No. For that very thing which has been observed somewhere...

That very same thing is imagined elsewhere. But how can there be an imagination of something that is absolutely non-existent, which is distinct from cognition and not an object of the intellect? // 138 //

Thus, since there is no other conceivable [entity], it follows that cognition itself, having the form of ignorance, must be conceived as ignorance; so he says: "Cognition. And he states the fault in that case with the words: "And therefore..."
What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "And not... [meaning] cognition cannot be apprehended by means of the exclusion of other cognitions.
He provides an illustration for this very point: "A tree. For the object 'tree' cannot be understood through the exclusion of trees. // 140 //

Furthermore, that cognition which appears as ignorance and is conceptualized as being ignorance would not possess the nature of knowledge. For a thing does not exist in that very form by means of which it is perceived through the exclusion (apoha) of something else; since the nature of "tree-ness" is absent in non-trees—such as jars and the like—which are the objects of exclusion.
Thus he says: "by way of exclusion" (apohya). //141//

And thus, since that which is intended to be non-knowledge lacks the nature of knowledge, it necessarily follows that it is indeed an object (*artha*). Therefore, by the very expression "non-knowledge," what is intended is actually an object; hence, there is no difference in meaning. Thus he says: "And therefore... Furthermore, even so, this proponent of the exclusion of non-knowledge (*ajñānāpohavādin*) must be asked: "What is the objective support (*ālambana*) of this cognition of non-knowledge? Certainly, you do not maintain that it has any external objective support whatsoever.

Knowledge is intended [as the object]. And since neither its taking itself as a part [of its own nature] nor its taking another cognition as its object is possible, he says "ajñāna" (ignorance) with the intention that he will explain this immediately thereafter. Therefore, for those who maintain that there is only knowledge (*jñānamātra*), there is no such thing as "ignorance" (*ajñāna*) which could serve as its object; thus he says "no. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely..."

The meaning of this is as follows: for we have already refuted the view that an object is something distinct from cognition. However, why should non-cognition, which consists of absence, not be apprehended by the very cognition of "non-cognition"? // 143 //

He refutes this with the words "bhāva" (existence). This is the intended meaning: for one who has denied those objects of perception—such as the earth, mountains, and oceans—which are well-known from childhood to old age, how could a subtle existence, perceivable only through logic, be an object of perception? Moreover, in his view, it is characterized by the absence of all description. Furthermore, as for the reason stated for cognitions of existence being restricted to their own internal parts:

This is no different for the cognition of the absence of that [object] either. Therefore, he says "svāṃśa" (its own part) to address how this [cognition] could have the non-existence of an external object as its objective support. // 144 //

Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), one must necessarily admit that even for a cognition whose object is ignorance, another cognition or its own part (*svāṃśa*) must be accepted as the apprehended object; thus he says, "by that" (*tena*). Let that very thing be the apprehended object—what is the fault? To this he replies, "its own nature" (*svarūpa*). Neither another cognition nor the self of the cognition can be made an object by a cognition whose object is ignorance, because [the cognition] has the nature of cognition. Since that which is contrary to its own nature cannot be apprehended, a cognition takes on the form of whatever its object is.

In this way, it establishes that [the object] is not to be grasped. Furthermore, how can a cognition whose form is ignorance be capable of making knowledge its objective support? That which is contrary to its own nature cannot be grasped. // 145 //

He demonstrates this very point with the words "just as" (*yathā*). Therefore, it is established that there is nothing to be excluded (*apohya*) when [the object] is mere cognition; thus he says "by that" (*tena*). And so, since there is no exclusion (*apoha*) when there is no object to be excluded, there is no similarity between the two cognitions—the apprehended and the apprehender—even in their nature as cognition; thus he says "of the apprehended and the apprehender. And thus, because both lack a common form...
It is logical to accept that the nature of cognition belongs to one or the other of the two—the apprehended or the apprehender;
thus he says: "Therefore... (verse 147).

Nevertheless, what is the certainty that it is the apprehending cognition and not the apprehended object? To this he says: "In this case. For the status of being cognition belongs to the apprehender, which is established for both parties, whereas for us, it is not established for the apprehended object. Thus, it has first been proven that cognition is the apprehender and the object is the apprehended. Or rather, why this obsession of ours? For the distinction between principles is [only] in accordance with our non-dualism (*advaita*).
That which was to be established has indeed been established. Since it is established, let there be whatever designation one pleases; thus he says: "the thing" (vastu). // 148 //

He demonstrates the designation according to his preference: "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Either both [the object and the subject] may be denoted by the word "knowledge," meaning both the object and the cognition; or rather, only the object is denoted by the word "knowledge," not the cognition itself. Or else, let it be stated that only the subject (*grāhaka*) is denoted by the word "object" (*artha*). Even so, there is no impairment of the position, because duality is established—this is the intention with which he says: "the subject. However, the Commentator [regarding] past cognition...

Momentariness is stated as the reason for the purpose of refuting the status of being an object of apprehension; for this reason he says: "Perceptual cognition has an external object as its domain, not another cognition as its domain. For that [cognition] is momentary;
it will not persist until the time of another cognition. He introduces that [point] with the words: "Of two cognitions. For [the former] is past.

The preceding cognition cannot be grasped by the succeeding one, because at that time [the former] is non-existent and thus impossible to grasp as if it were present; furthermore, since the object of apprehension appears as if present in the form "this is blue," [the former] cannot be grasped due to the momentariness of cognition. Therefore, because it is impossible for cognition to grasp [itself], he states that one must accept that cognition consists of the object itself, by resorting to our own view.

—Regarding the term "object" (*artha*): if it is argued that while a past cognition cannot be an object of apprehension, it is nonetheless possible for two simultaneously existing cognitions to stand in the relation of the apprehended and the apprehender, that is incorrect because simultaneous existence is impossible.

For how could we conceive that a subsequent [cognition], which derives its very existence from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), could arise together with that [preceding one]?

Because dependence is untenable in the case of simultaneity. Or, let there be the simultaneity of the two cognitions; even so, the relationship of the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyatā*) is not possible. For it has been stated that being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*) consists precisely in being a cause. And that is not possible when there is no temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*), because two things born simultaneously are independent of one another. This is what he says: "mutually" (*anyonya*). Why are they independent? To this he says: "action" (*kriyā*). For if there were some relationship between the two cognitions as action and its factor (*kāraka*)...

Thus, there would be a dependence [of the cause upon the effect]. And this [dependence] is not possible in the case of simultaneous arising (*sahotpatti*). Since the status of being a cause by means of imparting its own form (*svākārārpaṇa*) has already been refuted, one might object: "But even for you, if there is a causal relationship between the object and the cognition, there must be a relation of action and agent (*kriyākārakasambandha*. To this he says: "The object... etc. By whatever operation (*vyāpāra*) the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is "cognition" (*miti*). And what is this? It is what was stated regarding perception: "the birth of the cognition" (*buddhijanma*). That which is the connection (*saṅgati*) between the object and the consciousness within this cognition—that is [the operation] of these two.

The relationship of cause and effect. For that [cognition] is brought about by both the intellect and the object together. For as long as the object is not the domain of the intellect, it cannot be its object; and the intellect is the agent in its own production. Indeed, an origination that is without an object and without an agent is impossible. Thus, through this connection between action and its factors (*kāraka*), there exists a relation between cognition and the object.

The relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Thus, in the arising of the cognition of this object, its status as the objective factor (*karmakārakatva*) is precisely what constitutes its causality for that knowledge. "In this regard" means: according to the Mīmāṃsaka tenet. And this mode is not possible within the Buddhist system.

Since there is no such thing as the simultaneous birth of two things that have already been born, and because if simultaneity were to exist, it would be impossible for one of the two—when either is mentioned—to function as the cause of the other; with this intention, he says: "No.

Furthermore, even the determination that "this is the effect" and "this is the cause" is difficult to establish in the case of simultaneity, because there is no distinction in their mutual independence.

Indeed, when two horns grow simultaneously, it is impossible to determine that "this is the effect" and "this is the cause," since no distinction can be perceived; this is what he means by the term "restriction. Now, one might object: "If no distinction is perceived, then both might be the cause of both. To this he replies: "the pair. If the former were dependent upon the latter for its own acquisition of existence, [it would be the effect].
And the latter depends on the former; therefore, they constitute a circular argument (itaretarāśraya), which is difficult to resolve. // 152 //

[Objection: But surely, even here, the very fact of "occurring when that occurs" (*tadbhāvabhāvitā*) is the mark of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). And this "occurring when that occurs" exists even for two cognitions that arise simultaneously, because the latter comes into being at the very moment the former cognition ceases. Therefore, why would there not be the state of cause and effect in the case of simultaneity?

To this he says: "The fact of occurring when that occurs... [The full response is: True. The fact of "occurring when that occurs" is the definition of causality, but it is not devoid of temporal sequence (*paurvāparya*).

They state that the definition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) consists precisely in the fact that the existence [of one thing] is caused by the existence [of another], accompanied by a necessary restriction (*niyama*). Since there is neither priority nor posteriority in simultaneity, and certainly no such restriction, there is no causal relation. // 153 //

He presents an illustration for this very point—that both [factors] characterized as cause and effect are mutually dependent and not independent—by saying, "of the cow and the horse. Indeed, when a cow has been born previously and a horse is born subsequently, the horse does not become its cause on account of that priority and posteriority. The same applies to those existing as moments within a single continuum (*santāna*).

A moment arising in a different continuum does not have that [other] as its effect merely by virtue of its existence, provided there is no temporal sequence of priority and posteriority. Likewise, among the visible form (*rūpa*) and other qualities produced simultaneously with a jar, a mutual relationship of cause and effect is not admitted. For the whole substance (*avayavidravya*) is not the cause of the color of its parts.

This is because only those things that already exist previously in the form of horses and so forth are the causes therein in succession. These two examples are to be explained according to the distinction between one's own view and the views of others. By this, it is stated that for us, the mere fact of a thing existing when another exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitvamātram*) is not the defining characteristic of the relation of cause and effect. Therefore, whatever arises necessarily when something else is already present, [that is the effect].
He states that this [consciousness] has that as its cause and nothing else, saying: "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 155 //

Furthermore, as for the example stated by others—that even in simultaneity a cause-and-effect relationship is observed, as in the case of a lamp and its light—that is not established. It is not proven, because even there a subtle temporal distinction exists; for the light is the effect of the lamp, and it does not [exist] simultaneously with the lamp.

It is produced simultaneously. Just as when a lamp is lit, its radiance is produced immediately thereafter; therefore, he says "because of the cause," [implying] that there is no relation of cause and effect anywhere in simultaneity. If there is a difference in time, why is it not perceived? To this he says: "difficult to perceive. Just as when a hundred lotus petals are pierced one above the other in immediate succession, the difference in time is difficult to perceive.
The same applies to the lamp and its light. And just as in that case, the fact that the needle is not obstructed [by the cloth] serves as the proof for the difference in time,
so too, the fact that the light does not spread while the lamp has not yet been produced serves as the identical proof for the difference in time in both instances.
Regarding the lowering of one side and the raising of the other in a balance scale, there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect between these two, because both arise from a single cause.

For in that case, the person weighing them is the cause of both simultaneous states; or rather, it is a specific arrangement of the cords and the frame. For the cord, being positioned in the middle, holds the two sides evenly when it is centered, but when it is displaced to one side, it causes them to move unevenly.

Furthermore, it is not the case that non-existence is the cause of existence, nor is existence the cause of non-existence; thus, there is never a relationship of cause and effect between two things that arise simultaneously. // 157 //

Just as the causal relationship between preceding and succeeding cognitions cannot exist simultaneously, so too must the causal relationship between the two parts of cognition—consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender—be refuted. Since it is impossible for that which is not a cause to be an object of apprehension, he demonstrates this by applying the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) to the two parts, stating: "of the two parts."

The meaning is the refutation of [the categories of] means of knowledge (*māna*) and objects of knowledge (*meyatva*). If, however, it is argued: "Let there be no simultaneous relation where the former is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the latter;
rather, it shall occur through a temporal sequence. If it is asked how that which is non-existent—the past—can be an objective support, we say:

no, for this is possible by way of the imparting of a capacity (*śakti*). For the preceding cognition imparts to the subsequent one a capacity known by the name of 'latent impression' (*vāsanā*); thus, that which arises bearing that form has that [past object] as its objective support."
Therefore, he says: "And not... (158).

Why is it not so? To this he says: "the object of apprehension" (*grāhya*). For if the preceding [moment] were the object of apprehension through the transfer of its capacity (*śaktyarpaṇa*), then the object of apprehension would be something past.
Indeed, it is precisely that which is past which is grasped by the subsequent [moment] by virtue of its latent impression (*vāsanā*), just as a previous cognition is grasped by memory.

"Let the past be the object of cognition; what is the fault? To this he replies: "The state of being such" (*tādrūpyam*). The state of being such—that is, the state of having a past form—would be contradictory to consciousness and devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) for an object of cognition that appears as present. For how could the past be grasped by a cognition as something present, without its [past] nature being sublated? If it were not grasped in that way, it would simply be the past. How [then could it be an object]?

Since such a nature [of the cognition] lacks any means of valid proof, he says: "past," etc. The intention is this: an subsequent [cognition] arising by the force of the latent impression (vāsanā) deposited by a previous cognition would be of the very nature of memory.
And by memory, its own object is experienced as being permeated by pastness, in the form "that.
But here, it is not experienced in that way.

Because this is experienced as being "just like the present," how then can such a form (*tādrūpya*)—which is itself unexperienced—be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And this has been stated on the assumption that there is a latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) distinct from cognition; however, for those who maintain that there is only cognition (*vijñaptimātra*), there is no such thing as a latent predisposition existing apart from it. Nor is [the existence of such a predisposition] tenable.

Because a latent impression (vāsanā) without a substratum is impossible. Furthermore, the past cannot be the substratum for a latent impression because it is non-existent; nor can the future be so, precisely because it is non-existent. Nor does the former persist until the time of the subsequent birth, such that one could place a latent impression within it.

It can be understood that [the impression] perishes as soon as it is deposited, because of its momentariness. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "continuum" (*santāna*) distinct from the members of the continuum (*santānin*) which could serve as the substratum for the impression. Nor can a capacity (*śakti*) exist without a substratum.
This refutation of the impression (*vāsanā*) was already stated on the occasion of the rejection of the inference of objectless cognition; therefore, enough of this.

Here he raises an objection: "It would not be so in a dream. As for what you said—that [the dream object] is experienced through a memory permeated by its past state—that is not correct, because in a dream there is the appearance of something present. Nor is it right to say that a dream is not a memory, because other causes of the present moment are not apprehended;
for in that case, no cause of cognition such as a sense-organ or a logical mark (liṅga) is perceived, and the arising of cognition does not occur without a cause.

This is possible. Therefore, one must necessarily say that it is indeed memory (*smṛti*). And since memory also appears as if it were present, the same will apply here as well. He refutes this with the words: "Because of the reversal" (*viparyayāt*). True; in a dream, there is no cognition [of the object] as being past. However, due to a reversal, it appears in that way.

For erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*) and its opposite are indeed logically consistent when they have as their object a thing of one form while appearing in another form; thus, it cannot be understood from this that such cognitions are equal to those produced by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇajñāna*). What, then, is the nature of error in a dream?
He demonstrates this with the words: "In that case" (*tatra*). (160)

But how is it understood that this is an error? To this he says: "it sublates. For a subverting cognition arises there, [in the form]: "this is not so. We thus know that what is actually non-present appears there as being present. And this alone is the true nature of error: the manifestation of one thing in the manner of another. Thus it is well said.

"By way of the opposite. Nor can such a misconception be asserted regarding waking cognitions, for it has been stated that "waking cognitions are thoroughly well-ascertained"; with this intention, he says, "No. Thus it has been established that cognitions of past objects are not perceptions. Now he demonstrates this by means of a formal argument: "Therefore," etc. That which is past is not an object of perception.

"Because it is past. [The phrase] "like that which persists through another birth" means that there is no inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) due to the perception of yogins, because that has already been refuted. To prove this same point, he states another reason and example: "tadrūpa... etc. An object that is past is not the object of a perceptual cognition, because it is not known as having that [present] form. Whatever is not cognized in its own nature is not the object of a perceptual cognition, just like a future object. // 162 //

{2,160} Let it be granted that the past is an object of cognition; nevertheless, having defeated the Sautrāntikas, it is proper to state that it is the past cognition itself that is apprehended by [subsequent] cognition, and not the external object. For they [the Sautrāntikas] maintain that in the case of entities that continue as a stream through the production of successive similar moments, the object of apprehension is the past moment.

Thus they are established in this knowledge. It is better to rely on that very [knowledge] which is appropriate. For instance, with the intention of showing that the establishment of the grasped and the grasper is not at all non-worldly (alaukika), he says: "past," etc. Furthermore, even regarding the fact that knowledge has a past object, this must be considered: that past knowledge which is imagined as being grasped by means of the imparting of its own capacity (*śakti*).

Is that [consciousness] of the nature of the apprehended alone, or of the nature of the apprehender alone, or of the nature of both? With the intention that it is not tenable in any way whatsoever, he says: "the past. In that regard, with the intention that if it were of the nature of the apprehended alone, one would merely be accepting the object itself under a different name, he says: "the apprehended. [This refers to] that which has the nature of the apprehended alone.
For knowledge, being insentient in nature, would merely be another way of asserting the object itself under a different name. // 164 //

Moreover, the transfer of a capacity (*śaktyarpaṇa*) is not admitted in the case of a subsequent [cognition] that is to be grasped. And the transfer of a capacity is not possible for that which consists merely of the object of cognition (*grāhya*) and has not been consciously perceived, because it is impossible to deposit a seed of memory (*smṛtibīja*) for that which is not being experienced. With this intention, he says: "one's own" (*sva*). He demonstrates the very absence of the transfer of capacity through an example: "just as" (*yathā*). There is no transfer of capacity from that which has perished immediately after arising and has not been seen or cognized.

"By reason of its firmness," that is to say, because it is not experienced with greater clarity than ignorance itself. For they recite: "This is indeed the nature of things—that a more vivid experience deposits the seed of memory. That which is not of this kind does not bestow power [upon the seed], just as [memory does not arise] from a future object or from something previously unexperienced; likewise, it is the same for that which arises from another continuum. Thus, the undesirable consequence regarding the mere apprehended object has been stated.

Now he demonstrates that [the self] has the nature of being solely the grasper—[using the word] "kevala" (exclusive). For how indeed can that which has the nature of being solely the grasper become the object of grasping for the subsequent [moment]? The intention is that if that were the case, because its own nature would be destroyed, it would result in non-existence. // 166 //

Furthermore, he says "What [is this? because this nature of being solely a grasper (*grāhaka*) is difficult to establish. For the state of being a grasper depends upon an object to be grasped (*grāhya*). First of all, its own self is not the object to be grasped, because that too would likewise have the nature of being solely a grasper. He states the refutation regarding the state of having both forms: "The state of having two forms has already been rejected. This means it was refuted by the passage beginning with "This is not so," and so forth. Moreover,

If it possessed two forms, the preceding cognition would be cognized at that very moment, in its own time. In that case, it is not logical for it to require another subsequent cognition for its own self-awareness; thus he says: "it would be cognized" (saṃvedyeta). Furthermore, if the preceding cognition were to have two forms, then since the subsequent one arising from it would likewise possess that nature, the means of valid cognition (pramā) would terminate in the objective portion alone; so what would be the point of its having a past object? Thus he says: "if it has two forms" (dvyākāra). And if the preceding [cognition] had the nature of being solely the apprehended...
He states another fault: "The previous... and so forth.
"Entities possessing this or that form are produced from causes possessing this or that form;
such is the established rule. (169)

Now, how can the preceding [cognition], having the nature of being merely the object (*grāhya*), give rise to the succeeding [cognition] which possesses the nature of the subject (*grāhaka*)? If, however, the preceding [cognition] were merely the form of the subject, then it could not be the object of the succeeding one, because the relationship between object and subject is based on similarity (*sārūpya*). Furthermore, since the preceding [cognition] would be merely the form of the subject while the succeeding one would possess both forms, there would be a dissimilarity (*vairūpya*); thus, the succeeding [cognition] cannot have the preceding as its object.

It would be established. This is what he says: "By the grāhaka... Previously, when [the cognition] was considered as a mere grāhaka (subject), its status as an object (*viṣayabhāva*) by way of being a grasping (*grahaṇaka*) was refuted. Here, however, the distinction is that it is due to "dissimilarity" (*vairūpyāt*). As for the claim that the preceding [moment] is the objective support (*ālambana*) by means of the transfer of capacity (*śaktyarpaṇa*), that has already been refuted. Recalling that very point, he says something further: "And not... by someone.

Someone causes someone else to receive something by means of an activity (*vyāpāra*). However, no such activity is observed in the case of consciousness with respect to the transmission of its power (*śakti*), because, due to its momentariness, it does not persist until the time of the activity, and because no further activity is admitted. // 170 //

Furthermore, since this absence of the transfer of power (*śaktyarpaṇa*) has been established through elaborate argumentation as the very doctrine of "lack of objective support" (*nirālambanavāda*) in the Buddhist position, he says: "of the transfer of power. Now, that which was previously stated—that there is no relationship of cause and effect between the preceding and succeeding cognitions—and the refutation of the relationship between the perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfumer (*vāsaka*), [are here addressed].

He states the application [of the argument] in both cases: "In a continuum... and so forth. In a certain single continuum that has become the locus of dispute, there is no relation of cause and effect between two cognitions, because they are cognitions, like the cognitions in another continuum. Cognitions in another continuum do not have another continuum as their cause.

Because they do not act as producers for one another in that case. In this very same way, a formal argument (*prayoga*) should also be shown for the refutation of the relationship between the perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfume (*vāsaka*).

Here, the subjects (*dharmin*) are the cognitions themselves; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that they are not causes [of one another] within the same continuum (*santati*); "because they are cognitions" is the reason (*hetu*); and "like the cognition in another continuum" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). // 171 //

He now demonstrates, by means of a formal argument (*prayoga*), the distinction between the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) that has been established: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since cognition cannot in any way have itself as its own object, therefore that which is the apprehender of a form is distinct from that which is apprehended, because it is not cognized when that [form] is cognized. Whatever is not cognized when something else is cognized is distinct from that thing.

Like the grasper of taste and so forth. Since it has already been established that there is no cognition [of the self] when those [objects] are cognized, there is no suspicion of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*). Furthermore, the phrase "just as the grasper of taste and so forth" is to be connected with what will be stated later: "it is distinct.

In the same way, taking the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) as the subject of the proposition, one must demonstrate its difference from the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*); thus he says: "the object of apprehension.

Here too, the apprehender of taste and so forth serves as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For just as that [taste] is distinct from the experience of the apprehender of color when it is not being experienced [simultaneously], so too is the color which is its object of apprehension.
Even that [the cognition] is not at all reflected upon in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of its own apprehender. This has been demonstrated in the statement, "I do not even remember that.

Having thus established the difference between the apprehended and the apprehender individually, he now demonstrates it by taking both together with the words "the dyad" (*dvayam*). The dyad consisting of the apprehended and the apprehender is mutually distinct; this is the mutual reflection (*itaretaraparāmarśa*).

Because there is no mutual apprehension, like taste and so forth. Just as form, taste, and the rest are distinguished from one another when they are not mutually apprehended, so too are these two. // 174 //

Now, he demonstrates the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender in another way—starting with the word "eka" (one). The apprehended is distinct from the apprehender because it is not known to have the same nature as it. Whatever is not known to have the same nature as something else is distinct from it, just as the cognition of another mental continuum [is distinct from one's own]. Nor is the reason unestablished.

Because the object of apprehension has the form of blue and so forth, while the apprehending subject is experienced as being without such a form. In this very manner, taking the apprehending subject as the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*) should be demonstrated. He states another formal argument (*prayoga*): "Cognition" [is the subject]. "Cognition does not apprehend its own part" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*).

"Because [cognition] arises from cognition" is the reason. For Buddhists maintain that this [cognition] indeed arises from the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). That which arises from a cognition does not grasp its own part (*svāṃśa*), just as, for example, the own-potency (*svaśakti*) of a cognition. By "own-potency," one refers to the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the cognition. // 175 //

In this very way, the formal argument (*prayoga*) for the negation of being an object of apprehension (*grāhyatva*) is to be demonstrated; thus he says: "As for 'the object of apprehension' (*grāhya*). It must be shown that cognition is not apprehended by its own part (*svāṃśa*). "Those same [two] reasons and examples" means that the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because the Buddhists admit a latent impression (*vāsanā*) that is devoid of both [subject and object]. For according to the Buddhists, [cognition] does not apprehend its own part, nor is it apprehended by it.

And this should be understood as having been stated while adhering to the position of the ancient Buddhists who maintain that *vāsanā* (latent impressions) are distinct from cognition. However, our contemporaries do not consider *vāsanā* to be anything other than a specific immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-jñāna*), which is another name for its material cause (*upādāna*). Furthermore, we have already refuted that [position]. Otherwise, [regarding] the grasped and the grasper...

He demonstrates the distinction [between subject and object] with the words "Caitra" and so forth. The cognition of Caitra is the subject (*dharmin*). The thesis (*sādhya*) is that it does not bring about the awareness of that objective portion of cognition which has arisen from Caitra. This is because it is a cognition (*jñānatvāt*). Whatever is a cognition does not bring about the awareness of that [object], just as a cognition arising in another body [does not bring about the awareness of an object in this one]. In this very manner, the refutation of the powers of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*) should be demonstrated.

Thus he says: "by this very [means]. And this is the direction [of the argument] here: knowledge does not possess two powers, because it is an arising of knowledge, like its own power. Likewise, knowledge does not possess two powers.

Because it is cognition, like one of the two parts. For one of the two parts is indeed cognition itself. And this [cognition] does not possess two capacities, because two distinct types are admitted. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of fourfoldness. // 177 //

Now, one might object: "In this very same manner, since the self (*ātman*) is also a real entity (*vastu*), its possession of two capacities could be precluded just like that of a jar. To this, he says: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). For it has already been demonstrated that the self possesses a dual nature because it is the object of a cognition that is inseparable from our own cognitive act. That [dual nature] cannot be precluded by inference.

The meaning is that this would result in the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of contradicting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, in the case of cognition (*jñāna*), one cannot postulate a dual capacity as one does for the self (*ātman*), because there is a lack of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He says "but not here" to indicate that this has also been stated. Since a single thing thus having a dual nature is untenable, it must necessarily be accepted that the blue object and so forth are the apprehended (*grāhya*), distinct from the cognition itself.
And thus, a distinction between entities established by the force of valid cognition does not entail the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanāgaurava*). // 178 //
As for what was said—that a single conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is superior to multiple conceptual constructions—that has been refuted;

for indeed, an object established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not to be conceptually constructed. Nor can the conceptualization of cognition, which arises through the force of that [perception], be prevented. Even if they are unseen, very many things supported by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are to be conceptually constructed.
Thus it is. For this very reason, what was stated—that because [the form] is established for both [parties], it is logical to postulate that the form belongs to cognition—has also been refuted.
For if we were to see a form and then seek its substratum by asking "To whom does this belong?", then, because it would be established for both parties, the form would belong to cognition.

One might say this; however, perceiving the form through the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having a firmly established substratum (*pratiṣṭhitāśraya*), we do not seek another substratum for it. Furthermore, for us, cognition is not established until the form of the object is established, such that both might be established together. Indeed, that [cognition] is not experienced as being devoid of form; for by direct perception, the object itself is known, and that [perception] is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
It will be so. If that [distinction] is undesirable, then since there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its conceptualization, how could it be established for both parties?

To this he says: "Therefore," etc. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he takes up what was stated regarding the distinction of mere potency (*śaktimātra*). Now, beginning the detailed exposition for the avoidance of the aforementioned faults, he addresses what was first stated: "Knowledge, because it is a means..."

Thus, first it must be understood that because the attainment of the goals (*upeya*) depends upon the means (*upāya*), and since those goals are not perceived apart from their form, this [perception] is indeed the form of cognition;
he refutes that point first with the word "means" (*upāya*). It is true that cognition is the means for the accomplishment of the object.

However, the determination of the object to be attained (*upeya*) does not necessarily depend upon the apprehension of the means (*upāya*). For the eye, though it is the means for the discernment of form, is not experienced prior to that [discernment]. Furthermore, whatever must be understood first because it is the means is rendered inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by those very [means], such as the eyes; thus, it is not capable of proving the prior experience of the cognition that exists as the means. // 179 //

As for what was further stated—that since there is no cause for the non-apprehension of a cognition that has arisen and is unobstructed, it must therefore be apprehended—that is restated and refuted with the words "yad api" (as for that which...). The intention is as follows: It is true that a cognition has arisen and is unobstructed by anything; however, it does not follow from this alone that it must be apprehended, because its non-apprehension is logically established due to the absence of a grasper. It has already been stated that this [cognition] cannot possibly grasp itself by itself. Furthermore, [there is another point].

At that time, the cognition has indeed not yet arisen; for that [cognition] is a matter of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and it will only come into existence later. Therefore, even though the cognition exists, its non-apprehension is entirely logical due to the absence of a cause for its apprehension;
thus he says: "by that" (tena). // 181 //

If it was not apprehended at its own time, how then is it apprehended later? To this he says: "Not otherwise. Indeed, there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the subsequent ascertainment of knowledge, namely *arthāpatti* (presumption). That [presumption], which arises from the impossibility of the known object being otherwise, does not arise with respect to an object previously unknown.

It is indeed logical that [the cognition] arises subsequently, since it is only at a later time that apprehension occurs due to the existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the objection and its refutation have already been stated, so they are not elaborated upon here. // 182 //
Now, let it be granted for a moment that there is the existence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) subsequently;

however, why is there no apprehension of that which is unimpeded even previously? To this he says: "And not... For an object is not perceived merely because it is unimpeded, since even that which is unimpeded may not be perceived. [It is rather] produced by the convergence of a specific collection of causal factors (kāraṇasāmagrī).
For there is indeed the apprehension of entities; yet, even for those things that are not invariably connected [to it], they do not occur in its absence. What is impossible about this? // 183 //

What, then, is the causal complex for the apprehension of cognition? If it is cognition itself, what need is there for another cognition [to apprehend it]? Is it not the case that this very cognition is by its own nature luminous (*prakāśātmaka*)?
Let other entities, which are non-luminous by nature, require another illumination even if they are independent [of it]. For this very reason it has been said:
Nor is it of a non-luminous nature. Therefore, we do not perceive any cause for the non-apprehension of a cognition that has already arisen;

hence he says: "It is occupied. It is true that cognition is illuminating, yet it does not illuminate itself because it is occupied with the apprehension of the object. For [it is not so] in the illumination of external objects...

A lamp, being active, illuminates itself as well, because it requires the eye for that illumination. Therefore, it is entirely logical that even that which is luminous by nature requires something else for its own cognition. // 184 //

Alternatively, why should it be that cognition is merely "that which illuminates"? For its being so is proven by the fact that the object becomes directly present [to it]. Consequently, since it is established as having the very nature of experiencing the object, it does not illuminate even itself; thus he says, "of such a kind.
Even so, it might illuminate itself...

167} If, like the object, the nature of cognition were also experienced at the time of the arising of cognition, [the opponent] has already stated that "it is not so experienced. With this intention, he says: "And not... Furthermore, that which is the illuminator of one thing need not necessarily be the illuminator of everything; for the sense organs, such as the eye, are not [universally] illuminators.

Even [the categories] are intermingled from the perspective of their objects, because a fixed rule has been stated. Thus, here too, it is not untenable that cognition is the illuminator of the external object and not of the self; so he says with the verse beginning "satī" (line 10). However, the metaphorical application of the term "illuminator" occurs in some sense.
It must be stated that [the self] assumes the status of an agent with respect to manifestation; for otherwise, it has already been said that there would be an infinity of manifestations. // 186 //

As for what was stated—"And for that [cognition], there would be an establishment [of its existence] through another"—he restates that in order to refute it with the verse beginning "by another. For this is what has been said by others: "If indeed one cognition is produced by another cognition..."

Consequently, if one were to postulate a prior experience based on the recollection of each respective cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). However, when a single cognition makes known both the form of the object and its own form, then the entire recollection of the forms of the grasped and the grasper occurs with respect to that very [initial] cognition. In this way, the infinite regress is avoided. Therefore, a cognition is not to be known by another cognition. // 188 //

When this has been stated, he states the refutation: "In that case as well. As for the claim that if one were to postulate an experience for every instance based on the observation of memory here and there, it would lead to an infinite regress—that is incorrect.
Because memory is not established [in that way]. For memory occurs only with respect to an object already grasped; thus, it is impossible to remember a cognition that was not grasped.

However, in the case of remembering what was grasped, since memory is established only to the extent of the original grasping, there is no infinite regress, as will be explained later. Indeed, [memory] does occur...

It might be argued that at some time these two or three cognitions were previously experienced and are now remembered; however, the recollection of a continuum of consciousness is indeed extraordinary (alaukika). // 189 //

But if one first cognizes the cognition through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the knownness of the object (*arthajñātatā*), and then, by virtue of that knownness, postulates another cognition having that [first] as its object, and again, in this very same sequence, cognizes cognitions until one is fatigued—then, because there is recollection of all those cognitions that have been cognized, there is no infinite regress. To this he says [in the verse beginning with] "In the case of a jar," etc., in two and a half lines. As for the claim that there is recollection of cognitions that were previously uncognized:
He says "tadā" (then) to show that this is indeed impossible to state, being equivalent to the recollection of the son of a barren woman and so forth. // 191 //

As for what was stated by the Bhikṣu—that even in that case there is memory as if it were established—that is merely the speech of one who is deluded. Moreover, there is a basis for this delusion. For in that instance, the object is remembered; and since such remembrance would otherwise be impossible, its prior cognition is inferred. From that, too, the inference of a prior cognition [of the relation] follows. Thus, for those whose intellects are confounded regarding the connection here—

Even regarding cognition, there is an error of memory; however, even the recollection of the initial cognition need not be suspected, much less the recollection of the [entire] continuum. This is what he means by saying "an error of memory. Indeed, it is through the recollection of the object that this status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for that cognition and so forth manifests, such that even when there is an error of memory regarding that cognition, [the validity remains]. For when the cognition is being cognized by means of the recollection of the object, due to the contact with the object which is the content of that memory...
One is deluded into thinking that there is also recollection regarding cognition; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the cognition of cognition (*jñānajñāna*) is included here. // 192 //

With the intention that even through memory, since one grasps [the cognitions] up to the point of fatigue during the process of valid cognition, the transition to another object is possible, he says "as many as" (*yāvat*). This is the intended meaning: that many such cognitions do not arise; however, if they are desired to be known, there will be awareness of them up to the point of fatigue—that is, for as many cognitions as one perceiving them does not become weary. Even by following memory, one will perceive that many.
He clarifies this intention with the words, "that series" (*tat-prabandha*). Cognitions are known only so long as there is no fatigue;

thereafter, even when a great series of cognitions has been known, a break occurs due to fatigue, or due to a desire for another object, or due to contact with something else, resulting in the cessation of the knowledge of cognition. This is just as when delightful objects such as songs and the like are being experienced.
It is untenable that the cessation of a previous object occurs due to the desire for another object, for in that case, there would be no transition to another object. // 193 //

Furthermore, regarding what was said—that there too it is "recollection"—is that intended with reference to the first cognition, or with reference to the distributive repetition "there, there"? In the former case, there is no infinite regress, for the first cognition is indeed one; therefore, how could there be an infinite regress in its apprehension?
This is what he says: "In that regard" (tatra). // 194 //

If, however, you intend to refer to the very stream of consciousness itself and say that there is memory even with respect to that, we have already stated that this is not the case. Even granting this for the sake of argument, we say: if only many subsequent cognitions are remembered, then, because memory has grasping as its cause, we shall postulate the corresponding acts of grasping in order to establish those memories. Otherwise, how could it be so?

Memory will have as its object that which has been previously apprehended. However, even so, it is not logical to assume that cognition is determined independently of another cognition, because self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) has been refuted. Therefore, with the intention that it is better to accept a stream of cognitions as it arises from the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) rather than to postulate self-awareness, he says: "memory. And regarding the previous statement, "if [the object] such as a jar had been apprehended," if this were the case...

This being the case, it would be logical that there is also memory regarding that [subsequent cognition]. Thus, there is no infinite regress, because one remembers only as far as what has been cognized. However, even this is not the case, as has been shown. But now, if successive memories of objects are observed, then from that observation, the postulation of a stream of apprehensions alone is appropriate, and not the postulation of self-awareness; such is the distinction. // 194 //

If, however, it is argued: "True, there is this stream of apprehensions; however, those apprehensions have only the objects of the initial cognition as their domain. For in that case, it is only the cognition—not the object—that exists. It is the cognition itself that is determined through the form of the object and its own form. And the memory of that [cognition] has that [cognition] as its object, while another [memory] has that [memory] as its object, and so on. Thus, it is not [the case that the external object is perceived].

Anticipating the objection that there might be some cognition whose object is an external thing, he says, "Now" (*atha*). This is the intended meaning: the status of being an object is established through similarity (*sārūpya*). Therefore, if the first cognition were itself the object [of another], then, being non-different from that [first cognition] just as it is from itself, it would appear exactly like the first, namely as "a jar. The same would apply to the third and subsequent cognitions; thus, the successive cognitions would not be distinct from one another. But for the proponent of the external object (*arthavādin*)...
First, there is the cognition "jar," which has an object as its domain; second, however, is the cognition whose domain is that [first] cognition;

and third, the cognition whose domain is the cognition of the cognition. Even though cognitions are devoid of form (*anākāra*), it has already been stated that they possess an intrinsic differentiation just like those that do have forms; thus, the observation of an accumulation of forms is logically consistent.

When cognitions are sought to be known, it is not [the case] that this belongs to the Buddha; thus a contrary consequence (*viparītaprasaṅga*) has been stated. And this is said while accepting the self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) of the first cognition. Although this position regarding the objectivity of cognition (*jñānaviṣayatva*) was already refuted previously, it is now addressed again with the desire to state further objections.
It is proposed once again. // 196 //

Furthermore, this other point is understood: that the fault does not lie in the objects of cognitions. Thus he says: "vijñāna... (cognition). This is the meaning: for one for whom all cognitions have cognition as their object, his cognition of a jar or his cognition of the cognition of a jar does not differ, because both have cognition as their object. // 197 //

He demonstrates this very lack of distinction with the words "remembering. For when one has forgotten an object previously known, one remembers the cognition as being without form (*anākāra*), whereas one always remembers the object as having a form (*sākāra*); thus, [your position] is untenable. Indeed, the remembrance of a cognition whose object was forgotten is observed to be strictly without form. Likewise, even the remembrance-cognition "that is the jar" would have to be without form, since its object is the cognition itself. If it were to possess a form...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the memory-cognition of an object previously forgotten would possess an aspect (*sākāratva*), as there is no distinction [between the two cases]. Therefore, this distinction between a memory-cognition whose object is a jar and a memory-cognition whose object is a jar previously forgotten—which exists when cognitions have objects—would not occur if cognitions were themselves the objects.

Consequently, since one [memory] has cognition as its object and another has the external object as its object, the distinction between having an aspect and lacking an aspect is established. // 198 //

As for the reason previously stated—that there is a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) following the cognition—this too is not tenable. For this reflective awareness following the cognition is not produced by the fact that the cognition is an object of apprehension; rather, since cognition is the means for establishing the status of the object, the statement "that object is known by me" is a description of the object in accordance with that cognition.
