And it is only now, through memory, that there is an inference of the cognition regarding that object; however, previously, that object was not known preceded by a cognition. But when someone interrogates one concerning the existence or non-existence of such an object, then, because the object is the means for the cognition, the establishment of the object occurs preceded by the cognition: "That object existed."

Because it was previously understood by me, therefore it is not possible to postulate the prior apprehension of that cognition by means of this [subsequent cognition]. This is what he expresses with the words: "by one who has questioned the cognition. // 199 //

As for what was said—that on the view that cognition has a form (*jñānākāra*), the object of apprehension (*grāhya*) must be proximate and connected, whereas otherwise, one would have to admit an object of apprehension that is unconnected and situated at an extreme distance—he refutes this with the words "proximate" (*pratyāsanna*). The intended meaning is as follows: the relationship of apprehended and apprehender (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) does not exist in any way whatsoever if there is no identity (*ekātmya*).
It has been stated that [cognition] arises. In that case, what can we do? We must admit that even an unrelated and non-present object can be grasped;

for indeed, it cannot be said that things revolving in the mind from distant regions or from reports heard by day are not grasped, because that would contradict our conscious experience (*saṃvid-virodhāt*).

Thus, it has been stated that proximity (*āsatti*) and connection (*sambandha*) cannot exist [in the case of the past and future] because they are impossible. Nor would [the definition of a word] be abandoned; for connection is not everywhere merely the non-separation of location. Indeed, the relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is also a connection, and this exists between cognition and its object. For when cognition arises, there is the attainment of that [object], and this alone is its proximity (*sannidhāna*) with the object.

With the intention that "when that [cognition] has arisen, the object appears," he says: "the object. But what does this mean, "the object appears"? Is there an appearance of the object distinct from cognition? Or, if it is within consciousness itself, how can the form of the object appear? If that is so, then it does not exist; and since nothing else would appear in its absence, it would be a doctrine of non-existence (abhāvavāda). Therefore, this must necessarily be accepted: [The verse continues: *viṣayākāratā tasmājjñānasyārthāvabhāsitā | tadanyārthāvabhāsābhājjñānāstitve tu sā pramā ||* "Therefore, the state of having the form of the object is what constitutes the cognition's appearance as the object. Since there is no appearance of any other object, that [form] is the proof for the existence of cognition. [The commentary continues: For this reason, the Blessed One said: "O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the carrier of the burden. What is the burden? The five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*). What is the taking up of the burden? Craving accompanied by delight and lust, which finds pleasure here and there. What is the laying down of the burden? The complete fading away and cessation of that very craving, its relinquishment, renunciation, and release. And what is the carrier of the burden? The person (*pudgala*). Thus, the person is the agent of the action of laying down the burden, and the aggregates are the burden. Therefore, it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the twelve bases (*āyatana*) and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it is established that the person exists. Moreover, because the Blessed One taught the four truths, beginning with "this is suffering," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the three trainings—beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves"—it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four fruits of asceticism, beginning with "O monks, these four fruits of asceticism are to be realized by direct knowledge," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four pairs of persons and the eight types of individuals, it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four fruits of stream-entry and so forth, beginning with "O monks, these four fruits of stream-entry are to be realized by direct knowledge," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four foundations of mindfulness, beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four foundations of mindfulness," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four right efforts, beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four right efforts," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the five faculties, beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the five faculties," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the seven factors of enlightenment, beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the seven factors of enlightenment," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the eightfold noble path, beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the eightfold noble path," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four meditative concentrations," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four immeasurables," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four formless attainments," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the ten totalities," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the four analytical knowledges," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the six supernormal knowledges," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharmāḥ*), beginning with "O monks, you should train yourselves in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four fruits of the homeless life, beginning with "O monks, these four fruits of the homeless life are to be realized by direct knowledge," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four fruits of the householder life, beginning with "O monks, these four fruits of the householder life are to be realized by direct knowledge," it is established that the person exists. Furthermore, because the Blessed One taught the four fruits of the practice of the holy life, beginning with "O monks, these four fruits of the practice of the holy life are to be
Upon the arising of cognition, there occurs a certain unprecedented transformation in entities that is personally experienced by every cognizer.

Whether those entities are the forms of cognition or exist externally is another matter entirely. Even for those who assert that the awareness of an object—which is the result—is self-luminous, they too must necessarily point to some indefinable state pertaining to the object. How [could this be otherwise]?

Otherwise, an object would be established within the manifestation of consciousness. For one thing cannot be established through the manifestation of another, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). Consciousness is internal, whereas the external object is different. If it is argued that this [object] also appears [within consciousness]:

In that very case, then, that [object] too must be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). If it is argued that it is not self-luminous because it is dependent upon consciousness (*saṃvid*), then surely this is precisely what we wish to investigate: in what sense is it dependent upon consciousness? Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed dependent upon its own causal complex;

however, its manifestation (*prakāśa*) is consciousness itself, and is not dependent upon that [causal complex]. Therefore, for something that has not been previously attained, there must necessarily be some...

It must be admitted that there is an attainment (*prāpti*) regarding the arising of the result, since its perception depends upon this [attainment] and not upon anything else; this is the distinction.

And that very [attainment] is designated by us with terms such as "cognized-ness" (*jñātatā*). Therefore, it is established that both proximity and relation exist even by virtue of being an object (*viṣayatva*). // 200 //

Having restated the claim that the appearance of an object's form is possible even in cases of false cognitions, he refutes it with the words "artha... (the object...). This is the meaning: this [objection] which was stated—that the appearance of an object's form is impossible in cognitions such as that of two moons—is incorrect. For instance, first of all, there is no impossibility of the appearance of an object's form in correct cognitions; however, in certain false cognitions...

In the *Nirālambanavāda*, we have established—and indeed described—that the manifestation of an object's form occurs either through a mere alteration of place or a mere alteration of time; thus, there is no instance whatsoever where the manifestation of an object's form is impossible. Yet, this [position] is stated as being contrary to what appears: that an object situated in another location or elsewhere manifests [here].

"An object situated in one place is perceived elsewhere"—this is how you establish the external object in accordance with consciousness. Yet, how can it be said that such a [consciousness], whose range extends to another location and so forth, perceives an object elsewhere? For if this were so, what wrong has its own internal aspect committed that it should be rejected? Do not say so; for it has already been stated:

For us, the doctrine of non-referentiality (*nirālambanavāda*) alone follows from the sublation [of objects]; for the conceptualization of falsity proceeds by means of that sublation. And the sublation excludes only the connection with place and so forth, not the existence of external things. For that [sublation] negates the duality of the moon—as in "there are not two moons"—but it does not negate either the duality or the moon itself. How then could we deny those two as they appear externally? Therefore, there is nothing here that contradicts consciousness. // 201 //

It might be argued: "How can past objects, being non-existent, serve as the objective support (*ālambana*) for cognition? This has already been answered. For it has been stated that the nature of perception is to have a present and proximate object, whereas other types of cognition do not;
thus, [in those cases], there is no objective support at all.

This is what he says with the words "from perception" (*pratyakṣāt*). As for inferential cognition whose domain is the past and so forth, that is produced by a presently existing mark (*liṅga*) and the like.

It occurs precisely when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are non-existent. As for other cognitions—whether they be memories from the waking state or cognitions during sleep—they occur when latent impressions are present, because of the absence of any other presently arisen cause. // 202 //

For when objects that have never been experienced before are experienced, since no other cause such as a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is possible, there is no way out other than [concluding] that they are forms of cognition; therefore, he says "ya" (which). This is the intended meaning: even for you, what is the cause of such an experience?
Even the Buddhist considers a latent impression alone to be the cause of cognition. And a latent impression is not possible with respect to an object that has never been experienced before.

This is because the word *vāsanā* (latent impression) denotes a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by the cognition of an object. It might be argued: "The latent impression is not a mental impression born from cognition; rather, it is a specific cognition itself whose distinct capacity is to be inferred from its effect, namely the perception of an object never before apprehended. That is not so, because such is not understood in common worldly usage. Worldly people consider the latent impression to be nothing other than a mental impression originating from cognition.
It is not cognition alone. Furthermore, since the immediately preceding cognition does not possess that [object's] form, how could it be capable of producing a cognition that possesses that form?

"Entities possessing this or that form are produced from causes possessing this or that form"—this is your established tenet (*siddhānta*). If even this relationship of cause and effect is not accepted, then let cognition be entirely independent, even if it occurs only occasionally. What is the use of this obsession with dependence on the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)? Therefore, some *vāsanā* (latent predisposition) distinct from cognition must necessarily be admitted.

Once it has arisen, you too must admit that it initiates a cognition that is indeed similar [to its cause] by means of the concealment of a dissimilar continuum. And since that [initiation] is not possible regarding things never before experienced, our positions are equal. Nor is it the case that "it will be experienced," for this is intended to demonstrate the impossibility of an absolute latent impression (*vāsanā*).
But there is no utility whatsoever for a future experience in regard to a latent impression (vāsanā). // 203 //

But if the arising of knowledge is maintained while completely disregarding latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then that which was relied upon by the ancient Buddhists—the status of *vāsanā* as the efficient cause (*nimitta*)—would be contradicted; thus he says: "Without... (verse 204).

Furthermore, if one accepts the existence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then because that impression must have a cause in consciousness, it must be admitted that even an object not experienced in this life was experienced somewhere—in another birth or the like.
Thus he says: "Latent impression" (verse 205).

"What follows if this is so? To this he says: "And thus. Non-becoming is non-existence. It is not the case that the contact being experienced in a bad dream is absolutely non-existent for anyone. What, then, is the proof for its existence? To this he says: "Otherwise. For cognition, as an effect, is not produced without a cause; nor is its cause the currently functioning sense organs and so forth.

Something is indeed perceived. If it were not so in a dream, then even the latent impression (*vāsanā*) could not be the cause. And that [impression] does not arise without a prior cognition. Therefore, if this object is not known here [in this life], it must certainly have been experienced in another birth. // 206 //
In that case, how can things such as the cutting off of one's own head— which have objects of knowledge that are absolutely impossible to conceive—

be determined when their latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are impossible? Therefore, in such cases, it is far more appropriate to postulate only the form of the cognition itself, rather than the form of an external object.

Therefore, he says: "by way of being defective. This is the intended meaning: when it has been stated that cognition is in no way self-cognizing (*svasaṃvedana*), then it is precisely with regard to those objects such as earth and so forth situated externally that a defective cognition—due to some cause of defect—grasps an aspect (*ākāra*) existing otherwise. A non-defective [cognition], however, grasps it as it actually exists. There is never an experience of the form of the cognition itself. "Based upon that" means based upon earth and the other [elements].

This is the meaning. For it is precisely the subtle elements (*sūkṣma*) of earth and the other [gross elements] that are the cause in the production of the gross. By this, he refutes both their dependence on conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and their dependence on *pradhāna*. First, they do not depend on conceptual construction because they are not sublated. Nor do they depend on *pradhāna* because there is no means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*) for it. However, earth and the others are observed [to arise] through a sequence beginning with the subtler [elements].

Thus, the state of being an originator (*ārambhakatva*) in produced substances is based precisely on that [sequence] beginning with the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*). Furthermore, since the severing of the head, though understood as pertaining to another object, is perceived as being connected to oneself, this constitutes a different mode of determination (*anyathā vyavasthāna*). // 207 //

However, having set aside those objects such as earth and so forth, it is not logical to postulate a form (*ākāra*) within some other object consisting of either sound or cognition; thus he says: "those" (*tān*). He states the reason: "not" (*na*). No cognition devoid of the support (*upaṣṭambha*) of earth and so forth can establish itself; for [cognition] must have some substance, such as earth and so forth, as its objective domain.

For it is understood that some [cognitions] have qualities such as color and so forth as their object, some have universals such as "cow" and so forth as their domain, and others have actions such as upward throwing and so forth as their domain. // 208 //

Moreover, if all these forms appearing in cognition belong to cognition itself, while other entities such as earth and so forth are merely imagined, then since the object of all cognitions is equally extremely non-existent, by what distinction is it maintained that the objects of delusions such as dreams are extremely non-existent, such that we might be reproached thus: "How can the object in dream-cognition be extremely non-existent?"
"It is surpassed" (avasīyate); this is what he expresses with the words "of consciousness" (vijñānasya). Here, the meaning is "in the cognition of dreams and so forth. // 209 //

Therefore, it is established that even erroneous cognitions conceptualize an object that exists in one way as being otherwise, but they do not determine themselves; thus he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 210 //

If, then, all cognitions indeed have external objects as their objective support, what is it that is sublated by the sublater? To this he says: "And therefore... By the sublater, the external object is not rejected; rather, when the sublater exists, this mode of expression occurs: that otherwise, even though the object exists, this form is perceived by a cognition produced by a defective cause, and yet this cognition is not devoid of an object.
Thus [ends verse] 211.

Thus, first of all, the appearance of an object-form has been shown in delusions such as dreams, which are based on latent impressions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, the meaning of the subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) has been explained. He extends this very principle to sensory delusions involving objects such as a double moon, stating: "In the case of the double moon and so forth, it is likewise.
As for what was said—that the multiplicity of logical marks (*liṅga*) is not possible in a single object—therein follows the rebuttal.

He says: [the rule] "tārakādi" extends up to the word *syāt*. This is the intended meaning: even in the case of things possessing stars and so forth, the cognition of femininity and the like is indeed an error. Because gender distinctions are properties of living beings (*prāṇin*), they cannot exist in non-living things; therefore, what was seen elsewhere is superimposed elsewhere through error alone. Thus, it is precisely that femininity and so forth, seen elsewhere, which serves as the objective basis (*ālambana*) for the cognition of stars and the like.

But how can it be said that the cognition of femininity and so forth regarding stars and the like is an error? For in this case, no sublater is observed, as there is in cognitions such as that of two moons. Without such a sublater, however, only those who claim it is an error would themselves be subject to error; therefore he asks, "How? The intention is this: it is true; there is no delusion regarding stars and the like.

For it is precisely real [entities] such as femininity and so forth that are possible; for these are perceived from words such as *tārakā* (star), *tiṣya*, and *nakṣatra*, which possess feminine, masculine, and neuter genders respectively. And it is not reasonable to say that what is perceived does not exist.
As for the fact that they are not apprehended through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),...

This is not a fault, because [gender] has verbal testimony as its sole means of valid cognition (*śabda-eka-pramāṇaka*). Furthermore, an object apprehended by a single means of valid cognition does not become non-existent simply because it is not determined by another means of valid cognition. Therefore, since femininity and so forth are cognized by that very cognition which arises from verbal testimony alone, they are indeed ultimately real. However, this position—that [gender] has verbal testimony as its sole means of valid cognition—is utterly trivial. Indeed, not...

There is no capacity for words and their constituent parts to convey meaning when their relationship [to that meaning] has not been apprehended. Furthermore, a relationship cannot be grasped with a thing that is not known through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, this position is also quite weak; dissatisfied with it, he states another solution:
"by means of perceived [things]. In the case of stars and the like, there is no previously unperceived inferential mark (*liṅga*).

"By certain visible forms alone, through inference"—that is to say, the very visible forms that are about to be described constitute the inferential mark (*liṅga*). But what is the visible form by which femininity and so forth are intended? To this he says: "by contraction (*saṃstyāna*), expansion (*prasava*), and stability (*sthāna*). Contraction, expansion, and stability are the respective increases of the qualities (*guṇa*)—sattva, rajas, and tamas. And these qualities are common to both animate and inanimate beings alike, because they are recognized as having that same nature in all things.

For all things possess the distinctions of pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth; they exist as objects established as pleasant and so on, serving as the basis for sentient beings and as their producers. Indeed, even when not sought after, objects bring pleasure, pain, and delusion to sentient beings by virtue of being their basis and their cause. Furthermore, pleasure and the others are qualities such as *sattva* (purity) and so forth.

From the observation of that [state], the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) of all entities are determined. When an increase of *sattva* is perceived, which is designated as "contraction" (*saṃstyāna*), then masculinity is understood. When an increase of *rajas* is understood, which is "production" (*prasava*), then femininity is understood. When there is an increase of *tamas*, which is "stasis" (*sthāna*), then neuter-ness is understood. And that state of neutrality of entities is not the producer of any effect; it is merely the abiding in its own nature.

And this very nature is indeed observed in all things. For among living beings, men are seen to be dominated by *sattva*; women are composed of *rajas*; and eunuchs are composed of *tamas*, their entire activities being confused and obstructed. In the same way, the relative increase of *sattva* and the other qualities in the constellations Tiṣya and others should also be demonstrated, in comparison with other stars that possess little light.

For when the predominance of *sattva* is observed in a person, he is characterized as "Tisya" (masculine) because of his sharp radiance; but when the emergence of that very same *rajas* is observed, he is characterized as feminine, as "Tārakā"; and when there is an increase of *tamas*, he is characterized as neuter, as "Nakṣatra. In the same way, even in cases such as *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, the distinction of gender should be understood as consisting in the increase or decrease of the qualities (*guṇa*). Thus...
And thus, in every case, the three genders are established as ultimately real. For this very reason, the absence of sublation is also proven;

therefore, it is established that the cognitions of gender in words such as *tārakā* are not meaningless. In this very context, he shows the agreement of the elders [the Vṛddhas] with the words "just as. For Patañjali, having asked "What, then, is this gender? and having considered many alternatives regarding animate and inanimate beings, [proceeds].
Because there is no misconception upon seeing [the object], the logical mark (*liṅga*) has been described exactly as stated for both cases. // 213 //

And thus, he says "by that" [in the verse], indicating that even the three genders are logically established in this way. Now, one might object: let it be that the distinction of gender has different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) as its nature;

however, we do not tolerate a distinction of gender within a single substratum (*ekādhikaraṇa*). For whatever is the appropriate essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a thing, by that alone should it be eternally designated.

To this, he replies: "with reference to" (*apekṣā*). For, with reference to the various distinctions among those respective states (*bhāvabheda*), there occurs an increase of that particular quality (*guṇa*).
When [gender] is being observed, it is not untenable to determine a distinction of gender even in a single entity, just as one person may possess the status of being a son and so forth.

However, we do not accept this aforementioned nature of gender as ultimate, for we do not perceive gender in insentient things. Rather, we maintain that gender is simply a sub-species within the class of sentient beings. For we observe that there exists a commonality among the many groups of sentient beings—distinguished by differences such as humans, horses, buffaloes, cows, and boars—[which serves as the basis for gender].

The various intermediate forms, distinguished by differences such as femininity and the like, which are excluded from non-living things and which specific arrangements of breasts, faces, and so forth display as the means for [perceiving] bliss—since these do not exist in non-living things, we do not thereby apprehend a difference in gender. Is it then the case that the perception of gender in non-living things is merely an error? But surely that too [is valid] as long as no subverting cognition arises.

It is indeed difficult to pronounce. True. However, the statement regarding gender with respect to non-living things is figurative (*gauṇa*), just like the word "sacrificer" applied to the *prastara* grass-bundle or the single potsherd (*ekakapāla*), or like the word "fire" applied to a young boy (*māṇavaka*). For this is not an error, since it appears so even to those who are not deluded. But what is the quality (*guṇa*) on account of which the statement of gender is figurative in the case of non-living things? It is qualities such as tawny color (*paiṅgalya*) and so forth.

In the case of the boy (*māṇavaka*), the qualities of fire existing [in him] are the grounds for figurative speech (*guṇavāda*). But here, no such qualities of living beings are observed in non-living things by virtue of which figurative speech could be resorted to. Not so; for here too there is an understanding of qualities. For woman and man possess the properties of increase and decrease;

therefore, with the intention of expressing those properties, words with feminine gender and so forth are employed even in the case of non-living things, just as has been explained here in the present context.

And the absence of contradiction due to the difference in perspective is exactly the same. Furthermore, the use of a neuter gender term is intended to express an absolute diminution, because that is the nature of that class [of things]. This might be argued: "Since there is no figurative understanding regarding non-living things, how can there be figurativeness here?
Do you not have, O long-lived one, a cognition of an identical form regarding both living and non-living things? For for us, it is based solely on the verbal expression of the word.

The cognition of femininity and so forth is manifest in words such as *sruc* (a sacrificial ladle) and the like; however, no form that persists [throughout] is perceived in them in the way it is in living beings.

Therefore, the instruction on gender (*liṅgānuśāsana*) regarding non-living things is for the sake of establishing mere linguistic usage. But what, then, is the denoter of genders? This [question] is not applicable here.

Because the mere existence of that [gender] is useful for the subject at hand. However, if you ask what the purpose is, listen: as for those words denoting non-living things which are traditionally recorded as feminine, the authors of the grammatical rules themselves employed terms such as "feminine" (*strī*), "masculine" (*pumān*), and "neuter" (*napuṃsaka*) through figurative description (*guṇavāda*)—namely, "this is feminine," "this is masculine," or "this is neuter"—solely for the sake of establishing the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with other words expressing those same objects. Those [words], however, by their very nature, denote only their own primary referents (*svārtha*).

They say: because the figurative application (*guṇavāda*) of the traditional grammarians is so deeply established, it even produces the illusion that the *liṅga* (grammatical gender) is a denotative factor. This is the status of words consisting of indivisible parts, such as *vāk* and *sruv*. However, in the case of divisible words like *tārakā*, the suffix portion denotes femininity; since that [femininity] is impossible in the meaning of the base, it occurs in co-referentiality with it through a figurative function (*gauṇī vṛtti*).

He obtains [the result]. And the establishment of the *guṇavāda* has already been stated. Even regarding those specific modifications of suffixes (*pratyaya-vikāra*) such as in the case of *nakṣatram* and so forth, this same principle applies. This is because, according to the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*), the neuter gender for modifications such as the substitution of *am* for *ambhāva* and others is established, just as in the case of *ato 'm* (Pāṇini 7.1.24). As for those words denoting living beings, such as *aśvaḥ*, *aśvaḥ*, and so on—

Among those [words] ending in feminine suffixes, that very suffix expresses femininity. And since its own meaning is possible [in this case], it is expressed by the base (prakṛti) through its primary function (*mukhyā vṛtti*). Even in cases such as *aśva* and so on, the comprehension of the specific gender arises precisely from the modification of the suffix. Femininity and the like are indeed denoted by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), while the suffix [merely] indicates them.

It is not accepted that [the gender] is illuminated [by the suffixes], because the existence or non-existence [of the meaning] is observed only through the appearance and disappearance of the suffixes (*pratyaya*), and because the base (*prakṛti*) is determined by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) to express only its own inherent meaning. Therefore, it is only correct to say that the feminine suffixes such as *ṭāp* and so on are applied when the feminine gender is to be expressed. Furthermore, the author of the Vārttika stated that [the feminine form] might be seen elsewhere than in the case of "femininity" (*strītva*).

It should be understood that by saying this—namely, by stating that words whose observed mark (*liṅga*) is seen in living beings express [their meaning] only through a figurative function (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) when used in co-occurrence with a base word denoting a non-living being—it is not meant that there is an error (*bhrānti*) consisting in the superimposition of what is seen elsewhere. Therefore, the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) should not be questioned either, because such [superimposition] is observed in the case of figurative usage. Hence, in the cognition of "tārakā" and so forth, it is likewise [understood] as feminine elsewhere.

"The [word] would be seen"—this alone is the most excellent resolution. However, one should note that the incorrectness of the other two [positions] has been revealed solely through the presentation of the fact that, in some way, they take the word as the ultimate reality. // 214 //

As for what was further stated—namely, how cognitions such as "corpse" and so forth could be of real objects (*sad-artha*) regarding the very same body of a woman for a wandering mendicant and others—that is answered with the words "corpse, etc. Its meaning is this:

it is not untenable that an object of manifold form is experienced precisely as having manifold forms. However, a certain person, by way of a fixed disposition (*vyavasthā*), perceives a particular form...
Not everyone practices everything;

in this regard, the presence or absence of auxiliary latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the determining factor. For among wandering mendicants and others, a particular latent impression enters the heart of a specific individual due to some prior practice, and having arisen, it manifests in only a certain form within that very [individual].

[The Lord] shows [this] in the body of a young woman. For the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), having practiced the contemplation of the Self as distinct from the body, yet with an internal organ perfumed by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that [practice], thinks of the amorous woman as a "corpse" (*kuṇapa*), like a dead body. The lover (*kāmuka*), however, aided by the latent impressions instilled through the practice of passion, failing to perceive the distinction between the body and the Self, identifies with the body through egoism (*ahaṅkṛta*) and perceives the amorous woman as "I. But the dog, supported by latent impressions instilled by the excessive practice of eating flesh, which is its innate disposition, [perceives her as food].

The notion that "they desire to devour a woman who possesses broad hips and swelling breasts" is a state of consciousness directed toward a single object, following the specific arrangement of latent impressions (vāsanā) belonging to those such as wandering mendicants. // 215 //

He says: "What offense have we committed by asserting that consciousness is afflicted by the forms of blue and so forth, which are bound to latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? For you too have described latent impression alone as the cause for the appearance of forms.
To this he replies with the word "one's own" (*sva*).
This is the intended meaning: it is not [the case that] latent impression...

It has been stated more than once that a certain [mental] factor, in the form of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), is to be honored; and those who consider themselves experts in logic (*caurikā*) maintain that the imitation or similarity of that very impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by a prior cognition with respect to that same cognition is what constitutes "predisposition" (*vāsanā*).
Furthermore, that impression is the cause for determining a single previously practiced aspect within an object that possesses many aspects.

It is logical that [the form] exists; however, it is not tenable to say that a latent impression (vāsanā) manifests a form that has never been experienced or that is non-existent, as you gentlemen believe. Thus, there is a great difference between us. // 216 //

The cognition of "long" and so forth, which also has a single object, must be resolved in the same way through the difference in relative dependence; thus he says: "In the same way. In the cognition of long and short, there is a dependence on different limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). But in the distinction between "jar," "earthen," and so forth, there is a dependence on time and other factors; for even a single object is sometimes cognized as "this is a jar" and sometimes as "this is earthen," depending on the difference in time and other such factors.
The establishment of the diversity of awakening. // 217 //

Moreover, this is an unprecedented argument: that what appears as having multiple forms must therefore be a formless entity, and that these are merely the forms of cognition. For, since we observe a diversity in perception, it is more appropriate to postulate multiple forms rather than to postulate formlessness; thus he says:
It might be argued: "Let it be that multiple forms are non-contradictory even in a single [entity];

but how can there be the occurrence of many contradictory [forms]? To this he says: "Because of consciousness" (*saṃvitter*). That "this is contradicted by that" is witnessed by consciousness; therefore, wherever you have the conceit of contradiction, there is non-contradiction by the force of consciousness itself.
The intention is that we shall explain this very point. And this statement is made by way of a concession (*anvāruhya-vacana*);

for it has already been shown that there is no contradiction because [the objects] are distinct. It might be possible to postulate a formless nature for a single entity based on the perception of multiple forms, if there were a logical justification for the claim that "a single thing possesses a single form. Without such a justification, however, this assertion would be nothing more than a command from a sovereign. With the intention that this is illogical, he says: "possessing a single form" (ekākāram). // 219 //

For the determination of things depends solely upon consciousness. Therefore, whatever is established by consciousness in whatever form, it must be accepted as having that very form; thus he says, "For indeed" (*tathā hi*). Furthermore, even though an object is one, we do not maintain an extremist position (*ekāntavāda*) such that we could be reproached in this way: "How can one thing have many forms? For that [object] also consists of both the one and the many.
Thus, he says "na ca" (and not) to show that this applies to us, the proponents of non-absolutism (anekāntavādins). // 220 //

Therefore, it is established that the forms of objects, which already exist, are perceived as distinct and separate through cognitions caused by the presence of limiting conditions (upādhi) such as place, time, and state; he concludes this with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). Place and the other factors serve as the causes for the cognitions by means of the manifestation and concealment of the object's forms. // 221 //

"In that case, how is it when the forms such as 'jar-ness' appear simultaneously to perceivers? For those [forms] are not relative, since you admit they are intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). And it has been said: 'jar-ness, earthenness, substance-ness,' and so forth. What is the solution to this? To this he says: "Simultaneously" (*yugapat*). Even though here there is no dependence on external conditions (*aupādhikatva*) nor any emergence and suppression (*udbhavābhibhava*), nevertheless, regarding an object that possesses multiple forms, whichever [form] belongs to which [part of the] object...

When one remembers the word for a particular portion of an object, one cognizes it through conceptual construction as "this is such-and-such" and not otherwise; thus, the establishment of the conventional distinction is achieved. // 222 //

Right here he states an illustration: "constantly" (*nityam*). For although color and other qualities are constantly present in a jar, nevertheless they are not all experienced by everyone, because of the fixed distribution of objects among the sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
(223) Having thus shown the illustration, he applies it to the subject of the illustration: "in this way" (*evam*). (224)

[Objection: But surely the sense-faculties do not reach an object located outside; if [cognition] were to manifest without reaching [its object], there would be no limit [to such cognition]. Therefore, the comprehension of an external object in any way is not tenable. To this, he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the intended meaning: first, it is established by the force of experience that cognition has an external objective support (*ālambana*); it has been stated that this external objective essence is manifested by the sense-faculties only after being reached. And the fact that they function by reaching [the object] (*prāpyakāritā*) has been demonstrated. If, despite this, [your position] does not hold, then let it be so.

Nevertheless, cognition does not have multiple objects simultaneously, because that would contradict its nature as consciousness. We shall explain a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) belonging to the sense organs themselves— which do not reach their objects— that is inferred from the effects [of perception],
by the power of which they manifest external objects even though those objects are not reached.
Furthermore, the conceptual construction that cognition has its own part as its object is not supported by valid means of knowledge. // 225 //

Regarding what was also said—that speakers are indeed observed—he provides the following rebuttal: "They say. When worldly people say, "This object is blue because a cognition with that form arises," they do not say so while maintaining that the apprehension of the object is preceded by a familiarity with the form of the cognition. Thus he says this. // 226 //

How indeed do they say this? To this he says: "By way of being the grasper" (*grāhakatvena*). For when blue is known, one who has had a doubt raised by another or has himself become skeptical determines the reality of the object only after first ascertaining the validity of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is because such cognition is not otherwise [than valid] in its grasping of objects; it presents the object as it truly is, since that [presentation] is conditioned by it [the validity of the means]. And here, first...

To that extent, the blue object is presented by cognition. And in the same way, there exists a cognition persisting from the beginning until now which manifests as blue itself. Therefore, when one subsequently recognizes [the object] as "this is indeed blue," one takes that prior cognition as the means (*upāya*);
thus, it is not possible to establish the prior apprehension of the cognition by this [subsequent recognition]. // 227 //

Thus, the power of perception has been examined; and it has been determined that it is capable of functioning only with respect to external objects. Since the sublation of inference by perception is thus established, the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins) have not yet reached the conclusion that external objects do not exist—an inference based on signs. Therefore, bypassing the conceptualization of the experience of cognition as a means to establish their non-existence, they [proceed as follows].
He says that it is indeed appropriate to strive for that which is external alone, [stating]: "Laiṅgika... (verse 228).

It might be argued: "Ordinary people perceive an object as existing externally, whereas investigators, being unable to establish it through reasoning, conclude that cognitions have their own parts as their objective supports. To this, he says: "Just as" (*yathā*). The meaning is this: just as the cognition of that object arises in the world...

The investigators (*parīkṣakas*) should likewise speak in this manner; for those who assert that cognition is non-correspondent (*ayathārtha*) would not truly be investigators. This, however, is the essential nature of investigators: that they take refuge in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for in the absence of that, their status as investigators would be lost. Furthermore, worldly people do not perceive an external object as possessing an internal form. He recalls this very perception with the words "not of such a kind" (*na yādṛg*). The external object is not of the same kind as the internal form that is apprehended, because that [internal form]...
It has been stated that this [external object] is determined through another form as "this. However, the internal form would be determined as "I," just like our own self. // 229 //

Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Now, if it should be argued that 'this [cognition] is known precisely as it arises, and it makes another object known, like a lamp,' and so forth"—the author refutes that with the words "as it arises. The intention is this: that which is to be stated by the proponent of the denial of external objects must be consistent with the non-existence of such objects.

Furthermore, one who asserts that there is the apprehension of both the cognition and the object as they arise here does not thereby demonstrate the non-existence of the object; thus, it is not appropriate for the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) to say this. It might be argued: "This is not what is being said;

rather, we are merely stating that something else entirely different has entered into the cognition, which is not accepted by the proponent of the final conclusion (*siddhāntin*), and it is for the sake of refuting this alternative final conclusion that [the objection] is raised. To this he says: "How so? [It is] an irrelevant point that is of no use to the prima facie view.
The meaning is that for one who speaks, the refutation of another's established tenet constitutes a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna). // 230 //

Having thus raised an objection, he provides a resolution with the words "external" (*bāhya*). With this passage, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) addresses the Mīmāṃsaka who maintains the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādī*):

"Do you not admit that at the time of apprehending an external object there is an absence of obstruction to cognition, such that you say 'this is the form of the object'? For how could there be a non-apprehension of that which is unobstructed?"
And how could there be the apprehension of that which lacks a form? Therefore, the intention is that the postulation of the form of cognition alone is more excellent. // 231 //

To this, the *Bhāṣya* provides the following answer, which is not [correct]: "For no one perceives cognition (*buddhi*) when an object is unknown; rather, once it is known, one understands it through inference," and so forth. He states the intended meaning regarding that [passage] with the word "answer" (*uttaram*). Its meaning is as follows: the proponent of the established conclusion (*siddhāntavādī*), having understood the intention of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādī*), says:
"It is true that there is no obstruction to the arising of cognition."
However, at that time there is no apprehension because of the absence of an apprehender;

and that absence [of the apprehender] is due to the absence of its cause, namely the *liṅga* (inferential mark) which is the locus of terms such as "known-ness" (*jñātatā*). He states the intention of the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "arising itself," etc., by saying "anyathā": "Having established this in other systems of reasoning (*tarka*), the author of the Bhāṣya says 'arising itself,' and so forth. This...

The following is what is meant: this presentation of the view of a certain school of the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) was made by the author of the Commentary (bhāṣyakāra) for the purpose of refuting it. // 232 //
He presents the view of a certain school alone—“in them” (teṣu).

It is maintained that in other systems of reasoning, cognition is apprehended at the very time of the cognition of the object. For they think thus: “Consciousness, being self-luminous, establishes both itself and its object. And this has already been explained by us at length previously.
If this is so, what is the purpose of refuting it? Even so, duality is still established; therefore, he says:

"In that case" (*tathā*). For if it were maintained that both are perceived at the same time, then, since a formless cognition cannot be known and because only a single form is perceived, there would be only one thing possessing the form.

Furthermore, the non-difference asserted by the opponent on the grounds of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) cannot be set aside; in that case, the very existence of the object would be undermined.
For an object is not established by mere assertion alone—this refutation of that view is taught by the author of the Bhāṣya. // 233 //

Furthermore: [The opponent objects]—“Surely it is said that an object is known only when cognition has arisen, not when it has not arisen. Therefore, the Bhāṣya states that first cognition arises and afterwards the object is known.

This he challenges with the words “nanu” (surely). For an objection (*paricodanā*) occurs by way of pointing out an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*). But this is not undesirable for the Mīmāṃsaka, namely, that an object is known when cognition has arisen. Therefore, the objection is untenable.

The statement regarding priority and posteriority—that "first there is cognition, and afterwards the object is known"—is contradicted by the aforementioned simultaneous apprehension; thus he says: "priority and posteriority. By the commentary beginning with "as it is being produced," the simultaneous apprehension of both cognition and the object was asserted. How then can there now be priority and posteriority?
It is thus expressed. // 234 //
If, however, it is argued: "It was previously stated that the cognition, while itself arising, is known and makes the object known;

and here it is said that at the very moment of the cognition's arising, the object is known. But once it has arisen, that object—along with the cognition—is already passed over, as it were, since it is endowed with the property of momentariness.
How could it possibly persist until this day?"

The author of the Bhāṣya stated that "this object is known" by relying on the sense of the past tense as expressed by the suffix *niṣṭhā*. Therefore, there is no contradiction between what precedes and what follows;

nevertheless, the restatement of the already-stated meaning would be purposeless. Even so, in this other manner, that very same simultaneous perception of the object and its cognition is being expressed. And that has already been stated. Furthermore, there is no utility in this statement of another manner in its own right. This is what he says: "by way of momentariness."

Having thus raised an objection, he provides the resolution: "In this case as well. This is the meaning: just as in the passage "as it is being produced," the opponent did not raise an objection based on his own established tenet (*svasiddhānta*), so too here the Buddhist has not stated his own tenet when he says that an object is known once cognition has arisen. For if he had done so, he would have been accepting the very position of the opponent. With what intention, then, was this said? To this [he replies]: "Therefore..."

He says: "From the statement. This is the meaning: when the opponent, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), has stated this—that prior to [the object], cognition (*buddhi*) is not known—then a misconception arises in the listener of that statement, namely: "This proponent denies the knowledge of cognition prior [to the object];
therefore, I think he does not even admit the prior arising of cognition. For it is not the case that what is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) does not arise when it has come into being.

Nor is it apprehended. Thus, having developed a misconception from the statement of the opponent—the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin)—and having understood the proponent’s own position in an erroneous way, he asked: "Is it not the case that [you say] 'when cognition has arisen'? Previously, I heard from you Mīmāṃsakas that the arising of cognition is accepted; so why is it that this was not understood by me before? // 236 //

He elucidates the intention of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin) with the passage ending in "sahādarśanam. This, indeed, is the polished hope of this Buddhist: that there is a simultaneous arising and perception of cognition, because it is impossible for something that has arisen not to be perceived. Therefore, the point of contention here is only this much: whether the arising and perception of our cognition occur before or after the apprehension of the object, or rather, simultaneously with the apprehension of the object? And this...

The Mīmāṃsaka states that there is a cognition of the cognition subsequent to the cognition of the object. Therefore, this cognition of his must necessarily arise only later. Otherwise, how could there be a non-apprehension of that which has the nature of luminosity? Thinking, "I shall turn him away from this fallacious position," he first effects a displacement [of the cognition] prior to its arising. For it cannot be said thus: [2]

If it were claimed that the object is known even while the cognition has not yet arisen, this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And thus, it is easily established that the awareness of what has previously arisen occurs at that very same time.

Furthermore, if that awareness were established as occurring prior [to the object], it would certainly follow that there is no perception of the distinction between the two realities designated as external and internal.

For indeed, prior to cognition, the object alone exists; by its power, the consciousness is initially formless (anākāra). Therefore, the distinctness of their forms is established. Otherwise, since the distinction between forms would not be perceived, non-duality (advaita) itself would be established. Thus, he says "Therefore" (tasmāt), implying that even the objection regarding simultaneous apprehension can be explained with this same intention. // 240 //

He explains this very point with the words "simultaneously" (*yugapat*). Even when an object is apprehended simultaneously with its cognition, the form of the object is not perceived; for it has already been stated that "the distinction between the forms [of the object and the cognition] is not perceived. Furthermore, as has already been said, this rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), having its scope unimpeded for the Buddhist, refutes an object that is distinct from cognition and possesses a form. Precisely because of this, whether [the object is] prior or simultaneous—

In the experience of cognition, the object is lost; therefore, at the occasion of the final conclusion, the Commentator has established with effort that the prior existence of the awareness of the object itself is what must be proven. Thus he says: "Therefore... (241).
Thus, first, the objection and its resolution regarding the Bhāṣya passage beginning with "nanūtpannāyām" have been described. This is another subsequent section of that [work]:

"True. First the cognition arises; it is not first known. For there sometimes occurs this situation where an object, though already known, is said to be 'unknown'. He states the meaning of that [passage] as it was understood according to the literal text: "yas..."

Regarding the word "tu" (but): that portion of the Siddhānta text which serves as the response to this objection has already been examined previously, on the occasion of establishing the apprehension of the apprehender alone. For it was stated there:
"It will be argued here that cognition is not known prior [to the object];
in some cases, when there is an apprehension, only the awareness of the apprehender is perceived."

Thus it is said. What is meant by this is that there are indeed occasions when an object that has been known is said to be "unknown. This amounts to saying that only the bare cognition, devoid of the form of the object, is remembered. And it is said, "I do not remember [the object]. The commentary challenges the stated meaning with the words "But this is not so," etc., in one and a half verses. True; previously, the intellect...

Regarding the thesis that "cognition arises [simultaneously with the object] and is not known beforehand," this reason has been stated: namely, that even when an object is known, it is sometimes not remembered as if it were unknown;

therefore, cognition is not known beforehand. And this is mostly like the prattle of a child. For what indeed is connected here with what? That an object which was known is not remembered—does that imply that cognition existed previously? No.
Since it is not known [how this is so], there is therefore, for the time being, no direct proof for this proposition. // 243 //
Is this commentary, then, something that must simply be rejected?
No; he says "therefore" (ataḥ). This is true. This is not a direct proof for this proposition;
rather, by means of this text, the refutation of the proposition is stated by way of its result. Even by the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādin)...

In this context, it was desired that the form of cognition (buddhyākāra) [be established] by means of a prior perception of knowledge. That is now refuted by this [argument]: if cognition were to possess a form, then it would be remembered exactly as such. However, this is not the case on certain occasions, because there is a memory of the apprehending subject alone. Therefore, why do the deluded vainly insist upon a prior perception? Even so...
For it is indeed formless that this [cognition] is remembered, since it is remembered as being devoid of form and was not previously known [as having form]. What is meant by this?
In this manner, the intended proof of the cognition's possession of form is not established, because at times it is remembered as being formless. // 244 //

Regarding this, there is another commentary which says: "Furthermore, even if [the object] were of a single form, it would be the cognition itself that is absent, not the object, because [the object] is perceived. That is incorrect. For how can one who maintains the doctrine of duality deny the existence of cognition? Even so, his position is not established; moreover, in the absence of cognition, [the object] would be without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The establishment of the object can be determined; therefore, this must be explained, and so he says: "Granted" (*kāmam*). Here, the intention is not the absence of cognition, but rather that cognition is not established in the absence of an object—this is the point of the statement. It would be better to deny the cognition itself, since it is apprehended through the power of the perceptible object; for that upon which cognition depends cannot be [denied] while that very object exists.

"Taking up an object established by perception, one describes its non-existence. Furthermore: "And there is no apprehension of the form of cognition without a designation of the object; therefore, cognition is not non-designatable. And our perception is non-designatable; therefore, cognition is not perceptible"—this is the *Bhāṣya*. He explains that with the words "na ca" (and not). Cognitions...

For [cognitions] are not determined apart from the form of the object. Indeed, a cognition is never perceived as being distinct from the blue form itself, such that one could apprehend it thinking, "This is the name [of the cognition].

Rather, it is designated precisely by the form of the object, such as "the cognition of blue" or "the cognition of yellow. And thus, how can a cognition—which is determined solely through an eternal other-form—be an object of direct perception? For in the case of the cognition of a mirage...

A saline soil (*ūṣara*) perceived as water is accepted as an object of perception (*pratyakṣaprameya*), because it is the object of an error (*bhrānti*). And since that [error] itself is not perception, it is logical that an object is always perceived through its own nature (*svarūpa*) as being perceptual.
Thus, our definition of perception as "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) means "not expressible by the form of another," which is the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*. // 245 //
Thus, it has been stated that even when existing, [an object] is not perceived when analyzed through the form of another. Furthermore, there is this additional fault in your position:
that cognition is experienced precisely in accordance with its apprehension of what is non-existent, because cognition is intrinsically transparent by nature.

Since the state of being apprehended in the form of blue and so forth is merely imagined due to the disturbance of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he says this—up to the words "it is non-existent" because of the disturbance.
Therefore, it cannot be asserted in any way that cognition itself is the ultimate object of perception; thus he says: "by that. (247)
Furthermore, there is another point here:

the *bhāṣya* states that the cognition of a cloth occurs only when the specific causes, namely the threads, are employed; otherwise, even when the threads are being employed, a person with unimpaired senses might sometimes have the notion of a jar.
He [the author] raises an objection to this with the words "nimitta" (cause), etc., regarding this restriction of the causes such as the threads toward their effects.

190} That a particular cause produces only a particular effect and nothing else is common to both the proponent of cognition-only (vijñānavādin) and the proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin),
because for both, the accomplishment of the effect follows from their own inherent power (*nija-śakti*). For it is by its own inherent power alone that a particular cognition...

However, a cognition having the form of the threads and so forth produces a cognition having the form of the cloth and so forth, just as threads produce a cloth. The point is that, in this case, it is not possible to question either one of them [regarding its causal capacity]. // 248 //
He explains the very equality of the inquiry with the two verses beginning with "tantvarthaiḥ" (by means of the meanings of the threads). These two passages are self-explanatory. // 250 //

But if it is argued that the determination of effects for objects such as threads is stated by relying on a restriction of their causal capacity (*sāmarthya*), then [the author] says "of objects" (*arthānām*)—meaning that this is no more barred than the case of cognitions initiating other cognitions. // 251 //
Therefore, since the avoidance of faults is equal [for both sides], neither one can be further challenged; thus he says: "Therefore... (252).

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "deśa" (place), etc. This is the intended meaning: even that which is the cause of something is observed to initiate its effect only at certain times, not at all times—just as a seed [produces] a sprout. For that [seed], while residing in a granary, does not produce a sprout; rather, it does so only occasionally upon encountering a specific place such as a field, a specific time such as summer, and a specific auxiliary condition such as water, because [the effect] is manifested by place and the other factors.

This is not possible for those who maintain that [the world] consists of cognition alone; this will be explained later. Therefore, for what reason does the cognition of a jar arise only at certain times even for one who possesses the cognition of a lump of clay that has been produced? And why is there a subsequent cognition of the form of a sprout for a cognizer who already possesses the familiarity with rice seeds that have been produced? For in that case, there is no such thing as a staff, water, or other factors that could manifest the potencies of the causes.

[The opponent asks: "In dependence upon what do the causes delay? [The author replies: It might be thought that external factors such as place and so forth need not exist; rather, it is the cognitions of those [objects] themselves that will serve as the auxiliaries for the causes. That is not so, because due to momentariness, the coexistence of the assisted and the assistant is impossible. // 253 //

Not only do proponents of [intrinsic] meaning (arthavādin) have manifestors for the potencies of causes, but the potencies themselves are established by the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the effect; they are well-known to be fixed in threads and so forth with respect to effects such as cloth. Thus he says: "The potencies, too... (254).
But for you, the Buddhist, no ultimate power—whether distinct or non-distinct from consciousness—is established by which the determination of the commencement of an effect could be possible;
thus he says: "For you," meaning "having abandoned conventional existence. Conventional existence (*sadbhāva*) is that which exists by way of convention (*saṃvṛti*).
Having abandoned that [position], there is no ultimate power; nor is the establishment of conventional existence proven, as has been stated in the *Nirālambanavāda*. // 255 //

Moreover, you yourselves sing of "potency" (*śakti*) as being nothing other than latent impression (*vāsanā*). And since that [impression] has its source in prior experience and is capable of nothing other than the production of another cognition similar to it, he says "latent impression" with this intention. Now, one might object: according to your own view, just as in the case of the latent impressions of words regarding the cognition of objects, the specific restriction of causes such as threads to particular effects will occur precisely through the force of latent impressions.

Therefore, he says [the following] up to the end of the word "nimitta": "vāsanāyāḥ" (of the latent impression) is in the ablative case (*pañcamī*) expressing cause. This determinacy of the causal sign (*nimitta-niyatatva*), which has the latent impression as its cause, is untenable because of the very non-existence of the latent impression. And that non-existence [follows] from the absence of association due to momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and from the absence of a latent impression because the object to be perfumed (*vāsya*) and the perfumer (*vāsaka*) lack a common substratum (*anāśritatva*).

And the impossibility of a substratum has already been stated. The phrase "difficult to obtain" is to be connected with what will be said later. Furthermore, this latent impression (*vāsanā*) does not exist for the sake of favoring anyone else, because it is untenable for there to be a relationship between a fluctuating object of favor and a favorer. Therefore, with the intention that if it were independent and were to initiate an effect, it would have to initiate it toward everyone without distinction, he says: "Because it is not for the sake of another. (*apārārthyāt*)
Thus, it has been stated that the determination of effects is not produced by those [factors] precisely because of the absence of causal capacity.

Furthermore, regarding those factors such as space and time which we consider to be manifestors of the capacities of causes, he says—starting with "space"—that they too are not their determinants. // 257 //

The author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated "all this" and so forth with this very intention; thus he says: "having considered this. Since the equality of the objection has been thus refuted, he concludes: "therefore. And thus, because of the refutation of inference and because perception is incapable of operating upon itself, [the argument] does not hold by means of the first two [means of knowledge] favored by you.
He says "thus" (evam) to show that the emptiness of external objects is established by means of the two types of valid cognition (pramāṇa). // 259 //

Scripture, however, is restricted to [prescribing] practical application and is not an authority regarding such matters; thus he says, "of scripture. The meaning is that it is not [an authority] regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects. As for analogy (*upamāna*), its object is the similarity between two established things; it does not operate upon the existence or non-existence of a thing.

Furthermore, nothing called "emptiness" is established as something distinct from cognition, such that cognition could be analogized as being empty of it—just as a house is [said to be] empty by Caitra when he has gone abroad.

With the intention of referring to "within the temple," he says: "not by analogy. However, through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—which arises from the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of the various distinctions between entities—the entities such as earth and so forth are indeed established; thus, that [analogy] is an obstacle to emptiness.
Therefore, he says: "presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatti*). // 260 //

And thus, since emptiness has been shown to fall within the range of a sixth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "Therefore. Thus far, it has been stated that emptiness is not established by following the means of valid cognition. Now, having set aside what was said regarding the object of cognition (*prameya*), he introduces and refutes that [position] with the words ending in "evam" and "upeya": "In this way... The meaning is as follows: atoms are certainly not the objective supports (*ālambana*) of cognition, because they are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition for their existence.

It is not a collection of those [atoms], because nothing distinct from them can be established. Furthermore, the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) has been rendered impossible through the refutation of its mode of subsistence and other such objections.

Therefore, since external objects such as atoms—which would serve as the apprehended objects (*grāhya*)—are impossible, it is established by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) that all cognitions have the self as their objective support (*ālambana*).

Thus, even by those proponents who assert that emptiness has the objects of cognition as its basis, it must necessarily be admitted— by force of logic— that because an internal object of apprehension as described is impossible, because of the contradiction of a thing acting upon itself, and because the determination of "this" occurs through the form of another, the status of being an object of apprehension belongs to something other than the cognition itself; for a cognition without an objective support is impossible.
Since the method of refutation is the same for both [positions], he says:

"It has already been stated that atoms and the like cannot possibly be objects of perception, even as they are themselves parts; therefore, he says: 'They are objects of perception'. The intention here is this:
as for the fact that atoms are not perceived, that is already established for us as well, so what is the point of refuting that?

Even a collection (*samūha*), like a forest and so forth, is already refuted by the fact that it is not admitted [as a real entity]. As for that which is called the "whole" (*avayavin*)—another name for a collection—if it were real, we shall demonstrate how that is at the occasion of discussing the forest; thus he says: "real. (262)

Thus far, the establishment of external objects has been explained. Now, as for that which was stated in the Madhyamaka system—that because of the absence of external objects of knowledge, there is also an absence of the cognition [of them]—that has been refuted by the demonstration of the existence of external objects; thus he says: "iti" (thus). [The phrase] "in the cognition produced by the absence of external objects... [is explained as follows].

The meaning is that there is no conceptual construction of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). However, those Mīmāṃsakas who know the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of both—that which consists of knowledge and its object—it is they alone who are capable of bearing the burden of investigating Dharma; thus he says, "of both. This is the intended meaning: Dharma is the chariot, and the investigation of the *dhūḥ* (the pole) is a component part of it, synonymous with the yoke.
For by means of that, the chariot of Dharma is constructed.

For this [chariot] to carry that [burden], both of these—the knowledge and the object of knowledge—must be known in their true nature (*tattvataḥ*); for that which is merely imagined through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is not capable of bearing the yoke, and thus the chariot of Dharma would collapse. Indeed, a burden is not carried by two draft animals that lack the capacity; for there is no capacity in consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object of consciousness (*saṃvedya*) if they do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Therefore, that which...

It should be understood that what was stated when it was said "by way of conventional truth" (saṃvṛtisatya), and the refutation that it is not the case that conventionality lacks truth-status—that very point is here being summarized. // 263 //
Thus ends the section on the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
May it be auspicious.
Part III:
Chapter on Inference (Anumānapariccheda).

{3,1} Here, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, having concluded the section on the Vijñānavāda by summarizing the non-erroneous nature of perception with the words "therefore, perception does not err," formulated the definition of inference with the words "inference belongs to one who knows the relation," and so forth. He demonstrates its intended meaning [with the words] "perception... The point is this: in the text of the *Vṛttikāra*, it was stated that "perception does err."

And because inference and the other means of knowledge are preceded by that [perception], it was stated that they too must be examined, since their own deviation follows from the deviation of perception. In that regard, once the non-deviation of perception has been established, the suspicion of deviation has already been refuted on the grounds that [inference] originates from deviant causes; at most, only a deviation based on its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) remains possible.

That [objection] also is certainly not to be suspected regarding those things whose characteristics will be described below. For those who possess the vision of one who has awakened do not perceive contradictions in their cognitions, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly activity. We shall explain this for the others as well at their respective appropriate occasions.
Therefore, even inference and the other means of knowledge, being well-established in the world, need not be subjected to further critical examination.

And this [commentary] composed by the author of the Vārttika is a general exposition of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the Bhāṣya concerning the definitions and characteristics of all the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that are about to be discussed. For this very [work] is the common locus for the entire expansion (*prapañca*) of all the means of valid cognition that will be explained hereafter. By means of this verse, the occasion for the commencement has been established, and the expansion will now be explained in detail. This is what is meant: [The verse: "Having bowed to the one who is the cause of the manifestation of the world, who is the sole lord of the three worlds, who is the supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, and who is the self of all; having paid homage to the venerable teacher, the son of Umā, who is the source of the knowledge of the supreme Brahman, and who is the one who revealed the *Śiva-sūtra*—I shall compose this commentary on the *Bhāṣya*. [The prose: In this [verse], the word "world" (*jagat*) refers to the aggregate of all things, both sentient and insentient, which are subject to origination and destruction. "Manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is the appearance of that [world] as if it were external, due to the influence of beginningless ignorance (*anādyanirvācyāvidyā*). The "cause" (*hetu*) of that [manifestation] is the Lord (*īśvara*), who is the agent of creation, sustenance, and dissolution. He is "the sole lord of the three worlds" (*tribhuvanaikanātha*), meaning he alone is the master of the three worlds consisting of heaven, earth, and the intermediate space. He is "supreme Brahman" (*paramabrahma*), because he is the ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*). His "nature is consciousness" (*bodhasvarūpa*), meaning his essence is pure awareness. He is "the self of all" (*sarvātman*), because he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all beings. Having bowed to him, the author proceeds. Furthermore, "the venerable teacher" (*guruvarya*) is the son of Umā (*umānandana*), that is, Śiva. He is "the source of the knowledge of the supreme Brahman" (*parabrahmavidyānidhi*), because he is the one who revealed the *Śiva-sūtra*, which is the means for attaining the knowledge of the supreme Brahman. "Revealed" (*vivṛta*) means made manifest. To him, the author pays "homage" (*praṇipatya*), which consists of prostrating with the eight limbs of the body. Having thus stated the purpose of the work, he now states the connection between the preceding and the subsequent [sections]. "This commentary on the *Bhāṣya*" is an exposition of the intended meaning of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the definitions and characteristics of all the means of valid cognition that are about to be discussed. It is "general" (*sādhāraṇī*), meaning it applies to all of them. This is because this very [work] is the common locus for the entire expansion of all the means of valid cognition that will be explained hereafter. By means of this verse, the occasion for the commencement has been established, and the expansion will now be explained in detail. This is what is meant.
