The definitions [of the means of valid cognition] have not been formulated here to demonstrate a supramundane nature of the *pramāṇas*, as the Naiyāyikas and others do; for the Mīmāṃsakas accept those [means of cognition] that are established in the world and are non-deviant. Rather, they are intended to reject the examination prompted by suspected deviation.

The very nature [of perception] as it is well-known in the world is being demonstrated. Therefore, one should not suspect that there is any inconsistency between the definition of perception and the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). // 1 //

[728] Now, at this juncture of explaining the commentary on the definitions, the author of the treatise (*vyavahārin*), because it is the first topic, will investigate the definition of inference (*anumāna*).
In that context, it is stated: "of one who has cognized the relation" (*jñātasambandhasya*). Regarding this, we do not know what the meaning of the compound *jñātasambandha* is. It is not...

In that case, it would be either the person who possesses [the quality] or the aggregate [of parts], because there is no [explicit] substratum (*anupādāna*). For a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not occur when its external referent (*anyapadārtha*) is not explicitly taken up as a substratum.

But surely, the person—brought to mind through a relation with the intellect (*buddhi*)—or the aggregate, which is implied by the two members of the compound, is what is qualified. For the intellect, having been understood from its own word, brings to mind that which possesses it (*tadvant*), since it cannot establish itself without that possessor.

"Residing in its own substratum"—this does not entail the fault of [the action] lacking an object of acquisition (*anupādāna*). This is not so, because that which is being understood (*gamyamāna*) is not qualified. Indeed, fire understood through its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the referent of the word "smoke" is not qualified by the term "blazing. And he will say:
"A qualification of a meaning that is being understood is never observed."
Thus it may be thought: True, that which is not apprehended is not qualified; however, in this context, the related term is indeed apprehended.

For the syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: "Inference is the cognition of one part [of an object] from the perception of another part. Therefore, when there is the expectancy "of which part?", that very same part is qualified by the phrase "whose relation is known. But [one might object]: since it is subordinate to the act of perception...

A single constituent part cannot function as a qualifier. For a word that has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) does not connect with another word; indeed, it does not happen that when "king" has become subordinate to "man," the phrase "rich king" serves as a qualifier for "man"—as in the expression *rājapuruṣa*.

It is replied: There is no lack of connection simply because of its status as a subordinate member. For even a subordinate member connects with that which is required and capable of fulfilling that requirement.

It is indeed connected. Here, when it is stated "from the perception of one part," there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) as to which part [is perceived]. Even in the case of a semantic connection, this very expectancy is the cause. The technical designation *upasarjana* (secondary member), however, serves solely for the purpose of establishing its prior placement according to the rule *upasarjanaṃ pūrvam* (Pāṇini 2.2.30). For this very reason, the common usage "whose teacher's family? (*kasya gurukulam*) is logically justified.

For in that case, the guru has "belonging to a family" (*kulopasarjana*) as its very subordinate element, and "whose" (*kasya*) serves as its qualifier. Moreover, it is observed that a portion of the object of the act of seeing—the visible thing—is primary, while there is a connection with another word even for that which is non-primary and dependent, as in the example:
"the king's man is handsome. Therefore, the statement "from the perception of one part of that whose relation is known" is logically established.

This is not tenable. For it has been stated by the Teacher himself: "A subordinate term (*upasarjana*) is not connected with another word, just as in the case of 'the king's man' (*rājapuruṣaḥ*) when [the word] 'prosperous' (*ṛddha*) [is added]. And this has not been refuted. For if there were a qualification of the subordinate term, the word 'prosperous' would qualify the king. Furthermore, that which was stated—that expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) is the cause of connection—is incorrect.

Even for one who possesses such a desire, there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with another word if they are unfit; and here, its unfitness for connection is stated because it is subordinate to the act of seeing. Now, it might be argued: "This fault applies only when there is a single sentence (*ekavākyatā*); [in our view], inference is the cognition of one part based on the perception of another part.

Therefore, once the sentence is completed, when the expectation arises as to which part [is being referred to], the word "of the part" (*ekadeśasya*) contained within the sentence [provides the answer].

As for the qualification "of one whose relation is known," that is not correct, because the sentence containing the expectancy is not heard. That very same fault remains: the non-inclusion of the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*).

Where there is indeed such inclusion, its unsuitability has already been stated due to its being a subordinate element (*upasarjana*). Furthermore, in this case, the fault is precisely the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
And as for what was said—that perception (*darśana*) has the object perceived (*dṛśya*) as its primary referent—[that too is incorrect].

That too is incorrect, because in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the meaning of the final member is predominant. Furthermore, no connection with another word is observed based on an actual relationship of subordinate and principal; this is seen in the case of *rājapuruṣa* (the king’s man), where such a distinction is not perceived. [Objection: But surely the predominance of one part is understood through the word itself, for this genitive case in the object (*karman*) is characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix. [Reply: No, because it is not heard [in that way]. For in a compound, [the genitive] is not heard.

The genitive case-ending is heard [in the compound]. And a case-ending that is not heard does not express its own primary meaning; rather, its meaning is understood through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), as in the case of the term *niṣādasthapati*. However, by direct denotation (*śruti*), it is precisely the act of seeing, as delimited by the object of sight, that is understood as the predominant element.

The grammatical rule regarding the predominance of the subsequent member of a compound also follows from this very fact, because it is understood exactly so from the compound itself. Nor is it [the case that] the actual...

The predominance of a subordinate member [in a compound] is the cause for its connection with another word, either in a *sāpekṣa* (dependent) compound or otherwise. In the case of "whose teacher's family" (*kasya gurukulam*), there is no fault of *asāmarthya* (lack of semantic capacity), because the word *guru* is inherently dependent. For the meaning of "teacher" cannot be understood without including its correlative; since it is a relative term, it remains within the compound precisely while depending on that other required object.

There is no fault in [the word] "enters" (*anupraviśati*). However, the term "part" (*ekadeśa*) is not like this; thus there is a disparity. Therefore, the meaning of the compound *jñātasambandha* is difficult to comprehend. To this he says: "the cognizer" (*pramātā*). This is the intention: it is true that "part" is not the referent of another word (*anyapadārtha*). Rather, it is the cognizer himself, presented through his connection with cognition, who is designated as *jñātasambandha*. And even though it is already understood, by means of that which is non-deviating...

That which is presented by a mark (*cihna*) is indeed qualified. For instance, in the expression "Obeisance to the Pināka-wielder" (*namaḥ pinākapāṇaye*), the non-mention of another word for the referent of the compound is not a defect.

Furthermore, in the injunction "He takes up the Aindravāyava [cup]," how could the deity-indicative secondary suffix (*taddhita*), whose meaning is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, apply—having been brought over—to the Soma juice which has not yet been mentioned?
Now, [the sequence is: he buys the Soma, he presses it, and he purifies it.

It is stated that the juice of Soma, understood from the context, is the referent of the other member [of the compound] because [the word *dhārā*] means "he takes by means of a stream. Here too, it is not untenable for the cognizer—understood through its inseparable connection with cognition—to be the meaning of the *bahuvrīhi* compound. Some, considering as if they had found something rare what was merely said by the author of the Vārttika while standing in the position of the prima facie argument—that "what is implied is not qualified"—have merely pranced about [in vain].

Thus, this must simply be disregarded. For in our established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is precisely the individual (*vyakti*) as it is being conveyed that will receive qualification through case-endings and other words—such as in "two cows" (*gāvau*) or "the white cow" (*śuklo gauḥ*). And the same applies to the expression "the platforms are shouting" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*). As it has been said:
"No one indeed intends to express the existence or non-existence of the universal (*jāti*)."
For those two are indeed qualifiers of the individual that is being characterized by virtue of its permanence.

Thus, it does not occur that "this smoke is burning," because such a thing is not expressed. For the world ought not to be subjected to such scrutiny. However, if someone, out of impudence, intends to use the word "smoke" to indicate fire by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) and employs it accordingly, we do not forbid him.
But [if this were so], when the relationship has been cognized by the knower, the single part would not be specified; thus, for one who perceives a single part of the pervader—

If it were so, the recollection of the pervaded (*vyāpyasmṛti*) would result in being the inference (*anumāna*). But this is not accepted. For inference is the cognition of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) from the pervaded (*vyāpya*).

[The definition] "of one part whose relation is known" (*jñātasambandhasyaikadeśasya*) implies that even if the relation is established, there is the apprehension of a specific part. For in that context, by the genitive case in "of one whose relation is known," it is the pervaded itself that is presented as the relatum. Indeed, everywhere the genitive is observed to apply only to the pervaded.

It is said: We have already stated that we are not describing some extraordinary nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Rather, the well-known nature [of these means] is merely restated for the purpose of demonstrating that they are not subject to critical examination; for in the world, it is well known that inference (*anumāna*) consists in the knowledge of one part of the regulator (*niyāmaka*) upon the perception of another part of that which is regulated (*niyāmya*).

For even when there is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), that which is qualified (*viśiṣ�ṭa*) is obtained as a single unit. Moreover, [the sūtra] says "when the object is not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭe ’rthe*).

And it is not the case that a recollection of the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—based merely on the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) of one who perceives the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—has for its object something not in contact. This is because recollection does not have as its object anything additional to what was previously apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Rather, it is precisely from the pervaded, through the previously experienced necessity (*niyama*), that the mountain and so forth are understood as qualified by the pervader.

Therefore, it is established that there is the attainment of a specific part [of the pervader]. As for what was stated regarding the presentation of a distinction by means of the genitive case in the phrase "of a part whose relation is known," that is incorrect, because the genitive case can arise even from a pervader (*vyāpaka*). For there is indeed common usage such as "being produced is the reason for impermanence. And impermanence is the pervader of being produced. Therefore, when the term is employed without such qualification, [the meaning is established].

Even so, it is not untenable that through interpretation (*vyākhyāna*)—by virtue of a specific relationship—one obtains a specific [part of] a single locus (*ekadeśaviśeṣa*). For a specific understanding arises from interpretation, and not from doubt; thus it was well said that "the cognizer is one who has known the relationship.

He states another interpretation: "a possessor of parts" (*ekadeśin*). Since two parts cannot exist without a possessor of parts, it is appropriate for the implied possessor of parts to be the referent of the compound as a whole (*anyapadārtha*).

Now, if it is said that for one who has cognized the relation, "from the perception of one part" (*ekadeśasya*) [of the possessor of parts] (*ekadeśinaḥ*), then precisely that same fault of the compound would follow: either because that very part is subordinate to the act of perception, or because the relation of the possessor of parts depends upon its relata. This would indeed be so, provided that the genitive case were produced by a distinction from the part itself.

This sixth [category], however, is produced by the observation of a single part and its exclusion; nevertheless, it belongs to the whole (*ekadeśin*) through a traditional connection, just as in the expression "the sacrificial post of the Vājapeya. But what here is the "whole" whose relationship is known—is it the subject (*pakṣa*), or the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)?
It cannot be the subject, because its relationship is already being cognized. Nor can it be the similar instance, because, being already established, it is not something to be inferred.

This is not a fault. For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not grasped by a single observation; rather, through repeated observations, the pervasion of "mere smoke"—as distinguished from all previously known instances of place and time—by the state of possessing fire is determined. It is not, however, determined here that "this [specific locus] possesses fire now. Therefore, even for one who occupies only a part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśin*), the relation conditioned by the presence of smoke is known in a general sense; thus, he alone is one for whom the relation is known (*jñātasaṃbandha*). This is in a general sense...
Even when [the object] is grasped through spatial and other distinctions, an inferential recognition is not untenable in the same way that perceptual recognition is;

thus, there is no absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the "part" (*ekadeśin*) and the "single part" (*ekadeśa*) are intended as the locus (*āśraya*) and the located (*āśrayin*), rather than as the whole (*avayavin*) and its parts (*avayava*). // 1 //

Or rather, he says that this is a *karmadhāraya* compound—namely, "the known relation" (*jñāta-sambandha*). This is the meaning: since it is both "known" (*jñāta*) and a "relation" (*sambandha*), this is a *karmadhāraya*. And in this view, when the related entity (*sambandhin*) is to be understood, both the indicator (*gamaka*) and the indicated (*gamya*) are parts of the same whole. How so?

Because the relation, which has the related entity as its substratum, has both related entities as its two parts. For it is not the case that only one part of the smoke—which has the mountain as its substratum—is the indicator.

[Objection: "The mountain [is the locus]; however, smoke, being a part of that [mountain], is considered to be the thing to be contained. It is replied: The expression "part" (ekadeśa) applies even to the substratum portion. For example, it is used for parts which are the substrata of a whole, and for members of a collection; thus, there is nothing faulty. // 2 //

He says, "Or the two [are] the meaning of the other word," namely, "or the two. At the time of grasping the relationship, the pair consisting of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*), which has been perceived as mutually related, is called "the known relationship" (*jñātasambandha*). And its two constituent parts (*ekadeśau*) are the members of that collection (*samudāyin*). That this is so has already been stated previously. What, then, is the object of cognition (*prameya*) in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound or when the two are the meaning of the other word? It is certainly not the relationship or the collection.

It is exactly so. This is because those two [the relation and the whole] have already been understood previously, and because they are not now being understood through a distinction between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmivibhāga*). Nor is there another "partial entity" (*ekadeśin*), since that has not been mentioned. Nor is there an implication (*ākṣepa*) by means of the two parts, because the relation and the whole are free from further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*). Furthermore, the cognition of one independent part based on the perception of another independent part is not inference (*anumāna*).

Because it is already established. For he will say: "It is not merely a property (*dharma*), because it is already established. To this, it is replied: The meaning here is that inference (*anumāna*) is the cognition of another part in a certain [locus] arising from the perception of one part, based on either a known relation or a known related thing. Why?

This [is so] because of the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). For a single part (*ekadeśa*) in its own right is not "not proximate. Only in certain cases, such as a mountain and the like, does a single part become "not proximate. In that case, what is untenable about [the claim] that it is "because it has not been previously cognized"?

Furthermore, what kind of relation is intended here as a constituent of inference? Some maintain that it is inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). For they have stated it thus:

The restriction of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva) arises either from the relation of cause and effect or from an essential nature that acts as a regulator; it is established by non-observation [of the contrary], not by observation.

Thus it is said. For the establishment of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) does not result from either the non-observation or the observation [of a reason] in the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). This is because it is possible for even an indefinite [reason] to occur therein. Furthermore, the exclusion of all dissimilar instances is not established by the exclusion of some dissimilar instances, and it is impossible to apprehend all dissimilar instances simultaneously. Rather, [invariable concomitance is established] because smoke and so forth exist when fire and so forth exist, and do not exist when they do not exist.

When it is known that smoke and the like have a nature dependent upon that [fire], their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with it is established; for an effect cannot attain its own existence without that [cause].

Thus, in this case, perception [of smoke] in fire and non-perception [of it] elsewhere is the cause for establishing its production from that. From this, the establishment of invariable concomitance follows.
This establishment also holds in the case of identity (*tādātmya*), because it is logically impossible for something to exist while being identical to another if it were to occur without that other.

But surely, from odors that lack such a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), color, taste, and so forth would not be inferred. Indeed, color is neither its essence (*ātman*) nor its cause; how then can they be established from it? Listen to how they are established.
For, when [color] is inferred from taste alone—just as fire is inferred from smoke—the cognition of color occurs because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is identical, like the transformation of fuel.
Thus, there is no logical inconsistency. As they have said:

"The cognition of color and so forth, which depend on the same causal complex, occurs through the taste by means of the inference of the property of the cause, just like the transformation of fuel inferred from smoke."

Thus [it is said]. Now, it may be argued that while the cognition of smoke is possible because it and the transformation of fuel share the single cause of fire, color and taste do not have a single cause; for the tastes of the causes initiate taste in the effect, and the colors of the causes initiate color in the effect. So how can there be a commonality of cause? It is not by virtue of having a single cause that they depend on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), but rather from taste...
The cause of the taste, being inferred, is inferred as being conjoined with its material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*), which consists in the capacity to produce the form [of the substance].
Since only such a thing possesses causality, and since form is produced by that cause which possesses the capacity for activity (*pravṛttiśakti*), the form is established.
This, however, is untenable: first, as for the claim that an effect does not exist without a cause, from that [claim] alone, knowledge of that [cause] does not follow.
This has been stated. That is incorrect. For how can it be determined that an effect simply does not exist without a cause?
If it were to exist without that [cause], it would have to be either eternally existent or non-existent; and consequently, its very status as an effect would be lost. For it has been said by them:
"An effect must be either eternally existent or non-existent, because a cause is independent of anything else."
For it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.

Thus [it is said]: "Occasional occurrence is due to dependence; that which is independent, however, must be either eternally existent or non-existent, like the sky or a hare's horn. If this is so, then this rule of essential nature (*svabhāvaniyama*)—that what is independent is eternal and either existent or non-existent—is distinct from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). And as for what was stated—that the cognition of color from taste is due to dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*)—that...

This too is incorrect. Even if it is understood from its own effect that the cause of the flavor is accompanied by the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) in the form of the capacity for activity, how is the color-form (rūpa) understood? If you say it is understood from the cause, namely the capacity for activity, [we reply]: surely sound is neither the effect nor the nature of the color-form; so how could it be the means for its cognition? [If you argue] because the capacity for activity, which is the cause, does not deviate from its effect...

If this is argued, we say no. In that case, the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) would exist only between the effect and its own nature, even though it exists in the cause as well. If you say, "Let it be so," we say no; for it would follow that one could infer fire from smoke. If you say, "Let it be," then the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) is not the essential factor in inference. It might be thought: "The inference of form [as cause] does not proceed from the cause by virtue of the capacity for activity (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*); rather..."

In that case, taste is produced by the cause of taste acting in conjunction with the cause of color, which possesses color. Since even a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) is indeed a cause when qualified [by its effect], the causal cycle, mutually supported by [the qualities] such as taste, is thus perceived.

This is not so; because the effect and the cause do not exist simultaneously, it is impossible for the cause of color to possess that [taste]. By the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*), [it follows that...]

It must be said that color alone is the auxiliary cause. And in that case, the labor of inferring its cause is in vain. Even the claim that "color is the auxiliary" cannot be entertained by one who has not yet ascertained the invariable concomitance between color and taste; how much less so when that concomitance has already been ascertained? Furthermore, this [position] is directly contradicted by experience. Indeed, it is not the case that after perceiving taste, one proceeds to infer its cause through the medium of [perceiving] color.

The perception of color belongs to worldly people. Nevertheless, because of the necessary concomitance between color and taste, color is inferred from taste all at once. Furthermore, since the practice of inference is frequently seen to occur only between things that stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, the status of being an effect need not be disregarded as long as there is no deviation [in the concomitance]. Identity (*tādātmya*) must also be rejected, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the absence of any object of measurement (*meyābhāva*). For what indeed exists within the nature of a tree?

Once the nature of the *śiṃśapā* tree is known, this [object] remains to be cognized. This is because it is partless (*nirbhāgatvāt*). If it is argued that even though the entity is a single unity, its division is merely conceptual (*kālpanika*), we say no;

for there is no such partless entity, since the apprehensions of its parts remain valid and uncontradicted despite differences in location and so forth. Furthermore, inference itself relies upon conceptual distinctions.

Real identity (*aikātmya*) is not a causal factor (*anaṅga*). If it is argued that the conventional usage of "tree" is inferred [from "śiṃśapā"], how then can the conventional usage of "non-self" be inferred from "being a *śiṃśapā*"? For if there were identity (*tādātmya*), it would follow—just as with "tree"—that no inference could occur. This remains the case even regarding "fitness for conventional usage"; thus, this argument is trivial. In the same way, even the relations of cause and effect and so forth established by the systems of the Vaiśeṣikas and others [are untenable].
The various types of relations should be understood as having already been refuted; for they too are indefinite and thus not a cause for the arising of inference.

Let it be, then, that necessity (*niyama*) is a constituent of inference. No, because it is not apprehended due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First of all, perception arising from mere chance is incapable of determining this [necessity]. For indeed, one who opens their eyes suddenly perceives smoke in the kitchen together with fire.

It is concomitant; however, one does not know for certain that "this [effect] is necessarily produced by this [cause]. For the determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-niyama*) of all things is difficult to grasp;

even the great are not able to extract it instantaneously. Indeed, conceptual thought (*vikalpa*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that which is not within the scope of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), because the former is preceded by the latter. This might be argued: the determination of intrinsic nature exists because there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) across differences of place and so forth.
"It is determined. By what is it determined? Since all [cognitions] function merely through a continuity (*anvaya*).

Now, one might argue that the final cognition, accompanied by the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by each preceding cognition, becomes a determinative perception (*ālocanājñāna*), thinking "this is restricted by this," and from that, conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) will proceed. This is not so; for perception (*pratyakṣa*) depends upon the operation of the sense faculties.

Furthermore, there is no operation of the external sense-faculties elsewhere than where coexistence is observed. Nor does the internal organ function toward the cognition of an external object independently of those [faculties]. Moreover, even entities whose forms have been determined are experienced as becoming otherwise when there is a difference in location and so forth; therefore, it is not appropriate for those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) to resort to a fixed essential nature (*svabhāvaniyama*). Thus they say:
Since the potencies of things differ due to the distinctions of place, time, and other factors,
the establishment of entities through inference is extremely difficult to achieve.

Therefore, the relation that constitutes a constituent part of inference must be stated. Hence he says: "The relation. For pervasion (*vyāpti*) indicates a rule of concomitance (*sāhityaniyama*). Indeed, for one who perceives this, the cognition of one part arises from the perception of another part; thus, although the word "relation" denotes a general property, it here—within this section on the definition of inference—refers to a specific [type of] relation due to its association with what follows. Furthermore, the proof for its restrictive sense will be stated later.
Thus [ends the third].

If inference belongs to one who has cognized the relation, then that relation, being dependent upon two [terms], would constitute the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the inference of both; therefore, he says: "the pervaded," etc. (4).

Regarding this, he states the reason in the two verses beginning with "yo yasya" (that which belongs to which). That [which is pervaded]—namely, that which is equal or inferior in terms of space and time—is the object of pervasion (*vyāpya*).

First, there is the case where both properties possess the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakatva*), as will be illustrated later. The latter case, however, is like smoke and so forth.
For that [fire] generally exists at the same place and time as fire. Even when fire exists, it may be deficient in terms of those place and time;

that is, its place and time are not as extensive as those of fire—this is what constitutes its deficiency. For this very reason, it is not pervasive of fire, because it does not pervade all of fire's respective places and times. A pervasive entity, however, possesses equal or greater place and time.

In this case as well, the former [position] is exactly as previously stated. The latter, however, is like that of smoke in relation to fire. For smoke indeed pervades both the space and time of that [fire]. Even when smoke is absent, it is said to be "excessive" in terms of space and time.
And because these two possess such an essential nature, their character consists in being the pervaded and the pervader, and not otherwise.

For that reason, when the pervaded (*vyāpya*) alone is apprehended, there occurs the apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpaka*), because the latter does not exist even in the absence of the former. Indeed, this [pervader] does not exist beyond the space and time of the pervaded—just as fire [does not exist beyond the space and time] of smoke—in such a way that it could fail to indicate it even in its absence. But fire is not of such a nature; therefore, it is not the indicator of smoke.

[It] exists. But surely this distinction is not understood from the word "one who knows the relation" (*jñātasambandha*). For that [word] indicates merely the knowledge of the relation as a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), and not its state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatā*); so how is the distinction obtained? To this it has been said: [it is stated] by way of restating the worldly definition (*laukikalakṣaṇa*) for the purpose of demonstrating that [the definition] is not to be critically examined (*aparīkṣā*).

This is the commentary. In the world, it is established that inference is the knowledge of the pervader (vyāpaka) belonging only to one who perceives the pervaded (vyāpya) in a single part; for it is not otherwise. Having extracted the phrase "na hy anyathā" and joined it with what precedes, it should be explained as "tena" by depending upon that [preceding statement]. // 6 //

But surely, the cognition of the pervaded is also seen from the pervader, as in the case of "producedness" [being inferred] from "impermanence. For there is indeed the inference of the producedness of entities from their impermanence; and impermanence is the pervader of producedness. Therefore, the claim that "the pervader is the object to be known (gamya) and the pervaded is the means of knowing (gamaka)" is untenable. To this he says: "Because of being the pervader," etc. This is the intended meaning: True, ...

It is the pervader that possesses the capacity to indicate [the probandum], but not that which is apprehended as being merely the pervader. For when it is apprehended in that form, it is not contradicted even if the pervaded occurs in a greater extension of space and time. Nor does that which occupies a greater space and time serve as a prover;
for it has already been stated that [the probandum] exists even without it. But surely, it also possesses the state of being the pervaded? Let it be so indeed.

In reality, however, that form [of the pervader] is not apprehended; so how could there be the capacity to indicate [the probandum]? But when that identity [of the probans with the pervaded] is understood, the capacity to indicate arises through that very [identity], and not by way of being the pervader. Therefore, it is well said that only the state of being the pervaded (vyāpyatā) is a constituent of inference, and not the state of being the pervader (vyāpakatā). // 7 //

He demonstrates through a non-confused example that being the pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) is the essential factor, not being the pervader (*vyāpakatva*), by saying "clearly" (*vispaṣṭa*). Where the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader is not confused, there this is clearly observed: namely, that the pervaded is the indicator (*gamaka*) and the pervader is the indicated (*gamya*). For, in the case of "cowness" (*gotva*) and "hornedness" (*viṣāṇitva*), it is the pervaded—cowness—that leads one to infer the pervader—hornedness; however, hornedness does not lead one to infer cowness. [Hornedness] is the pervader.
For that [distinction] exists in measurement—inference. The meaning is that this distinction between the cognized and the cognizer is observed between "cow" and "horns. // 8 //

{3,11} Thus, because there is no confusion when the distinction between the signifier (*gamaka*) and the signified (*gamya*) is maintained, even in cases where a confusion of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs, it is established that "the state of being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*)" alone is the cause for the status of being a signifier. To this he says: "By that [reasoning]," etc.

Now, it has been stated that pervasion is a constituent part of inference. But to what does this [pervasion] belong? Is it to something conjoined (*saṃyogin*), something inherent (*samavāyin*), or something related through a relation (*sambandhisambandhin*)?
For we do not perceive a fixed rule here, since all of these could potentially be inferential indicators. Therefore, if it is something conjoined...

[The fire] is the pervaded (*vyāpya*). There would be no inference of color from taste. Now, [if you argue that] there is an inference of fire from smoke based on inherence (*samavāyin*), and an inference of a son’s Brahminhood from the Brahminhood of his parents based on the relation of one related to what is related (*sambandhisambandhin*), and so forth—this must be demonstrated.

Furthermore, "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) is defined as positive concomitance (*anvaya*); that is to say, it is "adherence" (*upaśleṣa*). And this [concomitance] does not exist with a fire situated upon the ground.

It is possible for the tip of a column of smoke to reach the sky; however, the rising of the stars situated in the heavens does not follow the shadow of a gnomon fixed upon the earth. Furthermore, when a pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs between two things, it must be either spatial or temporal. In the former case, an inference [of the future] would occur after eight watches (*yāma*) have passed, based on the rising of the present sun instead of the rising of the sun that is yet to come.

It would not be so. One must then be questioned regarding such claims as "the inference of fire from smoke in another [place]," and so forth. Therefore, he says by means of the two [verses] beginning with "by that": for indeed, since it is the mere state of being pervaded—regardless of the intended internal subdivisions—that constitutes the constituent factor of inference, for that reason, [it applies] to whichever one among conjunction and the others [is relevant].

By whichever one among those [two], and in whatever manner—whether as a state of contact (*upaśleṣa*) or otherwise—the pervasion (*vyāpyatā*) was previously apprehended through the other, that very [cognition] becomes the cause for inference. For contact is not pervasion; indeed, it has been stated: "This [pervasion] is a restriction of relation. And that [restriction] occurs even with that which is not in contact. For when X exists, Y comes to be.

And because [the effect] does not exist when [the cause] is absent, it is said to be "determined" by that. What is the use of [physical] contact here? Nor is there any intention to specify any one of location and so forth in this case. For, in whatever space or time the pervadedness of a given [entity] has been previously established, that very part of the pervader existing in exactly that much space or time causes that same part of the pervaded to exist in exactly that much space or time.

When a property is observed in another locus, such as the sky and so forth, it becomes a means of proof for the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) by virtue of its observation in relation to the locus of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

For a necessary rule (*niyama*) is indeed a constituent part of inference, and that is entirely the same for all cases; what is the use of further sub-divisions? Thus, there is pervasion (*vyāpti*) between smoke and the like—which have ascended no more than a certain distance from a location—and the swelling of a river, even though the latter exists at a much greater distance.

He demonstrates this by means of the rising of a constellation situated at an extreme distance from the shadow of the gnomon. Furthermore, by the phrase "at whatever time," he demonstrates the pervasion (vyāpti) even in cases such as the inference of the future rising of the sun. // 11 //

"Now, it has been stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this pervasion (*vyāpti*); therefore, he says: 'by repeated observation' (*bhūyodarśana*). But how can pervasion be known through repeated observation? For in that case, is each individual repeated observation the means of valid cognition, or is it the collection of observations, or rather another distinct means of knowledge—the final one—assisted by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the preceding observations?"

Or [it might arise] from repeated observation. In that regard, it has already been established that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not something to be apprehended through the observation of individual instances. Indeed, for one who suddenly beholds fire and smoke in a kitchen, the cognition "smoke is pervaded by fire" does not arise. Furthermore, what has not been experienced by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*) cannot be made an object of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*).

Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "collection of perceptions" (*darśanasamudāya*) composed of multiple perceptions, because it does not exist apart from those individual perceptions. Moreover, past, future, and present [perceptions] cannot be combined into a single unity. Therefore, one must consider which of the following is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*): the final perception aided by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by the preceding multiple perceptions? First of all, it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For that [direct perception]...

It is divided into two parts: the cognition of observation (*ālocanājñāna*) and that which arises from it, which is mixed with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). First of all, the former is not capable of ascertaining pervasion (*vyāpti*), because it lacks synthesis (*apratisandhāna*); for pervasion consists in the synthesis that "this is connected by this. Nor does the latter attain its own nature without depending on that [former]. And as for this assistance provided by the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), [it is as follows:]

This too is not tenable. For mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), whose nature is produced by the apprehension of the form of a particular object, deposit nothing but memory regarding that very object; they are not capable of apprehending another object. And since perception is the means of valid cognition for establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), how can pervasion be established through those [impressions] which do not have that [pervasion] as their object? Indeed, [cognition] arises accordingly from what is seen, inferred, or heard.

From the fruits of actions, one infers Vedic ritual acts in relation to specific individuals. Furthermore, the restriction of each particular animal or other such object to its respective fruit is not perceived directly, because it is beyond the senses. And as for this inference of the *apūrva* (unseen potency) from the subsidiary and principal elements of the Veda when a sacrifice is being performed—

That too would not be the case, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining pervasion (*vyāpti*). One must demonstrate such things as the inference of the absence of rain from the absence of clouds; therefore, pervasion is not established by perception. Nor is it established by inference, because that [inference] cannot arise—since its very existence depends upon [the knowledge of] that [pervasion]—precisely due to the absence of a means of valid cognition. As for verbal testimony (*śabda*), its object consists of future things yet to be produced, and thus it is not for the purpose of establishing a proven pervasion.

It prevails. Even analogy (*upamāna*), whose object is merely the similarity between two things established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), does not ascertain the existence of a thing. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) also arises from perception and has as its object a fact that cannot otherwise be accounted for.
And when there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) between two things previously determined together, there is nothing at all that can be called "unaccountable."

But surely, the state of being an effect is not tenable. For how can an effect exist when its cause is absent? Moreover, since the state of being an effect is to be understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*), the establishment of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the cause is based on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting in the inexplicability otherwise of the understanding of the state of being an effect produced by repeated observation. How, then, will pervasion be established in cases that do not stand in the relation of cause and effect? If repeated observations themselves [do not exist]...

If it is argued that they are not possible without pervasion (*vyāpti*), what indeed is impossible for them without pervasion? Their own nature (*svarūpa*) is established as being constituted by the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*). Furthermore, the manifestation of their own object is also [established] through themselves alone.

We see nothing that is untenable regarding that which is delimited by its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it sublated by another means of valid cognition. As for what would be untenable: it is not correct to say that a pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the nature of an entity (*bhāva-svarūpa*) is cognized through non-existence (*abhāva*).
In that case, it could not possibly be established by the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇika*).

It might be thought: "What is this pervasion (*vyāpti*) of smoke by fire other than the exclusion of non-fire? And since that [exclusion] is of the nature of a non-entity (*abhāva*), it is logical that it is cognized by means of a non-entity. This is not so, because it is of the nature of a real entity (*vastu*). For the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of smoke and the like is determined as a real entity by something [else]; otherwise, it would indeed be excluded even from the absence of a rabbit’s horn, and thus [it would follow that it is pervaded] by a rabbit’s horn as well.

It would be restricted. If it is asked, "How can that which is non-existent be restricted? what is the fault? For restriction is indeed exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and since that exists, what does it matter whether a rabbit's horn exists or not? If it is thought that restriction is exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), then what is this so-called "counter-example"? For that which is opposed to something by virtue of which it is restricted is its counter-example. [That which is] pervaded...

And just as smoke is said to be "not fire" because it is excluded from the absence of fire by means of a rabbit's horn—since that [horn] does not exist—the absence of fire is likewise indeed a counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Furthermore, since all counter-examples are incapable of being perceived, their exclusion cannot be understood through non-perception (*abhāva*), for it will be stated later that non-perception is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding non-existence. Therefore, there is no proof whatsoever for pervasion (*vyāpti*). If it is argued that it is mental [perception], [we reply:]...

No, because of the lack of independence regarding external objects. In this regard, it might be argued: "Even if the external senses are incapable of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with respect to various entities such as the past and future, the mind (*manas*), however, possesses an unimpeded capacity that is common to the discernment of all objects—past and so forth—in certain cases; therefore, the pervasion will be grasped by a perception (*pratyakṣa*) arising through its power. But that is not so.
Because the mind lacks independence with respect to external objects. Indeed, it has already been explained that the mind is not independent in its cognition of external objects;

as was stated in the passage beginning "together with the mind. For if the mind were held to be independent regarding external things, then everyone would be an all-seeing seer. If it is argued that the restriction [of experience] is due to latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), we say no, because those impressions are the cause of memory. In this regard, it might be thought: even if [the mind were] alone...
The mind is not independent in the determination of external objects;

nevertheless, being accompanied by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by successive prior experiences, it will function even with respect to the external world, just as [the mind] functions toward color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth when assisted by the eyes and other [senses]. Therefore, there is no lack of systematic order. But that is not the case, because [the mind] is the cause of memory. For those things which are the causes of mere memory are indeed influenced by prior experience.

The mental formations (*saṃskāra*) are not capable of providing assistance for the mind’s external apprehension, because it would follow that other objects of memory would also be apprehended. For indeed, the formation that serves as the cause of memory exists even in those cases. If that [formation] acts as an auxiliary to the mind in some instances of apprehension, why does it not cause other objects of memory to be apprehended as well? This argument is trivial.

But as for one who says: "The relation between fire and smoke is *sāhitya* (coexistence). And that is cognized at the very moment of their first apprehension. Furthermore, the relation between fire and smoke appears as undivided by space and time; for there is no thought that 'their relation exists here or now. Rather, it is precisely of those two which are present and proximate that [the relation] is grasped as 'this' (*idantayā*)."

The place and time of the two appearing [objects], as well as their relation, serve as qualifiers [of those objects] in the sense that "these two are related," or "there is no relation here at this [time]. Thus, a relation that is inherently natural (*svābhāvika*) is established as having an unconditioned form.
And when it is inherently natural, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not logically possible. What, then, has become a non-factor?

Thus, repeated observation is not a [direct] factor; rather, it is a factor by way of eliminating the suspicion that there might be an adventitious condition (*upādhi*). For fire, even when perceived as conjoined with smoke, is sometimes seen without smoke. In that case, an adventitious condition such as wet fuel enters into the situation.
Consequently, it is determined that the connection between fire and smoke is not intrinsic (*svābhāvika*). And because of seeing that [absence of smoke], [it is concluded] regarding smoke as well.

A doubt arises: "Perhaps its connection with fire is merely conditional (aupādhika). That doubt is removed by repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). Even when smoke is observed many times, no condition (*upādhi*) for its connection with fire is perceived. Furthermore, having searched diligently, since no condition is seen, it is determined that none exists. Thus, in this way...
It is established that fire is invariably concomitant with smoke alone; therefore, there can be no suspicion of deviation for that which is free from adventitious conditions (*upādhi*).

To this, he must be asked: is mere coexistence now the constituent factor of inference, or is it the necessary restriction (*niyama*) between them? If it were mere coexistence, then since that is already apprehended at the very first observation, one who perceives smoke again—even if they have not yet ascertained the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—[would possess the inferential knowledge].

It would have to be inference (*anumāna*). Now, if there is that restriction (*niyama*), from what is this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for it established? For no such thought as "this [object] is restricted by this [cause]" is seen to arise for one who perceives for the first time. A relation that is understood as being unrestricted by space and time is intrinsic (*svābhāvika*).

If it is argued that [the rule] is established through *niyama* (invariable concomitance), then since such a rule would have been understood at the very first instance, one would not require repeated observation. Furthermore, even in the case of fire as it has been observed, its connection with smoke may be deviant; and from seeing that [deviation], a suspicion of deviation regarding smoke also arises. If it is argued that repeated observation is required to eliminate that [suspicion], [we reply: this would be so only if [the relation] were not already determined.

Separation is observed for someone at some time, whether spatially or temporally. What assurance, then, can there be in other cases? But was it not said that this suspicion is dispelled by repeated observation? How is it dispelled? When fire has been understood to possess smoke hundreds of times, yet is seen without smoke; and in this case, there is no fixed rule [of concomitance] based on so many observations.
"Invariable concomitance is established.
[Objection: But surely, no limiting condition (*upādhi*) is perceived in the connection of smoke with fire, just as none is perceived in the connection of fire with smoke.
Therefore, why should that [fire] not exist even when smoke is present? [Reply: No, because factors such as location (*deśa*) and so forth are themselves suspected of being the limiting conditions.

Having observed the deviation from the connection with smoke in the case of fire, one suspects: "Perhaps even for smoke, there might be some limiting condition (*upādhi*) such as place, time, and so forth, regarding its connection with fire. For it is observed that in certain places, date palms (*kharjūra*) produce the fruit known as *piṇḍakharjūra*, and the sting of a scorpion is a cause of death; yet this does not occur in other regions. Smoke, too, would be like that.

Fearing that fire might occasionally arise even without smoke, they do not determine its necessary concomitance with fire even by a hundredth part. Since a suspected exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) obstructs the emergence of inference, what kind of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this, namely, "fire, being free from adventitious conditions (*anaupādhika*), is invariably concomitant with smoke alone"? It cannot be perception (*pratyakṣa*), for that is exhausted by [perceiving] mere coexistence.

It is not inference (*anumāna*), because that is impossible in the absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, if one were to postulate an endless series of further inferences for the sake of establishing pervasion, it would result in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) have already been refuted. Therefore, the means of valid cognition for ascertaining the relationship that is a constituent part of inference must be explained;
that is now being explained.

First, the proponent of the non-existence of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāvavādin*) must be addressed as follows: Does the cognition whose object is pervasion (*vyāpti*) simply not arise at all, or does it arise as doubtful, or does it arise erroneously? For the investigators have classified invalidity into these three ways, since no other possibility exists.

The first position is not tenable, because it contradicts the empirical usage of cognition. For it is commonly observed that one who perceives smoke in relation to fire determines, "this [smoke] is invariably concomitant with this [fire]," and having inferred the fire from that, engages in corresponding practical activity.
This would not be possible if there were no cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). By the very observation of such practical activity, doubt and error are to be ruled out.

Because such linguistic usage is impossible on the basis of those two alone, there is therefore no lack of validity (*aprāmāṇya*) for them. Validity, however, is divided into six types; we shall establish each according to its suitability within a particular cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). For instance, in the case of the pervasion of smoke by fire, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is [the means]; for it has already been explained that no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are possible here.

But surely, it has already been stated that perception is impossible because [the pervasion] is not apprehended at the first observation. For this very reason, it must be apprehended through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). But surely those [observations] have also been refuted by means of an alternative analysis (*vikalpa*), since neither individually nor collectively are they possible. True. It is not the case that the pervasion is apprehended individually, nor do the observations combine together. Rather, [it is apprehended] when [the cognition] is assisted by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by many previous observations.
In the final moment of perception, the fact that smoke possesses a nature invariably connected to fire shines forth in the mind—
just as the true nature of a gem appears to one who is examining it, or as the true nature of a word appears to one refined by the study of grammatical tradition.

The very state of being a Brahmin is like clarified butter melted from oil for one whose sense organ is assisted by the memory of the connection with mother and father, or like [butter] distinguished from oil for one whose sense organ is assisted by its taste and smell. For it is not the case that because all this was not manifest at first glance, it becomes otherwise later when it does appear. Nor is there any status as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

[The opponent] brings this about. But has it not been said that the latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) do not operate elsewhere than in memory? By whom, then, is an operation of the latent impressions admitted other than in memory? It is simply by causing [the object] previously and successively perceived to be remembered—namely, the connection of smoke with fire—that they assist the sense organ as it proceeds to generate the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*). [This occurs] even though [the perception] is separated by intervening acts of memory.

Moreover, it has been described that perception follows from the connection with the sense faculties, because it conforms to the manifestation of immediate presence which is the fruit of that sensory connection. And that which does not manifest immediately does not lose its status as perception simply because it manifests later, just as in the examples already cited, such as the Brahmin’s own nature.

But has it not been stated that perception arising from the first encounter (*āpātaja*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding pervasion (*vyāpti*), and that determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) is preceded by that [indeterminate perception]? How, then, can the latter also possess validity? Or does there exist, in the state of indeterminate perception regarding the perception of a Brahmin and so forth, an appearance of a form distinct from other persons—as there is in the case of an elder and the like—by which a subsequent determinate perception is set in motion? For instance, in that case, for one who perceives merely the physical body and remembers its connection to a lineage (*yonisambandha*)...
Just as the perception "this is a Brahmin" arises directly,

so too here, for one who has repeatedly observed fire and smoke, at the final observation there arises a direct perception whose object is the very nature of smoke— namely, that "this [smoke] is necessarily connected with fire"— concerning the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke which has been previously grasped by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*).
This much alone constitutes the state of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) being preceded by non-conceptual cognition.

That activity preceded by that [cognition] is indeed sought first for the purpose of recollecting names and so forth. And since that is accomplished here simply upon seeing the individual object (*vyakti*), due to the awakening of prior latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), there is no necessity for these two [the perception and the recollection] to have the same object. For this very reason, in the cognition of melted ghee as distinct from oil, one says "oil."

For one who mistakes [the substance] for "this," there is established the status of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) for the sense faculty conjoined with the odor; for in that case, there was no unmixed cognition of the form of ghee, due to the error that "this is oil. Therefore, it is only subsequently, by virtue of auxiliary factors, that [cognition] has as its object the individual entity presented by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*).
The perceptual cognition "this is ghee" arises as conceptual; likewise here too, there is no fault.

What, then, is made an object by the conceptual [cognition] here? It is the restriction: "This is restricted to this. For one who frequently perceives smoke in fire and observes its absence in what is not fire, a reflection eventually arises: "Could it be..."

"This is pervaded by that. Otherwise, how could it be that—despising the specific conjunctions of grass, wood, cow-dung fuel, and so forth, and disregarding various places distinguished by differences such as *jaṅgala* (arid land) and various times distinguished by differences such as evening—it pursues fire alone and does not occur in what is not fire?
Furthermore, beyond that, just as fire [is pursued] even while setting aside qualities such as smokiness and luminosity...

The heat residing in a potter’s kiln and the like does not abandon its nature, yet it remains restricted to that [specific locus]. In this way, the immediate certainty arises that "there is smoke because of fire. As for the objection that there is deviation in other locations and so forth—that has never been seen before nor heard of, and thus it does not even enter the realm of suspicion. Furthermore, for one who suspects deviation in this manner, there would be a lack of confidence in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to the observation of deviation in some cases. As for the fact that the restriction of essential nature (*svabhāvaniyama*), even when ascertained...

[Objection: "In other regions and so forth, [the poison] of scorpions and the like becomes otherwise. [Response: That is not so, because there is a difference in intermediate species (*avāntarajātibheda*). For that which is known to be invariably concomitant with something, and is uncontradicted, cannot become otherwise. However, the determination of the effect is caused by the presence or absence of power (*śakti*) due to differences in intermediate species; thus, there is no deviation anywhere.

But surely, why is inference (*anumāna*) itself not accepted? [The argument is: "Whatever is conditioned by an adventitious factor (*aupādhika*) deviates, just as fire [deviates] from smoke; but smoke does not [deviate] from fire in that way, and thus it is not conditioned by an adventitious factor. Let it be so. However, lack of certainty (*avyavasthā*) arises. In that case, let there be presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). This very observation of [the concomitance] in the presence of fire and the non-observation in the absence of fire, being otherwise inexplicable, establishes the necessary rule (*niyama*) with respect to fire. What here is inexplicable? The observation.
It is sufficient that it exists there;

for it is not the case that because something exists in one place, it must not exist elsewhere. If it is argued that its non-perception elsewhere is untenable, we say no; for the non-perception of other things is possible even when they are remote, due to a lack of sensory contact (*asannikarṣa*). This is so even among those things that are nearby...

If it is argued that non-perception in the absence of fire is untenable, we reply: no, because its occurrence is possible due to the absence [of the object]. For since that [fire] does not exist in those [places], how could it be perceived?

In that case, even if it exists, why should it necessarily exist elsewhere? What is the proof for this? Therefore, it is precisely the sense faculty, assisted by both perception and non-perception, [that establishes the nature of things].

It must be established in this way: that the determination of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing arises through direct perception (*aparokṣa*). But we do not understand this at all: what kind of intrinsic nature of the thing is being determined? It has been stated more than once that smoke is invariably concomitant with fire. What is meant by this is: whenever there is smoke, there is fire.
[Objection: Is it not the case that perception must be the relation with only that which is present in the immediate place and time? How, then, can there be a relation with the future and so forth?
For if that were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
[Reply: No. Because only the form (*rūpa*) of what is present is apprehended. It is simply the nature of smoke and such things that it is inferred in this way.
The form of walls and such things appears as if stable. For in them there exists a manifestation of a form that persists through a different time and is distinct from lightning and the like.
Because the proximate intermediate relation is not perceived, that form remains unperceived.
Indeed, if that [relation] were unperceived, there would be no sublation of the previously experienced silver in the form "this is not silver."
Because their objects are distinct. For at its own time, the silver was made the object by the prior cognition, not at the moment of the future sublating cognition;

how then could that which was never presented there be sublated? Even though it is connected with a different time, that which was determined by the prior cognition in that form extends even to the time of the future cognition; thus, having attained identity of object, sublation occurs.

[Objection: Surely, the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) is understood independently of anything else, just as heat is [understood] in the case of fire. And since the nature of smoke is not understood by one who has not grasped its correlate (*pratisambandhin*), how can it be the nature of a real entity? [Reply: Not so. For this is a relation; how could it be determined when the correlate is not understood? As it has been said:

"Now, the restriction (*niyama*) is stated according to our own view as being a relation. Therefore, what is there that is untenable in the claim that this positive nature of smoke's necessity with respect to fire is apprehended through perception? And it has already been explained how the exclusion of non-fire is not itself the restriction. [This is] by way of the exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
However, the restriction (*niyama*) is explained by investigators and taught to others precisely as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*).

Now, one might object: "But being restricted (*niyamyatva*) is also a status as a factor of action (*karmakārakatva*), and since that is of the nature of a capacity (*śakti*), how can it be perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)? No, for it is possible just like the perception of other factors of action. For even the capacities of other factors of action are not themselves directly perceived.

Therefore, even though the capacity [of the senses] is not directly perceived, it must be accepted that the causal factor (*kāraka*) is directly perceived. In this case as well, what is untenable about the idea that the object to be regulated (*niyamya*) will likewise be directly perceived? Thus, its status as a direct perception is established. Furthermore, regarding matters known through scripture (*āgamika*), there is a correspondence between each specific result and the respective ritual action (*karman*) to be known from the Veda.

Furthermore, because no connection to another action is perceived, it is understood from the scripture that "this fruit is pervaded by this very action," since there is an understanding of a fixed relationship between the means and the end. Moreover, because it is impossible to perceive the absence of two independent entities—such as the absence of clouds and the absence of rain—the cognition of pervasion occurs only between two positive existents (*bhāva*) in some manner. What is called the "absence of clouds" is simply a particular state of the sky itself.
The form of the sky is perceived as resembling a great ocean, motionless and free from wind, once it is released from the obstruction of clouds;

and the absence of rain is simply the dense, hard, and pale state of the earth itself. Since the nature of both these phenomena is indeed accessible through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that very perception serves as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) therein. This should be demonstrated in other cases as well.
Thus it stands. Let this be for now; we shall explain the other [topic] later. Thus far, the nature and the means of proof (*pramāṇa*) of pervasion (*vyāpti*) have been established.

However, this must be considered: of what is there pervasion by what? For two specific instances of fire and smoke known in one place are not seen in another location, such that a pervasion between them could be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, the locus of pervasion must be stated. To this he says: "In general," etc. It is true that there is no pervasion between two particulars;

rather, it is understood that there is a pervasion between two properties belonging to some subject in their general form, through the exclusion of their respective particular differences—namely, that the form of smoke is invariably concomitant with the form of fire. Thus, there is no fault whatsoever.
However, this is merely a general rule.
But he says "in some cases" (kvacid) because pervasion does indeed sometimes occur even between two particular [instances] of a permanent entity (sthāyin). // 12 //

Regarding this very point, he provides an example: "the rising of the Kṛttikās. For when, having observed the rising of the Kṛttikās, the proximity of Rohiṇī is stated—namely, that "Rohiṇī will rise immediately after"—in that inference, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of one particular by another particular. Indeed, there is no universal (*sāmānya*) between those two, because there is no evidence for a difference between individual instances. For it is recognized through direct recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) that "this is that same Kṛttikā" and "this is that same Rohiṇī. How could it be otherwise? Therefore, it is established that in this case, the pervasion exists only between two particulars.

If, then, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a constituent factor of inference, then indeed such pervasion exists between the state of being violence (*hiṃsātva*) and the state of being unrighteousness (*adharmatva*) in the case of external acts of violence; therefore, by virtue of being violence, unrighteousness would also be inferred in the case of [violence] within a sacrifice. Consequently, it would follow that the violence against animals dedicated to the deities (*daikṣapaśu*) and so forth is unrighteous. To this, he replies with the two verses beginning with "And because of pervasion" (*vyāpteś ca*). The intention is as follows: it is true that, at first glance, an error arises.
For it is indeed said that the nature of being unrighteousness (*adharmatva*) is necessarily concomitant with the mere fact of being violence (*hiṃsātva*); however, this is not so.

For it is by means of the already known state of being unrighteousness that the property of being violence is pervaded. And apart from the scripture (*śāstra*), no means for knowing that [unrighteousness] is possible.

Nor does there exist a scripture stating that the mere fact of being violence is a means to achieve what is harmful (*anartha*), because specific forms of violence are prescribed [in the scriptures]. This applies to a domain restricted by an injunction (*vidhi*).

And because there would otherwise be no scope for the prohibition; and because, in the absence of a prohibition, there would be no means of knowing that [certain acts] are instruments for achieving what is harmful (*anartha*). Therefore, since a general rule (*utsarga*) applies after having set aside its exceptions (*apavāda*), the prohibition "one shall not injure" takes hold over other forms of injury.
And thus, although the coexistence of the nature of injury (*hiṃsātva*) and unrighteousness (*adharmatva*) has been understood in the case of external injuries, [the prohibition remains applicable].

Nevertheless, being an act of violence (*hiṃsātva*) is not the determinant of its being unrighteous (*adharmatva*); rather, it is being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*). For even in the absence of violence, unrighteousness is established in cases such as drinking liquor solely by virtue of its being prohibited. Therefore, that alone is the [determinant] property (*dharma*), which is determined in the form: "only when this [prohibition] exists is the capacity for this [unrighteousness] to occur. That is to say, it is understood as being pervaded (*vyāpyatayā*). This is the meaning.
It is called the "instigator" (prayojaka). However, properties such as being "violence" (hiṃsātva) depend upon the pervasion (vyāpti) employed by others;

therefore, it is not possible for those [properties] to determine the pervading part of "unrighteousness" (adharmatva) and so forth. For external violence is not unrighteous merely because it is "violence," but rather because it is "prohibited" (niṣiddha). Consequently, there is no unrighteousness in any of the violences prescribed [in ritual], such as the killing of the sacrificial animal (daikṣapaśu) and the like. // 14 //

But those who employ such non-conclusive reasons (aprayojaka-hetu) wander for a long time, beset by easily found defects such as counter-reasons (pratihetu). For it is possible to demonstrate a counter-reason:
"The slaughter of the sacrificial animal is dharma, because it is enjoined, like the Agnihotra and other rites. Indeed, when the reason is conclusive, such [counter-arguments] do not arise.

Faults find no footing [in such cases], whereas they are indeed easily found in what is purposeless. This is what he says with the words "But those who... "Confidently" (*visrabdham*) is an adverbial modifier; the meaning is that they employ [the word] in such a way that confidence arises. // 15 //

It was stated that [the opponents] wander due to defects such as counter-reasons (*pratihetu*); he now sets forth those very defects with the words "In these... First, the counter-reason has already been stated by us. Furthermore, for those who speak in this manner, contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*) necessarily follows, because dharma and adharma have scripture alone as their authority. In some cases there is the subversion of what is desired (*iṣṭavighāta*), and in other cases there is dispute regarding the non-worldly (*alaukikavivāda*). // 16 //

He first states the example of contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*)—namely, "by virtue of being prohibited. And this has already been explained by us previously, according to the principle of anticipating what follows (*anāgatāvekṣaṇanyāya*). // 17 //

He states the example of contradiction with what is desired (*iṣṭavirodha*) as follows: "By the two reasons," etc. For in all cases, the falsity of erroneous cognitions depends upon sublation (*bādhaka*), a causal factor, or a defect (*doṣa*);

it is not established by the property of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) or by the property of having an origin (*utpattimattva*), because these two are common to both true and false cognitions. Thus, for the Buddhist who seeks to prove the falsity of that [cognition] solely on the basis of its being a cognition, the reason functions as one that destroys what is desired (*iṣṭavighātakārī*).

This is because [the opponent] rejects both the essential nature of the property (*dharma*) and the property-bearer (*dharmin*), as well as their respective specific qualities. Furthermore, since this involves the denial of earth and other elements well-established by the whole world, even a non-worldly dispute (*alaukika-vivāda*) must be shown to reside precisely here;

for worldly people do not tolerate a dispute such as "all cognitions are false. Indeed, a sudden sense of revulsion arises in those who hear such a dispute, just as in the case of "The moon is not the moon" (*acandraḥ śaśī*). Therefore, this is a non-worldly dispute. And so it has been said:
"And because it is well-known to the entire world, your thesis is certainly sublated in this case. (18)

He shows another example of contradiction with scripture (āgama) with the words "traivarṇika" and so forth. Indeed, there exist rituals such as the Soma sacrifice, enjoined by such [Vedic] injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice. Regarding these, when a doubt arises as to whether the qualification for them belongs to all four castes or only to the three [castes] excluding the Śūdra, the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it belongs to all four.

For all four castes desire heaven, and thus they are designated by the term "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). Since it was argued that one who desires heaven is understood here to be the qualified candidate, it was stated [in response] that the qualification belongs to those other than Śūdras. For those sacrifices are to be accomplished through sacred knowledge (*vidyā*) and fire; yet the lowest caste is without fire and without knowledge. How, then, could such a person be qualified for rites pertaining to the three fires (*vaitānika*)?

[Objection: But surely, by the very force of the qualification understood from the meaning of the Vedic revelation (śruti), there will be an implication of both the sacred fires and knowledge even for a Śūdra.

[Reply: No, because they are not prescribed for him. For the sacred fires and knowledge are prescribed exclusively for the three higher castes by such injunctions as "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa at eight years of age" and "A Brāhmaṇa should kindle the fires in the spring. Nor can these two come to belong to a Śūdra without restriction.

Thus it can be said: for who, having attained the connection with the fire of knowledge (*vidyāgni*), would venture to prescribe initiation (*upanayana*) or the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*)—which are restricted to specific times and stages of life—as being applicable to one of the lowest caste (*jaghanyavarṇa*) in the case of scriptural injunctions regarding desire (*kāmaśruti*) that are intended for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*)? Therefore, the fact that sacrifices and other rites are causes of heaven is conditioned solely by the status of belonging to the three higher castes, and not by mere humanity alone.

It is employed by one who belongs to the *śūdra* class. Suppose someone skilled in inference were to employ [the following argument]: "A sacrifice performed by a *śūdra* is a cause for attaining heaven, because it is performed by a human being, like a sacrifice practiced by those of the three higher castes. For such a person, there is a contradiction with scripture (*āgama*). But has not a contradiction with scripture already been illustrated?

What, then, is the purpose of this illustration? It is said: previously, a direct contradiction with scripture (*āgama*) was described regarding the inference of non-dharma (*adharmatva*) concerning Vedic violence;
