for it is clearly understood that the slaughter of the sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*), being enjoined, is a means to achieve a purpose—how then could it be non-dharma?

Because dharma is that object characterized by Vedic injunction (*codanā*). In this case, however, the fact that sacrifices and the like performed by a Śūdra are not causes for heaven is not directly refuted by scripture; rather, because the qualification belongs to the three higher castes, the exclusion of others follows by implication—this is the distinction. // 19 //

Now, under the guise of an irrelevant example, he shows other examples for the purpose of censuring the opponent with two verses beginning with "kṛta-": Cognitions such as "arising immediately after effort" and so forth—which are intended [as reasons]—do not establish the perishability of sound through their being objects of cognition; for that [perishability] is established by [reasons] such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva). And yet, "being produced" [is not present here].

This cannot be established by the observation of [destruction] immediately following effort, because there is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*) due to [the case of] space and so forth. If, then, perishability is necessitated by having parts (*sāvayavatva*), why are the worlds and the arrangements of the worlds—such as the earth, mountains, oceans, and so on—not perishable now? True. Everything that has parts is subject to the nature of destruction.
Even the earth, mountains, and so forth, having acquired specific conjunctions and disjunctions of their own parts, certainly perish part by part;

however, we do not admit the destruction of anything that is without a trace (*niranvaya*). In this same way, the destruction of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) should also be demonstrated through the process of addition and subtraction (*āvāpodvāpa*). Likewise, as for the impermanence of sound which has been inferred by the Vaiśeṣikas on the grounds of its possessing a genus (*jāti*) and its being perceptible by the senses, [it must likewise be understood as involving a gradual process].

That too is incorrect. For this [property], such as "possessing a genus" (*jātimattva*), is based solely on the existence of a real entity (*vastusansanmātra*) and is common to both the permanent and the impermanent;
impermanence is not established by this. What is meant by "based solely on the existence of a real entity"?

It is said to mean "based on ultimate reality" (*paramārthasat*). Only those things that are ultimately real—such as a jar, space, the self, and so forth—are objects of the senses and possess a genus.
They are not cognized through delusion, like the horns of a hare and so forth. // 21 //
Thus, he concludes the statement regarding the lack of proving power in that which is not a causal factor with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). This is the meaning:

whatever object, such as being prohibited (*niṣiddhatva*), is understood to possess the capacity for proof of something like demerit (*adharma*); that is to say, it is determined by such a capacity as "when this exists, that must necessarily follow. For it is precisely the capacity of the thing to be regulated (*niyamya-śakti*) that is designated as the "capacity for proof" (*sādhana-śakti*).
For only that which is understood as being restricted can lead to the restrictor, and not anything else;

thus, it is the restricted [quality] alone that is the indicator, and not the property of "being violence" (*hiṃsātva*) as it occurs in a general contingency. This is because [the indicator] is intended to be connected with "unrighteousness" (*adharmatva*) by virtue of its being prohibited.

For since the property of being violence is also concomitant through the same logical entailment (*prasaṅga*), this violence concomitant with that entailment does not serve as a prover for the property of being unrighteousness. // 22 //

Thus, first of all, the category of "relation" (*sambandha*), which constitutes a constituent part of inference in every respect, has been explained. Now, the statement "from the perception of one part [of a related pair], there is cognition of the other part" must be explained. In this regard, the following must first be stated: it would follow that inference is a cognition of a similar other part arising from the perception of an independent single part. But that is incorrect; for that [cognition] is merely recollection (*smaraṇa*).

How could there be inference? Now, if it is claimed that the object of inference is a subject (ekadeśin) qualified by another part (ekadeśāntara) based on the perception of one part (ekadeśadarśanāt), that is not so, because it has not been mentioned. For here, the subject has not been mentioned by any word; therefore, due to its non-mention, [the definition] is deficient.

Anticipating the objection that this is merely a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), he says: "is included" (*upātta*). Although the partisan (*ekadeśin*) is not explicitly mentioned by his own name, nevertheless, he is implied by the force of the meaning through the two words "part" (*ekadeśa*); thus, there is no fault of deficiency (*nyūnatva-doṣa*). // 23 //

He states the reason for the implication of the object (*arthākṣepa*) with the words "not for another" (*aparārtha*). For the mere nature of smoke and so forth, when not serving another [purpose], does not become the locus of the term "one part. Nor is the expression "one part" tenable through mutual dependence;
for no one has the cognition that "smoke is one part of fire. And as long as the fire is not apprehended, it cannot be [designated] as being one part of it.

Smoke can be apprehended; and once it has been apprehended, the absence of the object to be inferred [the fire] is established. Therefore, precisely because the status of being a "single part" (ekadeśatva) is otherwise untenable, it is proven that some substratum which possesses that single part must be apprehended as its locus. // 23 //

[Objection: Surely, the possessor of the parts (*ekadeśin*) may be implied by the two words "part" (*ekadeśa*). But from what is that unity [of the possessor] understood? Consequently, having seen smoke in one place, there would be no inference regarding another part-possessor located elsewhere. Furthermore, co-location (*aikādhikaraṇya*) of the two parts is not established, because it has not been mentioned. To this, he says: "That very same... (*sa eva*). The previously mentioned "possessor of the parts" is intended to have a singular number.

He refers back to the proponent of the "part" (ekadeśin) with the words "that very same. Indeed, that single entity is both the object of cognition and the means of cognition, because it possesses a dual nature. For it has those two aspects—the two selves which are about to be described—which justify its having a twofold form. [Objection: But was it not stated that the unity of the "part" is not obtained unless it is explicitly mentioned? [Response: No, because it is already included by the use of the singular number in the phrase "of one who knows the relation" (jñātasambandhasya). For in the case of the "part," the other term...
In the case of a single object,
singularity is conveyed by the singular number;

likewise, even in the case of the cognizer, when the substratum— the possessor of the parts— is implied by the word "part" uttered first, at the moment of requiring a second [word], [the same applies].

Even so, it is that very [self] revolving within the intellect which is understood as its substratum, and not anything else. This is because there is no reason for abandoning that [self], and because such is observed through linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). For example, when Devadatta has a bracelet on one hand and a ring on another hand, the hands are not understood to be distinct substrata; rather, Devadatta is understood to be one and the same. Therefore, it is established that [the self] is one.
Thus, a single part consists of the nature of both the goer and the act of going. // 24 //

It has been stated that [the subject] is both the object to be understood (*gamya*) and the means of understanding (*gamaka*). He demonstrates those two aspects as being of a dual nature with the words "by means of what is unestablished" (*asiddhena*). For if this [subject], the locus of a part (*ekadeśin*), were only established or only unestablished, then it would not possess a twofold character. However, because it is established through its form as smoke and so forth by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet unestablished in its form as possessing fire and so forth, it possesses a dual nature; thus, both [functions] are possible. He says: "Let the locus of a part be included by implication."
And that [middle term] is both the object to be known (*gamya*) and the means of knowing (*gamaka*). But how is it to be apprehended by cognizers?
Furthermore, no specific mode of its apprehension has been set forth by the author of the *Bhāṣya*. Therefore, there is yet another deficiency; to this he says: "apprehended" (*ātta*).
In that regard, indeed, the mention of a specific [instance] is relied upon.

Where there is an intention to express a distinction, that distinction is indeed intended here; for that partial entity (ekadeśin), depending on the speaker's intention regarding the cognizer, may be presented as either separate or non-distinct by the two terms "part" (ekadeśa). This is because the usage of inference is observed in both ways. // 25 //
He shows that very same twofold conventional usage with the words "it is impermanent. This passage is explained by its own literal reading. // 26 //

It has been shown that the object of cognition (*gamya*) and the means of cognition (*gamaka*) are apprehended through both difference and non-difference. However, a doubt arises as to how far the operation (*vyāpāra*) of inference extends. For even when there is the cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭārtha*), a means of valid cognition may terminate in the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) alone, just as the case of verbal testimony (*śabda*). Indeed, that [word] produces a cognition of an individual (*vyakti*) as qualified by its form (*ākṛti*).

Moreover, it is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that [the word] refers exclusively to the form (*ākṛti*). Therefore, here too, if it is maintained that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) refers exclusively to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just like that [case], then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*). For at the time of knowing the relation, fire alone is already established; what, then, would be accomplished by that inference?

However, if it is maintained that inference has as its object only the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*)—just as in the case of words such as "one with a two-piece staff" (*dvikhaṇḍa-daṇḍin*)—then, because the relation [between the sign and the signified] has not been grasped therein, [the inference is invalid].

[The reason would suffer from] being unestablished (*anumeyatva*). For smoke has not been observed as being concomitant with a specific fire-possessor such as a mountain; nor does there exist any universal (*sāmānya*) common to all fire-possessors.
Even if such a [universal] were to exist, it would again result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Therefore, they say:
"In this mire of the collapse of inference, the elephants that are the disputants have sunk."
If [the reason] pertains to a particular, there is no concomitance; if it pertains to a universal, it is a case of proving what is already established.

Therefore, he says: "pertaining to one part" (*ekadeśa*). This is the intended meaning: inference has as its object only that which is qualified (*viśiṣṭa*), just like words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) and the like.

Nor is there an absence of the apprehension of the relation (*sambandha*); for we have already stated that the relation is understood through the fact that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire," by setting aside all specific limiting conditions (*upādhi*). Even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), a relation can exist between infinite entities through some single limiting condition.

It is indeed apprehended. Even though it was understood in a general way that "that which possesses smoke possesses fire," nevertheless, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in its specific form as "this is that very one," its status as an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established; this has already been stated. Why, then, is it not accepted that the means of valid cognition terminates in the qualifier alone?
Therefore, he says: "Not indeed," [verse 27].

He demonstrates the very impossibility [of such a proof] with the words "not the property" (*na dharma*). For you yourself have stated that at the time of grasping the relation, only the property (*dharmamātra*) is established. In this very same way, one should demonstrate the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in the case of an inference of the property-bearer alone (*dharmimātra-anumāna*) or an independent inference of both; thus he says "likewise" (*tathā*). // 28 //
He states further refutations, corresponding respectively to the three cases where the property, the substratum, or both are the objects of inference: "of a single part," etc. (verse 29).

He explains this very point: "impermanence and so forth. For a logical mark (*liṅga*) must reside in a portion of the subject (*pakṣa*). Now, since the property called impermanence has been made the independent subject, how can "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*)—which is a property [of that subject]—be a logical mark that is not a property of the subject? Likewise, even if mere sound were made the independent subject, there would be no concomitance (*anugama*) of "being produced" with it.
It is possible to demonstrate this. For there is no necessary rule (niyama) that wherever there is "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), there must be "sound" (*dhvani*).

Likewise, there is no connection between both [the probans and the probandum]—which consist of sound and impermanence—and both [the reasons], which consist of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and positive concomitance (*anugama*).

Therefore, one must explain by means of a *tantra* (a single word serving multiple functions), connecting the word "connection" (*sambandha*), which occurs later, with the preceding and following terms.
Thus, it has been established that neither the property, the substratum, nor both—whether taken individually or collectively—can constitute the probandum. // 30 //

Now, why is it that the relationship between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*) alone does not constitute the probandum? To this he says: "The relationship. By the word "in the proof" (*mitau*), he indicates the statement of the means of proof (*sādhana-vākya*). Indeed, in a statement of proof, a relationship is not introduced by any name expressing a relationship, nor by a genitive case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*). For it is not formulated in this way: [text fragment]

"There is a connection between the fire and the mountain because of the presence of smoke"—nor does one say "the fire belongs to the mountain. Rather, people are seen inferring a location as qualified by fire and so forth; thus they employ the formulation: "The mountain possesses fire. Furthermore, it is not the connection itself that is inferred; therefore, it is said to be a "past connection" (atītena sambandha). Not only is it not included in the proposition (*pratijñā*), but in the example (*udāharaṇa*) as well, the concomitance of the mark (*liṅga*) with it is not indicated. For such an observation does not occur: [that the mark exists in the subject through that past connection].

"Wherever there is smoke, there is a connection with fire. However, it is the case that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire"—here, the location itself serves as the illustration. Thus he says: "And not even... Here, the word "iha" (here) refers back to the cognition. This is what is meant: in a statement of proof (*sādhana-vākya*), the relationship is neither presented as the probandum (*sādhya*) nor indicated as an example (*dṛṣṭānta*), nor is it [presented] contrary to its appearance.
It is appropriate for investigators to speak thus. // 31 //

Furthermore, this relation, when being established, is established either as mere existence (*sanmātra*) or as qualified by some attribute. First of all, the mere existence of a thing is not the object of inference. Nor does the relation possess two forms—one established and one to be established—such as the mountain and so forth, by which it might become the object of inference. Therefore, he says "not" [in the verse], meaning that the relation cannot be established in any way whatsoever. [Objection: But surely, if the relation does not exist, it is impossible to establish that which is qualified by it.
There is no such possibility that a mountain could be qualified by fire without being related to it; therefore, he says "therefore" up to the end of the passage. (Objection:
It is true that something is not qualified in the absence of a relation.

However, by this much alone, the fact that the relation is the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established; rather, the fact that the relation denoted by the possessive suffix (*matup*) is the probandum is grasped through implication (*arthagṛhīta*), precisely because it would otherwise be impossible for the qualified object to be the probandum, and not as something independent. He provides an example for this very point with the words "just as" (*yathā*). For words such as *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer") [denote] one qualified by a staff and so forth.

In this way, while expressing [the subject], they also acquire the relation by implication (*arthāt*), but they do not express it directly. Similarly here, when it is being proven that "the mountain possesses fire," the connection with fire is grasped through implication;
it is not that very connection which is being proven. Just as when a qualified object is cognized from words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), the relation is necessarily implied.

The meaning is that here too, when the qualified [object] is being established, [the cognition of the qualifier] arises as a necessary concomitant (*nuniṣpādī*). However, this must be considered: how is it that words such as *daṇḍin* ("staff-bearer") denote the qualified? For they end in a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*), and that suffix is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) in connection with the relation "this belongs to this.

Therefore, in this case, the meaning of the suffix is precisely the relation, and that is the primary [meaning]. According to the principle that "the base and the suffix [jointly express] the meaning of the suffix,"...
For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "They speak together [only] when [both] are primary. This statement is indeed intended to demonstrate the primacy of both only when they are denoted separately;
and the primary element is the meaning of the word. Therefore, it is logical that words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) and the like are merely expressions of a relation.
Furthermore, since a cognition of the qualified does not arise unless the qualifier has been apprehended, one must necessarily [express the qualifier] when there is a desire to denote the qualified.

The designation of the qualifier must necessarily occur first, since the comprehension of the qualified object is established from that very [designation]; therefore, it is impossible to assume that the word has the power to denote [the qualified] until that [qualifier] has been expressed. For this very reason, the view that the individual qualified by the form (*ākṛti*) is denoted will be refuted in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa*.

Furthermore, Pāṇini records in his *Smṛti* (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.1.119): "In the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), there is the denotation of a relation (*sambandha*) by means of the suffixes *tva* and *tal*. And how could [that relation] be [denoted] by those two?

In a derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*), a relation is denoted. If that which is denoted by the derivative suffix were not [the relation], then there would be no recollection of those two [the base and the suffix] when the expressed meaning is extracted; for it is said:

"The suffixes *tva* and *tal* occur in the expression of that quality (*guṇa*) because of whose presence a word is applied to a substance. Therefore, if the relation between the staff and the person were the expressed meaning of the word *daṇḍin*, [then the suffix would denote that relation].

This being the case, when that [relation] is extracted, the grammatical rule for the suffixes *tva* and *tal*—namely, "the state of being a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍitva*) or "one who is a staff-bearer" (*daṇḍita*)—is justified.

Just as the universal denoted by the word "cow" is extracted by the suffix *tva* as "cowness" (*gotva*), it follows that the relation alone is the denotation of words such as "staff-bearer. Therefore, how can it now be said that "the relation is merely an inseparable concomitant" (*nāntarīyaka*)?

To this it is replied: first of all, it is not possible to determine that the relation [between word and meaning] is denotable by following the *Smṛti* (Pāṇinian grammar). For that [grammar] is merely an instruction regarding words—namely, [the rule] "this suffix occurs when something belongs to this" (Aṣṭādhyāyī 5.2.94)—and not an instruction regarding meanings. Furthermore, a varying relationship of primary and subordinate status is observed between the *vṛtti* (the compound) and the *vigraha* (the analytical expansion). For example, in the case of *citraguḥ*, in the *vṛtti* it is understood that Devadatta or someone else, qualified by variegated cows, is the primary element.

In the analytical derivation (*vigraha*), however, in the case of "one whose cows are brindled" (*citrā gāvo yasya*), Devadatta and the like are subordinate as qualifiers of the cows alone; and those cows are the primary element. Likewise in the Veda: "The Soma which has the *Rathantara* as its *sāman*. Even though, according to the author of the Smṛti, in the derivation "this belongs to him" (*tad asya*), the relationship is indicated by the genitive case as being primary, [the analysis remains as stated].
Nevertheless, in a derivative formation (*taddhitavṛtti*) such as *gomat* ("possessing cows"), that which possesses [the cows] alone is the primary element, because it is so perceived.
For the word *gomat* appears as having the person as its primary referent, not as having the relation as its primary referent.
Even for the venerable Pāṇini, it was intended to demonstrate that the qualified entity alone is the denotatum by means of expressing the relation.

When the compound is being analyzed, the use of the genitive case is indeed unavoidable. Consequently, the illusion arises that its meaning is indicated as the primary thing to be expressed; therefore, the relation is not the expressed meaning according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*).
As for the claim that the qualifier is the first to be denoted: that is true, but in this case, the relation is not the qualifier.

For the staff (*daṇḍa*) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*), not a relation (*sambandha*). And that [staff] is already expressed primarily by the base form (*prakṛti*) itself. For this very reason, there is no fault of having to postulate multiple expressive powers (*abhidhāna-śakti*). Indeed, in the case of indivisible words such as *go* ("cow") and so forth, it is logical that even when a qualified cognition arises, only the qualifier is expressed; for in those cases, there is the fault of having to postulate two expressive powers for a single [word].

[It] exists. However, words such as *daṇḍin* (staff-bearer) possess constituent parts (*bhāga*). In these, distinct bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*) denote distinct qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and qualified (*viśeṣya*). What is there that is untenable in this? Therefore, a person qualified by a staff—which is denoted by the base and understood even earlier—is what is expressed by the word *daṇḍin*. [Objection: But in the absence of a relation, a staff is not even able to qualify a man.

True. However, the relation does not become denotable merely by that much. For it is not logical to assert that because cows not standing on the earth do not qualify their possessor, the earth itself must therefore be denoted. It is precisely because the cognition of the qualified object would be untenable in the absence of a relation [that the relation is required].

For this very reason, the relation (*sambandha*) is also included by implication (*arthāt*), but it is not explicitly denoted (*abhidhīyate*). As for the argument that the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) regarding the suffixes *-tva* and *-tal* would be untenable if the relation were not denotable—that is incorrect. For the rule prescribing the abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*) in words such as *gomat* is not intended to extract the denotable object itself; rather, it is for the purpose of extracting the denotable object through the phrase "because of the presence of which quality" (*yasya guṇasya hi bhāvāt*).

This is the recollection [of the rule]. Otherwise, since the meaning would already have been conveyed by this very [rule], the statement "in the case of primary derivatives, secondary derivatives, and compounds" (*kṛttaddhitasamāseṣu*) would become redundant. Therefore, when one relatum—qualified by its connection to a single cause—has been previously understood, and the other relatum is expressed, the connection grasped through the sense is not relegated to the category of what is directly denoted (*abhidheya*). This same principle applies to all derivative (*yaugika*) words as well.
It must be shown [as follows]. And it has been said:
"In all cases, it is the substance itself that is denoted by derivative (yaugika) words;
for it is not possible for the relation to be the denotation, because that would entail excessive complexity (atigaurava)."

Thus, since no other object of inference is possible, it follows that only the property (*dharma*) and the locus (*dharmin*), standing in the relation of qualifier and qualified, are what are to be comprehended through inference. // 32–33 //

He summarizes [the argument] with the words "by the qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) up to "are understood" (*gamyau*). Furthermore, this relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) has been accepted by some as being optional (*vikalpa*). For they think as follows: "In every respect, when a mere property (*dharma*) or a locus (*dharmin*) is cognized independently, faults such as proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) arise; but not when there is a cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). As for this 'qualified-ness,' let it belong to whatever thing, in whatever way, according to one's intention."

Nothing is faulty here. In every respect, the property (*dharma*) such as fire must first be understood in the subject (*dharmin*) such as a mountain by means of that very property, such as smoke. Whether that property is to be understood as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as the qualified (*viśeṣya*), there is no difference; for in both cases, there is an absence of independent inference (*svatantrānumāna*). Thus he says: "The word *aṅga* is determined by the end [of the verse]. (34–35)

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "In this regard. This is the intended meaning: for even the authors of definitions must follow worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exactly as they are found in the world; they should not do otherwise. For the world does not understand that fire is qualified by the mountain, but rather that the mountain possesses fire. Likewise, one should [state] the object already apprehended by oneself through inference using that very same [means].

Ordinary people, when establishing a point for another, are seen to employ a reason that is indeed qualified by the subject (*dharmin*), as in the inference of fire: "because it possesses smoke, it possesses fire. However, this [usage] would not be tenable if fire were being inferred merely as qualified by location. For, since fire qualified by the mountain is taken as the subject (*dharmin*) by virtue of its being the qualifier, [the reason is stated as] "because it possesses smoke."

Thus, the connection of that [subject] with the property of the reason (*hetudharma*) does not manifest clearly. For the status of being a reason belongs to that which is understood as a property (*dharma*) [of a subject]. Furthermore, a subject (*dharmin*) that has been taken up as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhāva*) cannot admit of a connection with the property of the reason, because subordinate factors have no mutual connection among themselves. Therefore, for worldly people, it is precisely from this specific formulation of the reason for the sake of others (*parārthahetuprayoga*)...
Such a mode of apprehension is inferred: that one understands even for oneself the locus (dharmin) as qualified by its property (dharma) alone, and not otherwise. // 36 //
If, then, the connection between the subject (*dharmin*) and the property of the reason (*hetudharma*) is not clear, by what [connection] would it be established? To this he says:

"Because of its primacy" (*pradhānatvāt*). When it is stated that "impermanence qualified by sound [is proven] because of being produced," the reason such as "being produced" would be connected with the property called impermanence—which, as the probandum (*sādhya*), is primary—and not with sound, which is secondary.

For it is proper that everything contained within a single sentence should be construed with the principal [subject] alone. And if there is a connection with the principal [subject], the reason lacks the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*). For "being produced" is not a property of "impermanence."

What then [belongs] to the sound? Therefore, it is logical that the subject (*dharmin*) itself, as qualified by its property (*dharma*), is understood by the cognizers themselves, and is likewise communicated to another. However, if it is argued:
"True, it is understood from the sentence that the reason’s connection is primarily with the property;

yet, by the superior force of the inferential mark (*liṅga*), the sentence will be set aside and the connection will be postulated with the subject alone. For the capacity for connection belongs to the property of the reason with the subject, not with the property."

Therefore, since there is no connection with the property (*dharma*), it might be argued that the connection will be with the property-bearer (*dharmin*) itself; to this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This is the intended meaning: it is true that the connection is established with the property-bearer. However, this very effort—namely, the breaking of the natural flow of the sentence—is itself a difficulty. For this reason he says: "This [connection] must be postulated. Otherwise, it would merely be a postulation of something as being otherwise than how it was understood.
The meaning is that this is a fault. // 37 //

Alternatively, by the inclusion of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason should be qualified as "because sound is produced" (*dhvaneḥ kṛtakatvāt*); however, with the intention that one does not observe practitioners formulating the argument in this way, he says: "of sound" (*dhvaneḥ*). As for the one who says:
"even when the subject is qualified as the probandum, at the time of demonstrating the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), wherever there is 'being produced'..."

When this is said, one might object that only the sound itself would be connected as the primary element, and not impermanence, because the latter is subordinate; to this he replies: "of the positive concomitance" (*anvayasya*). For at the time of demonstrating positive concomitance, they indeed apprehend the property (*dharma*) as distinct [from the subject]. In the formulation "wherever there is being produced, there is impermanence," there is no suspicion of a connection with the primary [subject]. Therefore, in the stage of the proposition (*pratijñā*):

When the subject (dharmin) is being proven as qualified by the property (dharma), that subordinate status which it previously held does not become defective in the statement of the example (dṛṣṭānta). However, it has been stated that logicians employ the logical reason (hetu) precisely without such qualification. In that case, when [the reason] is employed without qualification, there arises a suspicion of its connection with the primary property. As for the one who says that impermanence [is expressed] by the word ending in the genitive case (*dhvaninānityatvam*), [that is incorrect].

"The impermanence of sound is being qualified. And in this way, the connection of "because of being produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) with "sound" (*dhvani*) itself, whose case-ending remains unaltered, becomes clear. The connection with the property (*dharma*) would only occur through a proper modification of the case-ending;
and since that is improper, it must be stated [otherwise]. This position has already been refuted by the author of the Vārttika himself:

"Furthermore, because there is no basis [for it], there is no relation with the name, nor even a genitive case in the cognition. For if there were an indication by means of the genitive case, the relation itself would be the probandum (*sādhya*). And its status as a probandum has already been refuted. Having remained within the position that the probandum is qualified, the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*) by the property (*dharma*) is now being refuted.
Why then is the status of the relation as the probandum proposed once again here? Enough of this talk like that of a child! // 38 //

Moreover, when the fire's being qualified by a location (*deśaviśiṣṭatva*) is being proven, there is also the impossibility of all the types of subjects (*pakṣaprakāra*) that will be mentioned; thus he says, "of the fire. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate further refutations. "This" (*etad*) is a reference back to the definition that is about to be stated. To state those very types of subjects, he makes a concise promise: "qualified," etc. (39).

Now he demonstrates those very [positions] by dividing them, ending with the words "the fire which... This passage is self-explanatory. However, the distinction between the positions is to be understood by those who have applied their minds. Furthermore, in this context, the first two positions suffer from the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For fire is indeed established in some cases.

Even that which has been previously perceived as having its locus in a former place is already established; what, then, is the point of proving it? However, regarding the other five positions, there is a contradiction with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus he says: "But here... The fact that [the probandum] is already established is indeed very clear. (40–42)

He elaborates upon the contradiction [in the opponent's position] with the words "pervasion" (*vyāpti*). First of all, that which was stated—namely, "whatever is fire is conjoined with this [place]"—is incorrect. For all fires are not pervaded by this place, because the place lacks omnipresence and because all fires are not present here;
indeed, the existence of those [fires] is contradicted by their non-existence here. // 42 //

He refutes what was stated [in verse 3.33], namely, "that which has been seen by this," or "by that"—with the words "nor even by the former. The meaning is that even for fire that has been seen, there is no pervasion by this particular place. Regarding the statement "this which is [fire] is [qualified] by the mere place," he states the refutation with the words beginning with "nor" and ending with "by places": for this fire standing before us is not qualified by all places.
"Because of its absence everywhere. He points out the contradiction with the previous statement, "This [fire] is also [to the east]," by saying "with the former.
There is no qualification of this fire by the eastern location at all, because the eastern location does not exist here.

And in that case, the connection of the previously experienced fire with mere location has already been refuted by the same logic through the refutation of the connection of the fire standing before one with all locations; therefore, it was not presented and criticized separately. // 43 //

Thus, when the seven positions have been refuted, the eighth position remains: "This fire is qualified by this place. He refutes that with the word "this": it is not possible to establish that "this fire standing before us is qualified by this place. For it is not possible to point out that "this is fire" when its location is imperceptible.

[This is] to establish [the object] as being exceedingly distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*). However, as for the one who says, "The fire, having been remembered, is established by this [cognition] as qualified," he should be asked:
"How can that [fire], which was made an object of memory while existing only in its own place and time, be qualified by this [other] place?
Furthermore, by one who speaks thus, it has not even been considered that [this applies] to the former [place] either. This is because in an unqualified memory...

Moreover, the claim that "the property (dharma) is a qualifier (viśeṣaṇa) of the property-bearer (dharmin)" is not something to be established by reasoning, because properties are always understood precisely as qualifiers of the property-bearer; therefore, enough of this. With the intention that the location itself, previously perceived, ought to be the qualificand (viśeṣya), he says:
"of the fire" (agner). // 44–45 //

If fire were the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), then this would have to be its first moment of cognition, because a well-known thing is qualified by something not yet known. But here, at the outset, only the mountain is cognized. How then does it become the qualifier of the fire that is to be subsequently inferred? To this he says: "By the cognition of that" (*tajjñāna*). By the word *tat*, he points to the fire.
For at the time of perceiving fire, it is that very location which is cognized,
not the fire; therefore, of what [is there a cognition]?

The location (*deśa*) serves as a qualifier. For an object already cognized through perception is what is sought to be cognized through an unperceived property (*dharma*), in the sense of "of what nature is this property? In this way, it is that very location which is sought to be cognized and is indeed cognized, and not the fire. [Objection: But since the location is also already apprehended by perception, how can it become the object of inference? To this he says: "Of the location... For it is merely the essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) [of the location]...

The location is apprehended through perception, whereas its qualification by fire and so forth is inferred through inference; thus, there is no grasping of what has already been grasped. Therefore, it is the locus (*dharmin*) itself as qualified by the property (*dharma*) that is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and not the property as qualified by the locus.
Thus he says: "Therefore... (vv. 46–47).

And thus, it is the location itself as qualified by fire that remains the object of cognition (*prameya*). For that [location] is the locus (*dharmin*), since fire has it as its substratum; but fire is not [the object], because the location does not have fire as its substratum. Thus he says: "That [cognition] belongs to the location. Others, however, [hold that] even the previously perceived smoke is qualified by fire.

They consider the object of inference (*prameya*) [to be the qualified object]. With the intention that this too is indeed correct, he says: "And by others, [it is held] of smoke. The connection is: "that is the object of inference" (*sā prameyatā*). Here, he raises an objection: "But surely" (*nanu*). It has been stated that the object of inference is the qualified [object]. According to the maxim that "the qualifier cannot be grasped if the qualified is not grasped," the inferential mark (*liṅga*)—like the word (*śabda*)—would terminate in the qualifier alone.
This is indeed correct; for it will be stated in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that a word denotes only the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). // 48 //

He refutes this, saying "not so. He states the reason: "for not... For, out of fear of postulating multiple powers, it is accepted that the word's function terminates at the qualifier alone. The inferential mark (*liṅga*), however, produces the cognition of the sublated object by the force of a previously apprehended invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*). Therefore, the cognition of the sublator arises only with respect to that much which has been apprehended as being invariably concomitant.

He establishes [the following]: since the possession of smoke is understood to be invariably concomitant with the mere possession of fire through the relinquishing of all other adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is the possession of fire alone that is inferred; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Furthermore, it has been stated that the mere qualifier cannot be the object of inference because it would involve proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*).
With this intention, he says: {3,}

"And not [the subject]," he says. Even the qualificand (viśeṣya), such as a mountain, is already determined in its own essential nature; therefore, that too is not the object of inference. Thus he says: "the qualificand. (Verse 49)

Therefore, since [the mountain] is not known except in its qualified form, it is that very thing which is the object of inference; thus he says: "as being qualified. Here, an objection is raised: "But surely... It is incorrect to say that even smoke is inferred as qualified by fire, because [if it were so, smoke] would be a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself. // 50 //
He refutes this, saying: "This is not so. For smoke consists of both a universal and a particular nature;

therein, that which is made the subject (*pakṣa*) by way of its particular nature has the status of a reason (*hetu*) by way of its universal nature, and thus it is not a mere part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśa*). It has been established, then, that the object of inference is a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*);
however, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) remains unknown. Therefore, if it is claimed that smoke, the cognition thereof, and so forth, constitute inference itself, [that cannot be].

Consequently, there would be a difference in the object (*viṣaya*) between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*), and that is untenable. For this very reason, the Bhikṣu (Dignāga), having stated in the case of perception that a single cognition itself takes the form of both the means of valid cognition and its result, extended that same principle to inference as well by saying, "its result is like the former. If, however, the cognition of the inferable object itself were intended to be the means of valid cognition, then likewise there would be no separate result. Therefore...

The nature of inference must be stated; therefore, he says: "By means of smoke and the cognition thereof," etc. As for the claim made by the Bhikṣu that the result itself is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they share a single object, that must be refuted here just as it was in the case of perception. For ordinary people do not consider the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and the goal to be identical.

For who indeed would maintain the identity of an axe with the act of cutting down a tree? As for the avoidance of the objection regarding the difference in objects, that which was stated in the case of perception should be applied here as well. Just as in the view where the sense-faculties and so forth are the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the identity of object was established by showing that the operation [of the means] is directed toward the same object where the result is produced; in the same way, here too, in the view where smoke and so forth are the means of knowledge, the aforementioned [identity] follows from that very operation.

The identity of the object must be extended [to the case of inference]. Therefore, let either the smoke or its cognition, or the relationship or its recollection, be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since the status of being a means of valid cognition and its fruit depends on what one intends to express.

As for what was said—that there is an absence of a fruit in the case of cognition—the author of the *Bhāṣya* indeed shows that cognition itself is the means of valid cognition, because he states the reason: "cognition regarding an object not present to the senses. And there is no absence of a fruit.

Because only the [cognitions of] abandonment and so forth constitute the result. Nor is there any royal decree that the result must be of the same kind [as its cause]. For through utility, a result may indeed be either of the same kind or of a different kind. Or, even if the result were strictly of the same kind, the cognition of abandonment and so forth will still be the result; or it may be the memory of assistance and so on—with this intention, he says: "the cognition of the object of knowledge" (prameyadhīḥ). // 52 //

If the author of the Bhāṣya considers the cognition of the object (*prameyadhi*) to be the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how then is smoke and so forth accepted as a means of valid knowledge? To this he says: "Perception... We have already stated that being a means of valid knowledge depends upon what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣā*). Thus, when smoke and so forth constitute the most excellent instrument (*sādhana*), then that alone is the means of valid knowledge. Even by the author of the Bhāṣya, through the passage beginning with "either the cognition or the birth [of the cognition]," the lack of a fixed rule regarding perception was indicated.

By demonstrating this in every case, the lack of restriction has indeed been shown by means of parity. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya in accepting the validity of smoke and other such [inferential signs]. // 52 //
The Buddhists divide this inference into two types: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). As they say:

"Inference is twofold: that for oneself is the perception of an object through a mark possessing the three characteristics; that for others, however, is the communication of an object perceived by oneself."
Thus, with the intention that this twofold division is untenable, he says: "anumāna" (inference), etc. The meaning of this is as follows:

when one desires to demonstrate to others—such as teachers, disciples, fellow students, opponents, or disputants—an object grasped through inference by means of that very same inference, the subject (*pakṣa*), which is the qualified locus (*viśiṣṭo dharmī*), is cognized in the manner previously explained by us.

Thus he should be addressed. This is the underlying intention here: a statement of proof (*sādhana-vākya*) is employed solely to communicate to another a matter already grasped by oneself through inference. The other person, however, having reflected upon the three-fold mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) from that statement, [realizes] the probandum (*sādhya*) for himself.
Therefore, this inference of his is indeed for one's own sake (*svārthānumāna*). For the speaker as well, who has himself understood the object, it is likewise an inference for one's own sake.

We do not know which among these could be an inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*). If you say that speech is for the sake of others, no; because it is not an inference. We do, however, accept that speech is for the sake of others. As for what he says, namely that "because seeing is for the sake of others," [we reply: [The opponent objects: But surely, when one sees smoke and infers fire, and then speaks of it to another person, isn't that an inference for the sake of others? [The author replies: No, because that too is merely speech, and speech is not an inference. Furthermore, even if one were to speak of an inference for the sake of others, it would still be nothing other than speech. Therefore, since speech is not an inference, there is no such thing as an inference for the sake of others. Consequently, the statement that "seeing is for the sake of others" is not established. Thus, the reason provided is unestablished (*asiddha*). And since the reason is unestablished, the thesis is also not proven. Therefore, the inference is invalid. This concludes the critique of the inference for the sake of others. Now, the following is the critique of the inference for one's own sake. [End of section.]

But that [verbal testimony] is not inference, because it is produced from a mark (liṅga) that lacks the three characteristics and does not perceive the object. According to your own tenet, "inference is the perception of an object through a mark possessing the three characteristics";

therefore, how can speech be inference? If it is argued that verbal testimony is metaphorically called "inference for others" (parārthānumāna) because it serves another purpose—namely, its capacity to convey an object that has been made the domain of inference—[we reply: so be it.

Consequently, if speech that makes known an object already apprehended through direct perception were considered "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*), then direct perception itself would also result in being "for the sake of another. If, however, it is argued that direct perception is not for the sake of another because its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that [particular] is not within the domain of words, that is incorrect. For, in that case, [one would have to exclude] those who state things contrary to what has been grasped by direct perception.

It is not tenable to state that [the scripture] brings forth a contradiction with that [perception]. For one who asserts a matter contradicted by perception—such as "fire is not hot"—is refuted by having that perceived object established through verbal expression. However, that would not be possible in the case of an object of perception that is beyond the scope of words;
therefore, it must be admitted that even regarding objects of perception, speech does indeed speak. And thus, because speech concerning the objects of perception is for the sake of others...

Since who would deny that perception is for the sake of others, the two-fold division [of means of knowledge] is untenable. Therefore, he stated that only the aforementioned position should be maintained.
However, this must be addressed: what is this so-called "position" (pakṣa)?
To this it is said:

The meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the thesis (*pakṣa*). What is the proposition? It is a statement that presents the probandum (*sādhya*). As they say: "The proposition is the indication of the probandum. Therefore, one should state that the thesis is the probandum; thus it was said, "the thesis is what is to be expressed. He now introduces the statement regarding that: "In that regard" (*tatra*). In that regard, having first indicated the locus (*dharmin*) within the thesis, [he states] the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*).
"Fire and so forth are being enjoined; what is meant is: 'This mountain possesses fire.

However, some do not accept this statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*), which is another name for the proposition (*pratijñā*). They say: 'What is the use of this useless [statement]? Even without the statement of the subject, that which is required is indeed established. For the reason (*hetu*) is the means of proving the probandum (*sādhya*), not the statement of the subject. Indeed, this is not a matter based on scripture (*āgamika*)."

Because it would follow that the statement of the reason (hetu) is purposeless. If the ascertainment of the object were achieved through the statement of the thesis (pakṣa) in accordance with a reliable authority (āpta), the formulation of the reason would be useless; the opponent would then be occupied solely with ascertaining the virtues and faults of the speaker. However, since the final determination depends upon the reason, it is appropriate to examine the capacity of that very reason.

What is the use of stating the proposition (*pratijñā*)? Furthermore, the efficacy of the reason (*hetu*) is established simply by demonstrating its positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, since the probandum is established merely through the example (*udāharaṇa*) and the application (*upanaya*)—namely, "whatever is produced is impermanent, and sound is produced"—the proposition is useless. Rather, it is the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) of the reason alone that must be demonstrated; and that is done by means of the two types of examples and the application.
And since this has already been stated, enough with excessive detail.
If, however, it is argued that the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is for the purpose of announcing a dispute, that is not so; because it is not all-encompassing (*avyāpaka*).
For one might think: when this person asserts the proposition, "Sound is indeed eternal," then the other is a proponent of non-eternality.

"It is only after one has emerged [from meditative absorption] that discourse proceeds"—this is not so, because it is not universally applicable (*avyāpakatvāt*). This purpose does not pervade the statement of the thesis (*pratijñāvacana*), for it is impossible in the context of formal debate (*vāda*). For that [debate] concerns a student, and he must be made to understand reality (*tattva*) itself;
therefore, it is logical that reality is understood only after the power of the reason (*hetu*) has been demonstrated.
Why is dispute (*vivāda*) respected?

For one should not dispute with it. If you say, "It may exist in debate (*jalpa*)," no; because it is established otherwise. In this regard, it might be thought: "In debate, indeed, one who desires to engage in dispute formulates a thesis (*pratijñā*)."
And that is not so, because it is established otherwise;
for even in the absence of the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*), it is indeed perceived that one infers sound to be impermanent,
which is the reason.

Having stated, "Whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar," one applies the property of being produced to sound by saying, "And sound is produced. Thereafter, debate (*jalpa*) will certainly proceed. As for destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*), it proceeds in whatever manner once debate has been demonstrated. For the destructive critic has no goal to be established other than the refutation of the opponent. That which he...

When a certain matter is being established by means of the statement of a thesis (*pratijñā*), one who perceives the establishment of something contrary to their own position may become agitated and dispute.
Therefore, they object that the statement of the thesis is useless in all three types of debate and should be disregarded.
To this, we reply: you yourselves have stated that inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) consists in the illumination of an object already perceived by oneself.

It is logical that one who has themselves understood something to be qualified by some particular property due to some specific reason should likewise communicate it to another. However, in the absence of a thesis (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*) and other members would be without support, as if fallen into space. [Objection: But he did not previously know the probandum (*sādhya*) preceded by the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*); how then could he [communicate it] to another?

He speaks thus: "It is not so. Even if the words 'sound is impermanent' were not uttered during one's own apprehension, nevertheless, because this cognition is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), there certainly exists for the cognizer here a specific conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
however, since utterance is for the sake of others, that alone was absent in one's own apprehension. But another [person] does not [cognize] by means of what has not been uttered."
Since it can be communicated by means of a word, it is communicated by being uttered; thus, the mere utterance of the word is the only addition.
As for what was said regarding its lack of utility in debate, that is not so.

Because it is more useful. For since debate (*jalpa*) and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed between two parties desiring victory, one would not employ a statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) merely to delude the opponent. However, in a non-contentious discussion (*avivāda*), the student is not to be confused;
therefore, it is logical that the thesis is established most clearly by means of the statement of the proposition. Indeed, this is not a lack of verbal skill.

If we were to distress one who has approached us desiring to know that reality with obscure speech, it would not be useless even in the context of debate (*jalpa*). This has already been stated: for if the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) were absent, the reason (*hetu*) and other members would have no basis and could not function.

For they are subordinate elements that connect themselves only when there is a dependence upon the primary element, the probandum (*sādhya*); and that [dependence] does not exist if there is no indication of the probandum.

This is appropriate. For when the probandum (*sādhya*) has been stated, the reason (*hetu*) is connected in response to the expectation "from what [is it established]? Then, when the expectation arises as to "how is this [reason] the prover of this [probandum]?", the statement of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is required. Otherwise, however, due to the absence of a single purpose, there would not even be the status of a single sentence. To illustrate: when it is said, "Whatever is produced is impermanent," the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) [is understood].

It has been restated that [sound] is connected with impermanence; furthermore, by the statement "sound is produced," the connection of sound with its state of being produced has been restated. However, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for their mutual connection. One might suspect that these two sentences are unrelated, or the doubt might arise that both are merely restatements of their own nature—that what is produced is impermanent, and sound is also produced.

Or it would result in a different meaning altogether: namely, that just as that which is produced possesses the property of impermanence, so too does that which consists of sound; thus, one would arrive at the conclusion that all produced things consist of sound—a position that would be poorly established. Therefore, the denial of the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is a constituent part of the primary statement, is fitting only for nihilists who advocate the repudiation of everything, and not for others. For that [proposition] is the very essence of all worldly transactions. As they say:
The plaint is declared to be the essence of legal proceedings;
if that is abandoned, the plaintiff loses his case, while the defendant becomes the winner by crossing over it.
Thus, the manner of the proponent's statement is well-expressed: having pointed out the subject (*dharmin*), the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is predicated. // 53–54 //

But surely, if the subject (*dharmin*) is thus enjoined as qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*), there would be an understanding of its connection with the probandum alone, resulting in the exclusion of other properties (*dharmāntara*).

Consequently, when it is said "sound is impermanent," because of the restriction that it is *only* impermanent, properties such as being a quality of space (*ambaraguṇatva*) would not belong to it either. And since this would entail the rejection of the reason (*hetu*) as well, the establishment of the probandum would be impossible.

If the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) were not present, [the entity] might also be eternal; thus, the desired conclusion would not be established. Now, how is it that by the phrase "one [entity] is both eternal and non-eternal," the opposing position is implicitly rejected? True; for this very reason, when the restriction is applied to exclude that [opposing view], there would also be the exclusion of the other [possibilities]. Therefore, he says: "restriction" (*niyama*). Restriction is postulated solely with reference to the intention to express the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

Furthermore, [the presence of fire] is established even by other properties that are not contradictory to it. Thus, when "possessing fire" is being proven, only the mere absence of fire is excluded, and not other properties. Just as when it is said, "The cloth is white," there is a cessation of only its opposite—the absence of whiteness—and not of non-contradictory properties such as subtlety and so forth. And here, when it is stated "when the object is not in contact [with the senses]," what is the meaning of this? If it means that inference has as its domain only an object that has never been previously cognized, [then...]

That is not so. For at the very time of knowing the relationship, the connection between fire and the like is already understood as existing wherever smoke and the like exist; otherwise, the restriction itself could not be determined. Nor should it be said that the connection with place and time is something additional here, because while the connection of smoke with its location and so forth appears, that of fire does not. It is through the apprehension of the relationship that the connection of the entire space indicated by the smoke becomes known.
Because of this very determination. For this reason, some have explained the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) for the purpose of dispelling the misconception that [this cognition] is memory.
For memory generally occurs as being delineated by a reflection upon what is proximate;
it proceeds by means of the thought "that. And inference is not like this. Therefore, this is not memory. [Objection: But even if [the object] is not present...

In that case, memory indeed arises upon the mention of that [object]. As in the case of [the example of] "deprivation" (*pramoṣa*). It is not so. For in that case, because of the absence of a cause for direct perception, it is established that even though the cognition proceeds in the form of an experience, it is [actually] memory. Indeed, for sense organs that function by reaching their object (*prāpyakārin*), the capacity to manifest non-present silver and the like is impossible. However, the cause of memory is the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) produced by a previous experience.

It is maintained that memory alone is such [an invalid cognition] because its reflective awareness (*tad-avamarśa*) has been lost. However, this inferential knowledge (*laiṅgika-jñāna*), which arises by the force of present causes such as the logical mark (*liṅga*), proceeds in the form of direct experience (*anubhava*); it cannot be removed from being such [an experience] merely because of the absence of that [object]. And for us, direct experience is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, inference is designated as a means of valid cognition. If this is so, then let it be thus.

Such is the purpose of the term "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). No; for it would follow that [the cognition] lacks authority due to the absence of a result. A means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is that which has the result of a further determination (*adhikapariccheda*). If, however, mere determination were the result, then the same would apply to memory (*smṛti*), for that too arises as consisting precisely in the determination of its own object. It might be argued: "For us, a means of valid knowledge is indeed independent (*anapekṣa*)."
"And since recollection depends upon perception, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is not so, because [the same] consequence would apply to inference (*laiṅgika*).

For that too depends precisely upon the perception of a part (*ekadeśadarśana*) and so forth. If you argue that "recollection depends upon the grasping of its own object, but this [inference] does not," we say no; for here too there is dependence upon that. For even inference depends precisely upon a prior cognition of fire; for one who has not cognized fire [cannot infer it].

For one who has not yet cognized the relationship [between the word and its object], the cognition "fire is here" arises. Nor is it a royal decree that apprehension must be exclusively a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), for that would lead to the absurd consequence that even error would be so. Misapprehension is indeed an apprehension, yet it is not a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, we have already stated this while explaining the distinction between knowledge that accords with reality and knowledge that does not: that such a [misapprehension] is not non-existent. Moreover, regarding the object...

By the author of the Sūtra, in stating "it is unperceived" (*anupalabdha*), it was established that every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has only an object not [already] perceived as its domain. This too has already been explained during the occasion of its commentary. Therefore, the term "the grasping of an object not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭārthagrahaṇa*) must be explained; hence he says: "not in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). This is its meaning.

For an object that is proximate is of two kinds: either cognized through its true form (*tadrūpapramita*) or determined erroneously (*viparītanirūpita*). With the desire to avoid both of these, there is this expression "not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭavāk*). What, then, is the refutation of those [two]? To this he says: "of what is already cognized" (*pramitasya*). For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is required for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*) in order to determine what has not yet been cognized, not out of mere whim. And that [determination] occurs from a single operation of the means of valid cognition.
Thus, since it is established in this way, there is no dependence on another means of valid cognition. // 55–56 //

Furthermore, why would there not arise a dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which has already been cognized? To this he says: "By way of being of that same nature" (*tādrūpyeṇa*). This has been explained: for an object is cognized in two ways—either as being of that same nature or as its opposite. In that regard, when there is a determination of it being of that same nature, a further means of valid cognition is not fruitful, because the purpose of that [cognition] is accomplished by the previous determination alone. But in the case of a determination of it being the opposite...

However, since there would otherwise be no scope for any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the inclusion of the term "not already in contact" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) is purposeful, as it serves to exclude both [the objections of being either a memory or a perception].

But, one might object, it has already been stated that inference would thus be invalid because its object is something already in contact. This is not so, because the term refers to the specific context of the subject matter.

For although the property (*dharma*) previously apprehended is the object of memory, and the substratum (*dharmī*), such as the mountain, is established through direct experience, [inference still functions by grasping the connection between them].

Nevertheless, it has been stated more than once that the qualified [object] is made the object of cognition by means of inference. But surely, even the fire-qualified [mountain] was already cognized at the time of the convention regarding the relation. For in this way, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), he understood that "whatever possesses smoke possesses fire. Thus, his requirement concerns only that which possesses smoke; once that is known, the state of possessing fire is experienced as having been previously established through valid cognition.
True. However, although a place possessing smoke was previously cognized by way of its possession of fire, it is now recognized through inference.

And this recognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like perceptual recognition. For previously, the place was known as possessing fire in a form characterized merely by the presence of smoke; now, however, it is [known] specifically through inference that "this very place possesses fire."
What is there that is illogical about it being recognized? Moreover, this must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, how could one act after having known "this possesses fire"? For we observe that a person desiring to cook, having inferred the presence of fire, runs toward the fire.
Why is that?

If there were no distinction today from the previous experience, then indeed one would not [infer] "this is smoky, therefore it possesses fire," nor would one run toward the fire. If it is asked, "How does one engage in such practical activity (*vyavahāra*) regarding a fire that was not previously apprehended?"— it is not so, because of what occurred previously.

[Objection: It is understood [as the substratum] by way of being like smoke. If you say that one now perceives the mountain specifically through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and then acts toward the fire, [we reply: what does this seeker of fire have to do with the direct perception of the mountain? Therefore, one must admit that this cognition of its being possessed of fire is indeed distinct from the previous cognition, since it is on account of this that a specific practical activity (*vyavahāra*) arises; for [the previous cognition] had not grasped the object [in its specific form].

It must be stated that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This very point has been expressed by the inclusion of the term "not present to the senses" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). As for those who claim that its purpose is the exclusion of the suspicion that it is memory, for them, inference would result in having even a sublated object (*bādhitaviṣaya*). Indeed, the exclusion of that [memory-character] is not accomplished by any other member of the definition in the treatise on definitions.

[The object] is apprehended as something already produced. Therefore, the inclusion of the term "not proximate" (asannikṛṣṭa) is precisely for the purpose of excluding both types of proximate objects; thus, this is a sound interpretation. // 57 //

It has been stated that when [an object] is determined through its opposite, there is no room for another [cognition]. He states the reason for this in the words "at the root" (*mūle*). For the root of inference consists of the recollection of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth;

as long as the subsequent [inference] is delayed by being occupied with those respective operations, the preceding [perception], occurring more rapidly, seizes the object, and thus the very arising of the remote means of knowledge is obstructed—this will be explained immediately hereafter. How so?

Furthermore, inference would be sublated. For how can that which is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be sublated by another means of valid cognition? If it were so sublated, there would be no confidence in anything at all. If you argue that it is only a fallacious appearance (*ābhāsa*) that is sublated, then how is its status as a fallacious appearance established? If it is established solely through sublation, then this results in a circular argument (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, let it be that inference is sublated by perception, the senior means of valid cognition; but it cannot be sublated even by others that are inferior to it.

For what reason? To this he says: "of perception and so forth," ending with the word *syāt*. This is the intended meaning: that which is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is never sublated anywhere. For a means of valid cognition is indeed a cognition whose nature is ascertainment (*avadhāraṇa*). Therefore, where there is an ascertainment of some object by means of some aspect, [that cognition]—whether already arisen or about to arise—is [sublated] by that [ascertaining cognition].

Or rather, the sublation of knowledge might be stated. For sublation is of two kinds: sublation of what has been attained (*prāptabādha*) and sublation of what has not been attained (*aprāptabādha*). Sublation of what has been attained is, for example, in the case of the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. For in that case, the subsequent [cognition] acquires its own nature precisely by means of the destruction of the preceding one; thus, it is the sublater of that [preceding cognition]. And the subsequent [cognition], even when there is a difference of place and so forth, remains unsublated by its very nature.

And it first makes its own means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) appear. Thus, in the case of sublation by what has been previously attained, the word "ascertained" (*avadhārita*) excludes all three types of non-validity—that by which the object was determined by the subsequent [cognition]. For an object that is unknown, doubtful, or erroneous cannot be said to be "ascertained"; therefore, it is stated that for this [subsequent cognition], none of the three types of non-validity exist.
Thus, since it was previously made manifest by one's own cognition, it is the manifestation itself that is sublated therein; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the principle].

However, in the case of a sublation where [the object] has not been reached, as soon as the inference—which serves as the afflicted means of proof—begins to operate within its own domain, or as soon as a general rule begins to operate upon some particular object, [it is countered] by perception, or by inference, or by scripture whose every constituent part is established.

Or rather, when an object has been determined by a cognition that possesses a specific domain and arises rapidly, sublation occurs through that very cognition, characterized by the prevention of the subsequent one's arising. For a subsequent cognition whose path has been blocked by a stronger, more swiftly occurring means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) cannot possibly arise.
Thus, in a case where sublation has not yet occurred, the subsequent [cognition] remains unarisen; however, it is said to be "sublated" by way of the possibility of its occurrence.

Since the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is indeed [sublated] by direct audition (*śruti*), there is no sublation of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere. As for the claim that "it is not proper for the primary [means] to be sublated by the secondary," that is not so. For there is no fixed rule of relative weakness among the means of application (*viniyoga-pramāṇa*) such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, as there is in the case of these specific means of application. Rather, we declare that whatever occurs more swiftly, or which establishes itself by overriding what precedes it, is the sublater (*bādhaka*); the other is the sublated.

And for this very reason, we maintain that it is sublated by that very [means of knowledge]. Just as there is sublation of perception by what has been attained, so too is there sublation of a general rule (*sāmānya-śāstra*) by a specific rule (*viśeṣa-śāstra*), where the former has its probandum-component established by that same inference which has its own auxiliary-components established. Therefore, we shall state a thesis (*pakṣa*) that is indeed not contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is there a lack of confidence [in this], because sublation applies only to fallacious [cognitions] and because [the truth] is determined by a self-evident means of valid cognition.

Because the other is rendered non-manifest by means of knowledge (*jñāna*). This very point has been stated by the word "ascertained" (*avadhārita*). Now, it may be objected that even by a stronger [cognition], a weaker one is not necessarily sublated; for sublation occurs only when [the weaker] could otherwise have arisen. Therefore, through the determination of the respective objects, both [cognitions] will be established either by way of option (*vikalpa*) or by way of conjunction (*samuccaya*), without resorting to absolute sublation.

Therefore, he says: "of conceptual construction and so forth. Here, the aforementioned conceptual constructions and the like are not possible. First of all, two mutually contradictory forms cannot be combined in a single locus; for it is not possible that something be both audible and inaudible, or both eternal and non-eternal.

Nor can there be conceptual construction, because its object consists of affirmation and negation, which are impossible in the case of an established entity. Nor is there a fixed determination of the object.

Because the proof of both permanence and impermanence applies only to those things whose nature is color-form (*varṇātman*). Therefore, we state that there is sublation (*bādha*) precisely because [the reason] is impossible. Having thus established the sublation, it should be demonstrated through examples. Among these, he first demonstrates sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) with the words "ungraspability" (*agrāhyatā*). However, we do not understand this sublation by perception; for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [cannot have as its object] a thing contrary to its own domain.

It is correct that [the opponent's position] is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, "being an object of apprehension" (*grāhyatā*) is not itself an object of perception, because it is an object consisting of the relationship between the apprehended and the act of apprehending; and that [relationship] is not within the range of perception. For it is the sound (*śabda*) that is perceived, not its being an object of apprehension. For this very reason, it will be stated later that even the position that [sound] is not audible (*aśrāvaṇatā*) is not contradicted by perception. To this, it is replied: True.
The sense faculty is not the object of being grasped;

rather, the object of being grasped is its [the faculty's] object. Therefore, what is shown here is that the denial of the object of being grasped (*grāhya*) alone contradicts perception—meaning, it contradicts the inference that [all cognition] is without an objective support (*nirālambana*). On the other hand, the term "cognition" (*pratyaya*), derived from the word "not being grasped," expresses the very non-existence of that [object]. And what [is the nature] of the object of being grasped?
