An entity is other than this [non-]entity. For this non-apprehensibility of a rabbit’s horn consists in its not being an entity. It is precisely because of that absence [of being an entity] that there occur the designation and the cognition of "non-apprehensibility" in that case. Thus, by this method, it has been shown that only the position of the non-existence of the word is contradicted by perception; therefore, nothing is untenable. // 58–59 //

He states an example of contradiction by inference (*anumānavirodha*) with the words "of those" (*teṣām*). For those very [objects] such as sound and so forth, there is that which is contradicted by inference, such as "the non-audibility" [of sound].

Indeed, for one who intends sound to be the subject (*pakṣa*)—claiming it to be either inaudible or impermanent—that [position] is sublated by a counter-inference (*viparyayānumāna*) that occurs more swiftly. Others, however, consider this to be a contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣavirodha*); he refutes them with the words "for not" (*na hi*).
For sound is perceptible, but its "audibility" (śrāvaṇatā) is not; for the relationship between the sound and that which is audible is expressed by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.

This is because of the traditional rule (*smṛti*) stating: "In the case of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*), the relation [of the base] is denoted by the suffixes *tva* and *tal*.
And that [relation] cannot be apprehended through perception. Furthermore, the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

How could the relation of that [universal] to the word be perceptible? For a relation whose locus is both sensory and non-sensory is not perceptible, just like the relation between wind and a tree. Therefore, this is not a contradiction with perception. // 60 //

What, then, is the measure of audibility? To this he says: "That [is it]. Positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are observed: for sound is perceived by those who are not deaf and the like, whereas it is not perceived by those who are deaf and the like. For instance, when there is merely an impairment of the auditory organ, the cognition of sound is not seen in a deaf person, even though that person possesses the eyes and other organs. And when the auditory organ is intact, the apprehension of sound is observed, even in the absence of the eyes and other organs.

Therefore, by means of these two—positive and negative concomitance—it is understood that this property of being audible [is absent]. Now, one might ask: how is there a contradiction with inference in this case?
For positive and negative concomitance are not themselves inference.
However, the conceptualization of audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) arises from that [perception] and is mental;

therefore, someone who is deluded might claim that this [conceptualization] is indeed mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*). Such a person must be told: it has been stated more than once that the mind is not independent in its cognition of external objects. Whatever conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of something, that has that thing as its cause.

Thus, it is established in all cases that the auditory cognition of a word conforms to its object and is produced by its respective causes; this indeed constitutes the "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) of the word. As for the fact that the cognition is produced by hearing, this is therefore merely an inference. But is this not also the case elsewhere?

How is it to be understood that [a thing] has that as its cause, when it does not depend upon mental perception (mānasa-pratyakṣa) characterized by positive and negative concomitance? Listen: we indeed observe the production of a jar following the activity of a potter.
The causal relationship is perceived by the eye alone. For this "being an effect" of the jar consists in its arising immediately after that [cause];

and both that jar and its arising are indeed visible—so what is the use of the mind here? Therefore, when something exists, another comes to be, and when it does not exist, the other does not come to be.
The inference that "it has such-and-such a cause" is indeed valid, as its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is known through perception. And thus is the formal argument (*prayoga*):

sound is manifested by the means of cognition called hearing, because it is perceived only when that [means] exists; for whatever is such is manifested by that, just as a jar is manifested by the light of a lamp in the midst of darkness. And this [inference] is preceded by perception and preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Inference [of non-audibility] is established by that [audibility], because audibility is proven by it. Furthermore, this [inference of audibility] is stronger than the inference of non-audibility because its constituent parts are all established.

For as long as one intends to grasp the pervasion of quality-ness (*guṇatva*) by non-audibility, the production of that [pervasion] is obstructed by the cognition of pervasion produced swiftly by the inference of audibility.

In this very way, the inference of impermanence is also [sublated]. That which is based on reasons such as "being produced" (kṛtakatva) does not arise quickly due to defects such as being unestablished (asiddha) or inconclusive (vyabhicāra); thus, it is sublated by inferences of permanence that possess established members and arise rapidly.

For example, cognitions of the word "cow" (go-śabda) occurring at different places and times have the same object because they arise as the cognition "cow," just like a present cognition of the word "cow."
[This is established] by such arguments as: "The word 'cow' uttered yesterday exists even today, because it is the word 'cow', just like the word 'cow' uttered today," and so forth. // 60 //

He now announces the manner in which there is contradiction with words—namely, "in three ways. For contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) and so forth are well known as contradictions with words; thus they are designated in that way. However, these are not [merely] contradictions with words. For where a further proposition is sublated by a word established in some particular sense, [it is a contradiction with words].

In that case, there would be a contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabdavirodha*). However, when there is a contradiction with one's own words, the word has no established footing regarding any object, because its expression is self-contradictory. Even in the case of a contradiction with prior discourse, the determination must follow the relative strength or weakness of the reasoning between what precedes and what follows; thus, it is not a contradiction with verbal testimony. For in that instance, the object is not established by the authority of the word itself, since it is to be understood through reasoning (*nyāya*). [This applies to] worldly [convention].

Common consensus (*prasiddhi*), however, is neither a verbal testimony (*śabda*) nor a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*); rather, it is included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of knowledge]. Thus, by demonstrating a thesis that contradicts it, its nature has already been shown, and it is not appropriate to subsume it under contradiction with verbal testimony. For the thesis "the moon is not the moon" (*acandraḥ śaśī*) is not contradicted by verbal testimony; for verbal testimony does not express a relation between the word "moon" (*candra*) and Śaśin, such that a thesis which is not denoted by that [word] would be contradicted by it.

If the relationship were denotable by the word itself, there would be a contradiction with the nature of words, for it would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): the relationship [is known] from the denotation, and the denotation [is known] from the relationship. Therefore, these are not contradictions with the nature of words. However, because one rejects the former and accepts the latter through a consideration of the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) of the preceding and succeeding words, they are well-known as "contradictions with the nature of words" (*śabdavirodha*); this is the distinction established in other systems (*tantrāntara*).

It is said that there is a threefold contradiction with verbal testimony (*śabdavirodha*). However, in the ultimate sense, it is precisely the thesis asserting a meaning contrary to the statement of the Vedic meaning that is contradicted by verbal testimony. For the authority of verbal testimony is established therein; thus, one who asserts a contrary thesis is able to be refuted by it. And we shall explain this very point immediately hereafter. // 61 //

He shows those very three types [of contradiction] with the words "the proposition" (*pratijñā*). Among them, he states that the contradiction of the proposition alone is divided into three ways, using one and a half verses beginning with "as far as" (*yāvat*). This is the meaning: the contradiction of the proposition is indeed a contradiction with one's own speech.

And that is divided into three ways, due to the distinction between the act of utterance, the property (*dharma*), and the substratum (*dharmin*). The position is: "I shall remain silent for as long as I live."
It is sublated by the very thesis itself. For a thesis does not exist as long as it has not been stated; and by the mere act of stating it, silence is sublated.
Therefore, because there is sublation by the mere statement included within the body of the thesis, there is sublation by the thesis.
However, the position that all speech is false is sublated by the statement of a property (*dharma*); for if everything were false, even the statement of the thesis would be false.

If [the statement] were false, then nothing else could be false. Or, if that [statement] were not false, then there would be no universal falsity [of all things]. Thus, here, because of the consideration that the connection with the property (dharma) included within the proposition (pratijñā) is impossible, there is a sublation of the subject (pakṣabādha); this is what is meant by the "designation of a contradiction with the stated property. In the previous case, however, it was said "by the mere statement" because silence alone sublates the unqualified utterance. "Sublation of the self" means the sublation of the property (dharmabādhanam). Dharma...
This means that one who is thus improperly engaged brings harm upon oneself. The thesis "my mother is barren" is sublated by the statement of the subject (*dharmin*).
For as soon as "motherhood" is indicated, the state of being barren finds no footing. Nor should it be argued that the word "mother" is used here in a figurative sense, because I—[from whom...].
Because of the qualification "born" (*jāta*). When the subject (*pakṣa*) is thus qualified, it has been stated that there is a contradiction with the statement regarding the substratum (*dharmī*).

And this was said by way of a concession (*abhyupagamavāda*). However, the words of the mere chatterers (*jalpāka*), which exceed the authority of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, cannot be reconciled [with our position] through such means as being figurative (*gauṇatva*), for that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of all refutations (*dūṣaṇa*). For refutations arise only from negligence (*pramāda*) or ignorance (*ajñāna*).
When these [objections] are somehow resolved, there would be no fault whatsoever. // 62–63 //

He illustrates the contradiction with a prior statement (*pūrvasañjalpavirodha*) by means of the Buddhist's case. When the Buddhist has stated, "Sound is impermanent," and is questioned, "How can there be a cognition of an object from something momentary for which the relationship [between word and meaning] has not been grasped?"—if he then replies, "In that case, it must be permanent," then there is a contradiction with his own previous admission (*pūrvābhyupagamavirodha*). Even though, in this instance, one might follow the relative strength or weakness of the logical principles (*nyāya*),...

Although there exists a relationship between the sublated and the sublator, nevertheless, a proposition (*pratijñā*) that is internally contradictory in this way cannot even establish itself; thus, it does not require the application of logic (*nyāya*). For a matter that is at least conceivable within a proposition is established by means of logic; however, when a matter is inconceivable, there is simply no need for logic at all.
Because it is fragile by its very nature. Therefore, it is precisely the contradiction with the words that subsumes this [fallacy].

For their intention is that such a composition of words—being contradictory between what precedes and what follows—destroys the thesis even without a formal proposition. He states an example of contradiction with what is well-known to all the world, beginning with "The moon... In this case as well, the connection of words with a meaning contrary to the consensus of great people is shattered by its own inherent force.
"It is not a valid means of knowledge as long as it requires [further] dependence"; thus has the sublation by verbal testimony been illustrated. // 64 //

He states an example of contradiction with comparison (*upamāna*) as follows: "By one who has known [the cow]," etc. For, in the case of someone who has seen the form of a cow (*go*) in a city and now sees the form of a *gavaya* in the forest, the thesis that "the cow is not similar to the *gavaya*" is contradicted by comparison (*upamāna*). When the cow is beyond perception, its similarity is the object of comparison; but when it is perceptible, it is simply perceived directly. Therefore, the sequence "by one who has known the forms of both the cow and the *gavaya*" is intended. // 65 //

Now, wishing to discuss the contradiction by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti-virodha*), he first provides an example of that which is preceded by non-existence (*abhāva-pūrvikā*) in accordance with the Bhāṣyakāra, saying: "In the house... (verse 66).
He provides an example of that preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*): "In the case of fire... [and] "not burning. This means not endowed with that power.

He provides an example of that preceded by inference (*anumānapūrvikā*): "And in the case of sound, not being expressive. Having inferred through bodily movement the cognition of the object immediately following the hearing of the sound, one concludes that sound is the cause therein. Therefore, because all causal factors (*kāraka*) are invariably concomitant with action, [this is an instance of presumption].
The operation consists of the denoter and the denoted;
and since that [operation] is otherwise untenable, the existence of their capacity is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). // 67 //

Likewise, the position that seeks to deny the existence of the sense organs (*indriya*) is also contradicted by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by perception; thus he says, "the auditory organ," and so forth.

Although an example of *arthāpatti* preceded by perception has already been cited, he states this contradiction once more with the intention of showing that this same defect applies to the position denying the sense organs, under the guise of pointing out a flaw in the [present] thesis. In this very context, by means of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [he indicates] that which is preceded by comparison (*upamāna*).
The contradiction must be demonstrated—just as, for example, in the case of a cow compared to a gavaya, there is a denial of that [cow's] capacity to be apprehended by the cognition [of it].

He illustrates the contradiction preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "In the case of sound" (*śabda*). For, having established the expressive power [of sound] through another presumption (*arthāpatti*) based on the fact that the denotation of meaning would otherwise be inexplicable, one then establishes the permanence of sound through yet another presumption based on the inexplicability of that [expressive power].
It is understood. // 67 //

He illustrates the contradiction with presumption based on verbal testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) by saying, "contradiction by presumption based on what is heard" (*śrutārthāpattibādha*). But why is presumption being illustrated with such elaboration?

For the demonstration of its contradiction would indeed be established even by just one instance. Furthermore, no such elaboration has been shown regarding contradictions with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, contradictions with other means of valid cognition should have been stated with the same elaboration as presumption.
True. It is precisely by means of these sixfold divisions that the Vārttikakāra intends to demonstrate the contradiction here;

it is for the sake of illustrating this very point that the presumption (*arthāpatti*) arising from the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has been cited as an example. By that same method, the detailed exposition should also be shown regarding the other means of valid cognition.
For instance, contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) alone is divided into six types—excluding the sixth—by means of experience, memory, inference, and so forth.
For a proponent who is perspiring, the thesis that "fire is not hot" is contradicted by perception residing in direct experience (*anubhavastha*).
However, for one who is not near a fire, that very same thesis is contradicted by perception residing in memory (*smṛtistha*);
indeed, when this person asserts at the time of debate that "fire is not hot," the other party reminds him: "Do you not remember the heat of fire previously experienced, such that you speak thus?"
Having remembered that [taste], one then desists from the perceptible [object]; thus, there is "sublation by a perceived memory" (*smṛtapratyakṣabādha*).

However, "sublation by an inferred perception" (*anumitapratyakṣabādha*) occurs where, upon observing a particular movement on the face of a trustworthy person, it is asserted that their bitter taste and so forth—which were previously understood—is not present;
for by the deformity of the face, one's experience of bitterness is inferred. Therefore, the opposite position is sublated by an inferred perception.

As for sublation by what is heard (*śruta-pratyakṣa-bādha*): when someone denies a certain object and it is said, "This object was seen by the witnesses," sublation by the direct perception of the witnesses (*sākṣi-pratyakṣa*) is thus designated. This is not a case of sublation by verbal testimony (*śabda-bādha*), for in this instance they do not state the object itself, but rather their perception of it. Therefore, the decision follows precisely that perception. Perception...
Since that [object] is made known by them through its own specific term, this is indeed a contradiction with the perception already apprehended by verbal testimony.

As for analogy (*upamāna*), however, its object is merely the similarity to a thing already established by another means of knowledge; thus, it takes as its domain the similarity of something already established elsewhere. For example, in the recognition of a sickle or similar tool, one observes a certain kind of movement in oneself and [recognizes] that same [movement] in another.
Having seen [another], one compares [them]: "Just as in me, so too in this person, the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the axe and other tools has arisen through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Otherwise, how could one proceed on the following day to complete a task that was half-finished on the previous day? And here, having inferred through behavior an object belonging to another that corresponds to it, one compares its similarity to one's own cognition. Even though there might be a sublation (*bādha*) here by a direct perception known through inference, [the comparison still holds].

Although it cannot be shown [in that way], nevertheless, it can be shown in the determination of its similarity to one's own cognition; thus, it is stated that there is a sublation by perception whose existence is understood through that [cognition].
It is the very existence of perception that is cognized by means of comparison (*upamāna*). This is a case of sublation by perception understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

It should be demonstrated as follows: when many people seeking water are traveling along and one among them sets out to fetch it but delays, then, because that delay would otherwise be inexplicable, his perception of water is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In that case, the contrary position—that the pond is devoid of water—is sublated by the perception established through *arthāpatti*.
Since perception, which is positive in nature, cannot be apprehended through non-existence, the contradiction with that unapprehended perception is not cited here as an example.
Hereafter, we shall examine the sixfold division of sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*):

first, when fire inferred from smoke is denied, there is sublation by inference preceded by perception; second, when the heat of fire is inferred from that very fire inferred from smoke, a contrary position [is sublated].

It is sublated by an inference based on what has been inferred (*anumitānumāna*). However, where— after the application of a mantra has been perceived through the rule "He offers [the oblation] with the words *devasya tvā*," and the remainder of that mantra has been inferred, one then adopts a position contrary to it—
there is sublation by an inference based on scripture (*āgamānumāna*).

But when an obligatory rite (*nitya-karman*) has commenced and there is a deficiency of rice (*vrīhi*), and *nīvāra* grains—which resemble them—have been substituted, the injunction "one should sacrifice with rice" is inferred to have the *nīvāra* grains as its scope. For the parts of the rice, whose relationship [to the sacrifice] is known through their being the scope of that injunction, cause it to be inferred. Indeed, the rice grains do not constitute the scope of that injunction by their own nature alone.

The meaning of the Vedic injunction regarding rice (*vrīhi*) consists of the grains reduced to powder; since these [grains] exist even in wild rice (*nīvāra*), the injunction for rice is inferred as applying to wild rice by way of analogy based on the commonality of its constituent parts. Thus, in this case, the position that [the injunction] does not have that [wild rice] as its scope is sublated by an inference preceded by analogy (*upamāna*). However, the sublation by an inference preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has already been stated regarding the position that sound is audible (*śrāvaṇatva*). [This applies to cases] where, from a distance, one perceives the absence of a tree...

Having perceived [the object], the absence of its shadow is inferred; therein, by means of an inference preceded by non-perception (*abhāva*), the position that the shadow exists is sublated. Sublation by perception and by verbal testimony has already been shown in three ways. Another [instance of sublation] must also be shown by means of *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. However, the position that the *Aṣṭakā* and other such rites are non-dharma is contradicted by the verbal testimony inferred from the commonality of the performers, as established in the section on *Smṛti* (*Smṛtyadhikaraṇa*).

This has been demonstrated. For it is possible to infer that the *Aṣṭakā* and other such practices have their root in the Vedic word (*śabdamūla*), because they are performed by authors residing in Āryāvarta who are established in the Śāstra, just like the *Agnihotra* and other rites. However, there is sublation by scriptural authority (*āgamikaśabdabādha*) in cases where, amidst a dispute concerning the subject matter of a Śruti passage found in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), the existence of that Śruti is ascertained through the testimony of the authors of the Smṛti compendia.

For in that case, a contradiction with the eternal scripture known through authoritative tradition (āptāgama) is possible for the opposing position. However, regarding the contradiction with the word "likened" (upamita): when it is inferred from the Smṛtis of Manu and others—by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)—that there must be some Vedic source [for them], then the position that the root of the Smṛti texts consists of mere explanatory passages (arthavāda) is sublated by the word "likened," since the inferred root would necessarily be similar to the Smṛti statements themselves. This applies also to the position that the Viśvajit sacrifice has no fruit.

However, this is contradicted by a word established through presumption based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*). Since the existence of a word cannot be understood through non-existence (*abhāva*), the function of that [non-existence] lies in the determination of the word itself. In that case, regarding the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, where the entirety of the injunction has been determined as being absent, the position that the archetypal procedure (*prakṛtītikartavyatā*) applies is sublated. As he will state: "Because of the prescription of the whole, it is a new [rite]" (*apūrva*).

Regarding the term "Soma": the position that *nīvāra* grains should not be accepted as substitutes in the absence of *vrīhi* rice is contradicted by direct perception and comparison (*upamāna*). As for the sublation of comparison preceded by inference (*anumāna*), it occurs when, having inferred the motion of the sun through its arrival at different locations, one compares its similarity [of speed] at the beginning, middle, and end of the year; for just as the sun's motion is of a certain kind at the beginning of the year, so too is it in its middle or at its end.
In that context, regarding the phrase "at the end of the years," the position that there is a dissimilarity in their respective courses is sublated by an analogy preceded by inference.

However, the position that *pūtīka* plants are not similar to *soma* is contradicted by an analogy preceded by verbal testimony. For the similarity between *soma* and *pūtīka* is not perceived through direct perception. Nor...

And it is to be inferred. However, by the word itself, which establishes that the *pūtīka* plants are produced from the rays of the *soma*, their similarity (*sārūpya*) is established through the fitness of cause and effect. Therefore, because the *pūtīkas* originate from a cause and effect known through verbal testimony, the comparison of their similarity to *soma*—which would otherwise be the reverse—is contradicted by an analogy based on verbal testimony. [This applies to] those belonging to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.

For the position that "the ritual properties (*dharma*) do not exist at all in *satra* and *ahīna* sacrifices" is contradicted by the analogy of the *jyotiṣṭoma* and the *dvādaśāha*. Indeed, they proceed to the *dvādaśāha* by means of the analogy with the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and both the *satra* and *ahīna* [proceed to the *jyotiṣṭoma*] by means of the analogy with the *dvādaśāha*. However, when the sense organs of another person—qualified by similarity to one's own sense organs—are compared, the negation of that [similarity] is contradicted by the presumption-based analogy (*arthāpattyanumāna*). [This applies to the claim of] the non-existence of a creator of the Veda.

The thesis that [the subject] is not similar to the non-existence of things such as a rabbit’s horn is sublated by an analogy based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvakopamāna*). When the non-existence of both [the rabbit’s horn and the subject] has been understood through their non-existence, it is then that similarity is compared. Furthermore, the sixfold contradiction with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has already been described.
We shall explain the contradiction with non-existence (*abhāvavirodha*) immediately hereafter. // 68 //
He now illustrates contradiction by non-existence (*abhāvavirodha*) with the words "the horn of a rabbit, etc. This is a contradiction with the non-existence of perception (*pratyakṣābhāvavirodha*).

However, when it is being considered whether or not the sun has gone to such-and-such a constellation, and a person skilled in calculation understands through the inference of calculation that it has not gone because the [required] calculation is absent, yet a deluded person says it has gone—therein lies a contradiction with the non-existence of inference (*anumānābhāvavirodha*). [The same applies to] the thesis that bowing to a shrine (*caityavandana*) and so forth is a religious duty (*dharma*).

However, [the claim that inference is] contrary to the absence of scripture such as direct revelation (*śruti*) is contradicted by the statement, "The *darvīhoma* sacrifices possess the character of having a prior [similarity]," for no similarity of those [sacrifices] with any other ritual action is perceived in any way. On the other hand, regarding the existence of a similarity between a heap of straw and an elephant, the position that there is no [valid] analogy (*upamāna*) is contradicted. Likewise, [the claim that inference is contrary to perception applies] when sound does not come to the location of the ear.

Since the hearing of a sound in the auditory organ is established by the mere arrival of the resonance (*dhvani*) at the location of the sound, one who—on the basis of *arthāpatti* (presumption)—asserts that "a sound initiates another sound, and thus the final sound is eventually perceived by the auditory organ through a sequence," has that assertion sublated by the absence of *arthāpatti*. The absence of absence (*abhāvābhāva*) should be demonstrated as follows: when...

For when the absence of defects in the Vedas is understood through the absence of an author, then there is a sublation [of the opposing view] because the category of that which possesses defects is non-existent. // 69 //

Thus, first of all, the sixfold sublation of the connection between properties (*dharma*) has been elaborated. Hereafter, we shall explain the sublation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) and specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) of both the property and the substratum (*dharmī*). To facilitate easy comprehension, he provides a summary by mentioning what has already occurred and what is about to follow with the verse beginning "evam" (thus). Regarding the phrase "of those [properties] implied by the direct statement (*śruti*) and the sense (*artha*)," the essential nature is everywhere indeed the object of the direct statement itself; its specific qualities are also implied by the sense. This refers to the property and the substratum.

For it implies that specific property by which its own nature is pervaded; and that will be explained immediately thereafter. The analysis of the compound is: "the literal meaning [of the word] and the implied meaning. // 70 //

In this context, the sublation of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the property (*dharma*) has already been described; therefore, without performing that [sublation], he provides an example of the sublation of its qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*)—namely, "grass and so forth. For one who seeks to prove that snow possesses fire because it is seen to undergo transformations such as those of grass, there is indeed a sublation of the essential nature of the property by its very absence. Furthermore, its qualification—heat, which is implied by the sense—is sublated by the coldness perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Nor should it be argued that fire is seen in its radiance even when not hot, and therefore how can the specific property be implied by the object itself.
For even in the radiance, the fire is indeed hot;
however, because it is overwhelmed, the tactile sensation is not perceived.

Furthermore, it never abandons its heat, for that is its inherent nature (*svābhāvikī*). Nor should it be said that there is a non-perception [of heat] even in the presence of snow because it is overwhelmed by it; for a coldness contrary to that [heat] is actually perceived.

As for the presentation of a formal reason (*hetu*), it was intended merely to indicate the seed of that [objection] at the occasion of stating the defects of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*); thus, this [non-perception] occurs through the absence [of heat].
This is the sublation of a specific property of the dharma. // 71 //

However, since both types of sublation (*bādha*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*) have not yet been mentioned, he provides an example of such sublation in both ways with the verse beginning "adharma" (and a half). For it is generally understood that "violence (*hiṃsā*) is indeed unrighteousness (*adharma*).

When, having restated that unrighteousness enjoined [by scripture], such as the killing of a sacrificial animal (*daikṣapaśu*), causes suffering, it is then established that "that [suffering] is slight."

Even then, by virtue of being enjoined (*vihitatvena*), non-dharma (*adharman*) itself is sublated; its specific quality—namely, being a cause of suffering, which was implied for that purpose—is also sublated by that very same [enjoining]. For nothing that is enjoined can ever be a source of suffering, since an injunction has as its sole purpose the accomplishment of the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). This, then, is the sublation of both the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) and its specific qualities by means of scripture (*āgama*). Nor should it be objected here that the specific quality is only that which is directly expressed by the Vedic word (*śruti*); for that which is implied by the sense (*arthākṣipta*) is restated (*anuvāda*) for the sake of the injunction, because it is subordinate [to the directly expressed].

He illustrates the contradiction of both [the property and the subject] with respect to both by stating "ayathārtha" (unreal). For when it is established that all cognitions are false, then because the two cognitions grasping the property (*dharma*) and the subject (*dharmin*) are themselves false, and because the two cognitions grasping their respective qualifiers are also false, there occurs a sublation of both by both. And this "sublation of both through the statement of the property" is indeed a sublation by words (*śabdabādha*).
It has thus been established that for both [positions], there is a contradiction regarding their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). // 74 //

Furthermore, which two specific [properties] implied by the object are sublated? To this he says: "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*). The connection should be shown by modifying the word to "are sublated" (*bādhyete*). And in that context, it is stated: "from the perception of one part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*). In that case, the inclusion of the term "perception" (*darśana*) is redundant; it should simply be said "from one part" (*ekadeśāt*). For that is the logical mark (*liṅga*), not the perception itself; therefore, it must be explained.

Regarding the phrase "from the perception of one part," he says: "from perception" (*darśanāt*). This is the meaning: a part is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) by its mere existence; rather, it must be known in one's own cognition and made known in the communication to another. To include both of these, the term "perception" (*darśana*) is employed; and it is capable of including both.

This is because the term "showing" (darśana) is common to both the causative and non-causative senses. First, regarding one's own cognition (*svapratipatti*), the meaning is that when one part is seen, the resulting mental state (*buddhi*) is inference (*anumāna*). Regarding the formulation for the sake of others (*parārthaprayoga*), however, it is stated that the inferential cognition which arises after showing one part by means of the word "showing" in its causative form (*ṇijanta*) is inference. Thus, this word "showing," as uttered in that context, possesses two meanings.

This must be explained. By this [definition], that which is called the "unestablished" (asiddha) fallacy of the reason—wherein, in a certain part [of the subject], there is doubt, lack of conviction, or error on the part of either the proponent or the opponent, or both—is excluded. For such a [reason] cannot be demonstrated to another.
Or, it is "seen by oneself," which means it is known through one's own lack of confidence. In that regard, he provides an example of the two-fold perversion:

"because of coldness. Since both the word "fire" and the [actual] fire are [erroneously perceived as] cold and visible respectively, they are unestablished (*asiddha*) due to the perversions of both the proponent and the opponent. // 75–76 //

He states an example of the "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*): "By the state of being produced," and so forth. When a Vaiśeṣika employs the reason "sound is impermanent because it is produced, or because it is a quality" against a ritualist (Yājñika), that [reason] is unestablished for him in its own nature. However, when he himself states such a reason to another, then there is its non-establishment for him—for instance: "Sound is eternal because it is a substance, like space. For the Vaiśeṣikas do not...
They accept sound as a substance because they accept its status as a quality. "Of such a kind" means: of a kind that is not established for the opponent. // 77 //
He illustrates the "unestablished due to doubt" (*sandigdhāsiddha*) with the passage ending in *bāṣpādi*.

For when smoke is doubted as being vapor or the like—by both [parties] or by one, such that one wonders, "Is this a rising of dust, or vapor, or smoke?"—then it becomes unestablished due to doubt for both or for either one. Thus far, [the fallacy arises] through doubt and error.

The unestablished (asiddha) has been illustrated. However, when words with unknown meanings are employed out of ignorance, it must be demonstrated [as such]. "In three ways" means there are three modes by the proponent, the opponent, and both. Thus, it has first been stated that the reason is unestablished by its very nature; therefore, he says "evam" (thus). // 78 //

He states that the fallacy of the unestablished substratum (*āśrayāsiddhatā*) is also divided into three types by these very same factors—knowledge and so forth—which depend on both the proponent and the opponent, saying: "These very [factors]... (verse 79).

[Objection: Surely the reason (*hetu*) would be defective due to the unestablished nature of its own essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*), but what defect could there be for it due to the unestablished nature of its locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*)? To this he says: "Even when [the locus] is known. This is the intended meaning: a reason is not a means of cognition by virtue of its own essence alone, but rather as something known through its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). And that which has an unestablished locus cannot be known as a property thereof. [This is illustrated by the examples of] coldness and visibility.

Furthermore, [the reason] is indeed non-reason (*ahetu*) precisely because its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished. For coldness is established by its own nature in water, and visibility is established in color, tangible objects, and those things inhering in the same substrate as color. However, since these two are unestablished in sound and so forth by virtue of being properties of the subject, the statement that they are "unestablished in their own nature" (*svarūpāsiddha*) is made with the intention of referring to their nature as properties of that [subject]. Therefore, even in the case of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*), there is non-reasonhood due to the unestablishment of the property of the subject.
This is indeed logical. // 79 //

He now illustrates that [fallacy of] unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*)—the term "everywhere" being used according to the non-tenet (of the opponent). For when the Mīmāṃsakas, against a Buddhist, argue for the omnipresence of the self because an effect is perceived everywhere, then the reason has an unestablished locus for one of the two parties, since the self is not established for the Buddhist. However, regarding a certain worldly person who, being ignorant of the way of valid cognition, entertains doubt about the self, he says that when that very same reason is stated, the reason has a doubtful locus; this refers to "the worldly person and so forth" with respect to the self.
The meaning is "doubt. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), those among the non-Buddhist teachers (satīrthika) who also harbor doubt regarding the self are included.

Thus, the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) has been stated by way of doubt and error (*viparyaya*). Unestablishedness of the locus due to ignorance (*ajñāna*) must also be shown in the case of employing a term that is not recognized; for, against one for whom the word expressing the subject (*pakṣa*) is not well-known, such a type of reason (*hetu*) [is unestablished].
When this is stated, it is argued that there is a lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to ignorance. // 80 //

Now, if a reason (*hetu*) is defective because it is unestablished for one of the two parties, then in that case, even such reasons as "the self (*ātman*) is inactive because it is formless" would not function as valid reasons, since for the Digambaras the formlessness of the self is unestablished;
for they consider the self to be embodied (*mūrta*), being a transformation of the body. This is because [they hold it] to be a non-agent (*akartṛ*).

The claim that "the Veda is eternal" is not a valid reason for the Buddhists because it is unestablished for them; likewise, "sound is impermanent because it is produced" is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsakas. Thus, there would be nothing at all that could be established as a valid reason. Therefore, he says: "it is mere words. The meaning is this: a reason does not become unestablished merely by the words "it is unestablished for me. If that were the case, then nothing whatsoever would be established.

The conventional practice of inference could be established. However, when a particular [reason] has been determined by both the proponent and the opponent to be non-existent, the statement that such a [reason] is unestablished constitutes a refutation for the proponent; it does not follow from the mere utterance of the words "it is unestablished. // 81 //
Now, what is this "unestablished for both" (ubhayāsiddha)?
For there can be no agreement between two disputants on a single point;
indeed, even in a thousand lifetimes, a Buddhist would not consider the Vedas to be authorless.

Even a Mīmāṃsaka, even when his life-breath is at his throat, [would not admit] the produced nature (*kṛtakatā*) of sound. Thus, because there is no mutual agreement regarding such matters, the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) does not hold. Therefore, he says—the following is the intended meaning: it is not the case that proof and refutation are impossible merely because there is no mutual agreement between the two parties. For if, when a proof has been put forward by the proponent and its "unestablished" nature (*asiddhatva*) has been pointed out by the opponent, the proponent then establishes that very proof;

From that, the proof (*sādhana*) arises. However, if the opponent refutes [the argument] by stating a logical impossibility from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), then a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) of that [proof] is established. In this case, establishment by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone is what is required, not the acceptance by both parties. Even the statement, "that which is known by both to be non-existent," was spoken with the intention of establishing it through valid cognition.

It is not based merely on what is accepted [by one party]. For when something is established or sublated by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is generally observed that there is agreement between both parties. The word "other" (*itarat*) refers to that which is known as non-existent. That which is known by the proponent (*vādin*) as existent and by the opponent (*prativādin*) in the opposite way—that, when being established by the proponent, becomes a proof (*sādhana*). And this has been stated while standing within the framework of the logic of debate (*jalpanyāya*). In formal discussion (*vāda*), however, there is indeed agreement between both parties; thus, there is no such thing as "unestablished for one of the two" (*anyatarāsiddhi*) in that case.
As long as the proof does not establish the probandum, one is defeated due to the non-establishment of either [the reason or the thesis];
however, once that has been established, the refutation is averted. // 82 //
The objects to be excluded by the terms *asannikṛṣṭa* (not present) and *ekadeśa* (one part) have thus been shown.

Now, he shows the object to be excluded by the term *jñātasambandha* (known relation), ending with the word *sandeha*. For a relation is not known to exist between [a reason] that is a cause of doubt and one that is a cause of error;
indeed, it cannot be said that the common cause of doubt, such as *prameyatva* (knowability), has its relation with permanence (*nityatva*) known.

Since the relationship [of the probans] with the jars and so forth is already known through their impermanence, nor is "being produced" [known] through their permanence—because the cognition of the relationship is experienced in those very things through their impermanence—it follows that both members of that class do not have a known relationship;
thus, the phrase "having a known relationship" excludes them. And here, starting from the word *asannikṛṣṭa* ("not present"), one proceeds in reverse order.

The author of the Vārttika stated in his work on definitions (*lakṣaṇagrantha*) the purpose of employing a qualifier; for what reason? Because it follows the sequence of cognition. For one first cognizes the subject (*pakṣa*), and thereafter looks toward the reason (*hetu*).
Next is the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Therefore, for the purpose of refuting the fallacious positions (*asatpakṣa*), the term "not present to the senses" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) has first been explained. Then follows the statement of the reason (*hetu*): "from the perception of a part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*). Next is the statement of the example: "of one who knows the relation" (*jñātasambandhasya*). For it is in the example that the relation of the reason is known. Therefore...

In this way, defects of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadoṣa*), such as its being devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*) or the reason (*hetu*), are also refuted by this [definition]. Even when there is such a deficiency, the relationship can be known by oneself and explained to another. Furthermore, how many causes of doubt (*saṃśayahetu*) are there?
To this, he says: "Three" (verse 83).
He shows those very three types [of reasons], beginning with "the existent" (*san*). That which exists in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence (*tadabhāva*) is called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*);

for example, cognizability (*prameyatva*) in relation to permanence and impermanence. That which is excluded from both the probandum and its absence is "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), such as the possession of odor (*gandhavattva*) belonging to earth alone; for that is indeed excluded from all other substances, qualities, and actions that are similar or dissimilar to it.

"Two [reasons] connected with contradictory meanings": those which have been designated by others as "non-deviating contradictories" (viruddhāvyabhicārin) are to be illustrated immediately hereafter; therefore, they are not explained here. // 84 //

Therein, he first elaborates upon the "common" [inconclusive reason] by means of examples—starting with the words "prameya" and so on. The meaning is that these properties are common to both the probandum and its absence. // 85 //

In which probanda, then, do they have commonality? To this he says: "In the eternal," ending with the word "eternal" (*nitya*). But how is there a correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) when there is a disparity [in number]? To this he says: "The term 'non-eternality' (*anityatā*) is to be read twice. Thus, non-eternality is to be recited twice in its own place; from this, the correspondence is established. This is the meaning: when the argument "Sound is eternal because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*) is employed...

At that time, since knowability (*prameyatva*) is observed in both the probandum (*sādhya*) and its absence, it is common to both; therefore, it is not capable of leading to a definitive conclusion. For this reason, it is called "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*). And for this very reason, it is a cause of doubt. For doubt arises from the perception of a generality, the non-perception of specific features, and the recollection of specific features. As, for example, [doubt arises] regarding a post and a person due to the observation of the generality of height and girth.

Furthermore, due to the non-determination of the distinguishing properties (*bhedakadharma*) and the dependence upon the recollection of their specific differences, there arises a doubt consisting of non-ascertaining knowledge, such as: "Is this a post or rather a person? In the same way, for one who knows that "knowability" (*prameyatva*) is common to both the eternal and the non-eternal, there arises a cognition characterized by non-determination regarding those two alone, depending upon the recollection of their specific qualifiers; this is what is known by the name "doubt."

"Being produced" (*jāyate*) is a reason for doubt because it is a property of the object of cognition (*prameyatva*). And this is a reason for doubt that pervades both sides in their entirety. Likewise, the argument "sound is not produced by effort, because it is impermanent" is also exclusively common (*sādhāraṇa*), because it occurs in some things not produced by effort, such as lightning, and because it exists in all things produced by effort, such as jars. Thus, this [reason] pervades the entire class of dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) and occurs in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Thus it should be understood. Likewise, regarding the argument "sound is produced by effort because it is impermanent," impermanence is observed in all things produced by effort; yet even in the absence of such effort, it is observed in some cases, such as clouds, but not in others, such as space.

It should be understood that this [reason] is "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) when it pervades the entire class of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) but resides in only one part of the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*). However, that which resides in only one part of both [classes] is, for example:

"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal. For incorporeality does not pervade all eternal things, since it exists in space (*vyoman*) and so forth but is absent in atoms (*aṇu*); nor does it pervade all non-eternal things, since it is absent in jars, walls, and so forth, as well as in actions (*karman*) and the like.

Because [the reason] exists [in both]. And in all such cases, the very fact that the reason occurs in both [similar and dissimilar instances] is the cause for doubt; however, although the aspect of its non-occurrence exists, it is not a cause and is therefore irrelevant. For this very reason, those who propose a fourfold division of the common (sādhāraṇa) reason find it entirely useless for proof or refutation, and thus it should be disregarded.

For at the time of stating the proof, the non-occurrence [of the reason] in both the similar and dissimilar instances is of no use whatsoever to a proponent who abandons such a reason. Indeed, even by the slightest degree, a reason that exists in the dissimilar instance must not be abandoned. For the opponent who states the refutation as well, it is sufficient to state merely the occurrence in the dissimilar instance; what is the point of resorting to its specific sub-varieties? This was also stated by the author of the Vārttika regarding those [reasons] common to all [fallacies].

The detailed exposition of examples was presented to demonstrate that the very state of having two possible modes of occurrence (*dvayavṛttitva*) is the cause of doubt, and not with the intention of implying a fourfold classification. As it has been said:
"But for a single [reason], there is no utility toward the pointing out of a refutation."
And thus, it is abandoned in the means as well, because of its commonality and especially its particularity. // 85 //
The common [cause of doubt] has been explained;

now he illustrates the uncommon cause of doubt: "Earth is eternal. For odor is the specific quality of earth; since it does not leave earth to reside in any other entity—whether eternal or non-eternal—it is called "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa).
He said: "Let it be that 'possessing odor' is uncommon;
but how can it be a cause of doubt?
For it is logical that a common [reason], which relies upon both sides and produces a cognition of non-settlement regarding the two, is a cause of doubt."

But the uncommon [reason], being excluded from both [sides], is not capable of producing a cognition even in one [of them]; so how could it be a cause for doubt? To this he says: "In the production of certainty... For in the production of certainty, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are the two necessary factors; if even one of these is missing, the reason is not sufficient for certainty. For example, the common [reason], although accompanied by positive concomitance, is deprived of [negative concomitance].

Just as [a reason] lacking negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not capable of producing certainty, so too the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, being deficient in one member of certainty called positive concomitance (*anvaya*), fails to produce it and thus becomes a cause of doubt. // 86 //

[Objection: Was it not already stated that a common property (*sādhāraṇa*), which goes to both [sides] and produces a cognition in both, is the cause of doubt? But a unique property (*asādhāraṇa*) does not inform one of anything at all; therefore, it is not logical to say that it is a cause of doubt merely by being deficient in one factor. To this, he says: "The common [property], etc."—by means of two [verses]. This is the intended meaning: even a common property is not a cause of doubt simply because it generates a cognition in both [cases].
However, it is by way of demonstrating two contradictory [properties] that doubt arises;

for when both are demonstrated, since their coexistence in a single locus is impossible, doubt results precisely from this contradiction. And this is no different even in the case of the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason], for the uncommon reason, by excluding [the subject] from both [categories] and thereby indicating their absence, generates doubt precisely because the absence of both is impossible. Indeed, it is not possible for a thing to be both eternal and non-eternal.
"It does not exist," [one might say];

for indeed, the entire world is established through pairs of properties such as permanence and impermanence. Therefore, the non-existence of both is contradictory. Nor is there the existence of both, precisely because of that contradiction. Furthermore, there can be no acceptance of either one exclusively, due to the lack of distinction. Having encountered this dilemma, the person who relies on valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*)...
He doubts. And here is the meaning of the individual parts: just as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) and so forth, being observed as common [to both sides], are the cause of two cognitions.

In the *bahuvrīhi* compound, "having two cognitions as its cause" (*buddhidvayanimitteka*), the word "cause" (*nimitta*) indicates that the two cognitions are merely the cause of the doubt; it refers to that which has the probandum and its absence as its objects.

For it is precisely by taking two contradictory cognitions as the cause that doubt is produced through a common property (*sādhāraṇa*), since neither of the two contradictory [properties] can be established [in the subject].
Indeed, a single sound cannot be pervaded by both eternality and non-eternality, which are mutually contradictory;
for the superimposition of contradictory properties is never observed, as in the case of "eternal space" and "non-eternal produced substance. Therefore, from this, what is the cognition?

From that very fact, doubt is produced by means of the common [reason]. And this same [process] applies to the uncommon [reason] as well. For that too, having established its absence in both what is eternal and what is non-eternal, brings about a contradiction regarding the existence of both through that very route, and thus becomes a cause of doubt. However, they do not accept this status of the uncommon [reason] as a cause of doubt.

For doubt arises when both [alternatives] revolve in the mind without a fixed determination. Furthermore, nothing at all is placed upon the intellect by means of a unique (asādhāraṇa) property, because that [unique property] lacks any positive concomitance (anvaya) with anything else. Moreover, doubt is observed only regarding finite entities, by way of their exclusion (nivṛtti).

Furthermore, if doubt were produced by an uncommon [reason] that is excluded from everything, then a doubt directed toward all things would be produced. Yet, a doubt whose object is everything has never been observed before, because it cannot enter the mind. Nor can the absence [of a property] in all cases be understood merely through its exclusion from some single instance.

Doubt would arise from whichever [alternative] is the case. For when positive concomitance (*anuvṛtti*) is not observed, negative exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) cannot be established. Indeed, smoke, which persists in fire, is understood through its observed deviation to have a nature restricted to fire; thus, it is understood by implication to be excluded from those non-fires that are not perceived. But how can there be [exclusion] for that which is not positively concomitant with anything at all, [given that it must be] from those things whose non-perception is possible?
Exclusion would be understood from every [instance]. Therefore, it is not in this manner that an uncommon property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) functions as a cause for doubt.

However, if it is argued that because entities possessing uncommon properties are seen to partake in both permanence and impermanence, upon perceiving the earth as possessing those same properties, a doubt arises as to whether it is permanent or impermanent—then, in that case, [the reason] is due to its being an uncommon property.
Thus, doubt arises from what is common to many, not from what is unique;

for the unique property is one thing, whereas the possession of that [property] by many others is quite another. Therefore, if this [possession] has become the cause of doubt, what has been gained for the unique [property]? Alas! In this way, you have effectively accepted that only the common [property] is the cause of doubt.
Success! A non-common [property] cannot be a cause of doubt. Another opinion holds: "This is indeed a cause of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*).

There is, it is said, a type of cognition called non-determination; that is produced by this [non-common property]. For one who perceives such a property, there arises a cognition of an unascertained appearance, in the form: "Of what kind is this property? And this is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Because it consists of non-ascertainment (*aniścayātmakatva*). Nor is it doubt (*saṃśaya*), because [doubt] does not touch upon two sides [of a proposition]. Thus, this kind of non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*) is produced by the uncommon [cause]. But this is not tenable. For there is no such variety of cognition as "non-ascertainment" which it could produce. Non-ascertainment is simply the absence of ascertainment; and since it is of the nature of a prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), it is not something that can be produced. If, on the other hand, the negative particle (*nañ*) is intended to mean "other than," as in the case of [the term] *agrāhyaṇa* and so forth, then from ascertainment...

Otherwise, that which is denoted by the word [anadhyavasāya] would be nothing other than doubt itself. Furthermore, it has already been stated that its cause is not an uncommon [reason]. Now, if the negative particle *nañ* were used in the sense of the opposite—as in the case of "non-dharma" (*adharmādi*)—then the word *anadhyavasāya* would have to denote the opposite [of ascertainment], namely, uncertainty.

Furthermore, a mistaken apprehension (*viparītāvagraha*) is not produced by the uncommon [reason] (*asādhāraṇa*). If, however, non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*) is simply the determination of the absence of ascertainment—namely, "I have no ascertainment regarding this object"—then that absence of ascertainment is understood precisely through the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*); in that case, the uncommon reason has no function. Therefore, it must be established that the uncommon [reason] is merely a cause for the desire to know (*jijñāsāmātra*). For indeed, in one who perceives such [an uncommon object], there arises the question: "What kind of property (*dharma*) does it possess?"

The inquiry is: "Could there be an entity [of this kind] apart from this property? Even though such an inquiry may sometimes arise even from the perception of a pure locus (*dharmī*), it nonetheless certainly arises by way of the property (*dharma*) as well; thus, its status as a cause [for that perception] is not untenable. And it has been said:
"Therefore, ignorance leads to an inquiry that does not go elsewhere, directed toward those [objects] which have not yet been established."
"Doubt is appropriate because of generality; likewise, it arises from a counter-argument.

As for the statement here that the "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa) [reason] is a cause of doubt, that is the opinion of another school. For what is intended here is to demonstrate the object to be excluded by the term "known relation" (jñātasambandha);
thus, even if the uncommon reason is a cause of doubt, it remains entirely consistent [with the definition]. Let this be so for whomever it may be.

The meaning is that the term "known relation in every respect" (*sarvathā jñātasambandha*) excludes the [pseudo-reason] called *hetu*. However, the Śākyas consider the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) to be a cause of doubt, and they cite "audibility" (*śrāvaṇatva*) when the probandum is the impermanence of sound. As it has been said:
The Śākyas generally consider this [reason] to be inconclusive,
because it is excluded from both [the similar and dissimilar instances], just as it would be if it were present in both.
Thus it is; and this very point was raised by the author of the Vārttika himself at another place and refuted by the aforementioned objections. // 88 //
Furthermore, is it the case that those [reasons] cited possess the nature of being causes of doubt inherently? No; he says: "The doubtful... (89).

He states the reason, ending with the word "having obtained" (*labdhvāntena*), by saying "of the determination" (*nirṇayasya*). Where has this been seen? To this he says: "in the case of being devoid of action" (*niṣkriya*). For incorporeality (*amūrtatā*), when the probandum is eternity, is a cause of doubt because it is common to eternal space, non-eternal space, and motion; however, that very same property, when the probandum is being devoid of action, attains the status of a logical reason (*hetu*) once positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) have been established. Indeed, incorporeality is pervaded by being devoid of action. For neither the ether (*gagana*) nor the self (*ātman*), though incorporeal, undergoes locomotion (*parispandate*). And yet, incorporeality does not belong to things like chariots which possess [action] in that way.
It has been seen. // 90 //

He demonstrates that the uncommon [reason] is the cause for definitive determination (*nirṇaya*)—namely, "a portion of the earth" (*kṣityekadeśa*). For one who perceives a specific odor and has recognized the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there arises an inferential determination when a portion of the earth is established.

It has been stated that two reasons connected to contradictory objects, when applied to a single locus, constitute a cause for doubt. Regarding that, he provides an example: "Where... and so forth. For in a case where one person establishes that air is not the object of direct perception because it lacks color (*arūpatvāt*), while another establishes the opposite of that because of its tangibility (*sparśāt*), there occurs what the Śākyas call *viruddhāvyabhicāritā* (the state of being non-deviant despite being contradictory).

This has been stated. In that regard, doubt arises from the convergence of two reasons of equal strength, because there is no distinction between the two proofs in terms of their having well-established constituent parts. For the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that what is formless, when inhering in something formless, is not perceptible; and such is the case with air. Therefore, it is not perceptible. Furthermore, they declare that even the nature of action is visible to the eye due to its inherence in the same object as form. The same applies to touch.

The existence of air is indeed well-established; moreover, its pervasion is well-established by means of direct perception. Therefore, they possess equal force. Consequently, there arises doubt, because it is impossible for two contradictory [cognitions] to occur simultaneously in one place, and because their conjunction is untenable.

Furthermore, since conceptual construction is impossible regarding an established entity, even the relationship between the sublated and the sublator would be of equal status. Consequently, as both [alternatives] fluctuate due to this lack of finality (*anavasthā*), doubt arises because of their identity. As for the distinction between their relative strength and weakness, the contradiction with inference has already been described.
For example: "The Buddha’s word that 'the omniscient one exists' is correct, because it was spoken by him, just like the statements on momentary destruction and so forth."

When one person has said this, another declares: "The Buddha is not omniscient, because my statement is correct, just as fire is hot and water is liquid. In this case, the fact that [the reason] is stated by me is established for both parties; however, the fact that it was stated by the Buddha is not established for us. Therefore, because its constituent part (*aṅga*) is unestablished, the former proof is sublated by the latter, which possesses an established constituent part. As for the expression "the non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*), where two [reasons] are denoted by a single word ending in the nominative case—what of that?
We say: "The non-erroneous contradictory [reason] is a cause of doubt"—so the Śākyas claim. Is this not so?

For whose sake would it be a cause of doubt, since one of the two [alternatives] must be determined? Nor does the singular number intend to refer to a collection, because that [collection] lacks the status of being a term due to the words *viruddha* (contradictory) and *avyabhicārin* (non-erroneous). Indeed, by its two parts, it is precisely erroneous (*vyabhicārin*). However, there are two [types of] non-erroneous contradictories.

Thus it should be stated, and not in the singular. If it is argued that because each individual [reason] does not deviate from an object that is opposed by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), it is therefore called "non-deviatingly contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*), let that be so. However, it has been stated that a single [such reason] is not a cause for doubt. For this very reason, the author of the *Vārttika* speaks of two [reasons] connected with contradictory objects.

By using the dual ending in the name *saṃśayahetū*, it is shown that the state of being a cause of doubt belongs to two [reasons]. Here too, only the term *viruddhāvyabhicāritā* is mentioned; however, it is not stated as *viruddhāvyabhicārī saṃśayahetuḥ*. Therefore, in this context, it should be explained by implication (*yogyatayā*) as "the state of being non-deviant despite being contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritā*) belonging to these two, meaning "two [reasons] that are non-deviant despite being contradictory. // 91 //

Some describe this *viruddhāvyabhicāritā* (the state of being non-deviant despite being contradictory), which is a cause for doubt, as a distinct category (*jātyantara*) from both the common (*sādhāraṇa*) and the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Others, however, maintain that it is a sub-class of the common (*sādhāraṇa*), since it consists of two parts of a single aggregate. Still others, on the other hand, have maintained that this combined pair is not present in either [of the two alternatives] individually, and thus it is a case of non-concomitance (*ananvaya*), which is simply the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*).
He says: "Some [hold this view]. And in another passage, the author of the Vārttika has demonstrated his adherence to the position of commonality (*sādhāraṇya*). As he says:
"Because of its commonality, no distinction whatsoever exists for this;
for the whole, situated in the word 'common,' consists of two parts."

Thus it is said. Nor should it be argued that because the two [reasons] do not co-occur, this [reason] is exclusively *asādhāraṇa* (uncommon). For if the two were employed by a single [subject], then it might indeed be so; however, since they are seen to co-occur individually, when employed together by the two [subjects], it cannot be said that they do not co-occur. Furthermore, if it were *asādhāraṇa*, its status as a cause for doubt would be untenable, because that has already been refuted previously. Therefore, this is indeed *sādhāraṇa* (common).

We, however, consider it better to treat these as entirely distinct types [of reasons]. For just as it is not the case that they lack exclusivity because two [reasons] are not employed by one [person], so too there would likewise be no commonality [between them]. What, then, is common here? It is that each [reason], being pervaded by its respective [property], is employed individually.

And because a common [reason] is not employed as a whole collection [of both]. For this very reason, the fact that the counter-reason (*pratihetu*) and the contradictory reason (*viruddha*) are causes of doubt is stated here as distinct from the common [reason]; otherwise, since they would be included by that [common reason] alone, they would not be mentioned separately.
Furthermore, the manner in which doubt is generated here is indeed different: for while the common [reason] produces a cognition by being observed in both [sides], [the others do not].

However, the author of the Vārttika has stated that these two, by each presenting both [alternatives], are causes of doubt while remaining in the state of being "common" (sādhāraṇa), rather than being exclusively "common. 92.
But how is a decision reached in such a case?

To this he says: "The proposition" [is that which ends with] the conclusion. When the proposition (*pratijñā*), which is a member of the proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*), is sublated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as perception and so forth—as described under the section on the sublation of the thesis (*pakṣabādha*), then a decision must be made in favor of the other party through that defeat. As in this very instance:

To begin with, in the case of the example, when air is being directly experienced through the operation of the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*), the position that it is imperceptible is sublated by that very experience. For the direct perception of air does not differ from the direct perception of water arising from the tactile sense organ. Indeed, in this case, it is not a mere touch without a substratum that is experienced; rather, it is the substance which serves as the locus of that touch.

Furthermore, for one being struck by a powerful wind, the cognition of water clinging [to it] does not become distinct. Therefore, based on the result of the sense-organ's connection [with its object], it is determined that air is perceptible. In some cases, however, there is a sublation of the object by means of scripture, as in: "The human skull is pure."
When Pāśupata has stated, "Because it is a part of a living being,
like a fragment of conch-shell or mother-of-pearl," another person establishes that it is impure,

[arguing] "Because it originates from a living being, like excrement and so forth. In that case, since the subject matter of the former proposition is sublated by scripture (āgama), the determination of the meaning is made by the latter.
It is so. For when the matter of purity is to be distinguished, scripture alone is the refuge. When that [scripture] stands as an obstacle, an inference of purity cannot establish itself.
For they remember:
"Having touched a human bone that is still moist with fat, one should enter the water along with one's clothes."

Thus [it is said]. For Rudra indeed performed the Great Vow (mahāvrata), and the statement "he placed this head of a corpse" is merely an explanatory passage (arthavāda), not an injunction for the wearing of a corpse's head. And here, it is by means of the word "means" (sādhana) that perception and the other [pramāṇas] are referred to, as they establish their respective objects through their own nature. But how can perception and the others alone venture to subvert the thesis?
Since even in those cases sublation might be suspected on the basis of general observation, he says: "Because of the absence of sublation.
For no sublation is actually seen in them; however, the mere possibility of sublation at some time does not remove their status as valid means of knowledge. // 93 //

In this context, by the use of the singular number in the phrase "the reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) pervaded by its part (*tadaṃśena vyāptaḥ*)," it is shown that the reason is intended to be of a single number—that is, there is only one reason. For this very reason, two reasons that are contradictory yet non-deviant (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) do not constitute valid reasons, because they are multiple.
And this [position] is not tenable; for indeed, [there is no such thing as a] counter-reason... [3, ...]
The plurality of two contradictory [reasons] is not the cause for being a ground of doubt;

rather, it is precisely their capacity to introduce two mutually contradictory meanings. For when two contradictory meanings are introduced together in one place by two [reasons], people become doubtful therein—not because of the plurality of reasons, but because of the coexistence of both [meanings] even when each of the two grounds of doubt is individually understood. In some cases, this occurs simply from the convergence of both.

A definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) is observed, as in the case of verticality and the presence of a crow. For verticality alone is common to both a post and a person, and thus is not capable of producing a determination for either one. However, that same verticality, when accompanied by the perching of a crow, leads to the certain conclusion: "This is a post. Therefore, in this instance, while a single factor serves as the cause of doubt, it is through two factors combined that determination occurs; thus, the plurality [of causes] is irrelevant to the state of being a cause of doubt.

The state of having multiple contradictory probanda (*viruddhānekasādhyatva*) alone is the cause of doubt. For just as a single common [reason] existing in both the similar and dissimilar instances is a cause of doubt, so too, when two reasons with contradictory meanings both apply to their respective parts, their very presence in both is the cause of doubt; therefore, it is not correct to deny the status of being a reason simply because there are two of them. Thus he says: "In some cases... (*kvacid*).

Thus [it is said]. Now, it may be argued: "It is indeed reasonable that doubt regarding a post or a person arises from its verticality; however, doubt has never been observed to arise from the mere presence of a crow. True. But for one who wishes to establish that it is a post based on the mere presence of a crow, that [crow] alone is a cause of doubt; whereas when accompanied by verticality, it becomes a cause of certainty—it is only this much that was intended to be said, and thus there is no fault. Furthermore, regarding two non-contradictory [factors]...
In some cases, the status of being a logical reason (*hetu*) is observed even when two factors—whether individually or combined—are directed toward a single probandum (*sādhya*).

For example, in the case of verbal cognition (*śābdajñāna*), its status as inference (*anumānatva*) can be established by either [of the following] individually or by both together: its being produced from positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekaja*), and its being a means of valid cognition other than perception (*pratyakṣānyapramāṇatva*). Furthermore, when there is a duality [of reasons], the cause for their being fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) lies in this very [fact].

Multiple reasons should not be employed for a single probandum (*sādhya*). However, practitioners are seen employing various means of proof (*nānāsādhana*) to establish a single probandum as well as something else. Therefore, with the intention that doubt is based solely on contradiction and not on multiplicity, he says: "each individually. Previously, however, [it was said] regarding two causes of doubt taken individually.

Thus, it has been stated that the two [reasons] together constitute the cause for a definitive conclusion. Here, however, it is demonstrated that although each is individually indicative, they are also indicative when combined. // 95 //

Therefore, only those [reasons] that possess contradictory meanings should be shown as causes of doubt, and not merely by virtue of being different, as we have stated. Thus he says, "Therefore. Having explained the threefold cause of doubt, he announces the contrary types: "Some say there are six kinds of contradiction. This means that some maintain there are six modes of contradiction, consisting of contradictions regarding the nature of the property (*dharma*), the nature of the subject (*dharmin*), their own specific qualities (*svaviśeṣa*), both natures, and both specific qualities. Others, however, [hold that these are not distinct], because the two contradictions of both [property and subject] do not exceed the individual cases.

He says "or fourfold" to indicate that [others] have proposed a fourfold classification.
