He says "or even in one way" to show that we, however, maintain there is only a single type by the mere fact of the sublation of what was desired. The word "or" (*vā*) also serves to exclude the two previously mentioned positions. Furthermore, since the very subversion of the position—namely, that "it would belong to those who partake of the remainder"—is the cause of its being contradictory (*viruddha*), what is the point of introducing these intermediate subdivisions?

And they say that in all three modes, there is "contradiction" (*viruddhatā*) when there is a sublation of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) as presented by both the explicit statement and its implied sense; thus he says: "of that which is stated by the explicit statement and its sense. The nature of the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), and both together is what is stated by the explicit statement (*śrutya-ukta*);

however, their specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are for the most part stated by implication (*arthokta*). And those natures and their specific qualities are what are denoted by the term "meaning of the proposition" (*pratijñārtha*).
For all those [qualifiers] are intended by the speaker; however, specific attributes such as "dharma" and so forth are not explicitly included within the proposition (*pratijñā*) itself.

Thus, when this meaning of the proposition is sublated by the reason (*hetu*), the reason becomes contradictory (*viruddha*). Yet, we consider this to be somewhat like a contradiction. For how could a reason be contradictory when the meaning of the proposition is being sublated by that very reason?

It occurs. For it is appropriate to say that this [reason] "contradicts" (*viroddhet*) because it opposes the meaning of the thesis, or rather that it is a "sublater" (*bādhaka*). And it is not this very [reason] that is sublated by the meaning of the thesis such that it would become contradictory; for this [reason] is well-established (*prasiddhatvāt*). Indeed, the producedness (*kṛtakatva*) of a jar is well-established;
it cannot be sublated by an eternality (*nityatā*) that is itself unestablished. Therefore, this should be called a "sublater" (*bādhaka*), as stated by the author of the *Vārttika*.

It should be understood that it was stated [the reason] is contradictory merely by virtue of what is established for the opponent. In this regard, he first illustrates its contradiction through the sublation of the essential nature of the property (*dharma-svarūpa-bādha*) with the words: "If [it were] eternal... (97).

"But there is indeed a sublation of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*) when it is formulated in this way," he says—namely, "sublation. He demonstrates that very formulation with the three quarters [of the verse] beginning with "arthavat" (meaningful). For those who maintain that words denote the essential form (*svarūpa*) say: "In the cognition 'this is a cow,' an object qualified by the form of the word is understood. And it is not possible to denote a qualified object without denoting its qualifier."

It is possible that a word first denotes its own form (*svarūpa*) and only thereafter [denotes] the qualified object. Furthermore, the word "object" (*artha*) is subject to deviation, because for one who has not grasped the relationship [between word and object], the object is not cognized. However, the word's own form never deviates, since it is cognized even prior to the determination of the relationship.

And it is logical that the meaning of a word is non-deviant. Therefore, the intrinsic form (*svarūpa*) of words must necessarily be denoted; let there be the denotation of specific qualifiers at a time subsequent to that denotation. Having thus established their position, they state the formal argument (*prayoga*) at the end: "The intrinsic form of a word possesses meaning prior to the determination of its relationship [to a referent], for even one who has not grasped the relationship understands words joined with case-endings such as *su* and so forth. And when there is the connection with a case-ending...

In that case, purposiveness is observed just as it is after the apprehension of the relationship. But how, when formulated in this way, does there come to be a sublation of a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣabādha*)? To this he says: "And [purposiveness] is resorted to by way of its own nature. For when purposiveness is first resorted to by way of the object in its own nature, and what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is established as being merely qualified by purposiveness, [the sublation occurs].

From this, it is understood by implication that what he intends to prove is its possession of meaning through its own nature (*svarūpa*). And thus, there occurs a sublation of a specific property (*dharma-viśeṣa*) which is implied by the sense. But how is a specific property sublated when "by way of its own nature" is accepted? To this he says: "not its own nature" (*asvarūpa*). For "possessing meaning" [in this context] means having meaning through something other than its own nature, namely, through the state of possessing case-endings (*vibhaktimat-tva*).

By the force of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the word causes [the object] to be understood, because after the relationship has been grasped, another object is perceived. Therefore, by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), that very [object] is established as possessing case-endings. Consequently, this reason—that it possesses its own form as its meaning—contradicts the specific quality of "possessing meaning" (*arthavattā*).
Thus, there is a sublation of a specific property of the dharma. // 99 //

He states an example of the sublation of the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) with the words "ihapratyaya" (the cognition of "here"). For when one takes *samavāya* as the subject and seeks to prove its distinction from substance and so forth, and the reason (*hetu*) stated is "being the cause of the cognition of 'here'," with "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*)—as in the case of "this pot is here"—serving as the corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), then there is sublation of the nature of the subject; such is the intended meaning. // 100 //
But how, then, is there a sublation of the nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpabādha*) in this example?

To this, he says: "In this case too. In this example as well, because the nature of the subject—which consists of inherence—is brought to the opposite state, the reason becomes contradictory (*viruddha*). For it is observed that the status of being the cause of the notion of "herein" (*ihapratyaya*) belongs only to that which does not consist of inherence; thus, its identity with that [nature] is sublated.
"One would contradict" means that there is a sublation of the very nature of the subject (*dharmī*). // 101 //

And in this very case, one must also demonstrate the sublation of a specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*); thus he says: "And that which... For the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) maintain that inherence (*samavāya*) is of a single nature, just like the universal "existence" (*sattāsāmānya*). Yet even this specific property of its [the inherence's] is sublated because it would follow that it is differentiated, just like conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Thus, the reason is one that contradicts a specific property of the subject. // 102 //

He provides an example for the sublation of both the nature [of the property and the subject]—namely, "the self exists eternally. When someone proves to a Sautrāntika that "the self is eternal because it is partless, like space," then there is a sublation of both the property and the subject. For the Sautrāntika maintains that the absence of parts is connected precisely with the non-existence of space; thus, he would likewise conclude the non-existence of the self.
Indeed, space is merely the absence of obstruction.

The Buddhists, however, maintain that [the self] is not a different reality. Therefore, because the self is partless, there is a sublation of both: the sublation of its own nature and the sublation of its property of permanence. Thus, when this is being proven, there occurs a sublation of both specific qualities; he says "then" (*tadā*) to indicate this. For when it is argued that "the eyes and other [senses] are for the sake of another because they are composite, like a bed and so forth," then there is a sublation of both specific qualities—this is the meaning. But how, in this case, is there a sublation of both specific qualities?

Therefore, he says: "on a bed. For on a bed, such as a couch, the reason—"because it is a composite"—is observed to be pervaded by "being for the sake of another" in the case of a body composed of the great elements; thus, it would only establish that it is for the sake of something else which is itself a composite. Yet, what is intended to be established is its being for the sake of another, namely, the Self.

That would not be established. First of all, that specific property of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) which is intended—namely, being for the sake of the Self—is sublated by this very reason. Furthermore, even that specific property of the subject (*dharmin*), such as the eye and so forth, namely its being composed of ego-consciousness (*āhaṅkārika*), is sublated by this same reason. For being composed of a composite nature (*saṃhatātmakatva*) is observed to be pervaded by non-ego-consciousness in things such as beds and the like.
For those [objects] are composed of the elements (*bhautika*);

therefore, by that same illustration, the eyes and other sense organs would also be composed of the elements. The followers of Kapila (*kāpila*) maintain that the sense organs are derived from the ego-principle (*āhaṅkārika*), and their argument is as follows: this point means that [the status of being composed of the elements] is pervaded by both the state of being for the sake of another when combined (*saṃhatapārārthya*) and the state of being composed of the elements (*bhautikatva*).

In that argument where the reason (*hetu*) resides, the fact that it exists for the sake of both self and others (*ātmapārārthya*) is unestablished; thus, there is first of all a sublation of the qualification of the property (*dharmaviśeṣabādhana*).

Furthermore, the sublation of the qualification of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*) was indicated by the mention of "pervasion by material elements" (*bhautikavyāpti*) and will be explained immediately thereafter.
Therefore, not only is the existence for the sake of both self and others not established, [but the reason is also unestablished].

If both being non-composite in form and having the self as one's own purpose are intended [as properties of the body], then by the force of pervasion (vyāpti), it follows that the self itself must be composite;

thus he says, "non-composite" (*asaṃhata*). By this, it should be understood that an undesired consequence has been brought forward. This is what is meant: by this reason, the state of having the self as one's own purpose while being non-composite in form is not established; on the contrary, the self would instead become composite. // 106 //
He explains the sublation of the specific subject (*dharmiviśeṣabādha*) by stating "the state of not being derived from *ahaṅkāra*. This has already been explained previously. // 106 //

Thus, the contradictory (*viruddha*) reason, which is excluded by the phrase "whose relation is known" (*jñātasambandha*), has been explained in detail. Now, the fallacious examples (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*), which are likewise excluded by that same phrase, must be shown; for by means of them, the relation that constitutes a limb of inference cannot be made known.
Therefore, they too are excluded by the very words "whose relation is known. And this has already been stated by us previously. As it is said elsewhere:

And by the statement "the relationship between which is known," the three faults of the reason and the example, beginning with the "uncertain" (aniyata), have been refuted here by the author of the Bhāṣya.
Thus [it is said]. Therefore, in order to refute that [view], he first introduces the statement regarding the example (dṛṣṭānta) with the words "of the indicator" (gamakasya).

The meaning is that two kinds of examples must be shown in the proof-statement (sādhana-vākya) for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (vyāpti); namely, the example which, through similarity to or dissimilarity from the subject (pakṣa)—the locus of the property to be proven—is presented. // 107 //

Regarding that, he states the method of the concordant example: "In that regard" (*tatra*). Its meaning is as follows: the statement of the probans (*liṅga*) as being the means of establishing [the probandum] through its similarity with the example is the logical reason (*hetu*).
As they say: "The logical reason is the means of proving the probandum through its similarity with the example.
This amounts to saying it is the statement that makes known the probandum (*sādhya*). And its object is precisely the probans (*liṅga*). Having pointed that out...

The inclusion of the probandum (*sādhya*) is required in a positive example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), as in the formulation: "Whatever possesses smoke, that possesses fire," and so forth. To the question, "What is accomplished by including it in this way? he replies: "The subject" (*uddeśya*). It has been stated that the statement of the example is for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*). And when it is included in this manner, the subject—such as smoke—is stated as the pervaded (*vyāpya*); whereas the other [the property to be proved] is the included [pervader].

"Fire and so forth [are the means] by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*); thus, because it conforms to pervasion, such an adoption is indeed fruitful. Therefore, it has been stated that there exists a relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakatva*) between the object to be indicated (*uddeśya*) and the means of adoption (*upādeya*). // 108 //

What, then, is the nature of those two? To this he says: "yadvṛtta... (That which occurs in the relative clause...). By the terms *yadvṛtta* and *tadvṛtta*, there is the inclusion of words such as "whatever" (*yat-tat*) among those fully established [terms].

This is the meaning that results: whatever is first employed in connection with the relative clause (*yadvṛtta*), being primary and intended as the subject of reference, and whatever is subsequently employed in connection with the correlative clause (*tadvṛtta*), being joined by the particle *eva* (only/just), that is the term to be taken up as the predicate (*upādeya*).

And it should be understood that this very same distinction applies to all instances of things to be specified (*uddeśya*) and things to be taken up (*upādeya*), such as the sweeping of the planets and the threshing of grain. // 109 //

But what is the purpose of such a restriction on the application [of words], given that words are dependent upon the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*)? Whether they are applied in this way or that, they will certainly function according to the speaker's intent. To this he says: "He speaks. Words are not dependent solely upon the speaker's intention.

However, it must be stated that words function toward specific meanings only through their inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*), and therefore the desired result is not achieved by following the speaker's intention; thus, the manner of arranging the statement of the example is indeed essential. // 110 //

If, then, words were independent, so that even when an object does not exist in such a manner, the desired goal would be established by following the words, he says: "The state of being the probandum and the reason. This is the intended meaning: the power of the object does not function in accordance with the power of the word, nor does the power of the word [function] in accordance with the power of the object.
Therefore, just as the power of a word does not follow the meaning intended by the speaker, so too the determination of meaning does not follow the word;

rather, the relationship of probandum and probans regarding meanings such as "producedness" and "impermanence" occurs solely in accordance with the power of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not in accordance with the word. // 110 //

He demonstrates what follows when a word expresses its meaning solely by its own power, independent of the speaker, with the two and a half verses beginning with "tatrājñānāt. For instance, when a speaker who is ignorant of how to state an example intends merely to express the coexistence (*sahabhāva*) of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the reason (*hetu*), as in the formulation: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced."

Just as in the case of a jar, [one might say] "producedness" and "perishability" exist; or else, through a mistaken apprehension, one does not intend to express the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*). Even if such an intention were present, due to some cause of error, one would not utter a word capable of expressing pervasion, but would instead state only the mere coexistence (*sahabhāva*), as before.

Or, if one is mistaken and [thinks] the opposite—that perishability is pervaded by being produced—then not only is the intended [point] not established, but rather the unintended [consequence] follows from the reversal of the pervasion. The status of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) as the logical reason (*hetu*) would not obtain; instead, it would belong to the unintended "perishability" (*nāśitva*). It is for the sake of preventing such applications of unintended [reasons] that [the rule is stated].

"The rule for the application of examples is thus established. He concludes this very point with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The meaning is that what is accepted as a logical reason (*hetu*) must be expressed by way of its being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) by [the property], such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth. // 113 //
He demonstrates what occurs when objects are dependent upon words by means of the two quarters beginning with "yad etat. Its meaning is as follows:

for when the status of objects as probandum and probans follows solely from the power of pervasion (*vyāpti-śakti*), then even if the speaker has not merely shown their coexistence, [the logical relation is established].

However, while the statement of the example (*dṛṣṭāntavacana*) is indeed correct, the actual entities do not exist in a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) corresponding to that [example]; thus, it constitutes a fallacy of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā*).
This is to be connected with what will be stated hereafter. For instance, in the formal argument (*prayoga*): "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like an action (*karman*)."

In the examples—namely, like an atom, like a jar, and like space—they are respectively devoid of the pervasion of both the probandum and the reason from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). Indeed, since action is impermanent, it is devoid of the permanence that constitutes the probandum; however, the reason "because of being formless" does indeed exist therein. But atoms possess form; therefore, in their case, there is a lack of the reason.

The property to be proven (sādhya), namely permanence, indeed exists in those [atoms]. However, in the case of a jar, neither is permanence the property to be proven nor is incorporeality the reason; thus, there is a void regarding both. Furthermore, he will himself later explain the lack of pervasion (vyāpti) in the example of space. And in this very context, when the example "like space" is employed against the Sautrāntika who denies that [space], [the argument fails] due to the non-establishment of the locus (dharmin).
He says that there is the fallacy of the example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsatā) with the words: "tadasadvādinam" (regarding one who speaks of that as non-existent). // 116 //

He explains the lack of pervasion (*vyāptiśūnyatā*) with the words: "even when that exists. For even if space (*vyoman*) were to exist—and it would indeed be endowed with both the reason and the probandum because it is eternal and incorporeal—nevertheless, [the reason is absent] in respect to actions (*karman*) and so forth, which are incorporeal.
When impermanent things are being examined, there is no pervasion by the reason; thus, even such an example must be rejected.
This too is not capable of establishing the probandum, because [it lacks the necessary connection]. // 117 //
The example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), along with its fallacies, has been explained. Hereafter, he will explain the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

In this regard, first of all, this must be stated: must the statement of dissimilarity always be made just as the statement of similarity is, or not? In that context, those who maintain that the method of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is primary argue that it must always be stated.

He replies to them: "Similarity has been stated by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*). He thinks as follows: The statement of an example is for the purpose of making pervasion known; if that pervasion has already been made known by the statement of similarity (*sādharmya*), what is the use of stating dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)? Furthermore, similarity must necessarily be stated in order to make the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) known, because inference is primarily based upon that. This is because negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also established precisely through that [positive concomitance], whereas otherwise it would be difficult to comprehend. Therefore, if similarity accompanied by pervasion has been stated, [the purpose is fulfilled].

"Enough with the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya). When, then, should dissimilarity be stated? To this he replies with the three quarters [of a verse] beginning with "because of the observation of coexistence" (*sahabhāvitvadṛṣṭyā*). For when the speaker has stated the example correctly, the other—the listener—understands:
"By this, only the mere coexistence of the reason and the probandum has been stated, not the pervasion (*vyāpti*)."

Then, the connection is with what will be said later: "the establishment of the desired [conclusion] by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in order to make known the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent. Indeed, when one who has practiced the method of dissimilarity relies on that alone and not on a similar example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), then he says, "the establishment of the desired [conclusion] by way of dissimilarity"—or rather, "when he does not rely on that. Or, when the speaker...

When one who is poorly trained in dissimilarity (vaidharmya) does not know how to state similarity (sādharmya), and thus states by means of that similar example merely coexistence (sahabhāva) alone—pure and devoid of pervasion (vyāpti)—then, being questioned, he must establish his desired proof by means of that very dissimilarity; thus [the author] says: "Or the speaker," etc. (119).

Or, when one who is mistaken demonstrates a reversed positive concomitance (*anvaya*), even then, with the desire to rectify that [error], by subverting the previous erroneous cognition through a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*), he states that the desired proof is established—namely, "the reversed positive concomitance. Now, one might object: "If there is a reversal of the positive concomitance, let that very [concomitance] be presented correctly; what is the use of stating a dissimilar instance? True, this too would indeed establish the desired [point].

However, this was stated by us under a misconception—that what is intended is the absence of the reason when the probandum is absent; thus, even by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya), it certainly serves as a proof of the desired [conclusion]. As for that mere concomitance mentioned previously, it is useful precisely in the case of dissimilarity, as it functions to support that very thing which establishes the desired [conclusion]; thus he says: "mere concomitance" (sāhityamātra). // 120 //
Thus far, the occasion for stating the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya) has been shown; now he demonstrates the manner of stating it: "For the relation of pervaded and pervader... (121).

He states the reason for the contrapositive: "The state of smoke. For when the state of smoke is pervaded by the state of fire, then the absence of fire—that is, the non-existence of fire—is excluded from that smoke; thus, being excluded from where there is no smoke, it exists only where there is the absence of smoke.
In this way, it is pervaded. Indeed, that which occurs when something else is present and does not occur when that thing is absent is necessarily dependent upon it.

Therefore, it is said that [the former] is pervaded by [the latter]. Just as smoke, occurring only where there is fire, is established as being pervaded by fire, so too is the reversal of the pervasion between two absences established. // 122 //

And because there is such a relationship of pervaded and pervader between two absences, for that very reason the intended pervasion between two positive entities is established; thus he says: "In the same way, in the case of non-fire. When non-fire—that is, the absence of fire—is pervaded by the absence of smoke, smoke finds no room there due to the pervasion of its opposite, and thus exists only in fire; in this manner, its status as being pervaded by that [fire] is established. "In the same way" means just as...
The meaning is that the pervasion of non-existence depends upon the pervasion of existence, and likewise, the pervasion of existence depends upon the pervasion of non-existence.
Nor does this result in mutual dependence, because it is established as being beginningless, like the relationship between a seed and a sprout. // 123 //
{3,76} But what is the purpose of resorting to the reversal of pervasion between two absences? To this he says: "But the two pervaders...
For when a particular presence is the pervader, its absence alone is stated as the negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) by virtue of being the pervader;

in that case, the exclusion of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), such as non-fire, from the pervaded, such as smoke, would not have been stated at all. It is for the sake of stating that [exclusion]...

And the statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-vacana*) would be purposeful. For, just as in the case of "where there is smoke, there is fire," when it is stated that "where there is an absence of smoke, there is an absence of fire," the exclusion of the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), namely non-fire, from the pervaded (*vyāpya*), namely smoke, is thereby demonstrated. Therefore...

One who wishes to establish fire by means of smoke must state the reversal of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the absence of fire and the absence of smoke by way of a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus he says, "Therefore... up to the end [of the verse]. The meaning is that the relationship of the subject (*uddeśya*) and the predicate (*upādeya*) must be shown through the loci of occurrence (*yadvṛtta*) and the locus of the consequence (*tadvṛtta*), as follows: "Where there is no fire, there is no smoke. Furthermore, when stating that non-fire is pervaded by the absence of smoke, it must not be stated otherwise.

However, [the author] says "nor otherwise" to indicate that it is precisely by means of the mode of stating the subject and the predicate through similarity (*sādharmya*) that [the definition is established]; and this mode has been explained immediately above. (124–125)

He states the fault in speaking otherwise: "in the coexistence of non-fire and smoke. Just as in the case of the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), a word expresses its object through its own power and does not conform to the power of the object; thus it was stated that if one speaks merely of coexistence or if there is a reversal of pervasion (*vyāpti*), the desired [conclusion] is not established.
The meaning is that it is likewise here as well. // 126 //
Thus, even here, the meaning does not depend on the word; therefore, where the meaning takes the form of an example and is devoid of either both— the reason and the probandum— or one of them,
there too it does not assist the subject at hand, or else some other undesirable consequence follows.

Thus he says, "even where. The meaning is that even when a statement is correctly formulated, the desired conclusion is not established because the object [to be proven] does not depend upon it. He provides an example for this: "{3, 77} That which... In the very same argument—"Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal"—when such a dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is stated:

If one says, "Whatever is not eternal is also not formless, just like an atom," then the example is devoid of the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva-śūnya*), because since the atom is eternal, it is impossible to demonstrate the absence of that [non-eternality] therein. However, in the example "like cognition" (*buddhivat*), there is a lack of the absence of the reason (*hetvabhāva-śūnyatā*), because since cognition is formless, it is impossible to state the absence of that [formlessness].
The term *khavat* refers to the emptiness of the absence of both;
for since it is eternal and formless, the absence of both is difficult to apprehend therein. // 127 //

In this way, just as with a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one must demonstrate that [an instance] is fallacious even when there is a deficiency in pervasion (*vyāpti*). For it is for the sake of establishing that [pervasion] that the exclusion of the reason from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is stated. However, that which lacks exclusion even from a portion of the dissimilar instances is not pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, since pervasion is absent, the statement of such a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya*) is useless. With this intention, he says: "by the probandum" (verse 128).

And because such a [reason] is not pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*), it follows that even when the coexistence of two absences is observed in some instances, the relationship of indicator and indicated (*gamya-gamakabhāva*) does not necessarily hold everywhere; thus he says: "by that" (*tena*). For although that which is not eternal is also not incorporeal (*amūrta*), [the reverse is not true].
Just as one can demonstrate the coexistence of two absences in certain cases, such as "the jar or the wall," nevertheless, this does not apply to all [instances],
such as sound and so forth.

By this reason, [the subject] is intended to be understood as qualified by permanence. For some things that are formless, such as space and so forth, are permanent, while others, such as action and so forth, are impermanent; such is the sense. // 129 //

"Why is this not accepted? To this he says: "Because it is [mere] co-observation. For by the exclusion from only one part of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), only the mere concomitance (*sahabhāva*) of the reason is established. And that mere connection is not a constituent of inference. What then? It is pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor is this established by such mere association. He demonstrates this very point by means of an example: "Even though [the reason] is joined with corporeality and impermanence. This has already been explained previously. Here the Buddhists say: "What is this..."

It is said that when positive concomitance (*sādharmya*) has been stated through pervasion (*vyāpti*), negative concomitance (*vaidharmya*) is not required; for if there is even a hundredth part of doubt regarding the reason’s exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it lacks the capacity to produce knowledge. Therefore, the entire counter-example must be relied upon by the inferer to grasp that exclusion. And this is not difficult to ascertain.

Because it is easy to achieve non-perception of everything even for one who is situated in only one place. For indeed, the perception of all counter-instances (*vipakṣa*) is difficult, whereas their absence is obtained with ease. Nor should it be said that this non-perception is incapable of establishing the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of the reason due to being an "unqualified non-perception" (*ayogyānupalambha*). For we do not hold that the necessity of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-niyama*) arises from the non-perception of counter-instances; rather, it is based on identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*).

However, when there is a perception of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), which acts as an obstacle to the reason (*hetu*), it becomes impossible to grasp the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Since that [invariable concomitance] does not exist even for one who stands in only a single part [of the domain], the observation of its occurrence in the presence of the obstacle is what functions [to establish it]. Therefore, as soon as it is understood that smoke is the effect of fire, it is simultaneously known that its acquisition of its own existence (*ātmalābha*) is dependent upon that [fire] and does not occur in its absence. Not...

Furthermore, positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone cannot be the basis for the cognition of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because it is impossible [to perceive it] in the case of unique particulars (*asādhāraṇa*). For there is no perception elsewhere of the specific characters (*svalakṣaṇa*) of fire and smoke observed in the kitchen, once they have ceased to exist right there, by which means positive concomitance could be experienced. Thus, how can there be positive concomitance, and how much less so the negative concomitance based upon it? Moreover, among particular entities, there exists no such thing as a "universal" (*sāmānya*) that possesses a recurring intrinsic nature.

Since that [relation] would have to be determined as one of the constrained and the constraint, it would necessarily be of the nature of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it is only certain particularities (*viśeṣa*), characterized by some form of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), that indicate a certain particularity—namely, the exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*)—by way of such exclusion. Consequently, for the purpose of demonstrating this, it is logical that only a statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) should be employed.

Thus [it is said]. He replies to them with the words beginning "aśeṣa" and ending with "yukti. This is the intended meaning: although negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is a constituent part of inference, it is not established by mere non-perception alone, because its occurrence is also possible due to not having gone to that place. Nor does the absence [of the effect] when the cause is absent follow simply from the determination of its being an effect.

Because its absence [in the dissimilar instance] is difficult to ascertain precisely when there is no such distinction. For that which occurs when something exists and does not occur when it is absent is the effect of that thing; therefore, the absence [of the reason] when the [effect] is absent must be understood. Consequently, if it were an effect dependent upon that [subject], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatā*). Or, let us grant that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) follows from mere non-observation.
And its ease [of understanding] does not mean that reasoning (*yukti*) is not a necessary factor for inference. *Yukti*, *yoga*, *sambandha*, and *anvaya* are synonymous;

the point is simply that *anvaya* (positive concomitance) is not a non-factor. This is because the arising of inference for all cognizers occurs precisely by means of that [concomitance]. Therefore, for the purpose of explaining it...
The example by similarity (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*) must also indeed be stated; it cannot be rejected absolutely. And this statement is made as a concession (*anvāruhya*).

For the established tenet (*siddhānta*) is exactly as stated: in a correct application of similarity, dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) need not be required. This is because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) alone is primary, since negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established without it. For when the presence of smoke is understood [to be] through fire...
In the case of a relationship, the exclusion of non-fire is established by implication. Therefore, that [relationship] must first be shown by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*);

however, on occasion, dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is also stated when the opportunity arises. For those who read "anaṅgatvam" (non-membership), this is the explanation: for the membership of a mark (*liṅga*) in inference consists precisely in its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

For it is by means of those two that it becomes a constituent part (*aṅga*). Therefore, just as exclusion (*vyatireka*) is a constituent part, so too is reasoning (*yukti*), which is another name for positive concomitance (*anvaya*). [Objection: But even in the case of a linguistic mark (*liṅga*) consisting of words, since the positive concomitance occurring at a later time after the cognition [of the mark] arises, it is certainly not a constituent part; to this he says: "It will be explained regarding verbal [cognition]. For in the case of verbal [cognition], which is distinct from inference, the positive concomitance occurring at a later time after the cognition...
It will be stated that logical reasoning (*yukti*) is not a constituent factor (*aṅga*). As it will be stated:
"This construction of positive concomitance (*anvaya-kalpanā*) cannot be a constituent factor for the cognitions of meaning.

However, in the case of inference (*anumāna*), positive concomitance is everywhere a constituent factor for cognition. As for those who explain by supplying the words "therefore it is not a non-constituent factor" (*nānaṅgatvam anvayasya*) and stating that "logical reasoning will be discussed here regarding this very point concerning the word," [that is incorrect].

First of all, their criticism is merely the insertion of a logical connection (*anvaya*) that has not been heard [in the text]. Furthermore, no justification will be stated for the role of logical connection as a constituent part of verbal cognition (*śābda*), because its mention has already occurred right here by means of the term "known relation" (*jñātasambandha*). For this very reason, he will state that the dependence of inference upon logical connection is established. Therefore, the explanation is exactly as it was stated. // 132 //

As for the objection that it is only particulars (*bheda*) that possess the status of the signified and the signifier in inference, and that their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is impossible, he replies: "The consequence would be [the cognition of] particulars. There is no consequence of particulars being the signified and signifier in inferential cognition. This is because they do not pervade all places and times, as they are restricted to each individual instance.

Furthermore, it is impossible to experience a necessary rule (*niyama*) of one such [particular] with another through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). And in the absence of that, it cannot be a factor of inference.
"It is possible"—thus, for them, the absence of a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not a fault. If there is no consequence of cognizing particulars (*bheda*), then of what has this been shown?
There is no single, ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*) that follows after the particulars, because such a thing would be a conceptualized form (*vikalpākāra*). If...

Moreover, at present, inference arises precisely through the superimposition of a form known from the convention of pervasion (*vyāpti*). For, when this [inference] is scrutinized with precision, it is impossible [to find a real object], and thus it is merely an error (*vibhrama*). If this is so, then inference—which functions by superimposing an unreal form—is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). True. However, by the force of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), a certain particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed [indicated] by some conceptual form (*vikalpākāra*).

That which is apprehended through its universal nature (*sāmānyātman*), yet which—being merely delineated by the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*)—causes one to obtain the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is designated as "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). For us, non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is the cause of validity, and non-contradiction is the stability of purposeful action (*arthakriyāsthiti*). As they say: "Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge; non-contradiction is the stability of purposeful action. This is so.

And since in inference, the attainment of a real entity capable of causal efficiency is preceded by the appearance of that entity, inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As it has been said:
"Though it is an error because it apprehends something as what it is not, it is a valid cognition because it is non-contradictory.

Therefore, it is only particulars (*bheda*) that possess the relationship of the signified and the signifier. And since they do not constitute a basis for positive concomitance (*anvaya*), what was stated is indeed correct. Thus [the argument] concludes.

He says: "It exists. This is its meaning: this would indeed be so if there were no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*) distinct from the individuals. However, that [universal] does exist; this will be established in the *Ākṛtivāda* chapter by refuting all the objections raised by opponents.

And since its pervasion across multiple places and times is understood, it is not an unfit object for positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Nor is there a cognition of it in what is not that [the universal].

Because that [inference] possesses ultimate validity (*pāramārthikatva*). And thus, whatever straw or grass others resort to for the sake of establishing the validity of inference is likewise of little purpose. // 133 //
Another opinion holds that even when a positive example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) has been stated by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), a negative example (*vaidharmya*) must also be stated;

he introduces this view with the three quarters of the verse beginning with "some" (*kecit*). What, then, is the reason for this requirement? To this he replies: "by the desire to establish a restriction of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttiniyamecchayā*). // 134 //
He explains this very point with the words, "In the case of the reason" (*hetau*). For they think as follows:

when, in the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one states "where there is smoke" and then employs the restrictive particle *eva* by saying "there is fire indeed," then, since the reason is determined by the probandum—fire alone—the exclusion [of the reason] from everything other than fire necessarily follows.

And this is not possible, because it would entail the non-existence of even the locus of the property to be proven (sādhyadharma), which would result in the fallacy of the reason not being a property of the subject (apakṣadharmatva), and because it would entail the non-existence of the subject (pakṣa) itself. Therefore, the statement of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is meaningful only when it always restricts the exclusion to the absence of the property to be proven; for when that [statement] exists, it is made known that "in the absence of fire, smoke does not exist," whereas [without it] it might be thought that "it does exist. // 135 //

He refutes this as well, stating: "But that has little fruit. The meaning is that this statement of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), when formulated in this way, yields little result. Why does it have little fruit? To this he says: "Because... What has been established? To this he says: "For it is merely the absence of the pervader (*vyāpakābhāvamātra*). This was established in the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*) "The mountain possesses fire."

Just as the rule is postulated from its opposite, and not from that which is non-contradictory; therefore, even in a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), one must demonstrate only the exclusion of the absence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) from the smoke and so forth which are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), and not the exclusion of anything else. // 136 //

Establishing this very point by means of an illustrative statement, he concludes with the words "Therefore": "Thus, here— in the view of the wise according to the Mīmāṃsaka school— the three members of a syllogistic statement are generally considered to be the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), and the corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*)."
And this has been demonstrated by the author of the Commentary himself, because it is based on the three terms: the example, the reason, and the object to be proven.
Thus [ends verse] 137.

On this point, the commentary states: "That [inference] is of two kinds: that in which the relation has been perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣato dṛṣṭasambandha*) and that in which the relation has been perceived through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭasambandha*). Among these, an example of the former is [the inference of fire] from the sight of the form of smoke;

and an example of the latter is the recollection of motion in the sun, having observed that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by motion. By this, it is shown that there are two types of inference due to the two-fold nature of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*).

Regarding the statement "it has been said": here, some who consider themselves experts in policy (nītijña) believe that it is only a particular (svalakṣaṇa) that is grasped in some cases by means of inference as a universal (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa). To dispel that misconception, the author of the Bhāṣya stated this: "But that [inference] is of two kinds;

there is also inference whose object is a particular not previously perceived, such as in the case of [past] actions and so forth. But how can there be a perception of a relation with something whose particular nature has not been perceived?

Because an effect is observed to possess an origin. Even if the specific relationship with an entity whose own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not ascertained is not understood in detail, it is nevertheless observed in a general sense. For every occasional effect is seen to arise from something adventitious that possesses an origin, just as a cloth arises from the conjunction of threads. Therefore, Devadatta’s prior and subsequent disjunctions and conjunctions with successive locations [must likewise have such an origin].

Sometimes, when some adventitious cause is perceived, an inference is drawn; this they call an inference based on a relationship observed in a general way (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa-sambandha*), because its object is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that was not previously perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In the case of fire and such things, however, because the particular characteristic is determined through direct perception, they call it an inference based on a relationship observed through direct perception (*pratyakṣa-dṛṣṭa-sambandha*). And [this does not apply to] substance (*dravya*).

Thus, it must be stated that [sound] is the cause of conjunction and disjunction. For even when those [conjunction and disjunction] exist, [sound] does not occur. Nor can it be postulated that there is simply the arrival of another substance, because that is contradicted by the recognition of the previous substance. And it is not tenable to say that people do not perceive the difference because they are deceived by the production of successive similar [moments].

Because that cognition remains unerring even when there is a difference in location and so forth. And it has been stated by the author of the *Vivaraṇa*: "The doctrine of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is indeed refuted by recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Therefore, since no visible cause is possible, some invisible cause for conjunction and disjunction is inferred; and that is designated as 'action' (*karman*). For this very reason, action is not perceptible even in other locations."

Thus [it is said]. The author of the Bhāṣya demonstrates this: as he will state, "For those [actions] are not perceived," and on the occasion of establishing the existence of the *apūrva*, "We do not perceive the form of action," and "That which causes its substratum to reach another location is called action. This clearly shows that action is indeed inferred solely from the result of reaching another location.

It has been established that actions and so forth are exclusively the objects of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). To those who claim that, because there are two kinds of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), the twofold nature of inference is thus justified, he replies: "The twofold nature is not tenable.
The sense is that this aforementioned twofold nature is untenable. Why is it untenable? To this he says:

—By the three quarters beginning with "yathaiva" [it is meant]: just as indeed there is a relationship between fire and smoke that is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), so too is it between motion and attainment, because those two are also directly perceived. {3}

For we indeed perceive directly that Devadatta, as he reaches another location, thinks "he is going. This conceptualization of action does not differ from the conceptualizations of genus (*jāti*) and so forth; for it likewise conforms to the presence and absence of the sense organs and possesses an immediate manifestation. [Objection: But what else, apart from the conjunction with and disjunction from locations, belongs to Devadatta by way of action?

Moreover, we perceive form directly. It is inferred solely through the observation of its effect. Whether from the universal (*jāti*) or from the individual (*vyakti*), what form is experienced that could be determined as the object of direct perception? That [form] is indeed the very form of the individual.
If it is asked, "What is this [change] other than a different form (rūpāntara)?
then what about karma—is it formless? For even this [karma] is not at all distinct from that [form]; it is merely adventitious (āgantuka).

Therefore, those who cast the conceptualization of karma into the very camp of direct perception (pratyakṣa), just like the conceptualization of genus (jāti), [establish] the fivefold determinate cognition (savikalpaka).
We shall now divide perception (*pratyakṣa*). And it has been said:
"For one who is ascertaining Devadatta who has come within the range of vision does not perceive him as if he were beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), while reciting a poem composed by his own name."

Thus [it is said]. But if action were to be inferred from its effect, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it would be perceived like the sun or like Devadatta. And it is not observed that one perceives the sun as moving or vibrating in the same way one perceives Devadatta; for its orb is always seen to be stationary.
Yet, conjunction and disjunction are indeed perceived in relation to it as well—[is this not] equal?

From those two [moments], there would be an inferential cognition in both cases. Furthermore, when an action begins with disjunction and ends with conjunction, if that [action] were merely inferred from them, the cognition appearing as "it goes"— which has the manifestation of the present—
would not occur, for that [action] would then be past.

In that case, how could it be an object of a cognition whose form is "present"? For instance, in the case of fish in a stream of water that appears motionless, a cognition of movement would arise as an inference based on the perception of the continuous conjunctions and disjunctions of the water-particles; likewise, in the case of a post from which a hawk has flown away, an action would be inferred as being like that of the hawk, and consequently, even that [post] would become an object of the cognition "it is moving. If it is argued that the inference of action does not arise from mere disjunction alone, [the response follows].

"Rather, [disjunction arises] from conjunction preceded by disjunction. If that is the case, then there would be an over-extension (*prasaṅga*) in the instance where a single post, having been disjoined from one hawk, is conjoined with another; and also in the case of Devadatta who stands still after having moved. However, if it is argued that this conjunction of the soaring hawk with another location cannot be produced by a motion inherent in the post, [then our position remains intact].
"There is no inference of action there. Well then, let action be postulated even in the case of the *śyena* sacrifice;

however, in the case of a post (*sthāṇu*), it is simply a case of overstepping the logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). For one who perceives an obstruction and remembers the relation [of that obstruction], the cognition of the obstructing factor is certain. And since in the case of a post, there is the observation of an effect dependent upon a cause, the arising of an inference is not possible.
If it is argued that since conjunction and disjunction can occur in a post even through the action inherent in a hawk, there is no inference of an action residing in that [post], we say:

no. For the determination of inference does not follow from the specific purpose [at hand]. Rather, a pervaded mark (*liṅga*), wherever it is observed, brings about the presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) in each of those places. Indeed, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) functions by way of the impossibility of any other explanation.

Inference is not refuted. However, if it is argued that conjunctions and disjunctions arising in an uninterrupted sequence are the cause for inferring action, then in that case no motion at all would be inferred, because future conjunctions and disjunctions are beyond the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, only a limited number [of them] can be apprehended at the outset.

Now, [it might be argued that] there is an inference of action based on conjunction with and disjunction from one's own location (*svadeśa*). However, a hawk is not said to be the "location" of a post. Even so, this does not avoid the over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to fish, for water is indeed their own location. Furthermore, for those who maintain that space (*ākāśa*) is imperceptible, the cognition of action in a flying bird—expressed as "it goes"—would be untenable.

Because conjunction and disjunction with space are imperceptible, it is impossible to infer [motion] from them. Nor is the cognition "the bird moves" based on the apprehension of conjunctions and disjunctions of parts of light spread across the sky, because such a cognition occurs even in total darkness. Furthermore, according to your own tenets, there is no such thing as "darkness," since it is merely the absence of light. Therefore, it is impossible to determine that motion is caused by conjunctions and disjunctions with that [darkness].
To establish this, the twofold nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as an object of action is not tenable.

As for the statement that they are "not indeed [objects] of direct perception," which expresses their non-direct-perceptibility, we shall explain that very point differently in that same context. Furthermore, by the author of the Sūtras stating "the non-distinction of form and sound," direct perception...

Thus, it is established that [action] is indeed action (*karma*). Furthermore, in the section concerning the *apūrva*, the statement "we do not perceive the form of action" intends precisely the non-perception of the form of action as it exists manifested through its extension in a sequence of prior and posterior stages as enjoined;
for otherwise, if there were merely a negation of perception, action would be an absolute non-entity like the horn of a hare.

For it is not merely the perception by direct observation (*pratyakṣopalabdhi*) that is denied there. Nor is the statement "that which, having a substratum, causes it to reach another location" intended to mean that [motion] is to be inferred from its effect. What then? By means of the form of the substratum’s reaching another location—and not by way of its own nature—it shows that action does not exist as such; rather, it demonstrates the persistence of action in the form of the *apūrva*. Here too, in the case of Devadatta...

By stating that "one perceives the arrival at another location as preceded by motion," [the author] demonstrates that motion is indeed perceptible in the case of Devadatta. Otherwise, since the action in both Devadatta and the sun would be equally inferable, on what basis would the inference of motion in the sun be cited as an example of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* (inference from general observation)? For even in the case of Devadatta, it is precisely from *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* that [motion is inferred].

The establishment of movement [is thus refuted]. Therefore, it is well said that such a thing is untenable either according to the text or according to logic. For when two counter-correlatives (*pratiyogin*) are not mutually confused, there is a twofold distinction. However, in this case, that which is taken as the counter-correlative of one whose relation is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*)—namely, that whose relation is "seen in general" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭasambandha*)—there too, the relation between the movement and the attainment of form is indeed perceived through direct perception; thus, there is no [distinction] between the two counter-correlatives.
"Non-confusion," thus [it is said]. // 138 //

If, however, it is argued that even though perceptibility exists in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), because it does not apply to the subject (*pakṣa*)—since [the sun] is not perceived—the relation is not one "seen through perception" (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭa*); this is first raised as an objection: "If there is non-perception in the case of the sun. Now he refutes this: "No. He states the reason: "Even in the case of a place, [if it is] contemporary... That is, even in the case of a contemporary place—

The meaning is that while [the object] is currently being cognized, there is indeed no perception of it as present before the eyes (*apratyakṣatopalabdhi*). If, however, one maintains that there is a perception of the forms of fire and smoke as non-present in some place such as a kitchen, then that same [perception] exists in the case of Devadatta as well, because his movement is directly perceived; thus he says: "in some place" (*kvacid*). // 139 //

Thus far, it has been stated that what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣato dṛṣṭatā*) is conflated with what is perceived through general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭatā*). Now, he explains that even what is perceived through general observation is conflated with the inference of the form of fire—which is intended to be perceived directly—by means of the three quarters beginning with "yadi" (if).

For if it is maintained that the status of being perceived through general observation belongs only to the inference of motion in the sun in relation to another subject (*dharmyantara*), such as Devadatta; [then...]

In that case, it would indeed follow that even fire and smoke—though existing as the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*) in relation to other substrates such as a kitchen—would [be related] in this way. For generally, without intending to specify distinctions of place and so forth, this is understood as "that which possesses smoke possesses fire," just as the locus of reaching another place is the locus of motion. Therefore, this [relation] is indeed devoid of the status of being a counter-correlate (*pratiyogitva*).

"Both" implies the objection that a twofold division is untenable. Having thus raised the objection, he provides the resolution: "Therefore, they explain it in this way. The sense is that, precisely because the aforementioned twofold division is impossible, the twofold division must be described in the manner that is about to be stated. // 140 //

Therein, he first illustrates the relationship based on perception (*pratyakṣasaṃbandha*) with the words beginning "pratyakṣa" and ending with "yudhyate. For when one has previously formed a cognition through perception regarding two specific instances of fire and smoke— namely, that this fire has cow-dung for its fuel (*gomaya-indhana*), meaning its fuel is cow-dung, and that this specific smoke is produced by it— and then, after some lapse of time, [encounters them] elsewhere...

The meaning is that having gone somewhere and being present there, one cognizes that very specific fire by means of that very same specific smoke located in that place; thus, it becomes an inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*). By this, it is explained that only the "inference based on the observation of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) is expressed by the term "perceived through direct perception. For, by the word *pratyakṣa*, the particular (*viśeṣa*) is indicated.

For indeed, it is by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*) that such a specific intermediate distinction—consisting of the nature of having cow-dung as fuel and being produced from it—is capable of being understood, and not by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, through that [perception], such a distinction also becomes the object of inference (*anumāna*). Thus, it is entirely appropriate that the word "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇā*) to denote this specific [type of inference]. And the "inference based on the observation of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) serves as the basis for the "inference based on the observation of generalities" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).

The intended meaning is that the two-fold classification [of the counter-correlate] is thus established. Now, one might object: "The so-called *viśeṣadṛṣṭa* is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor is it a valid cognition at all, because its object has already been apprehended. For, by means of smoke situated in that very place, that same fire produced from cow-dung fuel is inferred in that very same place. Therefore, due to the absence of a difference in location, it lacks validity altogether."

Therefore he says, with the three quarters [of the verse] beginning with "tasya": the validity (*pramāṇatā*) of such a thing, which is perceived directly and whose existence might otherwise be doubted, arises from the cognition of that object. Even though there is no difference in space, its status as a means of valid cognition remains unimpeded because it removes the doubt of one who is doubting, by way of cutting through that doubt due to the difference in time. And this has also been cited by Vindhyavāsin as an example of "perception of a particular" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*); thus he says:
"Perceived through a particularity. // 143 //

If this is an example of inference from the perception of particulars (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), how then is there a mention of "grasping the form" (*ākṛtigrahaṇa*) in the Bhāṣya? For in that case, only the particular should have been shown. To this he says: "Of the two forms alone. This is the meaning: here, it is only between two forms (*ākṛti*) as presented by some internal particularity, such as having cow-dung for fuel, that there is the relationship of probans and probandum. For such is the cognition here: "This very same [thing] continues to persist until today."

The form of smoke, which is a transformation of cow-dung fuel, is perceived. Therefore, because the fire originating from that fuel persists [in the smoke], the apprehension of the form is not untenable. // 144 //

If that is so, then one should state as an example of *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa* simply another instance of fire and smoke, without intending to specify any internal distinctions; what is the purpose of using the sun as an example? To this he replies: "And even when it is another instance of fire and smoke. For just as there is a clearly manifest distinction between the forms of fire and smoke—produced respectively by the kindling of grass, wood, or cow-dung—which is self-evident to the consciousness of every cognizer, [so too is the distinction in the case of the sun].

It is not so with the attainment of a destination and its form. Therefore, since the inference of the mere form of a destination from the mere attainment and form [of the sun] is based on a relationship perceived through generality (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) in the case of the sun, it is indeed appropriate to cite the sun as an example.

Furthermore, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for grasping a relation in its generality? For there can be no grasping of a relation between two relata that have not themselves been grasped.
Nor is it possible for universals (*sāmānya*) to be grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the latter has only particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Nor is inference (*anumāna*) [the means], because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, he says: "The state of being an object of perception. [If one objects: "There would indeed be an infinite regress,"

If it is maintained that the apprehension of the universal occurs through inference, then, after establishing that its object is indeed perception by demonstrating that it is established as conceptual, the status of being perceptual is finally concluded; thus, the reality of the universal is proven. Now, one might object: "There is no such thing as a universal that is a real entity at all, because it cannot be determined as being either different or non-different [from the particular]. To this, he says: "And [it possesses] substantiality."

The fact that [the universal] is a real entity (*vastutva*) will also be established in detail in the section on form (*ākṛti*). Furthermore, by demonstrating that it is an object of perception, its status as a real entity has already been effectively proven even in the context of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In this case, the reality of the universal was indeed introduced for the purpose of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the statement, "there exists a real entity among universals. This, however, is a restatement intended to state the logical reason (*hetu*).

But as for one who is a rationalist (*haituka*) and does not respect the establishment [of things] through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from a logical reason (*hetu*), we shall establish both [the existence of the self and its eternity] by means of a reason alone; thus he says: "In this regard" (*atre*). 146.
{3,88} In that regard, he first states the reason for establishing the status of [the object] as a real entity: "of the inference of fire from smoke.
For the Buddhists declare that inference has a non-real universal (*sāmānya*) as its objective support, since they admit that a universal is merely the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, inference is indeed nothing but an error.

They say that inference is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it presents the form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) by the force of its relation [to that characteristic]. To those very people, this is said:

"The object of inference is a real entity (*vastu*), because it is a means of valid cognition other than non-apprehension (*abhāva*), just like the sensory cognitions of the ear and so forth regarding their own objects.
For whatever cognition is produced by the sense organs, such as the ear, with respect to their own respective objects, [that is a means of valid cognition].

That [cognition] has only a real entity as its objective support (*ālambana*). And whatever sense faculty is brought into contact with a particular object, that object is its own specific object (*svārtha*), because the sense faculties function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*). Therefore, in this context, the qualification "its own object" is intended to exclude cognitions such as those of a mirage (*mṛgatṛṣṇā*).

For if it were stated without such a qualification, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of non-existence and other means of valid cognition by having a real entity as their objective support would not have been stated, since erroneous cognitions lack both [of these characteristics].

For those [cognitions] are not valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor do they have a real entity as their objective support (*ālambana*). For when a sense faculty is associated with one thing, those [cognitions] arise having other objects as their domain. Such a cognition indeed has a non-entity as its objective support, yet it does not have an absolutely non-existent object. Thus, once it has been established that inference has a real entity as its objective support, it follows by implication that the universal (*sāmānya*) [is a real entity].

It is said that [inference] has a real entity (*vastu*) as its object. However, this status of having a non-entity as its objective support (*avastvālambanatva*) has been refuted by the author of the *Bhāṣya* through his employment of the term "object" (*artha*) in the definition of inference. The Buddhists maintain that inference has a non-object (*anartha*) as its domain.

They argue that although inference is an error—since it proceeds by determining a non-object (its own internal reflection) to be a real object—it is nonetheless a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it functions in connection with a real object and thus does not deviate from it.

To this, the following is the reply: the object of inference is the universal (*sāmānya*), which is an external reality itself, and not merely the form of a conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*). This will be established in detail in the *Ākṛti-grantha*. (147) Having thus established that the object is a real entity (*vastu*), he brings it forward and establishes [the point] by stating: "And the universal is a real entity. The connection with what is to be said later is as follows: the universal is a real entity because it is an object of cognition other than non-existence (*abhāva*), just like a unique particular (*asādhāraṇavastu*).

Thus [he says]. Now he demonstrates its status as an object of perception through the following formal argument (*prayoga*), by means of the three quarters of the verse beginning with "pratyakṣa. Whatever is an object of knowledge other than non-existence is indeed apprehended by perception; for example, the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa*) entity according to the Buddhists themselves. // 148 //

However, for the Buddhists themselves, who maintain that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the exclusive object of inference, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results; thus he says [the following] in five verses beginning with "The universal. This passage is self-explanatory.
But if it is argued: "If there were a dependence on inference for the sake of apprehending the universal that serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then an infinite regress would occur;
however, inference is not required for the sake of apprehending that [universal which is the object of inference]."

Since that [inference] is cognizable through conceptual construction arising from the perception of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth, it is not invalid, because it leads to the attainment of an object capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Nor is it a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object is not a real thing (*anartha-viṣayatvāt*). Therefore, since the logical mark (*liṅga*) is established by an indeterminable conceptual construction, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "Now" (*atha*). The intended meaning is this: first of all, it is not a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, non-valid cognition (apramāṇa) is possible; for when two contradictory natures are negated in one place, the occurrence of the other is unavoidable. Moreover, since that which is non-valid lacks the power to establish the object of knowledge (prameya), that cognition must necessarily be admitted as being valid (pramāṇa) itself.
And because perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna) are not admitted [by you], it would follow that it is indeed another means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).

Furthermore, just as that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) is accepted as a valid cognition when there is the awareness of its mark (*liṅga*), so too would it follow [as a valid cognition] regarding the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). And in this way, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) to be stated later would occur. By saying "whether from a valid cognition or from what is not a valid cognition," the proponent demonstrates that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses an undetermined dual nature. Therefore, let it be that the apprehension of the possessor of the mark is likewise exactly so.

"What is the fault? To this he says: "Even so. This is the intended meaning: even for us who are bringing about an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the consequence of the destruction of inference (*anumāna*) is what we intend. And even if another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were admitted, the destruction of inference would certainly still occur; for that very [other] means of valid cognition...
In that case, it would become the indicator of every instance of the probans (liṅga) and the probandum (liṅgin) in their general forms. // 155 //

If, however, the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) is held to be invalid precisely because it is admitted to have a single form, then the cognition of the marked object (*liṅgin*) derived from that mark cognized through an invalid means would also be false—just as the cognition of fire from what is perceived as smoke when it is actually steam. And in this case, there would be no inference at all. With the intention of stating that this would result in the permanent abolition of inference, he says:
—from that which is understood through the immeasurables. // 156 //

Here he raises an objection: "But surely... (*nanu*). The meaning is that just as the recollection of a relationship—which is itself not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*)—is accepted as a cause of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), so too will the knowledge of the logical mark (*liṅga*) be [a cause of valid cognition]. He refutes this: "In that case" (*tatra*). For recollection, arising from a prior cognition, is useful for inference by way of presenting that [prior object]; and since that [prior cognition] is indeed a means of valid cognition, it is logical that the resulting determination follows it.

And since this mode is not possible in the case of the apprehension of a logical mark (*liṅga*), he says: "But not... For in this case, even prior to the comprehension of the mark, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established that could be presented by a cognition based on a means of valid cognition. Nor should it be said that the cognition of the mark itself is merely a memory; for he says, "Because of its absence," meaning precisely because there is an absence of any prior means of valid cognition. // 159 //

But surely, since the cognition of the mark (*liṅga*) also leads to the attainment of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of smoke and so forth as previously apprehended by non-conceptual perception, it too must be nothing but memory;

therefore, in this case as well, a definitive determination (*nirṇaya*) from another non-conceptual means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed appropriate. To this he says: "It is mnemonic" (*smārtam*). Just as the present cognition of the relation is a recollection because it leads to the attainment of what was previously apprehended, [so too is the cognition of the mark].

Thus, for one who asserts that this inferential cognition (*liṅgajñāna*) is also a form of recollection (*smārta*) because it leads to the attainment [of its object] by way of being non-different from what was grasped by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), the capacity for recollection would be unavoidable even in the case of the son of a barren woman. For the established rule is that recollection has as its object that which has already been grasped. And since the cognition of the general character of the logical mark (*liṅgasāmānyajñāna*) does not have as its objective support (*ālambana*) a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) grasped by non-conceptual perception, how [could it be recollection]?

Regarding memory: if that which appears here has not been grasped, and that which was grasped does not appear, then it lacks the nature of memory. Furthermore, if memory were to have as its object what was never grasped, there would be the absurd consequence of remembering even the son of a barren woman. // 160 //

But surely, if the mark (*liṅga*) is held to be of a universal nature and is required for the sake of apprehending that [universal], then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) through inference, because that [mark] itself would be cognizable by another inference. Rather, it is the unique (*asādhāraṇa*) nature of the object itself that will serve as the mark in the cognition of the universal.

And since that [perception] is indeed direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no infinite regress. Therefore, he says: "And not... What is the reason for this? He says: "Because... A logical mark (*liṅga*) is one whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been observed. However, its inseparable connection with that universal (*sāmānya*) has not been observed in any way, whether spatially or temporally. This is because it is impossible for a unique [particular] to be continuous across other entities; thus, what is observed in one place...
And because it has ceased right there. // 161 //

Alternatively, if one accepts the perception of a relation, then [the universal] would fall into the state of being a general form (*sāmānyarūpatā*), just like "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth; thus he says, "Or it might be. He states the reason for this: "For not... (verse 162).

For this reason as well, he states that the unique essence of an object is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) with the words "And not... For smoke and the like, when made the basis for conceptual constructions such as "this is smoke," are observed to be the logical mark of fire and so forth. But how could that which is unique—being inexpressible in any form whatsoever—be a logical mark?
The phrase "its status as a logical mark is not tenable" is to be connected with what is to be stated hereafter. [Objection: But surely for animals... [text ends]
