Since inference is observed only in those who perceive a specific form accompanied by the mention of words, it is not the case that [the cognition] lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) simply because it is inexpressible;

therefore, he says with the three quarters beginning "vikalpa": this is the intended meaning—let it be granted that there may be no verbal expression for animals, yet they certainly possess a conceptualization of objects (*arthavikalpa*) consisting of the synthesis of what precedes and what follows. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate for them [to possess inference].

In inference, even that which is "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*) possesses the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*). However, how can the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason] be a logical mark, since it lacks the synthesis of preceding and succeeding moments and is devoid of conceptual construction regarding the object? For smoke that has not ascended into the mind as "this is that" does not become a logical mark for fire.
And such a thing is not possible in the case of the uncommon [reason].
Because that [consciousness] is not within the scope of connecting the preceding with the succeeding. // 163 //

Even in our own view, those specific particulars such as smoke which are conceptualized as having an uncommon nature (*asādhāraṇātman*) are not a logical mark (*aliṅga*) because they lack positive concomitance (*anvaya*); how much more so, then, is the uncommon nature of an object that is the exclusive domain of non-conceptual [perception]? Thus he says: "they are conceptualized. Precisely because of the absence of positive concomitance, even the cognition of an uncommon [particular] is not a logical mark for the cognition of the universal of the thing to be inferred (*liṅgisāmānya*). Thus he says: "for this very reason. // 164 //

If, however, for the sake of establishing the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa*) is admitted to have a universal form (*sāmānyarūpatā*), then—just as in the case of grasping the universal of the mark (*liṅgasāmānya*)—there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); thus, that too would remain unascertained. Therefore, he says:

"The universal... (*sāmānyeti*). But if, in some unique particular where the relation has been known through the universal, [the inference occurs] even by one who has not seen [the probandum] elsewhere...
The universal (sāmānya) is what is inferred. If that were so, then everything would be a communicator of everything, because there is no distinction;
thus he says: "or in some cases" (kvacid vā). // 165 //

Thus, it has first been stated that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the ascertainment of the mark (*liṅga*). Now, he says—"the experience of the relation"—to show that at the time of grasping the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), there is likewise no means of valid cognition for the knowledge of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). For when the possessor of the mark has not been apprehended, its related mark cannot be understood. And prior to the operation of inference, there is no existence of that [possessor of the mark] in its nature as a universal (*sāmānya*).
The intention is that there is no means of valid cognition for us, such as perception, [to establish the probans];
therefore, even when the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) is being understood, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress. // 166 //

Is it not the case that this conventional practice of sign (liṅga) and signified (liṅgin) is based solely on beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā)? Why such insistence here? For a certain latent impression, having arisen, manifests a conceptual construction (vikalpa) in the form of a particular sign, and thereby initiates a specific conventional practice of inference. As they have said: "This very conventional practice of inference and the object of inference..."

Since [the cognition] does not depend on external existence or non-existence by means of the principle of the property and the property-bearer as mounted upon the intellect, he says: "Nor even... Nor is the inferential cognition produced merely from latent impressions (*vāsanā*). For a latent impression is deposited by a prior experience.

This is a mental construction (*saṃskāra*). Since this [construction] cannot arise from a universal mark (*liṅgasāmānya*) that is absolutely non-existent—like a hare’s horn—how could the cognition of a mark (*liṅgajñāna*) possibly arise from mere latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? Furthermore, if the cognition of a mark is held to be based on that [impression], then the cognition of the marked object (*liṅgijñāna*) would likewise be established in the same way; thus, the recourse to inference as a valid means of knowledge (*anumānaprāmāṇya*), defined as "the perception of an object from a mark possessing the three characteristics," would be rendered purposeless.
Thus he says: "and the cognition of the possessor of the mark" (liṅgijñāna). // 167 //

{3,94} But surely this infinite regress is equally applicable to you as well in the inference of the absence of rain from the absence of clouds, since non-existence (abhāva) has non-perception (anupalabdhi) as its logical mark (liṅga). If another logical mark of the same kind were required, an infinite regress would result. To this he says: "Where... For where the absence of clouds is the logical mark for the absence of rain, that [absence] is not cognizable through a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called non-existence. Therefore, the defect of infinite regress based on the requirement of a mark of the same kind does not arise here. // 168 //

But for those who maintain that universals are perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there is no infinite regress for us; thus he says: "from what is apprehended by direct perception. This means "from this direct perception" (i.e., from the universal itself). // 169 //
"In that case, there would be an infinite regress in the inference of an inference (anumitānumāna);
therefore, he says: 'Even where... The meaning is as follows: the arrival at another location is indeed a perceptible mark (liṅga) that is "fundamental" (maulika), i.e., existing at the root;
by means of that, having inferred motion, when the motion in the sun is being inferred as the means of establishing it, there is no infinite regress. // 170 //

Now, one might object: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced; and its being produced is established by observing it [to arise] immediately after an action. If, in this way, "being produced" (kṛtakatva) were established solely through its occurring immediately after an action, then that action itself would require inference from another cause, leading to an infinite regress. To this, he says:
"The state of being a mark" (liṅgatva).

For in the inference [of sound] from the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), it is stated that "because some perceive action there," the mark (*liṅga*) is the state of occurring immediately after the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*). In that case, either the action qualified by the causal factors, or the causal factor qualified by that [action], becomes the mark by qualifying the state of immediate succession. And that is not perceptible. First, the perceptibility of the action has just been established; as for the causal factor—

In that case as well, the action itself is indeed perceptible, whereas its capacity (*śakti*) is imperceptible. Moreover, that capacity is neither a logical mark (*liṅga*) here nor is it something to be inferred.

Therefore, since both the action and the agent are perceptible, there is no regressus ad infinitum. For even for those who maintain that the object is to be inferred, there is no infinite regress, because [the process] terminates at the fruit (*phala*).
"Especially for us," [he said]. // 171 //

Thus, first, the untenability of inference has been stated in the absence of the generality (sāmānya) being a real entity and a perceptible object; now, with the intention that the entire collection of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would likewise become untenable if the generality were untenable—since they too depend upon the generality—and that it cannot be considered invalid according to the reasoning to be stated later, he says: "In this way" (evam). 172.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that other means of valid cognition are preceded by perception, and that universals are perceptible;
otherwise, an infinite regress would result. He concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). // 173 //

Thus, having established the perceptibility of the universal (*sāmānya*) by means of the object itself, he now addresses those who claim that only particulars (*viśeṣa*) are grasped by perception, saying: "By perception... If a particular is intended to be a composite substance (*avayavidravya*), and since we have already stated that it consists of a generic aspect dependent upon other constituent substances, how can it be said to be perceived? // 174 //

If, however, it is maintained that the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) are only the color and so forth of the whole (*avayavin*), that too is incorrect. For even those are indeed universals (*sāmānya*) in relation to their own specific qualities such as blue and so on; thus he says: "For color and so forth... (3.96). But if the view is held that blue and so forth are themselves the specific qualities, that is not so. Because even they possess the nature of a universal in relation to their own internal subdivisions of blue and so on; thus he says: "...their own specific qualities" (175).

If, however, it is maintained that the specific quality (*viśeṣa*) is merely the blueness of a single substance, such as a bee, that is not correct; for even that possesses the nature of a generality (*sāmānya*) in relation to the specific blues residing in its own parts, such as its wings. The blueness of a wing, too, is indeed a generality in relation to the blues of its constituent parts. And in this way, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) must be demonstrated starting from non-atomic [entities].
Thus he says: "And those too. Since atoms are partless, their form is indeed unique (asādhāraṇa).
But prior to them, even the form of the dyad (dvyaṇuka) is common to both; thus he says: "Of the dyad too. // 176 //

[Objection: Let it be that the particularity (*viśeṣa*) is indeed the nature of the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*); that very thing will be perceptible to us. To this he says: "And not by the ultimate [particularity]. For a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is pursued for the sake of practical activity (*vyavahāra*), not out of mere whim. And since there is no practical activity whatsoever by means of the ultimate particularity, what is the use of its perceptibility? [Objection: But surely even a cognition whose fruit is indifference (*upekṣā*) is indeed a means of valid cognition.

Therefore, he says: "And not... [The form of our atoms is not perceived when they reside in a gross object, as the threads are perceived in a cloth, whether individually or collectively; thus, there is no way for it to have a particular as its object. Now, one might object: "It is only the distinct atoms themselves, gathered together, that are apprehended, not a single effect-substance. Therefore, how can it be said that the universal resides in those things which possess parts? [To this we reply: It is precisely the gathered atoms, because they do not function otherwise, that are denoted by such terms as "particular," "specific," and so forth.
These [atoms] will become perceptible. Lest it be thought that a single atom might individually fall within the range of the senses, he says:

"by way of distinction" (*bhedeneti*). For it is always the single entity as a whole that appears to everyone, not the distinctions between atoms. Nor is it correct to say that non-distinction is grasped when it is not grasped through its distinctions; the point is that this would contradict conscious experience (*saṃvid-virodhāt*). Now, this very [perception] is the apprehension of distinction...

Regarding this non-differentiated manifestation, one might ask: what is the use of grasping at difference? To this he says: "Nor is it different," etc. The meaning is that difference cannot be cognized by a cognition whose form is non-differentiated, because the distinction between difference and non-difference would otherwise be untenable. // 178 //

[Objection: "But surely, even if there were no single [entity], this non-differentiated appearance could still arise by having a collection (*samudāya*) as its object. To this, he says: "A collection. For how can those who deny the universal (*sāmānya*)—which is indeed universally known throughout the entire world—have a "collection" as a distinct entity that could serve as the object of a non-differentiated appearance? Furthermore, since everyone always perceives a single substance, how could it be otherwise? To this, he says: "And not at all times..."

Furthermore, this collection (*samudāya*) would not be possible even without a single common genus (*ekajāti*). For there is no cognition of a "collection" regarding various heterogeneous things such as trees, jars, and clods of earth. Therefore, he says "na ca" (and not), meaning that if a collection is admitted, you would be forced to accept the existence of the universal "atomicity" (*aṇutva-sāmānya*). The particle "ca" (and) is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*). 180.

[Objection: Surely it is not possible to accept that substance, which has the nature of a universal, without a synthesis of its existence in multiple parts; nor is sensory perception capable of this, because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). To this, he says: "The universal... Even if, due to the postulation of a single underlying factor for many [individuals], that substance—which is connected to those various parts—is not grasped by being conceptually constructed as a "universal," nevertheless, it possesses a single form.

Since it cannot be denied that [the universal] is indeed apprehended even by non-conceptual [perception], one must demonstrate the sensory perceptibility of universals such as "cowness" (gotva), which reside in each individual, by means of the logic of the whole (avayavin) and the universal (sāmānya) that exists distributively across them. Although that universal is not apprehended in the form of the concept "this is a universal," in reality, it is the universal itself that is apprehended. However, at a time subsequent to the recollection of words and so forth...

The universal is apprehended by conceptualizing it through the reflective awareness (*avamarśa*) that follows many [individuals]. And this has already been stated in the proof of determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*).

Therefore, one should not say: "Let there be apprehension by the sense organs of the whole (*avayavin*)—which is synonymous with the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)—as a universal, but not of that which resides in each individual. (181)

{3,98} He says—"because there is no difference in the cognition in both cases"—namely, "by means of a collective [cognition]. By this, the following is established: why is the perceptibility of the universal not accepted in vain?
For even by those who desire particulars to be perceptible, the universal itself must necessarily be accepted as perceptible;
for when any [object] such as color-form (*rūpa*) is most carefully examined, it is found to be of the nature of a universal.
Furthermore, because a substance that is common to its various parts possesses that very nature,
and because a mere independent collection of atoms is never perceived, and because the denial of substance would contradict direct perception;
therefore, the whole (avayavin) and its universal, as well as all universals such as "cowness" inherent within it, are indeed directly perceptible.

The intended meaning is that [the objects] are indeed particulars (*viśeṣa*). And precisely because it has this as its purpose, one should not charge it with being redundant by pointing out that it merely demonstrates the perceptibility of the generality of the whole (*avayavin*)—which is a generality established in other passages. // 182 //

Now, surely you Mīmāṃsakas must necessarily admit atoms. Therefore, since they are established for both parties, why postulate a substratum (dharmin) when it is sufficient to simply assume that those very atoms possess the power to produce a single uniform cognition? For the assumption of a property (dharma) is indeed simpler than the assumption of a substratum. To this he replies: "And by the Mīmāṃsakas," etc. This is the intended meaning.
For whatever is presented by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is what we accept;
and it is not the case that, setting aside the gross [object], atoms alone appear in the cognition born of the senses.
Since we perceive gross objects upon approaching them, if atoms are postulated merely to conform to that perception, let them be;
however, we cannot venture to deny the fundamental gross object on the strength of such [atoms]. // 183 //

But for one who denies that what is directly perceived is gross by means of invisible atoms, it follows that even a hare would have to be denied by the notion of its horns; thus he says: "in the form of a collection. (184)

{3,99} Are atoms now like the horns of a hare? No, he says: "the aggregate" (*samūha*). For here, by the parsimony of conceptualization, a subject (*dharmin*) established by perception does not deserve to be abandoned. And once that [subject] is established, who would not accept that atoms are consistent with it? However, since there is no other means of establishing them, atoms are not necessarily [established].
It is said that they are intended. // 185 //
Therefore, whatever object is perceived directly as both the universal and the particular must be accepted exactly as such, in its state of direct perception;
one should not say that only the particular is perceptible and not the universal. Thus he concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore). // 186 //

Granted that perception is indeed unique (asādhāraṇa), nevertheless, it is not possible to deny the perceptibility of the universal (sāmānya). This is because universals such as "cowness" (gotva) are also unique when considered in relation to higher universals such as "existence" (sattā). Therefore, even if you maintain the position that perception must be unique, the universal of cowness and the like cannot be said to be imperceptible.
Thus, because it is established by the power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it cannot be denied; so he says: "Existence and so forth" (verse 187).

If it is argued that even though the universal (*sāmānya*) is apprehended by perception, it is not [considered] perception because it is not apprehended with the explicit mention of the universal, then this objection is raised: "The universal... He refutes it: "Or rather... For in that case, even the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa*) would not be perceptual. In that case too, during the state of non-conceptual [perception]...

Because there is no conceptualization of the exclusion of others (*paravyāvṛtti*), there is simply no distinct representation (*asādhāraṇollekha*). However, if it is argued that even though it is not conceptually constructed as having that [excluded] form, the conceptualizer nevertheless cognizes it by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), and thus it is perception; then, in that case, people would apprehend the object as having two forms, albeit indistinctly. Therefore, it is established that investigators can indeed describe it in either way.

"The object is indeed apprehended by perception in its two-fold form. With the intention of establishing that the observation of the relationship [between word and object] is generally established, he says: "Whatever object people understand in this [context], that can certainly be described in two ways.
The phrase "in this" means in perceptual cognition. (188)
Thus ends the chapter on inference in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the preceptor Sucaritamiśra.
006. Examination of Word (Śabdapariccheda).
Now begins the examination of word.
Since it has been stated here that perception and inference are not to be examined, this [section] is intended to demonstrate that scripture (*śāstra*) likewise is not to be examined.

The Commentary (*bhāṣya*): "Scripture (*śāstra*) is the cognition of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the cognition of words. Now, according to the view of the author of the *Vṛtti*, having asserted that the means of knowledge (*nimitta*) need not be examined, he stated that perception and the other [means of knowledge] are well-known authorities (*pramāṇa*), and that scripture is included among them; thus, [he argued] by way of the non-deviation of perception.

Anticipating the objection that [the treatise] should be examined, it is logical that the non-examination of the treatise is established immediately after its non-deviation has been stated, for that is the subject at hand;
why then should it be interrupted by inference? True, this is so. However, this sequence has been adopted in accordance with another system (tantrāntara).

For instance, the Lokāyatikas maintain that perception alone is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). They are awakened [to the truth] by the demonstration of the validity of inference, which follows immediately upon perception as relied upon by the Vaiśeṣikas and others. Indeed, the Vaiśeṣikas recite: "The means of knowledge is twofold: determination following observation and following after what was not observed. Likewise, others also hold that there are only two means of knowledge, namely perception and inference.

Just as even the followers of Akṣapāda have defined inference immediately after perception—stating that "inference is preceded by that (perception) and is of three kinds"—so too has inference been described here immediately after perception. Following that, the treatise (*śāstra*) is presented because it possesses a vast scope, is the subject at hand, and is conducive to the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). And thereafter, whatever else is to be stated...

Analogy (*upamāna*) was mentioned because it is well-known among many; for in the *Nyāyavistara*, it is stated that analogy is the means of proving what is to be proven through a well-known similarity. Following that, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) was mentioned according to the opinion of Pārāśarya, because it was stated by Kṛtakoṭi, who followed his view, immediately thereafter. As for the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāva*), its very nature is the absence of the means of knowledge consisting in existence (*bhāva*); therefore, the subsequent discussion follows after that.

What, then, is the purpose of following other treatises (*tantrāntara*)? It is said: for it is through their established renown that [the means of knowledge] are presented without further investigation.

By stating, "In other treatises these means of knowledge are thus well-known," the strength of their renown is expressed. Furthermore, by this, those who have emerged from meditative equipoise are established by various witnesses.
And here it is said, "from the cognition of the word" (*śabdavijñānāt*);

how, then, is that to be analyzed? Is it "cognition from the word" (*śabdād vijñānam*) or "the cognition of the word" (*śabdasya vijñānam*)? In the former case, the formation of the compound is untenable, for the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is compounded with [a word] expressing fear (*bhaya*). In the latter case, however, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even conceptual perception (*savikalpakapratyakṣa*) would be considered a scripture (*śāstra*).

For conceptual constructions (vikalpa) regarding objects not in contact with the senses, such as "cow" and so forth, arise from the cognition of words alone. To this it is replied: this is indeed a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*). Nor does the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) apply to determinate perception (*savikalpaka*), for that [determinate perception] does not arise from the word as a means of valid cognition (*śabdapramāṇa*);
rather, it arises from the sense faculty aided by the word. For just as the sense faculty, when assisted by odor, [perceives] oil that has melted...

Clarified butter separates [the milk]; in the same way, sound, in conjunction with [other factors], distinguishes universals (*jāti*) and so forth. Thus, the fruit of the connection between the sense organ and its object is the state of appearing as immediate (*aparokṣāvabhāsitā*).

And it has been stated at the end of the discussion on perception that this [immediacy] exists in conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*). Therefore, that very cognition which arises from the reflection upon the power of words and has for its domain an object not in contact [with the senses] is verbal (*śābda*). For this very reason, the mere knowledge of the word-meaning is not verbal; for that does not have an object not in contact [with the senses] as its domain.
For he will say: "It does not arise from a mere recollection. What, then, is verbal [cognition]?
We say it is the knowledge of the meaning of a sentence. But surely that [knowledge] arises from the knowledge of the meanings of the individual words?

It is not from the knowledge of the word itself. No, because the communication of the word-meanings is the intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*) of words, just as combustion is for firewood in the act of cooking. For it will be said:
"The communication of word-meanings is like the flame of firewood in the process of cooking."
Thus, there is nothing at all that is untenable.

However, this must be addressed: why is a specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) being formulated here when it is the occasion for a general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), since a treatise (*śāstra*) is indeed a specific type of word? If it must be explained, then even so, having stated the general definition, [the specific one] will be stated.
Furthermore, it is improper that a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*) should be defined at the very moment of defining the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), as if in great haste.

For here, the specific characteristics such as "being visible to the eye" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth are not being defined for perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others. Therefore, when perception and the rest have begun to be discussed in their general sense, it is appropriate to state the definition of sound alone among them.
"It is not [the fault] of the treatise. This is what he says: "In the case of perception and so forth. (1)

He states another objection: "sāmānya... (beginning with the word *sāmānya*). For only that whose general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is already known can be made to understand its particular (*viśeṣa*), and not anything else. Indeed, when a substance (*dravya*) has not been characterized, its particulars—such as earth and the rest—cannot be characterized. // 2 //

Thus, it has been stated that the designation of the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) as "the treatise" (*śāstra*) is untenable. Furthermore, he says—referring to what was stated [in verse 3]—"from the cognition of words," etc.—that even the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) does not apply to the specific object to be defined. // 3 //

What, then, is the definition of a treatise (*śāstra*)? To this he says: "Engagement" (*pravṛtti*). For that which teaches engagement and withdrawal is called a treatise—whether it be the eternal Vedic sentences or the non-eternal Dharmaśāstras and so forth—and not merely sound (*śabdamātra*). // 4 //
But surely, even sentences such as "He who desires speed [should sacrifice with a goat]," which express only the essential nature [of a thing], are accepted as scripture (*śāstra*);

why then is it said that "scripture consists in that which is an auxiliary to engagement (*pravṛtti*) and desistance (*nivṛtti*)"? To this he replies: "The essential nature," etc. "As an auxiliary to that" means:
as a part of an injunctive sentence (*vidhāyakavākya*). For there too, [it is said]: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu."

Thus ends the statement of the injunction (*vidhyuddeśa*). Therefore, passages such as "Vāyu is indeed the swiftest" constitute a single syntactical unit with that injunction. Consequently, it is appropriate that this too possesses the status of a scripture (*śāstra*). // 5 //

Now, it is true that explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) do not directly enjoin an action, nor do they enjoin any of its constituent parts—namely, the three factors consisting of the goal (*sādhya*), the means (*sādhana*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Since none of these [factors] are expressed by them, we do not consider those whose purpose is not action to form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction. To this, he says: "The scripture [is authoritative] regarding the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)."

up to this point. This is the intended meaning: although [the word] does not convey an action, nor anything connected with an action such as a means (*sādhana*) and so forth, nevertheless, these [words] form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*) with the injunction (*vidhi*), which is otherwise known by the name "verbal productive energy" (*śabdabhāvanā*). For the injunction impels the person...

To induce activity, [an agent] requires knowledge of the excellence of the object; and since the *arthavādas* are capable of producing that, they are useful for instigating engagement or cessation when they perform this function. Therefore, it is only when the *bhāvanā* is complete in its three components—that is, from the great sentence (*mahāvākya*) itself together with the *arthavāda*—that a person engages or desists, and not from the injunctive statement alone.
Thus, a statement that includes an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is indeed a *śāstra*. We shall elaborate upon this in the section concerning *arthavādas*.

Furthermore, a portion of this has already been shown in the commentary on injunctions (*vidhi*); therefore, enough of this excessive prolixity. Precisely because the knowledge of engagement and desistance arises from [the Veda] together with its explanatory praises, [it is authoritative].

For this very reason, even when there is the hearing of an injunction consisting of a mere suffix denoting an injunction or a mere word such as "yajeta" (one should sacrifice), it does not possess the status of a *śāstra*. For where even the statement of the three-factored *bhāvanā*— as an intermediate sentence— is incapable of inciting activity because it lacks the support of a corroborative passage (*arthavāda*), [it cannot be a scripture].
"How indeed will there be a capacity for the word and its conditions in that case? This is difficult to comprehend," he says: "Because [the cognition] does not arise from the word, etc. (6).

{3,104} Thus, he justifies the commentary (*bhāṣya*) which has been criticized on the grounds that the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and the object to be defined (*lakṣya*) are untenable, by stating: "It is unexamined" (*aparīkṣā*). This is the intended meaning: since the exegesis of the Veda is the subject at hand, only that which is useful for it should be stated; therefore, even bypassing the general introduction, he has defined the specific [subject] itself. For the composition of a definition is not intended here as an end in itself. Indeed, it is through the pretext of being unexamined that...
Definitions are being formulated. Even there, only that which is useful for the subject at hand has been established as the definition of a treatise (*śāstra*):
"The Veda is independent because it is not dependent on a person. // 7 //

If he does not speak things that are independent and devoid of utility, then what follows? To this he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). For when it is established that he, like a chatterer, does not speak what is useless, then if he were to state the definition of words as found in worldly speech, that would be useless for him who intends to explain the Veda. // 8 //

Now, one might object: "If that which is not useful [to the Veda] is not to be defined, then why are perception and the other means of knowledge defined? For no utility for them in relation to the Veda is observed. To this he replies: "Perception and the rest" (*pratyakṣādi*). The intention is as follows: there is indeed great assistance even in the mere determination of the nature of the Veda; for without that, it would not be possible—at the very outset, at the time of first receiving the sacred text (*svādhyāya*)—to determine even the phonemes, morae, and so forth.
Furthermore, at the time of knowing the meaning of the scripture, that which has not been ascertained would be of no use because it is not remembered.

Therefore, having considered the utility of perception and other means of knowledge regarding the phonemes, syllables, and so forth—both before and after [the mantra's application]—their definition was formulated.
Inference, too, is utilized for the inference of the remainder of a mantra applied to a specific ritual part (*pratīka*), such as in the injunction: "He offers with the words *devasya tvā*."

Comparison (*upamāna*) is also useful for comparing specific types of actions, such as those involving heroism and the like. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also useful for the postulation of a portion of a Vedic sentence that has not been heard.

Non-existence (*abhāva*) is also useful for determining the extent of words and sentences, and for determining that certain rites have unmanifest injunctions (*avyakta-codanā*) due to the absence of substances, deities, and so forth; such is the meaning of the two uses of the word "etc. (in the sūtra). // 9 //

And since no such utility exists for the definition of verbal testimony found in sentences like "bring the cow," that [definition] was disregarded and the definition occurring in the technical treatises (śāstra) alone was formulated;
thus he says: "But as for... (yat tu). 10.

Furthermore, he addresses the objection that "if the universal (*sāmānya*) is not characterized, the particular (*viśeṣa*) cannot be characterized," with the words: "And the particular... For the particular is not established when the universal is being characterized, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The particular, however, does not deviate from the universal; therefore, when that [particular] is characterized, the universal contained within it is characterized with ease. This is because, when there is a cognition of an object not present to the senses (*asannikṛṣṭe 'rthe*) arising from a prescriptive cognition (*vidhāyakavijñāna*), [it constitutes inference].

Since it has been stated that "it is the scripture" (*śāstra*), it can be understood from the sense of that [statement]—namely, from the mere knowledge of the words devoid of any specific injunction—that "[it is] verbal" (*śābda*); therefore, it is not mentioned separately. // 11 //

But was it not said that this is not a specific definition because there is no mention of a specific [object]? To this he says: "The general," etc. A qualifier is not necessarily one that is explicitly mentioned;
rather, it may also be obtained through the context (*adhikāra*), as will be explained in the case of the *Āgneya* and other [oblations]. That...

Even here, because the context concerns that which is characterized by *codanā*, it should be understood that even when "from the cognition of the word" is stated, the qualification "injunctional" (*vidhāyaka*) is intended. [Objection: If only what is useful to the present topic must be stated, then one should simply say "characterized by *codanā*"; why then is there a definition of "scripture" (*śāstra*)? To this he replies: "Injunction" (*codanā*). The sense is that these are synonyms. // 12 //

And this attainment of a specific distinction by way of the governing context (adhikāra) is also accepted by Jaimini, who employs the term *codanā* without qualification in the second sūtra; thus he says, "And as... He thinks as follows: although the word *codanā* denotes any sentence that prompts action in general, [the specific meaning is determined by the context].

Nevertheless, because the first sūtra introduces the immediate succession to the study of the Veda by means of the word "atha," the term *codanā*— by virtue of that very context— is restricted to Vedic injunction alone; likewise here, in this definition of the treatise (*śāstra*), since the topic under discussion is the authority of *codanā*, the terms "knowledge of words" and "knowledge of meaning" refer specifically to particular words and meanings.
The word "word" refers to that which prescribes, and the word "meaning" refers to that which is to be prescribed. // 13 //

Furthermore, regarding what was stated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) at the occasion of presenting the view of the Sub-commentator (*vṛttikāra*)—namely, that perception and the other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) are well-known, and that the scripture (*śāstra*) is included within them—it is shown that even there, the promise not to examine the specific scriptures was made solely with the intention of relevance to the subject at hand;
this is indicated by the words "perception and so forth. However, this must be considered: if scripture is a cognition produced by injunctive words, [then...]

Now, are the Vedāṅgas, Mīmāṃsā, and the treatises on ritual (karmānuśāsana) not *śāstras*, while worldly sentences such as "Bring the cow" and so forth are *śāstras*? If this were so, there would be a great contradiction with common worldly usage; for ordinary people do not apply the term *śāstra* to worldly sentences like "Bring the cow. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with your own words, since [the definition] resides in sentences such as "Bring the cow."

For they say that the definition of *śāstra* is such. In the Mīmāṃsā and other systems, we observe the metaphorical application of the word *śāstra* even to the Veda, or to something superior even to that. Furthermore, this word *śāstra* may be either conventional (*rūḍha*) or etymological (*yaugika*);
in either case, it is fit to apply to the Vedāṅgas and similar works.

For it has been described that in those [words] there is, as appropriate, instruction regarding their meaning, and that their conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) is preeminent. To this, it is replied: this is a case of "etymological-conventional" (*yogarūḍhi*) usage, like the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") and others;

therefore, it does not first result in over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "bring the cow" (*gām ānaya*). This is because, even though the etymological connection (*yoga*) exists, they are not employed by worldly people in those [specific senses].

Ordinary people consider only those [treatises] that teach human goals (puruṣārtha) to be "śāstra. Thus, by virtue of being its auxiliary limbs (aṅga), they too possess the status of śāstra. [Objection: But is it not the case that the definition of a śāstra is "that which prescribes" (vidhāyaka)?

And these [auxiliaries] do not prescribe anything at all. [Response: Not so; for all of them are devoted to the instruction on performance (anuṣṭhāna). This is the case with grammar (vyākaraṇa) as well.

For that which the virtuous would speak is what is taught by these [treatises]. Even in Mīmāṃsā, in every section (*adhikaraṇa*), through the exposition of reasoning (*nyāya*), there is everywhere only the instruction for performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, the rule is that whatever is a treatise (*śāstra*) is necessarily an instruction for engagement in activity;
however, the worldly convention—that whatever is an instruction is necessarily a treatise—is here restated by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*).

Furthermore, the definition of a treatise (*śāstra*) was not formulated independently of that [reliability]. Therefore, that sentence which has for its object an imperceptible thing (*asannikṛṣṭārtha*), which prescribes what is beneficial for man, and which is renowned in the world as a "treatise," is a treatise. On the other hand, that which has for its object an imperceptible thing, whether it be prescriptive or non-prescriptive, is verbal cognition (*śābda*).

This is the distinction (*viveka*). Just as in the case of perception, here too—in respect to the word, its cognition, and so forth—the various types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) should be demonstrated according to one's intention. One should not be dogmatic in insisting that cognition alone is the means of valid cognition. Furthermore, in the case of the preceding means of valid cognition, the subsequent cognition of the sentence-meaning is the fruit; and when that [sentence-meaning] is a valid cognition, the cognition of avoidance and so forth is the fruit. This is the distinction. // 14 //
Proponents of the doctrine of two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇadvayavādin*) maintain that this treatise is non-different from inference.
Desiring to refute them, [the author] sets forth their opinion with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*). This has been stated by them as a mere proposition;

however, the presentation of their reasons for non-difference will be undertaken on the occasion of refuting the reasons for difference stated by others. But why is such effort expended in presenting and then refuting the argument for non-difference?
Now, one might object that this non-difference has already been refuted by the Sāṅkhyas and others who maintain the doctrine of difference;
therefore, he says: "Difference. The meaning is that they have not correctly stated the cause of difference. // 15 //

He introduces those very grounds for differentiation mentioned earlier in order to refute them, ending with the words "pūrvasaṃskāra. For they have stated it thus: "In the case of a word, it is either the final phoneme conjoined with the preceding impressions (*saṃskāra*), or the sentence, or even the first phoneme."
Whether all [the phonemes] individually,
or together,
or the sequence of those very words, or the universal of sentencehood (*vākyatvajāti*), or a composite whole (*avayavin*) from which all distinctions such as individual phonemes have been shaken off.
Either the *sphoṭa* or the words themselves, acting in combination, express the meaning. These same alternatives should also be shown regarding the words;

likewise, the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), effort (*prayatna*), and so forth, are the causes for the production of sound. Since all of this is not observed in the case of smoke and the like, [the inference] is invalid due to that dissimilarity (*tadvaidharmya*).

Regarding the point that [verbal cognition] is inference (*anumānatva*), he states the refutation therein: "In this regard," etc. When the Buddhist has stated that verbal cognition is non-different from inference because it arises through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just like the inference of fire from smoke, this [opponent's] counter-argument is based on the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with smoke and the like.

This is the fallacy (jāti) called "balancing the heterogeneity" (vaidharmyasamā) or "balancing the alternative" (vikalpasamā). What, then, is a fallacy? A fallacy is a counter-argument based on similarity or dissimilarity. For when an argument has been put forward by a proponent, a logical consequence arises; because it arises, it is called a "fallacy."
And that *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is an opposition based on similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

When the proponent has stated a reason (*hetu*) by way of similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*), there occurs an opposition by the opponent through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For example, when the proponent says: "The self possesses action because it is endowed with qualities that are the causes of action, like a clod of earth."
The opponent's counter-argument by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) is as follows: "Just as a substance possessing action is seen to be non-pervasive,
such as a clod of earth,
so too is the self not [non-pervasive]."

Therefore, [the soul] is inactive. This is called the *jāti* known as "balancing the dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyasama*). Likewise, when a distinction regarding another property is introduced by the opponent, such that a distinction is also applied to the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), this is called the *jāti* named "balancing the distinction" (*vikalpasama*). For example, in this very same argument, the opponent says:
It is observed that some things are non-omnipresent and endowed with the qualities of action and cause, such as a clod of earth, while others are omnipresent, such as the self;
likewise, some will be possessed of action and some will be devoid of action. Thus, here too, when the opponent seeks to establish non-difference [between all things], [the same logic applies].
When an objection is raised based merely on the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with smoke and other [inferences], the fallacy (*jāti*) called "balancing the dissimilar" (*vaidharmyasama*) is incurred.

For the inference of fire from smoke is devoid of verbal formulation (*vākya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and so forth; but verbal cognition (*śābda*) is not like that. Therefore, it is not inference.

Likewise, "balancing the conceptual" (*vikalpasama*) should be demonstrated as follows: some [cognition] arises solely from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), while [others arise] from verbal formulation and conceptual construction.
Just as some [cognitions] are seen to be verbal,
while others— such as the cognition of fire through smoke— are not; in the same way, there will be some that are inferential.
"Something is not an inference. Because two types of genus are presented, it should not be said that the response is also a proof. // 16 //
But how is this [classification of] birth [justified]? For this is the proof: "Verbal cognition is distinct from inference because it possesses a different character, just like perception.
To this he says: "Smoke... [It is] not, first of all, by abandoning the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*).

They have stated a point of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). However, if dissimilarity were indistinct merely through some qualification, then even those [cognitions] whose nature is the object (*arthātmaka*) would have to be distinct from inference; yet this is not the case. For smoke and so forth do not become non-inferential simply because there is no difference [in their being objects].

Because it does not abandon the three characteristics [of a valid reason], "being produced" is a reason for impermanence; for even when the abandonment of the three characteristics is demonstrated, the distinction from inference is established. // 17 //

But for one who asserts a difference based merely on dissimilarity, that very statement of dissimilarity would result in being a universal (*jāti*); thus he says: "By means of the three characteristics. (18)

Furthermore, this other distinction between verbal testimony and inference has been stated: for in the case of inference, smoke and the like produce the cognition of a connection through a natural (svābhāvika) bond; however, from a word, the comprehension of an object is seen to occur even when it is employed according to one's own will;
therefore, there is a difference.

To this he says: "Just as... The intention here is as follows: even in this case, if a difference is asserted merely on the basis of some dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), then it is simply a matter of genus (*jāti*). Now, suppose this formal argument (*prayoga*) were made: "Verbal cognition is distinct from inference, because it conveys its object through the application of [the speaker's] will at pleasure, like the sense organs (*akṣa*). For the sense organs—such as the eye and so forth—convey only that very object toward which they are directed. That is incorrect; for even in that case, the conveyance of color-form (*rūpa*) and other objects occurs through the inherent power of their own nature. Or, if the reason is "conveying [an object] through the application of will at pleasure within its own domain," [it remains flawed].

Therefore, it is the same in the case of the logical mark (*liṅga*): when it is employed for the sake of another, it brings about the understanding of that very person toward whom it is directed. Now, if "convention" (*saṅketa*) is defined as the application [of a word] according to one's will, then the meaning [of the above argument] becomes this: wherever it is conventionally established, it causes the understanding of that very thing.

Consequently, there is an absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), for nothing other than sound itself makes an object known by following a convention. Alternatively, this is a *avīta* reason: inference indeed consists in a presentation that does not follow an arbitrary application [of the object], and this [word] is not like that.

Therefore, [the claim] that "it is distinct" is incorrect. This is because mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not indicative; for a logical reason (*hetu*) is required to possess both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*). Furthermore, this reason is never perceived as being pervaded by non-difference from inference, since nothing other than verbal testimony is ever established through arbitrary application. If it is argued that there is the establishment [of meaning] through hand gestures and the like according to convention, then that must be either a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) or inference. It cannot, first of all, be a separate means of valid cognition.

Because it lacks the characteristic of being tall, that which is known by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed inference (*anumāna*). This being the case, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that very [reason], and thus the exclusion of the reason from inference is not established. This is what was stated: "there is deviation due to the functions of the limbs. The functions of the limbs (*aṅgavṛtti*) are the movements such as contraction and extension belonging to the limbs, such as the hands and so forth. // 19 //

He explains this very point with the words "hand" (*hasta*) and so forth. It is precisely the functions residing in the limbs, such as the hands, that are called "hand-signs" (*hastasaṃjñā*) because they serve as a means for the cognition of specific objects. But how can this be an inference? For the configurations of the hands and other limbs are not pervaded (*vyāpta*) by specific meanings such as numbers and the like, since they sometimes occur even in the absence of those [meanings]. Rather, people understand the object from the configuration of the fingers and so forth by means of the recollection of the word that existed at the time of the convention.
[Objection: "They understand [the object] from the word alone. [Reply: That is not so.

For even without a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), one who is unlearned [in such conventions] perceives the meaning upon seeing the arrangement of a finger and so forth during ordinary usage (*vyavahāra*).
Nor is there any deviation (*vyabhicāra*) here; for no deviation is observed in the case of such an arrangement as that in which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) was understood.

This has been explained by him [the author of the *Ślokavārttika*] in the passage beginning "this [word] among other substrates (*dharmyantara*) is such. Therefore, this is indeed inference. This is what was stated: "That is its mark; such is the established rule. And having followed all of this, the author of the *Vārttika* offered a refutation:

for the comprehension of meaning from a word does not occur through arbitrary application. For words such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth function only in accordance with their own inherent power (*nija-śakti*).

They communicate their own meaning. However, as for arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), which—like hand gestures and the like—convey meaning by following convention, they are nothing other than inference; so what is the point of establishing a distinction between them? // 20 //
This is another cause of distinction:
for the determination of an object from a word depends upon a person,
whereas a logical mark (liṅga) determines the object by its own power alone.

"Therefore, because of its difference from that, there is a distinction. This too is an *avīta* reason (*avītahetu*). And it should be stated thus: "In inference, the determination of an object does not depend on a person, whereas in verbal testimony it does; therefore, it is distinct. He refutes this as well with the words "puruṣa" (person). A negative reason (*vyatirekahetu*) establishes an object precisely by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), just as [the reason] "vital breaths and so forth" establishes the Self as excluded from the body which is non-self. However, dependence on a person is seen to be a factor in the determination of an object even in inference, as observed in the case of the functions of the limbs. For whatever kind of convention exists for the communication of a particular meaning...
[The opponent argues: "It was composed by persons;

they understand that very [text] in dependence upon other persons. Therefore, even in this case, there is deviation [from the rule]. Furthermore, he says "pada" (word), because the reason is unestablished due to being non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). For words convey their meaning by their own power alone, not in dependence upon persons.
Even Vedic statements do not depend upon a person for the communication of their own meaning;
they depend upon an authoritative source only for the determination of their own form.
But surely, a word that has not had its relationship [with its meaning] grasped cannot convey a cognition; nor is there an understanding of the relationship that is independent of persons.
Even Vedic sentences do not convey their own meanings unless the relationship between words and word-meanings has been grasped.

Therefore, this relationship between words and word-meanings is indeed dependent upon persons, and thus there is no lack of pervasion [in the definition]. To this, he says: "The relationship... [etc.].
The intended meaning is as follows: first of all, a word and Vedic sentences are indeed independent in the communication of their meaning.

And just as the experience of the relationship [between word and meaning] here depends on a person, so too in other cases, such as inference, that [experience] is seen to be of a different nature. He demonstrates this very difference with the words "In this case... up to the end of the verse. "In this case" refers to [the cognition arising from] hand gestures and the like, which depends on a person.

For a convention (*samaya*) is indeed human-made. However, the relationship between fire and smoke depends on place; the relationship between the rising of the moon and the swelling of the ocean depends on time.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he indicates dependence on state (*avasthā*). Thus, by this it is meant: even in inference, the comprehension of the relation (*sambandha*) is of many kinds, due to the distinctions based on dependence on place and so forth. In the same way, here too [in the case of verbal testimony], there will be dependence on a person (*puruṣa*). This is the case with inference.
"Even so, the cognition of a relation is observed to be dependent upon that [object]. Furthermore, they have not even refuted the reasons for non-difference stated by others;
thus he says: "And it has been stated... (verse 22).

He presents that very reason for non-difference: "by means of the statement of a reliable person" (*āptavāda*). This is the meaning: just as in the case of smoke and so forth, the pervasion between two general properties is determined by setting aside their particular differences, so too in the case of verbal testimony, the pervasion between the general property of being the statement of a reliable person and the general property of non-contradiction is understood.
(The phrase *āptavādāvisaṃvāda* refers to this.)
And having understood it thus, even in the case of the Veda, non-contradiction is inferred because it is the word of the authoritative Lord (Īśvara);

therefore, this is indeed inference (*anumāna*). As long as non-contradiction is not inferred, the cognition that has arisen—even if it has an object as its domain—is simply not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) due to its lack of certainty. The general term [“non-contradiction”] is connected with each [instance]. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used in the elision of the gerund suffix (*lyap*).

112} Thus, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is as follows: although it is not possible to apprehend a relationship due to the differences among the specific instances of trustworthy speech and non-contradiction, nevertheless, because a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is possible between the two universals (*sāmānya*), it can be stated that these two possess the nature of inference (*anumāna*) through the cognition of those universals. // 23 //
But surely there is this ground for distinction:
inference is dependent upon the ascertainment of a relationship,
whereas words such as "apūrva" convey their own meaning without any dependence on the knowledge of such a relationship.

Therefore, to the objection that [the word] is distinct [from inference], he says: "And not so. Since words such as "cow" convey their meaning only when the relationship [between word and object] is already known, their status as inference is unavoidable; for even if one were to claim, by way of the example of *apūrva* (the unseen), that these too are distinct, that would not be correct. For the opponent is also able to argue that they are inference because they produce cognition dependent upon a relationship, just like smoke and the like. Furthermore, regarding the word *apūrva*:
He says "not so" [in verse 24], meaning that they do not differ from words such as "horse" and the like, because there is no distinction in their status as words (padatva).

What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "And not... Because these are indeed words, and a word whose relation [to its meaning] is unknown is not a revealer [of meaning]. Therefore, even by these [words], the object must be known only when their relations are already known, because they are words. But how can a relation with something previously unseen through other means of knowledge—such as the unprecedented heaven (*svarga*) and so forth—be experienced? It might not be possible; yet [it is].

If [the object] were not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then the "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) would be established by the evidence of *arthāpatti* (presumption), since the relationship between the action and its fruit as heard in scripture would otherwise be inexplicable.

Furthermore, heaven is understood from the supplementary portions of Vedic statements to be of the nature of unsurpassed bliss; thus, the apprehension of the relationship between these two [heaven and the action] as they are so understood is possible. Therefore, that which has been stated by others—that verbal testimony is not inference because it does not depend upon a [previously perceived] relationship—is [refuted].
He states that [the argument] "like the dice" is refuted because its reason is unestablished: "[The word] 'relation'... (verse 25).

Having introduced another reason for the distinction, he refutes it with the words "tulya" (equal). The analysis of the compound is: "sound," "proximity," "the cognition of that [sound]," and "the object and the cognition thereof. This too should be shown to be a non-reductio (*avīta*) reason. Its refutation should be understood as following what was stated in the refutation of superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Therefore, the claim of having an identical form is unestablished. // 26 //

Furthermore, he states that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because the intention to speak has ceased—namely, in the case of reflections. "Certainty" (*ekānta*) means a definitive conclusion;
since that [certainty] is its effect, and that is absent here, it is "inconclusive" (*anekānta*). How is it inconclusive?
Therefore, he says: "the original object" (*bimba*). For just as the original object is perceived in a mirror, exactly so is the face and such understood;

thus, there is a similarity here too between the signified (*gamya*) and the signifier (*gamaka*). Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) operating in the case of reflections is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, one might object: this is not inference, for the face is understood through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), being illuminated by the visual rays that are turned back by the light of the mirror.

This will be explained in the section on the word (*śabdādhikaraṇa*). Therefore, he says: "And not... The intention is as follows: when one has recognized the pervasion (*vyāpti*) through the similarity [of the reflection] to the fingers and so forth which are directly perceived, then one infers that the face situated in the mirror is also conformable to the original object (*bimba*). Otherwise, however, one might suspect that even the contact with the finger makes something of one form appear as something of another form. Therefore, not...
One should determine that it is of such a nature. // 27 //
Let it be that this is perception; what is the use of such subtle scrutiny?
We shall demonstrate an even clearer inference.

He says "perceptibility" (*pratyakṣatā*) because similarity is understood between the object to be inferred (*gamya*) and the means of inference (*gamaka*). By saying "of those that have gone," he demonstrates their imperceptibility (*apratyakṣatā*) for the purpose of establishing the object of inference (*anumānaviṣaya*). // 28 //
As for what was also said: "For in verbal cognition, a sentence uttered only once suddenly causes various objects to appear— both contradictory and non-contradictory—
just as in the cases of 'Dharma is an object characterized by Vedic injunction' and 'The white one runs.'"

It is not so in the case of inference. For smoke, having its pervasion known by a particular [fire], produces a cognition only with respect to that one [locus]. Therefore, there is a difference between verbal testimony and inference. And the formal argument is as follows: "Verbal testimony is distinct from inference because it sometimes presents multiple objects, unlike the sense-faculties. Or rather, the reason is *avīta* (negative-only), for the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is indeed singular.

"Just as smoke and so forth [are not identical], but sound is not like that, therefore it is distinct. Having set forth this [argument], he refutes it with the words "from a single sentence. The meaning is that even by this method, there is no distinction. // 29 //

"Why is there no difference? To this he says: "Of the mark (*liṅga*) as well. The sense is that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For the reason—namely smoke—simultaneously establishes fire-ness, heat, combustibility, and being a transformation of fuel. Likewise, it is contradictory (*viruddha*): [if one were to argue] "it is eternal..."

In the case of "Sound is [impermanent] because it is produced," it establishes permanence according to the speaker's intention, yet by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it establishes impermanence; therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, one might object: a contradictory reason does not establish multiple meanings.

For a logical mark (*liṅga*) becomes a means of cognition through the power of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Therefore, since "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) is pervaded by "impermanence" (*anityatva*), it is that [pervasion] alone which causes [the object] to be known.

However, the pervasion of a contradictory meaning for a single [mark] is impossible precisely because of the contradiction. First, he raises that doubt with the words "because of contradiction" (*virodhāt*). He states the answer with "it might be" (*syāt*). For the capacity of a word is understood to lie in the communication of the intended meaning.
Therefore, even he expresses only one meaning at a time; however, regarding other meanings, he too is simply non-conclusive due to contradiction. // 30 //

Furthermore, he says "And where... because by this reason, the distinction between numerous sentences that have a single meaning is not established. It is not only contradictory things that a word does not convey as many;
rather, it does not convey even non-contradictory things [as many]. This has been stated: "A word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding what is intended [by the speaker].
And from a sentence uttered only once, only a single intention residing in the speaker is inferred. Following that [intention], the object too is understood as being only one.

It follows that there is no instance anywhere of the simultaneous communication of multiple meanings; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished. To this, he says: "simultaneously" (sakṛt). // 31 //
Surely, there is indeed the manifestation of multiple meanings from a word; however, let it be granted that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) applies to only one [of those meanings].

And by this much, [the point] is established. To state [the distinction] through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from inference (*anumāna*), he says: "But as for that which... Just as, for example: {3, ...}
Just as, prior to familiarity with the correct analysis of linguistic expression, multiple meanings waver from a word,
so too is it observed that when a sign such as smoke is not clearly discerned, there arises the appearance of multiple possible objects.
For one who is in doubt from a distance— wondering whether this is smoke or a drift of dust— the mind remains unsettled between fire and a whirlwind.
"Applied thought" (vitarka) means: // 32 //

Likewise, he states that the failure to state an example in the case of sound is not a cause for [its] distinction from smoke and so forth, because of deviation (vyabhicāra)—thus he says: "dṛṣṭānta... [etc.]. How is there deviation? To this he says: "prasiddhatvāt" (because it is well-known). // 33 //

Now, it might be argued that while there is indeed a dependence on an example when a term is unfamiliar, in the case of the word [for Brahman], even that is absent; to this he says: "unpracticed. He demonstrates this very dependence with the words: "in this case. For where a doubt arises concerning an object whose meaning is not well-known, as long as one does not understand—after reflecting for a long time—that "this word is used by the elders in this sense," [one remains in doubt].
"One would not, for that reason, determine that object. Thus, it has been demonstrated that the proponents of difference have not correctly stated the causes of difference. // 34 //

He states that they have not even refuted the reasons for non-difference asserted by the Buddhists, saying: "Those stated by others. He sets forth those very reasons for non-difference in two and a half verses beginning with "Of word and inference. The meaning of this is as follows: just as the inference of fire from smoke is produced through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and because a single instance of smoke is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), [3, ...]
And it arises preceded by a connection;

likewise, knowledge arising even from a word arises in this very manner. Furthermore, that [knowledge] is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than perception, and it makes known an object not perceived through perception.

And verbal cognition has a universal as its object and is based on the three times; therefore, it does not differ [from inference]. This is an explanation of the meaning of the proof-statement (*sādhana-vākya*). The applications of the proof, however, should be demonstrated as follows: "Verbal cognition is inference because it is produced by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), like the inference of fire."

Thus, because it arises from the perception of a single instance, its being preceded by a [prior] relation is likewise the reason (*hetu*). Those two alone are the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Nor should it be said that [the reason] does not differ from "being preceded by a relation" because it is born of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

"Because the connection of inference consists of both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Previously, the reason was stated as being "born from a specific connection," whereas now it is stated as "being preceded by a general connection," without intending to specify the particularity. In this same manner, for the [remaining] three cases as well, the application of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should be performed as before. However, in the fourth case, the inference of fire is merely an illustration.
Inference based on future occurrence and inference based on past occurrence must also be demonstrated. // 35–37 //

Now, he introduces the refutation of the grounds for the distinction asserted by a certain faction of Mīmāṃsakas, beginning with the words "by some. He demonstrates that it is indeed a different object of cognition, using the phrase "from the two preceding ones. The intention is as follows: whatever operates upon an object not already determined by another means of knowledge is distinct from that other means, just as inference is distinct from perception. And since the scripture (śāstra) operates upon an object not determined by the first two [means of knowledge], it is therefore distinct from them. But what is the purpose of establishing its distinction from perception?

For no one maintains that non-difference [of word and meaning] exists, such that it would be refuted. It is replied: there certainly is a delusion among some, namely that this verbal cognition, which arises based on the operation of the auditory organ, is simply auditory perception.

Because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [auditory organ]. For this very reason, it does not occur for one who is deaf. Thus, by this demonstration of difference through perception (*pratyakṣa*), [the opponent's position] is refuted. For he thinks as follows: it has been shown that perception is the apprehension of an existing object; however, this verbal [cognition] has objects belonging to all three times, so how could it be included within perception?

A deaf person, however, does not understand the meaning because of not hearing the sound, not because of not hearing the meaning. And there is the formal argument: verbal cognition is distinct from perception, because its object is not determined by that [perception], just like inference. // 38 //

Therefore, having accepted this difference as being evident through perception, he refutes the cause of difference on the basis of inference—saying, "In that case also. He thinks as follows: if, because their objects are not determined by another means of knowledge, human statements were thus not to be considered scripture (*āgama*), then they would lack the status of scripture because their objects are determined by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

"But since it is only the Vedic sentences whose objects lie beyond other means of knowledge that differ, the reason [you have given] is too narrow. What, then, is this undesirable consequence you have brought forward?
Is it not indeed accepted that human speech lacks the status of *āgama*?
For *āgama* is indeed scripture (*śāstra*).

He will state that "the scripture is purposeful regarding what has not been [otherwise] obtained. However, since these [other means of knowledge] establish objects already obtained through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), they are merely restatements (*anuvāda*). For this very reason, the Vedic sentence itself is treated as the distinct subject (*pakṣa*) in the form "the scripture functions toward an object," because it is precisely its distinction [from other means of knowledge] that is useful. He says "so it is" to express this.
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "The cognition" (*pratyaya*). Thus, this proponent of the unreliability of human speech must be questioned:
"Is there a cognition of the object from those [words], or not?
It cannot be that there is none.

Because it would follow that all worldly conventions (*vyavahāra*) would be annihilated. Furthermore, since it is impossible for an existing thing to arise without a cause, a cause must be stated. And no cause other than speech (*śabda*) is logically possible for this [cognition]. Thus, the cognition produced by human speech is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), being born, free from doubt, and uncontradicted by another cognition; therefore, one cannot maintain that it is not based on scripture (*anāgama*).
"It is appropriate," [says one]. But the other, intending to show that [verbal testimony] is included within inference, says: "of the speaker's cognition. This is the intention:
for human statements are mostly inconsistent; therefore, they do not determine their object merely upon being heard. And an object that is not determined cannot be said to be known.

Since certainty alone constitutes knowledge, there is an absence of knowledge prior to the arising of that certainty; therefore, what is the use of an effort toward a cause? However, when the speaker himself is thus ascertained to possess a pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that he does not speak of what he has not understood—then, by means of his very statement, which is the effect of knowledge, one infers the knowledge that serves as its cause. Through the non-deviation of knowledge from the object, the object [is established].

[The object] is determined. And in that state, because the object is already known through the mark of cognition (*jñāna-liṅga*), the sentence is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*). Therefore, it is not *āgama*. But the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādin*) says: "How indeed could this [be so]? The intention is this: for it is cognition that, once apprehended, determines the object; and we shall explain that there is no cause for the apprehension of this [cognition] itself. // 39 //

Therefore, since [the word] itself is not understood, it cannot be the mark (*liṅga*) of the object; thus he says: "No. But was it not said that [the object] will be inferred from the word as an effect? To this he says: "Not the word. He demonstrates how neither [of these two] is a mark for both [cases] by means of the term "particularity" (*viśeṣa*). For inference occurs by virtue of pervasion (*vyāpti*).

And in this case, it would follow that the generality of the sentence is established from the generality of the cognition— since the generality of the sentence is understood as being pervaded by the generality of the cognition— and from mere cognition, mere objects [would follow];
but it is not so here.
Because it is the cognition and its specific object that are intended to be inferred, and because those two cannot be objects of inference due to the absence of a grasped relation [between them].
But surely, when a trustworthy person employs a statement, they employ it only after having known [the object]; thus, the relation is understood precisely through the specific cognition.
Therefore, that very [cognition] shall be inferred. If this is so, [then...]
In that case, the meaning must have already been understood prior to the sentence;

for it cannot be said that one employs a word in a manner other than [having known its meaning]. Moreover, if the meaning were not first known, how could the cognition [of the speaker's intention] be inferred? Would one infer, "This speaker knew something," or rather, "He knew this specific meaning"?

This [object] cannot be pointed out as something not yet apprehended. Furthermore, no specific quality of cognition can exist—apart from the contact with an object—which could be inferred. Nor is mere cognition devoid of an object inferred; nor is a specific object established on that basis. And cognition is not unascertained.

This is because the method for producing knowledge in one whose mind is characterized by doubt has already been demonstrated. Furthermore, no such doubt arises from the words of a trustworthy person (*puruṣavākya*).

As for the suspicion of invalidity that might occasionally arise due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it has been stated that this is dispelled by [the speaker’s] reliability (*āptatva*) and other such qualities. However, if it is argued that the understanding of a specific cognition occurs in this manner:
When it has been determined in this way— that this speaker does not employ words whose meanings are unconnected, nor those whose connections are not understood—
it follows that he must certainly know the connection between these words. Now, is the listener one who already knows the connection between words and word-meanings?

One does not understand the meaning from the words of a man at all. If that were so, then the supreme teachers [would be redundant]. However, the cognition that has arisen—being free from doubt and error—would not differ from the understanding produced by Vedic sentences. While a mere suspicion might somehow arise even regarding the Veda due to its being a "sentence" and so forth, its lack of authority is not established by that alone. "By those two" means by the [resultant] cognition and the word. // 40 //

Therefore, since perception and other means of valid cognition are impossible for the apprehension of the speaker’s intention, and since inference based on the object is untenable when that intention is not apprehended, the statement of a person—which brings about for the listener an object never before attained—is indeed scripture (*āgama*), just like the Veda. Thus he says: "By that... (verse 41).

As for what is also said—that the Veda, because its object is distinct, is indeed a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—that too is merely a wishful thought; thus he says, "And not even... The intended meaning is that it cannot be so stated.
Why can it not be so stated? To this he says: "The inferential mark (*liṅga*). When, by the previously mentioned reasons, everything without exception...
The point is this: since verbal cognition has thus been stated to be non-different from inference, how could its object possibly not be inferable? // 42 //

[Objection: But surely, since the Veda makes known an object not previously inferred by means of a mark (*liṅga*) in the form of its own meaning, it will be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this he says: "And not...
