For just as smoke-possessingness, being produced, and so forth, despite having internal differences, possess the nature of inference (*anumānatva*) without abandoning the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*), so it would be here as well. However, if it is argued that those [three characteristics] do not exist at all, [then the following applies].
In that case, it should be asked:
what is the purpose of introducing these intermediate distinctions? // 43 //

Others, however, whose powers are diminished, having resorted to non-difference itself, stand as partial proponents (*ekadeśin*); he shows this by saying, "it being thus established. For this is their intention: the authority of *codanā* has indeed been asserted, and that is certainly established even if the Vedic word is of the nature of inference (*anumāna*). For just as the Veda is authoritative from among words in general, so too is it here.

Thus, since the Veda is an inference from other inferences, what is the point of such great effort to establish their distinction? [Objection: But was it not stated by the Commentator that dharma cannot be inferred because it is yet to come into being (*bhaviṣyat*)? Therefore, if one accepts its status as an inference, there would be a contradiction with that; to this he says: "It will be. The meaning is that his refutation was intended with reference to an inferential mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the nature of an object. // 44 //
He refutes this as well with the word "saṃjñā" (name). The meaning is: if its status as inference is due to its subsequent mental generality (*mānasasāmānya*), then let it be so;

there is no fault in accepting that. However, if non-difference is desired on the grounds of the identity of their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), then since the defining characteristic of inference would be absent and another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would not be admitted, it follows that the Vedic words would simply lack authority. Thus he says: "by the defining characteristic. // 46 //

[Objection: But was it not stated that "the identity of definition [is established] because of the commonality of non-contradiction with the speech of a reliable person"? To this, he says: "āptavāda... (regarding the speech of a reliable person). The point is that by this method, the validity of human statements is established because they are of the nature of inference, but this does not apply to the words of the Veda. // 47 //

Why is it not established? To this he says: "But in the case of the Veda... Since there is an absence of a trustworthy person (āpta), it cannot be an inference based on the non-contradiction of a statement by a trustworthy person. Furthermore, since the experience of a relationship between the Vedas and supersensible objects is not established, they would simply be invalid. He will state in the *Vedādhikaraṇa* that the Vedas were not composed by a trustworthy person. // 48 //

[Objection: Having observed that certain portions of the Veda, such as the sentences concerning the "kṣepiṣṭha" [fire], have meanings corroborated by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), one may infer that other sentences as well—such as those concerning the *agnihotra*—possess true meaning because they are part of the Veda. Therefore, since there is an inference based on a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), [the Veda] is indeed inferential;
to this he replies with "nanu" (but...). 49.

He refutes this as well with the words "not because of the sun" (*nāditya*). The reason based on being Vedic scripture (*vedatva*) found in the passage concerning the sun-pillar (*āditya-yūpa*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Now, one might object: "This sentence does not have an unreal meaning;
for it will be stated in the *Tatsiddhi* Sūtra that the word 'sun' applies to the pillar figuratively (*gauṇa*) due to similarity.
To this he replies: "In the same way" (*tadvat*). Even the sentences concerning the connection between ritual action and its fruit would likewise be merely figurative.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, previously, by the power of the Veda’s own authority and its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the inferences regarding its lack of authority were refuted. However, if one were to concede that [the Veda] is an inference, then those [inferences against it] would also have an equal force and their spread would be difficult to restrain; thus he says: "Not from this... (verse 50).

Therefore, if one maintains that verbal testimony (*śabda*) constitutes a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) solely on the basis of a difference in its defining characteristic, then the Vedas would indeed be a means of valid cognition; furthermore, the status of being a means of valid cognition would be established equally for both worldly speech and the Veda. To this he says: "Therefore, even though the definition [of verbal testimony] has been adopted by others as 'verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person' (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*), nevertheless, because of the absence of a reliable person, the Veda would lack validity. Thus he states that such a definition should not be relied upon, concluding with "by that," namely, by the Vedānta. Furthermore, he states that even in the world, being a reliable person is not the cause of validity, saying: "in the world..."

He states the reason: "Previously. For, by virtue of being authoritative (*āpta*), there is merely the removal of any suspicion of sublation (*apavāda*). However, the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all cognitions is indeed innate; this has been explained in the discussion on the theory of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇyavāda*). What, then, is the definition of scripture (*āgama*)? To this he says: "Therefore. Cognition produced by faultless words is valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). // 53 //
He states that for a word of a single class, its validity alone is equal to that of inference, not its definition, saying: "by means of inference. (53)

Now, intending to state the distinction of the word (*pada*) from inference according to his own system, he states the reason for establishing that distinction: "The word" (*pada*). Although there is no need to establish its distinction [from inference] because the word is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the object of the word (*padārtha*), nevertheless, since others have conducted an investigation by citing examples of words, we shall establish its distinction precisely in that regard. "In this context" (*atra*) means "in the case of the word. (54)

Now he states the cause for this distinction: "the object" (viṣaya). He demonstrates the very distinction between objects with the words "sāmānya... (general, etc.). For it will be established in the *Ākṛtyadhikaraṇa* that the word has the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. // 55 //
However, it has been established in the section on inference (*anumānapariccheda*) that inference has as its object a subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*);

thus he says: "the subject" (*dharmī*). That which possesses a mark (*liṅga*) is the "marked" (*liṅgin*). There exists a mark that establishes that [subject] as qualified [by the property]. Now, one might object: in inference, it is the generality of the property (*dharmasāmānya*) that is inferred by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*); to this he replies: "Not yet," and so forth. As long as...
If that inference does not have that [dharma] as its object— that is, if it does not have a qualified object— it is not an inference at all;
it does not even have dharma alone (or dharma as its object).
It has been stated that this is because [the point] is already established. // 56 //

But is it not observed that even a single word has a qualified object as its scope? For example, when asked, "Which king is going?", another replies, "The King of Pañcāla. In that case, from the word "King of Pañcāla" alone, a person qualified by an action is understood;
therefore, he says: "from the general [term]" (*sāmānyāt*). That very... [3]

123} Whatever is understood in verbal cognition as something additional to the general sense is the specific domain of the sentence alone. For it is the sentence itself—through the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) with that [additional element]—that conveys the specific meaning, such as "the King of Pañcāla goes. Now, one might object: let there be such a connection for what has been heard;

however, even when another word is not heard, a qualified understanding is observed to arise from a single word, as for example when "the door" is said, [the meaning] "let it be opened" is understood.

Regarding this, how [is it so]? To this he says: "By implication" (*sāmarthyāt*). For a factor of action (*kāraka*) has its pervasion (*vyāpti*) known through an action; by the very power of that pervasion, it implies the verbal expression of the action. And from the sentence itself, in which the verbal expression of the action has been inferred, there arises the cognition of the specific meaning even in that case as well. // 57 //

Here he raises an objection: "Number, etc. He replies: "Not at all. For how could [the qualifier] be meaningful in a case where number and so forth are already understood? To this he says: "Even where... Indeed, a qualifier becomes purposeful through the possibility of its application and the possibility of its deviation. But a generic form (*ākṛti*) does not deviate from oneness.
Since duality and so forth cannot exist apart from unity, number and the like are qualifiers of the individual (vyakti) itself, which is implied by that [unity]. // 58 //
Thus, it has first been stated that the individual instance (*vyakti*) is qualified by way of *anurañjana* (coloring);

however, number and other factors qualify the action—that is, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—by being for its sake (*tādarthya*), since they are applied to it through direct statement (*śruti*) and the other means of proof.

As will be explained in the case of the singularity of the animal and in the case of "red" (*aruṇa*) and so forth, he says: "By being another word (*padāntara*)," [meaning] that they function as qualifiers through an extremely remote connection (*atyantaviprakṛṣṭaviśeṣaṇatā*).
"He shows," thus [it is said]. // 58 //

"In that case, a word such as 'gomat' (possessing cows), which has as its object a particular state of affairs consisting of the meaning of a sentence, will be an inference. To this he replies: "The meaning of a sentence" (*vākyārtha*). Even though this [word] indeed has a qualified object as its domain, it nevertheless lacks the nature of inference. For a subject (*dharmin*) that is already established becomes a thesis (*pakṣa*) when it is being proven as qualified by some unestablished property (*dharma*). But here, nothing at all is apprehended prior to the utterance of the word; yet, once the word has been uttered—

"If it is already understood as something distinguished (*viśiṣṭa*), what remains to be proven? [The author] shows that it is indeed already established by saying "to that extent" (*tāvān*). One who has not grasped the relationship [between word and object] does not understand the distinguished [object] from the word. But one who understands it having grasped the relationship does not understand anything more than what was already known at the time of linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*); how, then, could this be inference? // 60 //
Moreover, in this case, two distinct parts of a word—consisting of base and suffix—are understood as having two distinct meanings which experience the relationship of qualifier and qualified;
thus, a difference [between the two cases] is established. He says: "Because of the cognition of difference.
This, however, is appropriate to say regarding words such as *pācaka* (cook) and the like.

For in that case, the verbal root (*dhātu*) conveys the act of cooking (*pāka*), while the suffix (*pratyaya*) conveys merely the agent; however, the specific [meaning] is understood through the sense (*ārtha*). But in cases such as *gomat* and the like, it is traditionally taught (*smaryate*) that the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) occurs specifically in the sense of "that which possesses this" (*tad asya asti*). Therefore, how can it be said here that "it is exactly that much," implying no further scope than what was understood at the time of etymological derivation?

But this has already been stated regarding the meaning of words such as "cook" (*pācaka*). Furthermore, in inference, it is precisely a self-contained [object] such as a mountain that is apprehended as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and it is understood as qualified by a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) such as fire, which is recalled independently. Since there is independent apprehension of both [qualificand and qualifier] by means of a word, he says: "by the qualifier," etc.
The mention [of "grasping"] is for the purpose of indication;
the meaning is that it includes recollection as well. // 61 //
He states another discrepancy with the words "viśeṣya" (61).

Here he raises an objection: "Now [atha]... Even here, since it is the word itself, as first perceived, that is the object to be proven (*sādhya*) by virtue of being qualified by its meaning, there will be no violation of the sequence. // 62 //
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "The meaning of the proposition," etc. The meaning of the proposition is the *pakṣa* (the subject);

and that is the substratum (*dharmin*) qualified by its property (*dharma*). With respect to the qualified whole, it is called a "part of the substratum. That very thing [the part] would result in being the reason (*hetu*). For sound has been taken up as the substratum.

"That very [particular] is the reason. But surely, when from a distance the specific substratum of smoke is not perceived, then smoke is established as possessing fire and serves as the reason (*hetu*). That being the case, it will be the same here as well; therefore, he says: "the subject" (*pakṣa*). For the particular smoke currently being perceived is the subject (*pakṣa*); that which was previously known is the similar instance (*sapakṣa*); and the universal concomitant with that is the reason (*hetu*). Thus, the distinction between subject, similar instance, and reason is logically established. // 63 //

"But surely, here too we shall take a particular word as the subject (*pakṣa*) and state 'word-ness' (*śabdatva*) as the reason (*hetu*. To this he replies: "Word-ness. For it is a specific object that is intended to be inferred, and word-ness is not its indicator because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [Objection: In that case, then, let it be a subordinate generality (*avāntarasāmānya*), namely, 'being the word *go*' (*gośabdatva*").

Since it will be the cause, he says: "the nature of being the word 'cow'. Therefore, in this case, there is only a single individual that is to be qualified by the meaning and must be expressed as the reason; thus, with the intention that the status of being a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatva*) is unavoidable, he says: "the individual. // 64 //

[The opponent objects: "But surely, one single individual instance, differentiated by the differences among its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), will be made the subject (*pakṣa*. [The author] replies: "It might be so" (*bhavet*). He refutes this: "But not so" (*na tu*). The meaning is that a difference based on adventitious conditions (*aupādhika*) does not divide the real entity (*vastu*), because the cognition of that [entity] does not disappear. Furthermore, being qualified (*viśiṣṭatā*) occurs only when a relation exists; therefore, he asks: "Or how [could there be a relation]? (*kathaṃ vā*)—referring to what kind of relation there could be here between the object and the word. First of all, the object is not perceived in the location of the word.

For the word is in the mouth, while the object is on the ground; nor [is the object present] at the time of the word, because at the Kali age there is an absence of the object belonging to the Kṛta age. Thus he says: "Not, first of all," etc. (verse 65).

Now, if it is argued that a specific word is established through the cognition of its meaning—since such a cognition exists at the time of the word—the author anticipates this objection with the words "tatpratītiḥ" (that cognition). He refutes this as well with the word "param" (furthermore): if that which is qualified by the cognition is being inferred, then that cognition must first be apprehended as already established. And if it is known...

"What else is being inferred? [The opponent asks: "Is it not the case that the presently perceived specific qualities, such as rapidity (*druta*) and so forth, are made the subject (*pakṣa*), and their possession of a power to convey meaning is what is being proved? And as for the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)," [the text continues].

We shall take the universal "cow-word" (*gośabda-sāmānya*) as the reason, which is common to both [the proponent and the opponent], so that there will be no fallacy of the reason being a part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*); therefore he says, "not by way of communication" (*na pratyāyanena*). This is the intended meaning:

there exists no connection between the specific qualities such as rapidity (*druta*) and the like, on the one hand, and the object (*artha*)—which is based on place and so forth—on the other; rather, it is the state of being qualified by the power of communication (*pratyāyana-śakti-viśiṣṭatā*).
And yet, it is not possible for them either. // 66 //

To the question "Why is this not possible?", he says: "Of the particulars (*viśeṣāṇām*). Just as in the case of a large mass of smoke that has been made the subject (*pakṣa*), where fire exists below in one part of it, the smoke qualified by that [fire] becomes the probandum (*sādhya*); it is not so with the particulars such as fluidity and the rest, because they lack the capacity for signification. This is because, due to their deviation (*vyabhicāra*), they do not signify. However, that which is the universal (*sāmānya*) of those [particulars], namely the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), is qualified by the capacity for signification.
And regarding that position, it has already been stated that the very same thing would be both the subject and the reason; thus he says, "of the universal," etc. (67).
Therefore, concluding that a word qualified by its object is not an inferable entity, he says: "Therefore" (tasmāt) // 67 //

Thus, it has first been stated that sound is not the subject (*pakṣa*). But if it is argued that the object is made the subject and sound is the logical reason (*hetu*), that too is incorrect. He says "because it is not a property of the subject" (*apakṣadharmatvāt*)—and asks "how so? The sense is: how can it be determined? // 68 //

Why is this not determined? To this he says: "It is not an action" (*na kriyā*). Something connected as an agent (*kartṛ*) to a certain action becomes the possessor of something else, because relations such as that between owner and owned are preceded by the relation between action and its factors (*kāraka*). In that regard, he states that the relation between owner and owned is indeed preceded by the relation between action and its factors, saying: "The king. For first, in the act of supporting...
The king and his servant, having entered into the state of agent and object, experience the relationship of master and servant. // 69 //

{3,127} Thus, the relationship between part and whole is also centered upon action; so he says: "the tree. For the cognition arises that the tree, as the whole, resides in its parts. At other times, however, the cognition arises that the parts themselves, such as the branches and so forth, reside in it. Therefore, the relationship between part and whole is based on the state of being the agent of the action of residing. The same applies to conjunction.

He says "place" (*deśa*) because even this [inference] has action as its core: when smoke exists in a place containing fire, the agent existing there becomes conjoined with that place which contains fire.
Thus, other relations such as cause and effect are also preceded by the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*); so he says: "the effect," etc.
For *kiṇva* (ferment) is the seed of wine; being the agent in the transformation into the nature of wine, it is called the cause of wine.
Likewise, there is also the relation between a whole and its parts. An elephant, performing a portion of the army's task—namely, the victory over the enemy—is [said to be] of the army.
"It is said to be expressed as a relation. However, in the case of word and meaning, no such form of a relation is perceived.
Nor can it be asserted that a relation exists whose form is not determined; thus he says: "And not... [71] //

Furthermore, without a relationship [between the two], neither the genitive case in the analytical statement (*vigraha*) "the property of the subject" (*pakṣasya dharmaḥ*), nor the *tatpuruṣa* compound "subject-property" (*pakṣadharmaḥ*), is possible; thus he says: "And there is not... He concludes: "Therefore... (72). This means that both the compound formation and the analytical statement are untenable.
He summarizes: "Therefore... (72).

Others, however, state that this is a property of the word itself, namely that "the word has the object as its domain. This will be explained later when it is said that "non-apprehension [is the means] with regard to non-existence as the object of knowledge. He introduces this point with the words: "When [the cognition] has ceased..."

He says that this too is untenable: "By them also" (tair api). The meaning is that the relationship of object and subject cannot be established in any manner whatsoever. He explains how it is not established with the words:
"Not that" (na tat) // 74 //

Since it is impossible for [the word] to be related to the object in any other way, its status as having that object must be stated by means of the method of exhaustion (*pāriśeṣya*) as being the producer of a cognition whose object is that [thing].

And since such production of a cognition having that object is untenable without a relationship of denoter and denoted (*vācyavācakabhāva*), one must accept that relationship. Once that is established, the property of residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) is not a factor for the cognition; nor is there a cognition produced by that which does not reside in the subject.
He states that this is inference by means of the two verses beginning with "Therefore" (tasmāt). // 75–76 //

If, however, it is maintained that the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) alone is the cause for generating the cognition whose object is that [probandum], then, since the property of being a feature of the subject is itself untenable apart from that [cognition], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Therefore, this conception also does not hold; thus he says: "Because of its capacity to prove" (*gamakatvāt*). // 77 //

For this reason as well, there is no "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatā); thus he says, "And not... Those who have not understood the relationship between the signifier and the signified do not know the word as a property of anything other than its own essential nature (svarūpa). Therefore, the cognition that [the word] is a property of the subject would not arise with respect to the word. // 78 //
The cognition of the mere intrinsic nature [of the mark] is not the cause for the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in the case of smoke and so forth;

rather, it is the connection with the subject (*dharmin*). With the intention that this [connection] does not exist [in the present case], he says: "And not... [na ca]. Now, one might object: even here, at the time of initial learning, the connection with the subject as the object was indeed already understood. To this he replies: "Nor even... [na cāpi] // 79 //
This connection of the property with the subject appears even to one who has not previously learned the relationship, without depending on any prior connection;

yet that is not the case here, as he says up to the words "the cognition that [it] possesses smoke. Precisely because this connection of the property with the subject is independent of that [prior relationship], it is for this very reason distinguished from what follows, namely, the presence [of the reason] in similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Otherwise, there would be no distinction between them at all; thus he says, "by that" (tena). The three characteristics of a logical reason (*hetu*) are its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), its existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattā*), and its exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*). Among these, he points out that the subsequent characteristic—the connection with similar instances—follows upon the characteristic of being a property of the subject. // 80 //

But in the case of the word, it is not so; thus he says: "but not here. And this [non-eternality] is understood after the comprehension of the meaning, in dependence upon a prior relationship. Therefore, he says: "nor is it," because it is not an integral part of that [comprehension]. [81]

For this reason as well, he states that there is no "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatā*): "Nor is the subject [known]," and so forth. The sense is that, for the time being, a subject other than the object is not cognized. // 82 //
But that object which is to be conceived as the subject (dharmin), and by whose property (dharmatā) the word is understood to become the property of the subject (pakṣadharma)— [that is the object].

Even subsequently, that [object] must be cognized to be exactly of that same extent. Therefore, if it is first cognized precisely in order to understand its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*), then once that has been grasped, what is the use of a subsequent cognition of its being a property of the subject and so forth? For this reason, he says "And that which... in two verses (83–84), [arguing] that it is therefore not inference.
Now he refutes the positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—with the words "as for the positive concomitance. Why is it not established?
To this he replies: "by means of the operation" (*vyāpāreṇa*). // 85 //
He demonstrates this very point with the words "wherein. He states that it is not so here with the words "but not" (na tu). // 86 //

To the question "How is it not so?", he says: "Not at all," and adds, "This has already been stated previously. [The opponent objects: "But since the word is pervasive and the object is eternal, the connection between the word and its object can indeed be demonstrated. To this he replies: "It might be so," and then refutes it with: "In the case of all objects... (verse 87).
What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "By that" (tena). // 88 //
He raises a doubt regarding the relationship in another way: "Now, if it is thus... (89).
He refutes this as well, saying "not so. He states the reason for this with the words ending in "for it is seen by us" (*dṛṣṭo hi*).
Where has it been seen? To this he replies: "in one who is unlearned" (*avyutpanna*) [verse 90].

One might object: "In the case of the second and subsequent uses, the concomitance between the word, its meaning, and the cognition will be grasped. To this he raises the doubt with the words "dvitīyādi" (second, etc.). He refutes this as well with the words "śatakṛtvaḥ" (even a hundred times). Even after a hundredfold usage, one who lacks the desire to know does not perceive the relationship; and one who has not known the relationship does not cognize the meaning. // 91 //

"Is it not the case that for one who has cognized the relation, the cognition of the word does not deviate from the cognition of the object? And it is precisely this [cognition] that is accepted as being inference? To this he says: "Is it not the case? He answers: "If it were so. If there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) for one who has cognized the relation, then a different kind of relation between the word and its object must be admitted. // 92 //
To this he says: "It is not a constituent part. If it is not a constituent part, what follows?
To this he says: "By way of positive concomitance" (*anvaya*). The sense is that if there is no positive concomitance, cognition is not inference. // 93 //

But since the positive concomitance (anvaya) arises solely by following the capacity of the cognition previously apprehended, it is not the cause for the comprehension of the meaning; thus he says: "when known" (jñāte). // 94 //

He concludes: "Therefore" (tasmāt). However, in the case of inference, the capacity to produce knowledge is not established prior to the positive concomitance (anvaya); thus he says: "And not... (na ca) // 95 //

Now he refutes the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—with the words "negative concomitance. For indeed, when an object is not cognized, it is impossible to cognize the negative concomitance, since the cognition of the word cannot occur without the cognition of that [object]. If the object is already cognized, what is the use of resorting to negative concomitance? // 96 //

One might ask: "Are positive concomitance (anvaya) and negative concomitance (vyatireka) now useless regarding the word? To this he says: "The relation" (sambandham). Their function in the elicitation of the capacity (śakti) is the relation between the word and its object, which consists in the nature of the signifier and the signified. // 97 //

Having thus established that [verbal cognition] is not inference by virtue of its abandonment of the three characteristics of a logical mark, he demonstrates this through a formal argument: "Therefore," etc. Sound is not inference because it lacks the three features [of a logical mark], just like perception. This is because it avoids such an object [as that possessed by inference]. And "such" means exactly like that [perception]. Furthermore, the avoidance of such an object has already been described in the passage beginning with "for [inference] has a universal as its object. // 98 //

And this demonstration of the difference between the word and inference, which we have provided, is for the sake of displaying our proficiency; it is not because the word is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus he says: "When [the object] exists," etc. (verse 99).

He demonstrates how it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by saying "the word" (*padam*). He then states those very four types [of non-cognition] by saying "perception" (*pratyakṣa*), etc. // 100 //
He explains how there is no validity for one engaged in these matters, saying: "In that case... (verse 101).

But regarding that which was never seen before and is now perceived, its invalidity is characterized precisely by its non-arising; thus he says, "never seen before. Or rather, at that time, the cognition of the relation itself arises; thus he says, "the relation. Nor should it be said that the relation alone is the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for the word.

With the intention that this [object] is to be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he says: "the relation. He says: "the object which," because that object is understood from perception (*pratyakṣa*). // 102 //

He states that knowledge simply does not arise regarding what has never been experienced before and what is beyond the senses—thus he says, "beyond the senses" (parokṣa). However, regarding what was previously experienced though now beyond the senses, there is memory; thus he says, "beyond the senses" (parokṣa) [in the second case]. // 103 //

[Objection: But surely it will be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by producing memory itself; to this he says: "that which has already been cognized" (*pramite*). For memory has as its object that which has already been cognized, whereas it is an established principle that a means of valid cognition has as its domain an object that is [currently] in contact [with the senses]. How then is it not a means of valid cognition when its object has already been cognized? To this he says: "determination" (*pariccheda*). For a means of valid cognition has determination as its fruit. And nothing at all is determined by memory.
Because it brings about the mere presence of prior consciousness. // 104 //

Here, an objection is raised: "tādātviketi. Even if this object was previously apprehended, why should memory—which, like recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), makes known its existence at that [present] time—not be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? // 105 //

He refutes this with the words "as much as" (*yāvān*). Memory arises at another time, but unlike recognition, it does not at that moment determine the existence of the object, because it follows from a previous cognition. // 106 //

[Objection: Is it not the case that recollection (*smṛti*) arises solely from prior mental impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), whereas this knowledge of the word-meaning from the word, having a presently arisen cause, is indeed a direct apprehension (*grahaṇa*);
how then can it be called recollection? To this, he says: "The word. Let it not be recollection.
This apprehension (*grahaṇa*) also has no object beyond [what is already known], because there is no appearance of anything additional;

therefore, the word (*pada*) is not distinguished from other causes of recollection, such as similarity or prior observation, and thus it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). But surely, when either the action (*kriyā*) or the factor of action (*kāraka*) is uttered, there necessarily occurs in the mind a mental connection (*vyatiṣaṅga*) between one and the other. Therefore, how [is this so]?
It is said that no superiority is perceived; therefore, he says: "That which is superiority. The meaning is that this grace belongs to another word alone, not to a single word by itself. // 107 //

And this is told by us to our disciples out of mere friendship, not because the word (*pada*) itself is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). However, even if it were not a means of valid cognition, the meaning of the sentence would not thereby fail to be the meaning of scripture (*āgama*). For even by that [word] as a means of valid cognition, there must necessarily be an object of the word (*padārtha*). Therefore, a sentence that makes known an object not already apprehended by other means of valid cognition is indeed a means of valid cognition. Thus, [the sentence] is included within inference (*anumāna*).
Nor is there any deficiency in the word itself, because the meaning of a sentence is not something to be inferred; thus he says: "The means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa). // 108 //

[The opponent] asks: "How is it that the cognition of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārthajñāna*) is not inference? For even that [cognition] follows upon what has been perceived; therefore, it is indeed inference. To this, [the author] replies: "The meaning of a sentence" (*vākyārtha*). Words that have not yet had their relations grasped cause the meaning of the sentence to be understood. Therefore, the cognition of the meaning of a sentence is not inference. And it should be demonstrated in this way:
The cognition of the meaning of a sentence is distinct from inference, because it arises without the experience of a [logical] relation, just like sensory perception. // 109 //

But how can that which is unconnected be a means of cognizing another object? For in that case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; to this he says: "In the case of a sentence" (*vākya*). Furthermore, regarding those reasons for the non-difference of the cognition of word-meanings from inference that have been stated by others, he says:
"Of all [of them]," indicating that many of them are unestablished in the case of the cognition of sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). The cognition of sentence-meaning...

Indeed, [this cognition] is not produced from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), nor is it preceded by a [verbal] connection. Nor does it arise from the perception of [the object] itself, because its cause consists of the word-meanings understood from the words. Furthermore, its having a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object is unestablished, since its object is actually a particularized entity (*viśiṣṭa*).

As for its being a means of valid cognition other than perception and its capacity to bring about the cognition of objects not previously perceived, these matters are not definitive until the analogies (*upamāna*) and other such means have been established.

Furthermore, the cognition of an unseen object (*adṛṣṭārtha*) through that [verbal testimony] is rendered inconclusive even by fallacious inferences (*anumānābhāsa*). Likewise, even regarding objects belonging to the three periods of time, [cognition occurs] through nothing but fallacious inference. The same should be demonstrated regarding the cognition of word-meanings (*padārtha*). Moreover, the fact of being produced from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) even in those cases; for it has been stated in the determination of the power of words (*śabdaśakti-nirdhāraṇa*) that "the function of those two [concomitances] lies in the ascertainment [of meaning], not in the birth of the cognition. As for the quality of being preceded by a relation (*sambandhapūrvakatva*),...
But if that [reason] is stated without qualification, it is inconclusive (anaikāntika) by perception itself,

for even that [perception] is preceded precisely by the connection between the sense organ and its object. If, on the other hand, it means being preceded by a connection that is a constituent of inference,
then that is unestablished (asiddha).

For pervasion (*vyāpti*) is a constituent factor of that [inference]. However, pervasion is not the cause for the cognition of a word-meaning from a word. Furthermore, the property of having a universal as its object is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) precisely because of [the case of] verbal appearance (*ābhāsa*).

As for [the properties of] being produced by direct perception, being a means of knowledge other than direct perception, and making known objects not previously perceived, these are shared even by means such as analogy (*upamāna*) and so forth. // 110 //

Since the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises in this way for one who knows only the word-meanings even when sentences are not previously perceived, the Buddhists—clearly perceiving its distinction from inference and thus fearing that scripture (āgama) might be no different from inference—descend from that [position] and become distressed by the very investigation into the non-difference of words. For indeed: {3,}

They think thus: "Let it be granted for now that even a word is not distinct from inference; by this much alone, the statement 'here there is identity between verbal testimony and inference' indeed proceeds. Thus he says with derision: "In sentences...
This concludes the section on Verbal Testimony in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by Upādhyāya Sucarita Miśra.
007. Chapter on Comparison (Upamāna).
Now begins the chapter on comparison (*upamāna*).

"Comparison also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] by means of similarity," as stated in the Bhāṣya, for example: "The sight of a *gavaya* [produces the memory] of a cow. The intended meaning of this is as follows: comparison...

Nor is it to be examined [as a separate category], because there is no deviation from its being characterized by such a definition. As for the meaning of the individual components: it is that cognition which, when similarity is perceived in one object, produces in another object not currently in contact with the senses a cognition qualified by a similarity to the perceived counterpart—namely, "this is qualified by a similarity to that."

Regarding the phrase "it has an object of comparison" (*sopamānam*), the relative pronoun *yat* and the demonstrative pronoun *tat* are to be supplied. Nor should it be argued: "Since no specific object is mentioned, how is it understood that the cognition has as its object something qualified by similarity? For here, non-investigation (*aparīkṣā*) is being established by restating a well-known means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And in the world, it is well known that a cognition whose object is qualified by similarity is indeed comparison (*upamāna*). Therefore, there is no fault. [The phrase] "from the perception of one part" (*ekadeśadarśanāt*) has "the perceived particular" (*dṛśyamānaviśeṣaṇam*) as its qualifier.

If it is argued that [the term] is not included because it is not explicitly mentioned, we say no; for it is included in the example. For he says: "Just as the sight of a gavaya [is the cause] of the recollection of a cow. The meaning of this is as follows: *darśana* means "that in which something is seen" (*dṛśyate 'smin*), formed with the suffix *lyuṭ* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇe*). Thus, "gavaya-darśana" means "that of which the gavaya is the locus of being seen. The word-meaning of the compound is *sādṛśya* (similarity). This...

The meaning expressed is as follows: "the similarity perceived in the gavaya. Following this example, it is understood that in the defining statement (*lakṣaṇavākya*) as well, only that which is actually perceived is intended by the term "similarity. Furthermore, in the phrase "of the recollection of the cow" (*gosmaraṇasya*), the suffix *lyu* (denoting the agent) is applied according to Pāṇini 3.1.134 (*nandigrahipacādibhyo lyuṇinyacaḥ*). Thus, it refers to the cognizer who is remembering the cow. Just as the similarity perceived in the gavaya is similar to this [cow],...

"It produces the cognition 'this is a cow'. As for the connection [between words and objects], it was already stated previously that analogy follows verbal testimony because of the abundance of established usage. Here, an objection is raised: since this work is intended to present an investigation by way of restating well-known means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why is the definition of analogy as stated by the Naiyāyikas adopted?

Thus, it is appropriate to rely on that very definition of comparison (*upamāna*) which has been stated. For they have stated: "Comparison is the means of establishing what is to be established [the object of proof] through a well-known similarity. The meaning of this is as follows: through a similarity with a well-known object such as a cow, there is for someone who is ignorant [of the object], the establishment—that is, the communication—of something to be established that is not well-known, such as a *gavaya*, by means of a statement such as, "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*."
"Or, the cognition produced by that [verbal testimony] is comparison (*upamāna*). To this, one must state the reason for formulating a different definition while setting aside that [previous view];

therefore, he says with the two verses beginning "Of what kind? It is true that this was stated by the Naiyāyikas, but it is not logical, because it is not distinct from the verbal testimony (*āgama*) mentioned immediately above. For this [cognition] is a cognition of an object not present [to the senses] arising from the cognition of a word. Therefore...
In the Śābara-tantra, however, comparison (upamāna) is described in a completely different manner. // 1–2 //

He states that its status as scripture (*āgama*) is understood even according to the definition of scripture provided by the Naiyāyikas—namely, "scripture is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ*). For in this case as well, it is precisely through the cognition of a reliable person (*āpta-puruṣa-pratyaya*) that there arises a conviction regarding similarity in respect to the gavaya and so forth, which are otherwise unperceived. Indeed, [this would not occur] from one who is unreliable (*anāpta*).
(vi) Because it is non-contradictory. Therefore, considering that this statement belongs only to a reliable person (*āpta*) and is thus non-deviant, a certainty arises through its power;
for them as well, this is indeed scripture (*āgama*). // 3 //

Now, it might be argued that even in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, it is described that analogy (*upamāna*) is the cognition of another similar object arising from the perception of one similar object. This too is certainly not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it does not fall outside the category of memory (*smaraṇa*).
For just as memory occurs for one who is reflecting on something, so too there is memory of another similar object for one who perceives a similar object.

Therefore, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [recognition] and memory produced by means such as meditative absorption (*dhyāna*). Consequently, he states that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*)—namely, "because it arises from something similar. The definition of the Naiyāyikas, at least, does not fall outside the scope of scripture (*āgama*); however, the *Śābara* [definition] includes precisely what is not a valid means of knowledge. // 4 //
But surely, even a recognition that arises mixed with memory is seen to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it occurs through differences of place and so forth.
Likewise here, for one who has seen a cow in the city and then sees a *gavaya* in the forest, the cognition of its similarity to that [cow] is a valid means of knowledge;
therefore, he says: "place, time, etc. Indeed, the difference of place and so forth is not the cause of validity merely by virtue of its existence.
Rather, [recollection occurs] by way of being an object of cognition;

however, in this case, a cow qualified by another location and so forth is not being cognized, but rather that which was previously perceived in the city is remembered even now as being situated right there. // 5 //

He presents the view of a certain school of Naiyāyikas—beginning with the words "śruta" (heard). It is said that for one who has heard the statement of comparison (*atideśavākya*)—"As is a cow, so is a gavaya"—and who, having gone to the forest, possesses this knowledge of the gavaya colored by similarity, namely, "This gavaya is similar to a cow," this is *upamāna* (comparison). // 6 //
He refutes this as well with the words "perception" (*pratyakṣa*). First of all, the gavaya is perceived through direct perception due to sense-object contact;

furthermore, the similarity to a cow, having been understood from the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), is remembered. Thus, there is no object for comparison (*upameya*). Here he raises an objection with "But surely" (*nanu*). The intention is this: here, the gavaya is indeed understood as qualified by its similarity to a cow.

Nor is that [the cow] perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the cow is not present to the senses at that time. The object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the *gavaya* as qualified by that [cow]. For it is not determined by direct perception, since the latter has only the *gavaya* itself as its object. Nor is it remembered as something previously understood from scripture (*āgama*).
Because scripture has a general object, whereas here there is the manifestation of a specific [object] as "this" or "that. // 7 //

He refutes this by means of the [verse] beginning with "pūrva" (the first half-verse) along with the following half. Here, the following alternative must be considered: is something additional to what is understood from the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*) apprehended, or not?

If he says "no," then he argues that this connection (*saṅgati*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), as it is no different from memory. Just as the cognition of a word-meaning from a word is not a valid means of knowledge because its object is not additional [to what was previously known], even though it arises from a presently existing cause and is thus not strictly a memory.

Thus, here too, there is the cognition of the gavaya as qualified by its similarity to a cow, which is understood through the sentence of analogical transfer (*atideśavākya*). If it is argued that there is a distinction in the cognition of a particular (*viśeṣa*) based on what was previously understood as a universal (*sāmānya*), then that [particular] is obtained from perception alone; therefore, there is no room for another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). // 8 //

Now, it might be argued: "Since the similarity to that [cow] is not perceptible when the cow is not present, the gavaya qualified by that similarity cannot be apprehended through perception; therefore, there is scope for another means of knowledge. To this, he says: *yāvad dhi* ("for as long as..."). Whatever appears directly (*aparokṣa*) immediately following the operation of the sense organs is, for us, perception. And thus, since the gavaya is qualified by similarity, how could it not be perceptible?

It will be so. Since similarity exists in its entirety with respect to each birth (jāti), even though the cow is not currently perceived, the perception of the gavaya as qualified by that similarity is indeed possible; this is the intended meaning. // 9 //

Nor is there invalidity due to the confusion with the recollection of words and so forth, because the distinction between the perceived and the remembered has already been established in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*); thus he says: "of that which is being remembered.

The meaning is that when there is such a distinction, there is no invalidity. Furthermore, no fruit is observed even from the employment of the qualification of the specific sentence of scriptural extension (*atideśavākya*).
Thus he says: "Having heard," etc. (verse 10).

How is it not applicable? [The author says: "Even those who... If the perception of a gavaya as qualified by its similarity to a cow is intended to be *upamāna*, then it certainly exists even for those who have not heard the corresponding sentence, having seen a cow in the city and subsequently seeing a gavaya in the forest; thus, the result of the qualification is trivial. // 11 //

[Objection: "But surely, for those who have not heard the sentence of extended application (*atideśavākya*), there is no connection of the name [in the form] 'this is that gavaya,' whereas for others there is; thus this is a distinction. To this he says: "Now... [The author] refutes: "Not indeed... For they too know that which is intended as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*). Let it be granted that the status of being the named (*saṃjñitva*) is not connected. // 12 //
It might be thought: the very object of comparison (*upamāna*) is the relationship between a name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*). As it has been stated in the *Nyāyavistara*:

"The purpose of comparison is the comprehension of the relationship of designation (*samākhyā-sambandha*). And this has been explained: when it is said, "A *gavaya* is like a cow," one who perceives through sensory contact that which is similar to a cow understands that the word "gavaya" is the name for this [animal].

"One understands the relationship between the name and the named. Since it is not possible for one who has not heard the sentence of extension (*atideśavākya*) and does not know the word [to understand] the connection with the designation (*samākhyā*), [the author] states "not" as a qualification that possesses a result. He states the reason: "by means of similarity. [This is] from the sentence of extension.

Thus, when the object denoted by the word *gavaya* has been determined through its similarity to a cow, the relationship between the word and its meaning is indeed understood, even though it has not been apprehended in its specific individual form. For at that time, it is understood that "the object similar to a cow is what is denoted by the word *gavaya*. And this much constitutes the essential nature of the relationship.
Therefore, it is rightly said that the qualification is purposeless. // 13 //

[Objection: But surely, even for a relation that has already been known, its validity as a means of cognition (*prāmāṇya*) remains unimpaired when it is recognized [again]. To this he says: "And not... He states the reason for this: "Of the two capacities... For the relation between word and meaning is indeed the restriction of the expressive capacity (*vācaka-śakti*) and the expressed capacity (*vācya-śakti*).

And because that [relation] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is not recognized here through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); rather, that which was previously apprehended, neither less nor more, is merely remembered.
Is it then the case that there is no recognition whatsoever regarding objects beyond the reach of the senses?

If this were so, how could fire and other such things previously experienced be recognized through inference? And it has been said: "Even when an object previously ascertained—like that perceived by direct perception—is distinguished by differences of place and so forth, recognition may again arise from inferential valid cognition."
"Joy. And here too, he will say:
"By whatever means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) there is indeed the apprehension of intellect and action...
True. We do not say that what is beyond the senses is not recognized through recognition (pratyabhijñā).
This recognition— which arises from the senses and has a direct manifestation in the form "this is that gavaya, characterized by similarity to a cow"—
does not have as its object the relationship between word and meaning in the form of a *śakti* (potency);
rather, its object is simply the gavaya itself, which was previously known through its similarity to a cow.

Thus, for this very reason, he refutes that this relation has recognition as its object. However, since the gavaya here was previously perceived through its similarity to a cow, it is recognized; therefore, nothing is untenable. // 14 //

Now, it might be argued that the inclusion of the qualification [“heard”] is intended to exclude this from being perception: since this cognition of the *gavaya* is delineated by the word “heard,” it is not an object of perception, and therefore it will belong to analogy (*upamāna*). To this, he says:
“By the word... Even in a cognition permeated by words—{3, ...}

It has been described that cognition following the connection with the sense faculties is not produced solely by the reflection upon the power of words, and thus it is indeed perception; therefore, one might argue that we do not see any additional object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*) in any of the definitions.
To conclude that its object of knowledge is indeed unprecedented, he says: "Therefore" (verse 15).
If, however, it is argued that the apprehension of similarity is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and therefore it is not perception—
since perceptual cognition arises solely from the capacity of the object and the sense faculty,
and does not subsequently or previously reflect upon them— it follows that even when the substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived, similarity itself remains non-perceptual (*parokṣa*).
Thus, since that which is qualified by it (the universal) is not perceptible, analogy would have its scope; to this he says: "by determination" (*vyavasāya*).

This is the established doctrine of the Buddhists: that perception is non-conceptual and arises immediately upon contact. The Naiyāyikas, however, maintain that perception consists of determinate cognition (*vyavasāyātmaka*). Therefore, for them, why should similarity—not being different from universals and the like—not also be perceived through direct perception?
"It is cognized," so it is said. // 16 //

Even for those who maintain that [cognition] is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), this is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*); thus he says: "perception," etc. Thus far, having granted that similarity (*sādṛśya*) is a distinct entity, it was stated that comparison (*upamāna*) lacks validity due to the absence of an object, since it would be a perception of that [similarity]. Now, according to the Buddhist view:

He states the denial of similarity (*sādṛśya*) with the words "prameya" and so forth. Even for those who maintain that perception is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣavādin*), the status of comparison (*upamāna*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not intended, because similarity is not an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Therefore, while they compete [with us], how can comparison be a valid means of cognition?
And this is their intention: namely, that similarity is certainly not distinct from its substrata, because it is not perceived as such.

And if there were no distinction [between the universal and the individual], it would follow that the universal would be nothing more than its substratum. Furthermore, how does it subsist in its substrata? It cannot subsist in its entirety, because that would entail the consequence of [the individuals] being non-distinct;

for it is not tenable that what subsists in one thing in its entirety should likewise subsist in another. Nor can it subsist part by part, because parts do not exist [in a universal]. Moreover, this similarity is not any one of the categories of substance, quality, or action.

Because those [categories] were not enumerated among them by the experts in categories (*padārthapaṇḍita*). For we do not perceive similarity as being included within the nine substances, the twenty-four qualities, or the five motions. Nor is similarity itself simply a universal (*sāmānya*), for that [universal] is the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the cognition of that [object].
Likewise, similarity would be cognizable by the intellect; and if it were so, the same consequence would follow for [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like.

If it is argued that similarity consists in common parts (*avayavasāmānya*), we say no, because the cognition of similarity arises even when those parts are considered individually. If it is argued that similarity consists in a plurality [of common parts], we say no, even in the case of a plurality...

For when things are brought together in one place, independent of any counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the cognition of similarity arises. Indeed, there are such things brought together in one place,
yet they are not apprehended by the cognition of similarity.

For one does not recognize a cow as "similar" without depending on a distinct counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). If it is argued that similarities are [only] resemblances in dependence upon a counter-correlative, then is similarity now something relative? Certainly. If this is so, is it manifested or produced by that dependence? It cannot be produced, like duality by a dependent cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Because it is established by nature (*sahajasiddha*). Since manifesting factors such as light and the sense organs do exist, what else could it require? Furthermore, if similarity were merely the commonality of parts (*avayavasāmānya*), then in the case of twins, there would be the undesirable consequence of its non-existence due to the absence of such [common] parts. If one were to accept that even in those cases [there is similarity], then upon the destruction of one twin, the universal (*sāmānya*) would be destroyed, resulting in the abandonment of your own tenet (*siddhāntahāni*). Moreover, in the case of a painting and the like, there is an absence of transformed parts such as hands, heads, and so forth.

In the absence of a universal (sāmānya), there is an absence of similarity (sādṛśya). In this very same way, the same consequence must be shown regarding odor and the other qualities. Because the parts of the ears and so forth lack further constituent parts, they possess no similarity. Now, if it is thought: "It is true that similarity is not a universal of parts; rather, this is a distinct category (tattvāntara) altogether, different from substance, genus, quality, and action."

Or rather, it is a distinct difference in qualities. As the Guru has said: "Similarity is not a universal (sāmānya). What then? It is that very thing [itself], because of the oneness of 'cowness' and so forth. And thus, it becomes logically established that in this case, the meaning of the injunction (*vidhyartha*) is simply the conceptualization of similarity; the meaning of the injunction for the *śyenacit* is the construction of a hawk. This is because the individual hawk and its genus possess, by their very nature, a composite whole (*avayavin*) composed of parts such as wings, talons, flesh, blood, bones, head, back, feet, belly, and so on, which are brought together by means of bricks.

Because it would be impossible to accomplish. Moreover, if similarity is intended to consist in the commonality of parts, then since those [parts] are absent here, similarity itself would be difficult to establish; thus, the proposition "one should build a fire-altar in the shape of a hawk" would become an unachievable matter.

And in this way, the cognition of similarity would also be possible even in the case of partless things such as odors and the like. But that is not the case, because [similarity] is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*).

For if similarity were [independent], they would know the *gavaya* to be similar even without depending on the cow. For in that case, that entirety of similarity would be fully present [in the *gavaya*] alone; so what else would need to be depended upon? If it is asked, "How can it be understood as qualified by that similarity when the cow is not depended upon?", what is its connection with the cow? If it is said to be inherence (*samavāya*), [then...]

In that case, the cow too must be known by its similarity to the gavaya. Furthermore, why should that similarity which is said to be inherent (samaveta) depend upon the perception of the similarity residing in the gavaya? For it is not observed that because "cowness" is inherent in a brindled cow (śābaleya), there is a dependence on it even when perceiving a black cow (bāhuleya). Likewise, in the case of "this similarity to a gavaya exists in the cow," no reason for such dependence is found. Moreover, let the cow indeed depend [on the gavaya].

For one who has perceived a cow from a distance—even though he has already discerned the distinction between its various parts—the cognition of a gavaya as being similar to a cow would still arise. If it is argued that even the common features of the parts must be taken into account for that cognition, then the meaning of "taking into account" (apekṣā) must be explained.
If you mean that those common features of the parts are its manifestors (abhivyañjaka), [then...]
In that case, those [features] residing in the gavaya are its manifestors;
and since they exist in the cow as well, what is the use of perceiving them as residing in the cow?

Therefore, when the cow is perceived and its constituent parts are not perceived, the cognition of similarity to a cow would arise. For that similarity belongs to two universals (*jāti*), and since those [universals] are already perceived, what else remains to be expected? Furthermore, this quality of similarity which exists when there is a multiplicity of common constituent parts would not be possible if similarity were a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), because in that case similarity would exist in equal measure everywhere. It might be argued that [the causes of perception are] the manifestors (*vyañjaka*).

These [properties] belong to that [manifested object]. And when there is an excellence in the manifestor, there is an excellence in the cognition of the manifested; as it is in the case of a jar and so forth, so it will be here as well. That is not so. For it is not mere cognition that is being excelled here; rather, we perceive the very object itself as possessing a degree of excellence. Therefore, when the primary [object] is unavailable, one seeks out something similar, and thus [takes] what is very similar.

It is represented [as being similar]. That it is "not merely slightly similar" is also trivial. Therefore, similarity—which is a cause of error constructed solely by imagination, like a double moon or a fire-brand circle—is not epistemically valid. Since there is no object of cognition (prameya), there is no other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for similarity that constitutes a factor of analogy (upamāna);
this is what should be understood from the phrase "because it would result in the production of a form [of cognition] dependent [on something else]."
[730] It should be understood as "because it does not result in the production of form.

Here he states the resolution: "of similarity. This is the intended meaning: this is not merely imagined through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), because the two causes of falsity are absent. For cognitions such as that of a double moon arise from some defect when there is a difference in time and other factors.
[They] are sublated. But how could similarity—which, like genus (*jāti*) and so forth, is known by uncontradicted cognition—be otherwise?
And just as that [genus] is real for those who maintain that perception apprehends only unique particulars (*asādhāraṇa*), so too is similarity; why then should it be denied?
This very [similarity] is understood, free from doubt, and uncontradicted even in other places and times; thus, at least, similarity exists.

It should be conceptualized in such a way that it is logically consistent with the force of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For there is nothing whatsoever that is "inconsistent" when it has been perceived.
Regarding what was first asked—namely, "What is its essential nature?"—the answer is given: "By many constituent parts," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:

similarity is that connection of another class [of object] with many common constituent parts (*avayavasāmānya*). The mention of the common constituent parts of another class is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Similarity between individuals is indeed observed even in the case of the *Yama* twins and others. Thus, similarity is clearly observed even without commonality of parts, through the connection with commonalities of qualities, actions, and so forth, as in the case of paintings and the like. By this, the objection raised—that how can there be similarity in paintings and such—is refuted. Likewise, in the case of fire as well, a commonality of configuration and dimension (*saṃsthāna-parimāṇa*) should be demonstrated. As for the argument stated regarding the logical possibility [of similarity] when the acceptance of commonality of parts is admitted for the *Yama* twins:

This [objection] will indeed be refuted. However, it must be shown that even in the absence of a commonality of parts (*avayava-sāmānya*), the similarity between the qualities of a composite whole (*avayavin*) consists precisely in the commonality of the qualities of its parts. Furthermore, the similarity between rituals such as the *Saurya* sacrifice consists precisely in the commonality of properties such as the substance and the deity, because the "commonality of parts" is intended merely as an illustration. And for those who maintain that [the universal] is a distinct entity (*tattvāntara-vādin*), this [similarity] exists because [the universal] is dependent upon its substratum (*āśraya-pāratantryāt*).

It must be accepted as being included within the qualities (*guṇa*) themselves. A fifth category cannot exist, because it would be non-worldly (*alaukika*). It is established in the world that the categories of meaning (*padārtha*) are genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and action (*kriyā*). Therefore, since this [universal] is itself a quality, its inherence (*samavāya*) in both quality and action is simply untenable. Now, if one argues that it causes both quality and action to be perceived as similar precisely because they are inherent in a substance, [the response follows].

[Objection: Because of inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*). Just as a universal (*sāmānya*) that inheres in the parts [of one thing] makes known the similarity between the universals of "cow" and "gavaya," even though it does not inhere in them, it is said to do so because of "inherence in what is inherent in the same object. [Reply: No, because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for inherence in a substance.

For the universals of the parts, such as the ears and so forth, which inhere in the individual (*vyakti*), are directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*); however, similarity is [known] through the cognition of similarity.

It must be apprehended. Furthermore, there is no cognition of a substance that is similar to smell and so forth. Therefore, how could smell and the other qualities become similar by virtue of a similarity residing in that [substance]? Consequently, similarity is simply the commonality of parts (*avayavasāmānya*). But was it not already stated that this leads to the undesirable consequence of perceiving similarity even in a single object, because many commonalities of parts are perceived therein?
This has been refuted by one who says, "It belongs to a different genus. For similarity arises from the inherence in a different genus of those things that inhere in that different genus;

it does not consist of the mere essential nature (*svarūpa*), nor of a mere plurality [of common parts]. This will indeed be explained further below. Therefore, the mention of "a different genus" must be taken into account. As for the objection that "it is not produced by that," this is true; rather, it is manifested (*abhivyajyate*).
But that is as it has been said:
"Similarity is said to be the manifestation of many commonalities of qualities, parts, and actions, which are distinct from the primary universal."

Thus, for whatever is the cause for the perception of something, that is its manifestor. Therefore, even in each individual case, universals are indeed apprehended in their own essential form alone. However, by virtue of their inherence in other classes, they constitute similarity.

Furthermore, since an entity whose nature is inherence (*samavāya*) is not manifested in another genus unless it is conjoined [with its substrate], its dependence on that [substrate] is indeed logical.
Nor is something a non-entity simply because its manifestation depends on another thing; for Devadatta’s status as a father is not perceived independently of his son.

That [resemblance] is not a non-entity. Therefore, such things which are relative cannot be sublated. For this very reason, the cognition of "very similar" and so forth is possible based on the accumulation or non-accumulation of common parts. Thus, it is established that similarity consists of the commonalities of qualities, parts, and so on, as delimited by different universals and individuals. // 18 //
Now, in the phrase "this woman has eyes like lotus petals," the eye of the woman is compared to the petal, which is a part of the lotus;
and if similarity consists in the commonality of parts, that is not possible here.
Because it is itself a constituent part;

for there is no other constituent part, such as an eye, belonging to the eye itself. Therefore he says: "resembling. It is not necessarily the case that the similarity of a particular part to the whole is what constitutes similarity; rather, it has been stated that similarity consists in the commonality of parts. And that [commonality] belongs to the parts.

Furthermore, since the eyes and other [senses] indeed exist by virtue of the predominance of their own constituent parts and universals, it is logical that there is a cognition of similar parts in women and so forth; thus he says: // 19 //
Granted that similarity may exist in parts due to their connection with common intermediate parts;

however, even in the absence of those, a cognition of similarity is observed in various instances. How is this possible? To this he says: "In this way. This apprehension of common parts is not the governing factor. Rather, whatever commonality of qualities and so forth exists, it produces the cognition of similarity.

It produces that very similarity; therefore, there is not absolute identity here. Rather, the diversity of similarity must be accepted according to what is observed. For example—there is similarity of genus in the statement "A Brahmin is indeed fire," which means he is similar to fire. What is the similarity between these two?
"From one Brahman" means that their birth (*jāti*) or origin is from the mouth; this will be stated in the *Tad-siddhi* Sūtra.

But how is it understood that these two have a common origin? From scripture (*śruti*). For it says thus: "Prajāpati fashioned from his mouth the *Trivṛt* [stoma], among the meters; Agni, among the deities; and the Brāhmaṇa, among men."

In the world, similarity should be demonstrated between those of equal birth; however, the commonality of qualities is clearly manifest in the world in paintings and the like, and in the Veda, as in the statement "the sacrificial post is the sun.
As for the similarity of substance, it exists in the world between two people wearing identical ornaments.

And in the Veda it says, "The priests proceed wearing red turbans. Similarity of action exists in the world due to commonalities such as study and so forth, and in the Veda due to the commonality of swooping down and seizing, as in the case of the hawk and the sacrifice. For thus it is said: "Just as a hawk swoops down and seizes, so does this [sacrifice] swoop down and seize the hateful rival. Similarity of power, however, is seen in the world in expressions such as "Bhīma the wrestler."

And [this is] seen in the case of *soma* and *pūtīka*. For it is understood from the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) that the *pūtīkas* possess the power of *soma*, because they are understood to be its effect, and because the power of an effect conforms to that of its cause. And it has been said: "That portion of the *soma* which fell away became the *pūtīka*. Regarding similarity in their own properties, some have three crests and some have five; thus in the world there is mutual similarity among those with three crests and so forth.
And in the Veda, it is stated that for Vasiṣṭha, Atri, and others, Narāśaṃsa is the second Prayāja. For in that case, the similarity consists solely in the restriction of ritual duty (dharma-niyama);

and it has already been stated that the similarity between the primary (prakṛti) and the modified (vikṛti) rites consists precisely in the commonality of their duties. Furthermore, these factors—genus and so forth—whether occurring individually, in pairs, in groups of three, or collectively, being identical, bring about the manifold variety of similarity. // 20 //

Is it not the case that wherever similarity inheres, it is perceived by a cognition of "similarity"? If, moreover, similarity consists of the commonalities of parts, then since those [commonalities] inhere in the parts, they would produce the cognition of similarity only with respect to those [parts]. Or, if it is their abundance [that constitutes similarity], and that [abundance] resides in the commonalities of parts, then those [commonalities] alone would be the similar things. How, then, could there be a cognition of similarity regarding two different classes?

Therefore, he says: "Not the properties (*dharmāḥ*). This is true. For this very reason, similarity is neither the commonality of the parts called "properties" nor their abundance, because the cognition of similarity does not arise with respect to them. Rather, it is that other genus (*jātyantara*)—such as the *gavaya* and so forth—or another individual (*vyaktyantara*)—such as the *āgneya*, *saurya*, and so forth—which is endowed with a greater number of those [properties], that alone is grasped by the cognition of similarity. Consequently, similarity consists precisely in their inherence in another genus (*jātyantarasamavāya*). This is from the perspective of their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*).

Each of those commonalities individually is indeed the basis for the cognition of oneness, just like a primary universal (*pradhānasāmānya*). However, when they are aggregated and conjoined with another genus (*jātyantara*), they constitute similarity (*sādṛśya*);
and this [notion] is merely an elaboration of the statement "this consists of many commonalities of parts. // 21 //
Here he raises an objection with the words "of the twins. This is an objection from one who grasps only what is explicitly stated:

"If similarity belongs to a different class [of beings] due to the connection with many common parts, how can there be similarity between the two individual instances (vyakti) of the twins? But the other [responds]: "The mention of a different class is merely illustrative; why then this insistence on that point alone?"

Thus, he mocks [the opponent], saying, "This poor child," by the phrase "because it is observed. Wherever similarity is observed—whether in the universal (*jāti*) or in the individual (*vyakti*)—there alone should it be resorted to. Why do you fix your reliance on only one? This might be argued: "For entities such as universals possess a single nature; therefore, this similarity is likewise appropriately of that same nature. If, first of all, its nature is to subsist in only a few instances...

It is logical that [the term applies] to two individuals alone; or, if its nature is to reside in many, then it belongs to two universals (jāti) alone. However, since a partial application (ardhavaiśasa) leads to the conclusion that [the entity] is not a real thing (avastutā), he says: "In some cases, cognition... The intention is that both [possibilities] are established because there is no contradiction with actual experience (pratītyavisaṃvāda). // 22 //

[Objection: But surely similarity consists of universals (*sāmānya*), and these would perish with the destruction of the individual (*vyakti*). Therefore, the doctrine that the universal is eternal would be abandoned; to this he replies: "Universals. Let these [particular similarities] indeed be perishable, but other universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are certainly eternal; thus, there is no contradiction with worldly experience. // 23 //
But what is the distinction regarding other universals?

To this he says: "infinite" (*ananta*). For the substratum of [universals] such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is indeed infinite. Thus, even if one instance is destroyed, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in another substratum, destruction is not absolute. He says "by that" (*tena*) to show that our position is not a universal doctrine of eternal universals (*nityasāmānyavāda*). // 24 //
Alternatively, he states—“of the universal”—that even for universals belonging to parts there is no absolute destruction. He provides the reason: “of everything. // 25 //

If it exists there as well, there ought to be a cognition of similarity; therefore, he says: "of them" (*teṣām*).
