Through that [cognition], their similarity becomes something additional, but it is not the case that they do not exist individually. It is not only because the universal (*sāmānya*) is imperishable that the existence of its substratum in other locations and so forth is postulated; rather, since those [individuals] are indeed perceived in some objects even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he says: "those" (*tāni*). // 26 //
Now, it has been stated that the eyes and so forth possess similarity by virtue of the abundance of commonalities among their own parts;

but how will there be similarity for those parts themselves? To this he says: "similar" (sadṛśa). Just as the parts of a large whole are similar through the commonalities of their own parts, even so, in cases where a similarity of parts is perceived even within those parts, they too are similar through the commonalities of their intermediate parts; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. // 27 //
And this must be shown for as long as parts are [perceived] as non-distinct; thus he says "in this way. Beyond that, only the state of being an atom remains as the universal; thus he says "therefore.

Now, if universals were [simply] similarity, there would be the undesirable consequence [of similarity] in the case of "cowness" and so forth, because there is no difference in their reality; to this he says: "of the primary [principles]. This is the intended meaning: for us, [universals] are grounded in consciousness...

Therefore, that which produces a cognition of similarity is similarity itself. However, in the case of primary wholes (*pradhāna-avayavin*) where a single universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is perceived, there occurs the manifestation "it is that very thing," not "it is like that. Consequently, the primary universal is not the cause of a cognition of similarity, and thus it is not similarity. When there is a difference in those [universals]—that is, a difference in the primary universals—a cognition of similarity arises between the cow and the gavaya.

Nor is there a cognition of mutual similarity between those two. Therefore, where the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) resides, there is no cognition of similarity; and where there is a cognition of similarity, that [universal] does not reside there. Thus, it is established that the parts themselves, when aggregated, constitute similarity (*sādṛśya*), because they are the cause of the cognition of similarity. And so, regarding the basis for similarity [as stated] by the author of the *Nibandhana*:

Regarding the objection that if [the universal] were a distinct reality (tattvāntara), the same consequence would apply to "cowness" and so forth—which was stated as the reason—that has now been refuted. // 29 //

He raises an objection, stating "in a painting and so forth," on the grounds that since there is an absence of commonality among the parts (*avayava-sāmānya*) in a painting and the like, similarity (*sādṛśya*) is untenable. He answers:

"In that case too. Even though there is an absence of commonality inherent in the transformed parts, similarity is established by means of specific colors such as white and so forth, as well as dimensions, which reside in the earth-element portion [of the painting]. Now, what is this similarity? Is it similarity of genus (*jāti-sādṛśya*) or similarity of individual (*vyakti-sādṛśya*)?

Or rather, neither of these two [possibilities] is possible, because both are absent. For in paintings and the like, neither the universals such as "humanity" (*naratva*) nor their individual instances (*vyakti*) are possible. This is because an individual instance is that which inheres in parts such as hands created by its own nature, and a universal is that which inheres in such an individual instance. It is replied: here, it is the individual instance itself that is similar. Even though "humanity" does not exist here [in the painting],...

Since substantiality (*dravyatva*) exists, that individual is perceived as being similar [to others]. Generally, in such cases, it is the similarity of form (*ākṛti*) alone that is understood there. However, a skilled painter brings forth the similarity of the individual itself; for indeed, similarity consists precisely in the commonalities of parts taken together. Thus it has been said that even the commonalities of qualities (*guṇasāmānya*), when combined, constitute similarity. But in a painting and the like, only color (*rūpa*) is common, not smell and so forth. Therefore, he says: "color," etc.

Among form and the other [sensory objects], there certainly exists a similarity (*sādṛśya*) consisting in the equality of even a single one of them. It has been stated more than once that perception is based upon that [similarity]. Thus, in this case, in a painting and so forth, it is simply the generality of color (*varṇasāmānya*). In the case of specific fragrances such as those of flowers and so forth, or in milk, sugar, and the like, the similarity consists in the generality of taste (*rasasāmānya*). It is not necessary to follow [the view] that there must be a inherence (*samavāya*) of the generalities of all qualities. // 31 //

He states another refutation: "In the case of earth and so forth. For thus do the proponents of the theory that the effect pre-exists (satkāryavādins) argue: it is impossible to produce that which is absolutely non-existent, like a sky-flower;

therefore, the exclusion of the status of being an effect from what is non-existent implies its existence. Consequently, even the generalities (sāmānyas) of the parts of men and other beings are not absolutely...
They do not arise from non-existence; rather, they already exist within their own causes—the primary elements such as earth—and become manifested through transformation.

Furthermore, that manifestation resulting from transformation is to be determined precisely according to what is observed. And just as those [elements] are seen in Devadatta and others who possess hands and other limbs, so too [are they seen elsewhere].

Since this is the case regarding the various parts of a painting and so forth, why is it not accepted there? Therefore, even in the case of a painting and the like, similarity consists precisely in the commonalities of the constituent parts. // 32 //

He states the reason for its prior existence with the words "for not" (*na hi*). And this has already been stated previously. As for the objection that similarity—whether conceived as distinct or non-distinct—is reduced to non-substantiality through such alternatives, he provides the answer there with the words "of properties" (*dharmāṇām*). It is only all properties, such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, that possess plurality, and not the substratum (*dharmin*); nevertheless, there certainly exists a distinct internal status determined by property and substratum. This is the case with similarity as well. Therefore, it cannot be denied by this [objection], because in every instance, the lack of exclusivity (*anaikānta*) is established through non-contradictory cognition.
It is to be established. // 33 //

Thus, similarity having been established as a real entity (vastu), it is proven that for one who perceives simultaneously two existing substrata (dharmin) connected with the eye—whether both together or one alone—perceptibility (pratyakṣatva) is established; so he says:
"In the case of its being a real entity" (vastutve). //34//

In response to the objection regarding the function [of the word], he says: "It is like a universal" (*sāmānyavat*). He states the reason: "Because it is a counter-correlate" (*pratiyogī*). Thus, its logical establishment is similar to that of universals and the like. // 35 //

Since the complete coexistence [of the universal] in each individual is absent even when the cow-nature (*gotva*) resides in memory, it is established that the similarity residing in the gavaya—which is present before the senses—is within the range of the sense organs. Concluding this, he says "therein" (*tatra*), and now demonstrates the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for comparison (*upamāna*) according to his own view with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*). Thus, the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) occurs according to one's intention. // 37 //

[Objection: But surely the cow is remembered and the similarity is apprehended through perception; thus, we do not see any object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*). To this, he says: "By perception... (verse 38).
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "In perception," etc. (39).
But what, then, is the suspicion of deviation here, for the sake of whose refutation the definition is formulated? To this he says: "But where... (40).
He states the reason for the distinction between appearance and its opposite—namely, "the sublater" (*bādhaka*). Here he provides an illustration—namely, "just as" (*yathā*). // 41 //

But how is it that it has the appearance of that? To this he says: "standing nearby. The sense is that a subverting cognition arises in that case. However, in the absence of the cognition "it is not [so]," there is similarity to the ultimate reality;
thus he says: "it is not subverted. // 42 //
Addressing those who, believing that all [cognition] following upon observation is inference, desire to include this [perception] within inference, he says:

"And not... He demonstrates the impossibility of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth by saying: "Prior... For smoke and the like become properties of the subject—such as a mountain—which is the object of cognition, only after they have been apprehended prior to the arising of the inference.

And here, the cow is the object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore, prior to the arising of the analogy (*upamāna*), similarity is not apprehended as a property of that [cow]. Therefore, it is first of all not a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*). As for the possession of horns by the gavaya and so forth, their status as properties of the subject will be refuted later. // 43 //

He says "gavaye" [in the verse] because the similarity residing in the gavaya cannot be the inferential mark for cows qualified by that similarity, since it is not a property of the subject (apakṣadharma). And he says "pratijñārtha" [in the verse] because the similarity residing in the cow cannot be the inferential mark, as it would be a part of the very object of the thesis (pratijñārthaikadeśa). // 44 //
He says, "And the gavaya," because even the gavaya is not a mark (liṅga) of a cow qualified by similarity, since it does not reside in the subject (apakṣadharma).

He says, "Similarity," because its positive concomitance (anvaya) with a cow qualified by similarity has not necessarily been previously known. Thus, in either case, the object of knowledge (prameya) for comparison (upamāna) is either a cow qualified by similarity, or that [gavaya] qualified by the cow.
In both cases as well, the connection with the gavaya has never been perceived before. // 45 //

[Objection: But surely for those who perceive both simultaneously, the relation between the similarity and the gavaya is already understood; therefore, he says: "In one [person]. [Response: It is true that it is understood, but we have stated that it is not understood by everyone. Furthermore, if positive concomitance (*anvaya*) were a constituent factor of knowledge, then even a single person who has not grasped that concomitance would lack knowledge. [46]

If, however, it is argued that the connection of "hornedness" and so forth with the cow has already been apprehended, and therefore its being perceived in the gavaya will serve as a logical mark (liṅga) for the cow, that is not so. For those [features], being constituent parts, have their utility exhausted with respect to the cognition of the whole, the gavaya. Anticipating this objection, he says: "of hornedness and so forth. // 47 //

If, however, hornedness (*śṛṅgitva*) and other such properties are intended to be the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the cognition of a *gavaya* by their very nature, without being exhausted in that function, then—following the previously apprehended relation with those properties—the recollection of the cow would result in a state devoid of similarity. Thus he says: "If... To the question "How is it devoid of similarity?", he replies: "It is not a cow. And he states the sequence of cognition as follows: "Similarity... From the cognition of the horns and so forth... [3]

155} Depending on a cognition of similarity that involves a reversal [of perspective], the knowledge of a cow qualified by its similarity to a gavaya arises precisely from the cognition of a gavaya qualified by its similarity to a cow; it does not arise, however, from the mere cognition of [the cow's] horns and so forth. // 49 //

[Objection: But surely the horns and other parts are also mutually similar; how then can it be said that from them there arises a cognition devoid of similarity? To this he says: "similar," etc. If it is understood that the gavaya and others possess similar parts, then they are not cognized as being similar [to the cow] themselves; rather, it is only the parts that are similar to one another. Therefore, the possession of horns and so forth do not serve as inferential marks (*liṅga*) for the cognition of a cow qualified by similarity. Rather, from those [parts], there is merely the recollection of the cow, which is itself devoid of similarity.

It might be argued as follows: furthermore, in inference, just as smoke and so forth are understood as being a part (*ekadeśa*) [of the subject], the object of knowledge (*prameya*), such as fire and so forth, is likewise [understood] as being that very same part.
But here, the possession of horns and so forth are cognized as being parts of the *gavaya*. And yet, the cow—which is also a part of that [same whole]—is not inferred.
To this he says: "And not... (verse 50).

But if someone, out of impudence, should say, "One might infer exactly in this way," he says in response: "In this manner. This is an error because of the contradiction with non-existence. He says, "The cow standing in the city," meaning that the unqualified cognition of the cow standing in the city is merely a memory due to its similarity [to the cow seen before]. Because the object remains present, the cognition also [remains as such].
The designation [of the cause] by the name of that which resides in it is due to its being dependent upon that. // 51 //

Furthermore, what is the utility of analogy (*upamāna*) regarding the meaning of the Veda? If it is said that [analogy] serves to establish the application of archetypal properties (*dharmas*) to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), that is not so; for that is established by inference (*anumāna*) alone. A certain archetypal indicative mark (*liṅga*) seen in the modified sacrifice, being connected with those properties, will serve as the means of inferring them. It appears that this very point was intended by Jaimini as well, since...
He says this: "For whom there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*) through connection with the meaning. For here he clearly teaches the attainment of dharma by means of inference (*laiṅgikī*).
Therefore he says: "distinct" (*bhinna*). This is the intended meaning:

for one who perceives the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), the knowledge of that which is connected is inference. And in this case, [there is no such connection] for the sentences concerning the *saurya* sacrifice and so forth.

The connection [of the modified sacrifice] with the *vidhyanta* (concluding ritual procedure) of the *āgneya* and other archetypes is understood; however, this does not apply to the substance (*dravya*) and deity (*devatā*), nor to the action (*karman*) itself.

Therefore, how can the knowledge of that [archetypal procedure] be considered inference? The application of the archetypal *vidhyanta* must be determined through another means of valid cognition, namely comparison (*upamāna*).
For the modified principal rites (*vaikṛta-pradhāna*), when their own *vidhyanta* is not explicitly heard, do not reach completion without it. Whatever [is required]...

Having fulfilled their purpose by providing the *itikartavyatā* (procedural details) through the application of the *vidhyanta* (concluding ritual procedure) of the Āgneya sacrifice— this being established by analogy (*upamāna*) arising from the observation of similarities such as substance and deity— the [injunctions] for the Saurya and others become complete. For instance, in this very case, because of the similarity between the Saurya and the Āgneya sacrifices due to having a single deity (as indicated by the *taddhita* suffix denoting the deity) and consisting of vegetable substances, the properties of the Āgneya are [extended] to the Saurya by means of analogy.
[The following] are brought forward. And this is the meaning of the individual parts:

this [inference] has been stated as distinct from inference [as a means of knowledge] because it is employed in the thought, "How indeed might this collection of procedures, such as [the use of] fire and so forth, convey [the meaning] through mere similarity? Otherwise, since no such [procedure] is observed in connection with the *saurya* and other [subsidiary] injunctions, inference would not be possible.

There would be non-attainment [of the result] itself. Regarding the phrase "joined with fire and so forth": by means of the deity such as fire (Agni), one indicates the ritual action such as the Āgneya; by means of the ritual action such as the Āgneya, it is stated that there is merely the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) joined [with it]. // 52 //

He states another purpose: "Even a substitute (*pratinidhi*). When the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices have begun and there is a shortage of *vrīhi* rice, *nīvāra* grass—which resembles it—is substituted; this too is a fruit of analogy (*upamāna*). He states yet another purpose with the words ending in "is appropriate as a representation" (*pratikṛtir iti yuktam antena*): when the primary [material] is lacking and one must resort to a secondary meaning of the scriptural injunction, where [the similarity is established] by two or three very secondary and inferior commonalities.
A "counterfeit" (pratikṛti) is understood as a resemblance; in that regard, when a highly similar [object] is obtainable, that which is only slightly similar is considered false.
"That too is the result of analogy. But how can that which is only slightly similar be false?

For even when something very similar is obtained, that which is slightly similar is indeed understood as being like it. Therefore, let there be in that case a small degree of commonality of parts; to this he says: "the cognition" (*mati*). It is not only in reality that those two—the very similar and the slightly similar—[are distinguished], as in the case of [a woman and] a female servant (*strīva*).

[The cognition of] intensity or dullness [occurs] in that very same way—indeed, it arises immediately and swiftly in the primary form itself with respect to what is highly similar. The word *iva* is used as a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
Therefore, even when there is a cognition of similarity in a slight degree regarding what is only somewhat similar, there will be a cognition characterized by non-apprehension; thus, it exists.
The application of analogies pertains to both relinquishment and acquisition. // 53–54 //
Thus ends the chapter on Analogy (Upamāna) in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the Preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
Chapter Eight: On Presumption (Arthāpatti).

Now follows the section on presumption (*arthāpatti*). Here the commentary says: "Presumption is also the postulation of a fact based on the thought that a fact seen or heard is otherwise inexplicable.
For example, by seeing the absence of the living Devadatta from his house, one postulates his presence outside, which has not been seen."

The meaning of this is: even presumption (*arthāpatti*) need not be examined, because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*) by virtue of having such a definition. But what definition of presumption has been stated by this? Presumption is that which, when a fact is otherwise inexplicable, leads one to postulate another fact; for example, [the presumption] regarding the living Devadatta.
It has been stated that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is that which postulates an external existence when the absence from the house is not otherwise possible without that external existence.

If this is so, what indeed is this so-called "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*)? If it means that the existence of this [external presence] is not possible without that [internal absence], then this is merely an inference of a cause from its effect (*kāryataḥ kāraṇānumāna*) that has been presented.

It is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Now, if it is argued that while inference requires the knowledge of a relationship (*jñātasambandha*), presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) does not depend on the knowledge of a relationship, that is incorrect.
For when a relationship is unknown, it cannot be said, "This [fact] is not logically possible without that [other fact]."

For that very restriction of the relation known in the form "this is its effect," and so forth, cannot be established without its own cause, just as smoke [cannot be established] without fire. Therefore, it is stated in other words that this cognition arises solely from the force of the relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). This might be [objected]: inference has for its object a perceived particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), as in the case of fire and the like.

[Objection: Presumption (*arthāpatti*) arises with respect to things such as capacities (*śakti*), which have as their object a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that has not been perceived. [Reply: That is not so. Whether it be something perceived or unperceived, that which has a known relationship is understood through the impossibility of otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*).

For when a general effect, being impossible without a general cause, leads to the postulation of that [cause], since that [postulation] also arises through the knowledge of a relationship, how does it differ from inference (*anumāna*)? Furthermore, the fact that inference has as its object a particular characteristic that has not been perceived occurs in the case of inferring an action (*kriyā*).

It has already been described. Therefore, this [argument] is merely a mirage of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). True, if that which cannot be established without something else were to indicate that thing, then it would be a signifier. But in this case, that very thing which is not established is what is to be known.
Now, is external existence not established without the absence from the house? Certainly. For even in the house—
Since Devadatta exists, he must also exist outside;

therefore, his existence outside is established precisely by the observation of his absence from the house. But does the author of the *Bhāṣya*, by stating "seen or heard," not demonstrate that it is the indicator (*gamaka*) which is otherwise inexplicable? Not the indicated (*gamya*). [This is the view of] one who does not know the text.
"Beloved of the gods" (*devānāṃ priyaḥ*). The connection is as follows: "the postulation of an object [is] an object seen or heard. What is being stated?

That it is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for another object. [If one asks,] "With what, then, is the phrase 'it is not otherwise possible' (*anyathā nopapadyate*) connected? we reply: with "cognition" (*pramiti*). [That is to say,] it is the indicator (*gamaka*) of another object by bringing about its state of being otherwise impossible. Of which other object? If [you say] of external existence (*bahirbhāva*), [we respond:]...
The absence from the house does not render its [the person's] existence impossible;

for ordinary people do not perceive that the existence outside is impossible for one seen to be absent from the house, but rather that Caitra exists outside. Furthermore, by those who describe "presumption through otherwise-impossibility" (*anyathānupapatti*) as a qualification of the object to be known (*gamyaviśeṣaṇa*), [they imply] the indicator (*gamaka*).

If it is asked: "Is it that you simply do not accept *anyathānupapatti* (the impossibility otherwise)?"—if this were so, how could the existence of external objects be established? Or, if even that [external existence] is not established, then cognition occurs solely by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), and thus it remains an inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, for what purpose is the phrase "it is impossible otherwise" joined with a conceptual construction (*pratīti*) that is not being heard, while abandoning the actual indicator (*gamaka*)?

Now it is said: "The absence from the house, by bringing about the impossibility of another explanation (anyathānupapatti) for the existence of Caitra—who is related to another location—postulates his presence outside. To bring about doubt is to bring about the impossibility of another explanation;

for Caitra, who is generally seen residing in the house, comes to doubt his very existence upon seeing his absence from the house. Even when an object is perceived, the realization that its previously apprehended form is absent brings about doubt regarding Devadatta’s existence.

Since Caitra’s existence was previously understood through his connection with the house, the observation of his absence from there gives rise to a doubt regarding his presence—namely, "Does Caitra exist or not? This doubt is termed an "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*).
By producing this inconsistency consisting of a doubt regarding his existence, the absence from the house dispels that doubt by means of the postulation of his existence outside.

It establishes Caitra’s existence. In this case, the absence from the house, although its connection with external presence has not been previously apprehended, leads to the inference of that [existence] by way of raising a doubt regarding existence as something distinct. Alternatively, it is seen in two ways: either existence itself, rendered impossible by his absence from the house, postulates external presence in order to establish itself; or [the absence leads to the inference]. Thus is the twofold presentation.

For this very reason, there is a distinction from inference (*anumāna*). For in inference, smoke or the like does not lead to the cognition of fire or something similar by producing an "inexplicability" (*anupapatti*) in the form of doubt for someone, nor does it lead to the cognition of anything whose inexplicability has been produced. Rather, fire is inferred precisely from smoke that is beyond doubt. And just as in inference a mark (*liṅga*) of a certain nature is the means of cognition, so here [in presumption] it is that which is doubted.
Thus it must be accepted on the strength of perception.

But this is incorrect. For instance, as for what was said—that the absence from the house gives rise to doubt—this is untenable. How indeed can doubt regarding his existence be produced by that? Since Caitra was seen in the house, how...
If it is argued that [the object] does not exist here, we say no; for not everyone perceives it in this way, since even he by whom it was seen there [would perceive it].

He too, perceiving that [Caitra] is alive yet absent from that place, suddenly postulates his existence outside. Moreover—if there were doubt due to a contradiction with the nature of the object, we would see no reason for postulating external existence. For just as the absence from the house of one who is dead or about to be born does not indicate external existence, so it is for one whose actual presence is doubtful. Indeed, as long as Caitra’s existence is not ascertained, [the inference cannot hold].

One cannot establish Caitra’s presence outside merely by seeing his absence from the house. Furthermore, even for the sake of dispelling doubt, another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) must be sought here; it is not the external existence itself [that is established]. However, once the doubt has been removed, one understands through the observation of his absence from the house that he exists outside, as his existence is now certain. Now, regarding the mode of existence of one whose existence is thus certain:

"How can there be doubt? [one might ask]. "In that case, since doubt occurs even for one who does not see Caitra, what is the use of observing his absence from the house? Moreover, that observation is not the seed for the conceptualization of his existence outside. Therefore, inducing doubt—which serves as the very opposite of the conceptualization of his existence outside—is precisely what has been adopted as the means for establishing that [external existence]. Well done! Thus, we do not know what the meaning of the definition is."

Therefore, he says: "By means of a valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). We explain that [the word] "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) brings about understanding by inducing the state of being inexplicable otherwise. However, this is indeed a qualification of what has been seen or heard. Whatever object is known through the six means of valid cognition, if it is apprehended as being inexplicable otherwise—

That very [object] postulates another object in order to account for itself; the conceptual cognition (*kalpanābuddhi*) whose object is that [other object] is presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). But if this is so, does it not follow that a cognition arising by the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is inference? Not so. For the phrase "it is not otherwise possible" does not express invariable concomitance. Indeed, when it is said "it does not exist without this," [concomitance] is understood. What, then, is expressed by this [phrase]?
"It is not possible for what is seen or heard to exist without conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). But what is this "impossibility" (*anupapatti*)?

For there is no such thing as an impossibility regarding what is actually perceived. That which is perceived is indeed "impossible" only when it is contradicted by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For instance, Caitra's absence in the house is perceived through the means of non-perception (*abhāva*), yet his existence somewhere is established through inference because he is alive. This [inferred existence] is [contradicted] by the fact that no specific location has been determined.

It pervades even the house. This very contradiction between non-perception and inference is called "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*). Furthermore, doubt (*saṃśaya*) here is simply a conflict of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), characterized by the appearance of two unstable aspects regarding a thing that lacks a fixed nature. Alternatively, this is merely indecision (*anadhyavasāya*), belonging to one who is unable to direct the mind toward a single [conclusion] due to a lack of specific reasoning. Therefore, neither of these two [alternatives] is established here.

It is possible either to accept or to reject [the external object], since there is no difference in their status as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Thus, in this dilemma, the proponent of valid cognition postulates the object of inference—that it exists externally—just as one applies the general rule "one should not kill" to instances of killing other than those specifically prescribed. In this way, both [the existence of the external object and the validity of the inference] are established.
"It is a non-entity and yet an inference. This same principle must be demonstrated in every case. Furthermore, we shall explain later its lack of the three characteristics (trairūpya).
And here, it is said to be "perceived" (dṛṣṭa).

In this regard, we do not know whether what is intended here is that which is seen by the eye alone, or that which is seen by perception (*pratyakṣa*) in general. In the former case, there would be no presumption (*arthāpatti*) preceded by the ear and other senses.

In the latter case, it is preceded by inference and so forth. Now, if the word "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) is intended to include everything that has been cognized (*pramita*), then why is "heard" (*śruta*) mentioned separately?
For even what is understood through verbal testimony (*śabda*) is indeed cognized. If it is argued that this mention of "heard" is not for the purpose of intending a different category of object...
Rather, this is simply another synonym for "apprehension" (upalabdhi).

For people in the world are seen to employ the words "seen" or "heard" figuratively when they intend to express mere apprehension; no one [ever says] "I myself have not seen" or "I myself have not heard."

Regarding the phrase "one who takes back what has been given": with this very point in mind, the author of the *Ṭīkā* stated that "seen or heard" is a worldly expression. What is meant is that ordinary people are observed to employ verbal apprehension as distinct from other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This too is not tenable; for how could the author of the *Bhāṣya*, being so exceedingly skillful in his treatise on definitions (*lakṣaṇagrantha*), [fail to notice this]?
It cannot be said that one employs the word "heard" (*śruta*) without some other underlying intention;

therefore, he states the purpose for employing both [terms], beginning with the words "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*). This is true: that which is seen by all five means of knowledge, such as perception and the rest, is what is meant by "seen. The point is that the word "seen" is a synonym for "perceived" (*upalabdhi*). Nevertheless, from this "seen" [object]...

The fact that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) arising from what is heard is mentioned separately is intended to show its distinction from the previously mentioned presumption based on perception, by virtue of its being grasped through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This will be explained further below. Furthermore, the phrase "by means of five" was stated with reference to the first type of presumption; thus, this occurs at the occasion of providing examples of presumptions preceded by the six means of valid cognition. // 2 //

Now, he first illustrates that [inference] preceded by perception (pratyakṣapūrvikā) as the primary type, from the words "therein" up to "of fire. But what is this power (*śakti*)? It cannot be pointed out as having a specific identity (*idantā*) beyond the reach of the senses. [Objection: Is it not the case that this power is that upon whose presence or absence the presence or absence of the effect depends?

And such a thing is indeed directly perceivable. For instance, burning is observed immediately after contact with fire, and it is not observed when such contact is absent; thus, that very contact is declared to be the "power" (*śakti*), and not some distinct ontological entity (*tattvāntara*). And since that [contact] is perceptible, what need is there for presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)? No, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Just as the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of fire deviates [from the effect], so too does its contact. For it sometimes happens that fire comes into contact with substances such as medicinal herbs and yet does not burn. Therefore, in this case, a distinct ontological entity in the form of power is postulated through presumptive testimony.

Because it contradicts another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: burning is established by perception, yet it is negated by the absence of its cause. For that [absence] makes known the [negation of the effect] through the absence of the effect, since the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been ascertained. To explain further: the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of fire is not the cause.
There is no conjunction with that [cause], because of deviation;

nor is there anything else. Nor is it reasonable to say that it arises without a cause at all. For if that were so, it might not occur at any time; for dependence is the basis for its occasional occurrence.

But that which is independent must be either eternally existent or non-existent. Therefore, by the force of observing and not observing the effect, some form distinct from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of fire is inferred, such that the existence and non-existence of the effect are dependent upon the existence and non-existence of that [distinct form]. For if the existence of the effect were dependent solely on the essential nature, it would follow that it must always exist, since there is no difference [in the nature]. Thus, the mere essential nature of fire, being unobstructed, is the cause of burning, just as [the nature] of medicinal herbs and the like [is the cause of their specific effects].

If it is argued that [the seed] is obstructed, what is the meaning of "obstruction"? First of all, its own nature has not perished; we recognize that very same thing. For when a lamp is brought near a seed, we do not perceive any diminution of its form. Nor is a sprout produced by that [lamp]. If it is then claimed that, upon the proximity of another entity, a different causal complex (*sāmagryantara*) has simply arisen—

If it is argued that, for this reason, the effect of the previous causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does not arise, it is not so. For when there is contact with a mantra or the like, the destruction of the previous causal complex is not observed, nor is its effect perceived. Now, if it is said that the cause produces the effect even when devoid of the mantra and so forth, but nothing at all is done by it in that case—that is not correct; for [a cause] that performs no function...
Proximity obstructs the effect. For even other things that are indifferent may be present there, yet the effect does not fail to arise.

Nor does the notion occur that some entirely different thing has been produced by the destruction of the previous cause when mantras and so forth are in proximity; for the entire causal complex is recognized as such. And it has already been stated that the cause exists therein.

Nor is it logical to claim that either the prior non-existence of the mantra and so forth, or a causal complex qualified by that non-existence, is the producer [of the result]. This is because no functional operation is observed for a non-entity (abhāva) in the establishment of another entity.
Furthermore, even when a prescribed act is not performed, at that time another action is the cause of the transgression (pratyavāya).
The reason is as follows:
"When an insentient thing, failing to act at its own proper time, performs something else instead, it incurs a transgression by that very act; it is not produced by non-existence."
Thus [it is said]. But if—
“And that prior non-existence of the action which exists in the case of not performing what is enjoined, because it causes harm, is a real entity and therefore cannot be removed.”

From this observation, it is maintained that the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of the mantra and other such factors is the cause. Nevertheless, the subsequent observation of the effect would still not be possible. If it is argued that the destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) of the mantra and so forth is also a cause, then since that [destruction] did not exist previously, the effect would not have arisen prior to the employment of the mantra and other factors. For an sprout is never seen to arise even when any one of the earth, water, or seed is absent. Furthermore, while the presence of the previous mantra and other factors still exists...

Observing that the presence of the effect occurs when there is the presence of mantras and so forth—which are the opposite of those [non-causes]—we do not establish that the absence of those [mantras, etc. is the cause of the absence of that effect.

For it is not observed that transgression (*pratyavāya*) has the non-performance of what is enjoined as its cause, even when the performance of what is enjoined is present. And here is the formal argument:

whatever has the absence of X as its cause does not occur when X is present, just as transgression—which is produced by the absence of what is enjoined—does not occur when that which is enjoined is present.

[It is] by virtue of being produced [as such]. Nor is it the case that the effect occurs when there is the state of being a mantra and so forth. And thus, the state of being a mantra and so forth, being ineffective, would never obstruct the effect.

Therefore, the mantra is an obstructor of the causal power itself; its absence is not the cause [of the obstruction]. However, even that [mantra], when its power is snatched away by the impact of something more powerful, does not obstruct anything at all. And that which, being obstructed by something more powerful, does not even find itself—[how could it obstruct]?

Even in the absence of contradiction, the self [of the cause] should not be [assumed] by that [inference]. Let it not be that, even in the absence of a scriptural application (*viniyoga*) that opposes [the inference], there is likewise an absence of an inferential application (*laiṅgika-viniyoga*). Therefore, there is some excellence (*atiśaya*) in the causes, such that they do not initiate an effect through destruction or concealment; thus, the postulation of the burning power (*dahana-śakti*) from the burning perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is established. As for the inferability of power, however, it will be refuted later on. He now provides an example of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) preceded by inference.
Regarding the phrase "from what is inferred": by means of reaching another location, the sun's motion is inferred;

from that, its power [to move] is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Here too, "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) refers precisely to contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For movement among living beings is understood to be accomplished by specific instruments such as feet and the like. And this [sun], having been inferred to possess a mode of movement possessing those same characteristics, [is seen to lack such instruments].

The thought that it likewise ought not to move in that same manner is refuted by the postulation of its capacity: "Indeed, there exists a certain capacity in this [wind] by which it moves in a way contrary to other movers, approaching both the downward fall and the upward toss simultaneously. // 3 //

However, *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) has a distinct object from those [types of] *dṛṣṭārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is seen), and will be explained separately later;

thus he says, "based on what is heard" (*śruta*). He demonstrates that which is preceded by analogy (*upamāna*) with the words "the gavaya... When it is analogized that "the cow is similar to the gavaya," the capacity to be grasped by a cognition of similarity is postulated through presumption (*arthāpatti*). And such an inconsistency (*anupapatti*) arises in that case.

How is a cognition of extreme similarity produced with respect to the cow? For if it were to produce such a cognition, why would it not do so even at the first sight [of the cow], since the commonalities of the parts of the gavaya exist in the cow even then?

Thus, even though [the cognition] has arisen, it perishes due to a lack of logical support (*anupapatti*). It is established by the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*): there exists indeed some excellence (*atiśaya*) in the cow, whose manifestation is obtained through the perception of its counterpart, which produces a cognition similar to a *gavaya*.
Furthermore, as for this comparison—that among animals of the same class, the cow alone is similar to a *gavaya*—that too...
This is not tenable without the admission of a specific capacity (śaktiviśeṣa) belonging to it. // 4 //

He provides an example of that which is preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—namely, "denotation" (*abhidhāna*). Having observed the comprehension of meaning immediately following a word, its status as the cause of that comprehension is determined. Since causality is not possible without an operation (*vyāpāra*), an operation inherent in the word is inferred. And that [operation] is well known as "denotation. To establish that, the capacity of the word to denote is cognized through presumptive testimony. For, if it were merely denotative...
An inconsistency arises in the inference:

"This [word] is not the designator of this [object]. If it is argued that, just as before, once the relationship has been grasped, the word becomes a communicator even prior to the knowledge of that relationship, we say no; because that [relationship] is absent. For no relationship—such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or any other—is observed between this [word] and its object. Thus, since that [relationship] is untenable...
It serves to establish the postulation of a capacity (śakti). Indeed, there exists between these two a relationship consisting of the capacity of the signified and the signifier;

for it is because this [capacity] is not apprehended that the object is not understood. And thus, after the postulation of the capacity, since even the capacity would be untenable without the eternity of that capacity, the eternity of the word is cognized through another presumption (arthāpatti). // 5 //

He explains this very point with the verse beginning "abhidhā" (6–7). And he states that Jaimini himself will explain this in the section on *śabda* (the means of knowledge known as verbal testimony), saying: "of the observation... (6–7).

However, since the author of the *Bhāṣya* himself has already cited an instance of that which is preceded by non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā*), he does not cite one separately; thus he says: "By the absence of means of valid cognition," etc., in a verse and a half. The meaning of this is as follows: just as when Devadatta is alive, the postulation of his being outside—which was previously unperceived—is made upon seeing his absence from the house, so too the establishment of Caitra’s presence outside, which was shown in the *Bhāṣya*, is [to be understood] in relation to the examples under discussion.

The author of the Bhāṣya has cited this instance of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) which is preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*). However, the detailed exposition of the examples of *arthāpatti* was described under the section on the faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), beginning with the words "in the case of the non-existence of the knower and so forth," as an inference; thus he says: "among the faults of the thesis. (8–9)

{3,165} Now, while the distinction between presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and inference (*anumāna*) is to be understood, since it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*, he first states the distinction for that which is preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*), beginning with the word "abhāva. That presumptive testimony which consists in the indication of Caitra’s existence outside [the house]— derived from Caitra being apprehended by the means of knowledge of non-existence in the form "he is not in the house"— is also distinct from inference, because, like verbal testimony and comparison, it lacks the constituent factors such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
"It is divided. // 10 //

He demonstrates precisely why [the absence] is not a constituent part of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), etc., by saying "outside space" (*bahirdeśa*). For here, either Caitra qualified by outside space is the subject (*pakṣa*), or outside space qualified by him is the subject. Now, since the absence located in the house is a property of neither of these two, how can it possess the status of being a property of the subject?
The meaning is: "not in any way whatsoever. // 11 //
A mere non-existence that is not qualified cannot serve as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for Caitra’s being outside. Nor does his house function as its qualifier;

for a qualifier is dependent upon another, just as blueness is the qualifier of the substance *utpala*. Thus, in this case as well, it is logical that the house itself, which is a substance, is qualified by the non-existence that is dependent upon it.
Furthermore, because it is all-pervasive, the absence [of Caitra] is a qualifier of the house;
for that absence, which pervades the entire world excluding the single location occupied by Caitra, is capable of pervading the house.

The small house, however, cannot pervade the absence, which has such a vast domain. Therefore, just as the smoke, which is the pervaded, is understood to be qualified by fire, [so too is the house understood to be qualified by the absence].

By this reasoning as well, it follows that the house itself, as qualified by the absence [of Caitra], is the mark (*liṅga*) for the external existence [of Caitra]. And that house, qualified by his absence, is not connected in any way with either Caitra or the external location. For while there is indeed some connection of Caitra with the absence—since he is cognized as "the absence of Caitra"—the house, however, is not connected in any way [to that absence].

He states that [the absence] is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*) because it is understood as being connected with Caitra—this is expressed by the words "in the absence of that" (*tadabhāva*). Furthermore, he states that the absence from the house is not a property of the subject by saying "absence from the house" (*gṛhābhāva*). For a cognition of a property arises only when the subject has been apprehended; however, neither Caitra nor the external location are apprehended by means of the absence in the house. // 12 //

{3,166} But since the house itself is perceived there [by direct perception], the cognition of its property (the absence) occurs only with respect to that absence; thus he says: "The house is indeed apprehended. For it is not the case that Caitra is in the house itself, because that would contradict his absence; this is the intention behind saying "there. Since non-perception is understood as being connected to Caitra, it might serve as the inferential mark (*liṅga*); therefore he says: "And not here. Nor is the absence of perception a mark for [his] existence outside.
In the absence of this, it will be stated [later]. // 13 //

Therefore, he says "by that" (*tena*) to show that even non-perception in the house is not the cause. Furthermore, since non-perception is exhausted by the ascertainment of Caitra’s absence from the house, how could the cognition of his being outside be caused by it? With this intention, he says "from non-perception" (*adarśanāt*). He clarifies this intention with the words "not that" (*nāsau*). It is the very existence of Caitra, as ascertained through non-perception and no longer serving any other purpose, that constitutes the cause.

It is possible [to object that the reason is unestablished]. But since that is refuted by the fact that [the absence] is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*), he says: "of Caitra’s absence" (v. 14–15).

Thus, the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) has first been refuted; now he states that the subject itself is not perceived prior to the inference: "And not before," [verse 16].

Regarding this, an objection is raised: "The river. For in that case, even though the upper region has not been perceived, the floodwater—which is not a property of that [region]—serves as the mark (*liṅga*); likewise, it will be so here as well. // 17 //

He refutes this with the words "possessing rain. If it were inferred in this manner, there would be a contradiction with common worldly experience, for ordinary people do not perceive things in such a way. Therefore, he says "or rather. Since the cause of the observed rise in the river's water cannot be otherwise accounted for, rain above is postulated. This too was stated by one who follows the established tradition.

In the ultimate sense, however, this is indeed an inference arising from the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Nor is there the fault of the reason not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatā*). This is because the upper region is connected to the location connected to the flood;
for that which is unconnected cannot be a logical reason. // 18 //

Furthermore, he states that the absence from the house is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for [inferring] presence outside: "And [the case] of one who is alive," and so forth. For in inference, a logical mark must be of an ascertained nature to be indicative. And here, this absence from the house of one who is alive cannot be ascertained at all because of its contradiction with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For in that regard, such a doubt arises: "One who is alive must necessarily exist somewhere."

How could it not be so here? Thus, because there is no determination (*anadhyavasāya*), the absence of being inside the house is not established; therefore, due to its lack of proof (*asiddhatvāt*), it is not a logical mark (*aliṅga*). Furthermore, its establishment does not occur without including its "being outside"; and if that is included, then—as will be shown later—the object of cognition (*prameya*) would be non-existent. This is the intended meaning. // 19 //
But in inference, the nature of the mark (liṅga), such as smoke, is understood as established independently of the object of cognition (prameya); thus he says: "as possessing fire" (agnimattā). 20.

But if, even here, for the sake of establishing the independence of the reason, one intends the mere absence from the house—unqualified by [the condition of] being alive—to be the reason, then it is not conclusive; thus he says: "gehābhāva... (verse 21).

How does the absence from the house, when qualified by existence, establish presence outside, and how does it not do so when unqualified? He states the reason for both cases in the two verses beginning with "vidyamānatva": for in the cognition of the absence from the house as qualified by the attribute of existence, as long as the object of that existence is not established, the absence itself cannot even be cognized.

Thus, when the house is occupied by an absence that serves as the counter-positive (pratipakṣa) to Caitra’s presence, then Caitra’s presence cannot exist there; therefore, by the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) with respect to the locus, his presence must be outside. However, in the cognition of a pure absence (*śuddhābhāva*), there is no dependence on a locus at all, so what is the use of postulating an existence outside? // 22–23 //

But surely, the absence of Caitra from his house—which is certain to exist—would establish his presence outside by implication; however, for one whose existence is doubtful, that absence would lead to the inference of his being outside even without such dependence. To this, he says: "established. If there were doubt regarding Caitra's existence, [the argument would fail].

In that case, the cognition of its existence outside would not be established. Rather, when the cognition of its existence is indeed free from doubt, its presence is excluded—driven out—from the house by its absence and necessarily becomes an external state;

otherwise, there would be doubt even regarding that [external existence]. By this, it should be understood that the view held by some—that it is precisely the existence [of the person] which, having its presence in the house rendered doubtful by the absence from the house, postulates his existence outside—is refuted. And this has already been stated for the most part.
"By us," [it is said]. // 24 //

Therefore, it is established that non-existence (*abhāva*) which is independent of a living subject (*jīvananirapekṣa*) is fallible (*vyabhicāra*); and since that which is infallible is established only by way of entering into the category of the cognizable (*prameya*), it lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) because it differs from smoke and such.
Thus he says: "By that... (verse 25).

Thus, he concludes in order to establish its distinction from inference: "Therefore" [it is said]. This means that this means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) stands as something external to inference. // 26 //

Thus, since the non-existence in the house has been established as entering into the scope of the object of cognition (*prameya*), if that [non-existence] is accepted as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then an unavoidable circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*) results; so he says with the two verses beginning "pakṣe":
"But surely, in this way, there is also an entry into the scope of the object of cognition in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

For how will the non-existence in the house—which is not yet established and which is brought about by another means of knowledge through its own inconsistency—cause one to understand existence outside?"
Therefore he says: "Otherwise. For there are two ways in which something is untenable: some things are simply untenable, such that they cannot be established in any way whatsoever;
and some things are untenable only in the absence of a conceptual construction. Of these, that which is absolutely untenable is simply disregarded.
However, when something is possible given a certain postulation but impossible otherwise, that possibility is determined by the postulation of another [factor].
For it is precisely in this way that all worldly people and investigators understand. Nor is a contrary case observed in other regions and so forth.
Therefore, this is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And just as in inference, a mark (*liṅga*) whose nature is ascertained is the indicator.

Similarly here as well, something apprehended by one means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has its conceptualization (*vitarka*) aroused by another means of valid cognition. And there is no doubt regarding the validity of either one;
rather, there is merely a requirement for the justification of two things whose validity is already certain, [in the form of the question]: "How can both of these be made consistent?
This is like the case of the two scriptural injunctions regarding the taking and non-taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup. It is not the case that there, one must be abandoned in order to establish the other.

It is possible. Therefore, just as in that case, when it is required to explain how both [properties] can be established, both are established through a distinction in application; so too here, both [properties], which are established by valid cognition and whose existence is certain, are rendered consistent through the postulation of a different object, because they appear precisely in their respective forms. For the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are indeed distinct, possessing distinct causal complexes (*sāmagrī*); for this very reason, they differ from one another. [This concerns] the causes of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*).
Furthermore, there is neither doubt, error, nor ignorance;

and since these are likewise absent in the case of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), how can it be considered invalid? If it is asked, "How can a cognition arising from an unestablished relation be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?", we reply: the relation itself is not the cause of validity, but rather the absence of sublation (*bādhaviraha*). Since that [absence of sublation] is no different here [in *arthāpatti*] as well, no defect whatsoever appears to us regarding presumptive testimony. // 29 //

[Objection: Surely the absence from the house is not possible without [his] presence outside; therefore, it is an invariable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*). And that cognition of another object which arises from an invariable concomitant is inference. Therefore, this cognition of his presence outside is indeed inference. To this, he says: "without" (*avineti*). This is the intended meaning: some read [the definition as] "the perception of an invariable concomitant object is inference for one who knows it."
For those who know that [logical connection], it is intended that inference is the perception of the inseparable relation (*nāntarīyakadarśana*) by one who knows the necessity of that [relation].
However, in this case, it was not previously understood that the absence from the house occurs without the external presence;

for it is precisely at that time that, having postulated the external presence through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the state of being inseparable—namely, "this does not exist without that"—is postulated. Therefore, although it is real in its own nature, it was not previously understood.
It is not the cause for the arising of knowledge. // 30 //

[Objection: "In that case, for one who has already understood the relationship [between the two], there would be inference. To this he says, ending with the word *gṛhābhāva*: "Not indeed, by all means, is the concomitance of the two understood as a rule. The intention is that for one who has not understood their concomitance, this remains established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Even for one who has understood the concomitance of those two, the apprehension of their concomitance is not possible if the two themselves have not been apprehended; nor is the perception of the second possible upon the apprehension of one of them without presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). It is precisely through the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*)—namely, by the single fact of absence from the house—that [the person's being outside is known].

Or else, one of those two must be cognized as existing externally. If this were not postulated, then because one of the related members would remain ungrasped, there could be no cognition of their coexistence (*sāhitya*) at all. Therefore, for the sake of [establishing] coexistence, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) must be sought; thus, with the intention that it is established as a distinct means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he says: "And the means of knowledge... up to the end of the verse. He explains the underlying intention with the words: "By that... (vv. 31–33).
Now, one might object: "It is not necessarily the case that one of the two related terms must be apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone.
For it is possible for someone standing at the door of a house to perceive both [the absence and the person] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), thereby experiencing the relation;

and from that perceived relation, the inference of the person's presence outside follows from his absence from the house. Thus he raises this objection with the words: "gṛhadvārī" (standing at the door of the house). // 34 //

To this he replies: "Even then" (*tadāpi*). This is the intended meaning: while it is indeed possible to infer the existence outside from the absence from the house in this manner, there is no comprehension of all [objects] in this very way, because cognition occurs even for those who have not grasped the relationship [between the two]. Furthermore, this method is not possible for the comprehension of non-existence everywhere based on existence in one place.

For it is not possible to understand that existence is concomitant with the non-existence of the world in one place, because the non-existence of the world cannot be apprehended; this is the intended meaning. [Objection: But surely, it is understood in this way: when this [object] exists in one place, then it does not exist elsewhere, in its vicinity. And thus, once the pervasion (vyāpti) is known, there will be an inference of non-existence everywhere based on the perception of it in a single location.
Therefore, he says: "And not... For the pervasion of the reason is not established by the non-existence of one part through the non-existence of the three worlds. // 35 //
But if it is argued that no connection is perceived because of the non-existence of the world, and that this is due to its not being perceived—
surely, then, non-apprehension is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.

Just as Devadatta, being present in one place, is determined to be non-existent when he is not perceived in another location, so too, being present in one place while not being perceived anywhere else, it can be understood that he does not exist everywhere. For non-perception, unlike perception, does not require effort.
For perception, as an effect, depends upon its own causes—such as the contact between the object and the sense organ—and thus occurs only in one place, not everywhere.

However, the absence of perception does not depend on anything [specific]. Thus he objects: "But surely, in this case... Here, the word "here" refers to a specific location. Indeed, in this particular location, non-existence is understood through non-perception; and that [non-existence] applies everywhere as well.
It is the same. // 36 //

To this, he states the rebuttal: "Not by this [means]. Why is it not cognized? To this he says: "Because of that place. For it is the non-perception of something capable of being perceived that establishes its non-existence;

however, in the case of distant objects, non-perception is possible even though they exist, simply because they are incapable of being perceived; thus, there is no certainty of their non-existence. // 37 //
However, if all villages, cities, rivers, deserts, and other locations were reached, then Caitra’s absence from them could be established;
yet this is not possible to accomplish. With this intention, he says: "Having gone, having gone... (38).
Here he raises an objection: "Now, if... and so forth. The intention is this: first of all, a reason (*hetu*) that does not exclude itself from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) cannot be a prover;
nor is it possible to go and perceive all counter-examples.

Therefore, the absence of the reason from the counter-example must necessarily be grasped through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of something situated in only one part [of the counter-example]. It is just like that.

"It will also be the case here. "Smoke and so forth" refers to those things that are "excluded" (*vyatirekin*); thus, they are "smoke-excluders" (*dhūmādivyatirekinaḥ*). Since smoke and the like are excluded in the absence of fire and so forth, their exclusion is not established because they do not fail to reach the location where fire and so forth are absent. // 39 //

He addresses [this objection] with the words, "Of which... For according to the Buddhist, who maintains that exclusion (*vyatireka*) is primary, a reason cannot be a prover if there is no apprehension of its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).
This is because for him, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is the absence of another entity;
that is to say, the absence of that which is not fire, such as non-fire, in relation to an entity such as fire. Indeed, that [absence] is not possible without the exclusion of all non-fire.

For me, however, the reason is a concomitant indicator (*sahacārī hetuḥ*) which makes [the conclusion] known by means of a restriction based on mere positive concomitance (*anvayamātra-niyamena*). And that [restriction] is established by merely not observing [the reason] in dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), through just two or three observations. // 40 //

Surely, even for one who maintains the theory of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), it is indeed difficult to perceive smoke that is co-present with fires existing in infinite locations—both those not yet born, those already passed away, and those currently present. Now, if you argue that fires not perceived as co-present are nonetheless inferred simply from observing the co-presence of a few fires, then in this case as well, the relationship between Caitra’s absence throughout the entire world and his presence in a single location is perfectly established. For here too, while Caitra is present in one place, his absence is observed in several others.
And since one would thus infer the non-existence [of the object] everywhere by that much alone, he says: "But if this were so... (41).

To this, he states the rebuttal: "In the case of coexistence" (*sāhitye*). This is the intended meaning: our inference does not have the individual instance as its object, but rather the generic form (*ākṛti*) as its object;
and since the two forms are entirely inherent in each individual instance, the perception of their coexistence is indeed easily obtained.

For the concomitance of two forms is understood by a single observation alone. For this very reason, even a second or third observation is required when there is a suspicion of deviation, for the purpose of establishing a rule. Once concomitance is understood, a doubt arises: "Is this association of smoke with fire merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), or is it innate (*sahaja*)?"

In that case, because there is no deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) through repeated observation, and because there is no cause for the introduction of another limiting condition (*upādhi*), the cognition arises that its concomitance with fire is essential (*svābhāvika*). However, although the connection of fire with smoke has been understood at first, upon seeing a deviation in subsequent observations, a limiting condition such as "moist fuel" (*ārdrendhana*) enters into the relation. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of deviation due to differences in place and so forth.
For when two things have had their concomitance determined through a single observation, deviation is indeed seen in the case of fire;
therefore, if smoke were also to deviate from fire,
its deviation would likewise be observed after only two, three, or four observations.

And yet it is not so seen. Therefore, it is determined that this [subject] possesses a nature conjoined with fire. However, for one who lacks confidence even in this case, there would be a lack of confidence in all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alike, because deviation is observed in some instances of them. Furthermore, the exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyatireka*) is established by implication alone; for when one first searches for it, the dissimilar locations are infinite.

It would be difficult to establish. However, once the restriction of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaniyama*) is known, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is easily established because intrinsic nature is non-deviant.
For no one would ever suspect that fire could exist anywhere or at any time without its inherent heat.
"Because it occupies a limited space" means because it has a delimited location. // 42 //

But in the case of the existence in one place and the non-existence of the world, such a cognition of concomitance (*sāhitya*) does not occur; thus he says: "In this case" (*iha*). For here, the single non-existence is co-present with infinite locations, and is not of limited extent like the form of fire and smoke; therefore, concomitance is difficult to grasp in this instance. // 43 //

Here he raises an objection: "But surely," etc. The absence of Caitra in other locations is apprehended through inference. For it is inferred as follows: all remote locations are connected with the absence of Caitra, because they are distinct from the location occupied by him, just like the vicinity of the place where Caitra is currently staying. // 44 //

He refutes [the objection] with the words "contradictory" (*viruddha*). For how could there be the state of being a non-erroneous contradiction? To this he says: "in that same way," meaning "just as in the case of Caitra, so it is with respect to another location. Therefore, in all cases, non-existence is established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone;
there is no other way. // 45 //

However, if one maintains that inference is established by first grasping the concomitance (*sāhitya*) after having thus apprehended [the subject], then that must be preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);

and by this much, the validity of *arthāpatti* is proven. With this intention, he says—from "of the person" up to the end of verse 3.175. As for the one who says: "First, in the case of one's own self, a relation is observed between being present in one place and being absent everywhere else,"
Therefore, it must be explained how the non-existence of even another [object] is inferred everywhere. If it is by means of non-existence (*abhāva*),
it must be stated of what [that non-existence belongs].

First of all, the non-existence [of an object] in distant places cannot be understood through the cessation of perception, because precisely due to their distance they are not fit for perception; nor can its own non-existence in those places be understood. If it were present there, it would simply not be at a distance;
therefore, together with its presence in another location, its own body becomes fit for perception.
And because it would be perceived due to its suitability [for perception],
its non-existence is determined from this non-perception. If this is indeed another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
then that which exists in a particular location must be capable of being perceived by itself together with its substratum.
And it is not so here;
therefore, [Caitra] does not exist in other places. Thus, the non-existence in other places must be apprehended through inference, not through the non-apprehension of perception (*pratyakṣābhāva*).

And regarding that, the fallacy of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) has already been stated: "The various other places under dispute possess Caitra, because they are locations distinct from the place near Caitra."

"Like Caitra, like a location. And where doubt is raised by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*), there that which is supported by another stronger means of knowledge, such as perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, prevails;
and in this case, no other means of knowledge than presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is capable of establishing non-existence everywhere. For it functions in this manner:
This perception of Caitra in its entirety in one place would not be possible if Caitra were present in another location;
for entities are of two kinds: localized or all-pervading.
Pervasion (*vibhava*) is also twofold:

that which pervades all [space] and that which pervades its own substratum. The former refers to space and so forth; the latter refers to genus (*jāti*) and so forth. For that which is connected with all future conjuncts even though they have not yet arrived is well known as being pervasive (*vibhu*).
And by that [quality of pervasiveness], the self, space, and so forth are called "pervasive" (*vibhu*). First of all, Caitra is not like space;

for that which is spherical is understood to be fully contained within a single location. Furthermore, just as a whole does not exist in its parts, so too it cannot exist in another location. For if it had parts elsewhere, it would not be perceived here in its entirety.

Or rather, because it would be interrupted in the interval between [two locations], it would be something else. Furthermore, it cannot exist in the same manner as a universal (*jāti*). For a universal is formless;

having inhered in one individual (*piṇḍa*), it inheres in another individual. But how could this [motion] have inherence in another location? For this is not a universal. Its connection with another place is conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and that is not possible for what has not yet arrived.
For this [self] is seen to go and be joined with other places; therefore, it is not all-pervading (*vibhu*).

Consequently, since it is impossible for that which exists in one place to exist elsewhere in any way, its non-existence elsewhere must be admitted, and thus its cognition of the whole is established.

What, then, is the inconsistency here? No obstruction to complete cognition is observed here by anything whatsoever. Rather, it is only when there is a weak cause of obstruction that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) establishes itself by subverting that [obstruction] through the inference from existence (*bhāvānumāna*). And in this case, the inference from existence is weak.

Because it is contradicted by a counter-reason (*pratihetu*). However, where both [reasons] of equal strength encounter one another in a single instance, there the justification arises through the postulation of a different fact (*arthāntarakalpanā*); thus, nothing is untenable. In this way, the distinction of presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā arthāpatti*) from inference has been stated; now, in order to demonstrate its distinction from that [presumption] based on perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*), the proposition for that [latter] is set forth.

To this he says: "And where... Even in a case where the power of a cause such as fire is postulated because the effect such as burning is observed, there too presumption (*arthāpatti*) is indeed the primary means of knowledge. If, however, inference occurs subsequently, let it be so.
Furthermore, because it was cited in the *Bhāṣya*, the distinction of presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā*) from inference has been described first. // 46–47 //

Here, the proponent of inference presents the logical mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "of the effect. For they think as follows: inference is of two kinds, having for its object either a perceived particular characteristic (*dṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa*) or an unperceived particular characteristic (*adṛṣṭasvalakṣaṇa*). Of these, that which has a perceived particular characteristic as its object is the inference of fire by means of smoke and so forth.

And the inference of action and so forth from conjunction, disjunction, and the like, has as its object a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is not perceived. For an effect is known in its general relation to a cause; therefore, the cognition of it [the cause] from that [the effect] is indeed nothing but inference. He refutes this as well with the words:
"Not the relation... For he who has once seen a sprout from a seed will, on another occasion, [see it] again from a similar [seed].
Not perceiving [the sprout] through inference based on its own nature (*svabhāvānumāna*), one who infers that "this sprout must be produced by this [cause]" suspects here:
"How is it that the sprout is not born?
Thereupon, he postulates: "There exists some specific power (*śaktibheda*) inherent in the seed, by virtue of which the effect previously existed."

And [if you say] "it does not exist today," how can this cognition—which arises precisely from an investigation into the presence and absence of the ancient and present sprouts by one who has not even grasped a relation—be considered inference? Furthermore, all inference is dependent upon the apprehension of a relation;

it is not possible for there to be an inference between two related things when that relation has not been apprehended. Nor, in this case, is there a supersensible power (*śakti*) belonging to those two [the seed and the sprout].
