It cannot be experienced by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); for this very reason, it is also impossible to apprehend that which possesses the capacity (*śaktimad*).

Therefore, how can there be an establishment of both the capacity and its possessor from an effect whose relationship [to them] has not been apprehended? This is what he says: "Having seen... Now, it is indeed understood that the generality of the effect is [connected] with the generality of the cause...
"It is pervaded," it is said;
therefore, that will be inferred. True;

however, without the postulation of a capacity (*śakti*), the very designation "cause" does not cease to apply. For a sprout is that which exists when the seed exists, and its existence is not deviant from [the existence of] other things.

And since it is understood that [the sprout] has the seed as its cause, yet when it does not arise even though the seed is present, it deviates from that [seed] as well; thus, the very cognition of the cause falters.

One supports that [cognition] by postulating a potency (*śakti*). And once the potency inherent in the cause has been postulated, if the relationship is then understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), let it be so; for, as in the established doctrine, presumptive testimony is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the establishment of the potency.

He concludes that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), arising even without the characteristics of inference, is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "of presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatter iti*). // 49 //
He refutes the example cited by another commentator with the words "from inference" (*anumānāt*). For victory has its pervasion (*vyāpti*) known through defeat;

thus, having seen that [victory] in a single instance—such as a mongoose that kills snakes—one understands the defeat of the opponent. And from the observation of defeat, one understands the victory of the opponent. This, therefore, is not to be cited as an example of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). // 50 //
It was stated that presumptive implication based on what is heard (śrutārthāpatti) will be explained; he now provides an example of it: "Fat... (verse 51).

And regarding its object, there is a dispute; he sets forth that [dispute] for the sake of determining it alone, ending with the words "they conceive of it as an object. And since all [schools] maintain that it does not fall outside of scripture, he says:
"and from scripture. //52//

He states his intention regarding the acceptance of the non-difference of the scriptures with the word "mostly" (*prāyaśas*). Its utility in the Veda is great for the establishment of results, the unseen force (*apūrva*), the details of injunctions (*vidhyanta*), and so forth;
otherwise, if it were not a scripture, it would not be Vedic. // 53 //
Even if it were based on scripture (*āgamika*), he introduces a further disagreement with the words "of the statement" [54].
Here he shows the essential point: "Not, first of all... He states the reason: "For not... First, a sentence is not expressive;
how much less so when there are multiple meanings [55].

If it is non-expressive, how can there be a cognition of meaning from the sentence? To this he says: "padārtha... (the meaning of the word). And this will be explained in the *tadbhūtādhikaraṇa*. Now, if the meaning of the sentence concerning the night and so forth is not expressed by the sentence concerning the day, but is instead understood through its own meaning in the form of a connection between word-meanings, to this he says: "na rātryādi... (not the night and so forth). For the word-meanings such as "night" do not exist within the sentence concerning the day.
How, then, could there be any continuity of those [causes] therein? // 56 //

[Objection: But surely the meaning of the sentence regarding the night and so forth will be understood precisely through the connection with the meanings of the words "day" and so forth; to this he says: "Not day and so forth. (57)

He explains what was stated—that there is no multiplicity of meanings—with the words "anyārtha" (having another meaning). Therefore, he says "tasmāt" (therefore), indicating that this is the meaning of a different sentence altogether, and not of the sentence concerning the day. // 58 //

Thus, this is not the meaning of the root scripture itself; rather, one must determine which among the means of valid cognition—such as perception and the rest—is the authority for that other sentence present in the mind by which this meaning is understood. To this effect, he says: "of that" (tasya). // 59 //

In this regard, he states that perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing that [the Veda], saying "for not" (*na hi*). He further states that inference (*anumāna*) is also impossible because the sentence regarding the day, which would be connected to it, is not observed, saying "not inference" (*nānumānam*). // 60 //

But if one seeks a logical mark (*liṅga*) in the sentence concerning the day when the relationship [between word and meaning] is unknown, there would be a lack of restriction; thus he says: "If, however... (verse 61).

If, however, it is argued that one first grasps the very connection between the sentence concerning the day and the sentence concerning the night, and then infers [the latter] from that, this is indeed possible; yet, not all sentences of common worldly usage and the Veda are understood by everyone to be connected with all other expressive sentences. Therefore, how could those [sentences] be inferred from them?
He said: "And not," [verse 62].

For this reason as well, he says that there is no inference: "And not... For something qualified by a universal nature through which a relation has been known is what is inferred, not the mere existence of a thing.
And because the relation is not known here, both of these [conditions] are reversed. // 63 //

Since here the very nature of the sentence is the object of cognition (*prameya*), there is no subject (*dharmin*)—such as a mountain—that is previously established, independent, and unrelated, yet qualified by some independent property (*dharma*) such as fire; thus he says "previously established" (*pūrvasiddha*). // 64 //

Now, if one takes the heard sentence itself as the subject (*dharmin*) and proves its being qualified by the unheard sentence, then, because that [qualification] is unestablished, the thesis (*pakṣa*) would have an unestablished qualifier; thus he says "atha" (now).
Furthermore, when the heard sentence is being proved as qualified by the unheard sentence, no logical mark (*liṅga*) whatsoever is perceived, and there can be no inference without a logical mark.

If that very same thing is again intended as the logical mark (liṅga), then there is the fallacy of being a mere part of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñārthaikadeśatva), as was stated when a word was made the subject and its qualified meaning was being proven. Thus he says: "Furthermore... (kiñ ca).

The relationship of property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibhāva*) between the sentence concerning the day and the sentence concerning the night must also be rejected, just as it was for the word and its meaning; thus he says: "In the same way. Just as it was stated there that when the object, the property-bearer, is not apprehended, a word cannot be said to be its property, so too here, when the sentence concerning the night is not apprehended, [it cannot be a property].

The statement regarding the day is understood. However, if it is argued that this [statement] was first apprehended for the sake of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (pakṣadharmatā), then the intention is that there would be an absence of the object to be inferred (anumeya).
He clarifies this intention with the words: "not unapprehended" (nāgṛhīte) // 67 //

Moreover, it is described in that very same passage: "No relation exists apart from the connection between an action (kriyā) and its factors (kāraka). Therefore, just as it was stated that a word has no connection with an object based on an action—and thus [the object] is not a property of that word—so too must the status of the sentence regarding the day (*divāvākya*) as a property of the sentence regarding the night (*rātrivākya*) be rejected; this is what he says with the word "action" (*kriyā*). Furthermore, there is no relation here between the two sentences consisting of the nature of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), such as that which exists between a word and its meaning.

It is said that meaning is expressed by a word, but a sentence is not the denoter of another sentence; thus he says, "non-denotative. In the case of a word, however, since it generates the cognition of meaning, its being an object [of inference] is accepted, and thus the absence of an inferable [sentence] was shown. Here, however, because a sentence is non-denotative, it cannot be an object [of inference].
The distinction is that it cannot be understood in this way. // 68 //
If, however, it is argued that the sentence concerning the night is indeed understood from the sentence concerning the day,

and therefore that [sentence] also possesses the capacity to denote it— such that there exists a relationship characterized by the object and the subject of cognition— then it would follow that a single sentence is admitted to have multiple meanings.

For even the sentence concerning the night conveys its own meaning, and this is not logically tenable; with this intention, he says: "Because of [its] cognition. Now, it might be argued: "Let it not be that the sentence has that as its object by way of being expressive;
rather, that sentence is inferred from it."

Therefore, that mark (liṅga), being the object of inference, is indeed the mark itself; the statement regarding the day [the "day-vacana"] is designated as such because it possesses that property (taddharmatā).

As for the fact that its status as a property of that [subject] arises from being the object of inference, he says "anumeti" [verse 69], meaning that since the inference is already established beforehand, [stating] that property-status is fruitless.

Thus, it has been stated that the sentence as a whole lacks indicative mark (*liṅga*); now he says "by means of the word-meanings" (*padārthaiḥ*) to show that the status of being an indicative mark must likewise be refuted for the individual word-meanings contained therein. [Objection: But surely, even word-meanings whose relationship [to the sentence-meaning] has not been grasped can cause the sentence-meaning to be understood.
In this way, why do they not also lead to the understanding of the sentence regarding "night"?

To this he says: "The general," etc. A general action or a general agent, once apprehended, cannot be established otherwise than by obtaining a mutual connection; thus, it leads to the understanding of that specific [element].
And that which is the specific [element] is precisely what is called the meaning of the sentence. // 70 //

And since this mode of connection is not possible in the case of establishing the meaning of the sentence concerning "night," he says: "But not... Furthermore, he says: "Nor even... because no other relation—such as that of place, time, and so forth—exists between the sentence concerning "day" and the sentence concerning "night," nor between their respective word-meanings. // 71 //

It might be argued: "Even if the statement regarding the day is not the denoter of the statement regarding the night, we shall nevertheless postulate it, and from that, it will be understood. He raises this very objection with the words beginning "Now, if it were the denoter of this... and ending with "...another [statement]."

Regarding this, he states the refutation: "In the same way. First of all, there is no evidence whatsoever for the postulation of such another sentence; thus, setting that aside, he first brings about an infinite regress.
Furthermore, even that postulated sentence is not capable of making known the *rātri* (night) sentence, nor is it unrelated to it.
Thus, it is logical that only such [a statement] is indicative of it. Furthermore, if one postulates yet another sentence, the same fault recurs.
In this way, whatever sentence one wishes to postulate as indicative, that very thing cannot be indicative if it is unrelated; thus, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress. // 72 //

Now, if it is instead imagined that only the final [word] is the indicator (*gamaka*) despite being unrelated [to the rest], then it would be better to simply imagine that the first word of that same kind is the indicator; what is the point of imagining another sentence? And that is not tenable—this is the intention with which he says, "And therefore... Thus, for now, the status of the night-sentence as an object of inference has been refuted on the grounds of the impossibility of its possessing the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.

He says "anvaya... [etc. to show that the negation of both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) must also be demonstrated, just as in the case of the words themselves. For there is no positive concomitance such that the sentence concerning the day exists only when the sentence concerning the night exists, nor is there negative concomitance such that it does not exist when the sentence concerning the night is absent;

this is because there is no connection between their respective locations, times, and so forth. Nor is there a positive concomitance of cognition, since for one who is proficient in language, the cognition of the sentence concerning the day arises even when the cognition of the sentence concerning the night is absent.

The intention is that, because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) occurring at a time subsequent to consciousness are of no utility [for establishing its existence], this should be demonstrated by means of the phrase "like the word 'it' (*iti-ādi-pada*)" and so forth. // 73 //
Thus, it has first been stated that the sentence concerning the night is not cognized through perception, inference, or scripture;

now he shows that analogy (*upamāna*) is also not a means of valid cognition in this regard—up to the words "śrutavākye" and "tvam". He says "artha-sya" [etc. to show that the sentence concerning the night is not analogized even by way of its meaning, just as the sentence concerning the day [is not analogized].

And just as the analogy of the sentence concerning the night with the sentence concerning the day and its meaning has been refuted, so too the analogy of the meaning of the sentence concerning the night with those two must be refuted; thus he says "upamānatve" up to the word "syāt".
He concludes: "Therefore," etc. (75).

Therefore, since there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says "therefore" to indicate that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) alone is the refuge for understanding the sentence regarding the night. The fatness perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is contradicted by the prohibition of eating; and by that fatness, daytime non-eating [is contradicted].
Thus, due to this mutual contradiction, the very communication of its own meaning by the sentence concerning the day becomes untenable, and it brings in the sentence concerning the night.
Therefore, it is concluded that the statement regarding that night is to be inferred.
He now introduces and sets forth the refutation of what was stated—that [inference] has an object as its domain—by saying, "without this object.

This is the intended meaning: for fatness and the prohibition of eating mutually contradict one another, and the existence of both is obtained only through the postulation of an object; for in the case of a fat person, [eating] during the day is prohibited... [3]

184} Fatness results from eating at night alone, not from the mere statement about the night; therefore, it is logical that the meaning is derived through implication (*arthakalpanā*). Furthermore, just as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), though not explicitly stated by others, becomes the intended meaning of the scripture when it is understood through the inconsistency of the literal word-meanings (*padārthānupapatti*).

Thus, he says "vākyārtha... [verse 77] to address the question: why should an object that is cognizable through the non-logical inconsistency of the sentence-meaning (vākyārthānupapatti) not be included within scripture (āgama)?

First, he addresses the initial objection: "savikalpaka" [etc.]. For the cognition resulting from presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*) is indeed determinate (*savikalpaka*), and determinate cognitions are preceded by words. Therefore, since the presumption terminates in the word, the object established through the word itself is not the domain of the presumption. But surely, this is the same for all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of every means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Even by means of the sense organs and logical marks (*liṅga*), fire is understood only preceded by the word; therefore, even in those two cases, they must terminate in the word. Thus, in that context, it is the word residing in memory that is the non-revealer [of the object]; this is the same here as well. For just as the organ of action, being in contact with the object itself, illuminates only that object, and the logical mark, being connected with the object, makes that object known, so too is it here.
Not by means of the word;

likewise here too, an inconsistent meaning is rendered consistent only by another meaning, not by a word. Thus, presumptive implications based on what is observed (*dṛṣṭārthāpatti*) have only meanings as their objects. To this it is replied: It is true that the inconsistency of a sentence occurs only through its meaning, [and not] by means of another meaning.

It is not logical; rather, that sentence, being incomplete, requires another sentence, just as a word requires another word. For when it is said "he cooks," the expectancy is not satisfied by the mere perception of rice;
what then?
By the word "odana," a sentence that is likewise understood to be untenable requires another sentence altogether,

rather than that meaning in its own form. For this very reason, when the *nirvāpa* mantra has been transferred to a modified ritual (*vikṛti*) by extension (*atideśa*), [it requires] the original deity (*prākṛtadevatā*).

Due to the absence [of a word], when that word has ceased, the word *sūryāya* is supplied in its place. In the mantra for cutting, however, the word *chinadmi* is supplied in place of *iṣe tvā*. In the passage "He cuts first from the heart, then from the tongue, then from the chest," the word *avadyati* is to be supplied [to each clause]. It is not merely the meaning that is supplied; rather, *anuṣaṅga* (supplying) is the completion of the sentence in all cases.

This is because of the statement, "due to the equality of their application. However, in the case of perception and the other [means of knowledge], the object is not apprehended by means of its verbal form; even when it is grasped with a verbal expression, it is grasped precisely as the form of the object itself. Let the word, while conceptualizing that object, exist merely as a presence. If, however, the word were required there as well, animals would have no conceptualization of objects.

And that [word] does not exist, for even in their case, an effort is observed for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful. Indeed, thirsty cows go toward ponds and toward a place suitable for remedying that [thirst]. Therefore, since conceptual cognitions such as inference are seen even in those who do not know words, it is determined that there is no dependence on words therein. However, the cognition of presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*)...

It does not exist at all for animals, for this [cognition] arises from the derivation of words, and they do not possess that; this has been explained even in the context of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, there is no cognition through the presumption of a heard meaning (*śrutārthāpatti*) for others who have not mastered the language.

It is not observed [in them]. How much less so in the case of animals? Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is understood that there is a dependence on words in the case of presumptive testimony based on what has been heard (*śrutārthāpatti*). In the case of inference and the like, however, let there indeed be a recollection of words by virtue of the inevitable awakening of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); [but this does not apply to *arthāpatti*].

But there is no dependence on the word itself. Therefore, in this case, it is another sentence that is meaningful which serves as the justification for an untenable sentence, rather than a mere meaning or a mere word. For this very reason, even when the justifying sentence is heard by one who has not grasped the relationship [between words and meanings] and does not know the meaning, the logical inconsistency regarding the knowledge of the meaning of the untenable sentence is not pacified.
Even for one who has understood the meaning, there remains the conceptualization of an intention; therefore, the notion that the heard sentence is deficient does not cease.

Thus, it is established that in the case of presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), there is the conceptualization of a word. In response to the objection of another, he says: "when its purpose has been achieved. For as long as a word has not accomplished its function, cognition is understood [to persist].

That [sentence-meaning] is the *artha* (purpose/object). For the word *artha* denotes purpose (*prayojana*). Therefore, the meaning of a sentence is the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*). For as long as the word-meanings do not experience mutual connection, the sentence remains purposeless;

but once the relationship between action and its factors (*kāraka*) has arisen, the sentence has attained its purpose. Consequently, any further distinct object understood beyond that is not scriptural. Indeed, that which is understood through the impossibility of the meaning already grasped as being purposeful is not itself the purpose.

It exists; however, it serves to establish the purpose. Since no purpose can be found when the meaning of the individual words is untenable, it is logical that the previously understood sentence-meaning constitutes the subject matter of the scripture (*āgama*). What, then, is the distinction?
In any case, this is indeed the subject matter of the scripture.

We do not perceive any distinction between that which is mentally constructed (*kalpita*) and that which is heard (*śruta*). It is replied: if, when the matter consists of what is heard or received through tradition (*āgama*), its loss occurs due to negligence, then there is the cause for expiation based on the loss of what is prescribed in the *Yajurveda* and so forth; otherwise, however, it is the cause for expiation based on an unknown loss. And in that case, having prescribed a fire-oblation (*homa*) with each of the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) for a loss prescribed in the *Ṛgveda* and so forth, [it is said]: "If it is unknown, [one should offer] 'bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā'—the Great Utterances."

Having thus gathered [the arguments], he teaches the expiation: for the Veda is said to be "unknown" precisely because it is to be known through the presumption based on what has been heard (śrutārthāpatti), since it is not known as being any one of the specific categories such as the Ṛgveda and so forth. // 78 //
Here he raises an objection: "But surely... [he says]. First of all, there is no connection between the sentence concerning the day and the sentence concerning the night;
or even if it exists, it is not known.
And when the connection is unknown, [one cannot infer] upon seeing another thing...

The postulation of something else is not logical, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For that which possesses a dependent nature brings about the obstructing factor solely by the force of that dependence;

however, if one were to postulate something else through non-dependence, there would be no cause for such specific determination (*pratiniyama*). Therefore, this cognition of the sentence regarding the night is indeed devoid of any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*). // 79 //

He refutes [the objection] with the words "of the relation. The meaning is that "being a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇatva) consists in being a cause of valid cognition (pramā). Furthermore, the word *pramāṇa* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*). He demonstrates that the relation itself is not a cause for validity by saying "of perception" (*pratyakṣasya*). // 80 //
[Objection: "But surely perception is that which arises solely from the contact of the sense organ with its object; therefore, the relation [between word and object] is not a cause for its validity.

Thus he raises the objection up to the words "if it exists" (*asti cet*). He refutes this with the words "no, because of independence" (*nānapekṣaṇāt*). He demonstrates this very independence with the words "for not... (*na hi*). For it has been established that the relation is the cause for the production of valid knowledge in the case of inference.
And it is not so here. // 81 //
But he says that investigation occurring after the time of direct perception is not a factor of valid cognition: "By which also... (verse 82).
Moreover, in the position of those who maintain that the sense-faculties function without reaching [their objects], even the existence of the relation itself is non-existent;
therefore, just as they accept the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of perceptual cognition, so it will be here as well. To this, he says: "without reaching" (*aprāpya*). // 83 //

Therefore, disregarding [the objections], one must accept that a cognition which is connected, arisen, non-doubtful, and non-erroneous is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even when there is a difference in place and so forth; thus he says: "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). By the word "is born" (*jāyate*), he rejects invalidity characterized by non-arising; by the word "unbreakable" (*abhaṅgura*), he rejects doubt and error. // 84 //

Furthermore, the claim that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) is an extraordinary dispute. For the activity of those who proceed on its basis is never frustrated; and the capacity for successful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*) is precisely what constitutes validity.

There is a dispute regarding whether [presumptive testimony] is distinct from or identical to inference (*anumāna*), and we have already established our conclusion on that point; thus he says: "Nor even... (verse 85).

If this were so, then even in the case of inference (*anumāna*), the relationship (*sambandha*) would not be a constituent factor; therefore, he says: "But [it is] from that. For in that case, the cognition itself does not arise in the absence of knowledge of the relationship; thus, a cause for its production is certainly resorted to. However, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) there too is due solely to the absence of sublation (*bādhaviraha*). // 86 //

He demonstrates the utility of presumption (*arthāpatti*) for the Veda with the words "by means of tradition" (*smṛtyā*). Indeed, a vast portion of the Veda has the presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*) as its means of valid cognition; it would not be established without that [presumption].

For just as the revealed text (*śruti*) acquires its own existence through recitation, so too do these [portions] have the presumption based on what is heard as their means of valid cognition. As he said:
"Just as the recitation [of the Veda] is the means for understanding [the dharma], so too is the inherent capacity (sāmarthya) of the Śrutis.
For this very reason, they do not record even a single [verse], yet they might record a thousandth part.

Thus, for instance, having observed the Smṛti of Manu and others concerning the Aṣṭakā and other rites, and while searching for their foundational source (mūla), [one finds that such a source] is impossible [if one were to rely solely on the extant Vedic texts].

In cases such as error, a desire to deceive, personal experience, or other human statements, since the memory would otherwise be inexplicable without its own foundational source, the Vedic revelation (śruti) itself is postulated as that foundation. Likewise, by means of indicative power (liṅga) and the rest, the Vedic text that enjoins them is inferred— just as, for instance,
when a mantra recited in a specific context is taught by the rule of Vedic study (svādhyāyavidhi), it remains inexplicable without a purpose.

When, through a general understanding of the ritual’s assistance (*kratūpakāra*) based on its function (*kratu*), there arises a requirement for specific details, a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) is inferred to apply the mantra to its possible purpose,

by means of the connection "whatever it may be able to do" (*yac chaknuyāt*), after examining the mantra's inherent power. This is just as in the case of the *barhis* mantra, where [the injunction] is "one should cut with this."

This is application by means of indicative power (*liṅga*); but application by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*) is as follows: in that very same mantra, the word *dāmi* (I cut) is capable of denoting the act of cutting, and thus it alone is applied by means of indicative power, whereas the other words [of the mantra] are applied by means of syntactical connection itself, in the form of their co-occurrence with that word. Application by means of context (*prakaraṇa*), however, pertains to the *samidh* and other such mantras recited within the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

For they (the mantras) require a purpose, and the sacrifice requires assistance; thus, when there is this mutual requirement, the Vedic text is inferred as "one should assist the sacrifice by means of these. This is application by position (*sthānaviniyoga*).
For example, regarding the mantra "Thou art Dabdhi by name," which is studied within the sequence of the Upāṃśuyāja in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices:

for that mantra, the scriptural injunction (śruti) is inferred as "one should assist the Upāṃśuyāja with this [mantra]. As for application by designation (samākhyā), it is as follows: when the ritual items designated as "Adhvaryava" require an agent who is subordinate to them, the restriction of the agent is established by the designation itself.
It is performed. And there is a scriptural authority (śruti) on this point:

"The Adhvaryu priest should perform these. Furthermore, in the case of rituals for which neither the fruit nor the procedure has been explicitly stated—such as the Viśvajit, the Saurya, and others—a scriptural injunction capable of completing them is inferred, such as: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," and "One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer the Saurya oblation of cooked rice."

"The procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is like that of the fire-sacrifice (*āgneya*). There is a vast application of the Veda through such instances of presumptive testimony (*śrutārthāpatti*). Nor is this established by inference alone; for in this case, no connection has been observed between the unaccounted fact and that which must be presumed. And there can be no inference where a necessary connection has not been established.

Therefore, in this case, presumption (*arthāpatti*) alone is the refuge. Regarding the phrase "the perception of the relation": the state of being a perception exists only metaphorically in the intellect. He says, "all that," implying that if presumption were not accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), all of this would be inconsistent. However, if it is desired to call it "inference" by virtue of its general similarity to inference even though it is distinct by definition, let it be so.
"Thus, our other means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara) is established," he says with the word "evam.
Thus ends the section on presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the teacher Sucaritamiśra.

On this point, the commentary states: "Non-existence (*abhāva*) also [is a means of knowledge] because it is the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*), regarding the object 'it does not exist' which is not in contact [with the senses].
What, then, is indicated by this? It cannot be a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) itself; for it is not logical that a means of knowledge should be defined by the absence of a means of knowledge.
If it is argued that the previously mentioned absence of the means of knowledge is its definition, then in that case, this would apply equally to all means of knowledge.

For all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are indeed of the nature of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and thus they could all be called "non-existence of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*). Furthermore, there is no single definition common to all means of valid cognition by whose absence a sixth [category] would be defined. Moreover, that which is called a "means of valid cognition" is the establisher of some object of cognition (*prameya*);

we do not know what it is that is established by this [so-called "non-existence"]. [Objection: But was it not stated that it is the meaning of the word "is not," which is not in contact with the senses?

What is meant [by this]? That "non-existence" (*abhāva*) has as its object of cognition (*prameya*) the meaning "that which is not an object of perception and so forth does not exist. This is incorrect. The statement "it does not exist" means that "this is not cognized here. And it cannot be understood that there is an object of cognition for that which is not being cognized. Furthermore, of which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this the object of cognition?

If [you argue that it is] the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*), that is not so. For the absence of a means of valid cognition is the non-arising of a valid cognition; and for that to be itself a means of valid cognition appears almost as something supernatural. If you think: "The cognition 'it exists' or 'it does not exist' is established without dispute among all worldly people and investigators;
and it has already been explained in the Vijñānavāda that a cognition cannot be without an object, nor can its object be merely its own part," therefore—

It is precisely from the firmness of this cognition that the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is postulated; that [firmness] is the objective domain of non-existence (*abhāva*). They consider this cognition "it does not exist" to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while the non-existence of the jar and so forth is the object of knowledge. For this very reason, they divide non-existence into four types, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest. Indeed, a division of a non-entity is not possible. However, if non-existence is not accepted as a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*), [the following applies].

What, then, is the absence of curd in milk? That which they call antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). And for this reason, this absence of milk in curd is what is called destructional non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*). Furthermore, it must be stated: what is the objective support (*ālambana*) of the cognition "there is no jar here"? If it is the floor itself, that is not so, because [the cognition] would then occur even where there is a jar. If you say the objective support is the floor alone, then what is the meaning of "alone" (*kevala*)? If it is the floor itself...
That same undesirable consequence follows. Now, if it is the exclusion of other entities (*bhāvāntara-viveka*), then it is established that it is a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*);

and from that distinction, a distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) follows. For that [exclusion] cannot be experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is because direct perception is dependent upon the sense organs (*akṣa*), and since the sense organs consist of positive entities (*bhāva-rūpa*), their contact (*sannikarṣa*) can only be with a positive entity.
Not by means of non-existence. Furthermore, it is observed that even when its operation is absent, the cognition "it does not exist" arises;

for example, when someone has merely seen a house or similar object in its own form and then departs for another place, at that very moment, he is questioned regarding the absence of someone [who was previously there].

The absence of that [object] is thus determined. Therefore, a cognition of "it does not exist" which arises even in the absence of sense-object contact is not sensory (aindriyaka). Nor does it have any inferential mark (liṅga) as its producer. If it is argued that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the mark, we say no; because it is itself unapprehended. For a mark whose form is unapprehended cannot lead to the inference of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*), nor can one whose relation [to the object] is unknown do so.

Furthermore, non-apprehension in that manner does not reveal the existence [of an object] when it is itself known; for since it too is of the nature of absence, if it were to require another of its own kind, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress. Therefore, this must be accepted as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of establishing the non-confusion of entities.
And there is a well-known tradition among the Mīmāṃsakas: "Indeed, this is the sixth means of valid cognition. Hence, for the purpose of defining it...
"As for the claim that it is [known] from the text (*grantha*): that is incorrect. For by this [text], a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not be indicated.
Indeed, from the text, one concludes only the absence of a means of valid cognition, not the means of valid cognition itself.

Even when it is said "it does not exist," worldly people understand only the absence of the object of cognition (*prameya*), not some [positive] object of cognition. Therefore, first of all, there is no other means of valid cognition that accords with the text."
Nor does this accord with reason;

for it is only when a cognition is established that it is reasonable to investigate whether it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not. Furthermore, there is no such cognition as "there is nothing other than the perception of the bare ground. For that very [perception] manifests in two ways: as accompanied by something else and as unaccompanied.
Thus, when that [substratum] is perceived together with a jar or other objects, then the conventional usage "the jar exists" proceeds.
But when there is cognition of that alone, [the usage] is "it does not exist. Nor should it be said: "Even when subtle entities are present, cognition of that alone is observed;
therefore, even in those cases, it appears as 'it does not exist. For that very [substratum] appears in two ways. Indeed, the cognition of that alone is twofold.

It is perceived whether the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is visible or invisible. In that regard, when the counter-positive is visible, the cognition of that locus alone (*tanmātrabuddhi*) is itself the non-existence of the jar and so forth. Even for those who hold that non-existence (*abhāva*) is an object of cognition (*prameya*), the non-existence is ascertained as "it does not exist" precisely through the non-perception of what is perceptible. Therefore, this very cognition of the locus alone, which is established by all disputants, is designated as "it does not exist."

Furthermore, whatever cause is postulated for non-existence, let that very cause be accepted as the cause of the cognition of "that alone" (*tanmātra-buddhi*), which is established for both disputants.

Therefore, precisely where there was previously a cognition of a conjoined object, when a distinct cause intervenes, only the cognition of "that alone" arises; it is not, however, the non-existence of the jar or other such things [that arises]. (Necessarily...)
This must indeed be accepted. Otherwise, non-existence could not be apprehended, for the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) is the means of valid cognition in that case;
and it cannot be established by one who has not apprehended it. For even in the case of one who is fast asleep, there is [the absence of] a means of valid cognition... (text fragment).
[This refers to] the state [of non-perception]. Nor is there the certainty that "it does not exist. Therefore, a non-perception that has not been apprehended does not determine non-existence;

and since the apprehension of that [non-perception] would also be of the nature of non-existence, it would require another non-perception, leading thus to an infinite regress. Furthermore, if mere existence itself were to determine the non-perception, then even when the non-perception has ceased—
Otherwise, there would be no cognition that "Devadatta did not exist previously. Yet, such a thing does indeed occur.

When someone who was not seen in a certain place is later seen again, there arises a knowledge of his prior absence even though there is no [present] non-perception; that [knowledge] would not occur if there were no [prior] non-perception.

Therefore, it must be stated that this cognition arises solely from the reflection upon the prior non-perception. And in this way, it manifests that absence precisely as it is being apprehended. Furthermore, if there were an apprehension [of the non-perception itself], it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress. However, if one maintains that "non-perception" is simply the awareness of that [object] alone, nothing is faulty. For that awareness, being self-luminous and constituting the result, does not depend on another manifestation. Thus, it is the experience of that alone.

Thus, existence is self-luminous. And when it is reflected upon in the form of the non-perception of a jar or other objects, it is then designated as "non-existence. Therefore, non-existence is not a separate object of cognition (*prameya*). Nor is the cognition "it does not exist" a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because both [the subject and the object] are absent. This is merely an error of cognition consisting in the absence of cognition itself.
"We do not know what is perceived here, for it is like the illusion of perceiving darkness when light is not being seen. To this he replies: "What is it that is not known here?
According to what you have stated from the text, it is simply determined that there is an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
For some indeed maintain that non-existence (*abhāva*) itself is a means of valid cognition."

This very effort of the author of the Bhāṣya is for the purpose of refuting that [view]. How is it refuted by this? Listen. As for what some say—that the non-existence of an object not in contact [with the senses], which is beyond the scope of perception and the other means of knowledge, is itself a means of valid cognition—that is not so.

This [non-existence] is indeed an absence of means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva)—the meaning being that it is not a means of valid cognition. And the reason for its being non-valid has already been stated. This too is not tenable. If this meaning were explained in accordance with the text, then there would be a clear contradiction with the Bhāṣya in another section;

for the author of the Bhāṣya will say in the refutation of the Citrā sacrifice: "This might be so, if there were only five means of valid cognition. In that context, he clearly demonstrates that there are six means of valid cognition.

Nor is that intended as a conventional usage, for it is not tenable to claim that the number inherent in a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not differentiate its conventional application. Furthermore, in this case as well, no reason has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya regarding invalidity; nor is it tenable that the refutation of an opposing position occurs through a mere thesis (pratijñā).

Therefore, this must be explained. Here he says: "By means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇena*). This is the meaning: this is indeed the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*). As for what was said—namely, "How is that [non-existence] characterized by the absence of that [valid cognition]?"—that is true. The word "valid cognition" is not intended to refer to valid cognition in general; rather, although the word "valid cognition" expresses a universal, it is restricted to a particular instance by virtue of the context. [Thus, it refers to] the non-existence of valid cognition.

What, then, has been stated by this? It is the absence of the five previously mentioned means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). And there is one [means] which consists in the presence of the five; for all [the others] are indeed means of valid cognition regarding existence (bhāva-pramāṇa).

Therefore, the absence of a means of knowledge regarding existence is itself a means of knowledge regarding existence. And this will be explained in two ways further on: either as the non-modification of the self, or as the cognition that "it does not exist. Or [it is established] because there is the perception of the bare ground.
The cognition that "there is nothing else" is indeed [the means of knowledge]. What is its object? It is the absence of an object of cognition (*prameyābhāva*) arranged in four ways.

For if that were not present, the mutual confusion of cause and effect and so forth would certainly have been demonstrated by the author of the *Vārttika*. Furthermore, this worldly activity such as walking on foot, which is preceded by the ascertainment of the absence of thorns and the like, would also [be impossible] if non-existence were not an object of cognition.

This could not be so. If only the bare ground were perceived here and not the absence of thorns and such, then even when those [thorns] are present, it would be grasped by the cognition "it is not there. But the denial of the cognition is indeed contrary to experience;
for there is no difference in the manifestation of existence and non-existence. As for what was said—that the cognition of that alone is itself the [cognition] "the jar is not"—[that is incorrect].

"It is designated as such. In this regard, we do not know what is excluded by the word "mere" (*mātra*). If it excludes nothing, then it is meaningless. If, however, it does exclude something, then there must be an exclusion as its object;
otherwise, the conventional usage would be that it excludes only existence itself. This very [distinction] is what constitutes the cognition of a composite and the cognition of that "mere" [element].

This is the distinction: that [cognition] has a distinct object (*viṣaya*), and the exclusion of other objects is non-existence (*abhāva*). If it is argued that the object is cognition itself and nothing other than that, then even when there is the perception of a conjunction [of things], that [non-existence] would manifest as "it exists" and "it does not exist.
Furthermore, whatever is negated here is said to be "not there"; however, in the case of "the jar does not exist here," it is not the cognition itself that is being negated.

For if "it does not exist" were within the domain of cognition, there would be an absence of cognition itself. Now, if it is argued that the meaning of "the jar does not exist" is simply that "only the ground is perceived," ordinary people do not understand it in this way.
Furthermore, if this were so, there would be no desire to investigate whether a subtle entity exists or does not exist.
If there is no such thing as non-existence at all, then when an object is perceived, what is this further doubt regarding subtle things such as hairs or insects?
For the non-existence of other entities consists precisely in the perception of that [object] alone.

And that [absence] is indeed already known and not to be doubted, because consciousness is self-luminous; what else remains to be sought? If it is argued that absence is the cognition of that alone when the counter-positive is visible, and not when it is invisible—then what is the point of its being invisible?

When non-existence is not distinct from the absence of cognition. If non-existence were a separate ontological category (*tattvāntara*), then the non-perception of the perceptible would be required for its ascertainment. For the contact of the self, the sense-faculties, the mind, and the object is the cause of the production of cognition;

thus, when that [contact] is present—even though the sense-faculties and so forth are unimpaired, and even though the object sought has been diligently searched for—it is not perceived, then it is postulated that the non-perception is due to the non-existence of that [object]. Thus, in this way...

A subtle investigation is appropriate for the sake of establishing perceptibility. If [the object] were perceived as a mere substrate (tanmātra), then the qualification "perceptible" would become superfluous regarding its own nature. Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the cause of the non-existence [of an object] should be attributed to the cognition of that mere substrate alone on account of parsimony of conceptualization—that too...

This is incorrect. For it is not possible to disregard what has been established by valid cognition (pramāṇa) simply because it results in a parsimony of conceptual construction (kalpanālāghava). Nor is it logical to claim that whatever is the cause of non-existence (abhāva) is the cognition of "that alone" (tanmātradhī). For the striking of a hammer and so forth is indeed the cause of non-existence, yet such a cause does not produce the cognition of "that alone. Rather, the manifestation of the nature of objects such as the ground is caused by the sense faculties and other such factors.

It does not depend on the removal or striking away of a jar or the like. As for the claim that non-perception, when unascertained, does not determine absence—lest it follow [absurdly] even in deep sleep—that is incorrect. For an absence, being without a locus, does not manifest when its substratum is not apprehended; indeed, the absence of something appears in relation to something else, not independently. Therefore, he says: "It does not arise with respect to the form of a real entity."

Thus, nothing at all is manifested to one who is in deep sleep. And where would non-existence be delimited? Furthermore, it is the non-arising of a competent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines non-existence;
however, for one in deep sleep, there is no object suitable for a means of valid cognition.
Since that which does not manifest is not apprehended, how can a certainty regarding its non-existence arise?

Therefore, "non-perception" is not something unapprehended; thus, for one in deep sleep, the absence [of objects] does not manifest, but rather, this is not a case of the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyādarśana*). Furthermore, even when non-perception has ceased, there is the non-existence of what preceded it.

"It is now designated [as absent] even for that which is currently being perceived. That is not correct. For in that case, when many things capable of being perceived in the same way are being remembered, if one among them is not remembered, its absence is cognized through the cessation of memory—which is, in effect, the cessation of perception—just as the existence of other entities is cognized by means of memory itself.

The non-existence at that time and the cessation of memory certainly exist at that time; yet they are not themselves apprehended. Rather, it is the very absence of the object that makes known its prior existence; thus, there is no infinite regress. Therefore, it is correct to hold that the cognition "it is not" is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is non-existence, which is divided into categories such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth. This is the meaning: [The text continues: ...Therefore, this is the point: when one says, "This jar does not exist on this spot," the cognition "it is not" is the means of valid knowledge, and the object of knowledge is the non-existence [of the jar]. And this non-existence is of four kinds: prior non-existence, non-existence through destruction, absolute non-existence, and mutual non-existence. Among these, prior non-existence is the state of a thing before its production; for example, the non-existence of a jar prior to its being made from clay. Non-existence through destruction is the state of a thing after its destruction; for example, the non-existence of a jar after it has been smashed by a hammer. Absolute non-existence is the non-existence of one thing in another where it can never occur; for example, the non-existence of a hare's horn in a hare. Mutual non-existence is the difference between two things; for example, the non-existence of a horse in a cow, or the non-existence of a cow in a horse. Thus, the non-existence of the jar on the spot is a case of prior non-existence. And this non-existence is established by the cognition "it is not. Since this cognition is produced by the sense organ in conjunction with the spot, it is a perception. Therefore, the non-existence of the jar is perceived by the sense organ. Thus, the non-existence of the jar is indeed an object of perception. Consequently, the claim that non-existence is not an object of perception is refuted. In a case where the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) do not arise to cognize the existence of an object such as a cloth according to their respective capacities, it is possible for non-existence (*abhāva*) to function as a means of valid cognition in that regard;
by this, it is shown that the word "means of valid cognition" is used here in reference to the pentad of means of valid cognition. Regarding the nature of the object:

The statement "it is not born" shows that the mere cognition of the absence of independent existence is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, because he provides the definition of worldly means of knowledge, it follows that those means of knowledge do not arise—i.e., their non-arising constitutes the valid means of knowledge known as non-existence (*abhāva*)—only in cases where the capacity for such means is possible.
For it is precisely by such a means that worldly people understand that "it does not exist. This is also the meaning of the *Bhāṣya*: "Non-existence, too..."

It need not be examined, because it is non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*). For when there is an absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) regarding an object not in contact with the senses—an object termed "non-existence" (*abhāva*)—the cognition that arises when it is manifested in the form "it does not exist" is the valid cognition of non-existence (*abhāvapramā*). And for such a [cognition], deviation is impossible. Furthermore, even that which is obstructed produces a cognition by virtue of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*).
It is to be connected [with what precedes]. According to the maxim: "That which has a connection with something else is to be connected with it, even if it is distant. // 1 //

It has been stated that where there is a non-arising of the appropriate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the sake of cognizing the actual existence of an object, there "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition.
But what, then, is cognized by this [means] therein? Non-existence is, first of all, understood by its own respective means of valid cognition.
Therefore, he says: "The non-confusion of entities. (1)

He elucidates precisely the non-confusion of entities with the two and a half verses beginning with "curd in milk. This fourfold distinction between cause and effect and so forth that has been shown is designated as the "non-confusion of entities" (*vastv-asaṅkara*). That [non-confusion] is cognized through non-existence (*abhāva*), in the form of a hare's horn and the like. When the parts on the head of a hare are considered in that form, they are non-existence.
But in their own nature, they are indeed existent entities. // 2–4 //
But if non-existence (*abhāva*) were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), everything would be confused with everything else; thus he says in the two verses beginning with "In milk...

The word "thus" means that just as curd is in milk, so too milk would be in curd. From the statement "a horn on a rabbit" onwards, there follows the demonstration of a logical fault (*doṣaprasañjana*) regarding the failure to establish absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*). For if one does not rely upon the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence, there can be no absolute non-existence of horns and the like in rabbits and such beings.

[The argument] is established. Furthermore, the proponents of the doctrine that consciousness belongs to the primary elements (*bhūta-caitanya-vādin*) cannot be refuted. Moreover, the absolute absence of smell and the other qualities in the primary elements, such as air (*vāyu*), would not be established; for it is a settled principle that each of the four primary elements lacks one quality respectively, in ascending order. (5–6)

He states the fault in universal confusion with the words "na ca" (and not). This worldly transaction of ordinary people which is observed through the distinction of cause and so forth would not exist if there were universal confusion;
for instance, one who is commanded, "Bring the milk," brings only the milk and not the curd.
In the bringing of curd, there is no milk;
this would not be established if there were no mutual distinction between cause and effect and so forth. // 7 //
Now, is it not the case that so-called "non-existence" (abhāva) is not perceived as a distinct reality?
For we understand the bare ground through its own means of valid cognition,
whereas we do not perceive a jar when no such means of valid cognition exists.

But there is no other thing called "the absence of a jar" that exists within cognition. Even the statement "the jar does not exist" means that the jar is not cognized, not that the absence of the jar is cognized. Therefore, absence is characterized solely by the lack of all descriptive attributes; it is not some distinct reality. Hence he says: "And not... As for the claim that it is not apprehended by the means of knowledge that apprehend positive entities—that is true.

For this very reason, non-existence (*abhāva*) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*). Even the statement "the jar does not exist" does not mean that the jar is not cognized; for even if a jar exists, one may say that it is not cognized. Precisely for this reason, when asked "Does the jar exist or not?", one who has ascertained its absence does not designate it as "it does not exist," but rather indicates mere non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Therefore, the cognition "the jar does not exist" is indeed the apprehension of non-existence itself. And this [non-existence] is fourfold:

That distinction which has been described is not established in the case of non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all description. And there is a formal argument: "Non-existence is a real entity (vastu), because it possesses fourfold distinctions, like substance and the other categories. Furthermore, as for what they say—that there is no such reality as non-existence—this is incorrect.
For blue and other such things are mutually distinguished by their own nature, which is restricted to each respective object;
however, there is no such differentiator for non-existence (abhāva) from existence (bhāva).

Therefore, since we do not perceive anything excluded [from existence], how can we establish it as a separate reality? Its conventional usage, consisting of the employment of conceptual terms such as "it does not exist," is in some way based solely upon existence.

But it is not the case that there is a non-existence distinct from the non-existence that is restricted to a single form and unassociated with anything else. That [position] has already been refuted by the very refutation of the "partialist" (ekadeśin).

Furthermore, it must be explained how a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding "it does not exist," which lacks an objective referent, can be experienced; for the object of a conceptual construction is a form touched by words.

And that [conceptualization] does not exist here [in self-awareness]. Nor is the self capable of being associated with verbal expression through conceptualization, because it is unique (asādhāraṇa). Precisely for this reason, since conceptualization is non-conceptual with respect to the self, it declares self-awareness to be perception. As it has been said: "This [self-awareness] does not associate the self with verbal expression, because such a mode of operation is contradictory with respect to the self. If this is your view:
— "Conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding non-existence (*abhāva*), like those regarding universals (*jāti*) and so forth, have only superimposed objects as their domain;

therefore, conceptual construction regarding non-existence is not thereby vitiated. This is not correct. For whatever kind of thing is superimposed, it is distinct in each individual conceptualization;

how then could it be the objective support (*ālambana*) for a single word? If you argue that there is a determination of unity because one does not determine the differences between the imagined forms (*kalpitākāra*), then of what [is that unity determined]?

For those who maintain the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*), there is no single transmigrating agent who, by determining the unity superimposed upon the preceding and succeeding [moments], would employ a single word. Since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) are momentary, restricted to their own respective objects, and do not enter into the domain of one another, how could they effect a reconnection (*pratisandadhi*)? This being the case...

And the claim that [the object] is false because its domain is superimposed upon the opposite is indeed untrue. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that even what is called non-existence (abhāva) exists as a certain established form, like existence (bhāva), conjoined with the word "not" (na). For this very reason, when the question "What, then, is reality? is asked, [the answer is]: "But the being of the existent... (*satas tu sadbhāvo*).

The knowers of reality have relied upon reality in only two ways: as being or as non-being. Furthermore, if non-being does not exist, for what reason would there be the non-perception of a struck jar?
If it is argued that it is "because it has perished," then what is this "perishing"? If it is nothing at all, [then...]

As before, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being perceived. For we do not see any reason now why a jar—which has not lost its prior nature of causal efficiency—should not be perceived, provided that "destruction" is not accepted as some distinct reality (*tattvāntara*).

Thus, it is established that destruction is a distinct reality. And this was stated in order to refute the claim that non-existence is indefinable; it does not mean, however, that non-existence is a real entity (*vastu*).

Because it contradicts common worldly understanding. For just as it is contrary to worldly understanding to say "the moon is not the moon," so too is it to say that "non-existence is a real entity. For being (*sattā*) is what constitutes being a real entity (*vastutva*), and this [being] does not inhere in non-existence.

Because it would follow that there is no distinction between the existent and the non-existent; therefore, it is a non-entity (*avastu*). The claim that it is an entity (*vastutva*) is based on its performing a function (*kāryakaraṇa*), not in a primary sense. For even a non-entity is indeed capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), since we observe it produces cognition. Furthermore, in the case of failing to perform what is prescribed, it is precisely the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) that serves as the cause of demerit by functioning as a qualifier of another action. In the same way, the proof of its status as an entity in subsequent cases should be understood.

Thus [it is said]. For this reason as well, he states that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*), saying "of effects and so forth. The established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that the real entity itself consists of both existence and non-existence. In that case, how can there be a lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) for non-existence, which is itself of the nature of a real entity?
Is it now the case that there is simply no distinction between existence and non-existence?

We do not say "no," for there is indeed some slight distinction between these two by way of their being attribute and substrate, just as there is between color and other such qualities. But what is the relationship between these two—
is it conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)?

It cannot be conjunction (*saṃyoga*), because that is a property of substances. Nor can it be inherence (*samavāya*), because that would entail the consequence of [the object] being both existent and non-existent. For if there were inherence of non-existence, the thing could not be existent at all. It is not the case that its non-existence results from inhering in non-existence.

For a jar does not become non-existent through its inherence in a negation, because inherence is impossible in that which is non-existent. Rather, the non-existence of the jar arises solely from the blow [that destroys it]. As for that other entity which, being unstruck and not removed, is perceived in the form of a negation—how could that be non-existent? Therefore, everything, whether arising from its own cause or being eternal, possesses an unmixed nature.
Thus it is established that its nature is a property of an entity (*bhāvadharma*), just like birth and so forth; and from that, its status as a real thing (*vastutva*) follows. // 8 //

For this reason as well, he states that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a real entity (*vastu*), using the passage from "or rather" (*yad vā*) up to "real entity" (*vastu*). Non-existence, when apprehended in its universal aspect—as *prāgabhāva* and so forth—and in its aspect of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), possesses the nature of both universal and particular.

Consequently, for the purpose of an application regarding a real entity, the argument is: "Non-existence is a real entity, because it consists of universal and particular, like a cow and so forth. To prove that very same point, he states another reason: "because it is an object of valid cognition" (*prameyatvāt*). // 9 //
Is this not an unestablished reason?

For the relationship of universal and particular is indeed figurative in the case of non-existence. A universal form is observed to be denoted by a single word, such as "cow" and the like, while a particular form is denoted by various words, such as "Śābaleya" and the like. Therefore, even in this case, the relationship of universal and particular is merely figurative.

[This applies] to one who possesses discriminative knowledge. However, in the absence of such discrimination, this is merely an error based on the word "one"—namely, that non-existence has the nature of both a universal and a particular.

Therefore, he says: "And not... The sense is that an error or a metaphorical usage is postulated only when there is a subverting factor (bādhaka), and since that is not the case here, [non-existence is not so]. // 10 //

Thus, first, that which was stated in the Bhāṣya—that the meaning of "it does not exist" refers to an object that is not in contact [with the senses]—has been explained. Now, he explains the term "absence of means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇābhāva*): "the non-arising of perception and so forth. If it is asked what this non-arising itself is, he says: "it belongs to the self" (*sātmanaḥ*). For the self has a transformation consisting of cognition; thus, when the self [is directed toward] a surface or the like...

That non-arising of perception and other means of knowledge—which does not transform into the nature of a cognition such as "a jar"—is its abiding in its own form; this is designated as the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*).

And when that [absence] is a valid means of knowledge, the resulting fruit is the cognition "it does not exist. Alternatively, the cognition of an absence itself is called the non-arising of perception and so forth;
therefore, that [cognition of absence] alone is the means of knowledge.
The discernment is that the fruit is the cognition of [the object] as it truly is, beginning with its abandonment. // 11 //
Now, if an object consists of two natures, then it must appear as such all at once; what need is there for another means of valid cognition? To this he says: "By its own nature," etc.
By its own nature, that object—such as a cow—is existent, while by the nature of a horse and so forth, it is non-existent. Thus, within this very dual-natured thing, only a certain [aspect]...
Sometimes it is perceived, but there is no rule that it must be grasped as having a universal nature. // 12 //

But what is the reason that, although [an object] consists of two natures, only one form is perceived and not the other? To this he says: "Of whichever, wherever. For that which is manifest (*udbhūta*) is perceived, not that which is unmanifest (*anudbhūta*); as, for example, the color of fire at night is not perceived, while its touch is. Or rather, it is generally that which one desires to perceive. Therefore, of the existent and the non-existent, by whichever alone it becomes manifest, by that alone do cognition (*buddhi*) and designation (*vyapadeśa*) occur. What is this [statement]: "That which is cognized is experienced"?
For experience itself is not experienced;

rather, that [experience] is consciousness (*cetanā*), while the object is what is experienced. True. Experience too is experienced precisely because it would otherwise be impossible for the object to be attained. Thus, by this method, he demonstrates that it is indeed the manifestation of the object [that occurs], so there is no fault.
Thus [ends the thirteenth].
When one [of two things] that has become manifest is apprehended with the desire to grasp it, the other remains dissolved, existing in a state of conformity to it.
Just as when either of the two—general or particular—is apprehended, the other follows suit, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). We have stated this by way of a concessive argument (*anvāruhyavacana*).
However, in the cognition of both existence and non-existence, there is indeed the following of one or the other; thus he says: "of both" (*ubhayoḥ*). // 14 //

He demonstrates precisely this following of both [existence and non-existence] by means of the two phrases beginning with "this very [thing]. "This very" means unmixed with any other entity; for indeed, as long as the absence of other entities has not been established, a mixed nature cannot be determined.

Furthermore, there is no cognition whatsoever that consists of the negation "it does not exist" which is devoid of the support provided by the existence of the object to be negated and the locus of that negation.

It arises. By the word "something," he shows that there is indeed a cognition of an entity that is devoid of the accompaniment of non-existence, but this is not the case for non-existence itself. // 15–16 //

It has already been shown that an object consists of both existence and non-existence, and that something is experienced at some time or another. Now, he demonstrates the division of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for these two aspects: "by perception and so forth.
But how is this understood?
For when one whose eyes are wide open suddenly [perceives], "there is no jar here," [he understands it].
A cognition of the ground qualified by the absence [of a jar], such as "the ground is without a jar," is observed to arise;

this would not be possible if that absence were not perceptible. For when a qualifier is itself imperceptible, the qualified object cannot be perceptible, just as a person with a staff (*daṇḍin*) is not perceived when the staff is not perceived. Nor can it be said that there is no such qualified cognition at all.

Because there is no perception of the absence of a substratum. Furthermore, the self is the absence of an entity; how could that be experienced independently? For the properties of entities, such as form and so forth, are not apprehended as being independent. But the doctrine of the independence of non-existence is indeed [an assertion of] independence itself, for it demonstrates that the object consists of both the existent and the non-existent. And by stating "the aspect of existence" and "the aspect of non-existence," he clearly shows that the apprehension is qualified by that non-existence. Moreover, what is the proof for its independence?

For this [non-existence] is never cognized in that manner. Now, is it the case that non-existence is not cognized at all, or is it cognized independently? It cannot be the first alternative, because there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for its comprehension, which would lead to the undesirable consequence of its being eternally uncognized. Nor is there a cognition of independent non-existence when there is merely the negation of conjunction.

For non-existence (*abhāva*) consists precisely in the negation of the conjunction with a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), and since it is dependent upon its locus (*ādhāra-tantra*), it falls within the scope of sensory cognition when there is contact with the sense organ through the proximity characterized as being a qualifier of that which is conjoined (*saṃyukta-viśeṣaṇatva*). What kind of qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭa-jñāna*) is this? Is its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the non-existence itself, or the sense organ?

If it were non-existence (*abhāva*), then it would also have existence (*bhāva*) as its object; and this is not accepted. Therefore, when something is being perceived, that which is not perceived at that very time does not exist; thus, [non-existence] would be the manifester of both the existent and the non-existent. Consequently, we do not see any distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To this he says: "Not yet" (*na tāvat*). The word "yet" (*tāvat*) refers to the logical mark (*liṅga*). And that [mark] will be refuted later on.
Thus [it is said]. Here he states the reason: "Because [the capacity] pertains to positive entities" (*bhāvāṃśa*). For capacity is to be understood through the observation of its effect;

and that [capacity] of the sense organs is perceived only in the apprehension of positive entities, not in the case of non-existence (*abhāva*) either. However, we shall explain later that even without that [capacity], there is an apprehension of it. In this context, however, the intended meaning is that the relation between the sense organ and the object is contact (*prāpti*) accompanied by capacity.

As for the claim that two things associated with a single cognition possess a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is not so; for even a single cognition is seen to have multiple causes. We shall explain that this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) arises from a combination of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), the sense faculty, and the similarity [of the objects]. Furthermore, the distinction between what is being perceived and what is being remembered—even when both appear in a single cognition—has already been stated: "For those objects are indeed distinct. This is because [the object] presented by memory...
A person, such as "Dittha," who is not distinguished [by a qualifier], is not perceived. And a name is not perceived because it is something being remembered;

for when a qualifier is not grasped, that which is qualified by it is not understood, nor is it perceived. Thus, here too, when a real entity is being apprehended as qualified by an absence brought about by the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—

Nothing is untenable here. Even in the case of the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*), the referent of the cognition is indeed qualified by the attribute presented by the word "staff," but the staff itself is not [the primary object]. As for perception, let it indeed operate in both cases by virtue of its capacity;
however, the sense organs do not possess such capacity in both cases. In the cognition of absence, there is no dependence on that [capacity].
Because it will be explained [later]. Now, is there also in inference a specific cognition produced by the combination of perception and inference?

No; because inference arises dependent upon positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and it is precisely through a specific [concomitance] that the concomitance is followed. For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) "that which possesses smoke possesses fire" is understood. And it has been said:
"It is not so, for in this case there is no assumption of an infinite capacity in the inferential mark (*liṅga*).

Here too, in the cognition of a particularity such as "this possesses fire," there is indeed a dependence upon perception. This very fact—that it qualifies a substratum obtained through another means of knowledge—is the manner in which non-existence (*abhāva*) is cognized; thus, nothing is untenable. And as for what was stated, that there is sensory contact with non-existence by way of being a qualifier of that which is conjoined [with the sense organ], [that is also correct].

That is incorrect. For it is impossible for that which is unrelated to function as a qualifier, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasakti*). Otherwise, since contact is established simply by one who desires to know the qualifier, the recourse to the notion of "the qualifier conjoined with what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇa*) is entirely useless; therefore, enough of this. // 18 //
Not understanding the intended meaning, he objects with the words "But surely... For the contact between an object and a sense faculty is merely reaching [it].

And since non-existence is not distinct from existence, it follows that non-existence, like existence, has reaching by the sense faculty. To this, the reply should be given precisely by disclosing [the nature of] capacity (*yogyatā*).

Setting aside that [position] for now, he says "for not" with the intention of first refuting this very claim that there is absolute non-difference between existence and non-existence.
