For if there were absolute non-difference between existence and non-existence, then upon the contact of the sense-faculty with an existent thing, there would also be [contact] with its non-different non-existence.
But this is not the case, because even for non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no absolute lack of differentiation, just as there is none for form (*rūpa*) and so forth. // 19 //

He demonstrates that non-existence is indeed equal to form and so forth by saying "of two properties. The meaning is that even though the substratum of the two properties—whose natures are existence and non-existence—remains non-different, a difference between them is also accepted. He states the reason for this difference with the words "arising" (*udbhava*).
Even for existence and non-existence, [there is] arising...

The distinction between the perception and non-perception of [an object] when it is manifest (*udbhūta*) or suppressed (*abhibhūta*) is observed. This would not be possible if oneness were postulated; for a single reality cannot be perceived as both manifest and suppressed.

He states, "This very [is the cause]," indicating that this is the cause for the discrimination between these two. Furthermore, the independence of the cognition of absence from the sense organs will be explained later. // 21 //

And some maintain that this distinction among form and the other [sensory objects] is based on the difference in their perceivers. One can understand that this [same principle] applies to these two as well; thus he says: "of form and so forth. For some speak in this way: "Just as a single face appears as if divided due to the difference in limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as emeralds or rubies,"

Just as a single person is perceived as if divided into various roles such as son and so forth due to differences in perspective, and just as a single reality appears as if divided due to the difference of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the ear and other senses, so too here there will be a distinction between existence and non-existence that is merely conditional. [Objection: But if the distinction is merely conditional in this way, does it not follow that their essential unity is real? [Reply: Let it be so in this view.
Nevertheless, the establishment of form and so forth is indeed accomplished. // 22 //
And this has been stated by us as a statement made on the basis of a concession (*anvāruhya-vacana*);
for the distinction among form and the other [sensory objects] is not based on a difference in their perceivers, but rather is based solely on a difference in cognitions (*buddhi*).

For it is logical that a face, perceived as having a single form through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), appears differentiated due to the difference in its limiting conditions (*upādhi*). However, there is no evidence whatsoever for the oneness of color and the rest, since they are eternally distinct. And this difference in cognition is equally the cause of differentiation for both existence and non-existence; with this intention, he says: "merely by cognition. But what is this which consists of existence and non-existence, of which existence and non-existence are the two properties?

A single [entity] distinct from the collection of form and so forth is not perceived, because it cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of occurrence (*vṛtti*) and so on. Therefore, the substratum (*dharmin*) is the collection of form and so forth which are non-different in terms of location and other such factors, and it is not a separate reality; hence he says, "And not... The intended meaning is that here there is no subverting cognition, as there is in the case of a forest.

And although this was already stated in the proof of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), it is stated here for the purpose of establishing the locus of non-existence (*abhāva*); thus, there is no tautology. // 23 //

Thus, first, difference and non-difference have been shown through the existence of non-existence. He confirms those very points by means of the example of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, stating: "possessing existent qualities and substance. For it cannot be denied that form and the rest are different even with respect to their own nature, insofar as they are not non-different from the nature of the existent (*sat*) and so forth.

Thus, by the phrase "or [there is] difference," the non-difference [of things] in their nature as existence (*sat*) and so forth is not being rejected. In this way, even non-existence (*abhāva*), although distinct from existence because it is a property (*dharma*) of it, is held to be non-distinct with respect to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Regarding the phrase "in the form of substance" (*dravyarūpeṇa*):
color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory qualities] are non-distinct from substance, and that [substance] is non-distinct; thus, the meaning is that they are non-distinct in that form. //24//

If one does not rely on difference—just as with form and so forth—with respect to its own nature, then the cognition of existence and non-existence would not possess the character of being existent or non-existent in either case; thus he says: "If... (verse 25).

However, there is this distinction in cognition caused by the connection or non-connection with the sense organ; thus he says: "The connection with the existent. By this, that which they say—"we do not perceive the nature of non-existence as a differentiator from existence"—is refuted. This is because of the distinction between the forms of the existent and the non-existent: that which the ground is joined with by the sense organ is cognized as "existent."
That which is not perceived, such as a jar and so forth, is cognized as being non-existent. // 26 //
But surely, it is immediately after the operation of the sense organ that the cognition "the jar is not here" arises;

so why this distinction that the cognition of absence is not produced by the sense organ? For we do not observe the cognition of absence arising when the operation of that [organ] is absent, just as we do not observe the cognition of presence [arising then]. Even though absence is distinct from presence, [it is still perceived through the senses].

Nevertheless, its contact with the sense organ does indeed exist, either through inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*)—as is the case with color and so forth—or by way of being a qualifier of that [substratum]. Therefore, the cognition of it would be sensory; to this he says: "having apprehended" (*gṛhītvā*). The intention is this:

since absence cannot be apprehended if its substrata are manifold, there is a dependence on the sense organ here solely for the purpose of apprehending the substratum, not for the apprehension of the absence itself.

Just as the non-existence [of an object] cannot be apprehended when its counter-positive is not remembered—such that for the sake of remembering it, the awakening of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior cognition is also required—so too is the sense faculty required for the apprehension of the locus. Furthermore, mere contact is not the cause for the production of sensory cognition; rather, it is contact accompanied by capacity (*yogyatā*), as described in the section on perception. And the sense faculties do not possess the capacity to generate the cognition of non-existence.

It will be stated later that [the cognition] occurs even when those [senses] are absent. What is the meaning of "mental" (*mānasa*)? Does it mean that it is produced by the mind (*manas*), just like the cognition of pleasure and so forth? If this were the case, it would still be nothing other than perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, the mind does not possess independence with respect to external objects as it does with respect to internal ones. True. However, what is described here is the operation of the mind common to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), arising from the mere contact between the self and the mind.

Thus, it has been stated that the cognition of absence is produced by the non-existence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva) independently of the external senses. Furthermore, the expression "having perceived and having remembered" indicates a single agent for the two actions because of the non-difference between the property (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin). // 27 //

But how is it understood that the apprehension of existence depends upon the sense organs, whereas the apprehension of non-existence does not? For the presence [of cognition] when that [object] is present is common to both. To this he says: "By its own nature" (*svarūpa*). For one who, having ascertained the very nature of the house, has gone elsewhere and is asked, "Is Caitra there or not?"—

Then, when questioned about it, he realizes at that very moment its non-existence. For if the cognition of absence were dependent upon the sense faculties, it would not arise in the absence of their operation. Nor should it be argued that this is merely the recollection of a previously apprehended absence;
for an absence is not perceived when there is no recollection of the counter-positive (pratiyogin), nor is there recollection of the counter-positive at the time of perceiving the locus (āśraya).

It is so. For when many [people] are questioned, their non-existence [at that time] is stated; yet it cannot be assumed that there was a recollection of all of them at that moment. If, however, it is argued that the absence was understood in a general sense, and is now being recollected in a specific sense—
That is incorrect. For there is no such thing as a universal (sāmānya) called "non-existence" (*abhāvatva*);

rather, it is only the absence of specific particulars (*viśeṣa*) that are present in memory which is determined as non-existence. Nor is it logical to say that what was apprehended as a universal is remembered as a particular; for that memory arises from the seed of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā-bīja*) deposited by a prior experience.

It is not capable of apprehending even a slight degree of non-distinction. Therefore, at that very moment, preceded by the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the cognition of absence arises independently of the sense organs; this is indeed charming. This is what is meant by the statement, "it is apprehended at that very time.
And this has already been stated to mean that, through the cessation of the memory which is the fruit of perception, there is effectively a cessation of the operation of perception. // 28 //

{3,205} Thus far, the view that the cognition of non-existence is produced by the senses has been refuted. Now, he refutes its being inferential (laiṅgikatva) with the words "na cāpy atra" ("nor even here"). Here, an objection is raised: "bhāvāṃśe" ("in the positive aspect").
He replies with the section ending in "tadānīm iti matiḥ" ("at that time... thus the cognition"). There are two things here: the object to be negated and the locus of the negation.
Of these, the object to be negated cannot be the logical mark (liṅga).
For a logical mark (*liṅga*) must indeed be cognized. And at that time, the jar is not perceived;

for while that [the jar] is being perceived, its absence cannot be apprehended. Thus, here there is a contradiction between the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*). When the entity exists, its absence cannot be asserted as a thesis; yet if the thesis is maintained, it cannot belong to that which is non-existent and unperceived.
This is the nature of the mark (*liṅga*). Therefore, when non-existence (*abhāva*) is intended to be apprehended, the absence of that which is to be negated is not itself the mark. // 29–30 //

"Let it be then that the existence of the locus of the negation is the probans. To this he says: "And this is not [the case]. By "this," he points to the proximate entity presented by the other [party]. Just as it was stated that when the object is made the subject (*pakṣa*), the word is not a reason because it does not possess the property of that [subject], so too this existence of the ground (*bhūtala*) does not possess the property of the absence of a jar and so forth. Furthermore, inferential cognition acquires its very nature through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Furthermore, the connection of the entity on the ground with all non-entities is not known. How then could they be understood from that? To this he says: "together" (saha). // 31 //
Let it be granted for now that there is a connection with non-existence in some case, such as on a floor;
however, even regarding an entity like a jar whose existence has been known at some time, its non-existence is also understood in that place. Thus he says: "in some case" (kvacit). // 32 //
It is not only the case that when something has been observed here at some time, its absence there is understood;
rather, even for that whose absence there has never been previously observed, its absence there is understood. Thus he says: "Where... (verse 33).

But if it is claimed that the inference of one absence from a given entity is based on a relationship apprehended through some single absence, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasakti*); thus he says: "of something" (*kasyacid*). // 34 //

And he shows by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) that this is not the case, with the words: "Even when the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) has been apprehended, there is no cognition of the non-existence of another thing for everyone," up to the end [of the verse]. Furthermore, this positive entity (*bhāva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is related even to other absences (*abhāvāntara*).

Therefore, since it is inconclusive, it lacks the status of a logical mark (*aliṅgatva*) to indicate the absence of a jar or the like; thus he says: "Thus, due to deviation (*vyabhicāra*), it is not a logical mark. (35)

Furthermore, the apprehension of a relation depends upon the apprehension of the relata. Therefore, it must be stated what the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) is for the apprehension of the relatum called "absence" (abhāva). He says: "The relation... First of all, an inferential mark (liṅga) whose relation [to the probandum] is unknown cannot be a means of knowledge for its ascertainment; for if it were so, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya). With this intention, he says: "At that time... Therefore, he says: "In that case," implying that another means of knowledge must necessarily be sought for its apprehension. // 37 //

Now, he states the rebuttal of the Buddhist who maintains that non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is a logical mark (*liṅga*): "of perception and so forth. For logicians (*hetuvid*) divide reasons (*hetu*) into two types: the effect (*kārya*) and the essential nature (*svabhāva*).
And non-apprehension is simply the apprehension of one of two things that are associated within a single cognition.

And since its own nature and the nature of the object of cognition both manifest, it has the nature of both cognition and the cognized. For this [non-apprehension] does not deviate from the existence of the cognized object in the same way that it does not deviate from its own nature. Furthermore, its "connection" (pratibandha) with its own probandum—namely, the conventional usage consisting of the conceptual thought and word "it does not exist," or the suitability for such usage—is indeed identity (*tādātmya*). For this [non-apprehension] does not deviate from the conventional usage "it does not exist."

Just as [one infers] "being a tree" from [the presence of] a *śiṃśapā* tree. Thus, non-apprehension whose necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is known causes one who is deluded—who even when perceiving a vacant place still entertains the possibility of a jar—to infer either the conventional usage "it is not there" or its fitness for such usage. And so is the formal application of the non-apprehension of the absence of a jar and the like: that which is perceptible, being present, is not apprehended in a certain place; therefore, it is not there.

"It does not exist; nor is a visible jar perceived in the place where it would be perceived. He refutes this as well: "There is no connection of that [non-existence] with a qualifier. For the non-existence of a jar—which is intended to be inferred by means of non-perception, whether as the linguistic convention "it does not exist" or as its fitness for such a convention—is not understood to have a connection with even a single qualifier through non-perception.

How, then, can there be an inference of a specific [absence] from that? For that is the perception of the bare ground; and since we observe linguistic conventions such as "there is no" regarding various and manifold objects like jars and cloths, how could one specifically employ the convention "the jar is not"? If it is argued that this is the non-perception of the jar, and therefore it establishes the absence of the jar or the linguistic convention thereof—what is its connection with the jar? For that is indeed the perception of the location.
Only to that extent does it possess the nature of the non-apprehension of a jar. And since that [nature] is indistinguishable for everyone, why is it designated by one person alone?
This is so unless there is something called the "absence of a jar. Furthermore, why does the linguistic usage "the jar does not exist" not occur even when a jar is present?
If you say it is because of its opposition to the linguistic usage of existence (*sadvayavahāra*), then how can there be the linguistic usage of existence regarding the non-apprehension of a jar?

For even at that time, there is indeed the perception of the location. If it is argued that the perception of the isolated [location] is the non-perception of the jar, and that this does not occur when the jar is present, then what is the meaning of "isolated"? Is it not simply non-existence? If that is so, then the mention of "isolated" is redundant.

Therefore, this distinction—that the conventional usage "it does not exist" applies when a jar is absent, but not when it is present—is likewise difficult to establish. Furthermore, we do not understand by what specific distinction the inference of the conventional usage "it does not exist," which transcends the non-existence of the jar itself, is established; for that [usage] too would be something distinct from the entity [of non-existence].

Nothing [distinct] is perceived. Since fitness (*yogyatā*) is not something over and above that [cognition], when that [cognition] is cognized, it is cognized as such; thus we see nothing that remains to be inferred. However, the author of the *Vārttika*, having set this aside for now, stated another refutation. // 38 //

However, a connection is indeed established through non-apprehension by way of the generality of absence (*abhāva-sāmānya*); yet, no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises regarding the specific instances of that absence. Thus he says: "by way of the generality" (*sāmānyena*). But particulars cannot be made known by non-apprehension because they are inconclusive; thus he says: "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*). // 39 //
Moreover, a mark (*liṅga*) whose form is not cognized cannot serve as a mark in inference.
Therefore, this non-occurrence of perception and the other means of knowledge, being itself an absence (*abhāva*), must be cognized by another mark. For they say:

"Whatever negation there may be, it all arises solely from non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). And in this way, by following a series of similar successive marks in each respective case, there would be the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Thus he says with the two [verses] beginning "na ca" (and not). This was stated as a consequence—that non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension—but the view that non-apprehension is a distinct category of object different from other things has been refuted. // 40–41 //
In this way, even that absence which takes the form of a logical mark (liṅgin) must necessarily be understood first for the purpose of grasping the relationship [between the mark and the probandum].

Even when that [absence] is understood, since another logical mark of that same nature would have to be admitted, there is indeed an infinite regress. Therefore, because in some cases inference is necessarily absent, one must admit another means of valid cognition; thus he says: "The logical mark... (verse 42).
If, however, it is argued that the very cognition "it does not exist" is the inferential mark (*liṅga*), that is not so. For that [cognition] is the result;
how could the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge be its mark?
Indeed, a mark is accepted precisely for the sake of establishing that [object].

But once the cognition has been established, what is the use of an inferential mark (*liṅga*)? He says this: "No. If that [cognition] is the result, then what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

To this he says: "Of that very [same thing]. That of which it is the result is itself the means of valid cognition, because perception and the other [means of knowledge] do not arise [separately], due to the immediate succession of the result. // 43 //

Furthermore, even according to the treatises on the definition of inference established in the Buddhist tradition (*saugatasamaya*), that which does not arise from perception and the other [means of knowledge] cannot be considered inference;
thus he says: "possessing the three characteristics" (*trilakṣaṇa*). For they recite as follows: "Inference is the cognition of an object from a mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three forms.
Nor is non-arising—the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of a cognition—produced by anything.

"How much more so by a reason possessing the three characteristics. Now, it might be argued: "Non-apprehension is accepted as inference (*anumāna*) by virtue of being a reason (*hetu*), but it is not inference in the sense of being an inferential cognition (*anumiti*)," since the term is used here as a noun denoting the means (*bhāvasādhana*). Therefore, what is the point of refuting it? True;

its status as inference has already been refuted on the grounds that it lacks the nature of a reason. However, by this [verse], its failure to fall within the scope of the definition is being described. // 44 //
Here he raises an objection:

[the word] "means of valid cognition" (*māna*) implies that being a means of valid cognition is pervaded by the nature of existence (*bhāva*), as is understood in the case of perception and the other [means of knowledge]; therefore, [if existence is excluded], it follows by implication that [being a means of valid cognition] is also excluded—this is the sense. But the other [responds]: "We have already described how the non-confusion of absences is fourfold. Furthermore, there is no difference between the cognition of that [absence] and the cognition of existence."

Because of the commonality of the absence of sublation (*bādhaviraha*). And that [absence] is the cause for validity, not the positive nature (*bhāvasvarūpatā*) itself. That [positive nature], however, is not at all a causal factor for validity; it is somehow associated with those [cognitions] and thus invalidity does not arise simply by virtue of being a non-entity (*abhāvatva*). But when the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is a positive entity, that [cognition] is indeed invalid—this is the intended meaning. He says "the object of knowledge" (*prameyam*). This is entirely appropriate, as he states that in the case of a non-entity, the means of knowledge is a non-entity: "the object" (*meyam*). // 45 //

Just as non-existence is not a suitable means of knowledge when the object of cognition consists of existence, so too existence is not suitable when that [object] is non-existent; thus he says: "consisting of existence" (bhāvātmaka). // 46 //

It is not a royal decree that valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must consist solely of an existent entity (*bhāvātmaka*); rather, whatever has the fruit of determination (*paricchedaphala*) is indeed valid cognition.
And this is the same even for that which does not arise from perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth; thus he says: "Of that which consists of an existent entity" [verse 47].

It might be argued: "Since validity is observed only in the case of a real entity (*vastu*) and not in the case of a non-entity (*avastu*), such as non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the latter cannot possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If that were so, then for the Buddhists as well, the logical mark (*liṅga*) and its object of cognition (*prameya*) would not exist, for they too hold that these are not seen in a non-entity. To this he replies with the verse beginning "yadi" (if). He states the fault in admitting [the opponent's view] with the words "tathā sati" (that being the case). The meaning is that this worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—which was described as consisting of the distinction between cause and so forth—would not be possible. // 48–49 //

He states that "the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge" is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) even because it is not a property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*), by saying "of the means of knowledge. The intention is that when non-existence (*abhāva*) is made the subject, the non-arising of perception and so forth is not understood as a property thereof, because there is no relation between them. [Objection: But we shall prove the ground as qualified by non-existence.

And since that [absence] was previously apprehended, it will be a property of that [locus]; to this he says: "Where... For there is no non-arising of perception regarding the ground, because that [ground] is being cognized. // 50 //

"In that case, it will be a property (*dharma*) of the jar, because perception and other means of knowledge do not arise with respect to its object. To this he says: "That which... This is true. It might somehow be a property of that [object] where perception and the others do not arise;
however, it is not cognized here [in the case of the non-existent], because of the absence of both property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmitva*). For indeed...

Taking that [surface] as the subject (dharmin), its being qualified by absence is what is to be proven, because it is not perceived [as such]. Nor is the ground or similar locus qualified by that [absence], because at that time, the latter is absent from it. // 51 //

But that [non-apprehension] will be a property of non-existence, because it has that as its object. For when non-existence is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), it is indeed a logical mark (*liṅga*). However, non-existence will not be an object if it is not cognized;
and since the non-existence of the object of knowledge must be known, he says: "by means of non-existence" (verse 52).

But there is no other mode of relation with non-existence (*abhāva*) due to its non-arising, by means of which one could follow its being a property [of that subject] and thus have an inference; thus he says: "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*). For this reason as well, it lacks the status of being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharman*); thus he says: "not perceived" (*nāgṛhīte*). For smoke is not understood as a property of a mountain when the mountain has not been perceived. Now...
In the same way, it is said that non-existence is also cognized beforehand;
if that is so, then what has already been established is being proven. // 53 //
Thus, having established difference through both perception and inference, he demonstrates it by means of a formal argument (prayoga): "abhāvaśabda... (verse 54).

He states another argument, ending with "abhāvo 'pi" and "bhāvāt": therefore, it is established that non-existence (abhāva) is distinct from the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which consists of existence (bhāva); thus he concludes with "tasmāt. // 55 //

He demonstrates the utility of non-existence (*abhāva*) [as a means of knowledge] with the words "the rituals" (*karmāṇi*). This non-confusion of the fruits of all rituals, their mutual non-confusion, and the absence of a mutual relationship of principal and subordinate among them—none of this would be possible without the authority of non-existence as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (The phrase *yathā* implies *yāvat*, *tāvat*, and *yathāvat*.)
"Here" refers to a reference to the Veda. // 56 //

But surely, two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than comparison (*upamāna*) have been described by those who follow the opinion of Vyāsa, and the Sage [Gautama] has also accepted the status of *sambhava* (probability) and *aitihya* (tradition) as means of valid cognition;

therefore, the reason for rejecting them must be stated. To this he says: "By reasoning" (*yukti*). For it is only the sixfold system of means of valid cognition that accords with reasoning and is consistent with tradition (*āgama*). And tradition here refers to the Mīmāṃsā treatise.

Therefore, through both reasoning and scripture, the six means of valid cognition alone have been analyzed and deliberated upon here in this Śabara-bhāṣya; as for those two additional ones that are accepted by others, they are included within these very six. // 57 //

But where, then, is its inclusion? To this he says: "It occurs here. That cognition which arises from a hundred [based on] a thousand, and which is accepted as the means of valid knowledge called *sambhava* (probability), does not differ from inference (*anumāna*). A hundred is understood from a thousand because of their state of non-separation (*aviyutibhāva*), that is, because of their invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). Therefore, it does not differ from inference. Thus far, the means of valid knowledge called *aitihya* (tradition) has been discussed.
It is indeed untrue. [Examples such as] the acquisition of treasures, the subjugation of asura maidens, and so forth;
or that Draupadī had five husbands, and so on—if those were true, they would not [be established] by means of scripture (āgama).

It is divided [into two]. For this is authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*). And it has been said: "Even the speech of a person attains the status of scripture for a listener. Therefore, because they are included within inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*), it is established that there is no separate presentation of probability (*sambhava*) and tradition (*aitihya*). Thus ends [the section] in the *Kāśikā-ṭīkā* composed by the teacher Sucarita Miśra.
The determination of non-existence is completed.
The reading of the commentary (*bhāṣya*) is to be examined;
here the commentary says: "Now, let other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exist, but word (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition. Why?"

"Signless (*animitta*) because it is an apprehension of what is [already] present. This is its meaning: although, due to the non-deviation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), sound (*śabda*) is not a means of valid cognition by virtue of a property that exists in the general nature of all means of valid cognition, it is nonetheless not a means of valid cognition by virtue of a specific property inherent to itself. For instance, the meaning of the injunction "one should sacrifice with the *citrā*" is that cattle are produced by the *citrā* sacrifice. Even for a sacrificer who has performed the *citrā*, immediately thereafter—[with] all his sense faculties intact...

"Even animals are not seen; therefore, it must be the opinion that the sacrifice does not have animals as its fruit. This has been stated [in the Sūtra]: "It is not a valid means [of knowledge], because [the result] is perceived while [the cause] still exists. What is meant? For the instruments of perception, such as the eyes and so forth, exist for the animals. Yet, animals are not perceived immediately after the sacrifice performed by one desiring animals. Therefore, due to this contradiction with what was stated—
"The injunction regarding the variegated [sacrifice] is not an authoritative means of knowledge. This objection, moreover, appears to have its meaning already established;

for in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the author of the Commentary (Bhāṣyakāra) has already stated both the objection and its refutation with the words, "Is it not the case that [the Veda] speaks of things that are not so? and so forth. Anticipating the objection that this [present argument] is therefore redundant, he says:
"In regard to the next world. The meaning of this is as follows: in that context, the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" indeed has the next world as its fruit.

Thus, objections such as these have been raised from the perspective of outsiders to the Veda, such as the Buddhists and others. Now, however, injunctions regarding rites like the *citrayajña* that yield results in this life (*aihikaphala*) are being challenged. But surely, reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth can indeed challenge both types of injunctions alike.

Those very reasons were implicitly included there by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), who demonstrated [the point] by saying, "any worldly statement whatsoever. The author of the *Vārttika* also [states]:

Or rather, it has been explained that the authority of all Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) is dependent upon a person. Therefore, it is incorrect to say that only those [injunctions] whose fruits are in the next world are implied there. Furthermore, as for what was just said regarding the implication of those [injunctions] whose fruits are in this life—that too is untenable; for here too, a total implication has been made when it is said: "Since the Veda is thus seen to have transgressions, we consider that even such fruits as heaven do not exist. And by the author of the *Vārttika* as well:
If this were so, then one who asserts that even sentences concerning the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like possess a false meaning would be correct.

Therefore, they consider it logical that in both cases there must be a mutual refutation (*ubhayākṣepa*). What is this systematic distinction? To this it is said: It is true that there is a mutual refutation in both cases;

nevertheless, there is no redundancy because the reasons [for the refutation] differ. For instance, in that case, the reasons for the refutation stated by the opponents are "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth. [3...]
Now, however, by means of reflecting upon the power of the word (*śabdaśakti*), internal causes alone will be established as valid. And so it has been said:
"If immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not explicitly stated, it is [still understood] because of the comprehension of its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

For this capacity is the auxiliary factor for all verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) when they express their meaning. Thus, even if there is no scriptural statement (*śruti*) that the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) yields its fruit immediately, [the result follows].
Nevertheless, this is understood through the force of the sense (*arthasāmarthya*);

otherwise, how could it be that when she was present she did not yield the fruit, yet at another time, being non-existent, she will yield it? Furthermore, animals do not possess a cultivation (*bhāvanā*) that is impossible immediately [after death].
For heaven cannot possibly consist of the acquisition of various specific bodies, sense organs, and so forth that have not yet been projected;
therefore, let it not be immediately subsequent.
However, these sacrificial animals come into existence for the sacrificer right here, being unperceived immediately after their own causes.

Other causes, such as the acceptance of gifts and so forth, cannot be understood as having the variegated results [of sacrifices] like the *citra* sacrifice as their fruit, because they are not heard [in scripture]. However, this very reflection on the power of words has been demonstrated by the author of the *Vārttika*, while following the method of the logicians (*tārkika*), through formal arguments (*sādhana*) such as "or not the fruit of animal-sacrifices" (*na vā paśuphala*). Thus, when injunctions for the *citra* sacrifice—which have fruits in this life—have been addressed, other [injunctions] are implied by analogy with them.

The term "suchness" (*tathātva*) thus stands once again as a critique of the injunctions for the *agnihotra* sacrifice and other rites. And this [critique] is expressed by means of a critique directed toward results pertaining to this life (*aihika*). For this very reason, it is called a "critique of what pertains to this life. What is meant is this: this critique applies both to those things whose fruits are experienced in this life and to those whose fruits are experienced in the hereafter, precisely by way of prioritizing a critique of what pertains to this life.
Granted that results such as heaven in the next world may not be experienced immediately after the action; however, why is it that visible results such as cattle and the like are not experienced?

Since these are not experienced, they surely cannot be the fruit [of those actions]. Thus, by the failure of the injunctions regarding actions with visible fruits, there arises doubt regarding other actions whose fruits are in the next world.

The implication [of the objection] follows from that similarity. Previously, however, those [means of knowledge] were implied by relying on the extrinsic validity [of cognition], using the very reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) and so forth stated by the opponent. That is what was meant by "stated by others. He states another resolution: "In the *Sūtra*," etc. The intention is this:

in the *Codanā-sūtra*, the author of the *Bhāṣya*, for the sake of supporting the thesis, took into account—by looking ahead at what was yet to come—the objection and its resolution that the author of the *Sūtra* would later state.
These two have already been described. Now, however, since the author of the Sūtras states this himself, he has declared that this very point is the field for refuting all objections. // 1 //

In this refutation, the reason for the objection is precisely that which was stated previously; he sets it forth with the words beginning "citrā" and ending with "phalāni. This is the meaning: the injunctions whose objects are such things as the *citriṇī* sacrifice having cattle as its fruit are the subject (*dharmin*), and "false" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). This is because the object is not cognized by perception or other means of knowledge, even though those [injunctions] are authorized and capable of inducing activity.

If such [a statement] is false—just like the speech of one who intends to deceive—the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes injunctions (*codanā*) concerning the *agnihotra* and other rites within the scope of the argument. Now, it might be objected: the speech of one who intends to deceive is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) here; yet that speech is not invariably disconnected from perception and other means of knowledge, nor is it necessarily untrue. Therefore, the example is deficient in both respects. To this he replies: "In that case," [meaning] employed when the object is unreal.

Thus, the statement "the riverbank" and so forth is the example here. And since such a statement is generally employed by one who intends to deceive, it is said [in the text] "by one who intends to deceive. // 2–3 //
Now, he explains what was stated as "the objection regarding this world" (aihikākṣepa) by means of the words "or not": "The sacrifice performed for a painting is the subject;
it is to be proven that it does not result in cattle, because it does not bestow cattle at its own time."

"Like bathing and so forth. He states another formal argument (prayoga): "Those [animals]," etc. Those animals are not to be accomplished by means of the Citrā sacrifice, because they do not exist at the time of the production of the Citrā's result, just like the pleasure of satisfaction from heaven and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), satisfaction produced by eating is intended here. These two arguments are to be understood as those stated in the Bhāṣya: "The iṣṭi does not have cattle as its fruit," and "At the time of the ritual act, there must be the fruit of that act. Immediately following this, the author of the Bhāṣya stated: "For at whatever time the rubbing occurs, at that very time the pleasure of the rubbing [occurs]."

He applies that [example] as a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) to the two syllogisms with the words "by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇa*). In both syllogisms—"The variegated [sacrifice] does not have cattle as its fruit" and "Cattle are not to be accomplished by it"—there would be ease in the crushing [of the opponent's position] by way of dissimilarity; and such is the arrangement of the dissimilar instance here.

Whatever is to be accomplished is produced simultaneously with it, just as pleasure [is produced] by massaging. And whatever is to be accomplished, that necessarily exists at its own arising, just as pleasure exists at the arising of massaging. // 4–5 //
Now, it was argued that [the Veda] lacks authority because of contradiction with what has been stated. Yet, there is no contradiction here at all;
for the Word does not say that as soon as an action is performed, the fruit must arise immediately, but rather that "this belongs to him."

"Result" (*phala*); because the discussion concludes with this much. Therefore, it will yield its result at another time. This is what was stated: "If it is argued that it will yield its result at another time," and to this he says: "immediacy" (*ānantarya*). He refutes this: "not by capacity" (*na sāmarthyena*). Although immediacy was not explicitly stated, it has been understood here by implication; for as soon as it is said, "this is its result," it is understood by the very force of the meaning that it must occur immediately after this.

Thus [it is asked]: how indeed could that which is otherwise non-existent bestow its fruit at another time? Now, even if this were so, let the immediate succession obtained through presumptive force (*sāmarthya*) be sublated by the non-perception of an immediate fruit; but how can an injunction (*codanā*) that functions without distinction be sublated? To this he says: "By the word... For presumptive force (*sāmarthya*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nevertheless, since the capacity (*śakti*) is a cooperative factor for all verbal suffixes that express meaning, it is indeed a part of the word itself.

Therefore, just like the dipping with a *sruva* ladle, even in the case of non-substantial entities, the result is determined immediately after the object [is understood] by implication; thus, when that [capacity] is cognized, there is certainly a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). // 6 //

For this reason as well, immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is understood; thus he says: "At another time" (*kālāntare*). For if [the author] had heard the *liṅ* suffix in the sense that "it will yield a fruit here," then some kind of assumption might have occurred by virtue of its capacity. But now, since the statement concludes with "this is the fruit of this action," and because the fruits of all actions are perceived as being immediate, this applies even to Vedic rites such as the *Citrā* sacrifice.
Even when the action is being urged toward another, its immediate succession remains as a qualifying characteristic due to its inherent nature. // 7 //

Immediately following this, another commentary states: "There is even a certain Vedic statement that contradicts what is perceived, namely: 'This sacrificer, equipped with the sacrificial implements, goes directly to the heavenly world. He explains the specific distinction by which this was stated with the word "here" (*atra*).

For here, in the case of sentences such as those concerning the *citrā* sacrifice, lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) was asserted due to a discrepancy between the statement and reality; however, in the subsequent case of the sentence regarding the "sacrificial implements" (*yajñāyudhi*), [the situation is different].

The phrase "contradiction with perception and so forth" (*pratyakṣādivirodha*) clarifies the contradiction—namely, that "the journey to heaven. For while the reduction of the sacrificer, whose nature is unsurpassed bliss, to ashes—a state far removed from heaven—is perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), in the case of injunctions such as the *Citrā* sacrifice, there is merely the non-perception of an immediate result; however, no contradictory perception exists there. Thus, it might still be possible to postulate a result at some later time.
However, it is impossible that a body reduced to ashes could go to the heavenly world even after a long period of time; this is the distinction from the previous [position]. // 8 //
Furthermore, any other statement of this kind that contradicts valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is not authoritative—just as the commentary states: "gourds sink in water" and "stones float.
He explains that [with the passage] ending with the words "the sacrificial implements": the statement regarding the sacrificial implements is the subject (*dharmin*).
"False" is the property to be proven,
because it contradicts direct perception;
for that which contradicts direct perception is false.

"Just as 'the stones float' is a statement regarding rocks [that is false], it should be shown by way of similarity using 'just as' (*yathā*). He states the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) with the words "by way of dissimilarity": "That which is not false is not contradicted by perception, just as the speech of a reliable person (*āpta*). However, since previously the pleasure of massage was presented as an example by way of dissimilarity, the statement regarding rocks is also [to be understood] by way of dissimilarity.
In order to dispel the misconception that this was stated by the author of the Bhāṣya, the author of the Vārttika has demonstrated the distinction between similarity and dissimilarity. // 9 //
But is it not the case that the reason "because of contradiction with perception" is simply unestablished?
For there exists a conscious agent of actions who experiences the fruits in the next world;

it is with reference to him that it was said, "he will go to the heavenly world. Therefore, what is the contradiction? To this, he says: "from the body," meaning if the conscious being were indeed other than the body...
It might be so; however, there is no manner of connection between that [self] and the sacrificial implements,
whereas the body alone has a connection with the sacrificial implements such as the *sruk* and *kapāla*.

The connection with the possessive suffix (*matvartha*) is appropriate only with the intention that "the sacrificer is equipped with the sacrificial implements. Furthermore, the demonstrative reference "this very [one]" (*sa eṣa*) is an immediate indication;

this too is possible only because the body is perceptible, not because the Self is. This has indeed been stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "He designates the embodied one. Moreover, the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) refers to the agent of the sacrifice as the sacrificer.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the self to be the agent of a sacrificial act (*kratu-kriyā*) consisting of many sequential moments of action as previously described, because, being all-pervading (*vibhu*), the self cannot possess the actions that result in the disjunctions and conjunctions of prior and posterior locations. This is what [the author] states with the words "And not...
(*na ca*). Moreover, this has been stated by us while provisionally accepting the existence of the self.

But from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), even the existence of a self distinct from the body and the senses is difficult to establish due to the absence of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa); thus he says: "The existence [is not established]. This will be elaborated upon in the *Ātmavāda* [chapter], and so it is not expanded upon here. // 10 //

Furthermore, the *Bhāṣya* states: "And this [word] 'he goes' is not an injunctive term (*vidhiśabda*). He explains its intention with the words "If... The meaning of this is as follows: If, in this sentence concerning the sacrificial implements (*yajñāyudhivākya*), there were an injunctive term, then—since no immediate fruit is observed for the *Citrā* sacrifice and others—the citation of the sentence on the sacrificial implements for the purpose of presenting a contradiction by way of distinction would be untenable. Therefore, the refutation of the injunctive term is intended to support the author's own adoption of the distinction [between injunction and statement]. // 11 //

What is the distinction regarding the word of injunction (*vidhiśabda*)? To this he says: "Injunction," etc. For in the case of a word of injunction, since no specific time is mentioned, one may—by the very power of the injunction—postulate that the fruit occurs at another time, and thus avoid the contradiction with non-existence, as is the case with injunctions for the *Citrā* sacrifice and others. But here, [the text says] "he goes" (*yāti*).
Because it is stated as a present description, the contradiction with direct perception cannot be avoided; thus, there is a distinction due to non-perception. // 12 //

This was stated by us with the intention of [the analogy of] paintings and the like: that by postulating the future occurrence of the fruit when the word is an injunction (*vidhi*), the contradiction can be resolved. But here, because the state of being reduced to ashes is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is not possible to postulate that the fruit is the attainment of heaven by virtue of its occurring at a later time. For even by a thousand injunctions, this cannot be made plausible.

The meaning can be made understood. This is what he says: "And the result. What, then, is the result of refuting the status of [the Veda] as an injunctive word? To this he says: "By its power. For an injunction, which consists in the instigation of a conscious being, would—if it were untenable without one who experiences the results in the next world—lead one to postulate a self that is distinct from the aggregate of the body and the instruments [of action].

And for the purpose of negating such conceptualizations as that his going to the heavenly world might be metaphorical even while the body remains, or that his perceptibility might be figurative with respect to the self, there is the rejection of injunctive words. // 13 //

Furthermore, this portion of the Veda consisting of *mantras* and *arthavādas* is for the most part contradicted by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as "Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space, the sacrificer is the single-pot-sherd cake," and so forth. And all of that must here be diligently taken as the subject of the proposition (*pakṣa*) in the refutation of [the Veda's] authority regarding worldly matters, primarily on the grounds of its falsity.
With the intention that, by virtue of its falsity, the falsity of others will follow as a consequence, he says: "mostly" (prāyaḥ). // 14 //
The *Bhāṣya* states that "because of that similarity, there would be a lack of confidence even in the injunctions for the Agnihotra and other rites";

he explains its intended meaning with the words "this being so. For when the lack of authority in sentences such as those concerning the *Citrā* sacrifice has been established, then—since they are parts of the same Vedic corpus—it becomes possible to infer that the sentences concerning the Agnihotra and other rites also have false content.
Therefore, since the entire Veda would lack authority, there is the objection that Dharma is not "that which is characterized by Vedic injunction" (codanā-lakṣaṇa).
Thus ends the Citrākṣepavāda (The Refutation of the Variegated) in the Kāśikā commentary composed by the preceptor Sucarita Miśra.
018 Ātmavāda (The Discourse on the Self).

In this context, immediately following [the objection], the author of the Bhāṣya introduced a refutation of the objection by means of the eternity of the relationship, stating: "But the innate connection of the word with its meaning—that is the knowledge of it.
This is incorrect;

for it is appropriate to point out defects such as contradiction or lack of proof regarding that very [objection] immediately after the reason for the objection stated by the opponent. As for what [follows]:
Without refuting that [position], something else is stated; however, that is indeed irrelevant, and therefore he says: "In one's own position. The intention is this:

as long as the intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) of the Vedic injunction (*codanā*), characterized by independence due to its innate relationship [with its meaning], is not established, then even if the [opponent's] proof is refuted, the thesis that "Dharma is defined by the Vedic injunction" will not be proven.

Furthermore, it is his intention to explain a great deal more in this sequence, beginning with the determination of the relationship between word and meaning; otherwise, if it were treated differently, it would become as if fallen from the sky. And this will be explained on the occasion of determining the nature of the word itself.
Nor does this fail to connect with the preceding objection.

Because it is seen that there are two ways of offering opposition. As it has been said: "Opposition is twofold: either by subverting the opponent's reason or by stating one's own proof; of these, the latter is what is discussed here."

Nor will the refutation of the opponent's proof be undertaken here on the grounds that its reason (*hetu*) is unestablished; this will be discussed in the section on the "Refutation of Citrākṣepa. However, it was stated "for the time being" with the intention that it should be carried out according to this sequence. And he states that proof of his own position by way of a formal argument (*prayoga*) in order to please the minds of logicians, beginning with the words "not false" (*amṛṣā*). Here, the Vedic word is the subject (*dharmin*).
"Truthfulness regarding its own object" is the property to be proven;
because it does not depend on a speaker regarding its own object,
for whatever does not depend on a speaker regarding its own object is true.
Just as the cognition [arising] from a word is directed toward the meaning of that word. For a word is connected with its own object by its very nature;

it does not depend upon a speaker for the sake of conveying that [object], as will be explained in the section on the refutation of the [need for a] connection (*sambandhaparihāra*). The term "its own object" (*svārtha*) should be construed as qualifying both [the word and the cognition] through the principle of *tantra*. For if it were merely stated that "Vedic speech is non-false," it would result in the acceptance of the validity of the opponent's position.

This leads to the undesirable consequence of proving that [the Veda] has an unintended meaning. For the sentence "one desiring heaven should sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yajeta*) is not correctly accepted as having the sense "one desiring heaven should perform a sacrifice" (*svargakāmo yāgaṃ kuryāt*), because that would contradict the established conclusion of the sixth book [of the *Mīmāṃsāsūtra*]. For in that context, it will be established that [the meaning is] "one should bring about heaven by means of sacrifice" (*yāgena svargaṃ kuryāt*), since [the Vedic injunction] is independent of a speaker.

Thus, this unqualified reason that has been put forward would be nothing but unestablished (*asiddha*). For even Vedic sentences do not depend upon a speaker for the manifestation of their own form; nor do they depend on a speaker when their own meaning is to be communicated, because they are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) and because the relationship between word and meaning is eternal. Even the statement of a trustworthy person (*āptavacana*), which is of human origin and concerns an object already cognized by other means of valid cognition, depends upon the authority of the speaker. As it has been said:
In the words of authoritative persons, there is dependence on human beings. // 1 //

He states another argument, ending with the words "tatkṛta" (produced by that): the thesis to be proven is that the cognition produced by Vedic sentences is valid (*samyak*), because it arises from eternal sentences, just like the cognition whose object is the very nature of those sentences. For that [latter] cognition also indeed arises from the sentence.

Because a cognition devoid of an object does not arise. Furthermore, the eternity of the Vedic sentences will be established in the section concerning the Veda (*vedādhikaraṇa*). Regarding this very point to be proven, the previously mentioned reasons—stated during the occasion of explaining the *bhāṣya* passage "not because of difference" (*nānyatvāt*)—are as follows: because they are produced by causes free from defects, and because they are produced by speech not uttered by an unreliable person.
He says "here" [in verse 2] to show that the reasons must be demonstrated as follows: "Because there is an absence of sublation even when there is a difference in place and so forth."
Regarding this, the Commentary says: "It might be argued: there is no connection at all between a word and its meaning;
how then could it have either a personal (pauruṣeya) or impersonal (apauruṣeya) origin? He states the intention behind that [objection] with the words ending in "nityān."

The meaning of this is as follows: Having refuted the lack of authority of the Vedic injunctions (*codanā*) by means of the reason stated by the author of the Sūtras for the sake of establishing intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*)— namely, "because [the Veda] is independent" based on the eternality of words, meanings, and their relationship— now another opponent, such as a Buddhist, [objects] on the grounds that [the Veda] lacks the production of a relationship.

He stated that [the opponent's position] is false. And thus, at that time, the Vārttikakāra demonstrated by means of the Vṛttikāra’s view that intrinsic validity (*svataḥ prāmāṇya*) is to be established in this very context. Furthermore, regarding the avoidance of redundancy when it is said "and so it is stated by the Sūtrakāra," the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) was presented through the very grounds for objection raised against the doctrine of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ prāmāṇya*). And here too, the Bhāṣyakāra says: "Speak!"

Thus it is said: "It causes one to understand; it becomes the instrumental cause for the one who is understanding," and so forth. This very reason for intrinsic validity (svataḥ prāmāṇya), as stated in the *Codanāsūtra*, has been explained. // 3 //

He explains this very point up to the end [of the section] with the words "the relationship" (*sambandha*). For the existence of a relationship and its eternity were stated as reasons in order to refute the [notions of] injunction (*codanā*) and deception (*abhidhyā*). Both of these are not accepted by our opponents. Among them, the non-existence of the relationship has already been stated by this very commentary. As for its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), if it does not cause comprehension when first heard...

This will be stated by the words "then [it would be] produced. Thus, in this context, the non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the reason—"because of independence due to the absence of a relation"—is stated. Furthermore, it has been shown that when a relation does not exist, the cognition of an object stated by another does not arise. For it is by the power of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) that knowledge of one thing arises even for one who perceives a different thing. However, that which disregards the necessary connection...
If one who knows a little were to know everything, it would lead to an over-extension of the principle. (4–5)

In this context, the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra), having stated that relations such as cause-and-effect are untenable for the word, demonstrated that there is indeed an absence of a relation consisting of conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*). The Author of the Vārttika demonstrates this with the words "by impossibility" (*asambhavena*). Relations such as that of cause and effect, or the relationship between locus and located, are absolutely impossible in the case of word and meaning;
however, the relation of cause and effect is indeed accepted by those Grammarians who have a scent of Buddhism about them. They too say:
Although meanings and words are clearly perceived as direct objects of perception,
for us, the designator and the designated are nonetheless merely forms of cognition.

Thus it is said. For they think as follows: first of all, the phonemes (*varṇa*) are not the word, because each one individually lacks expressive power. Furthermore, since they do not exist simultaneously, it is impossible for them to initiate either a whole (*avayavin*) or a collection (*samudāya*). Precisely for this reason, universals such as "the word *go*" are impossible; and since the particularities of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth differ with every usage, they lack expressive power.

Since the cognitions, recollections, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of individual phonemes are rejected as being [mere] phonemes themselves— just like the phonemes— the final phoneme, even when accompanied by the impressions produced by the preceding phonemes,

lacks expressive power just like any preceding phoneme. Furthermore, because no single entity in the form of *sphoṭa* can be apprehended through the sequential process of synthesizing all the preceding phonemes and words,
sound (*śabda*) must consist solely of a cognition whose nature is the simultaneous appearance of the forms of multiple phonemes.

Even an external object—whose determination is rendered impossible by conceptual alternatives such as whether it is a genus or an individual, a part or a whole, a quality or a possessor of qualities, or whether it is distinct or non-distinct from these—is not possible; therefore, it consists solely of a cognition whose nature is the appearance of an external genus and so forth, arising immediately after the verbal cognition.

And since this kind of object is indeed produced by the word, they maintain that the relationship between word and object is simply one of cause and effect. But this [position] is utterly far-fetched and erroneous.

And this being the case, the cognition of an object would arise even for those whose own nature and power are unknown. For it is indeed observed that grains of rice, though concealed by earth and water, begin to produce effects such as sprouts even while their own nature and power remain unknown. Thus it is well said: "by the impossibility [of it occurring] for the remaining [causes]. But how is it that conjunction remains as the only possibility?

And because it is accepted through common experience. For ordinary people are seen to perceive the object as conjoined with the word through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), thinking, "This is a cow. Furthermore, some accept that the very connection between word and meaning is their mutual conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*).
This has been elaborated upon in the doctrine of superimposition (*adhyāsavāda*). Moreover, ordinary people generally consider conjunction alone to be the relationship.

Thus, that very relation which has been raised as an issue must be refuted; so he says, ending with the words "tasmin" (in that). He demonstrates the negation through an actual application [of the argument]: "na śabdaḥ" (the word is not...). For when a thing comes into contact with another, it is seen in the very location of that other, just as a rope [is seen] on a jar.

Nor is one of the two—word or object—seen in the location of the other, nor in a location immediately adjacent to it, like the middle finger [is seen] in the location of the forefinger. Therefore, their relationship is not established, just as between the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains; nor can the object be made the subject of the proposition (*pakṣīkārya*). Thus he says: "In this way. Alternatively, he says: "The two," meaning that both are mutually unconnected, since neither is observed in the location of the other nor in a location immediately adjacent to it. Here, the Commentator [Vātsyāyana] says: "If [it were] by means of the object..."

It was stated that if there were a [real] relation [between word and meaning], then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (*kṣura*) and "sweetmeat" (*modaka*), the mouth would experience both cutting and filling.

He explains the intention behind that statement with the words ending in "kṣura" (*kṣurety uktam antena*). Its meaning is as follows: here, the author of the *Bhāṣya* has implicitly included the reason "because [the object] is not perceived immediately after [the location of] that [word]" (*tad-deśānantarādṛṣṭeḥ*) in order to establish the relation between the word and its meaning.

And as for one who, due to the delusion of the cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)— namely, "this is a cow"— considers [the word] to be unestablished, he is thus instructed: if there were a relationship between the word and its object characterized by a direct contact (*upaśleṣa*), [then this would not be an error].
The object would also have to be located at the very place of the sound;

and since the mouth is the location of that [sound], then upon the utterance of the words "razor" (kṣura) and "sweetmeat" (modaka), there would follow the cutting and the filling of the mouth, yet these two do not occur.

Therefore, because the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) such as [producing] sweetmeats is not perceived, and because [the object] is not seen immediately following its location in the same place as the word, the logical reason (*hetu*) is established.

However, there is no cognition of coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the word and its referent at all. For we do not perceive an object colored by the word in the same way that we perceive a blue lotus colored by blueness. Rather, the cognition of those two arises in the form of "g" [the phoneme] and so forth, or as possessing a dewlap and so forth. In this regard:

"Regarding the *Siddhāntabhāṣya*, that relation which is to be designated here, you do not designate that [single] one," and so forth. He states the intention behind this with the words beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and ending with "inferiority" (*hīnatā*). Herein is the intention: for the relation intended by us between word and meaning is of the nature of a power (*śakti*) consisting of the signified and the signifier.

If what is being proved is the absence of a relationship characterized by conjunction (*saṃśleṣa*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). However, if it is merely the absence of any relationship [in general], then the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to [the existence of] relationships such as marriage and so forth. Furthermore, because the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains share a common connection with the same earth and other elements, the example is devoid of the property to be proved (*sādhyahīna*). // 8–10 //

But if, intending only the relationship between the signified and the signifier, one were to prove that "the word is not connected with the object," then there would be a contradiction with worldly experience; thus he says, "The signified... He states another refutation: "Contradiction... Here he states the reason, ending with the words "for not... The intention is as follows: man is indeed of four kinds.

[The audience] consists of those who have understood, those who have not understood, those who are doubtful, and those who are mistaken. Among these, the one who has understood is the proponent, while the others—being dependent [on him]—are the persons to be convinced;
and the thesis (pratijñā) is for the purpose of convincing them.

Therefore, whichever one among those [five members] is intended to be established as the final [conclusion], that very one must be established by means of words whose scope is the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*), and which are devoid of the relationship between signifier and signified (*vācyavācaka*).
Consequently, by those who employ the proposition, the relationship characterized as signifier and signified between word and meaning is resorted to;

thus, in refuting that [relationship], there is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavāgvirodha*). And this contradiction with one's own words occurs through denotation (*abhidhā*). For that contradiction is fivefold.
"By means of utterance, naming, the property, the substratum, and the expression of both. // 11 //

Now he elucidates the essential nature of the relationship between the signifier and the signified—[beginning with] "abhidhāna" [etc.]. Its meaning is as follows: in a single act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*), the word is either the instrument (*karaṇa*) or the agent (*kartṛ*), since the application of grammatical cases (*kāraka*) depends on the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). The object (*artha*), however, is exclusively the object (*karman*). Therefore, [it is established that] of these two, the word possesses the status of either object or instrument.

Or rather, [the relationship] is the state of being an agent (*kartṛtva*). It has been defined—by what will be said later—as "relationship. Alternatively, he says "in the cognition" (*pratipattau*) to mean that when the comprehension of a single object such as a cow is being accomplished, the word and its meaning—which are intended to be co-present like the red cow and the one-year-old heifer taken up by a single speaker—are restricted; this restriction between the two is their "relationship. This is because of their being taken up together (*upādānāt*).

Thus, by means of being "that which is taken up" (*upādīyamāna*), he shows the intention to express a qualification. For a qualification of that which is to be taken up is intended to be expressed, just as the singularity of the animal [is intended] in the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*). However, a qualification of the subject (*uddeśya*) is not intended to be expressed, just as the singularity [of the cup] is a qualification of the *graha* [vessel].

For the planets (*graha*) are the objects to be designated (*uddeśya*), since the act of wiping (*sammārjana*) is prescribed with respect to them. In this case, however, when there is a single objective to be understood, both the word and its meaning are to be taken together (*upādeya*), just as the animal is [taken together] in a sacrifice. Therefore, their concomitance (*sāhitya*) is intended as a qualifier; thus, as in the case of the red (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old cow (*ekahāyanī*), there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) regarding the relationship between these two. (But not /...)

In this way, when the red cow (*aruṇā*) and the one-year-old heifer (*ekahāyanī*) are heard [in the text], it is not logical to intend their conjunction (*sāhitya*). For in that case, the sentence is completed with respect to the aggregate (*samudāya*).
Moreover, the two word-meanings (*śabdārthau*) are not heard as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇatayā*) within the act of cognition (*pratītikriyā*).

How is the intention to express their co-occurrence (*sāhitya*) [inferred] in these two cases? It is not the mere fact of being heard that is the cause for intending a qualifier; rather, it is also the practical usage of meaning (*arthasaṃvyavahāra*). For instance, in the case of cooking and so forth, when one observes the usage of the action regarding the rice, the pot, and so on—even though they are not explicitly expressed—one understands the intended co-occurrence of the pot and the other items.
Thinking thus, when one desires to cook oneself, one brings all those things together. In the same way, here too, the child [infers the intention] from the elder who is the user.

Having inferred the cognition whose object is that [meaning] by observing the usage of a specific meaning, one first determines that the word is the cause [of that cognition], because it occurs immediately after the word. Furthermore, since the speaker’s purpose in this case is directed toward the comprehension of the elderly person being prompted, and since that comprehension is the primary factor, the concomitance (*sāhitya*) of the word and the meaning is intended when they are employed. Having understood this, one likewise [proceeds] when employing [words] for the sake of another.

It is well said that one brings about the understanding of another by taking up word and meaning as they enter the heart in conjunction, and by uttering the word; this is a desire for their coexistence, just like the desire for the coexistence of phonemes. // 12–13 //
But surely, by speaking thus, you have demonstrated only a connection with the act [of denotation] between word and meaning,
not a mutual connection between them. For instance, as for what was said regarding "in the act of denotation" (*abhidhānakriyāyām*),
by this it is merely described that both [word and meaning] are connected to the act of denotation in the form of object, instrument, and so forth.

There is no mutual relationship [between the means and the end]. Even when it is said that "[the means] are employed for the sake of comprehension," this merely demonstrates a connection with the act of comprehension by way of the roles of the communicator and the one to be communicated; it does not show a mutual [relationship], because a relationship is impossible without a relation of subordinate and principal (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). For he will say: "And because subordinate elements exist for the sake of another... (*Guṇānāṃ ca parārthatvāt*).

"Because there is no connection due to their equality. This might be the case: since all connections are preceded by a connection between an action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), it might be argued that only the connection between an action and its factors has been shown here. Let that be for now;
however, it must still be stated what kind of connection exists between these two at a time subsequent to that. Having restated all of this:

He refutes this with the words "tatra" up to "tayor antena. Its meaning is as follows: although there is no mutual connection between the factors (*kārakas*) because they exist for the sake of the primary object, nevertheless, whatever action whatsoever is grasped in the processes of comprehension and expression, [it is that which is connected].

And in that [relation], there exists between the word and its object a further connection characterized as mutual assistance, which arises subsequent to the relation between action and its factors (kriyākāraka).

Furthermore, this [position] is internally contradictory and contradicts other passages. For instance, it was stated here that the relationship between word and meaning consists in their being the beneficiary and the benefactor with respect to a single action (*kriyā*), since they are apprehended through that action; thus, the relationship shown to consist in mutual restriction is precisely their status as factors for the inference of the action.

For it has been stated that in the act of denotation, there is a relationship consisting of the status of object (*karmatva*) and instrument (*karaṇatva*). In another passage, he will state that the relationship is indeed the capacity (*śakti*). And in some places, he speaks of the very restriction of the word’s capacity as the relationship:
"The restriction between the capacities of the signified and the signifier is characterized by its result."
Speaking thus, it is also stated elsewhere:

"That which is the state of being the cause for a single designation, and that which is the state of being both object and agent; or rather, the restriction of the instrument and the object by means of a single expression."
"That is our [position regarding] the relationship between word and meaning.
Therefore, this must be analyzed: what kind of relationship between word and meaning is intended here by the author of the Vārttika?
To this it is said: just as in the case of a substance and a quality acquired through a single act of purchase, their mutual expectancy is fulfilled [by their relation].
The relationship is characterized by mutual assistance between the beneficiary and the benefactor. For that which is not dependent [on a substance] cannot accomplish the act of purchase.

Nor is a substance capable of accomplishing the act of purchase unless it is delimited by specific qualities (*guṇa*). Furthermore, even if a mere substance serving as a substratum is taken up through the power of its own quality, it is not included in the purchase [unless specified], as in the case of one's own cow.

Because of the restriction to a substance (*dravya*). Since the substance excludes [all but] a single quality (*guṇamātra*), even though that single quality is being employed, the act of purchase does not accept it because of its own restriction to the quality of redness (*aruṇimā*). This very fact constitutes a restrictive rule (*niyama*). Thus, here too, for the sake of accomplishing the act of expression which brings about the understanding of a single object, [the same principle applies].

The relationship that exists between the word and its meaning— which are intended to be taken together— following the connection between action and its factors (kriyākāraka), namely the state of being the beneficiary and the benefactor, is precisely what constitutes their relation.

What, then, is the mutual assistance between these two? Listen: for an object cannot be made known without a means of making it known, and a word cannot be a means of making something known without an object to be made known. Therefore, existing as the signified and the signifier, they become mutually the benefactor and the beneficiary of one another. And since this nature of theirs is fixed, it occurs through mere extreme proximity.

The relation is the designation of a restriction, but the restriction itself is not the relation. For this very reason, there is also the theory of the relation as power (*śakti*). Indeed, it is only when the powers of the signified and the signifier exist that there is a relationship of beneficiary and benefactor; the power itself is not the relation. Therefore, in this case...

Such talk as "power is the relation through the metaphorical attribution of non-difference due to proximity," "restriction is the relation," or "agency or instrumentality is the relation" is merely empty chatter. In reality, however, the relation is nothing other than the state of being the benefactor and the beneficiary.
But how is it said that this form is fixed for these two? For when a word has not yet been uttered, there is no relationship of mutual benefactor and beneficiary between the word and its object.
