Nor is it the case that they do not exist at that time, because they are eternal. Therefore, that [objection] is untenable. That is not so, because they exist by way of their potential nature (*śaktyātman*).
For even when a word has not been uttered, there exists in it the power to convey [meaning], and in the object, the power to be conveyed;
for this very reason, the relationship is said to be eternal.

But even so, when a single object is expressed by multiple words such as *kara* and *hasta*, or when a single word such as *go* expresses multiple meanings, how can non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) be understood? Therefore, since context and other factors are also required for the determination of word-meanings— given that in the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), a child does not employ isolated words, but rather [learns through] the method of insertion and extraction (*āvāpa-uddhāra*)— this...

It has been determined: when a word is employed with the intention (*vivakṣā*) of expressing a particular meaning, that is its meaning. And this intention is to be inferred from the context of the matter and other factors. When it is said, "Bring the cow to milk," it is understood by implication that his intention concerns an animal possessing a dewlap and so forth. When it is said, "I shall fight," [it is understood] by implication...

Thus, a cognition arises. In this way, because words are distinguished by differences such as meaning and context, and are endowed with various distinct potencies (*śakti*), one word is the denoter of another [meaning], and thus there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the word. Furthermore, the referent (*artha*)—such as the hand and so forth—is also distinguished by differences in its manifested states suitable for being denoted by that particular word; it is mutually distinct as the denoted object of words such as *kara* (hand), and thus the word does not deviate. Moreover, in a single...

It has been stated that this restriction applies to the action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, when word and meaning are employed within a single cognition or a single expression, there is no mutual deviation between them. Thus it was said: "That which is restricted in one [action]... (vv. 14–15).

Now, if it is argued that the relationship between word and meaning is a restriction based on a single causal action, then one would be relying solely upon invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), which is a factor of inference (*anumāna*). Consequently, the cognition of an object arising from a word—just like the cognition of fire from smoke through the force of that concomitance—would be nothing other than inference. To this, he says: "Nor even... He further states "it has been established" because this point has already been proven in the section on verbal cognition (*śābda*). Now, [the opponent objects]: "But if invariable concomitance is not required..."

What, then, is employed? The Commentator has stated: "The relationship between the name and the named. But surely even this relationship is useless. He raises this objection with the words "the name" (*saṃjñā*). The meaning is that it is an auxiliary part of that [process], being an auxiliary factor for making [the meaning] understood. // 16 //

How is it that [the word] lacks a constituent part? To this he says: "because they cause one to understand. This technical term (*saṃjñā*) is postulated because it causes understanding through the observation of linguistic usage. What follows from this if it is so? To this he says: "And this is not... What is meant by this is as follows: being a signifier (*gamakatva*) itself constitutes the nature of a technical term; it does not require any other relation besides that. // 17 //

And since this is so, the capacity to indicate [the probandum], like that of smoke and so forth, is preceded by another relation; this is what he states with the words "therefore. He states the fault in the case of their being equal [in status] with the words "it is not a factor" (*sānaṅgam*). Just as in the case of smoke and so forth, it is the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) alone that is the factor for cognition, and not the capacity to indicate which arises at a subsequent time.
"Thus it might be there as well. Now he states the rebuttal by means of the dissimilarity with smoke and so forth: "This is not [the case]. (18)

He demonstrates this very disparity with the words "it has been ascertained" (*nirūpita*). For in that case, regarding smoke and so forth in a location such as a kitchen, it is only after the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with fire has been ascertained that the capacity to indicate [the object] is produced by that [ascertainment]. Furthermore, he says "as the indicator" (*gamakatvena*) because the status of being an indicator is not apprehended in smoke at first. // 19 //
But in the case of sound, the opposite is true; thus he says with the verse beginning "here" (iha), which consists of one and a half [verses]. // 20 //

It has been stated that the initial acquisition of linguistic competence (*vyutpatti*) regarding a word occurs precisely through its capacity to convey meaning (*gamakatva*); he explains this with the following three verses. This is the meaning: for the acquisition of linguistic competence regarding a word occurs in three ways—either from the instruction of elders (*vṛddhopadeśa*), from their usage (*tadvyavahāra*), or from the co-occurrence with other words (*padāntarasamabhivyāhāra*). And in all these cases, it is the capacity to convey meaning alone that is first understood. To illustrate: in the case of instruction by elders, [one understands] "this is the denoted object (*vācya*) of this [word]," and "this is the denoter (*vācaka*) of this [object]."

Thus, it is precisely the relationship between the signifier and the signified that is understood. Even in cases where, upon hearing a certain sentence, one observes the purposeful activity of an elder directed toward an object and—by means of inferring his intention—conceives that he has understood an object such as a cow, there too [the understanding arises from the realization]:
"From this word, this person has understood this meaning."

Therefore, it is understood that "this is its meaning" based on the word's very capacity to convey knowledge (*gamakatā*). Even in cases where it is used in proximity to other well-known words—as in "the *pika* sings sweetly in the mango tree"—one who knows the meaning of "mango tree" but does not know the meaning of "pika" understands that the word "pika" is the conveyor of knowledge for that which sings in the mango tree; thus, one grasps only its status as a conveyor of knowledge (*gamakatva*).
It is established that the capacity to convey meaning exists everywhere; it is not [a matter of] linguistic derivation. // 21–23 //

But surely, it is your established tenet that the meaning of a word is the *ākṛti* (form). And its status as the denotable object cannot be understood without positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Therefore, it would follow that the cognition produced by the word must have that [form] as its primary object. To this he says: "In this way.
This is the meaning: here, the function of positive and negative concomitance consists merely in determining the isolated referent.
However, the capacity to denote an object that is intermingled with various universals (jāti) and so forth is indeed established. // 24 //

Indeed, the linguistic usage of words and their meanings is observed even among cowherds; yet they do not extract the meaning from words through the method of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Nor is it reasonable to say that words are non-expressive for them, since they are perceived in exactly the same way [as by scholars]. Furthermore, the determination of the meaning of words such as *pika* is based on the testimony of Mlecchas and others.

Since this will be explained later, he says [in the verse] "of many kinds" (*bahujāti*) with a half-verse. This is the intended meaning: worldly people seek only the practical activity (*vyavahāra*) of rejection, acquisition, and so forth;
and their practical activity is accomplished by a confused understanding of the object that arises at the very moment of uttering a word.
Thus, they pay no heed to the distinction between words used in their primary sense (*śrauta*) or their secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*). // 25–26 //

If that is so, for what purpose do they investigate? To this he says: "strength and weakness, etc. For those who abide by the scriptures are unable to perform the meaning of the scriptures if their capacities have not been determined; therefore, the investigation of the power of words is useful for their acceptance and rejection, and thus they investigate them. // 26 //

He elaborates on this very point with the two verses beginning with *kakṣyāntarita*. The meaning is as follows: generality (*sāmānya*) is of two kinds, the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*). The higher is called "Being" (*sattā*); the others are "substantiality" (*dravyatva*) and so forth. Although these are generalities, they also receive the designation "particular" (*viśeṣa*) because they are also causes for the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*);
thus, they are referred to by the term "general-particular" (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*).

And in that regard, the general and particular [meanings] are separated from the primary meaning of the general word by an intervening level. For example, when the word *sat* denotes existence (*sattā*), [qualities such as] substantiality (*dravyatva*) and so forth are mediated by that [existence].

And since the word, operating toward those [particulars] by the power of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), becomes weak; whereas it operates toward its own primary meaning through direct denotation (*śruti*), it is strong there. What, then, is this so-called indication? It is a cognition [of something] through an inseparable connection with the expressed meaning. As it has been said:

"The cognition of the inseparable connection with the primary meaning is accepted as the definition [of indication]. Thus, for those established in the treatises, a distinction is appropriate for the sake of specific practical application: how much is indicated through an inseparable connection with the primary meaning, and how much is expressed by the word through its own power? That very indication (lakṣaṇā) generally arises from a permanent relationship; therefore, it is said "from a permanent relationship. This refers merely to the relationship itself.

This, however, is the seed of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). He asks: "But what is the utility of distinguishing between the literal and the figurative in ritual performance? Listen: in common worldly usage, for instance, in the command "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas, and buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya," the word "Brāhmaṇa" is a scriptural term (*śruti*) that denotes the general class of Brāhmaṇas.

By means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the [scriptural injunction] applying to Kauṇḍinya as a particular instance of that [general category] becomes weak; thus, it is sublated by the direct hearing (*śruti*) of the word "Kauṇḍinya," which refers to a proximate particular. This is exactly the same in the Veda as well: the scriptural injunction "one should recite the *yajus* in a low voice" (*upāṃśu yajuṣā*), which resides in the general category of *yajus*, is sublated by the scriptural injunction "aloud with the *nigada*," which resides in a particular instance of it. Such examples are to be demonstrated.

By qualifying the particulars (*viśeṣa*) here with the word "general" (*sāmānya*), [the author] shows that there are no particulars whatsoever existing apart from the general. For there is a certain view held by some: "The ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) reside in substances and are eternal; and because they are the cause solely of the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*), they are indeed particulars. Indeed, the followers of Kaṇāda [hold that] the creation of the world proceeds from atoms (*paramāṇu*) through the sequence of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth.

They maintain that atoms do not possess a distinct form through their own nature alone; for it is impossible to produce a world with unmixed forms by means of atoms that are themselves indistinguishable due to their atomic dimension (*aṇutva*).
Therefore, they assert that there exist certain "particularities" (*viśeṣas*) inherent in the atoms which differentiate them from one another.
And these [particularities] are indeed perceived directly by those whose minds are cleansed of all impurity. To them, the following is said:

First of all, among entities that are dependent on the senses, we do not perceive particulars that exceed the intermediate universals. For earth and the other [elements] are distinguished from qualities and actions by their being substances (*dravyatva*);
and earth is distinguished from the other substances, such as water and so forth, by its being earth (*pṛthivītva*).

Trees are distinguished from other earthen things by their nature as trees, and *śiṃśapā* trees are distinguished from other trees by their nature as *śiṃśapā*s; in this manner, this discourse on particularity (*viśeṣa*) should be applied down to the level of atoms.
What is the use of further particularities here? For among atoms, even though they belong to a single genus, it is form alone that is differentiated due to the differentiation of their effects.
We shall infer [the following]: indeed, a prior entity whose form is undifferentiated is not capable of producing an effect that possesses a differentiated form.

Alternatively, there will be a quality called "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) which serves as the differentiator among them; this itself will be the "ultimate particularity" (*viśeṣa*). If it is argued that this [quality] cannot be established unless another particularity is required, then how will the ultimate particularities themselves be established without requiring further particularities? Or, if they do require [further particularities], there would be an infinite regress.

Therefore, this admission of further particulars is indeed feeble. It is well said regarding generalities and particulars: "The yogis see them," for those who have faith understand; we, however, are without faith, as we seek logical reasoning. (27–28)

It has been stated that those who understand sentences distinguish [the meaning] through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). He demonstrates those two—positive and negative concomitance—in the following two verses: "In that regard... and so forth. In that context, because the word "cow" is frequently used for the general category (*sāmānya*) such as "cow," and because it is also used for its particular instances (*viśeṣa*) such as the *śābaleya* (the brindled cow) even when the *bāhuleya* (the black cow) and others are absent;

Because [the word] is not applied to other entities even when the higher universal such as *sattā* exists—as seen from its non-application to other things—the word "cow" (*gośabda*) is known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the designator of the mere universal "cowness" (*gotva*), which is related to a single composite object (*ekāvayavin*) along with the dewlap and other features. Furthermore, by means of the inseparable mark (*avinābhāvinā cihna*) consisting of the dewlap and so forth, it indicates (*upalakṣayati*) cowness as being related to that same single object. Therefore, it is established that between the word and its object, there exists only the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*).
The relationship is understood first, and not the inseparable connection (avinābhāva). // 29–30 //

He concludes: "Therefore... Now, an objection may be raised: the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that there is a relationship between a name and the named; however, people in the world do not consider a name to be an indicator (gamaka), for smoke is not called the "name" of fire.

Therefore, he says: "the state of being a designator" (*abhidhāyakatā*). This is the intended meaning: when it is known that "this [word] is the indicator of this object," its status as a cause for cognition is not possible unless it is operative; thus, its operation and the operation of the word itself is called "denotation" (*abhidhā*). Consequently, because of the connection with the act of denoting, the specific quality of being an indicator—namely, the state of being a designator—is understood in the word. Since the state of being a designator is precisely what constitutes being a name (*saṃjñātva*), the relationship between the name and the named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*) is established.

Thus [it is said]. However, "inseparability" (*avinābhāvitā*) is the restriction of the relation, not the relation itself; this is what he states with the word "relation. And we have already explained here that this [inseparability] is restricted to the extracted meaning. It should be understood that the conclusion is reached by supplying the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). One should not suspect a difference in meaning between the terms "positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatireka*) and "inseparability," as they are synonyms. // 31–32 //

If the author of the *Bhāṣya* has implicitly included the usage "that which causes comprehension," he states it as "the relation" (*sambandha*). For words of arbitrary convention (*yadṛcchāśabda*), such as "Devadatta" and so on, express only that very thing for which they are designated. They possess no inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*) anywhere. Thus, the meaning of this formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the word "cow" and so forth is the subject (*dharmin*).
The thesis is that [the word] is not inherently capable of denotation;

the reason is "because it depends on another means. Whatever depends on another means is not capable by its own nature, just as the word "Devadatta" and so forth depend upon the apprehension of a convention. // 33 //

In this context, the author of the Bhāṣya raises the objection: "If a word is expressive, why does it not convey its meaning when heard for the first time? He then offers the resolution by stating, "In all cases, our observation is the authority," and so forth, explaining that a word conveys its meaning once its power has been grasped through the force of observation. He demonstrates this with the words "Just as... The meaning of this is as follows: first of all, is the expressiveness of a word even admitted?

If it is argued that this is due to the force of observing linguistic usage, this applies equally to the cognition of capacity; for we do not observe people who, without knowing the capacity, understand the meaning from a word. // 34 //

It might be argued as follows: "Lamps and the like, which are illuminators, are seen to illuminate their own objects even when their relationship [to those objects] is unknown; yet the word is of a different nature than these, and therefore it is not an illuminator. But that is not so.

Because of the distinctness of their capacities. For entities indeed possess diverse capacities. Thus, a lamp—though its relationship [to the object] has not been grasped because it serves as an auxiliary to perception—may indeed illuminate; yet, for that reason alone, it need not possess the same properties as the word. Therefore, this is not a valid objection.
Furthermore, since rice and other such things do indeed initiate their effects even when their own forms have not been grasped, why should the word not possess that same property?

It is not superimposed. For grains and the like are productive causes (*kāraka-hetu*), whereas a word is an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*). Therefore, [the opponent argues,] it depends upon the apprehension of its own form (*svarūpa*). If it is asked: "By whom was this commanded—that an indicative cause must depend upon the apprehension of its own form and not upon the apprehension of the relationship by the force of observation? [The answer is: It has not been so commanded.
This is the same regarding the dependence on the apprehension of a relation:

indeed, it is solely by the force of perception (*darśana*) that specific indicators such as logical marks (*liṅga*) and words depend upon the apprehension of a relation; the eyes and other [senses] do not. For in all cases, perception is our authority (*pramāṇa*). We do not accept that the eyes and other [senses] are causal factors (*kāraka*).
Since that which is the cause of knowledge alone is its indicator, he says this: "In its own nature," etc. (verse 35).

But surely, even before the apprehension of the relationship, is the word capable of denotation or not? If it is capable, what is the use of depending on the apprehension of the relationship? If it is not [capable], then this apprehension of the relationship would have to be considered the cause according to the principle of "coming from that" (*tadāgama*). To this, he says: "That which is the most effective means" (*yatsādhakatamam*). We do not perceive the word as being incapable prior to the apprehension of the relationship; nor does the dependence on an auxiliary factor destroy the inherent power of that which is already capable.

Why, then, does it not destroy [the capacity]? To this he says: "For not... (na hi). For if the requirement for an auxiliary were to destroy its own power, then every worldly or Vedic instrument (*karaṇa*) would lose its status as an instrument. Indeed, every instrument requires the assistance produced by the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). // 37 //

Furthermore—let us grant for now that the requirement of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) does not destroy the status of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*); on the contrary, even by virtue of that [requirement], there is no such thing as instrumentality at all, because the very nature of each individual instrument is defined by its dependence upon that [performance]. Thus he says: "with respect to each self" (*pratyātma*). But if this is so, since the effect cannot be produced without the coexistence of both, how can there be a distinction between the instrument and the manner of performance?

Therefore, he says [the following] up to the end of the verse with the words "external and internal" (*bāhyāntara*): that which is present for the accomplishment of an effect is the instrument (*karaṇa*), while anything else is external; this refers to the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).

Since even an external factor may, in certain cases, be intended as the instrument due to the activity of the causal factors (*kāraka*) based on the speaker's intention, he says: "or it may be so in some cases. (38)
This very point is demonstrated by the word "udvigna" (distressed). Even though the eye is an internal factor for the arising of knowledge, it is not considered the instrument;
rather, due to some specific degree of excellence, one intends to designate only the external lamp as the instrument. // 39 //

And this status as an instrument, which is based on the speaker's intention, is occasional. However, regarding constant activity, one understands that the internal eye is the instrument for the constant accomplishment of the effect; thus he says, "in constant activity. The meaning is that for the blind, there is no vision—that is, no seeing. // 40 //

[Objection: Granted that the eye possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*) in relation to the lamp and so forth because of its specific proximity (*asatti-viśeṣa*) to the effect, which is cognition;

however, since the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manas-saṃyoga*) is absolutely more proximate to the production of cognition, how can the eye have the status of an instrument in relation to that? To this, he says: "the body," etc. The intention is this: it is not merely specific proximity that is the cause for the status of being an instrument.
Rather, proximity is relative to external factors such as a lamp;
however, it is unique (asādhāraṇya) with respect to the internal conjunction of the self and the mind.
For the conjunction of the self and the mind is common to the cognition of taste and so forth, and thus it is not the cause of the perception of color by virtue of being non-deviant.

It can be understood that the eye alone, by virtue of its uniqueness, is the cause for the cognition of form; this has been stated in the passage beginning with "But the distinction between the eye, form, and so forth. // 41 //

Thus, having demonstrated in the example the division between the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), the specific contact (*sannikarṣa*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), he applies it to the subject at hand with the words "in the same way. By this, it is shown that even what was stated—that the grasping of the relationship (*sambandhagrahaṇa*) alone must be the cause according to the logic of scripture (*āgama-nyāya*)—may also occur by virtue of a particular intention. // 42 //

Furthermore—regarding the explanatory passage on the refutation which begins, "Just as the eye is not a seer without external light," etc., he states its intended meaning with the word "yathā" (just as). For the eye, although dependent on other means such as a lamp for the illumination of form, is capable by its very nature; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). He further states that the example is also deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) with the words "Devadatta. // 43 //

It has been explained in the *Adhyāsa* section that even for arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), the capacity for cognition already exists and is merely manifested through grammatical injunction (*niyoga*). Furthermore, in this context, the commentary states that the status of the eye as an instrument (*karaṇa*) is demonstrated by the word "eye. Now, since the eye and the lamp are equally causes of cognition, how is it that the eye alone possesses the status of an instrument? To this, he provides the following justification:

"—is manifestation. And although this was already stated in the commentary on the word *nityavṛtti*, it is mentioned here again for the purpose of supporting the *bhāṣya*; thus, there is no tautology. // 44 //

Thus, the relationship between the name and the named, having been established, was challenged by the author of the Bhāṣya on the grounds of its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), stating: "If it does not cause comprehension when heard for the first time, then it must be produced.

The author of the Vārttika demonstrates this with the words "puruṣa... (the person). And thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: that which is the relationship between the name and the named is produced, because it depends upon a person.
It is like the conjunction of a rope and a jar. // 45 //
Furthermore, regarding the *Bhāṣya* passage beginning with "For these two, word and object, are by their very nature unrelated," [the author] states its intended meaning:

"distinct," etc. This is the meaning: just as in the case of a rope-snake and the like, which occupy distinct locations and times, there is no commonality whatsoever such as place and so forth, so it is with those two, word and object. Therefore, just like that, they too are by their very nature unrelated. And the formulation of the formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: "Word and object are disconnected by their very nature."
Because they do not occupy the same place and time,
like a rope and so forth; those two [the object and its cognition] do not indeed share the same place and time,
because they are perceived as being based on different locations and so on.
It is exactly like that. // 46 //
"In their own nature, those two—the object and the word—are indeed unrelated"; this is the reading found in the *Kāśikāmātṛkā*.
Thus ends the *Saṃbandhākṣepa* (The Refutation of Relation) composed by the teacher Sucarita Miśra.
